chapters.html:
How a Mushroom Farm Works

AT A GLANCE This chapter is the map. It explains what a mushroom is, follows one strain from a frozen vial to a box of mushrooms, defines the words every later chapter uses, and shows how a farm is laid out and how its week runs. The numbers you will meet again and again:

  • Expansion: 1 agar plate → up to 12 grain masters (G1, 4 lb / 1.8 kg) → 12 spawn bags (G2, 6 lb / 2.7 kg) per master → 20 blocks (10 lb / 4.5 kg) per spawn bag.
  • Steam: ultra-pasteurize substrate until the slowest block core has held 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for at least 2-3 h, and no more than 4-6 h; sterilize grain at a core of 121 °C (250 °F) for about 35 min.
  • Knock: inoculate blocks at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), never above about 38 °C (100 °F).
  • Incubate: blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) at the bag surface.
  • Fruit: most staple species at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F).
  • Output: one 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room gives about 500-600 lb (230-270 kg) a week at full rolling capacity.

What a mushroom is

A mushroom is the fruit of a fungus, the way an apple is the fruit of a tree. The fungus itself is the mycelium: a mass of fine white threads (hyphae) that grows through its food, digests it and, when conditions are right, produces fruit bodies to spread spores. A grower's whole job is to grow a lot of healthy mycelium on a clean food source and then persuade it to fruit.

  • The scale of spore production is huge: one mushroom releases on the order of a billion spores, so about 100 shiitake on one log release about 100 billion.
  • A single spore grows into a monokaryon: mycelium with one set of genes. Only when two compatible monokaryons fuse into a dikaryon, with two sets, can the fungus fruit. This is why farms propagate strains from tissue and cultures, not from spores (genetics in Chapter 2 and Chapter 8).
  • The mass of the mushroom comes from the substrate (its food), not from the fruit room, so what happens during incubation sets the crop.
  • Mycelium breathes like people do, so a room full of colonizing blocks fills with carbon dioxide (CO2), like a crowded room. At commercial scale CO2 becomes the main thing to manage.
  • In nature, moisture drives fruiting. A substrate at 60-61% moisture is like a forest floor at field capacity.
  • A colonized filter bag is a synthetic log: the plastic is the bark and the block is the heartwood. Cutting the bag is like scarring a log: local gas exchange, plus light, triggers pinning (the start of fruiting).

Mushroom media are rich food, and they feed every mould and bacterium that lands on them, not only your fungus. That single fact explains most of the equipment on a farm: steam to kill competitors, filtered air to keep them out, and one-way flow so dirty areas never feed clean ones.

The production chain

AT A GLANCE Culture → grain spawn → substrate → steam → cool-down and inoculation → incubation → fruiting → harvest → sale. Each step multiplies the one before it, so an error early in the chain ruins far more product than one late in it.

The stages in order

Stage What happens Key number Covered in
Culture storage Each strain is kept frozen in cryovials of colonized grain in glycerol. -80 °C (-112 °F), about 3 mL of 10% glycerol per vial, thaw at about 30 °C (86 °F) Chapter 8
Agar work A vial goes to a slant, the slant to working plates. One slant gives 8-12 plates; cut transfers when growth is about 1 cm from the plate wall Chapter 7
Grain master (G1) Agar pieces go into a bag of sterilized grain. 4 lb (1.8 kg) bag; about 2 weeks to colonize Chapter 9
Production spawn (G2) One master is broken up into about 12 bigger grain bags. 6 lb (2.7 kg); 10-12 days for oyster, up to 4-5 weeks for maitake Chapter 9
Substrate Sawdust plus a supplement is mixed with water and bagged. Master's Mix 50:50 hardwood sawdust to soy hulls at 61-63% moisture; 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at most Chapter 10, Chapter 11
Steam Bags are heated to kill competing organisms. Ultra-pasteurize: slowest core 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h; sterilize: core 121 °C (250 °F) for about 35 min Chapter 12
Cool-down and knock Hot bags cool in filtered air, then get spawn, a seal and a shake. Knock at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), never above about 38 °C (100 °F); 1 G2 bag per 20 blocks (about 3%) Chapter 4, Chapter 11
Incubation Mycelium colonizes the block in a dim, steady room. About 19 °C (66 °F) at the bag surface, core no higher than 21-22 °C (70-72 °F); 10-14 days for blue oyster, about 12 weeks for shiitake Chapter 13
Fruiting Blocks are opened in a humid room with fresh air and light. 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) for staples; blocks fruit out over 2-3 weeks Chapter 14
Harvest and storage Mushrooms are picked on time and chilled fast. Cold store at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F) Chapter 15
Sale Fresh to chefs, markets and wholesalers; surplus dried. Dry at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) for 24-48 h to about 10% of fresh weight Chapter 22

Why the chain is a pyramid

The chain multiplies at every step. One plate feeds up to 12 masters, each master feeds about 12 G2 bags, and each G2 bag inoculates about 20 blocks. These are the working ratios that recur most often.

  • Spawn is mainly a carrier that moves the organism to the next stage. The nutrition it brings to the substrate is a secondary bonus.
  • One bad G2 spawn bag ruins 20 blocks, which is 60-80 lb (27-36 kg) of mushrooms.
  • A single cryovial can lead to about 60,000 lb (27,000 kg) of mushrooms. Showing staff this connects their job to the whole farm.
  • Hard rule on well-run farms: no G3 spawn and no substrate-to-substrate (block-to-block) transfers.
  • Because an error at the culture stage cascades through every later step, culture work gets the best equipment and the slowest, most careful staff.
  • Keep preservation and expansion separate. Preservation is a closed loop that returns to the freezer; expansion is a one-way line that ends in blocks.

The vocabulary every chapter uses

AT A GLANCE Learn these words before reading further. Each later chapter assumes them. Full definitions are in the Glossary.

Cultures and spawn

Term Meaning Covered in
Agar A gel made with nutrients, poured into dishes or tubes to grow mycelium in a clean, visible layer. Common media are potato dextrose (yeast) agar (PDA, PDYA) for fast strains such as oysters and malt yeast agar (MYA) for slow ones; plain agar with no nutrients gives thin, wispy growth that dies out. Chapter 7
Plate A petri dish of agar. The working ("feature") plate is the one cut up to start grain masters. Chapter 7
Slant A tube of agar set at an angle. The limited air in the tube slows the mycelium once it covers the surface, so slants keep for months in a fridge. Chapter 8
Cryovial A small frozen vial holding a strain on grain in glycerol at -80 °C (-112 °F): the master copy of a culture. Chapter 8
Liquid culture (LC) Mycelium grown in sugar water, used to inoculate grain: about 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) master. Chapter 7
Master, G1 A grain master: a 4 lb (1.8 kg) bag of sterilized grain inoculated from agar. Chapter 9
G2 A 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain bag inoculated from a G1. It is the production spawn, used in-house and sold to customers. Chapter 9
Spawn Colonized grain used to carry the fungus into the next stage. It is mainly a carrier; its nutrition is a bonus. Chapter 9
Spawn rate The share of the substrate's mass made up by spawn. More inoculation points mean faster colonization; the house standard is one 6 lb G2 per twenty 10 lb blocks, about 3%. Chapter 11

Substrate, steam and the lab

Term Meaning Covered in
Substrate The food the fruiting mycelium grows on: a carbon base such as sawdust or straw, usually with a supplement (soy hulls, wheat bran) that adds nitrogen for speed and yield. Chapter 10
Master's Mix The American default substrate: 50% hardwood sawdust and 50% soy hulls. Chapter 10
Block Substrate packed in a plastic bag with a filter patch: a synthetic log. 10 lb (4.5 kg) is the maximum size in small-patch bags. Chapter 11
Ultra-pasteurization (UP) Unpressurized steam that brings the block core to 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) and holds it for hours. It kills fungi and active bacteria, but not the heat-resistant endospores of some bacteria. Chapter 12
Sterilization Pressurized steam, 15 psi (1 bar) with the core at 121 °C (250 °F) or more for 35 minutes or more, killing essentially everything. Sterile media are an "open buffet" for anything that lands on them afterwards. Chapter 12
Cool-down Cooling cooked bags in HEPA-filtered, positive-pressure air before inoculation. Blocks are pulled hot from the steamer, never cooled inside it. Chapter 4
Knock Inoculating cooled bags with spawn. "Knock, seal, shake" is the sequence: spawn, seal, mix, then incubation. Chapter 11
HEPA A high-efficiency particulate air filter. "HEPA" is a generic word; read the label for the string of nines (lab grade is about 99.99...97%, for example 99.999997%). Chapter 4
FFU Fan filter unit: a fan with a HEPA filter, the basis of every modern clean room and of the flow hoods used for culture work. Chapter 4
Positive pressure Keeping a clean room at higher pressure than its surroundings, so clean air always pushes outward. Chapter 4

Incubation and fruiting

Term Meaning Covered in
Incubation The stage where mycelium colonizes the block in a dim, steady room. Think of it as a slow fruiting room in which CO2 and heat are the two things to manage. Phases: jump-off (most sensitive), exploration (white and fuzzy), and consolidation or maturation (dense, preparing to fruit). Chapter 13
Fruiting Opening colonized blocks in a fruit room so they form mushrooms. Cutting the bag gives local gas exchange and light, which trigger pinning. Chapter 14
Flush One crop of mushrooms from a block. One farm takes a single flush from every species except lion's mane, which gets two: about 2 lb then 1.5 lb. Chapter 14
FAE Fresh air exchange: bringing in outside air to push CO2 down. Fruit rooms run an exhaust on a CO2 controller, so the room "breathes" between a high and a low CO2 setpoint. Chapter 14
Plenum The clean space in front of the fruit rooms that captures and conditions fresh air for them. It is also where harvesting, grading, packing and drying happen. It is not an entrance, bathroom or office. Chapter 3, Chapter 14
Reefer A cold room or walk-in cooler held at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer, for incoming blocks and fresh mushrooms. Chapter 15

Three businesses in one

AT A GLANCE Culture and spawn, blocks, and fruiting are three businesses with different tools, space and filtration. Start with one you can run alone.

Mushroom cultivation is really three businesses, each with its own tools, space and filtration needs.

Business What it makes Notes
1. Culture preservation and spawn Stored strains, plates, grain masters and G2 spawn The hardest to keep decentralized; needs the cleanest lab. Many new spawn-only companies lack credibility.
2. Fruiting substrate (blocks) Inoculated blocks, sold or used in-house Needs mixing, steam and a clean cool-down and knock lab.
3. Fruiting and fresh sales Fresh mushrooms for chefs, markets and wholesalers The easiest stage to run small and local, and fresh mushrooms are much easier for a start-up to sell than cultures or spawn.
  • Start with one model you can run alone without hiring. Historically, most new farms chose to do everything ("spore to store") out of ego and an illusion of frugality, because they did not value their own time.
  • Spore-to-store can still work long-term for a small, lean, single-variety farm aiming at a fixed steady state, or for a remote farm with no reliable suppliers.
  • Most new farms buy blocks and fruit them out. Unless you make your own, you need a block supplier. Buying blocks frees a small farm to focus on fruiting skill and on customers, building demand before a big equipment leap.
  • A hybrid route: make about 100 blocks a week and buy the other about 150 (one pallet) to reach about 500 lb (230 kg) a week.
  • A middle option: buy grain masters (or liquid culture) from a spawn lab and make only bulk spawn, for example one run a week that produces a month of spawn for one variety.
  • Many farms that buy blocks and simply fruit and sell make a good living, so a small fruiting-only farm can make sense.

The business side is in Chapter 22.

How a farm is laid out

AT A GLANCE Four separate climates, product moving one way from steam to fruiting, and air moving the opposite way. Fruit-room air never mixes with the rest.

A block-making farm has four zones, each an independent environment with its own controls.

Zone Climate control Notes
Mix and steam Temperature and humidity unregulated, except for worker comfort Can be "dirty"; the place for a floor drain.
Cool-down and lab Recirculated, cooled and HEPA-filtered air, at positive pressure The cleanest rooms on the farm.
Incubation CO2 control plus cooling, held constant The stage that really needs a steady temperature.
Fruiting Fresh air (CO2), humidity and cooling regulated; can swing a little Fully decoupled from the other zones.
  • Keep four separate climates and never share air between fruiting and the rest.
  • Move product one way (steam → lab → incubation → fruiting) and move air the opposite way.
  • Treat the fruit room as a filthy environment. The job is to protect the rest of the building from it.
  • People are the largest source of contamination in mushroom production.
  • Plan roughly twice as much incubation space as fruiting space; the zones are not equal quarters.

A farm that buys in blocks needs only three spaces: a reefer (cold room) for incoming blocks and fresh mushrooms, a plenum that doubles as the work area, and the fruit rooms. Fruit rooms must connect to the plenum; the reefer is best kept away from both, mainly because of spore load.

The full layout rules are in Chapter 3, the lab in Chapter 4 and the air systems in Chapter 5.

How long each stage takes

AT A GLANCE For a fast species such as blue oyster, a plate becomes a master in about 2 weeks, spawn in another 10-12 days, colonized blocks in 10-14 more days, and the blocks fruit out over 2-3 weeks. Slow species such as shiitake need about 12 weeks in incubation alone.

Step Blue oyster (fast) Shiitake (slow)
Fresh plate establishing in the flow hood 3-5 days at about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), the hood's ambient 3-4 days at about 21-27 °C (70-80 °F)
G1 master About 2 weeks About 2 weeks
G2 spawn Typically 10-12 days 3-4 weeks
Block incubation 10-14 days at about 19 °C (66 °F) About 12 weeks (6-14) until 75-80% brown
Fruiting Blocks fruit out over 2-3 weeks Shocked into fruiting (cold, soak, smack)

What a working week looks like

AT A GLANCE Production rolls: at least one steam run a week, with each day given one main job.

  • Plan for a run every week from the start. One small farm planned to cook, cool, inoculate and incubate in a single space, taking turns so that hot blocks never cooled beside incubating ones: one knock, incubate the lot, empty the room, start again. That works for about a week, until a new customer wants more than one batch can give. Soon you need at least one run a week, back to back, and then cooling and incubation need separate spaces (the four climate zones).
  • A typical steam-to-knock rhythm: bags are pulled hot from the steamer at about 9 pm, cool overnight in front of the flow hoods in the lab, and are inoculated the next day.
  • A small farm can give each weekday one job: steam on Monday, cool-down and inoculation on Tuesday, spawn prep on Wednesday, agar and genetics on Thursday, and sales on Friday and Saturday.
  • One simple week had one fixed day for bulk spawn and one for all deliveries. Avoid hopping between tasks every day.
  • Map the tasks across Sunday to Saturday as lanes (for example substrate three days, harvest four, grading and packing two, deliveries three plus a market). Each lane can become a person, and combining lanes can remove a whole position.
  • A barrel-steamer week for about 100 blocks of 10 lb: day 1, mix, load and clean, then start the barrel around dinner time (it runs about 15-16 h); day 2, lab prep and spawn work; day 3, knock, shake and rack. One run gives about 100 blocks, about 200 lb (91 kg) of mushrooms a week.
  • For 100 blocks of 10 lb a week at 1:20 (one spawn bag per 20 blocks, about 3%; 1:40 for 5 lb blocks) you need about five 5 lb spawn bags a week.
  • A 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room runs as three weekly cohorts of about 250 blocks, giving about 500-600 lb (230-270 kg) a week.

How to plan a week in detail is in Chapter 22.

The numbers used most

The printable versions are in Chapter 24.

Item Value Covered in
Spawn storage 1-2 °C (34-36 °F); use within about 2 weeks (3 at most) Chapter 9
Substrate moisture 61-63% for most species; above about 68% invites bacteria Chapter 10
Block CO2 in incubation 1,500-3,000 ppm; never above 5,000 ppm where people work Chapter 13
Fruit-room CO2 Cycle about 450-900 ppm, 1,000 ppm at most Chapter 14
Fruit-room humidity Swing about 70-90% RH Chapter 14
Incubation space About twice the fruiting space Chapter 3
Block cost About $2.50-3 in materials. Count your labour and the real cost climbs toward the $8.50-9 bought-in price until about 2,000-5,000 blocks a week Chapter 22
Acceptable loss A steady 5% contamination rate can cost you your whole profit margin Chapter 16

How this book is organized

Part Chapters Use it for
1. Foundations 1 How a Mushroom Farm Works, 2 Fungal Biology, Genetics and History The big picture and background
2. Building the Farm 3 Planning the Farm, 4 The Lab and Clean Practice, 5 Climate Control, 6 Equipment Designing and equipping the space

4. Problems and Safety 16 Contamination, 17 Diseases, Pests and Water, 18 Safety, 19 Troubleshooting by Symptom Finding and fixing what went wrong
5. Species 20 Species Profiles, 21 Growth Metrics Growing a particular mushroom

7. Reference 24 Quick-Reference Cards, 25 Settings and Ranges, 26 Advice from Other Growers, 27 Source Library, 28 Glossary Looking up one number fast

TIP Mid-shift, go straight to Chapter 24 for a number, Chapter 19 for a symptom, and Chapter 20 for a species.

Key rules

  1. Keep four separate climates (steam and mix, lab and cool-down, incubation, fruiting) and never share air between fruiting and the rest.
  2. Move product one way (steam, lab, incubation, fruiting) and move air the opposite way.
  3. Never go past G2 spawn, and never transfer block to block.
  4. Measure the core of the slowest block with a logger on every cook.
  5. Pull cooked blocks hot into HEPA positive pressure and knock them as soon as they are cool: the same day, or the next morning after an overnight cool-down.
  6. Keep HEPA hoods running at all times and never spray them.
  7. Dose solids and water by weight so every bag has the same moisture.
  8. Incubate at about 19 °C (66 °F) with space between bags, and avoid temperature swings and bumps.
  9. Control fruit-room CO2 with an exhaust on a CO2 controller and keep the room at negative pressure.
  10. Change one variable at a time, and keep data before blaming the spawn.
  11. Wear a respirator when harvesting, especially shiitake and reishi.

toc.title: Black oyster and the Hokuto patent

chapters.html:
Fungal Biology, Genetics and History

AT A GLANCE Background knowledge for a grower: how fungi grow and breed, how oyster mushrooms and reishi came into cultivation, the recent history of small-farm growing, and a set of curiosities (fungi in space, the cicada fungus, the fastest mould on the farm). You do not need any of it to run a shift, but it explains why the methods in later chapters look the way they do, and it corrects the myths you will hear. The points people use most:

  • Treat every medicinal claim as unproven: the evidence is mostly in vitro or in animals.
  • Check names and dates against primary sources. Spoken names are often garbled (Jacquin, Kummer, Kaufert, Adaskaveg), and printed documents are more reliable.
  • Agar culture dates from 1894, steam-sterilized grain spawn from a 1932 patent, and dedicated oyster farms from the late 1970s-1980s.
  • Black oyster is a patented multi-species Hokuto hybrid (Canadian patent CA 2 878 902), not a simple oyster cross.
  • When a chemistry figure or unit conversion sounds off (bleach %, ppm, −80 °C, Gurley), recompute it yourself.

How to read this chapter

This chapter gathers the history, natural history and science that growers pass along: how oyster mushrooms and reishi came into cultivation, a student experiment that sent fungi to the International Space Station (ISS), the cicada fungus Massospora, mon-di genetics and many oddities. Mushroom lore mixes documented history with growers' own theories, campfire storytelling and outright jokes, so every item below that is not plain documented history carries a label.

Label What it means
Speculation An untested idea put forward by a grower. Worth testing, not established.
Fiction/joke Deliberate fabrication or parody. Never cite it as history.
Error A slip in a talk that the sources themselves correct (an on-screen slide, the book's own standard) or that simple arithmetic shows. The correction is given beside it and collected in Checking figures you hear.
Unverified / Unsupported / Overstated A name, number or claim that could not be checked, has no source, or goes further than the evidence.

RULE Treat any medicinal claim as unproven, check dates and names against primary sources, and never cite joke or parody material as history.

Fungal biology for growers

AT A GLANCE A fungus lives as mycelium inside its food; the mushroom is only its fruit body. Shape follows environment, moisture drives fruiting, and the rich media growers use feed every other microbe too. Fast reference: one mushroom releases on the order of a billion spores.

Mycelium, fruit bodies and spores

A fungus lives as mycelium: a network of fine threads (hyphae) that grows through its food and digests it. The mushroom you harvest is the fruit body, the part the fungus makes to release spores. These two sentences are the basic biology every later chapter builds on (see Chapter 1 for the farm view).

  • The mass of a mushroom comes from the substrate, not from the air of the fruit room. The brown layer on a shiitake block is a leather-like skin on the outside only.
  • Mycelium breathes like people do: it uses oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide (CO2), so a room packed with blocks behaves like a crowded room. CO2 becomes the dominant problem only at commercial scale (see Chapter 5 and Chapter 13).
  • Spore numbers are enormous. One mushroom releases on the order of a billion spores, so about 100 shiitake fruiting on one log release about 100 billion.
  • Fungal form depends strongly on environment, much more than in plant tissue culture. Fruit bodies grown in the dark look bizarre.
  • In nature, moisture drives fruiting (David Arora's field guide "All That the Rain Promises" makes the point in its title). A substrate at 60-61% moisture is like a forest floor at field capacity: as wet as it can be while still draining (see Chapter 10).
  • Mushroom work differs from a chemistry lab. A chemist only has to keep a sealed flask clean, but growers handle rich sterile media that will feed anything that lands on them, which is why mushroom labs need continuous filtered airflow (see Chapter 4).

Growth speed

Organism Typical growth rate Notes
Neurospora (a fast mould) About 3-5 mm per hour The mycelial "land-speed record" (attributed to John Donoghue). See Neurospora.

One genus, many oysters

  • Pleurotus species (P. ostreatus, P. djamor, P. citrinopileatus, P. eryngii and others) share essentially the same growth biology and differ mostly in colour and temperature preference. Many research papers simply write "Pleurotus sp.".
  • High-yield blue oyster strains are jokingly called "home wreckers" because they fruit four times.
  • Oysters and Psilocybe cubensis are the easiest mushrooms to grow. The oyster will colonize almost anything, which explains its popularity.
  • Master's Mix, 50:50 red oak sawdust to soy hulls, is the highest-yielding oyster substrate but also the richest and most fickle. Only cottonseed hulls or fermented straw compete with it (recipes in Chapter 10).
  • In P. ostreatus, the most robust strains (ones that never senesce and grow on anything) tend to yield poorly, with small mushrooms. An example is "JB", an old strain used by Far West Fungi.

Monokaryons, dikaryons and mon-di genetics

AT A GLANCE A spore grows into a monokaryon. Two compatible monokaryons join into a dikaryon, and only a dikaryon can fruit. Much of what growers say beyond that is open hypothesis. Practical strain keeping and breeding are in Chapter 8.

A single spore grows into a monokaryon, a mycelium with one type of nucleus. When two compatible monokaryons meet, their hyphae fuse and form a dikaryon, with two distinct nuclei in each cell, and only the dikaryon can form fruit bodies. This meeting of compatible hyphae is called plasmogamy.

A dikaryon can also pass one of its nuclei to a monokaryon it meets. This "di-mon" or Buller phenomenon makes a new strain without spores. The findings behind it come from only a few papers.

What growers suspect, and what is still open:

  • Speculation: shifts in which nucleus is "dominant" in a dikaryon may explain odd growth that gets labelled as senescence. The field has not yet defined what dominance means.
  • A related plate sign, fuzzy patches ringed by thick rhizomorphic (rope-like) lines, is read by some growers as the two nuclei drifting apart.
  • Do not assume the dominant nucleus is the faster grower. Selection might favour something else, for example defence against bacteria.
  • Speculation: blending (maceration) may read to the fungus like a disaster such as a fire, prompting an "escape" set of pins. This is compared with morels flushing for 1-2 years after burns. The idea is admittedly anthropomorphic.
  • Speculation: claimed fusions between genera (oyster x lion's mane, reishi x shaggy mane and others) form clamps but do not fruit, and might pass genes into later crosses.
  • Mating matters for yield. In 1968, Eugenio and Anderson found that compatible (mated) dikaryons yielded about 200 g more than non-compatible pairings.
  • Prediction: AI will predict mating outcomes from genomes. One supplier (Julian) already sells monokaryon cultures.

Substrate chemistry and growers' theories

  • Speculation: pelletizing destroys the sap-based antifungal compounds in softwood, so it should be no surprise that softwood pellets work as a substrate.
  • Raw peat and lime casing is "functionally clean": the specialized microbes that live in them do not thrive on rich substrate.
  • Raw amended (supplemented) substrate is not shelf-stable. In Southeast Asia, substrates are deliberately composted or fermented first.
  • Hydrogen peroxide chemistry: the enzyme catalase splits peroxide into water and oxygen, and the reactive oxygen species formed along the way damage lipids and DNA. Bacteria suffer more than fungal hyphae. Peroxide was approved for food processing around the 1940s-50s (date unconfirmed). See Chapter 17 for its use against blotch.
  • Unverified claim: a shiitake culture plated next to Streptomyces bacteria makes a metabolite specific to that pairing, as if fungi were "little chemists".
  • Speculation: mineral dust (calcium carbonate, silica) settling on caps may disturb the osmotic and polarity cues of the fruit body and cause topside gills as an epigenetic response. The grower write-up proposing this says itself that the molecular pathways are not established (see Chapter 17 on water quality).
  • Untested idea: would a shiitake mass of about 80 lb (36 kg) give bigger fruits?
  • Some people electrify shiitake logs to shock them into fruiting. Don't do this.

Early human uses of fungi

There is no real "origin date" for using or growing mushrooms. Written history starts only when Western science catches up, so most documented milestones fall in the 1900s.

Traditional uses fall into three groups: food (foraging), medicine and spirituality. A fourth group, "function" uses, covers tinder, dyes and materials.

  • Shiitake log growing in China is usually cited as the earliest cultivation. Speculation: it began when people noticed mushrooms on fallen (not standing) logs and started felling trees in the right season.
  • Log "beating" was a folk practice: growers banged naturally fruiting logs near fresh-cut ones. Without knowing it they spread spores, and perhaps also shocked the logs into fruiting. Growers also kept fruiting logs beside new ones. Treat the story as half-joking oral history; it is often retold.
  • Ötzi the Iceman carried birch polypore (Fomitopsis betulina), thought to be a purgative against intestinal parasites.
  • Tinder or hoof fungus (Fomes fomentarius), dried and flaked, smoulders very slowly and was used to carry fire. It is said that the Chinese used it for ignition before gunpowder (unverified), a point Paul Stamets has explained on the Joe Rogan podcast.
  • The reishi "mushroom of immortality" legend, as told in one reishi book: ravens laid antler-form reishi on the faces of slain soldiers, who rose again. Here "immortality" first meant resurrection, not health.

Books and theories on fungi in spirituality that growers often mention:

Work Subject
R. Gordon Wasson, Soma Amanita muscaria as the soma of the Rig Veda
Aldous Huxley, Brave New World The fictional drug "soma"
Wasson, Hofmann and Ruck, The Road to Eleusis Ergot in the kykeon drink of the Eleusinian rites
Albert Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child Hofmann's own account of LSD
Terence McKenna, Food of the Gods The "stoned ape" theory
John Marco Allegro, The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross Mushrooms and early Christianity

How oyster cultivation developed

AT A GLANCE Oyster cultivation is young. The species was described in 1775, pure agar culture arrived in 1894, the first oyster crops were grown in Germany in 1917, sterilized grain spawn was patented in 1932, and dedicated oyster farms with bags appeared only in the late 1970s-1980s.

Dedicated oyster farms appeared only around the late 1970s-1980s, so the industry is young. Commercial oyster growing became established in the US and Europe in the 1970s-80s. Kennett Square, Pennsylvania, was an early mushroom hub for button mushrooms, built with know-how from France.

Timeline

Year Who What
1775 Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin (often described as Dutch; the name is frequently garbled) First scientific description, as Agaricus ostreatus, on rotting trunks (especially walnut) in November-December. He noted that the stem looked like many fungi fused together.
1871 Paul Kummer, Der Führer in die Pilzkunde Erected the genus Pleurotus ("side ear") and many other genera still in use.
1894 Costantin and Matruchot (France) First pure mushroom cultures on agar, from tissue and from spores, steam-sterilized.
1890s-1909 Julius Oscar Brefeld First to go from spore to pure culture to fruiting. He went blind in 1909. His 1908 cultivation book has not been found.
1905 B.M. Duggar Showed that P. ostreatus spawn could be made on bean pods, leaves and manure (apparently not sterilized), stopping at the spawn stage.
1917 (WWI) Richard Falck, Brefeld's student Credited as the first oyster cultivator: outdoor P. ostreatus for German wartime food, using a trench method on wheat straw and stump inoculation.
about 1920s - Autoclaves are said to date from about this time.
1929 Bessie E. Etter Wood-rotting fungi fruited in the lab only when wood plus starch were present. Plain agar gave mycelium only. She used flasks of 500-1,000 cc (mL), with shiitake as the main example.
1932 James W. Sinden (Penn State) Patented steam-sterilized grain spawn (see Chapter 9).
1935 Frank Kaufert Described the spore system of Pleurotus corticatus (now placed under P. dryinus): about five routes to spore production, plus wood-block culture.
1958 Block, Tsao and Han Fruited P. ostreatus in about 2 weeks on sterile sawdust plus oatmeal in jars. Composted balsa gave 1.2 lb (0.54 kg). Seen as the US proof of block cultivation.
1963 Zakia Bano and Srivastava (India) Industrialized oyster growing on paddy straw in field plots, using P. flabellatus (now in P. djamor) and P. sajor-caju (now in Lentinus).
1968 Eugenio and Anderson Compatible (mated) dikaryons yielded about 200 g more than non-compatible pairings.
about 1970s - Liquid-nitrogen culture storage begins. Before that, strains were serially subcultured on agar and degraded (see Chapter 8).
about 1971 Paul Stamets and a colleague Studied clamp connections by electron microscope at a Washington college (one grower's account).
Late 1970s-80s - First dedicated oyster farms; bags arrive.
Late 1980s - New phenotype breeding largely stops.

What the original documents show

  • Duggar's 1905 work is a USDA bulletin, not a patent. Its title page reads "The Principles of Mushroom Growing and Mushroom Spawn Making", by B.M. Duggar, Professor of Botany, University of Missouri, USDA Bureau of Plant Industry. A table row in it reads "Pleurotus ostreatus: beans, leaves, manure etc.: rapid growth".
  • Calling Duggar's work a patent from the "University of Minnesota" is an Error: it is a USDA bulletin by a University of Missouri professor.
  • Sinden's US patent header reads "assignor to the Pennsylvania State College ... Mushroom Spawn and Method of Making Same".
  • Falck's German figures of stump inoculation show saw cuts made from three sides, spawn pushed into the cuts, and a disc placed on top.

Later developments

  • Morels resisted indoor cultivation for more than 100 years, though the triggers for outdoor cultivation are now understood.
  • Modern non-food uses of oysters include mycoremediation (cleaning up oil spills, popularized by Stamets), filtration and biomaterials.

Recent North American cultivation (oral history)

AT A GLANCE These are growers' memories of the last decade or two. Treat them as oral history, not documented fact.

Strains and suppliers

  • Strains used to move only by trade, between friends and on forums such as the Shroomery. There was no middle tier of spawn sellers between the industrial spawn makers and hobbyists.
  • Early global strain traders (for example Matt Noble, an Eastern European or Russian forum member) have mostly disappeared from the scene.
  • Shiitake strain 3782 was a "revolution" around 2013-14, giving more than 1 lb (0.45 kg) of mushrooms from a 5 lb (2.3 kg) block.
  • Good gourmet chestnut mushrooms were first seen in the Northeast about 8 years before these accounts were recorded, at New Hampshire Mushroom Company, grown in Northwest Mycological Consultants bags.
  • Maitake went from a "white whale" to a widespread small-farm crop in about two years, although an old Oregon farm had grown it for decades.
  • Chef Rob Evans (Duckfat, Portland, Maine) described Japanese villages with multi-generation maitake growers and restaurants devoted to maitake.

Steam, sterilization and clean air

  • Ten years ago, US practice assumed full sterilization in pressure cookers. Ultra-pasteurization in steam "double barrels" (credited to the forum grower known as "Roger Rabbit") was new. The older cubensis-era pasteurization at 71-77 °C (160-170 °F) kills much but leaves much alive (see Chapter 12).
  • Asian growers have long pasteurized substrate in lined-up barrels over a wood fire, with a small vent valve, and then hand-carted the barrels to the lab.
  • Before steam, one grower tried lime and dry heat, and others tried microwaving; all of these lead back to steam. That grower's first farm was in Chino Valley, Arizona, in 2012 (documented on the blog sandshrooms.blogspot.com).
  • A New Hampshire grower started the trend of using Sioux steam generators on mushroom farms about 10 or more years ago.
  • The old do-it-yourself flow hood recipe was a bare 99.99997% HEPA filter boxed in polyurethaned wood, with a salvaged squirrel-cage blower and a rheostat, checked with lighter-flame tests. Forum lore dismissed 99.95% filters, which in hindsight was dogma rather than necessity (see Chapter 4).

Substrates

  • Soy hulls plus sawdust became a default after Stamets' book Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms and experiments by other growers, because soy hulls were easy to source.
  • Earlier hobby growers used hardwood fuel pellets, which have a slick lignin skin.
  • Older shiitake practice browned blocks outside the bag until a 5 lb (2.3 kg) block had dried to about 1 lb (0.45 kg), then soaked it before fruiting (current practice is in Chapter 20).

Reishi in Eastern history

AT A GLANCE Reishi history is murky. Read the "zhi" colours as traditional categories and the "7,000 years of use" figure as weak evidence, not botany.

  • Reishi history is murky. Ancient texts lump many fungi and herbs together, so most early "reishi" references cannot be tied to a species.
  • Lingzhi is the Chinese name and reishi the Japanese one. "Zhi" broadly meant a fungus or plant of immortality, and immortality meant anything that restored balance and lengthened life.
  • In old materia medica (herbal reference works), reishi was sometimes grouped with psychoactive plants but given its own class.
  • The often-quoted "7,000 years of use" rests on Ganoderma spores found at three archaeological sites, dated roughly 6,800, 5,300 and 4,500 years ago (dates unverified). Spores in a dig do not prove human use.
  • Shennong, the legendary "divine farmer", is credited with the herbal classic. His dates are mythical (one account puts him before the Xia dynasty, about 1870-1600 BC), and nothing ties him reliably to reishi.
  • The Shennong Bencao Jing dates from the Han dynasty (about 200 BC-220 AD) and was edited constantly, so no original survives. It lists zhi as a "superior" herb.
  • Reishi became a prized status item because wild fruit bodies are rare and keep for a long time once dried. Foragers sold them to the elite, and Daoist hermits drove demand.
  • Speculation: early growers may have moved logs, or put fresh wood near wild fruitings. There is no proof of ancient cultivation.
  • Li Shizhen's Compendium of Materia Medica (1590) is called the first big Chinese pharmacopoeia. Japan later studied Chinese medicine (Kampo), and Japanese lore has hermits drinking reishi tea.

The six zhi colours

Zhi colour Organ or use in the text Note
Red Heart; sharpens wits and memory The only one clearly matching G. lucidum in the broad sense (sensu lato).
Green Eyes, liver
Yellow Spleen and abdomen; a carefree mind
White Lungs; cough and cold; will
Black Kidneys; urinary dribbling
Purple Joints, sinews, bones Thought to be a later addition, since it breaks the pattern.

Robert Rogers (presumably the author of The Fungal Pharmacy) argues that the colours were symbolic categories. Speculation: each zhi was a blend of herbs and fungi rather than a colour form of one species. Packets of red, green, black, brown and white reishi are still sold today.

Reishi in Western science

Year Who What
1781 William Curtis Named it Boletus lucidus.
1821 / 1867 - Moved to Polyporus, then to Fomes.
1881 Peter Adolf Karsten Erected the genus Ganoderma for the shiny (laccate) cap.
1889 Patouillard The double-walled spore became the defining trait of the genus.
1902 W.A. Murrill Described 7 North American Ganoderma species.
1929 Bessie E. Etter Ganoderma formed a 3D structure like a fruit body on agar when wood was present.
1943 An American study (unnamed) Wet conditions favour chlamydospores (thick-walled resting spores). Below about 85% relative humidity (RH), Ganoderma pore tubes grow hyphae instead of a proper pore surface (details unconfirmed; the source was hard to make out).
1949 Mary E. Stebbins and William J. Robbins Cultures can be preserved under mineral oil.
1950s S.R. Bose Differences among about 12 Ganoderma types.
1955 - About 40% of carbon converted to CO2 and mycelium, mid-range among the species tested.
1963 - Spore release peaks around midnight and is low by day, possibly tied to night-time humidity.
Late 1960s-early 1970s Chinese Academy of Sciences First full artificial life cycle with a spore-bearing cap. Earlier attempts gave only antlers and nodules.
1980s-2010 - Research grows with bag technology: genetics, mating systems, markers.
1986 Adaskaveg and Gilbertson G. lucidum and G. tsugae did not cross. Ganoderma is heterothallic (needs a compatible partner) and tetrapolar.
2000s - Studies of compound chemistry.
  • From the naming to about 1960 there is almost nothing on cultivation. The literature is mostly regional species records.
  • Bag or sawdust fruiting is much faster, but logs give more robust fruit bodies with more compounds, so quality-focused growers still use logs (growing notes in Chapter 20).
  • A mycologist photographed under ultraviolet (UV) light a reishi from an Ecovative kit that fruited in transit. The fluorescent colours show how compounds are distributed through the fruit body.
  • One grower's first tincture from wild reishi was very hard to process: it broke blenders and needed a double extraction.
  • Reishi is not much of an edible, though the trimmed outer flesh is described as having a foie-gras texture.
  • Mycelium materials (leather alternatives, packaging) are a growth area, led by Ganoderma's tough mat.

Compounds and medicinal evidence

RULE Treat every medicinal claim as unproven. The evidence is mostly in vitro (in a dish) or in animals, and responsible growers say so plainly.

  • Reishi compound classes: triterpenoids, steroids, phenols, nucleotides and polysaccharides/peptidoglycans. Reishi contains all the amino acids, notably lysine and leucine.
  • Across Ganoderma species, polysaccharide/peptidoglycan content runs 1.1-5.8% and triterpenes 0-7.8%, so content depends strongly on species. Over 100 triterpenes are known, 50 or more of them newly described.
  • The evidence points to immune modulation rather than direct anti-tumour action. Many studies are in vitro or in animals, small, and from one research group. There is some evidence for effects on blood glucose (mostly in animals), for liver and stomach protection, and for antiviral or antibacterial activity.
  • One grower's view, an opinion and not a finding, is that reishi supports overall body function rather than targeting a disease.
  • Medicinal claims generally rest on mostly in-vitro, unproven evidence. Good practice is to be honest with customers and callers about this.
  • Lion's mane (growers' understanding): two small classes of compounds that cross the blood-brain barrier (probably the hericenones and erinacines) upregulate neurite formation related to nerve growth factor. The source cited for this is a Fresh Cap Mushrooms video.
  • Open question: do late lion's mane flushes (for example the 13th) keep their beneficial compounds?

Reishi Madness: a mock advert (fiction)

  • Fiction/joke: "Reishi Madness" is a parody advert. It lists the usual health claims (immune, sleep, stress, blood pressure, anti-cancer and so on), calls them "as dubious as they are endless", and then parodies them. Typical use is said to be 1-3 drops a couple of times a day. Its makers do not endorse the claims.
  • Fiction/joke: it also covers the immortality folklore (about 4,000 years of use, as stated, and a raven myth compared with Odin's ravens), then stitches reishi into real events as jokes: the Brazilian lead-mask case, Betty and Barney Hill, the Patterson-Gimlin Bigfoot film and stories about the Vatican. None of this is history.
  • Speculation presented as fact: the "mummy's curse" deaths after Tutankhamun's tomb was opened (1922) are blamed on black mould. This is a popular theory, not established fact.

RULE Reishi Madness and parts of the campfire-style Massospora material are entertainment. Never cite them as fact.

  • Be careful with "beta-glucan" numbers. The common beta-glucan test (Megazyme) is not validated, and is unreliable on whole-food products made of mycelium grown on grain; most claims against mycelium-on-grain products rest on it. One California producer now studies health outcomes (cell-line work and a lion's mane cognition survey) rather than marker compounds.

Black oyster and the Hokuto patent

AT A GLANCE Black oyster (Black Pearl, Shimofuri) is a patented multi-species hybrid from Hokuto Corporation (Canadian patent CA 2 878 902), bred through P. nebrodensis to bridge oyster and king oyster. It is not a simple oyster cross. Growing notes are in Chapter 20.

  • The names Black Pearl, Black King, Cosmic Queen and Shimofuri are used interchangeably.
  • Hokuto Corporation described Shimofuri Hiratake as an eastern x western oyster hybrid (ostreatus x ostreatus), while others claimed king x blue. One grower who first repeated the website's line now thinks it was wrong.
  • Community evidence points to a complex hybrid. Buller-style crosses with kings and blues, made by the owner of Sprouted Mushrooms, gave only one mating pair. A 2023 sequencing of "Black Pearl King" sent to ALVALAB by a grower gave messy BLAST hits split between P. ostreatus and P. eryngii.
  • The patent is Canadian Patent CA 2 878 902 C, "Novel species of Pleurotus sp. and method for producing same". It is owned by Hokuto Corporation; the inventors are Ishikawa, Inatomi, Ouchi and Oku; the PCT application was filed on 2013-07-10, and the patent issued on 2016-11-29.
  • Claimed crossing scheme: (1) P. ostreatus x P. nebrodensis; (2) P. eryngii x var. elaeoselini; (3) = hybrid 1 x hybrid 2; then repeated backcrosses to ostreatus and eryngii. The deposited strains are NITE BP-1378 and BP-1379. A plain ostreatus x eryngii cross forms a dikaryon but does not fruit, so Hokuto bridged through nebrodensis.
  • Growers' working understanding (unverified): black oyster involves eryngii variants, European ostreatus and nebrodensis, and the exact parentage is uncertain.

The parent species:

  • Wild P. eryngii varieties are Mediterranean and North African and associated with the carrot family (giant fennel). King oyster is weakly parasitic on these plants. The claim that var. elaeoselini is found in Tunisia came from an AI search (unverified).
  • P. nebrodensis grows on limestone and volcanic soils from Sicily to Afghanistan, is endangered, needs a basic pH of 8-11, and fruits after hard frosts. Cap n Stem has released a culture of it as a curiosity.

Questions it raises:

  • Speculation: a near-sterile hybrid like black oyster may be ecologically safe, since it cannot cross within itself.
  • Speculation: dumping the sequences of a four-species hybrid into public DNA databases would muddy phylogenies (family trees of species).

Names, cultures and DNA work

Names in flux: chestnut

  • Chestnut taxonomy may shift. One community culture of "Pholiota adiposa" sequenced as something slightly different, and Alan Rockefeller's sequencing work is revising names, and the supposed toxicity, of some species.
  • Growers deliberately keep calling it P. adiposa while noting that the name is disputed.
  • Unsupported claim: people either tolerate chestnut completely or get very sick. It has been stated as "100% proven" with no source.
  • Wild chestnut-like Pholiota and wild burn morels taste better than cultivated ones. One explanation growers give is the missing microbial interactions in sterile cultivation.

Keeping cultures over decades

  • Dehydration was the first culture preservation method.
  • A long-running deep-freeze study recovered mycelium after 29-30 years, out of about 35 years of testing. The study is not named (unverified).
  • Cap n Stem keeps culture lines in cryo storage for a decade as rice-grain-sized pieces (methods in Chapter 8).
  • Culture collecting is shifting toward DNA sequencing and digital phylogenetics.

Influences on small-farm DNA work

Influences on one Maine farm's (Cap n Stem's) DNA work:

  • Alan Rockefeller's workflow of iNaturalist observations, DNA barcoding and GenBank uploads.
  • Oxford Nanopore pocket sequencers.
  • The Hamilton Morris podcast.
  • William Padilla-Brown.

Stroma

  • "Stroma" just means a mass of fungal cells, and the word is used loosely. Published work mostly ends with "unclear cause".
  • Older growers called it "Mycogone", but Mycogone is a genus of real Hypocrealean contaminants, which have caused region-wide outbreaks (for example in France). Prevention of stroma in spawn is in Chapter 9; contaminants are in Chapter 16.
  • Dr Jason Slot (fungal evolution and horizontal gene transfer; credited by one grower with finding the psilocybin gene cluster by nanopore sequencing) agreed to analyse Cap n Stem's stroma data cheaply, on condition that the results are published openly, with sequencing done by Novogene.

Wild species and ecology

Hericium and lion's mane

  • Three wild Hericium grow in the northern hemisphere: H. erinaceus (lion's mane), H. americanum (bear's head) and H. coralloides (comb tooth). They differ mainly in form and are handled almost identically in culture.
  • Wild lion's mane is rare in Maine and more common in southern New England. It grows in tree knots and wounds, and has been seen growing together with bear's head.

Other wild species

  • Wild maitake can produce heads of up to about 30 lb (14 kg), and they appear very fast.
  • One grower found Lactarius indigo on a university lawn. It is delicious but cannot be cultivated yet.
  • Chaga (Inonotus obliquus) is a sterile mass like a sclerotium.

Ecology notes

Ecology points growers raise:

  • Cultivated P. cubensis cannot simply be released into the wild to thrive.
  • Frank Herbert, author of Dune, reportedly poured blended chanterelles at the bases of trees and got fruits, and tried the same with Psilocybe cyanescens (according to a talk by Paul Stamets).
  • There is a story of spores mixed into chainsaw bar oil.
  • Shiitake is called a primary decomposer.

Fungi in microgravity

AT A GLANCE A student experiment from Swinburne University of Technology (Australia) sent mycelium to the ISS on the NG-21 Cygnus launch. The results had not been reported at the time of writing.

  • The experiment flew on the NG-21 Cygnus launch and was described by Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist at Swinburne University of Technology, in an interview during the launch broadcast.
  • Swinburne's SHINE program (running since 2017) has a student cohort design a space experiment each year. Earlier ISS payloads included teeth/bacteria, chia seeds (which failed by overheating), magnetorheological fluid and microgreens.
  • Ground trials grew mycelium on buckwheat and other grains in vials, testing added wood or coconut husk against grain alone.
  • The flight vials were 15 mL blue-capped tubes labelled "Trametes versicolor #2, #3, #5, 07/25/2024" and "Cordyceps #3"; the species were otherwise never named.

Logistics:

  • Rhodium Scientific handled the US approvals with NASA and the ISS National Lab.
  • In Australia, a regulatory colleague lodged the launch and return permits.
  • The cultures came via Russell at Aussie Mushroom Supplies, through its import and export link with a Maine farm (Cap n Stem).

The science:

  • Hypothesis: like many bacteria, fungi may thrive in microgravity. Changes in gene expression are of particular interest.

  • Rationale: fungi as fast food on the Moon or Mars, with spent mycelium becoming fire-retardant insulation or compost.

  • Post-flight plans: compare the genetics of flight and ground samples, run scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on mycelial density, and do chemistry. A denser network may not mean a healthier one.

  • Radiation on the ISS is modest, but beyond the Van Allen belts it could kill organisms. Fungi travel well lyophilized (freeze-dried), frozen or dried, and planetary protection rules would demand extreme containment.

  • Cap n Stem sent turkey tail, lion's mane and Cordyceps militaris, three strains it knows well, to the International Space Station for a school microgravity experiment. Shipping live cultures across borders risks customs holds, heat and irradiation.

  • After the trip, the turkey tail cultures had fully recovered within about five days, while the lion's mane was "just starting to get out from the grains".

Massospora, the cicada fungus

AT A GLANCE Massospora infects cicadas, replaces the end of the abdomen with a spore mass, and changes the insect's mating behaviour. Much of what growers pass around about it is campfire-style talk: mostly speculative natural history, with several factual slips corrected below.

  • Cicada basics: annual cicadas emerge every year, while periodical broods (for example the 17-year Brood X) emerge together. Nymphs feed on roots, adults live a few weeks, and males call using a hollow abdomen.
  • Massospora survives as resting spores in topsoil, which emerging nymphs pick up. Roughly 3-5% of cicadas are infected, mostly males (a hedged figure). For about a week the cicada acts normally; then the abdomen sloughs off to expose a chalky spore mass, a "flying salt shaker".
  • Infected males stop calling and flick their wings like females, which attracts other males, and they mate hyperactively. Speculation: the mechanism is manipulation of the central nervous system; whether the fungus drives the behaviour or merely influences it is left open.
  • Alkaloids: Massospora contains psilocybin in annual cicadas and cathinone (the amphetamine-like compound of khat) in periodical ones. Why the split exists is unanswered, and the amounts per insect are tiny.
  • An unnamed Boston researcher studies horizontal gene transfer. The claim is that psilocybin production arose as a discrete evolutionary event.
  • Psilocybin mycelium holds far less active compound than fruit bodies, and spores hold none, which is why spore syringes were legal.

Neurospora

Neurospora is a fast orange mould that shows up as a contaminant on farms (diagnosis in Chapter 16).

  • It grows by long, narrow leading hyphae followed by denser growth, at about 3-5 mm per hour: the mycelial "land-speed record" (according to John Donoghue). This figure is widely repeated.
  • It lives on tree bark and is an early colonizer at the edges of burns. Speculation (no evidence): a link with morels.
  • Beneficial uses: oncom (an Indonesian fermented press-cake), a Brazilian fermented cassava drink, Roquefort cheese (unverified), and use as a lab model organism since the 1920s.

Other curiosities

  • Fiction critique: the premise of The Last of Us (a Cordyceps fungus mutating to survive human body temperature) is scientifically silly, and it has shaped public fear of fungi.
  • A novel mould variant (Trichoderma or Aspergillus) appeared at about the same time at button-mushroom compost sites on several continents. Speculation: it spread from agricultural use of Trichoderma since the 1950s. The line that it "killed a bunch of mushroom farmers" is likely a garble for killed crops or businesses.
  • Big industrial growers clean each room fully after every crop, despite their automation.
  • One grower's first boss, at a maker of anaerobic lab equipment, travelled with a small anaerobic chamber of cultures in a suitcase.
  • Bagger names follow a lineage: a small builder's "Thor", then a Canadian container grower's "Odin", then Cap n Stem's "Fenrir", named after the wolf that kills the gods (machines in Chapter 6 and Chapter 11).

Checking figures you hear

AT A GLANCE Slips heard in talks that simple arithmetic or the sources themselves correct. When a figure sounds off (bleach %, ppm, −80 °C, Gurley), recompute it yourself.

Claim as made Status Correction
Bleach "2-4% = 200-400 ppm" Arithmetic 200-400 ppm is 0.02-0.04% (1% = 10,000 ppm). Doses are in Chapter 17.
Bleach "turns biocidal" at about 20% Garbled Bleach works at ppm levels, as the doses in Chapter 17 show.
−80 °C is "−250-something" Arithmetic −80 °C = −112 °F.
Sterile means "20 C for 15 min" Mis-hearing The standard is 121 °C (250 °F) for 15 minutes or more (see Chapter 12).
Higher Gurley rating = more filtration and more air Muddled A higher Gurley number (seconds) means less air permeability (see Chapter 11).
Duggar's 1905 work was a patent at the University of Minnesota Error The on-screen title page shows a USDA bulletin by a University of Missouri professor.
Chestnut intolerance is all-or-nothing, "100% proven" Unsupported No source was given.

Some talks include deliberate parody and fiction, and the speakers say so: reishi tied to UFO, Bigfoot and Vatican events; a list of reishi health claims its makers call dubious; and a Cordyceps zombie apocalypse the speakers call scientifically silly. Treat them as entertainment.

Key rules

  1. Treat every medicinal claim as unproven. The evidence is mostly in vitro or in animals.
  2. Check names and dates against primary sources. Spoken names are often garbled (Jacquin, Kummer, Kaufert, Adaskaveg), and printed slides and documents are more reliable.
  3. Take the documented Pleurotus milestones from the timeline, and treat growers' memories of recent decades as oral history.
  4. Read the zhi colours and the "7,000 years" figure as traditional categories and weak evidence, not botany.
  5. Black oyster is a patented multi-species Hokuto hybrid (CA 2 878 902), not a simple oyster cross.
  6. "Reishi Madness" and parts of the Massospora material are entertainment, so never cite them as fact.
  7. The mon-di dominance, "escape response" and dust-gill ideas are open hypotheses worth testing, not established findings.
  8. When a chemistry figure or unit conversion sounds off (bleach %, ppm, −80 °C, Gurley), recompute it yourself.

Open questions

  • The deep-freeze study (29-30 year recovery), the archaeological spore dates and the 1943 humidity study are not named or checked.
  • Whether nuclear dominance explains senescence-like drift is untested.
  • The cause of stroma is under investigation with Jason Slot, and no results had been published at the time of writing.
  • The results of the microgravity experiment have not been reported.
  • Why Massospora makes psilocybin in some cicadas and cathinone in others is unanswered.
  • Do late lion's mane flushes keep their beneficial compounds?
