chapters.html:
Planning the Farm and Its Layout

AT A GLANCE This chapter treats the whole farm as one building: which production zones you need, how much space each takes, how product, air and people move between them, what to look for in a building, how to grow in steps, how to fit a farm into a small space, and what working farms look like. Room-level detail lives in other chapters: the lab and cool-down in Chapter 4, climate equipment in Chapter 5, steam in Chapter 12, incubation in Chapter 13, fruit rooms in Chapter 14 and money in Chapter 22.

  • Plan four separate climates: mix/steam, lab/cool-down, incubation, fruiting. Never share air between fruiting and the rest.
  • Move product one way: steam, then lab, then incubation, then cooler or fruiting. No backtracking.
  • Give incubation about 2x the fruiting floor (3-4x for slow species) and more than the lab, and at least 3 weeks of space for a 2-week species.
  • Fruit-room cooler: 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer.
  • A 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room turns over about 250 blocks a week and yields up to about 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week.
  • Design from the ideal, then justify every corner you cut.

Why planning comes first

A mushroom farm is a chain of rooms. Each room has its own climate, and product must travel between them without picking up contamination. Mistakes in the layout cost money every single week, so it pays to get them right before you build.

  • Design from the ideal and work backward. Every corner you cut should have to be justified. Do not start out looking for corners to cut. Low-budget start-ups that hunt for the cheapest proof of concept end up fighting uphill.
  • The most common start-up error is to overestimate what fits in a small footprint. People underestimate the space needed for access, moving around, gowning and changing, and separate climate controls for each room.
  • People who buy buildings nearly always make incubation too small, and they ignore the sun's path and the roof colour.
  • Don't solve a shortage of space by taking turns. Cooling hot blocks in the room where others are incubating makes the incubation temperature swing up and down. Running in turns instead (one knock, incubate the lot, empty the room, start again) works only until demand grows, usually within weeks. Plan for at least one production run a week, with cooling and incubation in separate spaces.
  • Engineers often propose closed-loop air recirculation across the whole building, because it looks efficient. Biology (spore load, CO2 and temperature stability) usually kills such plans. One-way airflow is what makes rooms "rock solid".
  • Expect the layout to change within months as you grow. That is why cheap, modular, cleanable materials (steel studs, Coroplast, flashing tape) are the standard. After years of reshuffling rooms, Cap n Stem began designing a new facility from scratch in Lewiston, Maine.
  • Most new farms buy blocks and fruit them. Unless you make your own blocks, you need a block supplier. Block suppliers include Cap n Stem, Earth Angel and Far West Fungi, among others.

TIP To test a design, walk through a whole day (morning, afternoon and the next day) for each person who will work there. Much of what looks like inefficiency turns out to be useful redundancy.

  • Expect to rebuild. A Chicago farm learned so much about cooling, humidity and airflow in its first year, in a rented 37 m² (400 sq ft) space, that it tore out its grow rooms and built a second version. It had started six months before its first summer without proper cooling. Most farms rebuild, move and re-plan rooms many times; a floor plan cannot be fixed while you are still learning. One Florida farm moved its lab twice in two and a half years and was building its fourth grow room, with only two standing at any time.
  • Function before looks. Hand-built facilities often look rough, and even large, successful farms look chaotic inside. A facility has to work first. Polished rooms at well-funded farms are often just walk-in coolers with temperature controllers and probes.
  • Define the whole setup before comparing advice. What works in one room depends on every other choice: the fogger or mister type, continuous or cycled fresh air, the climate outside and the species mix. There are thousands of variables, and growers often talk past each other because their setups differ. A balance that works in one climate can contradict what a book says.

Three businesses, three kinds of facility

Cultivation is really "three business models in one":

  1. Culture preservation and spawn production.
  2. Fruiting-substrate (block) production.
  3. Fruiting and fresh sales.

Each needs different tools, space and filtration. Start with the one you can run alone without hiring (see Chapter 22).

Fruiting is the easiest of the three to decentralize (run at many small sites). Block production comes next, and spawn is the hardest.

The four climate zones

A farm that makes its own substrate blocks has four zones. Treat them as separate environments, each with its own controls.

Zone Climate control Notes
Mix / steam Temperature and relative humidity (RH) not regulated, except for worker comfort Can be "dirty". A steam annex is where a floor drain belongs.
Cool-down + lab Recirculating, cooled and HEPA filtered, at positive pressure See Chapter 4.
Incubation CO2 control plus cooling, held constant The stage that really needs steady temperature.
Fruiting Fresh air (CO2), humidity and cooling regulated; may swing a little Fully decoupled from the other zones.

Incubation is the most important room to control in substrate production.

A useful way to draw this is a four-column zone chart: MIX/STEAM "unregulated"; COOL/LAB "cooled + filtered" with a recirculation loop; INCUBATION "CO2 + cooling, constant"; FRUITING "CO2 + humidity + cooling, regulated", drawn with wavy lines to show that it may fluctuate.

Farms that buy blocks: cooler, plenum and fruit rooms

A farm that buys in blocks and only fruits them needs three spaces:

  1. A reefer or cold room at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer. This is a walk-in cooler or a CoolBot room (an air conditioner with a controller that lets it run cold) for incoming blocks and fresh mushrooms. A reefer is a refrigerated room or container.
  2. A plenum: a general work area that also handles air.
  3. The fruit rooms.

The plenum is where harvesting, grading, packing and drying happen. It also captures and conditions fresh air for the fruit rooms. It is not an entrance, a bathroom or an office. It can sit in front of the rooms, above them, or in a separate building ducted to them.

  • Fruit rooms must connect to the plenum. The cooler does not need to, and is best kept out of the plenum and away from the fruit rooms, mainly because of spore load.
  • Each fruit room generally comes as three sections: the heating/cooling unit, the plenum and the fruiting room.
  • The plenum can share space with a walk-in cooler or harvest area. It should not hold CO2-producing blocks or heavy activity. Monitor its CO2 and give it a fresh-air intake (see Chapter 14).

How much space each zone needs

Zones are not equal quarters. Incubation needs far more space than most people expect.

Rule Value Conditions
Incubation vs fruiting About 2x the fruiting floor Minimum. One consulting farm (Catawba Mushrooms) uses at least 2x, and 3-4x for slow species such as shiitake, maitake and chestnut.
Incubation vs fruiting shelf space About 2x the fruiting shelf space Another grower's rule. Err on the side of more, especially for slow species such as maitake and chestnut; a farm growing mostly fast-turning oysters needs less. Size up if you can afford it.
Incubation vs lab Incubation needs more floor than the lab In a small building, about two-thirds of the floor for incubation racks.
Incubation buffer 3 weeks of incubation space For species that incubate about 2 weeks, so a rack always has somewhere to go.
Slow species Incubation runs about 6-14 weeks Shiitake needs roughly 5-10 times more incubation space for the same output. The maitake figure is unclear (unconfirmed).
Chestnut, unripe Occupies a fruit room 4-5 weeks before harvest Versus 2-3 weeks if ripened in incubation first.
Fruit-room rotation Blocks take 2-3 weeks to fruit out Lay out a room as three weekly cohorts, with slack.
Cooler For two rooms of about 14 x 20 ft (4.3 x 6.1 m): block storage alone about two pallets (about 8 x 4 ft, 2.4 x 1.2 m, of floor); with fresh mushrooms about 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m) More if you buy blocks less often than weekly. More cooler space is always better.

Catawba Mushrooms reports that its own incubation is too small for its grow rooms, which shows how easy this mistake is.

TIP Build for growth. Make the grow room 25-50% bigger than you need today, and make incubation big enough to expand into, because demand tends to grow once a farm is known locally.

RULE Chestnut ripening decision. If incubation space is the bottleneck, fruit sooner. If the fruit room is the bottleneck, let blocks sit in incubation. If neither is, let them sit.

Permanent shelving fits more into a room, but only if the cooling is sized for the full possible load.

RANGE How full to fill a room. Standard: blocks and racks fill about 1/10 to 1/4 of the room's volume (Cap n Stem's rule for fruit rooms, applied with the same caution to incubation). In incubation, keep two hand widths between bags on all sides, and never let the load take more than about half of the room's cubic footage. The older one-third rule of thumb (attributed to Stamets) is still widely quoted. Context: a purpose-built 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room laid out at full capacity, with exhaust sized for that load, produces 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week, and dense layouts with tall racks work only where cooling and airflow are sized for the full load. These figures change how much floor you plan; details are in Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.

Reference room. One grower's reference grow room is 16 x 16 ft (about 4.9 x 4.9 m, 256 sq ft) and is fed by a 7 x 14 ft (2.1 x 4.3 m) plenum. The plenum is 98 sq ft, a room-to-plenum floor ratio of roughly 8:3. The room tops out at about 600 lb (270 kg) a week.

Product flow: one way, no backtracking

AT A GLANCE Product moves from dirty to clean to incubation and out, never back. Pull hot substrate straight into clean air. Move blocks in racks. Get contamination out of the building fast. Plan cold storage.

The ideal flow is linear: one way in, one way out, no backtracking. Walking through incubation to reach the lab carries contaminants with you. Put on a Tyvek suit (gown up) at the clean boundary.

  • In a small building, a U-shaped route can work for the clean spaces.
  • Work runs from cleanest to dirtiest (knock first, mix substrate second). Product flows from the cleanest rooms outward.
  • One room, one function. A farm that incubated racks inside its lab kept getting contamination from foot traffic and from removing contaminated bags. Blocks leaving a Bubba barrel (a steam barrel) at about 93 °C (200 °F) can push an incubating space from 19 °C (66 °F) toward 66 °C (150 °F) locally if both share a room.
  • If a building has only one entrance, put the fruit room at the far end and give it its own outside door. A door can be cut into a reefer container's wall. Harvest, grading, packing and truck loading then go out that door. Nobody has to carry dirty, spore-laden air back through clean areas or change shoes for each trip.
  • Group the dirtiest functions (steam, heat from outside, coolers) together, away from the lab. Keep incubation CO2 and fruit-room air flowing out of the building, never back toward the entrance.

Steam to lab

  • Pasteurized blocks, including ultra-pasteurized ones, may pass through a "dirty" or semi-dirty zone straight into the lab. Sterilized material must leave a double-door autoclave directly into clean space. If you can, put a small buffer closet between mix/steam and the lab (details in Chapter 4 and Chapter 12).
  • Distance matters. If blocks must travel about 400 ft (122 m) from steamer to lab, move them hot (93 °C / 200 °F or more after a hold of about 3 h) straight into a positive-pressure HEPA lab, handling them with welding gloves. A typical sketch of this problem shows a building with the lab inside and a separate steam box some way off.
  • CASE: Cap n Stem once carried racks about 10 ft (3 m) past an open window from the steam unit to the lab. The racks nearest the window got Neurospora. Another grower hauled hot blocks by Kubota tractor through snow to his lab, and his problems stopped. Lesson: hot blocks moved fast are safer than cooled blocks moved slowly.
  • For pasteurizing, use a shipping container rather than building or welding a custom steam box. Containers give more control.

Racks, carts and handling

As a farm scales, the aim is to touch each block as few times as possible. Use rolling racks wherever they fit.

  • Move blocks in racks or cages, not by hand-loading single blocks. Wheeled stainless racks of about 7 shelves (Metro-style shelves) roll from the steam chamber to the lab.
  • Rolling racks suit low ceilings of 8-9 ft (2.4-2.7 m) and cut handling. Bags are knocked straight onto the rack they incubate on, and finished batches are pushed straight to fruiting or the cooler. A thousand oyster blocks can be rolled into the cooler at once before a long weekend.
  • For a spawn or block supplier, mobile racks are ideal because the product leaves the building. Each bag stays on the shelf it was knocked onto, then rolls into the reefer for packing.
  • In fruiting, carts are the most important tool. Roll them out to a harvest/grade/pack area so spores stay off you and out of the plenum.
  • Tall stationary racks use high ceilings. Cap n Stem's Gardiner building has 20 ft (6.1 m) ceilings; standard Metro-style racks would hold only about 30% as many blocks. With tall racks a block is placed once and moved only at fruiting or packing. No safe 20 ft rolling racks exist.
  • Shelf size: 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) shelves leave too narrow an aisle for moving racks in and out of a container. Use 18 x 48 in (46 x 122 cm) shelves to keep a usable centre aisle.
  • A low ceiling limits rolling racks to about 4 tiers. Making doors as tall as possible allows a 5th tier, but then racks cannot roll from incubation into fruiting, so blocks get moved by hand.

Keep two sets of racks. A single rack that goes from steamer to fruit room and back sounds efficient but fails in practice.

  • Fruiting racks rust quickly in the humidity and caustic cleaning conditions, and dirty racks then carry rust and contamination into clean areas. Stainless steel is very expensive.

  • Incubation racks circulate through the clean side: cleaned in the vestibule, sprayed with isopropyl, held under filtration, then loaded at the knock and rolled into incubation.

  • Fruiting racks stay in the fruit room. Blocks are moved onto them at a transfer point.

  • Fruiting racks that will not move can be built more simply. If space is tight, put them on wheels just so they can be shifted to open an aisle.

  • Not every incubation rack will reach fruiting, because some blocks will be contaminated. Plan where those racks go so they do not pass back through clean space.

  • Put everything on wheels. A Maine farm rolls a whole room out every Monday and washes it down with a foamer and power washer in about 20 minutes. It builds racks of steel studs, not conduit or untreated timber, cleans up spilled substrate with a 200 L (55 gal) drum-type HEPA vacuum (about US$1,800), and fits plugged (bung) drains and filtered floor drains.

  • Removable shelves. Where full racks won't fit, a Houston farm used 1.2 m (4 ft) lengths of steel conduit with wooden ends that drop into fixed holders on the walls, so each shelf lifts out for cleaning.

  • Load racks outside-first. One Cap n Stem worker fills the outer slots of a rack up and down first, then the inside, which leaves even gaps and keeps handling consistent from steaming through cooling to inoculation. Bags loaded carelessly cause problems all the way down the line.

  • Use stem casters. Thick stem casters (about US$9-10 each) hold up; small threaded casters fail and drop racks.

  • Colour is not contamination. Blocks often discolour harmlessly. The Maine farm switched to black bags so staff stopped worrying about ugly but harmless colour, and stacked lion's mane blocks 6-10 high without harm from the brown liquid they leak.

Waste and contaminated material

RULE Get contaminated bags out of the building promptly. Make it a written procedure (SOP).

  • CASE: One Neurospora bag left over a weekend covered part of Cap n Stem's warehouse in spores by Monday.
  • Bag and bin Neurospora bags. Never cut them open and compost them near the facility.
  • CASE: At Cap n Stem's first shop (Westbrook, Maine), dumped infected bags formed a pile that was sucked into the air inlets. At Cascadia Mushrooms, a compost mound too close to the fruit-room ducts caused intermittent Neurospora on fruiting blocks. Keep compost as far as possible from air intakes.
  • CASE: Two years after a flood, mouldy wood-chip piles stuffed into old equipment in one corner were still a contamination reservoir until they were cleared.

Our farm: the spent and contaminated block route

FARM NOTE Two kinds of block leave the building, and they go by different routes because only one carries a risk to the next crop. Both routes must be written down as an SOP and posted by the door, because the rule in Waste and contaminated material is to get contaminated bags out of the building promptly and never leave them over a weekend.

Contaminated blocks and spawn (Neurospora, Trichoderma, bacteria, anything doubtful)

  1. Find it, do not shake it, and do not cut it open.
  2. Bag it where it stands, in the room where you found it, and seal the bag.
  3. Put the sealed bag in a lidded bin at that room's door. Do not carry an open bag through the lab or another room.
  4. Take the bin out the same day through the boiler room door, which is the farm's waste exit, by a route that never crosses the lab or the clean side. Log the lot code and species first (contamination targets).
  5. Dispose of it at the contaminated-waste site, far from every air intake (the intake rule). Never compost it by the building.
  6. Wash the bin and the spot, and note anything touched.

Spent blocks (finished fruiting, not contaminated)

  1. Take the block out when its last flush is done (getting the crop out).
  2. Count it against its lot code, so each lot's contamination and block counts match.
  3. Move it on racks or carts, not by hand, out of the building through the boiler room door.
  4. Take it to the spent-block site, which is also away from air intakes.

FARM NOTE Joseph's decision (6 Nov 2026): the waste exit for both routes is the boiler room door.

OPEN The site for each pile, and its distance from the fruiting and incubation intakes (750 CFM each) are not in any plan. Mark them on the site layout. Humidity stays near 88% all year in Playa Negra, so a wet pile rots and attracts pests fast: decide who empties the bins each day, and whether the contaminated site is a covered pit, a drum or something else. Check any local rules on burning or burying organic waste with the local authority before choosing.

Cold chain and shipping

Cooling is one of the most important things on a farm. You need coolers for outgoing pallets, for spawn before use and for blocks waiting to be packed. Home-built or hacked coolers are fine.

  • Cap n Stem pre-cools spawn in many 40 ft refrigerated containers, because home-built cold rooms are less even. Packed pallets wait in refrigerated containers for truck pickup.
  • A used 20 or 40 ft reefer container costs about $9,000. It has a 480 V refrigeration unit. With a step-down transformer to 240 V on about a 40 A breaker, it gives a lot of cooling and could be split into a cooled plenum and a walk-in. New walk-ins cost about $15,000-40,000, and up to $200,000.
  • Cap n Stem runs a line of working reefer containers (480 V units; the rear refrigeration unit is swapped out when it is damaged in transit) to hold colonized blocks and substrate. Being able to park production in cold storage is what lets a farm take days off.
  • If you buy blocks by LTL (less-than-truckload) freight, refrigerated or dry, the site road must take an 18-wheeler, or deliveries will not come. Shipping a pallet of about 150-200 blocks costs about $500-1,000 (up to about $1,600 has been quoted).
  • Owning a reefer or walk-in also makes it easier to schedule drying of surplus mushrooms.

Air flow between zones

AT A GLANCE Run two climate systems: one for production (lab, mix, incubation) and one for fruiting plus harvest/pack/grade. Recirculate within each, never between them. Cool incubation air may feed the lab; lab heat goes to mix/steam or outside, never into incubation.

Air should move the way product moves: from clean to dirty, and out. The table lists which paths are allowed.

Air path Allowed? Why
Incubation → lab Yes, if cooling is strong enough and the lab's heat is exhausted The lab tolerates high CO2, so this gives free cooling.
Lab → incubation No The hot substrate load in the lab would destabilize incubation.
Lab → mix/steam or outside Yes This is where lab heat should go.
Incubation ↔ fruiting No, either way Incubation air is too rich in CO2 for fruiting; fruiting air carries spores and humidity into incubation.
Fruiting Draw from the plenum or outside, exhaust outside, one way Keep fruit rooms at negative pressure relative to the plenum.

RULE A fruit room may share a wall with incubation, but its exhaust must go straight outside the building, never into incubation, because the air is full of spores.

A whiteboard version of the same idea shows a "SUB PROD" grid with four quadrants (INC. "high CO2, temp control"; LAB/COOL DOWN; FRUIT; MIX+STEAM "regulated for comfort"), arrows and X marks for allowed and forbidden paths, and a 3D sketch of a plenum floor above four rooms.

  • Run two separate climate systems: (1) production cooling for lab, mix and incubation; (2) fruiting plus harvest/pack/grade. Recirculate within each, never between them.
  • One long building can run like this: an unconditioned mix area, then a narrow lab, then incubation. HEPA units in the lab/incubation wall pull cool incubation air into the lab. Fruiting is kept separate from this CO2-rich cooled zone.
  • At Cap n Stem, the block incubation refrigeration also conditions the adjoining lab rooms. These rooms pull air from incubation and return it there while staying at positive pressure. This works for labs and incubation but not for fruit rooms.
  • A single air conditioner (AC) feeding a multi-zone plenum can serve several rooms if each room has its own damper and there is no recirculation back. Fruiting cannot be on it. Each room needs its own control to get even air exchange.
  • Fruit rooms are filthy environments. Isolate the rest of the building from them more than the other way round.
  • CASE: At Cap n Stem's old Westbrook site the fruit rooms were at positive pressure. Walls bulged and boomed, and fruit-room smells and spores leaked into incubation. Incubation there was partitioned with polypropylene curtain walls that swayed and buckled as the pressure changed.
  • Putting production and fruiting under one roof (for example, a lab at the back of a building with fruit rooms between the lab and incubation) is common and not advisable. It can work: one farm with this layout managed reasonably well.

Plenums in existing buildings

A plenum is a space where air is collected and conditioned before it goes into the rooms. Almost any spare volume can become one.

  • An attic can be a cooled plenum. It feeds filtered, positive-pressure air down into the lab and incubation, with air leaving toward the dirty steam side and out a window. Insulate the walls and the plenum heavily.

  • A plenum can be a side room, a barn interior, a basement, an attic or the end of a shipping container. Examples: a whole barn used as the plenum, with a fruit room inside it pulling air through a damper and exhausting outdoors; an AC in an attic ducted down a disused chimney to a basement fruit room.

  • If the plenum is in a separate building, duct the conditioned air across (over or under ground) and use an active intake fan. A passive damper cannot pull air through a long duct.

  • Bigger plenums are better. A small plenum needs more outside makeup air and therefore a bigger AC, so a larger plenum saves money, whatever some farms say.

  • Makeup air can come from a cooler, lower-CO2 part of the building rather than hot outside air.

  • One Texas grower bought a commercial duct manifold with a HEPA filter and a baffle (recirculate or pass straight through) and used his clean room as the plenum for the fruit room, ducting it straight across. It worked well.

People flow and working conditions

  • People enter clean areas through sluices (small changing rooms with two doors) and gown at the boundary. Do not route staff through incubation to reach the lab (sluice design is in Chapter 4).
  • Leave room in the plan for gowning and changing.
  • Staff split into semi-lab roles and dirty warehouse-floor roles. Some never enter the lab or fruit a block.
  • The lab is relentless: fans and lights are always on and there is no quiet place to recover. After the lab, staff may go into a loud walk-in cooler. Plan somewhere quieter to take breaks.
  • Spore exposure: harvest outside the fruit room or wear a respirator, and roll carts out to the pack area (see Chapter 18).
  • Manual handling shapes the layout. At one farm, sawdust barrels of 50-80 lb (23-36 kg) were hand-lifted onto stepped platforms (a back injury followed) or winched from rafters 22 ft (6.7 m) up (a near miss when a cracked barrel collapsed). A forklift was used once space was cleared. Plan forklift access and clear floor space around mixers and hoppers.
  • With high ceilings a super sack (a bulk bag of about one tonne) can be lifted straight over a hopper. Container farms can hang a super sack over a small self-refilling hopper.
  • Do not live on the farm. Cap n Stem calls it the "grave mistake" everyone makes, and keeps an hour's drive between home and work on purpose.

WARNING CO2 builds up where blocks incubate. The US OSHA workplace limit is 5,000 ppm. Cap n Stem's old Westbrook farm once ran about 7,000 ppm in incubation. A staffer who slept overnight in the incubation room (the warmest spot, with no CO2 meter) had sleep paralysis that a colleague blamed on CO2, and staff also napped on the incubation scaffolding. Never sleep in incubation, and monitor CO2 wherever people work.

Choosing and preparing a building

AT A GLANCE Look for a reflective, well-insulated roof, walls you can buffer, room for outside condensers, drains only where they belong (fruit rooms and steam, never the lab), good water and a road an 18-wheeler can use.

Roof, walls and climate

  • Roof. A black roof can reach about 66 °C (150 °F) on a 32 °C (90 °F) day, versus about 38 °C (100 °F) for a white or reflective roof. Insulate the ceiling at least as well as the walls. Hanging coolers cannot keep up under a hot roof. A lab built in Arizona with reflective panels stayed cool on 43 °C (110 °F) days. A typical sketch shows a building with a white roof over a black one, an arrow marked "insulation" and two cooler units inside.

  • Local climate. The coastal Bay Area (Far West Fungi) is very stable. Inland or extreme climates (Arizona, Texas, Florida, Nevada, and Maine's hot/cold swings) need a plan. Do not assume the builder considered heat. Buffer incubation from outside walls and duct the cooling in.

  • Walls. Cap n Stem's spawn incubation room backs onto an old brick wall facing a neighbour's always-open loading dock, so outside extremes leak in; they keep adding rigid foam. Concrete, steel and brick act as heat sinks or heat sources. Untreated concrete adds heat in summer and pulls it out in winter.

  • Ceiling height. With 15 ft (4.6 m) ceilings, temperature stratification (layering) in incubation is large, for example 16 °C (60 °F) at the bottom and 27 °C (80 °F) at the top, unless plenty of air is recirculated.

  • Block heat. Past a certain scale, incubation needs only cooling. A room of about 20,000 blocks held 19 °C (66 °F) from block heat alone through a two-day power outage at -18 °C (0 °F) outside, in New England.

  • Location can do the cooling. Far West Fungi sits on the California coast at Moss Landing, a sheltered bay where the temperature stays in the mid-teens °C (mid-60s °F) with steady fog, so the Pacific Ocean does most of the climate work. Farms have operated there since the 1960s and 1970s. Far West runs shipping containers with the doors wide open and the misting on, and only added air conditioners in recent years. Even there, temperatures can get out of control depending on how blocks are incubated (spawn on top or mixed through).

  • Hot warehouses. A Memphis warehouse reaches 43 °C (110 °F) in July, with every cooler and AC running. A Massachusetts grower's first summer in a warehouse, growing in tents, brought heat, humidity and mould in unexpected places, and constant cleaning; insulated walls became the first fundraising goal. His walk-in cooler had taken the wall budget because it cost about US$2,000 more at pandemic prices.

  • Dry heat is easier than humid heat. About 37 °C (99 °F) with near-100% humidity "feels like you're just inhaling water droplets". Coastal Florida gets cross-winds from both coasts, while New Orleans air stalls and air conditioners struggle.

CASE A California foothills farm cools its fruiting sheds with no AC at all. Under the roof joists the grower staples a perforated, two-layer foil radiant barrier, leaving a small air gap below the plywood, then a vapour barrier. While installing it, his thermometer read 46 °C (115 °F) on the plywood ceiling and 23 °C (74 °F) on the foil. With it, the fruit room stays about 24-27 °C (75-80 °F) on 43 °C (110 °F) days. A big roll cost under US$100.

Construction materials

  • Use materials that will not rot: steel studs and Coroplast (corrugated plastic sheet), sealed with 3M flashing tape, or SIPs (structural insulated panels). Cap n Stem imported SIPs from China at about $2 per linear foot.

  • Wood studs wick water from humid floors, grow mould and eventually force a tear-out. FRP (fibreglass-reinforced plastic) and heavy plastic panels are heavy and hard to install. Refuse contractors' wood backing. Details are in Chapter 14 and Chapter 4.

  • Many farms are built from duct-taped Coroplast rooms (Smallhold is one example).

  • Coroplast is flammable and not structural.

  • A small low-tech drying room can be a closet lined with Coroplast and cleaned thoroughly, with one outlet and a barrel outside to collect drain water.

  • Insulated sandwich panels. Click-together insulated panels with metal on both faces are easy to clean, watertight and quick to assemble, and can also build a walk-in cooler. They are standard in Europe and reached US farms through cannabis growing. In mild climates, hoop houses can avoid building permits for agriculture (in Washington State, for example), but insulating them is the problem.

Drainage and water

Space Drain?
Fruit rooms Yes. This is the first priority in a new build. Fit a P-trap so sewer air cannot back up. Optionally slope the slab to a channel of about 6 in (15 cm) or to a sump pit of about 16 in (41 cm) with a pump.
Plenum Not needed.
Lab / clean rooms No drains, sinks or faucets. Seal off any existing drain (see Chapter 4).
Steam area Use an existing floor drain only in a steam annex.

CASE The flood. In late winter, around 2017-2018, snowmelt from the hillside behind a farm came through the walls, and later through the back of the building, toward about 40 tons (36 t) of raw red oak sawdust stored on a concrete floor. Staff fought it with pumps, barrels, wet-vacs, shovels and forklifts. Berms of sifted wood chips failed because wood floats. A forklift hydroplaned and most staff were sent home. Lesson: check how water moves around a site before you store bulk material on the floor.

CASE Cap n Stem's Westbrook site combined spawn, block production and fruiting in a tiny space with no heat control, in a second-floor unit that kept flooding the floor below. They moved out.

  • Never rely on buckets and pumps for drainage upstairs. Cap n Stem's old second-floor facility drained into buckets with pumps; when the pumps broke, it flooded the business below.

Utilities

  • Electricity. Power needs are small apart from heating and cooling, which are the biggest costs. Fruit rooms need little electricity (lights, pumps, maybe a compressor for high-pressure misting). Standard 110-120 V service is usually fine, but consult an electrician.
  • Electric autoclaves (about 10 ft, 3 m, long) need 240 V at about 60 A (see Chapter 12).
  • The condensers and compressors of all cooling units must be outside the building, because they dump heat.
  • Have a generator that can run the air conditioning through outages. Split the electrical supply into many sub-panels, one per task, at the main breaker box.
  • Cooling redundancy. Oversize cooling: for example, pay about $2,000 more for 10 tons (35 kW) instead of 7.5 tons (26 kW). Use two units rather than one (see Chapter 5).
  • Water quality decides equipment life. Soft water at Westbrook let sauna-type steam generators run a long time; hard water at Gardiner scaled them up and killed units within about a week. Do not feed distilled or reverse-osmosis (RO) water to boilers, because it is corrosive; soften and treat the water instead (see Chapter 17).

  • Low water pressure fix: an IBC tote (a 1,000 L plastic tank in a cage) as a reservoir, with a quiet on-demand pump keeping the line pressurized. Cap n Stem's supply was about 6.66 gal/min (25 L/min).

  • An outdoor containerized boiler can freeze over winter weekends; protect it. Steam can be piped some distance: about 60 ft (18 m) to Cap n Stem's steam container.

  • Automate. The old Westbrook steam generator was not automated, so someone had to be on site about every two hours overnight to work the valves.

  • Check the electrical service before you sign. A Texas farm's 370 m² (4,000 sq ft) warehouse had 240 V, 200 A single-phase power, which looked like plenty; the farm needed about three times that.

  • Expect power prices to rise. A Tennessee farm saw its electricity price nearly double, from about US$0.06 to US$0.11 per kWh.

Storing raw materials

Material Space and storage notes
Raw sawdust A 33-ton walking-floor truckload occupies roughly 25 x 75 ft (7.6 x 22.9 m; 50 x 75 ft, 15.2 x 22.9 m, has also been given) at about 70% moisture. It needs a tractor, labour and space; "free" sawdust is not free. Before switching to pellets, Cap n Stem stored 30-60 tons, with no room to age it.
Same building, pellets About 30 tons of raw sawdust stacked floor to ceiling, versus about 60 tons of pellets in about 60 totes or super sacks (about 45 in, 1.1 m, high). Pellets at about 7% moisture store far more per square foot.
Combo pellets Must be stored indoors and dry. Months in a humid building is fine. Rats ignore them (Cap n Stem's observation, unconfirmed).
Raw soy pellets / grain Rats will bore through warehouse walls to get them. Pest control is an ongoing war.
Sorghum Insects attack it fast, even in dry, climate-controlled super-sack storage on racking. Churn it quickly; it really wants silos.
Any dry supplement or dust Microbial load is driven by moisture exposure. Keep it dry.
  • Storing raw sawdust indoors is ideal only within the material's shelf life, and a big open pile is exposed to any water that gets in.
  • One farm that switched from raw sawdust to combo pellets after the flood says it would never go back to raw sawdust.
  • Keep dusty work (mixing, bagging and dry-material storage) out of the air plenum. Either move it outside, or give materials a separate container that is kept dry, dehumidified and ventilated.
  • The cooking space will be hot and full of steam. Give it a heavy louvred exhaust fan, plus an inline fan (one grower uses a Hurricane) above the barrel, ducted to the exhaust.

Support spaces

  • An in-house wood and fabrication shop makes pallet assemblies, spacers and jigs from locally milled lumber.
  • A raised platform can hold two 2-yard (1.5 m³) mixers. Pallets of sawdust barrels are forklifted up, water and ingredients are added from above, and pneumatic baggers sit below (about 700 bags per morning; see Chapter 6).
  • In a small container farm, a covered outdoor area under an overhang is a good place for mixing, grading and packing. It keeps dust and packing traffic out of the containers.

Leases, landlords, permits and upstairs space

Most small farms start in rented space. Growers' experience with leases, landlords, permits and shared buildings:

  • Rent. A Florida farm leased three of four 9 x 12 m (30 x 40 ft) units in a clear-span warehouse for about US$1,600 a month; a 1,400 m² (15,000 sq ft) former bank nearby was about US$8,000 a month.
  • Know the landlord and the neighbours. Find out what else is in the building before renting. A mushroom farm next to a brewery gets a huge amount of CO2 and may end up sharing cooling through ducts. Landlords may object to holes in walls, installed air conditioners and electrical work.
  • Mushroom farming is not a two-storey business. Upstairs space in a warehouse is no use for incubation, because moving blocks up and down makes no sense. If well insulated, it might serve as a space for conditioning incoming air.
  • Permits and inspectors. In Austin, Texas, a farm worried that one inspector could apply boiler law to its low-pressure steam vessel even though the setup was to code, and its expansion needed building permits, an architect and an engineer. City ordinances may simply not recognize mushroom farming; a Tallahassee farm found its city opposed to farming or production uses.

CASE A Maine farm signed a 20-year lease on a bigger warehouse and "underestimated the build-out by like 500%". It dug up the slab for new trench drains and pumps and installed new electrical and water services, and owed its contractor about half a million dollars before bank financing came through, with the landlord's building dug up. It now has labs, a walk-in cooler, loading docks, several boilers and HVAC systems. The jump from about 45 m² (500 sq ft) to 280 m² (3,000 sq ft) is hard; each later jump, to 930 or 1,900 m² (10,000 or 20,000 sq ft), is harder.

Scaling up

AT A GLANCE Grow in big steps that add output without adding labour. Do not multiply small equipment. Stop tinkering once a system works.

How one farm's block production grew

Cap n Stem's block-making line went through five stages. Each step sped up production without adding much labour.

Stage Setup Output
1 (Westbrook) Tipping trough made of two 4 x 8 ft plywood sheets lined with polypropylene; sawdust carried upstairs in barrels and hydrated by hand About 30 bags of 10 lb (4.5 kg) per batch
2 Half-yard ribbon mixer, conveyor, hand-weighed bags, 2 people About 70 bags of 5 lb (2.3 kg), or about 35 of 10 lb, per mix
3 (Gardiner) 2-yard ribbon mixer plus home-built pneumatic bagger, 3 people 350 bags per morning
4 Two 2-yard mixers on a raised platform About 700 bags per morning, judged the practical maximum for mixers
5 "Fenrir" pellet-and-water filler, 8 heads, 4 people About 1,680 bags per morning

  • Each step should speed up production without adding labour. Extra staff erode profitability.

  • You cannot scale by multiplying small equipment: 2,000 blocks a week would need about 20 Bubba barrels. It is better to wait and make one larger leap to equipment that supplies two fruit rooms in one or two days than to step up one barrel at a time.

  • Labour does not scale linearly. If the farm is to grow, the owner should not remain the irreplaceable fastest worker (see Chapter 22).

  • A typical path for a solo grower: a tent at home, then a garage or home farm, then a dedicated building. Cactus Hat Mushrooms followed this path to a building on a 5-acre property in Brooksville, Florida.

  • Once the right systems are in place, production is easy: about 1.5 h to make 100 blocks at Cactus Hat. Stop tinkering with a working lab.

  • Hand spawning stays fastest at small and medium scale. Far West Fungi spawns by hand with 3 people in a corner.

  • Cap n Stem moved from a 1,900 m² (20,000 sq ft) building with 30 staff in Gardiner, Maine, to about 7,000 m² (75,000 sq ft) on 12 hectares (30 acres) in Lewiston, bought for about US$1 million. Around Seattle, a cost-effective 1,900-3,700 m² (20,000-40,000 sq ft) building cost about US$2 million at the time. Diesel and shipping costs keep rising.

Capacity numbers for planning

Use these to size rooms and equipment. Equipment costs and cost per block are in Chapter 12 and Chapter 22.

Unit Capacity
Bubba barrel (steam barrel) About 80-100 blocks of 10 lb (4.5 kg) per run; a run takes about 15-16 h. One run a week gives about 200 lb (91 kg) of mushrooms a week.
12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room 5 racks per row x 50 blocks = 250 blocks per row; about 250 blocks a week; about 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week at best.
Small building with 2-3 fruit rooms (harvest and pack moved out of it) About 1,000 lb (454 kg) a week.
Typical small-farm block purchase One pallet of about 140 blocks a week (one mix a week if self-made).
Pallet of 10 lb blocks 160-180 blocks (versus 320 blocks of 5 lb).
Steam container on a Sioux SF-11 boiler (also written SR-11) 10 ft container (20 ft at most), about 500 blocks, 8-10 h a run.
Steam container on a Sioux SF-25 boiler (also written SR-25) 20-40 ft container, 1,000+ blocks (up to about 6,000 per batch).
Incubation rack (pallet racking) 5 deep x 10 long = 50 blocks per shelf, about 500 blocks per rack, giving off about 1,000 BTU/h (about 0.3 kW) of heat per rack.
40 ft container fruit room Up to 13 racks of 2 x 4 ft, 650 blocks.

TIP A hybrid for a small farm: make about 100 blocks and buy about 150 more (one pallet) to reach about 500 lb (227 kg) a week, rather than doubling barrel runs.

AT A GLANCE Farm sizes, from growers across the US: a home operation makes about 45-90 kg (100-200 lb) a week; most small farms produce under 225 kg (500 lb) a week; at about 225 kg (500 lb) a week you have a real facility, and a solid team is built in the 225-450 kg (500-1,000 lb) range. Going much past that is a leap. Industrial farms produce hundreds of tonnes, and no single small farm can bridge that gap.

Farm size (per week) What it takes
34 kg (75 lb) One room holding lab, fruiting chamber and incubation, "on a good day" (Vermont)
36-45 kg (80-100 lb) A 1.8 x 3.7 m (6 x 12 ft) fruit room and a 2.4 x 2.4 m (8 x 8 ft) clean room doubling as incubation, sold at farmers markets and a few restaurants (Houston)
68 kg (150 lb) A basement farm at its peak (North Carolina)
68-90 kg (150-200 lb) A new Massachusetts farm's deliberate cap for its first two years, in 46 m² (500 sq ft)
225-270 kg (500-600 lb) Two people (High Country Fungi)
225 kg (500 lb) One fruit room at full capacity (Kansas City); grow by adding identical rooms
225 kg (500 lb) or less About two staff can make it work, depending on local markets and restaurants (Far West Fungi)
320+ kg (700+ lb) About 100 m² (1,100 sq ft) plus warehouse space, three full-time staff, a build-out of over US$150,000 (California)
450 kg (1,000 lb) Needs a large city market (such as Los Angeles), or the farm fails unless it owns its property or is a side income
2,270 kg (5,000 lb) The minimum to sell wholesale
  • Grow in steps, and stop at your size. Farms fail by growing too fast: going from 225 kg (500 lb) a week to 900-1,400 kg (2,000-3,000 lb) "is a whole different animal". Identify your cut-off size and stay lean below it; at some scales "the more you sell, the less you make" when chasing wholesale accounts. Learning at each step (5, 10, 30, 50, 100 lb a week and so on up to about 900 kg, 2,000 lb) leaves no gaps in understanding; a big budget at the start would have built the wrong farm. Nearby small farms do better cooperating (sharing block supply) than fighting.
  • Small and many can work. Maine has about 11 growers few have heard of, each selling a few hundred pounds a week, many with their own pneumatic baggers. Mid-size farms are the hardest to reach: Cap n Stem sees most farms either between about 90 and 2,300 kg (200-5,000 lb) a week or above a million pounds.
  • Plan for the people. Anything over about 45 kg (100 lb) a week needs a person or team for each part of the business. Investors always asked what happens "if you get hit by a bus". Plan how long a task takes the person you employ, not you.
  • Species changes everything. 225 kg (500 lb) of oysters is a different job from 225 kg of shiitake: shiitake takes five to ten times longer to harvest. Every increase in volume turns out different from what you expected, depending on the mix of species.
  • Automated lines need volume. Far West Fungi (about 18,000 blocks a week) advises that an automated bagging line needs a 7.6 m³ (10 cubic yard) mixer running all the time; without that demand it doesn't pay. At its height Kennett Square Specialties made about 80,000 five-pound blocks a week, including about 50,000 shiitake blocks before Chinese imports took that market.

CASE A Massachusetts grower who ran a shiitake farm quadrupled its output: easily 270 kg (600 lb) a week, some weeks 360 kg (800 lb) and bumper weeks up to 545 kg (1,200 lb), from about 480 blocks. Holiday staff shortages left him harvesting alone; cutting with shears gave him tendonitis that needed a cortisone injection and two months of physiotherapy. He would not grow shiitake again: it is messy and a lot of work.

NOTE White button mushrooms (Agaricus) are a different industry. A Washington farm produces about 113 tonnes (250,000 lb) a week at about US$1.25 per pound wholesale. In Pennsylvania a "double" grows 23-27 tonnes (50,000-60,000 lb) a week and is still small; each growing house takes about 150-175 m³ (200-230 cubic yards) of compost. Wholesale prices sat at US$0.90-1.00 per pound for about 40 years (about US$1.30 now), and growers who once picked 10-15 kg per m² (2-3 lb per sq ft) now need about 34 kg per m² (7 lb per sq ft) to break even; many skip the third flush in summer because disease and insects are too heavy. Small-scale Agaricus loses money ("it'll cost you $200 to grow $100 worth"), so don't try to compete. Kennett Square growers use strings of 20-30 small 18 x 18 m (60 x 60 ft) double-decker houses, each with one AC unit, and many now grow speciality species; some companies sell spawned and cased compost to farms nationwide, the way block suppliers sell fruiting blocks.

Small spaces and scheduling

  • Scheduling a small space is like Tetris. Know each variety's time to harvest so racks free up in time. In summer one farm must fit about 300 incoming blocks while about 300 spent blocks go to compost. A fixed footprint makes scaling hard, so plan for slow and busy seasons.

  • Keep backups: racks, fans, humidification. Small farms must weigh spare equipment against rent.

  • Reliable climate control means you have mushrooms when competitors' crops fail, and you can take their orders.

  • When spawn (sterilized) and substrate (pasteurized) work share one lab, plan on about two runs of each a week, never at the same time (see Chapter 4).

  • Use the climate for outdoor jobs. In Florida, two farms mix substrate in the yard under a carport, which is bearable even in winter.

  • A house can hold a farm, for a while. A Tampa grower produced at significant scale from a four-bedroom house: substrate under the carport awning, the lab next to the bathroom, fruiting in the sun room with portable air conditioners. He made his own blocks because none were available locally, and planned to move to land.

  • Incubation is usually the bottleneck. A California farm in about 100 m² (1,100 sq ft) plus 55-75 m² (600-800 sq ft) of warehouse runs incubation and fruiting space at about 1:2, the reverse of the usual 1:1 or 2:1 in favour of incubation, and knows incubation limits it. It loads eight racks a week into incubation and pulls eight out, on a 30-day turn.

  • Space for growth. A North Carolina farm uses about 560 m² (6,000 sq ft) of an L-shaped former furniture warehouse it is buying, with a path to about 1,950 m² (21,000 sq ft) plus 0.8 hectares (2 acres) for containers, hoop houses and shiitake logs. It borrowed about US$100,000 and finished a 5-year plan in 2.5 years; its founder worked more than 380 days straight in the first year. An Australian farm was told by growers worldwide to add 30% or more to every space, or leave room for extra buildings.

Worked examples

Converting a 100 sq ft milk barn

A client wanted to cook (in a Bubba barrel), cool, knock and incubate inside an old milk barn of about 100 sq ft (9.3 m²), roughly 10 x 10 ft (3 x 3 m). The room had a door, a central ceiling hatch to the attic, a concrete tub, and windows on two sides.

Problems found:

  • Blocks at 93 °C (200 °F) would heat the incubating space.
  • Incubating blocks and cooling blocks would sit a few feet apart.
  • A floor drain sat in what would be the lab.
  • The filter could only be changed through the clean space, via the attic hatch.
  • A window AC would ice up under the steam load.

Fixes suggested:

  1. Remove the concrete tub (about a quarter of the floor).
  2. Put the barrel in a small steam annex by the drain and window.
  3. Make knock/cool and incubation separate rooms.
  4. Give about two-thirds of the building to incubation racks.
  5. Consider a U-shaped flow.
  6. Fit a 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) HEPA unit in the ceiling to pressurize and cool the small lab.
  7. Use the attic as a cooled plenum.
  8. Size cooling at about 3 tons (10.5 kW), using a couple of mini-splits or a small walk-in evaporator rather than window units.
  9. At 80 blocks per run and 80 blocks per rack, provide at least 3 well-spaced racks.

Shipping-container farms

Containers are popular for indoor farming because they are cheap (a few thousand dollars) and modular.

  • A two-container mushroom farm could be split into a lab quarter, incubation, and a sterilizer at the back. Capacity is the limit unless spawn or blocks are bought in. That was one reason the Cactus Hat owner turned down a buy-out offer from a container vertical-farm company.
  • Container fruit room. Wall off 4-6 ft (1.2-1.8 m) at one end of a 20 or 40 ft container as the plenum; the rest is the fruit room. There is no room for a walk-in cooler, which must sit outside.
  • In the reference container design only the plenum really needs insulation.
  • A design seen in Florida had the heat exchanger at the back and the plenum at the front. It created two very different climates at each end and is not recommended. Container heat-exchanger layouts are in Chapter 5.
  • Containers are also used as steam vessels. Do not cool blocks in them: they have wooden floors and leaky doors (see Chapter 4).

The reference 40 ft container fruit room is laid out like this:

  • Overall 40 x 8 ft (12.2 x 2.4 m).
  • A conditioned plenum 4 ft 8 in (1.42 m) deep at the door end, holding a heat pump, a CO2-controlled fresh-air damper fan and a 1,000 CFM variable-speed intake fan beside a fully gasketed door.
  • 13 numbered racks of 2 x 4 ft in two rows, with an aisle of 2 ft 4 in (0.71 m).
  • Two 700 CFM CO2-controlled exhaust fans, one on each side of an end door.
  • Capacity note: "Up to 13 2x4 racks for 650 total block capacity".

CASE A container farm benchmark. A review of a farm of three 40 ft containers plus one 20 ft container found 640 sq ft (about 59 m²) for incubation and fruiting and 480 sq ft (about 45 m²) for production, lab, cooling and plenum. That is small for a whole farm. Realistic output was about 400-600 lb (180-270 kg) a week of lion's mane, oysters and black oyster. Container farms are expandable and repeatable, but this layout probably needs a fourth 40 ft container for incubation to keep the fruiting container full.

TIP Two buildings can be simpler than one. When building from scratch, consider two separate buildings or containers a short walk apart (for example 0.6 m, 2 ft, joined by a concrete walkway): one for substrate, cool-down, lab and incubation, the other for fruiting. Each gets its own climate system tuned to its own conditions, instead of one shared system that has to balance them all, and it is easier to add a building later.

WARNING Ready-made fruiting containers can be wildly overpriced. One grower was quoted US$235,000 for a container farm. Container vertical farms sell each container as the equivalent of 20-40 hectares (50-100 acres) of field, which makes them a cheap-looking way into indoor farming. One Florida container farm wanted to put an entire mushroom operation (a quarter of one container as the lab, a section for incubation, the sterilizer at the back) into one or two containers; the mushroom grower it approached doubted how much that could produce and declined.

  • Containers are not new for mushrooms. Growers have used them for decades, including containers dug into hillsides.
  • Neighbours and permits. A Denver farm's first expansion was shipping containers in its back yard. The city said containers were a grey area that couldn't be permitted ("you'll find out if you have a bad neighbour"); two weeks later a complaint brought a cease-and-desist order. An appeal to the city's board of adjustment let the farm keep the containers for 2.5 years while it bought land and built a barn. A Detroit farm on agricultural land had regular visits from the police and township until it painted every container the same flat grey; after that, "nothing from anyone". Keep the site tidy, hide rubbish, paint containers one colour, and check local rules before putting up a sign.
  • Disconnected boxes cost time. A Jacksonville farm's layout of separate containers, trailers and a walk-in cooler means walking outside in heat and rain and moving blocks many times; the grower estimates it costs about 1.5 hours a week. Other farms line containers up with a covered walkway between them, which works better. A Tallahassee farm that ran its lab and substrate in a trailer on a friend's lot, 15 minutes from its fruiting rooms, wasted a lot of time carrying and driving bags across town.
  • Running cost. A California farm's first fruit room was a container lifted over the house into the back yard by a 95-ton crane, two inches from the gutter. It came with its own AC, plus an added 3-ton condenser. In summer the AC cost about US$600 a month while the whole farm earned about US$2,000 a month: "I'm spending like $1,900 a month to make two grand."
  • A first container farm. Smallhold's first farm was a 6 m (20 ft) container on a borrowed lot with about 10 cm (4 in) of insulation, tiled inside like a shower ("completely unnecessary", but it looked great). It had to grow through summer and winter, so it needed heating and cooling, on poor wiring that kept tripping (which is where the company's sensors and controls began). Humidity came from a hose feeding a trash-can fogger with a float valve and a fan; keep the fog off the float. Cooling was an air conditioner, later with a CoolBot controller.
  • Fit-out for a buy-in farm. A Colorado grower kitted out a "plug and play" container for a ranch with top-quality sensors and radiant floors; the owners only wanted to buy ready blocks and fruit them.

CASE A buried container. A grower in eastern Washington buried a 2.4 x 12 m (8 x 40 ft) shipping container in a hillside, in soil at about 10 °C (50 °F). Earth weighs about 2,100 kg per m³ (3,500 lb per cubic yard), so 90 cm (3 ft) of soil puts about 1,600 kg (3,500 lb) on every 90 x 90 cm (3 x 3 ft) of roof, and container walls are thin sheet. He ran two beams of 5 cm (2 in) square steel tube with 6 mm (1/4 in) walls along the roof with a header and supports, and when the sides began bowing in during backfilling he wedged 2x6 boards across inside until the fill settled. Two well-casing pipes, 25-30 cm (10-12 in) across, ran from the back up through the soil and stood above the surface, drawing air through like a chimney from windows at the front, with no fans. With ground contact "it was total geothermal": at -32 to -40 °C (-25 to -40 °F) outside, the room stayed about 10 °C (50 °F) with no heat, and 3,000-4,000 colonizing bags kept the insulated half warm. Later, used for a lamp-lit plant grow, the earth absorbed the heat and held the room near 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) on 38-43 °C (100-110 °F) days, then released it at night to stay near 21 °C (70 °F).

Home, closet and tent scale

  • Closet labs without positive pressure only recirculate room air. If that is what you have, make everything that enters (you, clothes, materials) as clean as possible, and add an anteroom if you can (see Chapter 4).
  • The minimalist room rules apply even at 20 bags a week at home: a cool-down room with only HEPA, a knock room with only the workstation and sealer, and incubation with only racks.
  • At very small scale a window AC or portable ducted AC is fine for incubation, but keep only a couple of racks and do not cram the room. Window ACs, even with CoolBot-style controllers, ice up under a load of hot blocks.
  • Grow tents are harder than they look at scale: constant cleaning, flexing and tipping. Hobby growers should move to a proper room. If you grow maitake in tents, it needs its own tent.

Example facilities

AT A GLANCE Real layouts to learn from: a block and spawn producer (Cap n Stem, Gardiner), its cramped first site (Westbrook), a buy-in fruiting farm (Wild Fruitings), generic fruiting layouts for start-ups, and short notes on other farms.

Cap n Stem, Gardiner, Maine: a block and spawn producer

This walk-through follows product in order.

  1. Pellet storage and bagging. Super sacks of combo pellets are augered into a wooden hopper. Load-cell stations drop pellets to a set weight, then spray water to the moisture target. Four stations side by side let one operator keep pace with a Japanese-style bagger (Cap n Stem's claim). The stations are a row of funnel hoppers on a wooden frame, each with its own controller box and a bag hanging beneath.
  2. Steamer. A fabricated shipping container with a metal floor, steam entering at the top and exhaust low at the far back, filled with racks. It is held at about 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for 2-3 h. The unloading side outside the lab is a dirty area.
  3. Substrate lab. Bags are pulled hot (around 9 pm), cool overnight in front of flow hoods and are knocked the next day. A 7.5-ton (26 kW) AC takes its return from the lab and feeds a plenum; 8 flow hoods in two areas draw from that plenum. The return is restricted to keep the lab at positive pressure (see Chapter 4).
  4. Fabrication shop and coolers. An in-house wood shop, and many coolers.
  5. Block incubation. Large refrigeration holds block surfaces near 19 °C (66 °F) and also conditions adjoining lab rooms (spawn cool-down, other incubation). Pioppino blocks ship at about week 3.
  6. Packing and shipping. Perforated block cartons; pallets stacked with an air channel down the middle; packed pallets wait in refrigerated containers; local pickups go in Gaylord bins (large pallet-sized boxes). A typical outgoing pallet is strapped, built of vented cartons and labelled with the customer's name.
  7. Grain spawn line. Jacketed kettles are filled from an on-demand heater at about 85 °C (185 °F). Drained grain is lifted in barrels to a mixer, then goes to a pneumatic bagger, then onto racks into a vacuum autoclave with space between shelves for even steam (see Chapter 9).

More details of the Gardiner farm:

  • Substrate incubation is held at 19 °C (66 °F) by four evaporators with condensers on the roof. The air is unfiltered, which is fine for substrate. A separate spawn room needed its own AC to reach about 16-18 °C (the low-to-mid 60s °F).
  • The spawn lab rooms run in this order: the hood room (genetics work, cryogenic freezer) at the highest pressure, then a dedicated cool-down room, then inoculation. All spawn incubates inside the lab.
  • The substrate lab has about nine 2 x 4 ft hoods along the wall opposite the entrance. They pull from a pre-filter room cooled by an outside AC of 3.5-4 tons (12-14 kW).
  • Spawn incubation uses tall stationary racks that exploit the 20 ft (6.1 m) ceilings: tall green pallet racking with wooden slat decks and ducting overhead. The new facility also has rows of galvanized rolling racks with about 7 wire shelves on casters.
  • CASE: A 7.5-ton unit serving spawn had a duct running down the middle of substrate incubation. Heat radiating from the duct caused growth differences from row to row until someone spotted it.
  • A high-pressure boiler (about $100,000) is built into a shipping container so it can sit outside. Steam goes about 60 ft (18 m) to the steam container.

Cap n Stem's earlier site: Westbrook, Maine

Westbrook shows most of the mistakes this chapter warns against.

  • It combined spawn, block production and fruiting in a tiny second-floor space without heat control, which kept flooding the floor below.
  • The fruit rooms were at positive pressure and leaked into incubation. Incubation was divided with swaying plastic curtain walls. The steam generator needed tending every two hours overnight. CO2 reached about 7,000 ppm.
  • The "Neurospora wars": incubation was overrun, made worse by dumping infected bags outside, where spores reached the air inlets. The root cause was bad bag seals (see Chapter 16).

Wild Fruitings Mushroom Co, Maine: a buy-in fruiting farm

This farm sits about 10 minutes from Cap n Stem and buys in Cap n Stem blocks. It was formerly Maine Mushroom Company, run by Shawn and Kat.

Two estimates of its layout exist; both were rough figures given in conversation, so treat the dimensions as approximate.

  • Estimate 1: two fruit rooms of about 14 x 20 ft (4.3 x 6.1 m) and a plenum of about 20 x 28 ft (6.1 x 8.5 m), maybe bigger. A traditional walk-in cooler has its compressor outside. There are two doors in the dividing wall, and exhaust fans on the back wall blow straight outside. A plenum window is kept permanently cracked open to hold plenum CO2 down.
  • Estimate 2: a 15 x 24 ft (4.6 x 7.3 m) open outbuilding that doubles as the plenum, a cooler of about 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m), and two 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit rooms (one in use), exhausting out the back. A plan of one 12 x 24 ft room shows three rows of five racks, labelled Week 1, Week 2 and Week 3.

Generic fruiting-facility layouts for start-ups

  • Split rectangle. One half of the building is the plenum; the other half is split into fruit rooms 1 and 2. Air is drawn from the plenum side and exhausted through the far outside wall. Example building: about 40 x 20 ft (12.2 x 6.1 m) with an internal dividing wall.
  • Standard room. 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m), with its 12 ft wall facing the plenum (where the intake damper goes) and an exhaust fan of 800-1,000 CFM blowing straight outside (see Chapter 14).
  • Worked plan. The plenum is on one side with two wall units holding it at 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) and a condenser outside. Fruit rooms F1 and F2 sit on the other side, each exhausting outside. The plenum's units total 18 kW, and each room holds 300 blocks. The final layout is a 28 x 40 ft (8.5 x 12.2 m) building with the plenum (with a recirculating unit), F1 and F2 exhausting through the far wall, and a walk-in cooler box at one end.
  • Sizing example. Two 12 x 24 ft rooms side by side plus a plenum of about 24 x 24 ft (7.3 x 7.3 m), with two cooling units for redundancy totalling about 3.5 tons (12.3 kW).

Other farms worth knowing

  • A large Agaricus farm growing king oysters. Agaricus "doubles" (paired growing rooms) of about 80 x 80 x 25 ft (24 x 24 x 7.6 m) with wood shelving and concrete, heavily insulated. A roughly 30-ton (105 kW) HVAC unit with a fresh-air damper feeds a perforated PVC manifold down the centre of the room. About 11 return-duct filters are cleaned daily. There is no active humidification, because the wet wood and concrete supply moisture (see Chapter 14).
  • European caves (France and elsewhere). Big headroom and natural humidity, no engineered air exchange, and beautiful king oysters.
  • Far West Fungi. 3 people hand-spawn in a corner; a stable coastal climate.
  • Mycelia (Belgium). Extensive facility plate maps (see Chapter 4); a clear contrast between stripped, equipment-only rooms and a personalized manager's room.
  • An upstate New York farm. Incubation packed solid with no fans. Do not copy this.
  • A large farm with evaporators inside its fruit rooms. Spores clog the coils so badly they strip them weekly. Use a plenum instead. Smallhold had the same problem with evaporative coolers inside rooms (unconfirmed).
  • Dutch and other European substrate companies, and Mycopia. Dense trolleys in incubation, which work only because ventilation channels are left through the pack.
  • Cascadia Mushrooms. Shiitake was 50% or more of production. Compost near the fruit-room ducts caused Neurospora.
  • Arizona. A lab built with reflective panels stayed cool on 43 °C (110 °F) days. Another grower's lab had an AC return inside it (see Chapter 4).
  • A New Jersey farm. Its lab problems came partly from cheap hardware-store "HEPA" filters.
  • Facilities worth studying: Cap n Stem (Maine), Mycelia and Mycopolitan, and one other grower's production space.

Farms abroad: what Japan and Australia teach

What growers have seen on very large, specialized farms abroad, mostly from an Australian grower's tour of Japan:

  • Specialize. Japanese growers grow one or two species; they believe growing many means never mastering any. Many farms in Asia grow a single species, often in low-tech greenhouses or shade houses. One nameko farm makes 3 tonnes a day with 20 employees and robotic harvesting, packing and grading, and still supplies only 1/27 of Japan's daily nameko demand.
  • Big is cheap per kilo. Japanese farms run at peak production with very low prices: a nameko farm producing about 136 tonnes (300,000 lb) a week makes only about US$1 million a year and loses money on sales in summer, but keeps running to keep its staff. US prices are high by world standards, so good substrate pays on high-value mushrooms.
  • Maitake at scale. A Japanese maitake farm produces one tonne of fresh maitake a day with only about 30 kg of second grade. It mixes up to 30% ground spent shiitake logs into fresh oak sawdust, because maitake digests cellulose and lignin poorly and the shiitake has already broken them down. It moves blocks between rooms through staged incubation, uses strong light for fruiting, and finds incubation the most difficult part.
  • Bottle farms are a different scale. A bottle system was quoted at about US$1 million for the know-how and bottles alone, and about US$4 million with all the infrastructure; it only pays at large scale. A US bottle farm of 23,000 m² (250,000 sq ft) on two floors employs close to 200 people.
  • You don't need state-of-the-art technology. Some multi-generation Japanese farms humidify with tubs of misting fog. Keep rooms clean but not hospital-sterile; some farms with moss on the walls grow top-quality mushrooms with no blotch. If you are bleaching rooms daily and still have problems, look at the substrate, the heat treatment and the spawn instead, and change one thing at a time.
  • Plastic waste. Japan burns stripped bag plastic in furnaces to heat buildings, which would be illegal in Australia. So-called biodegradable bags break into microplastics, and no compostable bag yet survives an autoclave.

Key rules

  1. Plan four independent climates (mix/steam, lab/cool-down, incubation, fruiting), and never share air between fruiting and the rest.
  2. Lay the building out for one-way flow: steam, then lab, then incubation, then cooler or fruiting, with no backtracking and gowning at the clean boundary.
  3. Give incubation about twice the fruiting space and more than the lab, and size it for at least 3 weeks of production (much more for shiitake).
  4. One room, one function: do not incubate, cool and knock in the same space.
  5. Put lab heat into mix/steam or outside, never into incubation. Incubation's spare cool air may feed the lab.
  6. Choose or modify buildings for a reflective, well-insulated roof, buffered walls, outside condensers, and drainage only where it belongs (fruit rooms and steam, not labs).
  7. Store substrate dry, off the water path and away from rats and insects. Pellets take far less floor than raw sawdust.
  8. Move product in racks and carts, and get contaminated bags and compost out of the building and away from air intakes.
  9. Size cooling with redundancy (two units, or one size up), and plan cold storage for spawn, blocks and outgoing pallets.
  10. Scale in big steps that add output without adding labour. Do not multiply small equipment.
  11. Check site access (an 18-wheeler for freight) and water quality before committing to a building.

Open questions

  • No floor-area ratios exist for a complete spore-to-store farm. The space rules here come from a 100 sq ft consultation and from fruiting-only layouts.
  • Room fill: this book uses 1/10-1/4 of the room's volume as the standard, with two hand widths between bags and never more than half the room for incubation. The 500-600 lb a week from a 12 x 24 ft room is that room's full capacity; what fraction of its volume that layout fills was not stated. See How much space each zone needs, Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.
  • The dimensions of the Wild Fruitings example differ between the two estimates.
  • The design of Cap n Stem's new Lewiston, Maine, facility has not been published.
  • Electrical service sizing for a whole production facility (boiler, autoclave, refrigeration) is not covered beyond figures for single pieces of equipment.
  • Planning approval and building codes (for example, fire concerns about Coroplast raised in Canada) are covered only in passing.
