chapters.html:
The Lab and Clean Practice

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the rooms where cultures, spawn and substrate are opened and inoculated: how to lay them out, how to keep them at positive pressure with HEPA air, how to cool cooked substrate without re-contaminating it, how to choose, run, protect and test flow hoods and fan filter units, and how to gown, clean and work at the hood. It ends with the people side: hiring and keeping staff who can do repetitive clean work well.

  • Clean HEPA air must push out of the room (positive pressure). Supply about 20% more air than the room returns.
  • No recirculating AC, mini-split or return duct inside the lab or cool-down room.
  • Pull cooked substrate hot (93 °C / 200 °F or more) straight into HEPA air. Knock at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), roughly room temperature in a lab that isn't hot, and never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.
  • Hood air speed about 90 ft/min (0.45 m/s) where you work; work within one bag length of the filter.
  • Never spray a HEPA filter. Test with agar plates.
  • Disinfect with 70% isopropyl or bleach at no more than about 400 ppm. Never mix bleach with ammonia.
  • Keep only what the task needs in each room.

What a clean room is and why mushrooms need one

A clean room is a space supplied with filtered air that is as free of particles as practical, plus a routine of disinfection. How strict it needs to be depends on how critical the work is. Aerospace and medical clean rooms are far stricter than a spawn lab.

The core design idea is positive pressure (overpressure). The room sits at a higher air pressure than its surroundings, so clean air is always pushing outward, ideally through an exit you chose. A lab design has three priorities: "positive pressure, positive pressure, and also positive pressure"; after that come construction, HEPA units and the workstation, and disinfection and cleaning.

  • Fan filter units (FFUs) with HEPA filters are the basis of every modern clean room and mycology workspace. An FFU is a fan in a box that pushes air through a HEPA filter. They began as ceiling units giving overhead positive pressure in labs and were adopted by mushroom growers.
  • Mushroom media differ from chemistry work. A chemist only has to keep water out of a sealed flask, but sterile grain and agar are rich food for any organism, so you need a continuous flow of filtered air.
  • People are the largest contamination source in mushroom production. Protective clothing (PPE) matters most when working with sterilized media. Humans shed large numbers of bacteria through their skin every second (a point from Roger Rabbit's notes).
  • Once a lab is built correctly it tends to stay clean. HEPA filters stay clean unless you damage them.

RANGE How much equipment you need. For production, use constant filtered airflow (recommended). The old method shown in classic books (The Mushroom Cultivator; Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms), a sterile white closet wiped with Lysol or a still-air box, is the worst approach for production, because anyone entering immediately sheds contaminants; constant filtered airflow replaced it. At the other end, a beginner cloning wild or store-bought mushrooms does not need high-grade filtration: a cleanable surface is enough. Technique matters more than equipment; equipment mainly buys scale.

Three kinds of lab

Lab type Used for Cleanliness bar
Spawn / sterile lab Agar, grain masters, G2, sterilized media Highest. Every room and corridor over-pressurized from its own HEPA. Tyvek, masks and gloves mandatory; staff change in a sluice.
"Dirty" substrate lab Knocking (inoculating) ultra-pasteurized substrate Lower than the spawn lab but still kept clean. A single room returning air to the AC. Strict gowning mainly at the hoods.
Closet lab / still-air Hobby culture work Recirculates room air through a hood. Only as clean as the air coming in.
  • The substrate lab is sometimes jokingly called the "MERV, who cares" lab (MERV is a lower grade of air filter), but it must still be clean.
  • Sterilized media are axenic (free of all other life). That makes them an "open buffet" for any organism. They leave a double-door autoclave straight into a HEPA-positive clean room and are handled with a stricter process (full-body PPE at Cap n Stem) until the bags are sealed.
  • Pasteurized blocks are more forgiving. Hot blocks kill much of what touches them, so they can cross a clean but not pristine area on the way to the lab.

Positive pressure

AT A GLANCE A fan outside the room pushes air through a wall-mounted HEPA into the sealed lab. The air is cooled before the filter, in a pre-filter room. A restricted return keeps the lab about 20% positive. Supply high, exit low in the opposite corner. In a suite of rooms, step pressure down by at least about 20 Pa per room.

How to pressurize a room

RULE Lab HEPA units must not be recirculating units standing inside the room. A fan outside the room pushes air from another space through a filter mounted in the wall. That pressurizes a sealed room. Recirculating-only HEPA fans are a common mistake. Recirculating hoods alone do not pressurize a room.

  • You need both: a wall-mounted, outside-fed pressurizing unit, and a HEPA workstation for the work itself. Size the linear feet of HEPA to the number of people knocking, and prefer variable fan speed.
  • Simplest build: cut a square hole in the dividing wall and set the FFU into it from behind, so everything on the lab side is HEPA air. Picture the room as a box with an FFU in the back wall (rated "99.99...%") and air flowing out at the door.
  • FFUs are made to sit in a wall cavity about 5.5-6 in (14-15 cm) deep, which fits 2 x 6 framing. They pull from another space, blow into the lab, and the air returns via the plenum. They can also sit on a table on 3/4 in (19 mm) Trex decking, using their rear mounting tabs.
  • For a tiny lab, a 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) HEPA in the ceiling can pressurize the space with downward flow and cool it from the top.
  • The simplest way to keep a clean room positive is one FFU mounted in the wall, pushing HEPA-filtered air from the neighbouring room into the lab: "small thing, big impact".
  • FFUs and hoods can draw their air from a cooled neighbouring space through a box or flex duct behind them, run up high. You do not need an open corridor between the two rooms, and the lab stays positive.
  • Avoid recirculating HEPA units in an inoculation lab for another reason too: their dirty back face collects contaminants. These are released in a power outage and pulled back through when power returns.
  • Spawn incubation can use the same design: a separate positive-pressure room fed by wall filters with fans behind them (near-laminar flow). The air returns to a pre-conditioning / pre-filter room to be re-filtered rather than using fresh makeup air. Picture a "spawn" room inside a larger loop, with a filter/fan bank on one wall and an adjoining pre-filter room with return arrows.

The pre-filter room and the AC

HEPA fans draw from a plenum: either the surrounding building or a dedicated room. That air must already be at the target temperature: comfortable for a knock room, or incubation temperature if mycelium incubates there. All temperature control happens outside the HEPA-filtered space. The loop is: AC → plenum → HEPA → room → hallway → back to AC.

The substrate-lab version. A "pre-filter room" behind the hood wall holds the AC supply and the coarse pre-filters on the backs of the hood fans. Because the hood fans pull from it, it runs at negative pressure and draws air in through cracks. That is acceptable, because every bit of air reaching the lab passes through HEPA. Cap n Stem's AC, about 3.5-4 tons (12-14 kW), sits outside and is ducted straight into the pre-filter room, so hood air leaves at the AC supply temperature (for example 13 °C / 55 °F). "Pre-filter room" is a clearer name than "plenum" or "preconditioning room".

A sketch of this lab shows: the door and sluice in one corner; a row of hoods along the opposite wall; the room at about 90 Pa static pressure; the pre-filter room behind the hood wall; and an outside AC marked 3.5 tons. In cross-section it reads LAB | PRE-FILTER | OUTSIDE: the AC pushes into the pre-filter room, the filter in the dividing wall delivers into the lab, and a return duct runs from low in the lab back to the AC.

Other versions of the same idea:

  • Farm version. A 7.5-ton (26 kW) AC takes its return from inside the lab and feeds a plenum. 8 flow hoods in two areas draw from that plenum into the lab. The return is slightly restricted so the lab stays positive. The plenum doubles as pre-filter and pre-conditioning space.
  • Pasteurization version. AC supply goes into a walled pre-filter / pre-cool room. HEPA fan units of matched capacity (for example 3,000 CFM) carry that air into the lab, and the AC return comes from the lab. Match fan speed and static pressure. This speeds block cooling and works for sterilization too.
  • Borrowing cool air. A long building can run: mix area, a narrow lab, then incubation, with HEPA units in the lab/incubation wall pulling cool air from incubation and returning it. High CO2 does not matter in the lab, so this gives free cooling for staff and substrate cool-down. At Cap n Stem the block incubation refrigeration also conditions adjoining lab rooms (spawn cool-down, other incubation), which pull from incubation and return to it while staying positive.
  • Direction matters. Incubation's spare cooling may be pulled into the lab if the substrate heat load in the lab is exhausted. Lab heat must never be pushed back into incubation; it goes to mix/steam or outside. Building-level air paths are in Chapter 3.

TIP Tell an HVAC contractor plainly that the pre-conditioning room is a pre-filter space whose air returns to the same point. Size the plenum and the pressure difference together so the equipment is not overworked. The return must cope with positive pressure, or the fans overheat.

  • Positive-pressure rooms stress the HVAC, because they constantly push conditioned air out. Direct the exhaust deliberately and, for efficiency, return it to the conditioning source. A clean incubation room also needs its own ventilation for CO2.

Procedure: balancing the return

  1. Run a return duct from low on the lab side back to the AC. Typical return ducts are 10-20 in (25-51 cm) square.
  2. Fit an adjustable damper so the return can be restricted.
  3. Match the AC supply to the filter flow, for example 100 units each, measured at the filter with an anemometer (air-speed meter).
  4. Throttle the return to about 80 units, giving roughly a 20% positive difference.

CHECK Air should rush out of the lab when you open the exit. These numbers are illustrative; what matters is that the lab returns clearly less air than the filters supply.

WHY An unrestricted return leaves the lab at zero or negative pressure. Then door openings, gusts or a nearby roll-up door push dirty air in.

Hot-load relief. Freshly steamed blocks, around 93 °C (200 °F), dump a lot of heat into the lab. For the first few hours, let lab air exhaust outdoors rather than return to the cooled space. A passive relief port is enough: a screened "dog door" or a cheap plastic gravity damper that opens under pressure, not routed through the vestibule. Close it once the blocks have cooled, and normal return resumes.

Airflow inside a room

  • Put the inbound HEPA high on a wall or in the ceiling, and the exit low in the diagonally opposite corner. This gives a steady current without turbulence that would lift settled particles.
  • A narrow hallway can take the outflow, absorb pressure drops and loop the air back to the plenum.
  • Spawn incubation in a positive-pressure HEPA room: supply high and let air leave low. Cold air sinks and counters the heat from the spawn.

Pressure cascades in multi-room labs

  • The most critical rooms are fed directly by HEPA at the highest pressure. Their outflow passively pressurizes successively less critical rooms.
  • Keep a steep gradient: at least about 20 Pa per step, because pressure collapses within seconds of a door opening. Making doors hard to close is wasted effort. A typical example: rooms at 120 Pa and 90 Pa off a plenum and hallway.
  • Cap n Stem's spawn lab priority order: (1) the flow-hood room (genetics work, cryogenic freezer) at the highest pressure; (2) a dedicated, empty, very clean cool-down room where autoclaved grain cools overnight, drawn with two exits; (3) the inoculation room.
  • In the spawn lab, every room and corridor is over-pressurized from its own HEPA, and air flows back through a central corridor and out the way you came in. The substrate lab, by contrast, is one room with an AC; the spawn lab is several HEPA-fed rooms off a corridor.

Measuring and tuning pressure

  • Low air-pressure differences are measured in pascals (Pa); psi belongs to autoclaves. For a single room, feeling a strong rush of air at the exit is enough. For several rooms, use a handheld digital manometer with two tubes, one in each room.
  • Example readings: a substrate lab at about 90 Pa. A cool-down room needs clean, well-filtered positive-pressure air, perhaps in the range of 90 Pa (unconfirmed), but not anthrax-grade.
  • Two control levers: supply airflow (fan speed, set with a rheostat) and outlet size. Outlets are "dog doors": holes in walls with adjustable Coroplast flaps. Some facilities automate this.
  • Restricting outflow raises a room's temperature. That is useful in a clean incubation room (colonizing mycelium makes heat) or in a Maine winter. Opening it dumps heat. In high summer Cap n Stem opens adjustable panels on the spawn room to lower its pressure, which drops the temperature a couple of degrees within minutes; they reverse this in winter.
  • Air exchange rate = total HEPA fan airflow (CFM) / room volume. Example: 800 CFM into a 4 x 4 x 4 ft room (64 cu ft, 1.8 m³) = 12.5 air exchanges per minute. The same calculation applies to fruit rooms (for example 12 x 24 x 10 ft).
  • A lab and a fruit room are designed along similar lines. The fruit room's aim is to stop CO2 and spore backflow; the lab's aim is filtration and linear airflow (see Chapter 14).

Heat added by pressurization

  • Positive pressure raises the exchange rate but traps heat, and the filter fan itself adds heat. Over-pressurized spawn rooms run hotter than expected.
  • Fan motors and friction through the HEPA add heat: 18 °C (64 °F) supply can arrive at 19 °C (66 °F). Pulling 19 °C (66 °F) substrate-incubation air through a fan and HEPA into a spawn room gave 20-21 °C (68-70 °F). Fix: chill the pre-filter space hard (for example to 16 °C / 60 °F) so the gain of about 1 °C (2 °F) still lands at the target of about 17 °C (62 °F).

Never put a recirculating cooler inside a clean room

RULE Do not put recirculating AC units or recirculating fans inside a clean room or cool-down room, even temporarily. The coil collects fragments shed by people and redistributes them. Contamination builds over a grace period, then takes off. Condition the air in a pre-filter room behind the HEPA wall instead.

  • A mini-split or heat pump inside the lab blows unfiltered air through a dirty coil and filter. In a small closet lab, an internal recirculating AC competes with the flow hood and spreads unfiltered air.
  • Ceiling ducts blowing conditioned air down onto flow hoods cause endless contamination unless the duct connects to the back of the filter.
  • CASE: A photo of an Arizona grower's lab showed an AC return duct inside the lab. Even with a HEPA positive-pressure intake, the return collected contaminants from foot traffic on its coils and blew them back. Growers in this position tend to change steam time, recipe or spawn supplier instead of finding the real cause.
  • Summer failure mode: warm pasteurized blocks heat the inoculation room. Provide cooling, but not with a unit inside the lab, because it creates air plumes.
  • Substrate incubation is different. Blocks with filter patches do not need HEPA air, so cooling units can sit in the room and recirculate (see Chapter 13).

Laying out the lab

AT A GLANCE Enter through a sluice, keep steam physically apart, give each room one job, keep rooms bare, make the knock table one row deep, and hold the lab at about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F).

Insulate against the outside. Outside conditions leak in. Cap n Stem's Gardiner spawn incubation room backs onto an old brick wall facing a neighbour's always-open loading dock, and they keep adding rigid foam. Concrete, steel and brick act as heat sinks or sources. Roof and climate are covered in Chapter 3.

Sluices, airlocks and one-way movement

A sluice (ante-chamber) is a small room with two doors between the dirty side and the clean side.

  • A sluice with two swinging doors stops the sudden pressure drop that happens when a single door opens and lets dirty air back in. Put it at the opposite end of the room from the filtered air supply. It is not essential for every lab, but it is worth it in production.
  • Sluices or airlocks (entry, exit and pass-through chambers) buffer dirty outside air. Movement through them is one-way, with separate exit sluices for product, equipment and racks.
  • Order the work from cleanest to dirtiest (for example, knock first, mix substrate second). Product flows from the cleanest rooms outward.
  • A pass-through window sealed with 3M flashing tape lets substrate bags on a cart on one side be handed to a Tyvek-suited worker with a stainless cart on the other, without anyone crossing.

The two-room entry routine is in Gowning and PPE.

Separating steam from the lab

  • Keep steaming physically apart from the cooled, filtered lab. Seal bare concrete, line the walls with Coroplast, make the lab airtight, and vent steam and heat outside.
  • Ideally a small buffer closet separates mix/steam from the lab, with the lab at higher pressure so dirty air bleeds outward. A steam box in a corner can be emptied through a semi-dirty area with little risk.
  • With pasteurization, the unloading side outside the lab can be a "dirty" area; bags go straight from the steamer into the lab. With ultra-pasteurization, blocks can be pulled through a small door onto a clean rack the moment the cook ends, and the steam room itself can stay relatively dirty.
  • A double-door airlock between steamer and lab is not essential if blocks come out of the steamer hot and go straight in.
Process Conditions Route to the lab
Ultra-pasteurization Under 1 psi (7 kPa), 100 °C (212 °F) May pass through a dirty zone into the lab.
Sterilization 121 °C (250 °F) at about 15 psi (103 kPa), 35 min at the core Must leave a double-door autoclave straight into clean space.

Steam processes are covered in full in Chapter 12.

One room, one function

  • CASE: A farm incubating racks inside its lab kept getting contamination. Removing contaminated bags and constant traffic carried spores onto the knock table.
  • Even a perfectly clean incubation room will have some contaminated bags (for example, Neurospora pushing through a torn patch). Having them a few feet from blocks cooling for tomorrow's knock is a major contamination route.
  • If the cool-down area and lab share a space, you cannot work in the lab while substrate is cooling, and the space needs a recirculating AC system.
  • Cap n Stem incubates all its spawn inside the lab rather than in outside air, so the lab temperature also sets the spawn growth schedule.
  • When one lab must do everything (substrate cool-down, inoculation, grain and spawn, agar), split the work by day rather than by room. For example: steam on Monday, cool-down and inoculation on Tuesday, spawn prep on Wednesday, agar on Thursday. One consulting farm (Catawba Mushrooms) runs a single lab day each week. See Chapter 26.
  • Doing pasteurized substrate work and sterilized spawn work in the same lab is where "weird anomalies" start. Cap n Stem did it for years and it worked, provided the two are kept apart in time and the flow hood is treated as sacred, with no dust. Plan about two runs of each a week, never at the same time.
  • In a narrow lab, one long bench works better than two separate hood stations: for example two 2 x 4 ft FFUs side by side acting as one 8 ft (2.4 m) hood. A straight-line layout keeps the work flowing and forces one job at a time; awkward layouts end up training staff in "gymnastics".

Keep it bare

  • The cool-down room needs only HEPA and a clean floor. The knock room needs only the HEPA workstation and the sealer. The incubation room needs only racks. Tools and instruments live in the hallway. The same logic applies at home at 20 bags a week. Cluttered labs such as Mushroom Mountain (Tradd Cotter's), which does not mass-produce spawn, are the opposite model.
  • Avoid the cluttered "artist studio" lab with a hood in the middle and things piled round it. Clutter is where mistakes and contamination come from, even though several popular online growers work this way.
  • No décor or personal items in clean spaces: no photos, calendars, decorative lighting (such as the lighting in North Spore's lab), or cats. At Mycelia (Belgium) the contrast between a stripped, equipment-only room and a personalized manager's room is plain to see.
  • The more official and scaled the operation, the more the lab must be simplified to stay consistent over time. Complexity and kitsch erode consistency.
  • People romanticize labs, partly because of YouTube. Most beginners' labs are dirtier and less efficient than they look on camera. A lab is not a cosy library.

Space, tables and temperature

  • Start-ups overestimate what fits in a small footprint and underestimate the space needed for access, movement, gowning and separate controls (see Chapter 3).
  • If a filter can only be changed by pulling it down through the clean space (for example, via a small attic hatch), solve that at design time.
  • Make the knock table only one row deep, so workers physically cannot stack blocks behind each other. People drift to shortcuts in monotonous work. A typical sketch shows a single row of blocks along the hood, with a second row crossed out.
  • Table depth versus air speed. Air velocity fell from about 120 ft/min (0.61 m/s) near the filter to about 60 ft/min (0.30 m/s) at 36 in (91 cm). Do not work deeper than one bag length from the filter: 12 in (30 cm) bags on a 36 in table leave about 18 in (46 cm) spare. A grower who opened about 400 bags at once on a deep table is the example of what not to do.
  • Keep HEPA coverage continuous from opening to sealing. A gap between the spawning and sealing stations works for a while, then causes losses.
  • A pneumatic sealing jaw allowed a vertical sealing station that handles one bag at a time with laminar flow across the work surface, but the cycle time per bag became the bottleneck (see Chapter 11).

Lab temperature. Aim for about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F). It suits healthy growth, and staff in Tyvek can tolerate it. In the mid-20s °C (mid-70s °F) a suit becomes miserable, especially when knocking bags. 19 °C (66 °F) is a practical compromise, not a magic temperature at which everything thrives.

Example labs

  • Cap n Stem's substrate ("dirty") lab: Coroplast over steel studs, seams taped with 3M tape, and about nine 2 x 4 ft flow hoods along the wall opposite the entrance, pulling from a space behind that wall. Everything entering is sterilized, pasteurized or (staff) freshly laundered.

  • A comb-tooth (lion's mane) lab: a wall of three perforated-face filter panels above a long stainless table, and white walls with seams sealed by 3M tape.

  • A knock area: two workers at a stainless table in front of a wall of flow-hood filters, with racks of clear spawn bags alongside.

  • Culture work at Cap n Stem is done in a high-end hood (the "$10,000 hood"), because early mistakes multiply downstream. Spawning is done in the FFU-pressurized clean room in front of another bank of FFUs, so the work gets double HEPA filtration.

  • After years of shuffling rooms in its current building, Cap n Stem began designing a new facility (in Lewiston, Maine) from scratch.

  • Cap n Stem's sterile-pellet lab (where sterilized pellets are hydrated and then spawned) works like the inside of an HVAC unit. The air conditioner pushes about 3,000 CFM (1,400 L/s) into a back pre-filter room. Full-wall flow hoods in that room draw from it and push about 3,500 CFM (1,650 L/s) into the lab, which keeps the lab at positive pressure. The lab's return air goes straight back to the air conditioner.

  • A tent lab (Wumbo Genetics): a 3 x 3 m (10 x 10 ft) tent lab and a 2.4 x 2.4 m (8 x 8 ft) incubation tent share a small 0.6 x 1.2 m (2 x 4 ft) plenum tent. All the air is conditioned in the plenum and then sent to both tents to hold them at positive pressure. One conditioned air supply serves two rooms, which saves space and electricity and keeps the work cleaner.

Construction materials and finishes

  • Use inorganic, easily cleaned materials: Coroplast walls, 3M flashing tape on the seams, steel studs. They are cheap, quick and modular, which matters because the farm layout will change within months as you grow. Cap n Stem wasted time and money on other materials early on. The same three materials are used for fruit rooms.
  • Doubled steel studs, joined with tin-snip tabs and self-tapping screws, are strong enough to hang heavy wall HEPA units.
  • No floor drains, sinks or faucets inside clean rooms. Drains harbour bacteria and mould, and the high airflow dries rooms anyway. If a lab already has a drain, tape or seal it off rather than relying on a P-trap, or at the very least bleach it daily.
  • Epoxy-coat concrete floors. Mould grows in bare concrete; epoxy seals it, rolls on easily and cleans easily. The rule: "No drains! Epoxy on concrete!"

WARNING Coroplast is not structural, and it is flammable and melts. In a fire, get out. Building-code concerns have been raised in Canada.

Cooling cooked substrate

AT A GLANCE Cool-down is where most widespread contamination starts. Pull blocks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, straight into positive-pressure HEPA air. Never let them cool in the steam vessel and then carry them through dirty space. Inoculate once they are down to about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), roughly room temperature, and never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.

Why cool-down is the weak point

  • Improper cool-down is the source of most widespread contamination. Blocks become vulnerable as they cool toward roughly 38 °C (100 °F) and a little above.
  • As blocks cool, the air inside the bag contracts and draws outside air in through the filter patch. Whatever is in that air is pulled into the block.
  • When blocks fail, start the diagnosis with the production method (sterilized or ultra-pasteurized) and the cool-down speed, not with the ingredients.
  • In warm climates, cooling bags outside a clean room is even worse, because warm outside air is drawn into cooling bags more aggressively.
  • Filter patches are not hermetic. A wetted patch (in a humid cooling room, or on hot substrate at about 60-62% moisture) becomes a direct path for mould drawn across it by fans.

Hot transfer: the method to use

Option How Risk
Hot transfer (recommended) Pull blocks hot, at 96-99 °C (205-210 °F), or 93 °C (200 °F) or more after a hold of about 3 h, straight into a HEPA-filtered, positive-pressure room to cool. Handle with welding gloves. Hot blocks are less likely to pick up contaminants in transit than cool ones.
Cool in the vessel The vessel is back-pressurized with HEPA air while it cools. Moving the cooled blocks through dirty space afterwards still risks contamination.

Procedure: hot transfer and overnight cool-down

  1. At the end of the cook, pull the racks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, within 3 hours at most.
  2. Let the steam pour off the blocks.
  3. Roll them onto racks sprayed with 70% isopropyl, in front of positive-pressure HEPA air.
  4. Cool overnight. At Cap n Stem, racks are pulled at about 9-9:30 pm and cooled with air at about 18 °C (65 °F) in front of the flow hoods; blocks reach about 37 °C (99 °F) by 8 am and are knocked at about 9:30 am.
  5. Before knocking, check the block temperature with an infrared thermometer. Inoculate at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), roughly room temperature; never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above (see the RANGE below).

CHECK Even with hot handling in a dirty space you might lose about 5 of 150 bags. The rule: "Always cool down hot in front of an overpressurized HEPA lab."

RANGE Block temperature at inoculation. Recommended: about room temperature, which in practice means 27-32 °C (80-90 °F) (full table in Chapter 11). Upper limits in use: below 38 °C (100 °F) at most; about 30 °C (86 °F) as an empirical upper limit; others accept the 32-37 °C (90-something °F) range. One grower finds that even 27 °C (80 °F) can be too hot to inoculate, so measure every time. Knocking at 38 °C (100 °F) or above kills spawn, and the result is often mistaken for contamination (see Chapter 11).

RANGE Where to cool. Pasteurized blocks in a substrate lab cool overnight in front of the lab flow hoods before inoculation. For sterilized material, a separate HEPA cool-down room is better (pass-through autoclave, racks, bag tops folded over, and no hands opening bags), because cooling bags in front of laminar flow can dry them out.

  • Do not cool pasteurized blocks inside the pasteurization vessel. A wet, dirty container overnight contaminates them. Shipping containers have wooden floors under the metal, water troughs and leaky doors, so they pull in dirty air as they cool.
  • A closed steam box takes about 8-10 h to drop from 93 °C (200 °F); some farms leave blocks in for 48 h. That also over-cooks them.
  • Barrel-cart pasteurizing: roll the cart into the lab, lift the barrel off, and cool the blocks under HEPA.

Dedicated cool-down rooms

  • A separate cool-down room matters when the autoclave runs all day while staff inoculate, because hot bags coming out at 66-121 °C (150-250 °F) would overheat the workers. With one run a day, you can cool and knock in the same room.
  • Plenum layout for a cool-down room beside a clean work room: both rooms at equal pressure and airflow. Cool-down air (blocks come out near 100 °C / 212 °F) is exhausted outside rather than recirculated, while the work room stays cool (about 16 °C / 60 °F) and returns its air via transfer grilles to the plenum. The reasons: worker comfort, off-gassing smell, and keeping hot air from crossing the building during constant traffic.
  • Heat load: 2,000-5,000 bags per cycle entering at 93 °C (200 °F) or more swing the room from hot and humid to cool and dry as they cool.

Cool-down failures

CASE Cap n Stem's own lesson. One summer day, blocks sat in the steam unit until they were below about 66 °C (150 °F), then were carried past an open window to the lab about 10 ft (3 m) away and cooled there. The racks pulled first, nearest the window, went to Neurospora within about 2 days of inoculation; those at the back were affected less. Lesson: move blocks while they are hot, and never past an opening.

CASE A customer cooled bags overnight in a shipping container to about 10-27 °C (50-80 °F), then moved them across a dirty space. After switching to moving hot blocks into the lab, they struggled to cool them, so they added hoods and filters. But clogged pre-filters killed their positive pressure, and the lab no longer protected the blocks. Lesson: hot transfer only works if the lab stays positive.

CASE A Midwest farm's blocks colonized weakly and looked "greasy", and many species (even reishi) did not fruit. Cause: hot blocks waited 1-3 days, not hours, before going from the ultra-pasteurizer to the filtered cool-down room. Heat-loving (thermophilic) bacterial endospores survived and got a head start.

CASE A farm cooking 5-10 lb (2.3-4.5 kg) blocks in barrels pulled "HEPA"-filtered air into the barrels during cool-down to keep them at positive pressure, then moved the cooled blocks to the lab. It worked, slowly got worse, then failed. The suck-through intake filter (likely 99.95-99.97% or worse) was probably compromised.

  • Pulling air through a HEPA (for example, HEPA shop-vacs attached to a steam box for cool-down) seals poorly and contaminates everything.
  • One grower switched to hauling hot blocks by Kubota tractor through snow into their lab, and their problems went away.

Procedure: testing the cool-down air path

  1. Seal some bags completely before cooking. Optionally put a datalogger in one.
  2. Cook and cool them with the batch.
  3. Incubate them without opening them.
  4. Read the result: growth in these sealed bags means the air drawn in during cooling is contaminated.

CHECK If contamination shows across everything, suspect the equipment, not the working hood.

Handling cooked blocks

  • Move blocks in racks or cages rather than hand-loading individual blocks; tired or careless staff eventually contaminate. Cap n Stem builds wheeled stainless-angle racks of about 7 shelves that take Metro shelves, so whole racks move from the chamber to the lab (see Chapter 3).
  • Never return a dropped block or rack to the batch. Floor contact can contaminate everything. Discard it or use it elsewhere.

Flow hoods, fan filter units and HEPA filters

AT A GLANCE Buy tested, lab-grade, blow-through HEPA units with many nines; do not build your own. Use a horizontal hood. Keep it running all the time at about 90 ft/min (0.45 m/s) where you work. Protect the bottom edge of the filter, vacuum out spills, never spray it, and test it with agar plates and an anemometer. A well-treated HEPA lasts about 10 years.

Terms and ratings

  • FFU means fan filter unit. "HEPA" is a generic word, like Ziploc. Read the label for the string of nines and the final digit (5, 7, or all 9s): higher is better.
  • HEPA filters are rated at 0.3 micron. ULPA (ultra-low particulate air) filters let through only virus-sized particles.
Filter or label Rating as stated Comment
Lab-grade laminar-flow HEPA (recommended) 99.99...97% (many nines), for example 99.999997% The grade to insist on for lab hoods.
Standard HEPA 99.95-99.97% at 0.3 micron The standard HEPA rating, but inadequate for lab use in the stricter view.
Old forum DIY spec 99.99997% Hobby forums used to dismiss 99.95% filters.
Lab Rat "Nomad" label 99.99% at 0.1 micron Small portable hood.
Cheap hardware-store "HEPA" 99.7-99.9% Linked to a New Jersey farm's lab problems.
Some units sold as HEPA About 98% Works until it leaks, then cannot be recovered.

RANGE How good the filter must be. Standard for a production lab: lab-grade, many nines (99.99...97%). The gap between 99.95-99.97% and 99.99...97% is large; few filters on the market are rated at the higher level for suck-through use, and cheaper filters only work until they fail. 99.95-99.97% is the standard HEPA rating. Context: for small hobby hoods, the old forum insistence on 99.99997% over 99.95% was more doctrine than necessity. Whether 99.95-99.97% is acceptable for blow-through lab hoods is still open (see Open questions).

Blow-through versus suck-through

  • Laminar flow means pushing air through a filter that is gasketed all round. A proper FFU (the fan pushing through the filter) traps contaminants on the back face, where they stay unless the front is damaged.
  • With suck-through filtration (HVAC style), a power outage lets the filter lose its seal against the fan housing, so air slides around it. A filter designed for blow-through laminar flow is not equivalent to one that air is sucked through.

Horizontal versus vertical hoods

Hood type How it works Use
Horizontal (recommended) Blows from the filter toward the worker. Protects the culture and forgives hands or heads above the work: particles blow away rather than down. Cap n Stem's horizontal hood runs at about 90 ft/min (0.46 m/s). The standard choice in mycology. Lets Cap n Stem staff without microbiology training work with essentially no issues, which helps when hiring.
Vertical (downflow, perforated table) Protects the user, but blows anything above the work (hands, hair, skin) down onto plates. Needs different hand movements; most people know horizontal. Can work with good technique and Tyvek, but beginners on a college vertical hood contaminated about half their plates. Cheap tabletop units from China cost about $3,000-5,000 and suit automation.

Inside a hood

A large horizontal hood (a Baker EdgeGARD; Cap n Stem's is a battered used unit that their staff rebuilt) works like this:

  1. Intake slats under the work surface stop big particles.
  2. A cut-to-size foam/cotton pre-filter sheet comes next.
  3. A grate stops the pre-filter being sucked into the blower.
  4. The blower pushes air up the back plenum and out through the HEPA wall. There are no pre-filters on the HEPAs themselves.
  5. Side panels and return grates in the work surface pull air back to the blower to recycle it.

From outside, it has a stainless perforated face and a top light; opening the slotted lower panels shows the pre-filter area. A free-standing FFU, by contrast, is a white box with a round fan grille.

  • A generic flow hood is: a fan with a rheostat, a sealed air gap, a perforated dispersion plate (metal with drilled holes), a gasketed HEPA, and a table. Without the plate, air concentrates in the centre and is weak at the edges, creating currents. A 3D sneeze guard helps at the edges.
  • Modern FFUs have a fan with a backing plate that throws air into the plenum for even distribution.
  • Cap n Stem's cabinet hood recirculates under its perforated table and has side guards and outward "blowback" fans that push air out as hands enter.
  • Hoods have a raised grid that keeps hands 6-13 mm (1/4-1/2 in) off the filter.
  • A typical culture-work hood set-up: a stainless horizontal hood with a spray bottle, a jar of sterile swabs, a ceramic infrared tool sterilizer, scissors on a wipe, slants in a rack, and plates stacked at the back against the filter. Some labs have a stainless hood with a perforated back panel and purple lighting.

Face velocity

Face velocity is the speed of the air leaving the filter, measured with an anemometer.

Measurement or target Value Conditions
Target About 90 ft/min (about 0.45 m/s) At the working zone. Too low or too high gives turbulence.
Too fast Well above 90 ft/min The grate causes turbulence and swirls.
Too slow About 70 ft/min (0.36 m/s) Heavier particles from the worker can settle on the work.
Big hood, near the filter About 126 ft/min (0.64 m/s) Highest close to the filter.
Big hood, about 6 in (15 cm) out 90-130 ft/min (0.46-0.66 m/s) Lower in the middle where the fan is; drops sharply toward the outer edge.
Table depth effect About 120 ft/min (0.61 m/s) near the filter, about 60 ft/min (0.30 m/s) at 36 in (91 cm) Work within one bag length.
Lab Rat Nomad About 96-104 ft/min (0.49-0.53 m/s) Across the face and at petri-dish distance; very even.
Conversion 0.3-0.5 m/s is about 60-100 ft/min About 70-90 ft/min is the commonly quoted working band.
  • Adjust the variac (variable transformer) or fan speed so about 90 ft/min falls where you actually work.
  • Cap n Stem's Gardiner hood has a static-pressure gauge on the filter's back pressure and automatically raises motor speed to hold 90 ft/min. Rising back pressure means the filter is loading.

Run hoods all the time

RULE Leave hoods running all the time. A HEPA unit switched off (to save power, or because it has no rheostat to slow it) passively absorbs humidity, moisture from cooling blocks, and spores from patches and contaminated blocks. When it is restarted it can compromise the knock table. If needed, run it at low speed.

  • A small lab hood draws about 3.5 A, which is negligible on the power bill, so leave it on rather than running it only for the two hours you work.
  • Running hoods catch particles shed by people in street clothes under a lab coat. If a hood has been off, switch it on and wait an hour or so before working. Constant production makes always-on easiest.
  • In a closet lab without positive pressure, running the hood 2 h before entering does not help much, because you bring skin, socks and beard in with you.

RANGE Warm-up time. Fixed hoods: never switch off (recommended), or wait an hour or so if you do. A portable Nomad unit in a closed small office: run it 20-30 min before culture work; one unit passed a plate test after a 20 min run.

Pre-filters and maintenance

Filter Change or check interval
Wall FFU pre-filters pulling from a dirty space Much more often; check weekly.
One grower's FFUs: 1 in (25 mm) MERV 8-11 pre-filters Changed every week; an anemometer catches a restricted filter.
In-room hood pre-filters Every 3-4 months, sometimes 6.
  • Leave room for a pre-filter on the flow hood's intake.
  • Clogged pre-filters can kill positive pressure (see the cool-down case).
  • Prevention routine: track contamination by season; have a way to check airflow and pressure; change pre-filters and filters; clean ducts; recheck after any building change (for example, an autoclave set through a wall leaving a gap).
  • Spore loading on cooling equipment outside the lab: build a box around an evaporator's return side with an opening for a coarse furnace pre-filter, and swap the pre-filter when it is loaded (see Chapter 5).
  • Hot, humid climates: buy HEPA filters and pre-filters made for high humidity (specific mini-pleat designs) rather than standard or home-built ones. Heat and moisture build a film on ordinary filters, and small labs have failed because the pre-filter or the humidity rating was wrong.

Protecting the filter face

  • The most abused spot on a mini-pleat HEPA is the bottom edge at table level, where grain splashes into the face and bags get rammed into the frame, causing ruptures.
  • Fix: tape a 2 in (5 cm) stainless angle iron to the table along the base of the filter as a bumper, keeping bags about 1.5 in (4 cm) off the frame. In Cap n Stem's substrate lab a stainless angle runs along the base of each FFU, so staff can push blocks close without hitting the filter, and stray grain bounces off.
  • Vacuum spilled grain or sawdust out of the filter promptly. Never pick at it with a knife, and do not blow it out with compressed air. A trapped millet seed becomes a mould source. Keep a vacuum at the hood.
  • A badly ruptured filter cannot be repaired with superglue or caulk. Replace it.

CASE Contamination rose until the farm was overproducing to compensate. Spilled grain had built up at the base of the knock-table HEPA, because cleaning had degraded as training passed from person to person, and staff slammed blocks into the filter until it cracked and air passed through unfiltered.

Never spray or wet a HEPA filter

WARNING Do not spray isopropyl or anything wet into a HEPA. Moisture swells the pores and weakens the membrane; alcohol may react with the cellulose matrix; and wet spots can be colonized (Neurospora will grow on almost nothing). Alcohol is always diluted with water, so spraying it always wets the filter.

  • Wet filter media wicks contaminants through, like a lateral-flow test, turning the filter into a contamination source.
  • Neurospora drawn into a wet filter can establish and grow there; it has been seen growing on the back of filters.
  • HEPA filters are not dirty, so there is nothing to clean. A social-media post of a "busted filter" caused controversy, and even an experienced collaborator did not know this rule.
  • Abused filters (spore-laden or humid air, sprayed with disinfectant) fail fast.
  • Some growers (for example, in Facebook groups) say spraying alcohol on the filter is fine. It is not.

Lifespan and costs

Item Value
Well-treated HEPA life About 10 years; 7-10+ years for hood wall filters.
Abused HEPA Loses uniform flow within a year.
Cap n Stem's record No HEPA replaced in 2.5 years; replacements only from damage.
Hood wall filter replacement About $700 in filter material.
New large hood About $6,000-20,000 (odd lab units range from $1,000 to $50,000).
FFU from the source About $850; replacement filters about $300-400.
Imported resold FFUs $1,200-1,400, and subpar compared with US-made tested units.
Vertical tabletop hood (China) About $3,000-5,000.
Lab Rat Nomad About $100; the largest model is about 2 x 3 ft (0.6 x 0.9 m).
Cost logic An $850 filter over 10 years is about $80 a year; contamination costs far more.
  • Choose by scale: a couple of hundred dollars (a Nomad), about $800 (an FFU), or many thousands (a big hood).
  • Farms that accept a fixed 25% contamination rate should diagnose their technique, filter and room instead.

Buying, building and suppliers

  • Used hoods appear at auction, sometimes badly abused. Clean them thoroughly, and check the side panels for rust holes that would let air bypass the pre-filter. A cheap used unit is still a bargain even if it needs new filters.
  • Do not build your own flow hood, even if you are a skilled woodworker. It is hard to fit and seal, and builders get attached and never suspect their own hood. Buy pretested units; good makers replace defective ones.
  • The old DIY recipe (a bare 99.99997% HEPA, a box of polyurethaned wood, a salvaged squirrel-cage blower, a rheostat and a lighter-flame flow test) carried electrocution and fire risk. Today a couple of hundred dollars buys portable hoods, mini-pleat filters and FFUs.
  • Do not trust a seller's word that something "should work as a HEPA filter". Do not bet a scaling business on an unknown filter.
  • Suppliers: Filter Sales USA / International Filter Sales (filtersales.com; the source most resellers use), Flow Cube, Lab Rat Flow Hoods, Bonsai Filter (now said to be part of Midwest Grow Kits), Baker (EdgeGARD hoods), and bulk imports from Alibaba. See Chapter 23.

Small and portable hoods

  • The Lab Rat "Nomad" has a 3D-printed casing, a computer-style fan, a perforated distribution grid behind the filter and mesh in front. Work only in the middle of the face.
  • It can run in the field from a car inverter or power bank, for cloning wild mushrooms onto plates and parafilming them on the spot.

Procedure: validating a portable hood

  1. Run the hood for 20 min.
  2. Place 6 open agar plates on the work area: at the corners and along the centre lines.
  3. Leave them open for 3-4 h (the original test was done in a dirty warehouse).
  4. Close, seal and incubate the plates.

CHECK No growth in the middle or at the edges means culture work is possible with that hood. Growth only at the edges points to ungloved handling, not the hood.

Testing filters and rooms

AT A GLANCE Agar plates are the best test; plates are cheap and filters are not. Add an anemometer for air speed. Test before you blame spawn or recipes.

Procedure: plate test at the hood

  1. If the hood has been off, run it first.
  2. Expose clean agar plates in front of the filter for 30 s to 2 min at different positions (or about 60 s each across a hood about 4 ft, 1.2 m, wide), or leave them on the work surface for 15-20 min.
  3. Also place plates on tables, at the edges and around the room.
  4. Cover, parafilm and incubate the plates, then map what grows.

CHECK Longer exposure means lower risk tolerance; a day-long exposure catches occasional shedding.

  • Cap n Stem buys blank pre-poured plates from a partner company, Tip of the Cap.
  • Facility plate maps. Mycelia (the Belgian spawn company) did these extensively. Cap n Stem places plates at doorways, vents and room corners about every 6 months. The best spot is the outflow "dog door" that all the air leaves through. Test when nobody is working, so people do not skew the results.
  • Anemometer. Check that face velocity is even across the filter. A vane anemometer is cheap; buy a mid-priced one (vanes in a casing are more accurate). For example, an Extech AN300 thermo-anemometer held at the hood. Do not confuse it with a manometer, which measures pressure.
  • Particle counter. A cheap counter (about $30 online) can be held in front of the filter. Simply walking into a room can spike one to about 900. Particle counters are more rigorous, but proper ones are pricey.
  • Smoke, incense, ribbons. These show laminar flow over the filter's life. The lighter-flame trick shows flow but says nothing about contamination. Some people push smoke through filters to see the flow; do not do this to your filters.

Diagnosing filter and room problems

  • Recurring green, brown, black or orange moulds usually mean bad filtration or negative pressure. If pressure is known to be good, look for breaks near the bottom of the filters (see Chapter 16).
  • Observe before replacing a filter. Find the path of least resistance for contamination: where the positive pressure and any recirculation come from.
  • Damaged filters or irregular airflow give sporadic infiltration. Whole lots can also be ruined by bad technique (see Sterile technique).
  • Farms resist suspecting their own filter. Test it anyway.

CASE A farm saw rising rates of every kind of fungal contaminant. Its lab had a wall of recirculating hoods (which create no pressure), yet air rushed out through a poorly gasketed glass "dog door". The air came from a ceiling "overpressure" duct fed by a fan pulling air through a so-called HEPA on the roof, rated 99.95-99.97%. Installing a well-gasketed mini-pleat HEPA at the top of the duct, with the fan blowing through it, stopped the contamination. The same farm had its lab at the back of the building and its fruit rooms between the lab and incubation. Lesson: blow through a good filter; never suck through a poor one.

Gowning and PPE

AT A GLANCE In the spawn lab: change in a sluice into full-body hooded Tyvek, face mask, gloves, booties and dedicated lab shoes. In the substrate lab: freshly laundered clothes, a shower, or Tyvek, with strict gowning at the hoods.

Procedure: entering the spawn lab

  1. Room 1 of the sluice: take off outer clothes, hat and shoes.
  2. Room 2: put on full-body hooded Tyvek, lab shoes (Crocs), booties, gloves and a face mask.
  3. Walk one way into the lab. Leave by the exit route, never back through the entry.

CHECK Gowning supplies sit on a shelf at the boundary: labelled bins of Tyvek suits by size (XL, XXL), disposable masks (from Uline) and hair nets. A correctly gowned worker enters in a full white suit and black nitrile gloves.

  • Cap n Stem's lab PPE: full-body hooded Tyvek (said to filter at roughly HEPA level, about 0.3 micron; unconfirmed), a face mask (an N95 is overkill), gloves and booties. Tyvek raises body temperature by roughly 6 °C (10 °F) above the room.
  • Shoes: use dedicated lab shoes. Crocs work well because they are cleanable. Feet bring in more contamination than anything else.
  • Substrate lab: staff wear freshly laundered clothes, shower, or wear Tyvek. Strict gowning matters mostly when working at the hoods. Spawn lab: changing into Tyvek in a sluice, masks and gloves are mandatory.
  • Soaking yourself in alcohol before work is unnecessary ritual. A clean suit does the job.
  • Small lapses (popping in ungowned to grab a phone) become habits. Wool socks over Crocs in the lab is the kind of thing that rightly alarms a careful lab worker.

RANGE Gloves. Production lab: gloves are required (recommended). Small culture work: some growers work without gloves if their hands are soaked in isopropyl ("no gloves, no problem"). In a portable-hood plate test, the only growth that could appear was traced to ungloved handling.

Cleaning

AT A GLANCE Mop after every session; disinfect every surface weekly (after every knock in a substrate lab); fruit rooms far more often than people think. Use 70% isopropyl or bleach at no more than about 400 ppm.

Cleaning routines

Space Routine
Spawn/culture lab (Cap n Stem) Vacuum and mop after every session (slants, grain knocks, order picking). Weekly full disinfection of every room, including walls and ceilings (equipment excepted).
Other farms' labs Monthly full disinfection. The interval depends on scale and the target contamination rate.
Substrate lab After each knock, mop the whole room, walls and ceiling with bleach or isopropyl (mops or sticky mats). Alcohol footbath at the entry.
Fruit rooms Far more than people think: daily if possible. Bleach spray at about 250 ppm, power-wash or wipe the walls, push water to the drain, and rotate cleaning agents.
Fruit rooms (another grower) Fully clean walls, floors and racks before loading new blocks. Bleach on floors, sometimes alternating with vinegar. Walls spot-cleaned, not weekly.
Maitake room Every single day, because of Trichoderma and airborne contaminants.
Large industrial farms The whole room, top to bottom, after every crop (for example Mycopia).
  • One grower estimates that about half of all farm time goes to cleaning (another jokingly put it at 43%).
  • Fans and ducts are the hardest to clean. Spray or wipe fans regularly, or it becomes a big job. A noisy fan is often the first sign of failure; cleanliness protects machinery as well as crops.
  • Equipment outside the lab: a Coroplast heat exchanger is pressure-washed every other day over a gravel pit. A drum fogger can take a coarse intake filter and should be easy to pull out and clean (see Chapter 5).
  • Remove contaminated bags from the building promptly. Cap n Stem once left contaminated bags in the warehouse over a weekend, and one Neurospora bag covered that part of the building in spores by Monday (see Chapter 3).

RANGE Footbaths. Labs: an alcohol bath or footbath at the lab entry is part of the routine in some labs. Fruit rooms: isopropyl footbaths at the doors make little difference; a clean plenum and steady one-way airflow matter more.

Disinfectants

Agent Use and notes
70% isopropyl The US default. Short surface action. For surfaces, gloves, bag ends and racks.
Bleach The other US default. Fruit-room water treatment about 150-200 ppm; fruit-room spray about 250 ppm. For cleaning, do not exceed about 400 ppm. If you can easily smell it, it is too strong.
Quaternary ammonium ("quats") Used by European farms. Stays active in a bucket all day, so less spraying is needed. Some Belgian farms prefer quats to isopropyl. No concentrations are given here.
Hydrogen peroxide An antiseptic that kills bacteria, viruses and moulds on contact but breaks down quickly to water and oxygen. It does not keep surfaces clean and does not sterilize.
Lysol Used in still-air boxes. Its chemistry is uncertain (possibly quats). Not a sterilizer.
Vinegar Alternated with bleach on fruit-room floors by one grower.
  • Do not confuse the three main agents. In everyday farm terms, peroxide is an antiseptic, isopropyl a sanitizer and bleach a cleaner.
  • Work in ppm. 200-400 ppm bleach is 0.02-0.04%, not 2-4%. Effective bleach solutions are a few hundred ppm; nothing near 20% belongs in a cleaning routine.

WARNING Never mix bleach with ammonia or ammonium cleaners. It releases a toxic gas. One person got sick doing this. A grower in Arizona hurt himself using undiluted pharmaceutical-grade bleach.

Sterile technique at the hood

AT A GLANCE Stage everything first. Sterile items go nearest the filter with nothing upstream. Keep yourself downstream. Work slowly. Shake bags away from the airflow.

  • Stage first. Put every supply inside the hood before starting, so you are not repeatedly leaving the filtered zone. Park finished plates to the side, still in front of the filter.
  • Placement. Anything sterile or biological (culture, fresh plate, open grain bag) goes closest to the filter, with nothing upstream of it. Keep sterile items in the zone near the filter, never out front. Keep yourself downstream: only filtered air should touch the work.
  • Edges. Air speed falls with distance from the filter, so keep blocks, spawn bag, alcohol bottle and hands close. Leave a margin between the spawn bag and the edge of the filtered zone (people quote 4, 6 or 12 in; 10, 15 or 30 cm); the edges are the weakest part. Do not line up rows of open bags deep on the table.
  • Lids and openings. Open plate lids toward the filter, and set the lid face-up or leaned against the filter. Keep an open slant's mouth facing the filter. Open grain bags angled slightly toward the filter, not toward or away from yourself.
  • Tools. Sterilize tweezers or scalpel before every touch, in a ceramic infrared (Bacti-Zapper-style) sterilizer, a bead sterilizer or a flame. Then cool the tip on a fresh agar plate, or in 70% isopropyl in a tube at a "cool-down station", so it does not scorch the culture. One common set-up dips tweezers in a 50 mL conical tube of amber liquid, most likely isopropyl (unconfirmed).
  • Bags in transit. Plates travel between rooms in SacO2 filter bags. Spray the bag and the scissors with alcohol before cutting, in case they touched the Tyvek suit. Spray the grain bag before opening it.
  • Spawn bags. Soak the end of the broken-up spawn bag in isopropyl and snip a small corner to pour (see Chapter 11).
  • Pace. Work slowly and deliberately. You cannot see air currents, and fast movements create eddies that pull dirty room air into the work zone. The hood is for careful culture work, not fast production.
  • Shaking. Shake bags of sterile media or spawn away from the laminar flow, so you do not pump dirty air into the work zone. Some solo operators fold, pinch and shake in a way that gets away with it at small scale.
  • Common technique failures: shedding from hands, holding the spawn bag outside the laminar flow, fingers in bags, and not checking seals.
  • Jar and lid assemblies. Sterilize with lids loose and foil-covered (or filters foil-covered, or tube assemblies wrapped separately). Then tighten, reassemble or fit filters inside the hood.
  • Minimal kit. An isopropyl-wiped work surface with a glass slab on top is enough to take clean clones from store-bought or wild mushrooms.
  • A typical working scene: gowned workers (white suit, black nitrile gloves) at a flow hood with a perforated stainless back, a spray bottle and scissors on a wipe, transferring cultures and cutting Parafilm with gloved hands.

Procedure: settling fresh plates

  1. Parafilm each fresh plate twice.
  2. Leave the plates 3-5 days in the flow hood to establish.
  3. Seal them in a SacO2-type filter bag.
  4. Move them to incubation (see Chapter 7).

RANGE Temperature in the hood area. The flow hood area runs about 21-27 °C (70-80 °F) in one lab and about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) in others; another describes it as slightly warmer than culture incubation, which is just under 21 °C (70 °F).

People in the lab

AT A GLANCE Lab work is repetitive, invisible and sensorily harsh. Hire with paid test days, explain why each step matters, limit chatter during inoculation, and design tables and routines so that shortcuts are impossible. A 5% contamination rate is roughly an entire profit margin.

Why lab work is hard on people

  • Some hires fail in the lab for sensory reasons: headaches from the lighting, nausea from disinfectant smells, discomfort with constant white walls, white noise and suit confinement. Others show slowly building anxiety and an urge to leave.
  • The core challenge is doing the identical task the same way every time without losing focus.
  • The environment never lets up: HEPA fans never stop, lights never go off, and there is nowhere to take a break. After the lab, staff may go into a loud walk-in cooler (see Chapter 3).
  • A 1980s cleanroom design manual (title unknown, section 3.3 "Attitudinal Factors") makes these points:
    • Personnel are operators, maintenance technicians and engineers (three groups).
    • White garments create anonymity.
    • Assembly-line repetition causes problems of task identity and significance.
    • Do/don't training worsens attitude.
    • Operators cannot see product quality, because problems are below the visual threshold, so work becomes ritual in an "informational void".
  • The "cannot see quality" point fits spawn especially well: neither contamination nor success is visible when the work is done.

Hiring

  • Talk the lab up in the interview as if it were a BSL-4 (maximum containment) lab, and watch whether the candidate frays. It usually shows quickly.
  • Use paid test days. Bring the candidate in, walk them through everything the job involves, then ask honestly whether they could do it. Watch body language in the lab: engaged and energized, or eager to leave? Some people love the "spaceship" feel.
  • Hiring for "culture fit" (active, outdoorsy, kind, into mushrooms) did not predict lab tolerance, and hiring instinct is usually wrong.
  • Spawn lab staff are a different personality from substrate crews: hire calm, steady people. Staff split into semi-lab roles and dirty warehouse-floor roles.
  • Horizontal hoods let staff without microbiology degrees do clean work, which widens the hiring pool.

RANGE Experienced lab hires. Someone from a working lab can be a positive hire. Be wary, though, of people who come from a spawn lab confident they have it all figured out, as they can be too casual; some of the best lab staff at Cap n Stem came from Walmart and pallet-loading warehouses, while an experienced hire has also worked out.

Keeping work accurate

  • Staff always look for shortcuts. Stacking blocks behind each other on the knock table to fit more is busy-ness that does not help, so design the table so it cannot happen (see Space, tables and temperature).
  • Repetitive work induces a trance. Long conversations or audiobooks during, say, bag 700 of 1,000 lead to errors when something changes (such as inoculating twice as many blocks per spawn bag) and to mislabelling.
  • No talking while pouring or inoculating spawn (a written procedure at Cactus Hat Mushrooms). One Cap n Stem owner does not talk at all when pulled into inoculation.
  • Media trade-off. The most controlled setting would be white noise only, but people need to talk and bond, and a new hire who always wears headphones can become isolated and resentful. Mixing crews alternate between all-phones weeks and slower, chattier weeks. Music is fine for purely repetitive tasks like shaking bags, as long as you keep count.
  • Explain why repetition and small details (for example, how bag folds are done) matter; small errors can damage the business. Some people enjoy a fixed pattern.
  • Connect each role to the whole. Farming is siloed: some staff never enter the lab or never fruit a block. Showing a cryovial and explaining that it can lead to about 60,000 lb (27 t) of mushrooms gives meaning to the work. The 1980s manual's remedies were thorough whole-process training, rotating staff through all tasks, and communication systems such as intercoms and windows.
  • Staff mistakes are training failures (Extreme Ownership by Jocko Willink is a useful read). Written procedures and redundancy matter, because eventually the owner is not the trainer. Cleaning standards degrade as training passes from person to person (see the filter case).
  • Data engages technically minded staff and gives them ownership. Standards slip over the years, and data catches what written procedures alone miss. An autoclave's paper cycle printout engages staff and visitors.

Team culture and leadership

  • Cap n Stem has named leads for critical areas (autoclave/boiler and heavy equipment; crops) but decides things collaboratively, less hierarchically than the 1980s manual's model.
  • Anonymity in suits means you often cannot tell whether your mistake is linked to someone else's. Many labs answer this with employee ID numbers and cameras; Cap n Stem deliberately does not, to avoid a surveillance culture.
  • Leaders should step in when a bad micro-culture forms. Useful tools: ironic humour about "fascistic cleanroom" rules, and silliness (calling out "Dad!" in Tyvek, counting bags aloud with new staff).
  • Owners should still do floor work occasionally (fold bags, run the hood) to avoid their own task-identity problem. One owner spent six hours on the hood when over half the staff were out, and found it a relief.
  • Slim margins and fast turnarounds push people into panic fixes that then persist as rituals. Example: an older teaching of inserting a flat Tyvek sleeve over the grain inside the bag to "filter" the cooling air; in steamers it does nothing (see Chapter 11).

WARNING A 5% contamination rate is roughly an entire agricultural profit margin. Do not accept it as "not bad".

Key rules

  1. Pressurize the clean room with outside-fed HEPA units pushing air in, and restrict the return so the room supplies more air than it returns (about 20% more). Recirculating hoods alone do not pressurize a room.
  2. Never put a recirculating AC, mini-split, evaporator or return duct inside the lab or cool-down room. Condition the air in a pre-filter room behind the HEPA wall.
  3. Supply high and exit low in the opposite corner. In multi-room labs, step pressure down by at least about 20 Pa per room, checked with a manometer.
  4. Pull cooked substrate hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, straight into positive-pressure HEPA air to cool. Do not let it cool in the vessel and then carry it through dirty space. Knock at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.
  5. Buy tested HEPA/FFU units with many nines (lab-grade, blow-through), not DIY or unknown "HEPA" filters.
  6. Keep hoods running all the time at about 90 ft/min (0.45 m/s) where you work, and work within one bag length of the filter.
  7. Fit a stainless angle iron along the filter base, vacuum out spilled grain, and never spray anything onto a HEPA.
  8. Test with exposed agar plates (at the hood and around the facility) and an anemometer before blaming spawn or recipes.
  9. Build with steel studs, Coroplast, flashing tape and epoxy floors. No drains or sinks in clean rooms. Keep only what the task needs in each room.
  10. Gown in a sluice (Tyvek, mask, gloves, dedicated shoes), work cleanest to dirtiest, and keep incubation and contaminated bags out of the lab.
  11. Mop after every session and disinfect all surfaces weekly (or after every knock in a substrate lab), with 70% isopropyl or bleach at no more than about 400 ppm. Never mix bleach with ammonia.
  12. Hire with paid test days, explain why each step matters, limit chatter during inoculation, and design tables and routines so that shortcuts are not possible.

Open questions

  • Pressure targets exist only as examples: 90 Pa for a substrate lab, a 120/90 Pa cascade, and "at least about 20 Pa per step". The figure of about 90 Pa for a cool-down room is unconfirmed, and no full set of pressure metrics has been published.
  • Filter grade is unresolved: whether 99.95-99.97% HEPA is acceptable for blow-through lab hoods, or only the many-nines grade.
  • The lab temperature of 19 °C (66 °F) is a comfort and growth compromise; there is no data behind it.
  • There are no figures for how much air exchange a cool-down room needs per bag or per BTU of hot substrate, beyond the 3,000 CFM example and AC sizes of 3.5-7.5 tons (12-26 kW).
  • Whether bags should cool in front of hood laminar flow or in a separate cool-down room is not settled (see the RANGE in Hot transfer).
  • Quats are an alternative used in Europe, but no concentrations or products have been given.
  • The claim that Tyvek filters at HEPA level is unconfirmed.
  • The exact model of high-humidity HEPA and pre-filter that Cap n Stem recommends for hot, humid climates has not yet been confirmed.
