chapters.html:
Climate Control and Monitoring

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the hardware that holds temperature, humidity and CO2 in incubation rooms, labs and fruit rooms: heat loads and sizing, walk-in evaporator ("reefer") units, mini-splits and heat pumps, heating, plenums and room pressure, heat recovery with a Coroplast heat exchanger and HRVs, humidifiers from pond foggers to TAC misting and Hart high-pressure systems with Pola wet/dry-bulb controllers, CO2 controllers, and the sensors and data loggers that check it all. Room layout is in Chapter 3, Chapter 4, Chapter 13 and Chapter 14; this chapter keeps to the air-handling equipment and its rules.

The rules and numbers used most:

  • Cooling, not heating, is the hard part almost everywhere.
  • Never recirculate fruit-room or clean-room air through a cooling coil inside that room. Condition air in a separate plenum and pull it through rooms one way.
  • Automate CO2 before anything else: fruit rooms about 450-900 ppm, incubation about 1,500-3,000 ppm, never above 5,000 ppm.
  • Plenum: CO2 at or below about 450 ppm, humidity about 40-50%.
  • Allow about 1 °C (2 °F) of heat gain through every fan and HEPA stage.
  • Humidify with fine, filtered, treated, non-recirculated mist (150-250 ppm bleach or ClO2 in the water), and check every controller with an independent logger.

Why climate control is the hard part

AT A GLANCE A fruit room throws away conditioned air all day, blocks make heat and CO2 that feed each other, and a cooling failure turns a packed room into an oven. Oversize and duplicate your cooling.

  • A conventional fruit room is an energy sink: it conditions fresh air to temperature, then dumps it outside full of CO2. One grower compares it to heating a house in winter with every window open.
  • Energy is "near impossible to chase" in a mushroom facility: each extra air exchange costs more, and hot climates (a Texas summer) get expensive. An HVAC specialist usually does the sizing.
  • Cooling is the hard part almost everywhere, from Canada to El Paso.
  • Heat and CO2 feed each other. More metabolism makes more CO2 and more heat, and the extra heat drives still more metabolism. A packed room must stay ahead of this loop.

  • Redundancy. Buy two units rather than one, and oversize. For example, pay about $2,000 more for 10 tons (35 kW) of cooling instead of 7.5 tons (26 kW).

  • Failure. If the HVAC fails, a dense incubation room becomes intolerably hot surprisingly fast. Have a backup way to move air in and out of the building. Shiitake is the first species to suffer.

  • Spares. Keep backups of fans and humidification gear. When the compressor of a high-pressure humidifier broke at Cap n Stem (a Maine farm), the farm limped along on a Hydrofogger.

  • Overpower the conditioning. Cap n Stem's advice for incubation is to give the air system more capacity than it seems to need. In winter it heats the incoming fresh air, in summer it cools it; the set point stays in the middle, but the job flips with the season. If the room drifts too far either way, timelines change: oysters incubate faster and blocks start fruiting in incubation. Ordinary building HVAC rarely does this well and is expensive.

  • Most farm emergencies are climate failures. Most calls Cap n Stem receives come from farms fighting contamination, and the answer usually involves the climate system: compressor size, room size, how many blocks a room can hold, and above all enough air conditioning. A large share of its consulting work is rescuing farms after something broke, even something as simple as a humidifier left switched off.

  • Ask for the engineer. A good HVAC contractor may still ask whether a fan is "just a fan". Ask the equipment company for its engineer, especially at firms that build refrigeration (reefer) units. An engineer does the arithmetic: sizes the system for the hottest and coldest days, explains what it can handle and how hard it will run, and does not guess. Spending this money without knowing what the equipment will do is a gamble.

The four climate zones and which way air may move

AT A GLANCE A farm has four independent climates. Air may flow from cleaner and cooler to dirtier, never the other way, and fruiting air never mixes with anything.

A farm is four independent environments, each controlled for a different job.

Zone What is controlled How tight
1. Mix and steam Temperature and humidity are not regulated; the space is only made comfortable for workers. Loose
2. Cool-down and lab Recirculating, cooled and HEPA filtered. Tight
3. Incubation CO2 and cooling held constant. Tight
4. Fruiting CO2, fresh air, humidity and cooling regulated. Allowed to swing a little

Rules for the direction of air between zones:

  • Excess cooled air from incubation may be pulled into the lab, as long as the heat from substrate in the lab is exhausted.
  • Lab heat must go to the mix/steam area or outside, never into incubation.
  • Fruiting must be fully decoupled: it draws from outside and exhausts to outside, one way.
  • Run two separate climate systems: (1) production, incubation and lab cooling; (2) fruiting plus harvest, pack and grade. Recirculate within each system, never combine them, and never feed CO2-rich cooled incubation air into fruit rooms.
  • A single AC can feed a multi-zone plenum serving several rooms if each room's damper is independent and nothing recirculates back. Fruiting cannot share it.
  • Each room needs independent control to get even air exchange in every room.
  • Engineers often propose whole-facility closed-loop recirculation for efficiency. Spore load, CO2 and temperature stability usually kill those plans. HVAC contractors may over-engineer and will not understand why you refuse to recirculate fruit-room air, so tell them explicitly what each space is for.

RANGE Recommended: never use recirculating HVAC for fruit rooms. Recirculation is fine, and is the most efficient approach, only for clean air: inside the conditioning plenum, in incubation and in the lab. Some designs also put heat-pump heads in rooms. Published advice from the author of two cultivation books to HEPA-filter and recirculate fruit-room air is rejected here, because fruiting air is full of spores.

Heat loads: how much heat blocks make

AT A GLANCE A 10 lb (4.5 kg) block makes roughly 2-10 BTU/h (0.6-2.9 W) while it colonizes, with a peak around day 11. A few blocks don't matter; thousands make incubation a cooling-only problem.

Heat per block

Basis Figure Conditions
Per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, ideal differential about 2 BTU/h (0.6 W); low at first, spiking near the end as the last patches close 19 °C (66 °F) outside the block, core rising to about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F)
Per lb of substrate about 1 BTU/h, i.e. About 10 BTU/h (2.9 W) per 10 lb block A second figure, "3.5 BTU per 10 lb bag", is unconfirmed.
Per lb of dry substrate about 2 BTU/h; a 10 lb block holds about 3.3 lb (1.5 kg) dry, so about 6 BTU/h (1.8 W) per block
Per rack of about 500 blocks (5 deep x 10 long x 10 shelves) about 1,000 BTU/h (293 W) More in poorly ventilated pockets.

RANGE Recommended: size cooling with a generous margin. Block heat output is stated as about 2, about 6 or about 10 BTU/h (0.6, 1.8 or 2.9 W) per 10 lb block in different sources, a threefold spread, and none of the figures comes from a stated measuring method.

Scale changes everything

  • 10 blocks make negligible heat; 200 are noticeable in a small room; 20,000 are an order of magnitude more.
  • Case: a about 20,000-block incubation room held 19 °C (66 °F) from block heat alone through a about 2-day power outage at -18 °C (0 °F) outside. Past a certain scale, incubation needs only cooling, even in New England.
  • Most incubation rooms mainly need cooling because bags are exothermic (they give off heat). Heating matters only in large spaces or long cold seasons.
  • Peak heat comes around day 11 for spawn and days 11-12 for oyster blocks.
  • Grain is a "hotter" medium than wood-based substrate and ideally incubates cooler, at about 16-18 °C (the low-to-mid 60s °F). That forced Cap n Stem to give its spawn room its own AC.
  • Pioppino makes far less heat per pound; a row full of it ran cold one winter.
  • Hot blocks from the steamer are a large short-term load: 2,000-5,000 bags per cycle entering at over 93 °C (200 °F) swing a room from hot and humid to cool and dry while they cool.

The building matters too

  • A black roof can reach about 66 °C (150 °F) on a 32 °C (90 °F) day, against about 38 °C (100 °F) for a white reflective roof. Insulate the ceiling at least as well as the walls, since hanging coolers cannot keep up under a hot roof.
  • Case: a lab built in Arizona with reflective panels stayed cool on 43 °C (110 °F) days.
  • Permanent shelving packs more blocks in, but only if cooling is sized for the full potential load. Otherwise colonization times vary widely.

Sizing examples

AT A GLANCE One ton of cooling is 12,000 BTU/h (3.5 kW). Real farms below show what worked and what was too small. The strongest lesson from working growers: go big on AC.

Space Equipment Notes
Two fruit rooms, about 300 blocks each, held about 18 °C (65 °F) about 18 kW (about 5 tons) of MrCool DIY mini-split heat pumps Holding about 16 °C (60 °F) may need more.
Small fruiting facility One or two 9-18 kW heat pumps, or a ducted package unit, or walk-in evaporators with an outside condenser
Two 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit rooms plus a about 24 x 24 ft (7.3 x 7.3 m) plenum Two units for redundancy, about 3.5 tons (12.3 kW) total
Room receiving hot steamed blocks about 3-ton (10.6 kW) system: a couple of mini-splits or a small Heatcraft evaporator Window ACs ice up.
4,500 sq ft (418 m²) incubation room A single 7.5-ton (26 kW) unit: overloaded Shiitake browned unevenly up the racks; top blocks showed every stage at once.
Large incubation, 4,000-6,000 sq ft (372-557 m²) Reefer-style evaporator system Standard split HVAC tops out at holding about 18-20 °C (65-68 °F).
Lab with 8 flow hoods 7.5-ton (26 kW) AC with its return from inside the lab, feeding a plenum Return slightly restricted for positive pressure.
Lab with a hood wall about 3.5-4 ton (12.3-14.1 kW) AC outside the building, ducted into a pre-filter room Hood air leaves at the AC supply temperature (example 13 °C, 55 °F).
Agaricus-style double room about 80 x 80 x 25 ft (24 x 24 x 7.6 m), at a large Pennsylvania farm about 30-ton (106 kW) HVAC with fresh-air damper Perforated PVC manifold down the room centre; about 11 return filters cleaned daily.

Advice from working farms:

  • "Go big on AC" is the strongest message from High Country Fungi (Avery's farm). Its 1 ton (12,000 BTU/h, 3.5 kW) mini-split cooling both incubation and lab is too small, and the AC in its pre-chamber was undersized. If the AC is properly sized, most other problems are manageable.
  • Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan's farm) uses about 60,000 BTU/h (17.6 kW) of AC for two grow rooms and 2 x 12,000 BTU/h (2 x 3.5 kW) for incubation. A mobile 12,000 BTU/h LG unit next to the king oysters holds them at 18 °C (65 °F). The farm's note also says "55 °F ambient" (13 °C), which is unclear.
  • In a hot, humid climate, generous cooling is an advantage rather than waste, especially when one cooled plenum also feeds the lab.
  • To pre-cool the AC's intake air, one grower suggests a 1 hp water chiller loop through a heat exchanger; a glycol chiller is another option to look into.
  • One grower can only get his grow rooms below 16 °C (60 °F) at certain times of year. For the height of summer he built a 1 hp water chiller on a closed loop to a heat exchanger, used as a "cold exchanger". In an earlier building (a former brewery), his fruit room was a thick insulated-panel walk-in once used to chill beer. It came with a large air handler inside (about 3 m, 10 ft, long with three fans) and a multi-ton chiller on the roof (probably water or glycol), and it could take the room as cold as he wanted. Used commercial refrigeration like this is worth hunting for.

CASE A Washington farm (Cascadia Mushrooms) had its first consultant lay out the farm and size the cooling, then built it in insulated greenhouses with a bought climate-control kit of thermostats, timers and temperature sensors. It worked for years, until the farm started packing the rooms much fuller: "then there just wasn't enough cooling capacity", and the system had to be re-engineered. Older designs assumed long, multi-flush blocks in loosely filled rooms. Modern farms push one big first flush and pack rooms fuller, so the heat load per room is higher. Size for the room as you will actually fill it.

CASE At Cap n Stem's first building (about 280 m², 3,000 sq ft, in Westbrook, Maine) the temperatures "just could not be regulated". A big HVAC system was already there, but nobody knew how much heat the blocks made. The farm switched to a more forgiving shiitake strain (3782) and brought incubation temperature under control.

  • A Florida farm (Nearby Naturals) spent about a month laying out its AC: the main unit outside the warehouse with the pipework running in. Neither founder was an engineer, which is why that month was needed.
  • A Houston farm (Flying Saucer Farms) ran a 2-ton AC (24,000 BTU/h, about 7 kW) in its first 1.8 x 3.7 m (6 x 12 ft) fruit room, with disc foggers blowing in from outside the room. Slime kept growing on the surfaces and the room needed constant cleaning.

Choosing cooling equipment

AT A GLANCE Use walk-in evaporators with outdoor condensers for incubation and anything below about 20 °C (68 °F). Mini-splits suit small, temperate fruiting setups. Avoid window units and CoolBot rooms except at the very smallest scale. Every condenser goes outside.

Equipment Best use Main limits
Walk-in evaporator ("reefer" unit) with outdoor condenser Incubation and anything held below about 20 °C (68 °F) Recirculates only; coils clog with spores; no economizer
Mini-split or heat pump Small, temperate or cold-climate fruiting setups; heats and cools Installers often botch them; struggles in deep cold
Package unit, ducted Recirculating plenum cooling Can carry an economizer (a damper that cools with outside air when it is cool enough)
Window or portable AC, CoolBot room Only very small incubation (a couple of racks) Ices up under hot blocks; little airflow
Evaporative cooler True desert
Used refrigerated container Cheap cooled plenum plus walk-in 480 V unit needs stepping down
  • Any cooling unit's condenser and compressor must sit outside the building, since it dumps heat.

Walk-in evaporator ("reefer") units

  • What they are: a fan-and-coil evaporator inside, with refrigerant lines to a compressor and condenser outside (on the roof or the ground). They throw a lot of air a long way; mounted high, they reduce the top-to-bottom temperature difference. A typical cutaway shows a ceiling-mounted unit (Chandler brand) inside, with the evaporator at about 2 °C (35 °F), linked to an outdoor compressor.
  • They are the simplest, most affordable way to hold temperature, compared with water chillers or conventional HVAC.
  • They can be set anywhere from about 19 °C (66 °F) down to freezing. Models differ in coil size, depth, fan speed and refrigerant, which changes how much they dehumidify. Heatcraft is the preferred maker at Cap n Stem.
  • They discharge air at about 13 °C (55 °F) and can hold blocks at 19 °C (66 °F). Ordinary HVAC reaches maybe 20 °C (68 °F) at best (it prefers about 22 °C, 72 °F) and struggles on 38 °C (100 °F) days.
  • They cool to 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) more easily than a package unit reaches 20 °C (68 °F), which suits hot climates (Arizona, Florida, Southern California). Before these units, Cap n Stem staged fans everywhere.
  • Case: Cap n Stem's substrate incubation is held at 19 °C (66 °F) by four evaporators with roof condensers. The air is unfiltered, which is fine for substrate. Heatcraft high-efficiency units recirculate the incubation air, with occasional exhaust to hold 2,000-3,000 ppm CO2.
  • Spawn incubation at 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) needs refrigerant-coil cooling rather than standard HVAC. It is hard, because the room's positive pressure flushes air out constantly.
  • Case: before Heatcraft rooftop units, overheating blocks in summer were a serious problem at Cap n Stem. A partner even proposed coring a void in each block to cut internal heat; it was not adopted.
  • With enough air exchange these systems can run without heating in mild climates, but fresh air must still come in. Economizers do not fit evaporator-type units. One farm (Wild Fruitings) keeps a plenum window cracked to keep plenum CO2 down.
  • Spores clog them. Walk-in evaporators only recirculate. In a spore-laden space the fins and coils clog even if mushrooms are picked early. Fix: build a box enclosing the evaporator's return side against the wall, with an opening for a coarse furnace pre-filter that is simply swapped.
  • Do not put evaporators inside fruit rooms. One large farm strips spore-clogged coils weekly, and another farm initially ran evaporative coolers inside fruiting rooms that were constantly fouled and rebuilt. Use a plenum instead: fruiting does not need temperature control so tight that it justifies risking expensive equipment.

WARNING Never run cooling pipes through racks. Condensation would rain onto the bags.

  • Used refrigerated shipping containers cost about $9,000 for a 20 or 40 ft (6.1 or 12.2 m) unit with a 480 V refrigeration unit, stepped down to 240 V on about a 40 A breaker. They give plenty of cooling and can be split into a cooled plenum and a walk-in. New walk-ins cost about $15,000-$40,000, up to $200,000.

  • A Colorado farm at about 2,500 m (8,200 ft) incubated thousands of blocks in a barn through summer without trouble. Once it had many more blocks and a boiler running, heat became the problem, and it fitted large evaporative ("swamp") coolers and big louvre vents. Its verdict: plan the air handling first, not last.

  • Evaporators and mini-split heads inside fruit rooms must be cleaned about twice a week because of spores; one New York farm with mini-splits in its fruit rooms had heavy bacterial blotch on king oysters. A Texas farm solved the same problem with walk-in-cooler style units feeding the room from outside it.

Mini-splits, heat pumps and package units

  • Mini-splits and heat pumps (MrCool DIY, Mitsubishi and others) both heat and cool, and suit temperate and cold climates such as rural Maine. They are cheap and DIY-installable; HVAC installers often botch them.

  • Case: Cap n Stem's fruit rooms used two heat pumps. In Maine both heating and cooling matter, but summer cooling was the bigger problem. At -28 °C (-18 °F) outside the heaters could not hold temperature; below about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) growth halted, and some weeks there was nothing to sell.

  • A package AC unit, ducted in and recirculating, is another plenum option, and package units can carry an economizer.

  • Case: a 7.5-ton (26 kW) unit serving spawn runs on auto (heat/cool) because of a shared wall. Its duct ran down the middle of substrate incubation, and the heat it radiated caused row-to-row differences in temperature and growth until staff spotted it.

  • Modes through the year: cool only in summer, auto in shoulder seasons, heat in winter.

  • In a true desert, use evaporative coolers.

  • High-efficiency mini-splits still have to pay back their installation cost through power savings. For a small California farm that never added up, so it spent the money on reflective foil insulation instead (see Insulate and shade first). Heating and cooling is the biggest issue for farms that grow out of tents into warehouses, because the power cooling takes is so large.

Window units and CoolBot rooms

  • CoolBot rooms (a window AC with a controller that drives it colder) are discouraged ("quit now"): window ACs move too little air, their built-in filters fail and energy use is high. If you use one anyway, add return filtration and do not undersize it (unconfirmed).

  • Window ACs, even with CoolBot-style controllers, ice their coils almost at once when hot steamed blocks load a room with heat and moisture. They then need daily defrosting and give no cooling meanwhile.

  • At very small scale a window or portable ducted AC is fine for incubation, if you keep only a couple of racks and do not cram the room.

  • Farms cool in many improvised ways. Many use CoolBot units (a window air conditioner with a controller that lets it run colder); some push a shop-type refrigeration unit into a spray-foamed room.

  • Window units can carry a very small farm. A Pennsylvania grower ran them in his first basement and they "did OK", though he had far too many blocks packed in. At scale, forced air from a refrigeration unit wins.

Cold storage

  • Cold storage (a reefer or walk-in at 1-4 °C, 34-40 °F) is one of the most important things on a farm: for outgoing pallets, spawn before use and blocks awaiting packing. DIY coolers are fine. Keep it out of the plenum and away from fruit rooms because of spores.

Heating

AT A GLANCE Heat only where you must, never with combustion heaters in a fruit room. Small electric heaters on the fruit-room intake, a boiler radiator in the plenum, or simply trapping clean-room air all work.

WARNING Do not heat fruit rooms with propane "hot dog" greenhouse heaters or other combustion heaters. They put CO2 into the space unless properly vented and controlled.

  • Cold-climate option: 120 V plug-in thermostatic heaters on the fruit-room intake, for example raising 10 °C (50 °F) plenum air to 13-16 °C (55-60 °F). Filter them so spores are not cooked onto the coils. A typical drawing shows the plenum at 10 °C (50 °F) and intake heaters delivering 13 °C (55 °F) into the rooms.

  • A Canadian container grower heated his plenum with a hot-water radiator fed from a boiler.

  • Restricting a clean room's outflow raises its ambient temperature. That is useful in a clean incubation room, or for heating in a Maine winter; opening the outflow dumps heat. In high summer Cap n Stem opens adjustable panels to lower spawn-room pressure, and the room drops a couple of degrees within minutes; in winter they reverse this.

  • A dehumidifier gives off heat. Case: in a closed drying closet one drove the temperature to about 38 °C (100 °F) against a 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) target. The fix was to crack the door, with a small fan near the bottom pulling air in. Make-up air should ideally be filtered; pull more if the source room is dry, less if it is humid.

  • Fans and HEPA pressurization also add heat; see heat gain through fans and HEPA.

  • Cheap heat from waste wood. A New Hampshire farm burns about 44 cords of free arborist and town wood a year in a wood boiler (about US$40 a cord in labour to cut, split and stack, against about US$300 to buy). The boiler feeds radiant floor heat and a 400,000 BTU/h closed-loop heat exchanger on the air intake that warms 2,000 CFM of air from -23 °C (-10 °F) to 32 °C (90 °F). Its 25 cm (10 in) concrete walls store about a week of heat. "It's easier to do that than it is to make it cold."

  • Freezing. A California farm had to switch its air system off on freezing nights. Once it was forgotten: by morning a 1.5 m (5 ft) run of icicles hung from the fan, water was blasting out, and every one of more than 1,000 forty-pound blocks in the room was frozen and went to the cattle.

Hot and humid climates

AT A GLANCE Most of the advice in this book comes from Maine, with cold winters and mild summers. Farms in Florida, Texas, Louisiana, Brisbane and other hot places agree on five things: cool far harder than a northern farm, treat humidity as the hard part, insulate and shade before buying capacity, plan for the day a unit fails, and choose species and strains for the season.

What growers in hot places agree on:

  • Cool harder than you think. Every hot-climate farm that fruited well through summer ran far more cooling than a northern farm of the same size. One Florida farm's rule: work out the cooling load, then buy about double.
  • Humidity is the hard part. Hot, humid air is worse than hot, dry air: it breeds moulds. Big cooling units also strip moisture from the air, so incoming air has to be cooled and then humidified again, not just chilled.
  • Insulate and shade first. Roof foil, insulation and indoor locations cut the load before any AC is bought.
  • Plan for failure. A unit that quits on a hot day can overheat a room in hours (see Power cuts, alarms and backup).
  • Choose species for the season. Some growers switch to heat-tolerant strains or drop cold-loving species in summer.

What growers in hot places found

  • Florida, Orlando (Nearby Naturals). The farm "totally over-designed" its fruiting chambers with far more AC than seemed necessary, and had what it believed were the coldest fruit rooms in Florida. That is why king and black pearl oysters, which like it cold, grew well there. The advice it was given by a more experienced grower: the first thing to get right is "temperature, temperature, temperature". Work out what you need and buy double, and cool the air in an anteroom before it enters the fruit room. Farms that skip this end up with 27 °C (80 °F) fruit rooms. In Florida heating a fruit room is never needed; all the effort goes into cooling.
  • Florida, Jacksonville (Sun and Sky Mushrooms). The farms that do it properly hold their grow rooms near 16 °C (60 °F) even in summer, with much more AC than a typical setup. It is expensive, but it pays as long as product keeps moving. Stopping for a summer month is not an option either: restaurant buyers switch to whoever still has mushrooms. A Tallahassee farm set the same target for its grow rooms: fully automated and steady at 16 °C (60 °F).
  • Texas, Austin (HiFi Mycology). In a Texas summer a grower can spend six months "waiting for things to break", hoping the grow room stays below 21 °C (70 °F), with no spare capacity to try a demanding species such as maitake. Starting in an uninsulated garage in November gave at least a month before the heat; insulation was the first job. With outdoor highs near 43 °C (110 °F) for three months, doors cannot be left open the way farms in coastal northern California do. When this farm expanded to about 930 m² (10,000 sq ft), the plans included a 40-ton chiller or a refrigerated container. Instead it split the farm: fruiting and colonizing in the new building, substrate and lab in the old one five minutes away. With no lab to protect, the new building's air only has to deal with CO2.
  • Texas, Houston (Flying Saucer Farms). About four months a year bring 38 °C (100 °F) outside while the fruit room must stay at 18 °C (65 °F) or less. The farm changes how it cuts the bags with the seasons, depending on how much conditioning the incoming air needs. Coastal Texas "is not hospitable", and tips from growers in milder places often don't transfer.
  • Brisbane, Australia (Little Acre Gourmet Mushrooms). A subtropical city with hot summers and no real cold needs "so much cooling" that even incubation must be cooled, unlike a coastal California farm whose incubation is a shade house outdoors. The farm now runs many refrigerated containers outside the building just to keep things cool. Keeping things cool at scale is one of the hardest parts of the business, and most people don't budget for the cost of refrigeration.
  • California foothills (Foggy Dew Fungi). This grower used to shut down for two or three months every summer. Now he fruits through summer with heat-tolerant strains that can fruit in 32 °C (90 °F) weather. Not every species has to be grown year-round; a seasonal crop can even build demand ("we don't always have shiitake, but when we have it, they look forward to it"). Customers notice when a different blue oyster strain changes the look of the caps.
  • Maine (North Spore). Cooling is the constant problem in mushroom growing. In its first summer this farm had no cooling at all and turned to window air conditioners, even free ones picked up from the roadside.
  • Mississippi coast. Two growers working indoors in a house found the coast so humid they needed no humidifier at all, and the mushrooms grew big. But with no way to exhaust the air, both began wheezing, and they stopped growing indoors. After two days away, white oysters had covered every surface in spores, and pink oysters left a pink layer. See Spores and health.

RANGE Fruit-room humidity in a very humid climate. Standard: swing relative humidity between about 70% and 90% with the exhaust cycle (Chapter 14); holding 90% all the time invites blotch. Context: in Houston, where outside air already arrives at 80-85% RH, one farm runs "a little wetter" and lets the room run down only a little. It reports no blotch and sees blotch only in winter, when the air gets drier, so it believes deep wet-to-dry swings are what let blotch bloom. Cap n Stem's answer: big cooling systems strip moisture, so humidify the incoming air before it reaches the crop; the room should take "a breath", not ride big waves.

Precooling the fresh air

Precooling means cooling, and ideally drying, the outside air before it reaches the main air conditioner, so the AC is not fighting hot, wet air. Three farms show the options.

CASE A New Hampshire farm's grow room 4, 2.4 x 2.4 x 4.9 m (8 x 8 x 16 ft) holding about 1,800 fruiting bags, always ran too warm and grew "spaghetti blues": 1 cm (half-inch) caps on 25 cm (10 in) stems. Its 60,000 BTU/h (about 17.6 kW) air conditioner could not blow air cold enough when the outside air was warm and humid. The fix was a home-made "poor man's heat pump": the fresh air is drawn from a spot in the field through pipe buried in the ground and under the floor slab before it reaches the AC. On a 32 °C (90 °F) day the air entering the AC was 17 °C (63 °F) and dry; on a 35 °C (95 °F) day the grow rooms held 14 °C (58 °F). The whole system draws 81 W and had run for five years without being switched off. Most of the cost was the digging.

CASE A Detroit farm sits low on a water basin with a high water table. It pumps well water at about 12 °C (54 °F), chills it further with a geothermal (water-source) heat pump, and runs it through a chiller coil that conditions the air going to the grow rooms. On a 38-41 °C (100-105 °F) Michigan summer day the air entering the rooms is still about 10-12 °C (low 50s °F). The used water goes to neighbouring crops and soaks back into the same water table. In winter the same loop heats the water with on-demand and conventional water heaters, so the fresh air arrives at the room set point all year. One more 4-ton unit was expected to run four grow rooms. The farm is clear that this only works because it has abundant cold well water; it does not suit city farms or most rural ones.

  • Cold water through the shelving does not work. Running cold well water through the racks is a common idea. The plumbing is complicated and fragile, and incubating blocks still need large volumes of air moved past them: "It still can't beat that forced reefer unit blasting air." Ground or well cooling can work for the air supply, but at scale forced air from a refrigeration unit wins.
  • Never pipe walk-in cooler air into a grow room. The cooler freezes up quickly.

WHY A precooler works only when its cold source is much colder than the room. Detroit's well water is 12 °C against a 14-16 °C fruit room, and New Hampshire's soil is cold. A cold source can only cool air towards its own temperature, and it only dries the air if it is colder than the outdoor dew point. Shallow ground water usually sits near the yearly average air temperature, so in a hot, humid lowland it may be only a degree or two below the room and above the dew point, and gives little benefit. Measure the water or soil temperature before you build. Where it is too warm, the Coroplast heat exchanger, which uses the room's own cool exhaust air, is the better precooler. (This is general physics rather than growers' experience.)

Evaporative cooling

When water evaporates, it takes heat from the air around it. Misting or fogging a room therefore cools the air as well as wetting it. How much it cools depends almost entirely on how dry the air is to begin with.

RULE In a true desert, use evaporative coolers. Everywhere else, size a refrigerated system. (Cap n Stem)

How it works. Water needs heat to turn into vapour. When fine mist evaporates into air and no heat is added, that heat comes out of the air. The air's total heat content stays the same, but its temperature falls while its humidity rises. The lowest temperature it can reach is the wet-bulb temperature, the point where the air is fully saturated. The worked figures below are standard psychrometric arithmetic (general physics rather than growers' experience) for air going into a room and being misted until it reaches 90% RH.

Air going into the room After misting to 90% RH Lowest possible (wet bulb)
19.7 °C (67.5 °F), 50% RH 14.5 °C (58 °F) 13.5 °C (56 °F)
19.7 °C (67.5 °F), 40% RH 13.0 °C (55 °F) 12.1 °C (54 °F)
19.7 °C (67.5 °F), 60% RH 15.9 °C (61 °F) 14.8 °C (59 °F)
11 °C (52 °F), about 95% RH (straight off a cooling coil in a humid climate) about 11 °C: no drop 10.6 °C (51 °F)
  • A grower's plenum read 19-20 °C (67-68 °F) on a day his grow room read 14 °C (57-58 °F). Part of that gap was humidifier water evaporating in the room; he keeps his plenum near 50% RH. The 50% row of the table matches: evaporation alone explains a drop of about 5 °C (9 °F). Mixing warm supply air with cold room air does not add to it; mixing only blends the two.
  • Dry climates: evaporative cooling is close to free cooling. Pads, wet walls or fog can take a large share of the cooling load, which is why Cap n Stem recommends it for deserts. A southern California farm, where humidity is 30-40% most of the year, uses evaporative cooling to avoid spending heavily on energy, and the dry air may also mean fewer endemic mushroom diseases and pests (though moulds remain). Cap n Stem's first farm, in the high desert of Chino Valley, Arizona, cooled the whole area around its lab with big swamp coolers at the back of a greenhouse clad in metal panels, and it "worked abnormally well".
  • Hot, humid climates: outdoor air is already near saturation, so there is little room for more water to evaporate. A cooling coil has to condense water out of that air, and the air it delivers is nearly saturated and cold, so misting it gives no further drop. The mist still absorbs some of the heat the room picks up after the air comes in (from blocks, lights and walls), but it adds no cooling capacity. Size the refrigerated system as if the humidifier were not there.
  • Never put the humidifier and an AC coil in the same air. A coil that recirculates misted room air condenses the water back out and works harder. (This follows from the physics above rather than from growers' reports.)

TIP A nursery grower's trick for wet walls: run the feed water through black ABS pipe laid in the sun so it arrives warm. Warm water evaporates faster, so the air leaves the wall cooler. A California farm using it measured a 14-17 °C (25-30 °F) drop in its rooms. Talk to nurseries and greenhouse growers: their cooling solutions often transfer.

NOTE Field studies from outside the mushroom sources agree. Greenhouse fogging trials found that temperature falls by part of the gap between the dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures, and the drop grows the drier the incoming air is; reported drops reached about 6-6.6 °C below outside air (Öztürk 2003, Turkish Journal of Agriculture and Forestry 27:49-57; Abdel-Ghany and Kozai 2007, Environmental Control in Biology 45:9).

Fruit-room plenums

AT A GLANCE A plenum is a separate conditioned space that feeds the fruit rooms. Keep it at roughly fruit-room temperature, CO2 at or below about 450 ppm and humidity around 40-50%. Fruit rooms pull from it and exhaust outdoors, never back into it.

  • What it is. The plenum is a separate space (a side room, barn interior, basement, attic or part of a container) conditioned to roughly the fruit-room target. The fruit room draws makeup air from it and exhausts outdoors, never back into the plenum. The plenum's heating and cooling must keep up with the room's air-exchange rate.
  • Its first job is recirculating air through the AC. When a fruit room calls for fresh air, that room's damper opens and CO2-rich air leaves the building.
  • Examples: a whole barn as plenum with a unit recirculating inside it; an AC in an attic ducted down a disused chimney into a basement fruit room; an attic as a cooled plenum feeding filtered, positively pressurized air down into lab and incubation.
  • Size. The plenum need not match the fruit room, but bigger is better: a small plenum needs more outside makeup air and so a bigger AC, and a larger plenum saves money, whatever some farms say. A room not packed full needs fewer air exchanges.
  • Catawba Mushrooms makes a grow room's plenum at least half the grow room's floor area.
  • The plenum can share space with a walk-in cooler or harvest area, but do not store CO2-producing blocks in it or work heavily there. Monitor its CO2 and give it a fresh-air intake.

RULE Keep plenum CO2 at or below about 450 ppm. A room can never get lower than its supply air.

  • Safeguard: a about 250 CFM (425 m³/h) squirrel-cage fan wired to a CO2 controller brings outside air into the plenum. Slightly positive pressure in the plenum is better than negative.
  • Humidify the plenum lightly to about 40-50% RH (a small standing humidifier or a fine mister on low). Then fruit rooms are not fed near-0% air, which causes heavy wall condensation, rotting structure and longer humidifier run times. A typical plenum drawing shows 40-50% RH in the plenum and about 75% in the fruit room, with the jump from 0% marked as the thing to avoid.
  • High Country Fungi conditions a plenum before the grow room, with a large wicking humidifier holding it at about 50% RH; the evaporation also cools the air.
  • Catawba Mushrooms draws plenum air through an 8 in (20 cm) intake into a filter box, and feeds the grow room through an adjustable damper.
  • If the plenum is in a separate building, duct the air across (over or under ground) and make the intake an active fan, since a passive damper cannot pull through a long duct.
  • Avoid a plenum at one end of a room and a heat exchanger at the other (seen at one farm): it creates two different climates.

TIP A plenum mini-split runs on its own thermostat, which reads the temperature at its remote, not in the grow room, so expect the two to differ. One grower's plenum read 19-20 °C (67-68 °F) on a day his grow room read 14 °C (57-58 °F). The gap comes from warm plenum air mixing with the cold room air, how fast that mixing happens, and evaporative cooling from humidifier water. Learn your own offset and set the plenum to suit.

Container farms

  • A container farm can build a small plenum inside the container. Insulating the whole container is mostly unnecessary; insulate only the plenum.
  • Reference container layout: a plenum at the entrance holding a high-efficiency heat pump, a CO2-controlled fresh-air damper fan, a thermostat-controlled 1,000 CFM (1,700 m³/h) variable-speed intake fan into the room and a fully gasketed door; two 700 CFM (1,190 m³/h) CO2-controlled exhaust fans at the far end.
  • A Kansas City farm built its grow room of Coroplast in a windowless interior corner of a warehouse, so the room holds its temperature well. Fresh air comes from outside, and the plan is one mini-split feeding several grow rooms. Its rooms run about 18 °C (64-65 °F), and the growers would like them colder.

Fruit-room pressure and fans

AT A GLANCE Run fruit rooms at negative pressure: a CO2-controlled exhaust fan blows straight outdoors and makeup air comes in from the plenum through a backdraft damper. For a 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) room: 800-1,000 CFM (1,360-1,700 m³/h) CO2 exhaust plus a about 500 CFM (850 m³/h) thermostat exhaust. No circulation fans inside.

RULE Run fruit rooms at negative pressure. An exhaust fan pulls air out to the outdoors and makeup air enters from the plenum through a damper. "Negative" is relative: it means lower pressure than the surrounding building.

WHY A positively pressured fruit room pushes CO2-, spore- and humidity-laden air into the plenum and ruins it. Case: the old Westbrook fruit rooms at Cap n Stem ran positive; their walls bulged and boomed, and smells and spores leaked into incubation.

  • Put a backdraft damper on the intake. It opens when air is pulled and closes to stop room air leaking back.
  • Two exhaust fans placed symmetrically either side of centre give more even one-direction flow, with fewer hot or high-CO2 pockets, than one off-centre fan.
  • No oscillating or circulation fans inside fruit rooms (a cannabis-grower habit). Mushrooms prefer still air between exchanges; many fans dry and stress the fruits.
  • Fruit-room exhaust is hard on fans. Case: opening a full shiitake room released a spore cloud that coated and seized a fan. Keep a backup fan.

Procedure: setting up the air system of a 12 x 24 ft fruit room

  1. Fit an intake from the plenum with a backdraft damper at one end of the room.
  2. Fit a CO2 exhaust fan of 800-1,000 CFM (1,360-1,700 m³/h) at the other end, blowing straight outside. Ideally put it on a speed controller so it modulates about 400-1,000 CFM (680-1,700 m³/h) depending on how full the room is.
  3. Wire the CO2 controller to switch that exhaust on (setpoints in CO2 setpoints).
  4. For temperature, add a separate about 500 CFM (850 m³/h) exhaust fan on a thermostat, with its own damper. Two independent exhausts are easier to wire, redundant and independently controlled. One fan on both a thermostat and a CO2 controller is possible but harder to wire.
  5. Make intake CFM equal to or greater than exhaust CFM. Use a passive intake or variable-speed fans.
  6. Put filter boxes on the intakes (for example AC Infinity 10 in, 25 cm, inline filter boxes), and use dampers to keep the room negative.
  7. Leave out circulation fans inside the room.

CHECK With the exhaust running, air should rush in through the intake damper and the room should sit below the pressure of the surrounding building. A handheld digital manometer reads the difference in pascals; see measuring air and pressure.

RANGE Recommended: an active exhaust fan, the only good way to regulate CO2 and keep the room negative. The cost is that the fan collects spores, and negative pressure, though it makes the most sense, is the hardest arrangement on equipment. Some large growers consider this small-farm "lung" design wrong; it is meant for small farms buying blocks, not for big facilities with large AC systems.

RANGE Recommended: cyclic ("lung") exchange. Run bigger intake and exhaust fans from a CO2 meter. When CO2 is satisfied the fans stop, humidity climbs until the humidifier shuts off, CO2 rises until the exhaust restarts, and humidity drops: a cycle of evaporation and condensation that gives healthier fruit than constant exchange, which strips the room and leaves RH flat around 80-85%. Many large growers run constant exhaust instead. Evidence for cycling: early king oyster failures at Cap n Stem ran 250 CFM (425 m³/h) fans constantly before the farm had CO2 meters, and a French-Canadian grower cleared lion's mane blotch and malformation by switching to cyclic exchange. Exception: for maitake, run a about 500 CFM (850 m³/h) fan continuously in a 12 x 24 ft room (rather than 1,000 CFM) to balance humidity and evaporation, accepting slightly high CO2.

Fan sizing and fan life at working farms

  • Exhaust fans are always undersized (High Country Fungi).
  • High Country Fungi's 16 x 16 ft (4.9 x 4.9 m) room has two 10 in (25 cm) fans of about 700 CFM (1,190 m³/h) each, each on its own speed controller. Both exhausts sit at floor level at the far end of the room and blow out through the same wall, with two reverse-ducted intakes and hooded, dampered vents. The fans run off CO2 controllers, and the CO2 sensor hangs dead centre of the room.
  • High Country Fungi replaces its Hurricane inline fans twice a year, because the wet air wears them out.
  • EC fans (Catawba uses Fantech FKD) are made for speed control and can later be run from a PLC (a programmable logic controller, the small industrial computer that automates a farm).
  • Always exhaust fruit-room air outdoors, for the sake of spore load. Never send it through a filter and back into shared space, because filters are not impervious (Cap n Stem).

Large-room and duct designs

  • Large-room example (a large Pennsylvania farm): a about 30-ton (106 kW) unit feeds a perforated PVC manifold down the room centre, giving smooth, barely perceptible, mostly recirculated airflow. There is no active humidification (wet wood shelving and concrete evaporate enough) and no blotch. The same materials in a small room would not do it.

  • One Canadian container grower's original container used a full-length perforated supply duct with holes increasing in size along it, and a low perforated return. Ductwork clogs with spores in humid air.

  • Check exhaust fans daily. A New Hampshire grower found one stopped because the room "didn't smell right": brown, spore-filled water from the exhaust had run back into the room.

Air for labs, cool-down rooms and spawn rooms

AT A GLANCE No cooling unit or recirculating fan ever goes inside a clean room. Condition air in a pre-filter room or plenum, push it through HEPA filters, throttle the return so the lab stays about 20% positive, and pre-cool about 1 °C (2 °F) extra for every fan and HEPA stage. Lab layout and clean practice are in Chapter 4.

RULE Never put a recirculating AC, mini-split or recirculating fan inside a clean room, lab or cool-down room, even as a stopgap.

WHY Its coil and filter collect particles shed by people and redistribute them. Contamination builds over a grace period, then flourishes. In a small closet lab an internal AC also fights the flow hood. Case: a lab with an AC return duct inside it kept blowing contaminants back, even with a HEPA positive-pressure intake. Growers in that position change steam time, mix or spawn supplier instead of spotting the real cause.

The pre-filter room design

  • Recommended: a pre-filter room behind the hood wall holds the AC supply, with coarse pre-filters on the backs of the hood fans. It runs negative and draws in air through cracks, which is fine, because everything reaching the lab passes through HEPA.
  • HEPA fans must draw from a plenum already conditioned to the target temperature: comfortable for knock rooms, or incubation temperature if mycelium incubates there. All temperature control happens outside the HEPA space. The air path is: AC plenum → HEPA → room → hallway → back to the AC.
  • Ceiling ducts blowing conditioned air down onto flow hoods cause endless contamination, unless the duct connects to the back of the filter.
  • Positive-pressure rooms stress the HVAC, because they push air out constantly. Size the pre-conditioning plenum and the pressure differential together, and make sure the return handles the positive pressure, or fans overheat. Direct the exhaust air deliberately and return it to the conditioning source. An incubation clean room additionally needs its own ventilation for CO2.

Procedure: setting a lab's positive pressure with the return duct

  1. Run a return duct low on the lab side back to the AC. Typical return ducts are 10-20 in (25-50 cm) square.
  2. Make the return adjustable and restricted, so the lab returns less air than the filters supply.
  3. Match the AC supply to the filter flow: for example 100 units each, checked at the filter.
  4. Throttle the return to about 80 units, for about a 20% positive differential. (The 100 and 80 are illustrative units, not a measured flow.)

CHECK An unrestricted return leaves the lab neutral or negative. Confirm the lab is positive with a manometer (see measuring air and pressure), or by a strong rush of air at the exit.

Heat gain through fans and HEPA

  • Fans and HEPA filters add heat: air leaving a 18-19 °C (65-66 °F) room arrives warmer in the next.
  • Examples: pulling 19 °C (66 °F) incubation air through a fan and HEPA into a spawn room gave 20-21 °C (68-70 °F); a 18 °C (64 °F) supply can become 19 °C (66 °F) on arrival.
  • Pre-cool hard in the pre-conditioning space (for example to 16 °C, 60 °F) so the air still lands on target (about 17 °C, 62 °F).

RULE Allow about 1 °C (2 °F) of heat gain through every fan and HEPA stage, and pre-cool accordingly.

Spawn incubation rooms

  • Spawn incubates in a separate positive-pressure room fed through wall filters with fans behind them. The air returns to a pre-conditioning/pre-filter plenum to be re-cooled and re-filtered, rather than using fresh makeup air.
  • Do not put recirculating cooling units inside the spawn room.
  • Supply air high and let it leave low: cold air sinks against the heat of the spawn.
  • Over-pressurized spawn rooms run hotter than expected, since the filter fans add heat.
  • Substrate blocks with filter patches do not need positive-pressure HEPA air, so cooling units can sit in the substrate incubation room and simply recirculate.
  • Shared cooling: a block incubation room's refrigeration can also condition adjoining lab rooms (spawn cool-down, other incubation). These pull air from incubation and return it while staying positive, and HEPA units in the shared wall give free cooling to lab staff and to cooling blocks. This works for labs and incubation, never for fruiting.

Cool-down rooms and hot blocks

  • Blocks come out of the steamer at about 100 °C (212 °F). Exhaust the cool-down room's air outside rather than recirculating it, while the adjacent work room stays about 16 °C (60 °F) and returns its air through transfer grilles to the plenum.
  • For pasteurization, the AC supply goes into a walled pre-cool room, and matched HEPA fan units (for example 3,000 CFM, 5,100 m³/h) carry it into the lab, with the AC return from the lab. Match fan speed and static pressure.
  • Warm pasteurized blocks overheat inoculation rooms in summer. Provide cooling, but not with a unit inside the lab, which creates air plumes.
  • Keep the lab around 18-19 °C (65-66 °F): staff in Tyvek can tolerate it, and above the mid-20s °C (mid-70s °F) a suit is miserable.
  • Case: when a customer began moving hot blocks into the lab, they struggled to cool them, added hoods, and then clogged pre-filters killed their positive pressure. In warm climates, cooling bags outside a clean room is worse, because warm air is drawn in harder.
  • Steam and cool-down practice is covered in Chapter 12.

Air-exchange rate and pressure tuning

  • Air-exchange rate = total HEPA fan CFM / room volume. Example: 800 CFM into a 4 x 4 x 4 ft room (64 cu ft, 1.8 m³) is 800 / 64 = 12.5 exchanges per minute. The same arithmetic applies to fruit rooms.
  • Pressure tuning: "dog doors" (wall holes with adjustable Coroplast flaps) set how much air leaves each room, plus rheostat fan-speed control. Some facilities automate this.

Incubation air

AT A GLANCE Incubation, unlike fruiting, needs plenty of moving air to break up heat and CO2 pockets. Fans blowing 18 °C (64-65 °F) air hold block surfaces at 19 °C (66 °F). Control CO2 with a CO2-triggered exhaust or HRV. The full incubation process is in Chapter 13.

  • Incubation needs a lot of recirculating air. With 4.6 m (15 ft) ceilings stratification is huge, for example 16 °C (60 °F) at the bottom and 27 °C (80 °F) at the top, giving bad blocks top and bottom.
  • Oscillating fans help break up stratified pockets, and sealed bags do not dry much if room CO2 is steady.

CHECK Signs of stratification: same strain, batch and day, but top-shelf bags are dense, swollen with liquid and starting stroma while bottom bags are still patchy.

  • Fans barely reach a block insulated by its neighbours. Five 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks deep get very hot in the middle; 4-5 lb (1.8-2.3 kg) blocks far less.
  • The interior of racks is always the hardest place to ventilate, but lab-like gushing airflow seems to harm shiitake buckling. Aim for just enough movement for even temperature and CO2.
  • Fans blowing 18 °C (64-65 °F) air hold block exteriors at 19 °C (66 °F). Denser substrate needs stronger cooling fans and a slightly lower temperature; looser, leaner mixes tolerate 20-21 °C (68-69 °F) ambient.
  • Case: an upstate New York farm's incubation room was packed solid with no fans. Don't do this.

WHY "No circulation fans" applies to fruit rooms, while substrate incubation needs them. That is a difference of purpose, not a contradiction: fruit bodies want still air, and dense incubation racks need heat pockets broken up.

Advice from working farms:

  • Put fans in incubation (Catawba Mushrooms). A mini-split should sit at the front or rear of the room and push air down its length, rather than blow straight over the racks. Fans help break up temperature and CO2 layering, and a damper intake from the plenum, or a portable AC on the far side venting outdoors, can purge CO2.
  • High Country Fungi keeps incubation simple: air-condition the room and monitor CO2.
  • Cap n Stem lets incubation recirculate through its mini-splits, which is the biggest energy saving available, and pulls in no fresh air. The room is kept just slightly negative, so CO2 leaves only through door leakage or a CO2-triggered exhaust (around 3,000 ppm) and never flows back into clean areas. A normal door leaks enough oxygen.
  • Put fans in tight incubation rooms, overhead or blowing corner to corner. CO2 doesn't simply sink but hangs in pockets "like a ghost" and has to be mixed. Mushroom mycelium wants rapid air movement, unlike what cannabis growers expect (Cap n Stem).
  • A second, backup cooling unit in incubation is a good idea (Cap n Stem).
  • A small-farm example: a basement incubation room on one 1 ton (12,000 BTU/h, 3.5 kW) mini-split held about 17 °C (63 °F) in summer, with outdoor air at 24-27 °C (75-80 °F) and 80% RH, helped by the dehumidifier in the plenum.

HRVs and makeup air in incubation

  • Incubation CO2 control needs an exhaust or makeup fan, ideally an HRV (heat-recovery ventilator; an ERV, energy-recovery ventilator, also works) that swaps room air for outside air while exchanging heat, triggered by a CO2 controller. A typical setup drawing shows an HRV with its duct and fan, and the CO2 band 1,500-3,500 ppm.
  • Treat incubation as a slow fruiting room where CO2 and heat are what you manage.
  • Makeup air can come from a cooler, lower-CO2 part of the building rather than from hot outside air.

WARNING Without an evacuation system already in place, a cooling shortfall on the hottest days leads to the heat-CO2 spiral and bad blocks.

Heat recovery: the Coroplast heat exchanger

AT A GLANCE A Coroplast heat exchanger (CHE) is a washable stack of fluted plastic sheets that lets warm, spore-laden exhaust air pre-heat (or pre-cool) incoming fresh air without mixing. Coroplast costs about $9 a sheet. Wash it every other day. Its about 85% recovery figure is unconfirmed.

  • Origin. The design comes from a Canadian container grower and was explained in a recorded interview.
  • What it is. A stack of fluted 4 x 8 ft (1.2 x 2.4 m) Coroplast sheets with alternate layers blocked. Return air (rich in CO2 and spores) runs one way and fresh intake air the other, trading heat without mixing.
  • Why not a commercial exchanger. Fruit-room spore load clogs metal-fin units within hours, and they cannot be flushed. The Coroplast stack can be washed.
  • Without an exchanger you can simply duct in makeup air with a CO2 meter in the plenum, and duct the exhaust out. It works, just less efficiently.

Procedure: building a Coroplast heat exchanger

  1. Cut full 4 x 8 ft (1.2 x 2.4 m) sheets and shorter sheets. Coroplast costs about $9 a sheet.
  2. Make "sandwiches" with spacer strips (PVC lumber or composite decking) at the edges. Hot glue holds surprisingly well; Gorilla-type glues are also fine.
  3. Alternate full sheets and sandwiches, and stack to the required width.
  4. Set up the air paths: odd layers carry return air from a duct at the top down through the flutes and out the bottom; even layers (open at the sides, blocked at the top on the far side) carry fresh air up from the bottom and out the top into a duct to the plenum or room.
  5. Size the stack: add up the flute cross-section and match it to fan CFM (for example a 500 CFM, 850 m³/h, intake), return airflow and room volume. The original unit had about 30 sheets; units the same designer built for a large farm were about 80 sheets thick. A bigger stack carries more air and can serve a larger room or two rooms.
  6. Stand it vertical: cold dry air enters low, and warm humid air enters high and travels down, which also helps wash-down. Laid on its side it loses that long runway.
  7. In cold climates, build it from black Coroplast and shield the intake sections.
  8. Install it outside the container on cinder blocks over a pit of gravel or sand.
  9. Fit a bottom baffle that turns the exhaust (which leaves low so spores drop out) back up and away, so it is not drawn into the fresh intake.

CHECK Every other day, lift the top flap and pressure-wash the flutes so spores wash down into the gravel.

What it saves

  • Worked example: -18 °C (0 °F) outside, 16-21 °C (60-70 °F) return air and about 85% recovery give incoming air of around 10 °C (50 °F). Only about 6 °C (10 °F) of extra heat is then needed, from a small heater. In summer the same works for cooling, with a small AC on the outside of the plenum.

RANGE Treat the performance figures as estimates. The about 85% recovery figure is second-hand and uncertain, and the saving from a $1,000 to about $200 monthly conditioning bill is a hypothetical, not a measurement.

Fitting it to a container

  • Retrofit to the reference container: put the exchanger where the CO2-controlled fresh-air damper is, duct its fresh outlet into the plenum, remove the rear exhaust fans and run a full return duct from the back of the room to the exchanger.
  • The original design only works with a hydrofogger in the plenum. His constant cross-draft exchanged the room air about every 6 minutes. When its designer tried a plain humidifier at one point, the cross-breeze trapped humidity in a local bubble and the room stratified. The layout runs CHE → plenum (heat, humidity) → fruiting container, with a top supply duct and a floor return.
  • Adaptation for high-pressure fog: take CO2-rich return air from the back of the room into the exchanger, and deliver fresh air through an elbow pointing down near the door, setting up a rolling vortex down the room. Put the fog nozzle near the door so the air carries the humidity evenly. This was worked out with one farm.
  • Duct-fed high-pressure misting causes uneven saturation.

Humidification

AT A GLANCE Most unexplained blotch at scale comes from the humidifier, not the spawn or blocks. "Proper" humidification means fine mist, in-line filtered and treated water, no recirculated room air, and accurate measurement. Keep ultrasonic units outside the room. Dose humidifier water with 150-250 ppm bleach or ClO2. Hart settings: air 80-85 psi, water about 25 psi, 1-2 heads per 12 x 24 ft room. Fruiting humidity targets are in Chapter 14; blotch itself is in Chapter 17.

What good humidification means

  • "Proper humidification" means four things: fine mist, in-line filtered water, no recirculation of room air, and accurate measurement.
  • As you scale, unexplained blotch and contamination often trace to the fruiting-room humidifier rather than to the spawn or block supplier. When blotch gets out of hand it is usually the humidification method: where the air comes from and how it is filtered, and where the water comes from and how it is treated.
  • Fine atomization gives a "dry fog" that evaporates rather than pooling. Controlling the atomization rate is what makes the other treatments work, because it raises the threshold at which condensation collects; the room feels dry. Standing water always causes problems.
  • Example: in a room run by a coarse fogger the fog is so dense the shelves are barely visible, and a hand held in the stream gets wet. In a room run by a Hart high-pressure system, a hand in the stream does not get wet.
  • Cold air holds less moisture, so unchanged humidification causes condensation on the fruit: mildly, mycelium growing from caps; worse, bacteria and rose comb. Use finer atomization.
  • Yellowing on oyster caps is a key indicator of poor humidification and early blotch. Case: in a fogger room, a block near the humidifier had succumbed.
  • At $600-700 for a fogger you may as well buy a high-pressure fog system; it is not overkill even for tent growers. Dumping untreated city water into a humidifier is asking for blotch, and a about $500 upgrade pays back fast.

  • Steam is not mist. A Maine farm once ran a hose from a sauna steamer straight into a fruit room. It was far too hot, and the steam condensed and soaked everything. Standard: steam used for humidity goes through a fine atomizer so it saturates the air without wetting surfaces (Humidifier options); a bare steam hose into the room is the failure case.
  • Low-pressure misters make water. The same Maine farm's first fruit rooms used low-pressure misters that put a lot of water on the floor. The floors sloped to buckets with float-valve pumps, which stuck and overflowed, flooding the floor below many times.
  • Grow-shop atomizers belong outside the room. Atomizing humidifiers made for indoor plant growing are wrecked by mushroom spores. Put them outside the room and duct the mist in.
  • A Hart-type system as a first-room system. A Kansas City farm running a high-pressure fog system found it took time to dial in, with many nozzles and settings, but it shows how much control is possible and worked far better than humidifier tubs in its tents, which grew a jelly-like slime that had to be scraped off. Tents are hard to clean, and keeping blotch down in them took effort.
  • Mushrooms use about 2.6 L of water per kilogram of crop (0.7 gal per lb), humidification included, against roughly 15,900 L per kilogram (1,900 gal per lb) for beef.

Ultrasonic units: placement and fixes

  • Keep ultrasonic humidifiers outside the fruit room. Inside, they humidify dirty room air and blow it over the crop; recirculation is the worst case.
  • Feed the vat with a about $2 float valve, and put a coarse replaceable filter on the air intake.
  • An untreated fogger is one of the biggest bacterial vectors, and the usual cause of weekly "I have bacterial blotch" calls.
  • If the drum must be inside, duct its intake to outside air so it pushes fresh humidified air in. This is the same logic as avoiding a recirculating AC in a lab.
  • Case and fix: a Vermont farm had a Hydrofogger inside the room. Fix: box off a corner with Coroplast and a wall vent, and duct the Hydrofogger up and out into the room so it draws from the box. Optionally filter the box intake against insects. Make the unit easy to pull out and clean, and add bleach if cleaning daily.
  • Case: at Medlock's farm, ultrasonic discs in a barrel under a tarp ran condensate back into the barrel and concentrated particulates. Rose comb became so bad that every species except chestnut grew inverted caps.

CASE A West Virginia grower stopped fog falling out of the air by releasing it high and evenly. The fog first mixed in a 200 L (55 gal) plastic drum holding about 38 L (10 gal) of water and plenty of headspace, fed by a five-disc ultrasonic fogger ("more than enough"). From the drum it entered the room through a 15 cm (6 in) galvanized pipe near the ceiling, drilled with many holes, so the humidity spread instead of "dumping like a waterfall". The CO2 exhaust was the same perforated pipe standing upright in the middle of the room, pulling evenly from every corner, and a plenum above dropped dry air in. The result was almost no visible fog and dry floors ("I like to be able to walk into my grow in socks"). He also ran a slow fan through washable filters, changed every couple of days, to cut the spore load, and avoided strong airflow on the crop because it deforms lion's mane.

The Hart high-pressure system

Components. A cigarette-pack-sized "drip-free" stainless mixing box in the room, a 12 V solenoid valve, a compressed-air input, a pressurized water input, a ball valve to tune water flow, and screw-in misting heads with different spray patterns. It fires a dry fog from a top corner when the humidity controller calls; a hand held in front barely gets wet. New Hampshire Mushroom Co., Madison Valley Mushrooms (unverified) and Far West Fungi use it. A typical installation shows the mixing box with its water (H2O) and air inputs and 12 V solenoid, later with a peristaltic pump loop dosing bleach or ClO2 into the water.

Setting Value Conditions

Water pressure about 25 psi (1.7 bar) Works across 5-30 psi (0.3-2.1 bar).
Heads per room 1-2 heads For a 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) room.
Compressor about 26 gal (98 L), about 4.5 SCFM (standard cubic feet of air per minute; 127 L/min) minimum, running 50% of the time or less See the RANGE below for larger sizing.

RANGE Compressor for a high-pressure fog system. Standard (Cap n Stem): a rotary compressor of about 100 L (26 gal) and about 4.5 SCFM is the suggested minimum for one small room. Context: many nozzles or several rooms need far more air. One Texas farm's nozzle plan needed about 40 CFM, far beyond a hardware-store rotary compressor of about 10 CFM, which is also probably not rated for continuous running; Catawba Mushrooms sizes about 5 HP with a tank of 300 L (80 gal) or more. Other growers have had to rebuild an old piston compressor's motor every year, and a Dutch consultant recommends a screw compressor for large systems.

  • The same Texas farm's humidifier history shows the usual path: ultrasonic discs (2, then 12, then 24 discs), carbonator pumps at about 150 psi (10 bar), then commercial foggers from the cannabis trade, with a cheap paint-sprayer nozzle suggested as a test of air-atomizing.

Procedure: plumbing a Hart system

  1. Water line: run 1/2 in (or 3/4 in) PEX to the room. Copper also works.
  2. Fit a ball valve for service isolation.
  3. Reduce to about 1/4-3/8 in.
  4. Fit a filter housing, which doubles as a reservoir.
  5. Fit a push-and-set pressure regulator; set water to about 25 psi (1.7 bar).
  6. Run 5/16 in ID x 7/16 in OD (about 8 x 11 mm) tubing and barbs to the mixing box.
  7. Air line: compressor (about 90 psi, 6.2 bar) → quick-disconnect → union → air regulator → union → solenoid → union.
  8. Set the air regulator to about 80-85 psi (5.5-5.9 bar).
  9. Mount the controller, air filter/regulator, solenoid and water filter on one plywood board for easy service.

WHY The unions let you swap the regulator and solenoid, the parts most likely to fail. The solenoid is the only electrically controlled part: when it opens, air rushes through and draws water to the nozzle.

CHECK When the controller calls, a dry fog should fire from the top corner, and a hand held in front should barely get wet.

  • Nozzles: they come in two micron sizes. Clean clogged ones by soaking them in vinegar, and swap in a spare. Units are reported running 8-10 years.
  • Compressor: it need not be huge. One demonstration used a Kobalt about 26 gal (98 L), about 4.5 SCFM unit, the suggested minimum. Size it to run 50% of the time or less; extra tank volume helps. A rotary compressor at about $300-500 is another suggestion.
  • Costs: heads about $300 each (unconfirmed); a Hart kit about $400-500; a Pola controller about $400; plus the compressor, which is useful for other things.
  • Case: One farm had chronic blotch, tried ClO2 and H2O2 sprays, and the blotch went away after installing Hart. If blotch persists with this system, check the water source (see water for humidifiers).
  • Catawba Mushrooms recommends Hart Environmental over hydrofoggers to reduce blotch risk. With other humidifiers, it recommends a Pola HP57 humidistat with a wet/dry bulb sensor (sold by Far West Fungi).
  • High Country Fungi used a Hart system on an air compressor but burned out a compressor from overwork. It now rates the TAC misting system (from California) as superior, and would use Hart only if TAC isn't available. It also found the air had to be dehumidified before its mister would switch on.
  • Hart has had the market almost to itself (sales were described as about US$1 million in a year), and its makers have been slow to address compressor failures.

RANGE Recommended: a TAC misting system first, because it needs no compressor and compressor burn-outs are the main Hart failure. Hart is the proven alternative and has cleared blotch on several farms; if you choose it, size the compressor generously (next RANGE). Avoid foggers and ultrasonic barrels for routine fruiting. See Chapter 25.

RANGE Compressor size. Recommended minimum: about 4.5 SCFM (127 L/min) on a about 26 gal (98 L) tank, sized to run 50% of the time or less. Catawba Mushrooms says the compressor needs about 5 HP (3.7 kW) and an 80+ gal (300+ L) tank; given the compressor burn-outs reported by other farms (three at one North Carolina farm, one at High Country Fungi), err large. See Chapter 25.

RANGE Nozzle size is uncertain. The finest Hart nozzle is quoted as roughly "0.022" (units not stated) in one source and about 0.03 micron in another, both unconfirmed; the steam atomizer is put at about 0.3 micron (unconfirmed). Treat all three as unverified.

Humidity controllers and sensors

  • Cheap digital controllers (Inkbird) fail within a couple of months. The most accurate method is the old wet-bulb/dry-bulb sensor. A combined temperature/RH controller from an Italian company (name not given) also exists.
  • Pola HP57 (confirm the model number with the supplier): a combined temperature and humidity controller using a wet/dry-bulb sensor, a small hanging water vat with a wick tube. The wet bulb gives 0-100% RH; the dry bulb gives temperature (roughly 10 to about 49 °C, 50 to about 120 °F). "Oldest technology is the best": it is more accurate and cleanable than cheap electronic sensors.
  • Mount the Pola sensor as far from the misting nozzle as possible, typically in a ceiling corner, and keep it clean. Example: with the door open, its display read "66.4H" and the system immediately called for humidity.
  • Coarse fogger droplets make ordinary hygrometers inaccurate (one grower's claim).
  • A Pola HP57 controller is just a two-wire relay switching on and off, so a mister with a digital sensor can usually be spliced into one (Cap n Stem).
  • Give each Inkbird controller a second, independent sensor, so a drifting probe gets caught. Govee sensors work well. Use a gel humidity protector on exposed circuits (High Country Fungi).

Pola wiring as narrated (unverified: check the real wiring diagram before copying this):

Wet bulb red/black 1 and 2
Solenoid hot 6, with a jumper from 7 to the plug's hot (black)

  • The solenoid leads were unmarked and found by trial. The person wiring it is colour-blind and matched brown to red and blue to black at the sensor junction.
  • Seal controller and sensor boxes against humidity: silicone in the gland grooves, cable glands or flex conduit, and cover screws tightened evenly. The board is as sensitive as an Arduino.

RANGE Recommended: control humidity from a humidistat (ideally a wet/dry-bulb controller), not a timer. Timers (for example 30 min on/10 off) run humidity very high and worsen blotch as temperature rises. As a budget stopgap, a cycle timer on a fogger (adjustable from seconds to hours, for example 10 min on/20 s off in the driest season) can work if checked often, because the seasons change the load.

  • Not every small room needs a humidistat, but every room needs a CO2 meter. A Florida farm found a phone-linked humidistat drove it to distraction with alerts at 3 a.m. ("only 55% in chamber 2") and dropped it with relief. Cap n Stem's minimum kit for a small room is a CO2 meter, without which nothing else can be set. Its own recommendation for running misting is still a wet/dry-bulb humidistat, the most accurate control; read the Florida story as "a small room can manage without one".
  • Controls that work together. Custom mushroom controllers let heating, cooling, humidification and CO2 equipment work together in ways off-the-shelf or proprietary units can't. Many products sold at indoor-farming trade shows, such as fabric duct socks and poor humidifiers, are inefficient for mushrooms.
  • VPD control. A West Virginia grower switched to controllers that run on vapour pressure deficit (VPD) instead of relative humidity, because VPD allows for air temperature: an RH target set for 18 °C (65 °F) is too wet when the room falls to 9-10 °C (48-50 °F) at night. Plant VPD controllers cover a wide range, but mushrooms sit at the very wet end, so they need finer steps than 0.1.

Water for humidifiers

RULE Filter and treat humidifier water. High-pressure misting heads, Hydrofoggers and ultrasonic vats all foul with sediment and minerals.

  • Treatment chain for all incoming water: physical filter → softener (if the water is hard) → carbon scrub. The fruiting branch then adds RO (reverse osmosis) or steam. Problems arise when any stage fails: a softener skipped, a poor filter, a broken RO unit, steam spitting water on fruit. Boiler-side water treatment is in Chapter 12.
  • Why: young primordia draw water from the block, but developing fruits react to the humidity in the air, so sediment and microbes in humidifier water affect them. Blotch and rose comb come from the humidity, not the block. Blotch moves in water droplets: it is practically waterborne rather than airborne.
  • RO is the best, if semi-wasteful, fix for blotch and rose comb. It wastes roughly 2 gal per 1 gal produced (unconfirmed), and the reject water is mineral-rich.
  • Inline UV is the cheapest good first line, sized by gallons per hour. It is non-chemical and not equivalent to bleach. It is mainly worthwhile for deep wells; city water has a low microbial load.
  • Disinfect the water: 150-250 ppm bleach in the fogger vat is standard at large farms; ClO2 is an organic-certifiable alternative. Dose with a peristaltic pump (like an IV pump, $30-200; about $50 on Amazon) into the small auto-fill line, calculating the dose from the bleach label. A typical teaching board for this reads "150-250 ppm BLEACH (ClO2)" on the drum, names the blotch bacterium (Pseudomonas tolaasii), and crosses out Lysol and peroxide.
  • Use multiple barriers: treat the water before the fogger's auto-fill bucket, and filter the intake air.
  • Even with filtration plus steam or RO, farms often still add bleach, peroxide or non-activated ClO2.
  • Case: A New Jersey farm on a shallow dug well fixed persistent blotch by injecting hydrogen peroxide (or ClO2) into the humidifier line.
  • Case: A small grower in North Carolina dumped and cleaned a 10 gal (38 L) reservoir every 3 days and refilled it with water plus 1.5 quarts (1.4 L) of 3% drugstore peroxide, giving about 0.1% H2O2, which is about ideal. Their decimated blocks recovered within about two weeks.

WARNING Peroxide is a treatment, not a fix. The root causes are water and air filtration, drainage, trapped drains, negative pressure and humidifier design.

RANGE Standard standing dose: bleach (150-250 ppm) or ClO2. Context: in an outbreak, about 0.1% hydrogen peroxide for a short time is a proven rescue and is listed among standard humidifier treatments. One older source said not to dose fogger water with Lysol, hydrogen peroxide, Pine-Sol or vinegar, calling peroxide a no-go without giving a reason.

CASE A grower's lion's mane began forming hundreds of small mounds, some of which turned to bacteria, and his blue oysters became blotchy. He checked water filtration, light, evaporation, black and clear bags, airflow and cleaning products before finding the cause: the UV lamp treating the humidifier water had burned out. A new lamp killed the bacteria in the water and both crops returned to normal. Lion's mane pulling away from the substrate has been traced to the same water-and-bacteria cause. Check UV bulbs on a schedule. Problems differ by water source (well, chlorinated city water, run-off, drought), and farms that don't treat water suffer crop loss after crop loss.

CO2 control

AT A GLANCE Automate CO2 first. A CO2 controller switches the exhaust or intake fans between a fan-on and a fan-off level. Fruit rooms: fan on about 900 ppm, off about 450-600 ppm, 1,000 ppm absolute max. Incubation: 1,500-3,000 ppm, never above 5,000 ppm. Plenum: at or below about 450 ppm.

RULE Automate CO2 first. It is the number one thing to automate, and essential once you have several rooms or want a holiday. A fruit room without a CO2 meter is unacceptable: every fruit room needs a controller to switch its fresh-air fans.

  • Case: without a CO2 controller, rooms produce deformed fruit, such as a single about 4 lb (1.8 kg) black oyster "washer".
  • Do not trust your senses ("I can feel it") or "the mushrooms will tell me". CO2 cannot be set by a fixed exhaust rate, because CO2 output changes with block age, and a fan running constantly wastes conditioned plenum air when the room is half empty.

The controller

  • Recommended meter: the CO2Meter.com square "Grow Room Controller" (model RAD-0501). It tolerates humidity and spore load, reads high ranges, and switches an exhaust or intake fan on a differential (the gap between its fan-on and fan-off levels). It is the only meter Cap n Stem recommends, and the same unit serves plenum, fruit room and incubation.

  • Example display: the unit reads the room's current level (for example 650 ppm) and holds a "Lo" setpoint (for example 800 ppm).

  • It uses cannabis terms. "Veg" mode (wide differential, high ppm) suits incubation; use veg mode to reach incubation setpoints. "Flower" mode (narrow differential, low ppm) suits fruiting.

  • Price: About $230-300 (about $300 in one source, about $230-250 in another).

  • Move as much fresh air as you can while holding temperature. A New Hampshire grower's rule for fresh air is to move the most air through the room that the cooling can keep at temperature. A room holding several weeks of blocks has to find a middle setting, because what suits blocks on their first day of fruiting (high humidity, some CO2) is wrong for blocks on their last. The one item he tells new farms to buy is a CO2 meter wired to the exhaust fan, so the fan switches on automatically and the room breathes like a lung.
