Plenum at or below about 450 The supply limits the room's low point.
Substrate incubation, recommended about 3,000 about 2,000-2,500 2,000-3,000 band.
Substrate incubation about 3,500 about 1,500 With an HRV; well under 5,000.
Substrate incubation 4,000 2,500 "Veg" mode example.
Substrate incubation room 1,500-3,000 ideal Lower causes problems; higher means more heat and unsafe air.
Substrate incubation (Cap n Stem) exhaust at about 3,000 Room kept slightly negative.
Shiitake incubation room about 2,500 ideal max 5,000

RANGE Fruit rooms: standard exhaust on at 900 ppm, off at 600 ppm, with 1,000 ppm the absolute maximum (a cycle of roughly 450-900 ppm). Other figures: a low end of about 450-500 ppm, a 400-900 band, and a 400-1,000 band (the last possibly a slip for the fan's CFM range); working farms run 1,000 on/600 off or hold about 600. Incubation: standard exhaust on at 3,000 ppm, off at 1,500-2,500 ppm depending on how much CO2 you tolerate; bands in use range from 1,500-3,500 ppm (with an HRV) to 2,000-4,000 ppm (a "veg" mode example).

  • 20,000 ppm of CO2 sounds like a lot until you breathe on a CO2 meter and see how much CO2 your own breath carries.

Incubation CO2 and safety

  • In incubation, room CO2 around the bags should stay no higher than about 2,500-3,000 ppm (in-bag levels are much higher). Above that, metabolism goes haywire and staff get uncomfortable.
  • A too-wide swing drives metabolic heat, so set a fairly narrow band.
  • CO2 safety: the OSHA workplace reference is 5,000 ppm (time-weighted). 10,000 ppm is a range where some organisms' cells die.
  • Case: Cap n Stem's old Westbrook farm once ran about 7,000 ppm in incubation, and staff napped on the incubation scaffolding as well as on a couch.
  • During a power outage CO2 climbs fast, because blocks keep respiring with no exhaust. Plan for power cuts: CO2, not just temperature, is the risk when fans stop.
  • Monitor CO2 where people work. Case: a staffer who slept overnight on a couch in the incubation room (its warmest spot) had sleep paralysis with a loud buzzing "presence". CO2 was the likely cause, and there was no meter in incubation.

WARNING Never sleep in incubation. Put a CO2 meter in every room where people work.

  • Lion's mane: a too-wide differential, or a fan outage, gives uneven maturity ("dreadlocks"). It recovers within about a day once fixed.

Power cuts, alarms and backup

AT A GLANCE Blocks keep making heat when the power goes off, so a room without cooling warms up fast, and a failure on a summer day can cost weeks of production. Fit alarms to coolers and rooms, decide in advance what a generator will run, and never leave a farm unattended in peak season.

  • How fast it goes wrong. Most growers don't realize how fast rooms heat up until the first power cut. A late failure on a 10-week shiitake run wastes the whole pipeline; a fast crop loses about two weeks. A room packed with blocks is "a recipe for disaster" when anything fails, and one California farm has taken calls on New Year's Eve that a chiller, pump or air handler was down with tens of thousands of dollars of crop at stake. No amount of money buys complete redundancy.
  • Decide what to save. In a big Pennsylvania farming district, summer power cuts are routine on days above 32 °C (90 °F), with hundreds of farms running 25-30 ton cooling units on the grid. Before it had enough generators, one farm towed a portable generator around at night, hooked up backup air conditioners and iced down cooling coils, gambling on whether an outage would last three hours or three days. Decide where a generator does the most good and save the rooms producing the most heat. That farm now has a large generator and is paid to come off the grid during summer peaks.
  • Cold weather can help. During a three-day winter outage at about -18 °C (0 °F), Cap n Stem held incubation at 19 °C (66 °F) by opening doors, and ran a generator only for the cryogenic culture freezer.
  • What a failure does to the crop. A California farm that has lost power six or seven times, with no generator, found its starved fruit rooms grew long stems with small caps, like trumpets; it sold them to chefs as "trumpet blues".

CASE A Maine farm kept US$20,000-40,000 of mushrooms in its cooler, and the owner drove to the farm up to five times a night to check the cooler door. After one cooler failure he put alarms on everything; each failure happened once, never twice. It also meant he could never be more than about 16 km (10 miles) from the farm, and the fatigue ended in a car accident. Alarms that reach your phone let you sleep.

CASE The one time a Colorado grower took a holiday in season, the humidistat stuck on and humidified non-stop. The mushrooms were sopping wet, and a new employee who had run out of boxes packed 9 kg (20 lb) of wet oysters into hardware-store moving boxes. Never be away in season without someone trained to check every control.

Monitoring and measurement

AT A GLANCE Measure CO2, temperature and humidity, and trust no single instrument: check every controller against an independent logger. Temperature matters most. Use loggers inside bags to diagnose uneven growth, a manometer for room pressure, an anemometer for hood airflow (about 90 ft/min, 0.45 m/s), and agar plates to find where contamination comes from.

What to measure, and why records matter

  • The key data points are CO2, temperature and humidity. Temperature is the most important one (for sterilization, incubation and shipping).
  • Data rarely gives guaranteed answers except to prescribed questions, but it grounds diagnosis.
  • Most farms keep few operational records, and start only after certification or a disaster. Graphs engage technically minded staff and give them ownership, and at scale data is a check that SOPs (standard operating procedures) alone do not provide.
  • Keep backup instruments, because data can be wrong. A handheld IR thermometer can read 29-35 °C (84.6-95.4 °F) on the same forehead, but it is fine for spot checks in incubation rooms and for confirming blocks are above 93 °C (200 °F) when a steam chamber opens.

Temperature loggers

  • MadgeTech loggers (models, prices and steam use are in Chapter 12) also serve climate monitoring: verify room thermostats against a logger; log temperature inside bags versus outside; place one in a shiitake block for its full about 3-month incubation and through fruiting. MadgeTech also sells humidity and gas loggers.
  • Seal a logger or thermocouple inside a bag at inoculation to watch the internal temperature surge, then fall. G1 bags started from an agar wedge make no heat at first, but later make nearly as much per pound as heavily spawned bags. Loggers can also ride in colonizing grain or substrate bags, and in fruiting blocks.

TIP Mark the logger bag unmistakably (a white paint marker, a big black X). Case: one farm's crew inoculated the logger bag, mixed it in with the rest, and three days later broke open every block without finding it. Better to fruit them and look later, or buy another logger.

CASE Uneven substrate incubation: one corridor cold and the next hot (14, 16 and 21 °C, 58, 60 and 69 °F, measured against a about 19 °C, 66-67 °F, set point). The cold spots slowed chestnut and pioppino, costing pioppino about a week. People first blamed the spawn; the cause was supplemental AC ducting, not the Heatcraft units. Lesson: log before you blame suppliers.

  • Handheld IR thermometers jump around: 29-35 °C (84.6-95.4 °F) on one forehead, and 34, 28, 28, 24 and 25 °C (93, 82, 83, 76 and 77 °F) in another quick test. They are as unreliable as a type K readout, but fine for spot checks walking incubation rooms.
  • Cheap type K loggers (about $150) give absurd readings with a frayed lead, and their probes break after about 10 uses.

Shipping temperature

  • Temperature is the variable that always bites when shipping spawn, blocks, cultures or fresh mushrooms. Keep substrate under 27 °C (80 °F) in transit. Refrigerated freight, and vented cartons with air channels down the pallet, keep blocks longer.
  • Box test: spawn with gel packs in an insulated box, left out over a weekend, held temperature well. Gel packs chill, then buffer, then give out, so heat stress usually comes at the end.
  • Pre-chill spawn before shipping, because packed, active spawn heats itself, and ship fast. Cap n Stem pre-cools spawn in 40 ft (12.2 m) refrigerated containers; home-built cold rooms are less even.

Measuring air and pressure

  • Room pressure: differentials are measured in pascals with a handheld digital manometer (two tubes, one per room). For a single room, a strong rush of air at the exit is enough.
  • Flow-hood face velocity: target about 90 ft/min (about 0.45 m/s), checked routinely with a vane anemometer. Example: one big hood read about 126 ft/min (0.64 m/s) near the filter and 90-130 ft/min (0.46-0.66 m/s) across the working zone, falling sharply at the edges.
  • One hood has a static-pressure gauge on the filter's back pressure and automatically raises motor speed to hold 90 ft/min. Rising pressure means the filters are loading.
  • A cheap (about $30) particle counter held in front of a filter is a quick check. Simply walking into a room can spike one to about 900.
  • Incense smoke or tied ribbons show laminarity (smooth, one-direction flow). The lighter-flame trick shows flow but nothing about contamination. Pushing smoke through your filters is not advised, nor is the old joke of smoking a cigarette in a fruit room to judge air exchange.

Procedure: plate test for airborne contamination

  1. Expose open agar plates in front of the filter and around the room: 30 s to 2 min, or 15-20 min on the work surface, or a whole day to catch occasional shedding.
  2. At Cap n Stem, plate doorways, vents and room corners about every 6 months; the outflow "dog door" is the best spot. Do it when nobody is working.
  3. Close and incubate the plates, then map where growth appears.

CHECK Clean plates in front of the filter mean the filter is sound. Plates are cheap; filters are not.

Procedure: cool-down air-path test

  1. Seal some bags before cooking (optionally with a logger inside).
  2. Cook and cool them with the batch.
  3. Incubate them unopened.

CHECK Any growth means the air drawn into the bags as they cooled is contaminated.

  • Prevention routine: track contamination by season; check airflow and pressure; change pre-filters and filters; clean ducts; recheck after any change.
  • Keep compost piles far from air intakes. Case: intermittent Neurospora at Cascadia came from a compost mound near the fruit room's ducts. Neurospora has also been seen growing on the backs of filters. See Chapter 16.

Maintenance

AT A GLANCE Fans, ducts, coils, filters, heat exchangers and nozzles all load up with spores. Clean on a schedule, and treat a noisy fan as a warning.

  • Fans and ducts are the worst things to clean. Spray or wipe fans regularly, or it becomes a big job. A noisy fan is often the first sign of failure. Cleanliness protects the machinery as well as the crop.
  • A conventional recirculating HVAC system inside a fruit room clogs fast: a $30,000 unit could be dead within about a month.
Item Task How often
Coroplast heat exchanger Lift the flap and pressure-wash the flutes Every other day
Return-duct filters in large rooms Clean Daily
Coarse pre-filters on evaporator returns and heaters Swap As spores load them
Hart nozzles Soak clogged ones in vinegar; keep a spare When clogged
Ultrasonic humidifier domes Clean Constantly
Fans Spray or wipe Regularly
Inline fans in wet exhaust (High Country Fungi) Replace Twice a year
Agar plate check of doorways, vents, corners Plate and incubate About every 6 months

Key rules

  1. Plan for cooling first; at scale, incubation needs no heating at all.

  2. Use walk-in evaporator units with outdoor condensers for incubation and anything below about 20 °C (68 °F); mini-splits suit small, temperate fruiting setups.

  3. Never put a recirculating coil, AC or fan inside a fruit room, lab or cool-down room; condition air in a plenum or pre-filter room instead.

  4. Keep fruit rooms negative: CO2-controlled exhaust out, damper-fed plenum air in, no circulation fans.

  5. Keep plenum CO2 at or below about 450 ppm and its humidity around 40-50%.

  6. Buy a CO2 controller for every fruit room and incubation room; fruit at roughly 450-900 ppm, incubate at roughly 1,500-3,000 ppm, never above 5,000.

  7. Allow about 1 °C (2 °F) of heat gain through every fan and HEPA stage, and pre-cool accordingly.

  8. Humidify with fine, filtered, treated, non-recirculated mist; move ultrasonic units outside the room and dose their water (150-250 ppm bleach or ClO2).

  9. Measure humidity with a wet/dry-bulb controller, not a cheap electronic sensor, and site it away from the nozzle.

  10. Oversize and duplicate cooling units, and keep spare fans and compressors.

  11. Check controllers against an independent logger, and log in-bag temperatures when diagnosing uneven growth.

  12. Wash heat exchangers, fans, filters and nozzles on a schedule; a noisy fan is a warning.

  13. Cool harder than you think in a hot climate: size with plenty of spare capacity, insulate and shade first, keep fresh air on CO2 control, and humidify the dried incoming air before it reaches the crop.

  14. Plan for power cuts and unit failures before they happen: alarms that reach your phone, a backup unit or generator, and a known order for what to save.

Open questions

  • Block heat output varies threefold between sources (2, 6 or 10 BTU/h per 10 lb block), and no measured method is given.
  • The Coroplast heat exchanger's about 85% recovery and its cost saving are unmeasured.
  • Hart nozzle sizes and the Pola model number are uncertain, and the Pola wiring was narrated by a colour-blind installer and should be checked against the manual.
  • Peroxide in humidifier water is both recommended and rejected.
  • Cyclic ("lung") versus constant fresh-air exchange is still unsettled among large growers, and the maitake advice runs a fan continuously.
  • Metrics for checking fruit-room pressure were deferred and never given.
  • A detailed, published build guide for the Coroplast heat exchanger is not yet available.
  • The labels "90 PA" and "SS" on a typical lab pre-filter layout drawing are unexplained.

chapters.html:
Equipment

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the production machinery and tools of a block and spawn farm: sawdust handling, mixers, pneumatic and Japanese baggers, the Fenrir dry-bagging filler (including its wiring), grain kettles, bag sealers and tumblers, racks and carts, small lab tools, building materials and fabrication, drying gear, and a price list. Steam generators, boilers and autoclaves are in Chapter 12; cooling, humidification and CO2 hardware are in Chapter 5.

The rules used most:

  • Measure substrate by weight (solids and water), not volume, so every bag has the same moisture.
  • Buy fewer, bigger, simpler machines rather than multiplying small ones.
  • Keep backups of anything a crop depends on.
  • Clean machines daily, because a dirty mixer or hopper contaminates everything that passes through it.
  • Mix grain gently for 5-10 min, then bag.

Buying principles

AT A GLANCE Fix your systems and stop tinkering. Spend on steam before a mixer. Scale in one big step, not many small ones. Keep spares of critical kit.

  • Once the right systems are in place, production is easy: one grower makes 100 blocks in about 1.5 hours. Keep systems fixed rather than constantly experimenting; once the lab (filters, band sealer) is built, stop tinkering with it.
  • Spend on a boiler before a mixer. Mixer prices rose from about $8,000 for Cap n Stem's 2-yard (1.5 m³) unit to about $30,000, and a pellet system can run on cheap wooden hoppers.
  • You cannot scale by multiplying small equipment. One larger leap is better than several small steps (details in Chapter 12).
  • Keep backups of racks, fans and humidification. Case: when the compressor of Cap n Stem's high-pressure humidifier broke, the farm limped along on a Hydrofogger, which did poorly. Small farms must weigh spare kit against paying rent.
  • Manual bagging (standing under a bagger all day, folding, racking) is heavy repetitive strain, so automation also reduces injury. Payback comes through speed and redeploying staff; amortize machines over 2-10 years.
  • Supply-chain changes (sawdust sources disappearing) can force extra purchases: Cap n Stem bought extra mixers and sifting equipment for this reason.
  • Fuel choice: natural-gas equipment can often be converted to propane by changing orifices and fittings; one grower did this on a steam kettle.

WHY To decide whether a piece of equipment is worth buying, work out what its absence would cost when something fails. A bought-in block costs about US$8.50; if a heat wave kills 10,000 blocks in incubation, the loss is far more than the cooling unit that should have been installed months earlier. Assume anything you don't provide for will fail, and work backwards from that.

Raw material: sifting, moving and storing

AT A GLANCE Raw sawdust needs sifting and heavy lifting; pellets in super sacks need neither and store twice as densely. Never put hands on a hoisted load.

Sawdust sifters

Cap n Stem went through four sifter designs for raw sawdust. The substrate side of this story is in Chapter 10.

Version Design Outcome
v1 A table with a 6 x 8 ft (1.8 x 2.4 m) frame holding a mesh screen; sawdust shoveled on Slow, manual.
v2 A screen shaken by an old pump motor through an angle-iron linkage Loud, shook itself apart, bogged down, and a fire hazard when stalled: "don't ever do this".
v3 A flat conveyor into an RPC (reusable plastic) crate, then tilted so chips run off one end and sawdust falls through into barrels The flat version just filled crates with chips; the tilted version worked.
v4 A trommel: a rotating drum of rolled perforated steel with welded internal ribs, belt-driven on a stand with guards; sawdust falls into barrels and chips exit the low end The right height, but it fills only two barrels at a time instead of four.
  • The trommel is a large steel drum on a wooden frame with roller supports and a belt drive; underneath, sawdust slides down a chute.
  • Scale: a 33-ton (30 t) load of sawdust was sifted one batch at a time. The farm dropped super sacks and loaded with two forklifts and two dump trailers.

Moving material

  • Barrels of sawdust weigh about 50-80 lb (23-36 kg), about 75 lb (34 kg) typical, and had to be raised to the mixer feeding the bagger. A winch hung from rafters about 22 ft (6.7 m) up kept failing because barrel handles broke. Most barrels were lifted by hand onto stepped platforms, which caused a back injury, until a forklift could be used. Pallets carried four barrels.

WARNING Near miss: a cracked barrel on the winch tipped, a worker steadied it by hand, the barrel collapsed and the hook cinched, nearly catching his hand. Work stopped for the day. Never put hands on a hoisted load, and retire damaged barrels.

Storing material

  • Storage density: a building held about 30 tons (27 t) of raw sawdust floor to ceiling, but the same space holds about 60 tons (54 t) of pellets in about 60 totes or super sacks (about 45 in, 1.1 m, high). Pellets also come in 30 and 50 lb (14 and 23 kg) bags.
  • Block production at Cap n Stem starts from super sacks of combo pellets augered up into a wooden hopper. Shipping-container farms can hang a super sack over a small hopper that refills itself as it empties.
  • Clumpy super sacks of supplement were probably wet at some point; do not use them.
  • Much bulk grain arrives in poor condition (totes of millet with insects and mould clumps, sorghum full of bugs). Ask experienced growers for sources.

Mixers

AT A GLANCE A ribbon mixer makes recipes homogeneous but costs about $30,000 for 2 yards today, wastes water and time on clean-out, and caps a line at about 700 bags a morning. Dry bagging with pellets removes the mixer altogether.

From hand trough to dry bagging: one farm's history

Stage Equipment Crew and output Cost
1 (Westbrook) A tipping trough of two 4 x 8 ft (1.2 x 2.4 m) plywood sheets lined with about 1/4 in (6 mm) polypropylene sheet (joints taped), with a hoist on a pneumatic button to tip it. Sawdust was carried upstairs, raked and hydrated by hand from a ceiling hose. about 30 x 10 lb (4.5 kg) bags per batch; carrying barrels injured a worker's back Not stated
2 A half-yard (0.38 m³) ribbon ("mirrored helix") mixer, with conveyor and foot pedal to a spout; bags hand-held, weighed and corrected 2 people, about 70 x 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags (about 35 x 10 lb) per mix Listed about $6,000, bought for about $3,000 through a gardening catalogue
3 (Gardiner) A 2-yard (1.5 m³) ribbon mixer feeding a home-built Donahue-style pneumatic bagger (the conveyor was dropped) 350 bags in a morning with 3 people (2 folders keep up with 1 mixer) about $20,000 then, about $30,000 now
4 Two 2-yard mixers on a raised platform; sawdust barrels forklifted up; water and ingredients added from above; pneumatic baggers below; teams alternate lines about 700 bags per morning, judged the practical maximum for mixers Not stated
5 The Fenrir dry-bagging filler, no mixer (see the Fenrir) 4 people, about 1,680 bags per morning about $10,000 build including development
  • A typical stage-4 platform layout shows the two mixers raised above the baggers. Working views show a red ribbon mixer agitator turning pellets under a water stream, a flexible auger tube, and a red-framed bagging machine.
  • The half-yard mixer was built for soil and would not hydrate properly without someone's arms in it breaking lumps, but it made recipes homogeneous.
  • A 1-yard (0.76 m³) mixer (as bought by one spawn company) is barely bigger than a half-yard.

RANGE Mixer prices. Budget about $30,000 for a 2-yard mixer today; every source agrees on this current figure. Older and other figures: Cap n Stem's 2-yard mixer is put at about $8,000 in one source and about $20,000 "then" in another, and a generic substrate mixer at about $13,000+, all without clear dates.

Mixer practice

  • Mixers waste a lot of water and time on clean-out after each mix and each day, especially with raw inputs.
  • Mixers trap old wet material. Case: a chunk of wet combo-pellet mix stuck in Cap n Stem's mixer turned foul. Clean daily for a steady state, plus an intensive weekly clean of key equipment. Grain and starch make mixer cleaning a big job.
  • Case: a farm alternating between a dry-bagging filler and a mixer used near-boiling water in a mixer with a grime layer. The pellet mix came out much darker before cooking: a nutrient-rich cake that steam could not fully deal with.
  • Soy hull pellets in the old helix mixers needed nearly all of the recipe's water added to the soy first (run about 20 min) to break them down; then the dust was added and topped off. Otherwise the soy stayed dry and the sawdust too wet. Oak in combo pellets helps them break apart. See Chapter 10.
  • Wet-bag mixing order: dry ingredients first. When combining pellets with raw dry sawdust, hydrate the pellets first, then add sawdust, so mixing takes a long time.
  • With pellets plus measured water, additives (calcium, molasses) can be dissolved into the water supply, for example dosed from an IBC tote like a hydroponic system.
  • Working views show a drum being tipped into a red ribbon mixer, and a clear bag filling under a mixer discharge chute.

Grain in a mixer:

  • Grain needs only a few minutes in a mixer to blend: 5-10 min with gypsum and powders spread across it. Then stop and bag.

  • Pull a bucket sample to check homogeneity and remove clumps.

  • Running the helix continuously grinds grain to chaff, and over-mixing collects broken material into "pizza crust" clumps.

  • Use a gentle mixer (a helix; paddle mixers are acceptable). Aggressive mixing smashes grain into paste.

  • A layer of chaff builds up in the grain mixer, a nuisance.

  • The full grain mixing procedure is in Chapter 9.

  • Ribbon mixer prices from one US maker (late 2020s): about US$18,000 for 1.5 m³ (2 cubic yards), US$23,000 for 3 cubic yards and US$27,000 for 4. A 2-cubic-yard batch fills about 140 ten-pound blocks. A square, adjustable mild-steel bagging hopper added to a mixer costs about US$2,000 from a small builder against about US$3,500 from the mixer maker; round hoppers with sharp corners let wet substrate cake on the sides.

  • Old mixers wear out at the worst moment. A New Hampshire farm's 40-year-old ribbon mixer fried its bearings, and the grower spent about 18 hours grinding the hardened shaft free.

Weight versus volume: wet and dry bagging

AT A GLANCE Dose solids by weight and water by weight or flow meter. Volume works for pre-hydrated grain but not for dry pellets. Bags of slightly different weight yield the same if their moisture is identical.

  • Wet bagging: a fully hydrated premix comes from a mixer and is then bagged.
  • Dry bagging: dry pellets go into the bag, then water is added in the bag. Machines that do this include the Fenrir and those built by Eric Meyer and Mossy Creek.
  • Pellet-plus-water hydration in the bag, with no mixer, is what makes the Fenrir possible. Substrate-side detail is in Chapter 10.
  • Volumetric dosing of dry pellets is inaccurate, because pellet size, dust and density vary. Bags meant to be "10 lb" came out about 8.7-9.0 lb (3.9-4.1 kg), or 4.2-5.1 lb (1.9-2.3 kg) dry, and a fixed water volume then gives wildly varying moisture. Several small-builder dry baggers are volumetric.

RULE Measure solids by weight, and water by weight or with a flow meter (1 g of water = 1 mL). "Twins, not sisters": every bag gets the same moisture content, even if total weight varies slightly.

WHY Exact moisture is what makes yields consistent from block to block. Blocks within about 2.5-3 lb (1.1-1.4 kg) of each other (9 vs 11 lb, 4.1 vs 5.0 kg) yield almost the same if the moisture is right. Moisture targets are in Chapter 10.

Grain: volumetric dosing works

  • Spawn bagging is volumetric: a sliding doser between mixer and bag, about the size of a beer can, adjustable to trim (for example a quarter pound, 0.1 kg, over). Bags are then checked on a second scale.
  • Volumetric dosing works for grain because the grain was hydrated uniformly beforehand.
  • In the grain line, the mixer discharges from the bottom into a pneumatic bagger that slides in and out on air and fills an adjustable volume per bag, set by bag size and grain type.
  • A spawn bag set of 84 takes two kettle boils of about 20-30 min each plus 15-20 min of bagging.
  • Spawn weight precision matters more than block weight. G2 bags are held at about 6 lb (2.7 kg) so expansion rates stay fixed; under-spawning or hand-spawning gives variable colonization. See Chapter 9.

Pneumatic baggers

AT A GLANCE A pneumatic bagger is the simplest way to move a fixed volume of mix into a bag: one bag every 4-6 s, for about $2,000 on top of a mixer. It must stop for every mixer batch, and you can build one yourself.

  • Concept: the simplest way to move a fixed volume of material from one place to another, with few moving parts. A shuttle drives a tube back and forth through a polypropylene sheet, giving consistent volumetric fills. Sometimes the bottom of a mix needs re-incorporating.
  • An earlier double-piston version, with small, fast "pea-shooter" pistons at too high a pressure, was overcomplicated and disliked by staff.
  • Speed: a pneumatic bagger can fill a bag every 4-6 s, but must stop for each mixer batch (100-200 bags), so its effective rate is lower.
  • Price: About $2,000, on top of a about $13,000+ mixer, for the conventional wet-bagging route.

Building a pneumatic bagger

Part Specification
Frame rails Galvanized Unistrut, 1-5/8 in (41 mm) channel, two levels
Legs 1/2-13 threaded rod with nuts and about 1.5 in (38 mm) OD washers
Tabs 1.5 in (38 mm) stainless angle iron with 9/16 in (14 mm) holes centred on the leg
Shuttle and still boards 3/4 in (19 mm) HDPE; chutes 1/4 in (6 mm)
Piston A pneumatic cylinder, sourced from Grainger (name as heard) or Fright Props

Procedure: building the frame and boards

  1. Build each threaded-rod leg joint as a "sandwich": lock nut, washer, angle-iron tab, washer, nut, with spacer pieces holding the rail spacing. Threaded-rod legs let you raise, lower or shorten the frame.
  2. Grind the zinc coating off galvanized parts before welding, with a 60-80 grit flap disc.
  3. TIG-weld (one builder uses an Eastwood 200) with 1/16 in (1.6 mm) mild-steel filler on the stainless-to-galvanized joints. Wear eye protection.
  4. Cut holes with an annular cutter on a Bridgeport-head mill, using cutting oil so the cutter does not overheat and lose its temper. Clean off the oil with acetone or lacquer thinner.
  5. Fit a bottom cross-piece with a locating hole so the lower (still) board cannot slide when the piston fires.
  6. Tack the piston in place, check it, then weld fully. Orient the tabs so they pull the assembly together.
  7. Make the chute of the mixer or hopper smaller than the bagger's inlet, so all substrate falls through and none spills past the frame or platen. Mount a metal or plastic collar to the top rim.

WARNING Zinc fume and dust are harmful. Grind off zinc before welding galvanized steel, and wear eye protection.

CHECK The finished unit stands on wood blocks with a hopper on top; the horizontal piston moves the shuttle board on the upper level, and the still board with its drop chute sits below. Every fill should drop cleanly into the bag with nothing spilling past the frame.

  • Board alternatives: plywood or MDF could substitute for HDPE, but MDF swells like a sponge when wet unless sealed (for example with polyurethane). Two layers of 3/4 in (19 mm) MDF make a cheap welding and assembly table.

  • Fixing a warped HDPE board: soak it in about 93 °C (200 °F) water for a few minutes until soft, then over-correct slightly, since HDPE has shape memory.

  • Tool note: Milwaukee angle grinders burned out fast in one shop (two were cooked building a steam-box base).

  • For a one-person farm labour is the biggest cost. A California grower's pneumatic (Thor) bagger cut a week's bagging from four or five hours of hand packing to about an hour. The same small builder had sold about 90 of these baggers in under a year, some as far as Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Mexico.

Weighing fillers: the Fenrir

AT A GLANCE A weighing filler drops dry combo pellets into each bag until a load cell reads the target, then adds exactly the right weight of water. No mixer is needed, every bag gets the same moisture, and one head bags about 200-240 bags an hour. The open-source Fenrir head costs about US$1,340. Weight versus volume explains why weighing matters.

Where it came from

  • Three generations of bagger are named after Norse myth. One small builder made the "Thor" bagger. A Canadian container grower built the "Odin" as a joke. Cap n Stem's simplified version is the "Fenrir", after the wolf that kills the gods at Ragnarok.
  • The Odin had two hoppers with separate augers, one for red oak sawdust and one for soybean hulls (50:50), then a scale, then water: three measurements per bag. It was slow (about 20-24 s a bag) and expensive to fabricate. It was sensitive to mismatched motor speeds and to non-pellet materials compacting, and its drops were too big for the bags. Cap n Stem ran it for nearly a year.
  • Pre-blended combo pellets made a single feed stream possible, which is why the Fenrir could be so much simpler.
  • Before that, an in-house system let the farm set any target moisture from about 20% to 100% and allowed for the moisture already in the pellets. It was a row of bag stations, each with a load-cell platform and an overhead solenoid valve and water line feeding an open bag of dry pellets.

How it works

  • The kit: a controller (the "brain"), a load-cell scale with a bag holder, and an auger trough with a water head. You build the hopper yourself. Cap n Stem's is wooden, about 8 ft (2.4 m) high and 12 in (30 cm) wide, and wood works fine for it.
  • Mechanics: the controller drives a motor that turns an auger in a trough running from the hopper to a 3D-printed chute head over the bag. Water comes by PEX pipe to an on/off solenoid and out of a perforated nozzle in the bottom of the head. The bag holder is shaped so the opened bag tucks around it and does not fold. 3D-printed dividers could cut down pellet bounce. The STL print files and the Arduino code are open-source.
  • One cycle:
    1. Pellets fall until the scale reads the target, then the auger stops.
    2. The controller waits about 1.2 s for pellets still in the air to land.
    3. It works out the water as target total weight minus pellet weight, corrected for the pellets' own moisture.
    4. It opens the solenoid, then pulses it to finish exactly. A learning routine corrects for in-air pellets over time.
  • Pellet moisture setting: combo pellets hold about 7% water, and pellets in general 7-11%. Measure your own by oven-drying a sample (see moisture testing) and enter it in the menu.
  • Modes: accuracy mode; dry-weight only (pellet-only bags, for dry sterilization or for watering the next morning); and water only.
  • Moisture trials: because the set point is adjustable, you can bag test batches at 61-65% to find each strain's best moisture. Cap n Stem bags at 61-62% to allow for drying during incubation.
  • The load cell is a 5 kg cell costing about US$50, so bags over about 5 kg (11 lb) can't be weighed; no larger-cell option has been described. Never jam anything into the cell's gap. Mount it to minimize side-to-side tipping and centre the bag holder on it. Keep the auger outlet low and the water flow moderate, so the impact doesn't throw off the reading.
  • No central brain. Each head runs on its own controller, so one failure doesn't stop the line.
  • Water pressure: if pressure is poor, use an IBC tote as a reservoir with a quiet on-demand pump to keep the line pressurized. Cap n Stem's supply gives about 6.66 US gal/min (25 L/min). The lines could also take preheated water from a boiler. The solenoids are one reason to filter incoming water (water treatment).
  • Grain: some users dry-bag millet with a Fenrir (dry grain plus water, hydrated by pressure during autoclaving). It tends to stratify, leaving a soggy bottom and a dry or undercooked top, and one well-known grower doubts it works well. One YouTube grower promoted dry bagging for years. Some cordyceps growers use it for rice-based media. Hydrate grain before bagging instead (Chapter 9).

TIP Many growers bag Master's Mix with a Cap n Stem filler and Cap n Stem's own pellet blend. For a new farm, one grower rates the Thor bagger as the best option.

  • The larger Odin bagger works the same way: a load cell under the bag runs the pellet auger until the dry weight for a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block at 62% moisture is reached, about 4.42 lb (2.0 kg) of pellets at about 7% moisture, and then the water is added. Uniform inputs such as pellets are what make this automation possible.

A Fenrir line looks like this: a plywood controller box with a small screen; an aluminium bag holder on a load-cell platform with upright fins; a black 3D-printed chute head; a black steel auger trough with a blue PEX water line and a brass solenoid fitting. Wiring a controller box

These notes come from a narrated build. The wire colours and terminal orders could only partly be checked against what was visible, so treat them as unconfirmed and check the published build notes before you wire one.

Component Detail
Stepper driver StepperOnline DM542T digital stepper driver. It drives the auger's pulses and speed, cued by the controller.
Controller A small screen unit from Seeed (it looks like a Wio Terminal). Arduino-like, with a speaker.
Boards A load-cell board (bag weight) and a water board (switches the solenoid), Grove-style, on a grey 3D-printed plate.
Power 12 V supply for the controller; a 24 V transformer (about 360 W) that can run three, maybe four, heads.
Printed parts Controller holder and bezel (with the Fenrir rune logo), board back plate, wire-harness holder.
Enclosure Anything. Cap n Stem's is plywood with a front door that holds the controller.

Procedure: wiring a Fenrir controller box

  1. Gather tools: hot glue gun, small and medium flat and Phillips screwdrivers, a pick, wire strippers, drill bits and an impact driver.
  2. Fit a terminal block at the back of the box with hot and neutral jumpers, fed from the 24 V transformer. Run all the internal red and black power leads through one hole to that block.
  3. Set the stepper driver's DIP switches fully and its side switch to 5 V. Mount it centrally (two screws are enough). Mount the 12 V supply above it, with its leads near the exit hole. Add a female-to-male USB extension so you can reach the controller to reflash it.
  4. Bring the motor's four-wire harness (blue, black, red, green) in through a hole drilled low on the right side. Connect it to the left-most removable terminal of the driver in the narrated order black, green, blue, red. The driver takes its red and black power from the transformer terminal.
  5. Make the controller-to-driver signal cable: three wires (red, white, green), with a capacitor between green and white (negative to white, positive to green) to steady the signal. Keep the capacitor leads from touching. In the driver terminal the wires go in reverse order, with white sharing the fourth terminal from the left (daisy-chained, as narrated). Some terminal clamps must be unscrewed fully so the gate lifts before the wire goes in.
  6. File or tape printed parts if your printer is imprecise. Hold the delicate signal wires with a printed clip, and bolt the controller and board plate through the door with wing nuts. The left board is water and the right board is load cell (the narration contradicts itself once).
  7. Wire the solenoid with the water board acting as a switch in the hot lead between supply and solenoid. Put a flyback diode across the split solenoid wire, so a voltage spike fries the diode instead of the solenoid. Leave slack so the door can open.
  8. Finish the rear wiring: three red and three black leads ganged on the terminal block, jumpered to the transformer feed, under a plastic guard. Re-tighten every rear terminal with the impact driver, because once the box is on the wall you rarely see that side.

The opened box shows a green and black driver board, two small blue boards and red power leads.

CHECK Nine times out of ten a misbehaving filler has a loose wire. Make every terminal tight, strip wires to the right length, and leave no frayed or bare copper touching a neighbour.

Japanese automatic baggers

  • Cap n Stem's base machine is a Japanese automatic bagger, imported through Far West Fungi. It was described as the first and only 10 lb (4.5 kg) substrate bagger, modelled on the maker's 5 lb (2.3 kg) units, and had been in use about 2 years at the time.
  • Throughput: 900 bags an hour, set by the machine's cycle. It picks up a bag, opens and loads it, fills it, and ejects it for folding and loading onto steam or autoclave racks. It originally compressed the fill too; Cap n Stem removed the compressor.
  • The hidden cost is the feed. Feeding the stock machine at 900 bags an hour with pre-hydrated mix takes two or three mixers of 2-4 cubic yards (1.5-3.1 m³) each, with chain lifts or augers into its rotating "cake pan" hopper. That is about US$100,000 of mixers on top of a US$40,000-80,000 bagger, plus conveyors: about US$200,000 for a full stock setup. Farms balked at it, and prices are expected to rise with tariffs.
  • Reliability: redundant, simple, sensor-based and pneumatically driven, so they rarely break. They need compressed air, occasional lubrication of the pneumatic slides, occasional sensor adjustment, and a 240 V three-phase supply (which can be stepped down for the vacuum).
  • Bags: until recently these machines needed Japanese or Chinese bags that open reliably. Unicorn now makes machine-grade bags that open easily (filter grades XLS, A, B and T were mentioned). Getting bags to open fully is a major labour and automation problem; bigger bags open better.
  • Automatic spawners also exist: a conveyor opens the bag, spawns it and closes it. Far West Fungi and Cap n Stem are not convinced they beat a hand crew, because they are fairly slow unless you run several. A typical one is a bagging and spawning machine with a hopper and conveyor.

A weighing head for a Japanese bagger

  • Nicknamed the "Pelomatic", this adapter puts a Fenrir-style head on a Japanese bagger. It doses pellets and water into each bag so a dry-bagging farm can keep up with the machine, and it needs only a conveyor to a small top hopper. It is claimed to suit 400-900 bags an hour. The demonstration used about 100% oak pellets (slow to absorb) at arbitrary settings.
  • Design: pneumatic pistons (as under the mixer in Cap n Stem's original system) combined with auger feed. Four dosing buckets on load-cell scales rotate to keep pace with 900 bags an hour. They are fed by four auger motors with built-in drivers, daisy-chained to one central controller. Water comes from two solenoid-driven PVC tubes with flap valves, which fill to about 6.5 lb (2.9 kg) in 2-3 s; the amount is adjustable in the Arduino program.
  • Feeding it: the small top hopper is limited by the machine's height. The bagger's existing laser level sensor (originally for the cake pan) can trigger the feed conveyor to keep it topped up. With a high ceiling, a super sack can hang straight over the hopper; otherwise use a boot with an auger or a flap conveyor.
  • The adapter runs, and can be diagnosed, separately from the Japanese controller. It removes the pneumatic shuttle that carried hydrated substrate, which was the main sensor trouble spot.
  • Labour claim: it doubles what four people can do and cuts bagging to about one person folding bags and swapping super sacks. With two people it halves labour and doubles output compared with the Okta line.
  • Status when described: 2-3 more weeks of programming and sensor work. The goal was a drop-in kit (unplug some parts, add a panel) for 5 or 10 lb Japanese baggers, handling any combination of weight and water. The prototype showed the top of the bagger with a black funnel, red pneumatic lines, a blue water line and a white feed hose. No field results had been reported.

Grain-cooking equipment

How to hydrate grain is in Chapter 9; this section covers the hardware.

  • Jacketed kettles reach a rolling boil in about 2 min and keep boiling even after about 200 lb (90 kg) of cold grain is tipped in. They run back to back: barrels of raw grain are dosed in, and the drained hot grain is lifted to the top of a mixer.
  • An on-demand water heater fills the kettles at about 85 °C (185 °F) so they boil sooner. These heaters wear out.
  • Kettle cooking is fast, precise and self-cleaning. Use a false bottom to avoid scorching, stir, or add grain only once the water is at a rolling boil. Cut the heat early (for example at 16 of 20 min) to allow for draining time.
  • A hot steam-jacketed kettle (jacket at about 35 psi, 2.4 bar) quickly dries out any grain left in it, and starch sticks to the walls. Drained grain typically drops into barrels (green Uline barrels under the kettle outlet in one farm).
  • Kettle boiling is laborious, needs full attention and is dangerous: one farm's spawn staff have burns.
  • Hot-water soaks lose heat fast when they meet a large mass of cold grain. Hold the soak temperature with a jacketed vessel or heaters, and stir or aerate.
  • Grain cleaner: a small grower using local grain can buy or build one for a few hundred dollars. A vacuum lifts light debris while heavy kernels fall through sieves.
  • Draining a tote: when a 1-ton (900 kg) tote drains from the bottom, lighter, damaged kernels rise and all come out at the end. Problems then concentrate on the last day, even though the lot records looked normal.
  • Electric pressure cookers are a simple small-farm option: large MegaChef units (12 qt is a common size). Give each cooker its own 15 A circuit; anything with a heating element needs its own circuit, and two cookers probably can't share one. Larger options are an All American 75X pressure sterilizer, or a 30 gal (114 L) Megapot with a false bottom on a Bayou Classic SP40 burner for 50-75 lb (23-34 kg) loads. See Chapter 9 for the method.

Bag sealers

Method Experience
Band sealer (recommended): Bosch Doughboy 550 The only band sealer one experienced grower would buy. Bosch's packaging arm became Syntegon, whose newer model is better but pricier and more complex.
Fold twice, fold the sides, zip tie pulled tight with a zip-tie gun Airtight, so gas passes only through the filter. The earliest method, still used by some growers.
Handheld jaw impulse sealer Miserable: held down by hand, overheats after about 80 bags, PTFE strips break, hands get burned.
Impulse sealer that overheated Burned micro-holes in bags; part of the cause of one farm's long fight with Neurospora (Chapter 16).
Electromagnetic clamp sealer (North Spore used them early) Looked like too little clamping pressure.
Jaw sealer retrofitted with a pneumatic piston and adjustable delay (John Donahue's design) Allowed a vertical station that keeps laminar flow across the work surface, but the cycle time per bag became the bottleneck.
Electromagnetic impulse sealer about 24 in (61 cm) wide (somewhere between 20 and 36 in, 51-91 cm), two bags side by side Nearly doubled speed, but new hires misaligned bags (sealing two together, missing edges): the farm's first real training and procedure problem.
  • The band sealer carries each bag through the sealing band and a ceramic cooling section, then drops it into a tumbler. The tumbler mainly acts as a holding station so bags don't pile up and pop.
  • Unicorn has changed its plastic a lot, which makes substrate bags harder to seal; bags have arrived too thin, too thick or the wrong size. Test every new bag lot on your sealer.
  • A vacuum sealer for packing dried product (for example reishi antlers) needs dialling in, because it has many settings. Check each sealed bag for punctures by eye and by hand. A bench scale (a Torrey was in use) sits beside it.

WARNING A pneumatic jaw sealer closes at roughly 90 psi (6.2 bar). One grower deliberately put a hand in to test it and crushed his fingers. Don't.

RULE Buy a band sealer rather than struggling with handheld impulse sealers, and train new staff on bag alignment.

Tumblers and shaking

  • A tumbler can never fully mix spawn through a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block in an XLS-A bag. Bags go from the tumbler to a table for a hand shake, which is a big labour cost.

  • Tumbling works better with 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags. One grower built a tall tumbler on John Donahue's idea: a culvert pipe of the right length, pitch and speed, with snaking inside, mixes evenly enough that bags just need inspecting and shelving.

  • A tumbler is only a holding place for bags; a 10 lb bag still has to be shaken. One grower's tumbler was a set of barrels welded onto a treadmill.

  • Shaking 100 bags should take about 45 minutes, but it is hard work unless it is done every day. New staff who get through their first week of shaking usually stay at least a year.

Mechanical spawners

  • One farm tried John Donahue's volumetric pneumatic canister spawner, fed from stainless hoppers. Every hopper needed sterilizing (peracetic acid, then drying, which is near-sterile at best). One bad spawn bag risked cross-contaminating many blocks, and it slowed the line. The farm sold it to another grower and went back to spawning by hand (Chapter 11).
  • An open idea: put sterile pellets, water and spawn precisely into a pre-sterilized (for example gamma-irradiated) bag, so it mixes itself and only needs sealing and shelving.

Racks and carts

Incubation racking

  • Pallet racking: About 4 ft (1.2 m) deep and 10-12 ft (3-3.7 m) tall, with 7-8 shelf levels. Use slat or strapping decks, not solid ones, so air moves up and across. Leave at least two hand widths between blocks on every side, including above. A 10 ft (3 m) span holds about 10 bags a row (bags are about 9 in, 23 cm, wide; the figure was uncertain and might be 20). A typical layout is cross-braced racks 4 ft deep and 12 ft tall with 4 ft (1.2 m) aisles, or tall green-framed racking with wooden slat decks under overhead ducting.
  • Another grower uses pallet racks about 48 in (1.2 m) wide and 10 ft (3 m) tall, about 5 blocks across, with aisles and lights on both sides. Overstuffing racks lowers output compared with fewer, healthier blocks.
  • With 20 ft (6 m) ceilings, one farm built tall stationary racks; standard Metro-style racks would have held only about 30% as many blocks. The cheapest option is pallet racking with 2x4s and strapping. That farm now imports metal racks from China; they need some work but give consistent airflow and spacing and no splinters.

Rolling racks

  • Why roll: less handling and flexible placement. Examples: keep G1 grain racks somewhere warm until they make their own heat, then roll them somewhere cooler; incubate maitake in dim light, then roll it into bright light to trigger pinning; roll a thousand oyster blocks into the cooler before a long weekend; put inoculated bags straight onto the rack they will grow on, which speeds up knock days; push finished batches straight to fruiting or the cooler.

  • Rolling racks suit low ceilings (8-9 ft, 2.4-2.7 m); no safe rolling rack about 20 ft (6 m) tall exists. They allow denser packing because aisles can be dropped, but only if cross-ventilation channels are left through the pack. They are often the wrong size and end up shoved into corners.

  • A common type: galvanized steel racks with about 7 wire-deck shelves on orange casters, packed closely.

  • For a spawn or substrate supplier, mobile racks are ideal: each bag stays on the shelf it was knocked onto, then rolls into the refrigerated container for packing.

  • Steam racks: wheeled racks of stainless angle (about 7 shelves) that take Metro shelves let whole racks move from the steam chamber to the lab (Chapter 12).

  • Rolling metal shelving racks move blocks from incubation into the fruit room and pull away from the walls for the weekly wipe-down. Plan production per rack: blocks per rack and yield per rack.

Fruiting carts

  • Rolling carts have been called the most important fruiting tool. Roll them out to a harvest, grading and packing area, which keeps spores off you and out of the plenum.
  • Keep one species per rack and give each rack to one lot, so the whole rack is harvested, cleaned and reloaded together. Fixed conduit racks lead to forgotten, overgrown clusters at the back.

RANGE Racks in the fruit room. Recommended: keep fruiting racks in the fruit room and don't cycle incubation racks through it, because humid, caustic fruit rooms rust shelving and stainless steel is very expensive. In practice, black galvanized-look wire shelving in one fruit room showed only a little rust after a year, "nothing serious".

WARNING Use large casters. Racks on small casters are the ones that failed, at 2 a.m. during a harvest. Loaded rolling racks have tipped over while being loaded or moved, for example during a night harvest of about 300 shiitake blocks (600-700 lb, 270-320 kg). Keep spare racks so rescued blocks have somewhere to go.

Drying racks

  • About 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) frames with 10-12 shelves of heat-tolerant polypropylene composite mesh (sold for curing cannabis), fixed with stainless screws. See drying.

Small lab tools

Flow hoods, filters and lab layout are in Chapter 4; this is the small kit.

  • Tool sterilizer: a Bacti-Zapper-style ceramic infrared sterilizer, or a benchtop bead-style unit with a perforated metal cylinder, replaces an open flame. Cool the tip on fresh agar or in 70% isopropyl alcohol at a "cool-down station".
  • Blender rig for agar slurry and breaking up mycelium: a regular-mouth Ball jar with the blade base and gasket of a cheap Oster blender screwed on as the lid, sitting on the motor base. Any regular-mouth jar size fits. See Chapter 7.
  • Before scalpels, one grower cut agar with soft-handled dental tools (they burned up in an alcohol lamp), then forged a stainless blade with an oxy-acetylene torch. Learning to fabricate and weld is valuable for a mycologist.
  • Aerated liquid-culture lids:
    • A polypropylene Ball-type lid with a silicone gasket and three drilled holes, each fitted with a threaded through-valve.
    • Two 1/4 in (6 mm) silicone tubes run to the jar bottom. Air enters through a 0.22 µm PTFE filter and leaves through a second filter.
    • Buy "1/4 in" valves (really 6 mm, from China). Put a silicone washer on the thread, push up from underneath with the flat side of the crush nut against the lid, and tighten until the gasket just starts to bulge.
    • Single-barb fittings seal better than double-barb. Female luer-lock-to-barb adapters take the filters.
    • The draw line gets an outward one-way valve with a luer cap and ends just above the jar bottom.
  • Air pump for those lids: an EcoPlus Pro 40 aquarium pump with 12 valved outlets runs up to 12 jars. Use a non-barbed fitting at the jar inlet so excess pressure can't burst the glass. Use 1/8 in (3 mm) ID tubing in Shore A70 silicone, not A50, which is too rubbery.
  • Magnetic stirrers work better on the lowest setting; high makes a constant vortex. Aeration should just make a layer of bubbles on the surface.
  • Hood bumper: tape a 2 in (50 mm) stainless angle iron to the table at the base of each HEPA filter. It keeps bags about 1.5 in (38 mm) off the frame, is easy to clean, and makes stray grain bounce off. Keep a vacuum handy for spilled grain. A badly ruptured filter can't be fixed with superglue or caulk.
  • Airflow meters: buy a mid-priced vane anemometer; encased vanes are more accurate, and neither the cheapest nor the dearest is best. An Extech AN300 thermo-anemometer is one example. Use a handheld digital manometer for room pressure differences.
  • Flow hood prices: new about US$6,000-20,000 (odd lab units US$1,000-50,000). Used hoods at auction are bargains even if the filters (about US$700 of material) need replacing, but clean them and check the side panels for rust holes that let air bypass the pre-filter. Baker (Maine) makes EdgeGARD hoods. The Lab Rat Flow Hoods "Nomad" is a 3D-printed case with a computer-style fan, about US$100, the largest about 2 x 3 ft (0.6 x 0.9 m), measured at about 96-104 ft/min (0.49-0.53 m/s).
  • Filter sources: Filter Sales USA; Bonsai Filter (said to be owned now by Midwest Grow Kits); Lab Rat Flow Hoods; bulk from Alibaba.
  • Genetics bench: a miniPCR 8-tube thermocycler run from a phone app (protocol named for Alan Rockefeller); a small benchtop microcentrifuge; a vortexer; and a hot-water bath with a float. See Chapter 8.
  • Gowning supplies: Tyvek suits in several sizes, Uline disposable masks, hair nets and nitrile gloves.
  • Keep rooms bare: the cool-down room needs only HEPA and a clean floor; the knock room only the HEPA workstation and the sealer; the incubation room only racks. Store tools in the hallway.

WARNING Home-made flow hoods carry electrocution and fire risks (rheostat wiring, flame tests indoors). Coroplast is not structural and it burns; in a fire, get out.

Instruments

Monitoring is covered in Chapter 12 (logging steam runs) and Chapter 5 (climate); these are the care points.

  • MadgeTech loggers: tight gaskets make them liquid-proof, but don't drop them, open the sensor housings, or contaminate the sensors and washers. Batteries are non-rechargeable and long-lived, about US$20 to replace. The maker repairs units cheaply and turns replacements round fast. Wash them with soap and water to remove film from grain or hardwood. The PR140 failures one farm had came from a gasket not fully tightened or a dead battery; daily pressure cycling wears batteries.
  • Probe loggers are expensive but a great tool. Some growers manage without one by borrowing one now and then.
  • Use an anemometer to check hood and fan filter unit (FFU) airflow, and give each Inkbird controller a second, independent sensor. Govee sensors work well, and a gel humidity protector keeps moisture off circuit boards.

Building materials and fabrication

  • Wall skin: Coroplast (fluted plastic) in 4 x 8 ft (1.2 x 2.4 m) sheets, about 2 lb (0.9 kg) each, fixed to steel studs at 2 ft (61 cm) centres with stainless self-tapping screws. About US$8-11 a sheet (a COVID-era price) from sign shops; pallets are cheaper from large sign companies.

  • Seams: 3M flashing tape: stretchy, self-healing and very strong once stuck. Buy it from lumber yards rather than hardware stores. The same three materials (steel stud, Coroplast and flashing tape) build labs too.

  • Use materials that won't rot: steel studs and Coroplast, or structural insulated panels (SIPs). One farm imported SIPs from China at about US$2 per linear foot (30 cm).

  • Doubled steel studs, joined with tin-snip tabs and self-tapping screws, are strong enough to hang heavy wall-mounted HEPA units.

  • Welding and machining notes (grinding off zinc, TIG welding, annular cutters, reshaping HDPE) are in the bagger build.

  • Every mushroom farm of any size needs a fabrication shop and builds things constantly. One grower trusts no humidifier he didn't build himself; a Houston farm built its own controllers and welded its own systems to suit its climate. Keep a tidy, covered store of spare parts and scrap for building your own equipment. Off-the-shelf climate packages for mushrooms are still rare: unlike indoor plant growing, you cannot yet order "this AC system to cool this many square feet".

Drying equipment

  • Batch capacity is set by the dehumidifier's capacity in pints per day (PPD). Home units remove about 20-40 PPD (9-19 L a day). A ceiling-mounted, attic-style unit does about 100-130 PPD (47-62 L a day) for around US$500, and it is worth spending a bit more for capacity.
  • A plugged-in dehumidifier is safer than improvised wooden drying boxes with a hot plate and fan, which are a fire hazard.
  • Buy a dehumidifier with an auto-drain (a clear tubing outlet) run to a barrel or floor drain. A dehumidifier works like an air conditioner in reverse and gives off heat while it removes water.
  • A small industrial blender grinds reishi offcuts into powder. See Chapter 15.

Key rules

  1. Measure substrate by weight (solids and water), not volume, so every bag has the same moisture.
  2. Buy fewer, bigger, simpler machines, and keep backups of anything a crop depends on.
  3. Clean mixers and hoppers daily.
  4. Mix grain gently for 5-10 min, then bag.
  5. Buy a band sealer rather than struggling with handheld impulse sealers, and train new staff on bag alignment.
  6. Give racks large casters and slatted decks, and keep spare racks.
  7. Don't build machines that rely on one central controller; independent units keep running when one fails.
  8. When an automated filler misbehaves, check for loose terminals first.
  9. Fit an angle-iron bumper in front of every HEPA filter face.
  10. Grind off zinc before welding galvanized steel, and wear eye protection.
  11. Give every heating appliance (grain cooker, hot plate) its own circuit.

Open questions

  • The Fenrir wiring colours and terminal orders were narrated rather than fully shown; check the published build notes.
  • The weighing head for Japanese baggers was still 2-3 weeks from completion when described; no field results were given.
  • The 5 kg load cell means the Fenrir can't weigh bags over about 11 lb (5 kg); no larger-cell option has been described.
  • The throughput of competing dry baggers has not been measured.
