chapters.html:
Culture Work: Agar, Liquid Culture and Cloning

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the front end of production: agar media and plating, incubating and reading plates, moving cultures onto grain, plain and aerated liquid culture, agar slurries, cloning wild or shop-bought mushrooms, and choosing strains. The numbers and rules used most:

  • Start every expansion from a fresh plate that came straight out of storage. Never chain old plates.
  • Put the inoculum in the centre of the plate and parafilm it twice. Let it establish 3-5 days in the hood, then incubate at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F).
  • Cut transfers when the leading edge is about 1 cm from the plate wall, from the outer ring.
  • Two 1 x 1 cm cuts per 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1 master gives about 12 masters per plate; 1 G1 makes about 12 G2 bags; 1 G2 makes about 20 blocks. No G3.
  • Liquid culture: 0.5% sugar, a 10-14 day cycle, 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain master.
  • Test every new or revived strain by fruiting it before you trust it.

Storage of cultures, senescence and genetics are covered in Chapter 8. Grain spawn itself is covered in Chapter 9, and the clean room and flow hood in Chapter 4.

Why culture work matters

A mushroom farm runs on a living culture: the mycelium of one chosen strain, kept pure and multiplied step by step until it fills thousands of blocks. "Culture work" is everything done with that mycelium before it reaches bulk grain: growing it on agar (a jelly of seaweed gel and nutrients in a petri dish, called a plate), on slants (agar set at an angle in a test tube), in liquid culture, and moving it on to grain.

The culture chain

The standard chain is: cryovial → slant → working ("feature") agar plate → G1 grain master → G2 grain spawn → substrate blocks.

  • A cryovial is a small frozen tube of culture kept at -80 °C (-112 °F) (Chapter 8).
  • A G1 grain master is the first bag of grain inoculated from agar. A G2 bag is grain spawn inoculated from a G1. The G2 bags inoculate the substrate blocks.

Why G1 masters exist at all: going straight from agar to G2 would mean cutting agar for every bag and coming back later to shake each one. Pouring one G1 into about 12 G2 bags and shaking once avoids that second visit.

RULE One farm's hard rule: no G3 spawn and no substrate-to-substrate (block-to-block) transfers.

Loops and lines

Think of cultures as "loops and lines". Preservation and refreshing is a closed loop that returns to the freezer. Expansion is a one-way line that ends in blocks. Keep them separate: every culture you hold should belong to one or the other. The loop is explained in Chapter 8.

The risk multiplier

One plate feeds 6-12 G1 masters, which feed spawn bags, which feed blocks. A bad plate can ruin "upwards of 240 bags", and the full chain beyond that is far larger. This is why culture work gets the best equipment and the slowest, most careful staff.

  • One farm (Cap n Stem) does its culture work in its most expensive flow hood, a "$10,000" unit, because early mistakes multiply downstream. Spawning happens in a clean room pressurized by fan filter units (FFU), in front of another bank of FFUs, so the work has two layers of HEPA filtration.
  • To help staff who never enter the lab see the whole operation, the same farm shows them a cryovial and explains that it can lead to around 60,000 lb (27 t) of mushrooms.

WHY Because one plate feeds dozens of grain bags and thousands of blocks, a mistake at the culture stage is the most expensive mistake on the farm.

Expansion numbers

AT A GLANCE The working ratios that recur most often are 2 cuts per bag → 12 G1 per plate, 1 G1 → 12 G2, and 1 G2 → 20 blocks.

Step Ratio Conditions / notes
Cryovial → carriers 5 toothpicks per vial; or 5-6 carriers; or 5-10 rye grains Each toothpick goes to its own slant
Slant → plates 8-12 plates; "up to about 10" (4 were made in one demonstration); "about a dozen", averaging 8 at present From one slant
Held-back expansion dish → dishes About 4 (could go to about 20, but that is a huge output) Test-and-expand line (Chapter 8)
Plate → 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1 masters Up to 12 at 2 cuts per bag; about 6 at 4 cuts per bag Same protocol for all species at one farm
Plate → G1, shiitake 6-8 (one farm uses 6) at 4 cuts per bag Slow strains
Plate → G1, test line 1 plate → 1 grain master; also "about 4 grain masters per dish" in an expansion drawing Test bags
Plate → G1, lion's mane "Up to 30-some" per plate Stated once; inconsistent with every other figure, so don't plan on it
Liquid culture → grain 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain master The industry-standard dose; equals the volume of one farm's culture syringe
G1 (4 lb / 1.8 kg) → G2 (6 lb / 2.7 kg) 12 bags (range 6-24 mentioned); about 20; 12-20 12 is the usual figure
G2 → substrate blocks About 20 blocks per G2 bag (1:20) Blocks are 10 lb (4.5 kg) for comb tooth

Whole-chain examples

  • 4 grain masters → 80 G2 → about 1,600 blocks.
  • About 480 masters per vial: 5 toothpicks x about 8 plates x 12 masters.
  • 6 masters x 12 = 72 G2 bags; 72 x 20 = 1,440 blocks.

RANGE G2 bags per G1: standard 12. Context: on millet about 20 works, because its many small grains give many inoculation points; one talk on culture preservation uses about 20, and another farm runs agar → 4 lb grain master → about 20 G2 bags. The full range quoted is 6-24. Masters per plate: 12 at 2 cuts per bag or 6 at 4 cuts; a single quote of "30-some" is an outlier. Plates-per-slant and masters-per-plate figures vary between sources, so do your own arithmetic when you plan: for example 6 masters x 12 = 72 G2 bags, and 72 x 20 = 1,440 blocks.

A typical expansion drawing shows the tree from one held-back dish to 4 dishes, then 4 grain masters (GM), then 80 G2 bags, then 1,600 substrate blocks. Notes beside it sum up the start of the chain (1 cryovial → 5 toothpicks → 5 slants → about 50 plates → hundreds of G1s) and the test line (1 plate = 1 GM = 20 G2).

Plate generations at other farms

  • Another farm makes 5 second-generation plates (P2) from each first-generation plate (P1) by cutting a wedge for each, and also drops wedges into jars. It keeps one P2 in use and refrigerates the rest until needed.
  • A third farm normally works plates from P1 to P4, but has run lines out to P30-40 without trouble.

TIP P30-40 is the exception, not the plan. The safer habit is to return to a fresh plate from storage for every expansion (see Key rules).

Agar media: which for which species

Agar is a nutrient jelly. The nutrients come from malt, potato or similar, with a little yeast. The common media are:

  • MYA, malt yeast agar; MEA, malt extract agar.
  • PDA, potato dextrose agar; PDYA, potato dextrose yeast agar; PYA, a potato-yeast agar.
Species / group Medium Notes
Slow strains (shiitake, some lion's mane, maitake) Malt yeast agar (MYA) Malt nutrients are released more slowly, so the older centre of a slow plate stays fed.
All Hericium (lion's mane, comb tooth) MYA Gives more robust, stable growth; slower strains generally go on MYA
Comb tooth MYA preferred; any malt agar works Slower than oyster; benefits from extra nutrients
Fast strains, oysters PDA / PDYA Black oyster was revived on PDYA
Chestnut PDA/PDYA, MYA or PYA all fine Charcoal agar has been used but is not needed
Maitake MEA preferred over PDA MEA gives more dynamic, rhizomorphic (rope-like) growth
Lion's mane, shiitake MYA with activated charcoal (black plates) or blue-dyed agar Contrast makes faint mycelium and the leading edge visible; it does not change how the mycelium grows
  • Falling back to the other medium (MYA instead of PDYA, or the reverse) is fine if needed.
  • Plain agar-agar with no nutrients gives thin, wispy mycelium that dies out. Use a nutrient medium such as PDA or MEA.
  • Faint species such as lion's mane and shiitake can also be read by holding the plate up to a light.

WARNING Gentamicin (an antibiotic) in agar is a last-resort rescue for heavily contaminated cultures, not a routine additive. One grower used it once to clone a wild Ganoderma near Topsham, Maine. It worked, but the isolate was weak and was dropped.

TIP Use MYA for slow or faint species (shiitake, lion's mane; maitake on MEA) and PDYA for fast ones. Add charcoal when you cannot see the edge.

Buying versus pouring plates

  • Cap n Stem buys its agar plates and slants from Tip of the Cap (name as heard) rather than pouring hundreds a week. At about $1 per plate, staff time is worth more elsewhere. The farm poured its own early on, and also tried Northeast Laboratories, who did not understand mushroom needs.
  • The same farm produces about 400 or more agar dishes per week, plus slants.
  • A smaller farm does all lab work on one day (Tuesday). It pours 5 sleeves of plates, seals them with grafting tape and stores them in a gasketed tote. It transfers half the culture collection one week and the other half the next. Chestnut, maitake and enoki are moved every other week, to fit production.

Sterile technique at the hood

AT A GLANCE Work in a horizontal laminar flow hood (a cabinet that blows HEPA-filtered air across the bench toward you). Keep anything sterile or living closest to the filter, sterilize the tool before every touch, move slowly, and parafilm every plate twice.

Setting up the hood

  • Use a horizontal laminar flow hood. Put anything sterile or living (culture, fresh plate, sterile grain bag) closest to the filter, with nothing upstream blocking the clean air.
  • Open plate lids toward the filter, and set the lid face-up or leaning against the filter. Keep the mouth of an open slant pointed at the filter.
  • Stage every supply in the hood before you start, so you don't keep leaving the clean airflow. Park finished plates to one side, still in front of the filter.
  • A typical set-up: the worker is gowned in a white Tyvek-type suit and black nitrile gloves at a stainless hood with a perforated back wall. A spray bottle and scissors sit on a wipe. The hood holds sterile swabs, the infrared sterilizer, slants in a rack and plates stacked against the filter.
  • In a working lab you will see gloved hands moving cultures between petri dishes in the hood, cutting parafilm with scissors, and racks of labelled tubes.

Sterilizing tools

  • Sterilize tweezers or blades in a ceramic infrared sterilizer ("Bacti-Zapper" style) before every touch. Then cool the tip on a fresh agar plate, or by dipping it in 70% isopropyl alcohol (IPA) in a tube at a cool-down station, so it doesn't scorch the culture.
  • A benchtop electric sterilizer with a perforated metal cylinder can replace an open flame; long forceps fit into it.
  • A 50 mL conical tube of 70% IPA beside the sterilizer is the usual cool-down dip.

Procedure: plating a transfer

  1. Stage the fresh plates, the source culture, the sterilizer, the cool-down tube, scissors and parafilm in the hood.
  2. Sterilize the tool in the infrared sterilizer; cool it on agar or in 70% IPA.
  3. Open the lid toward the filter.
  4. Pick the tool by the type of growth: an inoculation loop for strains with fluffy aerial mycelium such as oysters; tweezers or cut agar chunks for flatter, two-dimensional mycelium such as lion's mane and shiitake. A loop lifts the aerial mycelium cleanly without digging into the agar.
  5. Place the transfer in the centre of the new plate.
  6. Seal the edge with parafilm, twice. Parafilm keeps microbes out but lets air through.
  7. Re-sterilize the tool before the next touch, every time.

WHY Centre placement gives even radial growth. Off-centre, one side reaches the wall and stalls; centring also gives the biggest outer ring to cut from later.

RULE Work slowly and deliberately. Fast movements disturb the airflow. The hood is for careful culture work, not for speed.

Moving plates between rooms

  • Plates travel between rooms inside SacO2 filter bags. Spray the bag and scissors with alcohol before cutting the bag open, in case they brushed the Tyvek suit. Re-sterilize tweezers between every use.
  • One farm keeps its cultures in SacO2 "microsacs" even though it moved its spawn bags to Unicorn bags.

Portable hoods

A portable hood (the "Nomad") can run for 20-30 min in a closed small office before culture work. It can also run in the field from a car inverter or power bank, to clone wild mushrooms onto plates and parafilm them on the spot.

Low-tech culture work

Technique matters more than equipment; equipment is mainly for scale.

  • Minimal kit: a work surface wiped with isopropyl and topped with a glass slab. Gloves are optional if hands are soaked in isopropyl. Clean clones can be taken from grocery-store mushrooms or from wild specimens such as Laetiporus (chicken of the woods) on logs.
  • Beginners cloning wild mushrooms do not need high-grade filtration; a cleanable work surface is enough.
  • Before owning scalpels or pre-sterilized blades, one grower cut agar with soft-handled dental tools from a pharmacy (they burned up in an alcohol lamp), and later forged a stainless blade with an oxy-acetylene torch. Learning to fabricate and weld is useful for mycologists.
  • The "Uncle Ben's 90-second rice" method uses pre-sterilized commercial rice pouches as grain. It breaks the conventional sterile rules but works for hobbyists. Treat it as a challenge to dogma, not as a production method.

Procedure: testing a hood with settle plates

Plates are cheap and filters are not, so check your hood and rooms with open plates.

  1. Pick spots across the face of the hood (centre, edges, corners).
  2. Expose open plates at each spot. For a hood about 4 ft (1.2 m) wide, 60 s per spot is one choice; other timings in use are 30 s to 2 min, about 1 min, or 15-20 min on the work surface. A day-long exposure catches occasional shedding.
  3. Cover, parafilm and incubate the plates.
  4. Map what grows against where each plate sat.
  5. About every 6 months, also place plates at doorways, vents and room corners, ideally when nobody is working.

RANGE Exposure time per spot: about 1 min is the common choice (60 s per spot on a 4 ft / 1.2 m hood). The range runs from 30 s to 2 min, to 15-20 min on the work surface, to a whole day. Longer exposure means lower risk tolerance.

CHECK A good hood passes a hard test. One lab worker ran a Nomad hood for 20 min, then left 6 open plates in front of it for 3-4 h in a dirty warehouse. Nothing grew in the middle or at the edges.

Incubating plates

AT A GLANCE Fresh or revived plates sit 3-5 days in the warm hood to establish, then go to 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) until the edge is about 1 cm from the wall. Run Hericium plates a little warmer.

Stage Temperature Duration
Fresh or revived plates in the flow hood to establish About 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), the hood's ambient 3-5 days (for example over a weekend)
Same, chestnut A "slightly warmer" hood 3-4 days
Same, shiitake About 21-27 °C (70-80 °F) 3-4 days
Same, pioppino Flow hood or warm room Short, then about 1 week in incubation
Plate incubation after sealing 18-21 °C (65-70 °F); chestnut "just under 21 °C (70 °F)" Until about 1 cm from the edge
Hericium agar Warmer than grain or blocks: about 20-21 °C (68-70 °F), with 21 °C (70 °F) ideal; the same notes also list 18 °C (65 °F) Small plates don't self-heat, so they need warmer air to reach the same mycelial temperature
  • During the first days in the hood the mycelium is switching its enzymes to the new food and leaving the grain. Grain-to-agar transfers show a visible lag for this reason. Oysters may already show a couple of inches (about 5 cm) of growth in that time.
  • Hericium plates kept too cool pin early, grow in bands, or crawl.
  • Shiitake plates run faster at about 25-27 °C (the high 70s to 80 °F) and slower in a 16-21 °C (60-70 °F) incubation room.
  • Plates moved from warm air into a cooler room collect condensation.

RANGE First days in the hood: recommended 3-5 days at the hood's ambient, which on one farm is about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F); shiitake hoods run about 21-27 °C (70-80 °F). One source calls 80-85 the "standard incubation temperature", but this sits oddly beside the 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) used for everything afterwards and the 19 °C (66 °F) block guidance elsewhere; treat it as the hood's ambient rather than a target. After sealing, incubate at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F).

Reading plates: timelines and appearance

Species (medium) Time to fill / reach the edge What healthy growth looks like
Comb tooth (MYA) Visible after about 3 days; full plate about 2-2.5 weeks; 3-3.5 weeks if cool, an early 2 weeks if warm Faint and wispy like lion's mane, with cord-like veins giving thick and thin patches (normal). A typical plate shows white, radiating, fluffy mycelium on amber agar about two-thirds across, with cord-like streaks.
Lion's mane (MYA + charcoal) Edge in about 1.5-2 weeks Wispy and nearly transparent; a faint white plate, easiest to read held up to the light
Shiitake (MYA, charcoal) 3-4 weeks (as little as about 3) Faint and loose
Chestnut Edge in about 1.5-2 weeks (faster in the warm hood) Fine threads off the grain in week 1, then a "white water" wave of fluff while the centre flattens; light-coloured, vein-like main lines with fuzz; yellows as it does in bags
Pioppino About 2-3 weeks Fluffy, cottony, white and radial, with the first wisps from the cutting
Black oyster (PDYA) A couple of inches (about 5 cm) within the 3-5 hood days Thick, white, clearly visible threads growing out evenly and lying tight to the agar, not fluffing until they reach the edge. A fully colonized plate is dense white, filling up to the lid.
Maitake (MEA) Slow on every medium Rhizomorphic on MEA; takes 1-2 weeks to visibly recover after the agar is cut
King oyster Run-of-the-mill and forgiving at lab level Exposes any off variable, because it needs a steady metabolic rate (like maitake and pioppino)

TIP Faint, wispy lion's mane mycelium can look like contamination in blocks too, yet it colonizes a block in about 10 days. Don't bin it for looking thin.

When to transfer: the 1 cm rule

RULE Take transfers, or move the plate to the fridge, when the leading edge is about 1 cm from the plate wall.

WHY While growth is still spreading, the edge is in rapid cell division. Once it touches the wall it stops spreading and switches to thickening the mat. This rule is one of the most widely repeated in culture work.

  • Cut from the outer ring just behind the leading edge, where division is most active.
  • Transfer only from the leading edge, and don't let the mycelium reach the plate edge. Lion's mane in particular won't work once it has hit the edge.
  • Comb tooth plates go to the fridge, to production or to customers at about 2.5 weeks (up to 3 if cool). Plates kept for one farm's own storage may run a bit further, but are still stopped short of the wall.

Plates past their peak

Once a plate passes the 1 cm point it ages. Some aged plates are still usable; some are not.

Sign Meaning / action
Fluff clusters, primordial fluff, the centre fluffing up to the lid Plate is past peak; still usable. An aged lion's mane plate can be covered in dense white fluff clusters, with small fruit bodies on the agar.
White inner secondary ring (shiitake), later browning Still usable, but the plate is ageing
Secondary skin on a king oyster plate Peel it off; fresh tissue is underneath
Pioppino hitting the wall Gets fluffier ("pillow"), maybe slightly yellow, never a tough mat
Lion's mane fruiting on the plate Still usable if you cut from the outer edge, away from the primordia (baby fruit bodies)
Yellowing or yellow metabolite droplets Do not use
Overgrown oyster plates Mat, yellow and may form stroma if not refrigerated
Plate older than 3 months House rule on one farm: discard

RULE Discard plates that have yellowed, show metabolite droplets, or are older than 3 months.

  • Hericium on agar or in liquid culture left too long will form fruit bodies, even pushing past the plate film.
  • Pioppino plates refrigerated at the 1 cm stage filled in to the edge after about 3 weeks in the fridge, but had not hit the wall.
  • Refrigerating shiitake plates can stress them into secondary overlays.
  • Don't keep reusing old plates; keep each culture line fresh.

Stroma versus consolidation

  • Stroma (a tough, leathery mycelial crust) is very rare on agar. When it does appear, blame plate age, heat or poorly mixed media, for example undissolved lumps of malt extract. Well-made, evenly mixed agar and liquid culture essentially never show it.
  • A dense secondary mycelial layer that can be peeled off a plate is "mycelial consolidation". It is healthy, not stroma.

From plate to grain

AT A GLANCE Cut about 1 x 1 cm squares from the outer edge. Two cuts per 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1 normally, four when speed matters or for slow strains. Open the bag toward the filter, seal, label and incubate. Grain itself is covered in Chapter 9.

Item Value Conditions
Cut size About 1 x 1 cm squares from the outer edge The zone of most active growth
Cuts per 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1, normal 2: one against the front face of the bag, one against the back, so growth is visible Up to about 12 masters per plate
Cuts per 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1, rushed 4: front, back and sides About 6 masters per plate; faster colonization
Cuts per G1, shiitake 4 6-8 masters per plate
Cuts per G1, pioppino 2, sometimes 4 Plate at about 2-3 weeks; pioppino sits between the slow and fast strains
Test masters Pieces about 3x the normal size, one on each face about halfway down Speeds colonization for single test bags
Liquid culture to grain 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain master See Liquid culture

The same inoculation rate is used across all strains on one farm, done in the clean room in front of a HEPA wall.

Procedure: inoculating a G1 grain master from a plate

  1. Spray the sterile grain bag with alcohol and open it angled slightly toward the filter (not toward yourself, and not away).
  2. Sterilize the tool and cool it on the centre of the plate.
  3. Cut about 1 x 1 cm squares from the leading edge: 2 per 4 lb (1.8 kg) bag normally, 4 for rushed bags or shiitake.
  4. Drop the agar chunks into the bag, one against the front face and one against the back. In practice, unsealed rye or milo grain bags sit opened toward the filter, the chunks go in, and the bags are sealed.
  5. Seal the bag with the open end still facing the filter.
  6. Label it with the strain, fold it and send it to incubation.

CHECK Comb tooth and black oyster G1s: leave them unmoved for about 1-1.5 weeks, shake, then allow roughly another 1-1.5 weeks to finish.

WARNING Chestnut mycelium is easily upset. Shaking a G1 too soon after the agar cutting, or a thermal shock, often leads to odd growth, cell death and contamination. Let it establish first.

TIP A clear label convention, as seen on one bag: "Comb Tooth G1 121323-HCFF-2", that is species, generation, date (MMDDYY), strain code and bag number. Another bag reads "B-BO #2, 8/12".

Liquid culture

AT A GLANCE Liquid culture (LC) is mycelium grown in a sugar-water broth. The standard here is Cap n Stem's: 0.5% sugar, a 10-12 day cycle (never more than 14), and doses 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain master.

  • Ordinary LC is aerated only by shaking the vessel. Shaking vents CO2 and breaks up mycelium settled at the bottom, so the dense layer does not go anaerobic (airless).
  • There are two schools on LC media: complex recipes said to produce vigorous mycelium that adapts to any substrate, and simple low-sugar solutions. Cap n Stem chose simple, and that is the standard in this book.
  • To limit genetic drift, start every LC batch from an agar plate that came straight from cryo storage.
  • Inoculum: one generous scalpel scrape of surface mycelium from the newest growth near the plate edge (about a quarter-plate area was mentioned). No more is needed.
  • Incubate LC in the flow-hood area or in any climate-controlled incubation space.
  • LC does not dry out with too much air exchange, unlike grain or substrate.
  • Rye takes liquid culture well and is popular with growers of Psilocybe cubensis.
  • Many growers use LC for lion's mane, which thrives in it and darkens the broth (sometimes needing refreshing). Farms built around agar can stay with agar.

WARNING Serial liquid-culture expansion (LC from LC from LC) is a fast route to degeneration in Cordyceps militaris (see Chapter 8).

Parameter Value Conditions
Sugar concentration 0.5% (Cap n Stem's standard) Tested from 0.5% to 8%; common practice is 2-4%, and some use 1%
Cycle length 10-12 days, no more than 14 About 6-7 days growing/aerating, plus 6-7 days hold before drawing into syringes
Dose to grain 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain master Industry-standard dose for fast colonization; the volume of one farm's syringe

RANGE Sugar: standard 0.5% (Cap n Stem). Common practice elsewhere is 2-4%, some growers use 1%, and trials ran up to 8%. Cap n Stem tested the range and found low sugar markedly cut contamination and made the mycelium grow "purposefully". Cycle length: recommended 10-12 days, 14 at most; earlier figures of 4-6 days, 12 days and a 15-day maximum were also given before settling on this.

CASE Mossy Creek Mushrooms (Tennessee) keeps 343 strains and runs liquid culture this way:

  1. Take a needle biopsy (a tiny sample picked up on the tip of a needle) from a slant or dish. A needle sample is smaller than a scalpel cut and carries less contamination; the grower even works dish to dish in open air with a needle.
  2. Let the jar rest 3-4 days without stirring (10-14 days for pheasant's back).
  3. Once a dime-sized "jellyfish" of mycelium appears, stir once a day. The culture is ready in about 14 days.
  4. Pre-fill 10 syringes. Seal the first three in a bag in the fridge as emergency stock.
  5. Test each batch on agar and on grain at the same time, which saves days compared with testing one after the other.

The farm has also started growing liquid culture in bags.

RANGE Sugar in liquid culture. Standard (Cap n Stem): 0.5%. Context: Mossy Creek uses about double the usual sugar, but only because it never expands LC from LC; every batch starts fresh from a slant and is used once. If you expand LC from LC, stay at 0.5%.

Aerated liquid culture (ALC)

ALC means air is actively pumped into the culture, with gentle magnetic stirring. The motivation was reports, and some literature, claiming faster growth and denser mycelium with more clamp connections (small bridges on the hyphae that mark a healthy dikaryon). One spawn farm ran a trial comparing ALC with plain LC, partly as product development for its culture syringes.

The idea came from a grower group who were getting attractive aerated cultures.

Setting up ALC jars

  • Run the magnetic stirrer at its lowest setting; high makes a constant vortex. Keep airflow minimal: just enough for a layer of surface bubbles.
  • Lids with internal tubes (air line and syringe-draw line) make it hard to fit several half-gallon (about 1.9 L) Ball jars into a small pressure cooker. Pop the tubes off, wrap them separately, sterilize, and reassemble in front of the hood.
  • A typical rig: two wide-mouth Ball jars of pale yellow broth with red lids and tubes, on magnetic stirrer plates with stir bars, labelled "PO-BO 7/12" (species code unclear).
  • Dosing grain: a syringe injects through a black self-healing port into mixed grain.

The ALC versus LC trial

Trial stage Result
Grain (6 lb / 2.7 kg masters, 20 mL each) ALC started slightly slower; overall colonization about the same
Black oyster blocks, colonization ALC lagged early; both fully colonized at the same time
Round 1 fruiting (9 ALC, 9 LC blocks, top-fruited at a partner farm) Pinning took a while. ALC total weight was greater, and the heaviest single block was ALC.
Round 2 (5 each, about 2.5-3 weeks incubation, side-fruited, harvested a day late) ALC 2.87, 2.75, 2.58, 2.60, 2.74 lb = 13.54 lb (6.14 kg); LC 2.87, 2.80, 2.67, 2.61, 2.73 lb = 13.68 lb (6.21 kg). Effectively a tie.

WHY The clearer lesson was not ALC versus LC. Longer incubation (and side fruiting) raised black oyster yields, by an estimated 0.5-1 lb (0.23-0.45 kg) per block.

  • Still open: how many months ALC syringes keep in the fridge, and whether any benefit lasts. A larger repeat was proposed: 3 weeks' incubation, then top fruiting.
  • Aeration is being tested to relieve the stagnant state of submerged mycelium. For dedikaryotization, though, flasks must stay still (Chapter 8).

ALC lids (Myco-op style)

These lids let a pump feed filtered air into a jar and let you draw culture into a syringe without opening the jar.

Component Specification
Lid Regular Ball-type polypropylene lid (autoclavable), silicone gasket, three drilled holes with threaded through-valves
Internal tubes Two 1/4 in (6 mm) silicone tubes to the bottom; the draw tube ends just above the jar floor so it doesn't suck against the glass
Air in / exhaust 0.22 µm PTFE filter on the inlet; a second filter on the exhaust
Draw line One-way (check) valve flowing outward, with a luer cap
Pump EcoPlus Pro 40 aquarium pump, 12 valved outlets (6 per side), up to 12 jars; run continuously or on a timer
Tubing 1/8 in (3 mm) inside-diameter air tubing; Shore A70 silicone preferred over A50 (too rubbery)
Jar inlet fitting Non-barbed, so excess pressure can't burst the glass
Demonstration jar 2,000 mL

Procedure: sterilizing and running ALC jars

  1. Cover the filters with foil, or sterilize the filter assemblies in a separate empty foil-covered jar.
  2. Pressure-cook the jars, then fit the filters in front of the hood.
  3. Inoculate with agar, or with a syringe, inside the hood, and keep the filters dry.
  4. Connect the pump; keep fittings tight if it runs on a timer, to avoid suck-back.
  5. To fill syringes: in the hood, block the exhaust, attach the syringe to the luer on the one-way valve and open the air slowly. Jar pressure pushes LC into the syringe. A 60 mL syringe fills quickly, and about 150 syringes have been claimed from 1,500 mL. Bigger filters fill faster.
  6. Cap the valve and the syringe afterwards.

CHECK That 150-syringe claim works out at only 10 mL per syringe, so check your own count against the jar volume before planning on it.

  • Advantages claimed over stir plates alone: no injection port being stabbed repeatedly, and positive pressure keeps the LC aerated and sterile as long as the filters stay dry. Sealed, filter-fed jars can therefore incubate outside the clean area. These lids are popular with cubensis growers.
  • Weak point: purchased LC can't go in through the one-way valve. Swapping in a female luer barb lets dirty air flow back when the pump is on a timer.
  • Larger-area 0.22 µm filters exchange air better and build less pressure. Small filters can pressurize a jar enough to pop a loose part. For "bio jars" not used for syringes, one filter in and two out is an alternative.

Agar slurry

An agar slurry is a fully colonized plate, agar included, blended in sterile water and used directly to inoculate substrate bags instead of grain or sawdust spawn. It has not been shown to match grain-spawn yields, and many species do not tolerate it.

WARNING Treat agar slurry as experimental. It worked only for chestnut in one farm's trials, and it changed the fruit form.

Procedure: making and dosing an agar slurry

  1. Build the blender rig: a regular-mouth Ball jar of water with the blade base and gasket from a cheap Oster blender screwed on as the lid. It sits directly on the blender motor; any regular-mouth jar size fits.
  2. Sterilize the water jars for about 35 min at about 15 psi (1 bar) in a pressure cooker, lids slightly loose and foil-covered. Tighten the lids in the hood afterwards (tight lids on hot glass are hard to open and can break).
  3. Use one fully colonized plate per jar of about 400 mL (the original trials); one demonstration used half a plate.
  4. Wipe the plate with alcohol and remove the parafilm. Flame the scalpel (or use a bead or ceramic sterilizer) and cool it in the agar centre. Cut around the oldest, central area, drop the agar into the jar, and tighten the lid in the hood.
  5. Blend: pulse, check, swirl, pulse again until fine. Blender speed, blade sharpness, pulse time and species all need trials. The result is a milky white slurry.
  6. Dose about 45 mL per substrate bag (earlier trials used about 50 mL).
  7. Seal the bag with an impulse sealer and shake very thoroughly. An even spread of fragments is the critical step.

WARNING Blending too long kills cells; this probably happened in one farm's slurry trial.

CHECK Expect a long lag while damaged cells regrow and possibly recombine.

What happened in trials

Species tried Result
Chestnut The only species that colonized: nothing visible for about 2 weeks, then suddenly fully colonized
Four oyster types Only scattered fuzzy spots
Shiitake Only scattered fuzzy spots
Lion's mane Nothing

CASE In a trial on 5 lb (2.3 kg) chestnut blocks from the same expansion, slurry blocks gave many small, very uniform clusters of about 20 caps. Normally spawned blocks gave bigger, robust clusters of about 5 caps. That is a clear change in form. Whether it reflects a switch in the dominant nucleus or reconsolidation is unknown. Lesson: anyone making LC or slurries should watch for changes in fruit form.

RANGE Which method gave which chestnut form is not fully settled. One account describes "bigger caps, bigger stems" versus "skinnier caps, normal stems" without clearly saying which came from slurry. The more detailed account says slurry gave the smaller, more numerous caps.

  • Slurry can be seen as a "pre-dedikaryotization": blending a dikaryon's cells is the first step of splitting it, and in dedikaryotization one monokaryon commonly wins (Chapter 8).
  • Slurry is worth trying on any species, cubensis included. A side-by-side comparison of slurry against grain spawn was planned.

CASE A second trial reached the same result. Chestnut (Pholiota adiposa) slurry poured onto 5 lb (2.3 kg) sterile bags sat dormant for about 10 days, then colonized "practically overnight" and fruited normally, with no grain spawn needed. Yields matched grain-spawned blocks, though the fruit bodies were shaped somewhat differently. No other species or genus has done this in Cap n Stem's hands. Growth after blending also seems more vigorous.

Cloning a mushroom

AT A GLANCE Cloning means growing a culture from a piece of a living mushroom. Clones can come from grocery-store or wild mushrooms. Take inner tissue, make at least two cuts, give quiet plates a week, and transfer repeatedly until one clean organism remains; then re-plate once more to confirm.

Procedure: taking a clone

  1. Choose the freshest, cleanest specimen you can.
  2. Cut the specimen in half. Take tissue from the innermost part, farthest from every outer surface; the outside carries bacteria and foreign spores.
  3. Take at least two cuts from any specimen, especially a poor one, so one failure doesn't end the attempt.
  4. Place each piece in the middle of its own agar plate. For example, an orange fragment of chicken of the woods sits mid-plate on clear agar; later a scalpel moves an agar wedge carrying the orange tissue onto a new plate.
  5. Parafilm, incubate, and watch for mould, bacteria or mycelium.

TIP You can clone in the field with a portable hood running from a car inverter or power bank, and parafilm the plates on the spot (Portable hoods).

Four typical outcomes

Case What happened Lesson
Best case Fresh, still-growing chicken of the woods with no bugs, bacteria or mould grew clean mycelium from the first cut. Re-plated, it matched the first plate, and only then was it called "cloned". Re-culture to confirm before calling it done
Worst case An older maitake with surface mould, carried unrefrigerated for a couple of days. One cut was overrun by mould. A "dead plate" is unrecoverable
Slow case The second maitake cut showed neither mould nor growth at first. After about a week a microscope showed normal hyphae starting, and that section grew out. Dense fruit-body tissue can take time to revert to vegetative growth; don't bin quiet plates early
Most common case Lots of bacteria and other growth around the tissue, for example on shrimp of the woods (Entoloma abortivum), which already involves two fungi Clean it up by transfers

Under the microscope, a good clone shows thin, branching hyphae radiating from the edge of the tissue piece. A white colony with a cloudy halo around it is probably bacteria.

Procedure: cleaning up a dirty plate

  1. Let the mycelium outrun the bacteria; it usually does, or it throws up aerial tufts.
  2. Lift aerial tufts with a sterile loop without touching the agar, which may carry bacteria. A blue disposable loop picking up a small white tuft is the typical move.
  3. Where mycelium runs across the agar, use a sharp scalpel for precise cuts.
  4. Plate each transfer separately and watch it.
  5. Repeat until only one kind of growth remains and it matches the target. Expect several rounds: most wild clones carry a hitchhiker.
  6. Label clean-up plates clearly; one lab's plate reads roughly "SOP-outside-clone" (reading unverified).

TIP Optionally isolate each other organism on the plate (for example two bacteria and a mould) to map what the mushroom was living with.

What a clone can and can't do

  • Tissue propagation keeps a phenotype (the visible traits) you like. Growing from spores always recombines the genes, so you never get a true copy.
  • Cloning refreshes a line but never returns it to its original state. Storing a snapshot close to the original isolate is the better way to keep a phenotype (Chapter 8).
  • Wild isolates often smell wonderful but fruit poorly. A wild lion's mane from a beach colonizes Masters Mix blocks but won't fruit. A fragrant wild oyster grew on 50:50 but fruited poorly. Colonizing a substrate does not mean the strain will fruit on it: match substrate and fruiting trigger to the strain.

Production strains that began as clones

  • The chestnut culture used by Cap n Stem was cloned from a market sample in a walk-in cooler at Rosemont Bakery and Market, Portland, Maine.
  • The HeCNS lion's mane was cloned from the wild by Leighton Banks.
  • The JC shiitake was cloned in 2018 from log-grown shiitake bought through log brokers; many plates were made and one selected.
  • Cap n Stem's comb tooth is a wild clone from Denmark.

Choosing strains

AT A GLANCE Choose strains for your substrate, climate and market. Test each new or revived strain by fruiting it. Keep an alternative strain ready to rotate in during disease outbreaks. Species-by-species growing details are in Chapter 20.

General principles

  • Phenotype must be matched to substrate. Not every strain likes a given recipe, and oyster-centred thinking misleads small farms. A whiteboard summary of the idea reads simply "Phenotype : Substrate".
  • In Pleurotus ostreatus, the toughest strains (they never senesce and grow anywhere) tend to give poor yields of small mushrooms. Example: "JB", an old Far West Fungi strain recently acquired by Cap n Stem.
  • High-yield blue oyster strains are jokingly called "home wreckers": they fruit four times, and commercial growers cannot compete without that yield.
  • Cap n Stem keeps its house blue oyster despite its sensitivity to stroma, because its 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) fruits underpin customers' businesses. Small, dainty strains don't pay the same.
  • Phenotype selection can reduce spore load. A truly "spore-less oyster" is near-mythical, though large spawn companies are said to be good at low-spore strains.
  • Lion's mane works as an indicator species: a farm-wide problem may show only on lion's mane while hardier species cope, so don't assume the culture is at fault.
  • Rhizomorphic growth, prized by psychedelic growers, is not necessarily a sign of a healthier strain or substrate.
  • Run test grain bags (one plate to one master) routinely to confirm strains are not senescing: check expected stage times, healthy full fruit bodies and expected yields. That way the guidance you give customers comes from your own grows.

RULE Rotate strains against disease. Bacterial blotch can hit one strain and spare another, so switching strains during an outbreak removes losses immediately (even at lower yield) while you fix the root cause. Running the same genetics year after year eventually gets targeted, so rotate occasionally even with good practice. Example swap: from "3044" to "POCNS", "3015" or "King Blue" (codes unverified). See Chapter 17.

  • Very aggressive strains and heavily bred, long-domesticated lines seem more prone to blotch (anecdotal).

Shiitake strains

"LE" in strain codes stands for Lentinula edodes, the shiitake.

Strain Origin (as told) Character
3790 (LE3790) Mycelia (Belgium); originated in Japan (taken out by Mycelia and others, which Japan disliked) The most widely grown shiitake in North America and Europe. Fruits slightly colder; medium-large, meatier, denser ("donko"-style) mushrooms of better quality. More finicky, but higher yield and quality when dialled in. John Donahue calls it a "hot", vigorous, almost oyster-like strain. Far West Fungi grows it exclusively.
3782 Mycelia (Belgium); obtained from Brian Simpson at a Georgia farm; spread by Aloha Around 2013-14 a "revolution": 1+ lb (0.45 kg) from a 5 lb (2.3 kg) block on raw red oak plus red wheat bran. Many small, wafer-thin caps; a forgiving "training wheels" strain that tolerates moisture or heat errors; suits farms running around 29 °C (85 °F); more, smaller pins.
KOM From a Texas farm (possibly Korean origin, unverified) Expected to become a flagship standard strain within 1-3 years; tolerates low moisture
321 John Donahue / Northwest Mycological Consultants Cascadia's strain; average colonization (about 12 weeks), very pretty gourmet quality, low yield; still in use
JC Cloned in 2018 from log-grown shiitake by two Cap n Stem growers (Erik and Tyler) Big mushrooms, but niche compared with 3790 and KOM
"Straw" Aloha Medicinals Common in the late 2000s. Occasional 1 lb (0.45 kg) flushes of big mushrooms from a 5 lb (2.3 kg) block, but thousands of blocks gave none or one. One grower sold them at about $8/lb ($18/kg), including to a restaurant that thought they were log-grown. Another grower went back to breeding from it.
  • A whiteboard comparison: 3782 is small and plentiful, with "higher yield" later corrected to "moderate yield", and "tiny" on 10 lb (4.5 kg) ultra-pasteurized blocks; 3790 is medium-large, fewer, with moderate yield.
  • Mycelia offers about nine shiitake strains, not all bred in-house, and is said to have tried crossing 3782 x 3790 (Cap n Stem is sceptical). Its breeding protocol was described as very thorough.
  • Shiitake has around 40 grades in Japan.

RANGE Yield, 3782 versus 3790: recommended reading is that 3790 gives higher yield and quality when well managed, while 3782 gives a moderate yield of many small mushrooms and forgives mistakes. One whiteboard first called 3782 "higher yield" and then revised it to "moderate", with 3790 also listed as moderate.

Lion's mane and other Hericium

Hericium species differ mainly in morphology (shape) and are handled almost identically in culture.

Strain Origin (as told) Character
HeCNS (the Leighton strain) Wild clone by a Maine grower (Sagadahoc County was referenced), gifted to Cap n Stem when they left the industry One of the two most widely grown US lion's mane strains; a new benchmark for wholesale yield. Compact pom-pom fruit, tiny spines, several good flushes; handles and stores well. Ideal 13-18 °C (55-65 °F), sweet spot about 16 °C (60 °F). Sold under many names (for example "Tree Beard") because spawn companies rename strains.
POW ("HePow") Not stated The other common US strain. Tolerates slightly warmer conditions; good wholesale yield; less dense, spinier fruit.
"Lion's Pride" / HELP Thought to come from the same Maine line, naturalized near a farm in the US South (Mississippi/Alabama, unverified) Tolerant of heat and humidity; a flexible "fail-safe" strain; lower fruit quality in Cap n Stem's hands
129 Northwest Mycological; Cap n Stem's first Tough, less fickle, lower yield; still kept
9514 Mycelia (Belgium) Similar to 129
Comb tooth HcFF From a Danish farm, wild-collected in Denmark Stable, good fruiter. Very vigorous, high yield, high quality; keeps producing in warmer and varied conditions where erinaceus strains taper off. More farms are adopting it.
  • Some farms love one of Leighton or POW and hate the other.
  • A story sometimes told that Cap n Stem cloned HeCNS itself in Gardiner is a joke; Leighton Banks made the clone.
  • A typical strain map groups Leighton, POW and HELP together as one family that differs mainly in morphology.

King oyster, maitake, chestnut and others

Species Strain Notes
King oyster "Conch" From JT at Mushrooms Naturally, promoted on CMGN years ago; became the US standard and is still grown more than 2603 in the US. Auto-fruits in incubation even in rough conditions, and those deformed fruits usually don't regrow.
King oyster Mycelia 2603 (the code may be 2602) A soggy, neglected block lost its first malformed fruits but regrew good ones days later
King oyster "Siberia" Obtained by trade and given to North Spore; since lost
Maitake Mycelia "9827" The most significant strain now, and Cap n Stem's second most popular; very forgiving and behind the maitake boom
Maitake "Shogun" In Cap n Stem's cryo, just starting expansion; tolerates warmer fruiting than 9827
Maitake "494" Old Northwest Mycological strain; inconsistent; behaves differently
Maitake Other Northwest Mycological numbers; "Oakshire" Said to perform badly; Oakshire untested
Chestnut "PA CNS" Lineage: John Donahue (NMC) → Eric Milligan at New Hampshire Mushroom Co. → cloned by Erik Lomen of Cap n Stem → distributed worldwide. Also described as cloned from a Portland market sample and shared through NMC, CMGN and others.
Pioppino "AACN" From a wild collection via another grower; may not be true Agrocybe aegerita; yields very high
Reishi Ganoderma lingzhi From John Donahue, who got it from other growers in the 1980s; anecdotally high in some triterpenes
P. nebrodensis Cap n Stem release Endangered relative of P. eryngii from limestone and volcanic soils; reportedly needs a substrate of pH 8-11; fruits after a hard frost; low yield, a curiosity
Oyster "Steel Blue" Erik Lomen's first strain: nearly white when hot, deepest blue when cold; weak yields

RANGE King oyster, Conch versus 2603: recommended reading is that Conch is the better strain when the process is excellent. Which of the two is more forgiving is not clear from the sources.

  • Many Pholiota species can be grown but give only odd or one-off fruits. The PA CNS chestnut strain gives full commercial flushes, which is why it was prized on the East Coast.
  • King oyster is huge in Europe and East Asia under slow traditional methods. Testing many European and Asian strains on Masters Mix would probably turn up a strong performer (speculation).
  • Maitake strains are among Cap n Stem's top three spawn sellers.
  • Reishi variants exist: One grower grew a kidney-bean-shaped Ganoderma isolate from upstate New York for a long time.
  • Selling cultures can draw public dispute: a Cordyceps culture sold by one farm led to an online argument with a forum member who grows Cordyceps (and who had once applied to work there).

Strain sourcing, trade and naming

  • In the 2000s strains moved only by trade between friends and on forums such as Shroomery. There was no middle tier of spawn sellers between industrial makers and hobbyists, and Northwest Mycological barely served small growers.
  • Early strain traders such as Matt Noble (an Eastern European/Russian forum member) swapped cultures worldwide. Most of those collectors have since vanished.
  • Spawn companies rename strains, so one strain may be sold under many names.
  • Strains shared freely spread widely: one grower sees strains he mailed out years ago fruiting at farms across the country.
  • Cap n Stem plans formal, "high-tech" breeding and cloning, and will give new strains memorable names rather than number codes (and not cannabis-style names).
  • Spawn-industry consolidation is a concern: Sylvan buying companies worldwide, Amycel's patent-style strain protection, and Stamets once requiring a waiver to buy spawn.
  • One farm (Avery's) gets all its genetics from Cap n Stem in Maine: blue oyster POCNS, lion's mane "POW" (code unconfirmed), and Cap n Stem's house cultures of chestnut, pink and golden oyster, plus black pearl "58" (code unconfirmed), pioppino, golden enoki and maitake.
  • Another grower brought maitake 9827 over from Europe earlier, and a large maitake producer got it from them.

WARNING Moving cultures across borders needs phytosanitary paperwork. Maitake cultures were once hand-carried back from Mycelia in Belgium after a contact there advised skipping that paperwork; this was an illegal import. About half the strains brought back were excellent and half mediocre. Cultures have also been smuggled back from Europe, and one lab boss travelled with a small anaerobic chamber of cultures in his suitcase. Strains should not be hoarded, but import them legally.

Culture work as a business

  • Cultivation is three businesses in one: culture preservation and spawn, block production, and fruiting with fresh sales. Each needs different tools, space and filtration. See Chapter 22.
  • Keeping cultures takes about the same time at small or large scale: five varieties means five culture lines kept fresh. Consider making spawn only for one or two main varieties and buying the rest. Don't make spawn for species you also buy as blocks.
  • A middle path: buy grain masters or LC from a spawn lab and make only bulk spawn yourself, for example one run a week producing a month's spawn for one variety.
  • Fresh mushrooms are far easier to sell than cultures or spawn when starting out, and many new spawn-only companies lack credibility.

History of agar culture

  • 1894: Costantin and Matruchot in France produced the first pure mushroom cultures on agar, from tissue and from spores, using steam sterilization.
  • A piece of gill placed on a plate keeps shedding spores if its basidia (spore-bearing cells) had already formed.
  • 1929: Bessie E. Etter grew fruit bodies of wood-rot fungi in the lab. Plain agar gave mycelium but no mushrooms; wood rotters needed wood (sawdust or ground wood) plus a starch such as cornmeal or oatmeal. She grew them in 500-1000 cc flasks with one mushroom from the neck. Her main example was shiitake; Ganoderma formed a three-dimensional, fruit-body-like structure on agar when wood was present.
  • Reishi: the Chinese Academy of Sciences started work in the late 1960s and achieved full artificial cultivation (a spore-bearing cap) in the early 1970s. Lab attempts from the 1930s to the 1960s produced only antlers or nodules.
  • Fungal morphology depends heavily on environment (for example, fruit bodies grown in the dark look bizarre), unlike plant tissue culture.
  • Mushrooms produce different enzymes depending on their food. One claim is that a shiitake culture plated beside a Streptomyces culture makes a specific antibiotic-like metabolite.

Key rules

  1. Start every expansion (plate, LC or grain) from a plate that came straight out of storage; never chain old plates.
  2. Put the inoculum in the centre of the plate, parafilm twice, let it establish 3-5 days in the hood, then incubate at about 18-21 °C (65-70 °F); run Hericium plates a little warmer than grain.
  3. Cut transfers from the outer ring when growth is about 1 cm from the wall; refrigerate plates you are not using at that point.
  4. Use MYA for slow or faint species (shiitake, lion's mane; maitake on MEA) and PDYA for fast ones; add charcoal when you cannot see the edge.
  5. Discard plates that have yellowed, show metabolite droplets, or are older than 3 months.
  6. Two 1 cm cuts per 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1 (12 masters per plate), four cuts when speed matters or for slow strains; G1 to 12 G2, G2 to about 20 blocks; no G3 and no block-to-block transfers.
  7. For LC, keep sugar low (0.5%), finish the cycle in 10-14 days, and dose about 20 mL per 6 lb (2.7 kg) master.
  8. Treat agar slurry as experimental: it worked only for chestnut in trials and changed fruit form.
  9. When cloning, take inner tissue, make at least two cuts, give quiet plates a week, and transfer repeatedly until one clean organism remains; re-plate once more to confirm.
  10. Choose strains for your substrate, climate and market, test each new or revived strain by fruiting it, and keep an alternative strain ready to rotate in during disease outbreaks.

Open questions

  • No LC recipe beyond "0.5% sugar" is available: sugar type, additives, vessel volume and the agitation schedule for plain LC are not stated.
  • The ALC trial was small (n = 5-9 per group) and confounded with incubation time and fruiting method. The fridge life of ALC syringes is still being tested.
  • Agar media recipes (MYA, PDYA, amount of charcoal) were not stated.
  • The meaning of the "70F / 65 / 68 agar" numbers noted for Hericium agar was not explained.
  • Which slurry method gave which chestnut fruit form is unclear, and no yield figures were given for slurry blocks.
  • Several strain names and codes are as heard and unverified.

chapters.html:
Storing Cultures, Strains and Genetics

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers keeping strains alive and true to type (cryopreservation at -80 °C (-112 °F), slants, sterile-water storage, refrigeration), recognizing senescence and drift, the basic genetics of monokaryons and dikaryons, mechanical dedikaryotization and breeding, and a basic DNA workflow (extraction, PCR, gel electrophoresis). Much of the genetics in this field is still speculation, and it is marked as such. The rules used most:

  • Freeze a snapshot of each strain close to the original isolate and always expand from it, rather than serially subculturing.
  • Bank colonized rye berries in about 3 mL of 10% glycerol per 5 mL vial at -80 °C (-112 °F).
  • Thaw fast in a 30 °C (86 °F) water bath.
  • Test a revived strain by fruiting it (one grain bag, about 4 blocks) before releasing it.
  • Refresh banked cultures regularly: check every 6-12 months; treat anything past 2-3 years as suspect.
  • Keep spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), never 6 °C (42 °F).

Plate handling, the 1 cm rule and expansion numbers are in Chapter 7.

Why preserve cultures

  • Every cell division adds a little genetic damage. Freezing a snapshot close to the original isolate and always re-expanding from it (a "tight loop") keeps a line stable. Serial slant-plate-slant transfers or re-cloning do not: cloning refreshes a line but never returns it to its original state.
  • One farm keeps culture lines in cryo storage for up to a decade, as tiny pieces the size of a rice grain, cycling back to them so production stays close to the original phenotype.
  • Think of preservation as a closed loop (freezer → plate → re-bank → freezer) and expansion as a one-way line to blocks. Keep every culture in one or the other (Loops and lines).
  • Preservation is expensive in dishes, agar, slants, bags and labour, so many growers neglect it and only notice when their cultures senesce (age and decline).
  • Large spawn companies (Amycel is probably the one meant) do not genetically modify strains. They select mutations, store them cryogenically and test which work on which substrates.

Storage methods compared

AT A GLANCE -80 °C (-112 °F) cryo is the main method. Sterile water at about 1 °C (34 °F) is the next best and the only one for species that don't survive cryo. Slants in the fridge are the simplest.

Method Temperature How long it holds (as stated) Notes
Cryovial, colonized rye (or toothpicks) in glycerol -80 °C (-112 °F) About 2-3 years comfortably, then "iffy"; about 3 years; a decade for tiny pieces; study samples recovered after about 30 years The main method at Cap n Stem, where all cultures are banked this way
Sterile/distilled water with agar plugs About 1 °C (34 °F), fridge Months to years "Next best thing to cryo"; best for species that don't survive cryo
Slants Fridge 6-8 months used without trouble; now refreshed more often Limited air makes the mycelium slow down
Yeast-bank freezer -40 °C (-40 °F) Better than a fridge An option via breweries or yeast banks
Liquid nitrogen Not stated Not given An option, and part of the history
Plain agar (chestnut) Fridge "A long time" Only for exceptionally stable strains; optionally with wood or grain in the slant
Mineral oil Not given Not given Historical (1949)
  • -80 °C (-112 °F) is the lowest temperature you need for cryoprotected mycelium. Most small growers only have a fridge at about 1 °C (34 °F).
  • A typical comparison drawing sets the two options side by side: a petri dish divided into squares for plugs, for the -80 °C (-112 °F) freezer, and a test tube of plugs under water for the 1 °C (34 °F) fridge.
  • Cryo is cost-inefficient unless your culture use justifies it. Some culture banks (Cap n Stem is one) will store other people's cultures, without selling them unless asked.

TIP Temperature conversions on this topic are often misquoted: -80 °C is -112 °F.

Cryopreservation at -80 °C

Carrier: toothpicks versus rye berries

A carrier is what the mycelium grows on before it goes into the vial.

  • The two common carriers are toothpicks and rye berries. Cap n Stem used toothpicks for years and has recently switched to rye.
  • Why rye: its internal capillary or cell structure adds its own cryoprotection, it hydrates evenly and it colonizes densely. Toothpicks of weaker species can be lacklustre. Sorghum was also tried; rye worked better.
  • Poor revival (low vigour, apparent cell damage) usually traces back to poor sample preparation. For thin, delicate Hericium mycelium, well-hydrated, fully colonized rye is essential. A side-by-side of under-hydrated versus hydrated toothpicks showed visibly different growth and speed.

Procedure: preparing colonized grain for the vial

  1. Put cuttings from a fresh plate in the centre of a blank agar plate. Pour hydrated, sterilized rye berries (from the spawn line) in a ring around them.
  2. Incubate until the mycelium covers the berries, colonizes their interior and grows a little past them.
  3. Bank promptly. Left too long, the fungus digests the berries to mush and the grain loses its protective structure.
  4. In the flow hood, with sterile tools, drop colonized kernels into vials of cryoprotectant. Make sure they are fully submerged: shake down floaters, and shake to coat.
  5. Seal the vials and put them in the -80 °C (-112 °F) freezer.

CHECK The number of new vials equals the number of berries you placed, in the scheme that puts one berry in each vial.

Cryoprotectant

A cryoprotectant is a liquid that protects cells from ice damage during freezing. Glycerol is the standard one.

Parameter Value
Glycerol concentration 10% v/v in water
Mixing 900 mL water + 100 mL glycerol per litre; RO (reverse-osmosis) or distilled water recommended
Vial About 5 mL plastic screw-cap cryovial
Fill About 3 mL per vial (0.3 mL of it glycerol); 3.5-4 mL in one chestnut protocol
Carriers per vial 5-10 colonized grains; or one kernel per vial (two protocols); or 5 toothpicks (toothpick method)
Storage -80 °C (-112 °F), vials in cryo boxes ("suitcases")
  • How glycerol works: water molecules cluster around glycerol rather than around each other, so large, damaging ice crystals don't form. Glycerol enters the cells; other cryoprotectants act outside them.
  • 10% glycerol is the standard cryoprotectant across the mushroom and biologics industries and, from research, the most effective.
  • The outcome depends on species, density of the sample, freezing rate and storage temperature (-20 °C (-4 °F), -40 °C (-40 °F), -80 °C (-112 °F) or liquid nitrogen). Studies are small and contradictory, so aim for a robust, repeatable protocol rather than complete theory.
  • Still open: the best cryoprotectant concentration, other ingredients, and freezing liquid culture versus grain.

RANGE Glycerol strength: recommended 10% v/v. Some protocols use 5%: water plus 5% glycerol with wheat or rye grain (formerly toothpicks) in one shiitake protocol, 5% in an earlier lion's mane protocol, and 5% used by one lab worker. Some industry people use 30-35%, but the literature reports cell death at around 25-30% in some species, such as shiitake.

Cryo equipment

  • A typical cryo set-up: a -80 °C (-112 °F) chest freezer (one is Thermo-brand) in a room marked with tape lines on the floor; white and red cryo boxes, lifted frosted from a rack; screw-cap cryovials.
  • Slants are short, green-capped tubes of tan agar held in a rack, each labelled with its strain.
  • The flow-hood room, which holds the cryogenic freezer and the genetics work, is the top pressure priority at Cap n Stem: the first room to protect with positive pressure (Chapter 4).

Thawing and revival

AT A GLANCE Thaw fast at about 30 °C (86 °F), use the oldest lot first, plate the carrier in the centre, give it 3-5 days in the warm hood, then 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). Compare every revived vial with its expected profile before you expand it.

Procedure: reviving a cryovial

  1. Pick the earliest lot vial first.
  2. Thaw it fast: put the vial in a water bath at about 30 °C (86 °F) until it is fully melted.
  3. Grain carriers: place the grain in the centre of a fresh plate and wait a few days for mycelium to emerge.
  4. Toothpick carriers: put each of the 5 toothpicks onto its own slant, giving 5 independent revival tests per vial.
  5. Let revived plates sit 3-5 days in the warm hood, then move them to 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) incubation (Incubating plates).
  6. Watch revived slants for health and survival. The healthy ones become the source for master spawn, more plates and more slants; discard weak ones.
  7. Compare every revived vial against its expected profile before expanding, because one vial can lead to hundreds of masters.

WHY A slow thaw leaves ice crystals melting and re-forming, which damages the mycelium.

TIP The cryo process is still evolving. Thaw time and slant incubation conditions after thawing have not been fixed.

How species behave in cryo

Species Cryo behaviour reported
King oyster No cell-line degradation in cryo or refrigeration, no odd agar growth; among the most consistent
Chestnut Among the most consistent; exceptionally stable even before cryo
Maitake Stores well in cryo and always recovers; stable on agar for long periods
Oysters Some revived with irregular growth, patches of programmed cell death, browning or blackening (partly blamed on one farm's earlier poor cryo routine)
Pink and golden oyster Don't survive cryo; use sterile-water storage
Cordyceps militaris Degenerates fast; preserve early

Re-banking and the test-and-expand line

Procedure: re-banking (the loop)

  1. Once a revived plate looks right, move a wedge to a fresh plate strewn with sterile rye berries.
  2. When the berries are colonized and the plate is fluffy, transfer them to new vials.
  3. Refreeze. The loop runs cryovial → agar plate → plate with rye berries → back to cryo.

Procedure: the test-and-expand line

Cap n Stem adopted this soon after it began selling spawn.

  1. Thaw one vial, cut the grain in half and plate it on two dishes: dish 1 (T, test) and dish 2 (E, expansion).
  2. Hold back dish E.
  3. Take dish T to one grain bag, then to about 4 substrate bags.
  4. Fruit the blocks and check yield and form.
  5. Only if they pass, expand dish E (about 4 dishes from it; see Expansion numbers).
  • If a vial has sat 18-24 months and you doubt it, expand it to one grain master and about 4 substrate bags, fruit them, and confirm the yield before trusting the line.
  • Track every vial, test and expansion in a spreadsheet, database or Gantt chart.

How often to refresh

RANGE Recommended: cycle each banked culture through the refresh loop at least yearly, ideally checking every 6 months, and treat anything past 2-3 years in the freezer as suspect until a test fruiting proves it. Reported holding times: about 2-3 years comfortably with recoveries getting "iffy" after that (two protocols); about 3 years (a chestnut protocol); lines kept for a decade (as tiny pieces); and a long-running freezer study with samples recovered after about 30 years (quoted as 29-30 and 29-35 years).

Without a -80 °C freezer

  • Make cryovials yourself (flow hood, liquid cryoprotectant) and ask a local brewery or yeast bank to keep the box. They store yeast at -80 °C (-112 °F) (some at -40 °C (-40 °F), still better than a fridge) and often have room. Cap n Stem uses friendly breweries in Maine.

  • Or use a culture bank: Cap n Stem, North Spore and a Belgian bank (probably MYCELIA bvba) are options.

  • Our farm has no freezer. See Our farm: the culture bank without a freezer for the slants-and-water-tubes bank used here.

Slants

A slant is a test tube of agar set at an angle, giving a long surface for the mycelium.

  • Slants keep a long time because the limited air in the tube makes the mycelium slow down once it covers the surface.
  • Slants 6-8 months old have been used without trouble, but one farm now refreshes them more often, as a matter of risk tolerance. Refrigerated distilled-water storage is arguably better, and cryo better still.
  • One slant yields 8-12 production plates (other figures are in Expansion numbers).
  • For a very stable strain such as Cap n Stem's chestnut, plain agar storage, optionally with wood or grain in the slant, is fine for a long time.

Procedure: making storage slants

  1. Make 3-5 slant tubes per culture.
  2. Cool freshly poured slants at an angle in front of the flow hood.
  3. Inoculate and colonize them for 2 weeks.
  4. Refrigerate; in one farm's experience they keep for years. Vacuum-sealed food containers work for storage.

RULE Keep both slants and water tubes of each strain, so storage doesn't depend on one method.

Sterile-water storage

AT A GLANCE Small agar plugs from the leading edge, in sterile water, in a screw-cap tube backed off 1/8 turn and parafilmed, at about 1 °C (34 °F). Holds months to years. The best option for pink and golden oyster, which don't survive cryo.

Procedure: storing plugs in sterile water

  1. Grow the plate only partway; it should not be thick or matted.
  2. Cut small agar squares from the leading edge, or slice the plate "like a pizza".
  3. Put them in an autoclavable screw-cap test tube; one low-tech version uses a 50 mL screw-cap centrifuge tube.
  4. Fill with sterile (or distilled) water.
  5. Back the cap off about 1/8 turn, then parafilm it.
  6. Store at about 1 °C (34 °F) in a clean fridge, or in a lunchbox inside a fridge.
  7. To use: pull one plug per new plate with a flamed tool. Make backup tubes.
  • The water keeps plugs hydrated and oxygenated and stops three-dimensional growth; mycelium also likes the hydration.
  • This method is also called "liquid agar preservation". It is the next best thing to cryo and the best option for species that don't survive cryo (pink and golden oyster). Shiitake stored this way tested "pretty stable" over months.
  • It preserves cultures that would otherwise dry out on parafilmed plates, and has given one low-tech grower years of backups. A genetic library is worth building and doesn't require thousands of dollars.
  • A low-tech set-up: agar wedges cut with a torch-flamed long blade in front of a small framed HEPA unit, dropped into a 50 mL tube of water labelled "LOW-TEK".

CASE Early on, one grower moved cultures by cutting agar cubes from plates (poured in a glove box), dropping them into sterile water in a slant tube and carrying them on a plane. The culture survived a long time. A plate cut into chunks going into a slant tube of sterile water is the whole method.

Short-term cold storage of plates and spawn

AT A GLANCE Keep spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), not 6 °C (42 °F). Use G2 within 2-3 weeks of refrigeration. Watch lion's mane for fruiting in the fridge.

  • Before shipping, pre-chill spawn in 40 ft (12 m) refrigerated containers, because packed, active spawn self-heats. Gel packs chill, then buffer, then give out, so heat stress tends to hit at the end of transit.
  • Temperature is the variable that always causes trouble when shipping spawn, blocks or cultures, especially in summer.
  • One farm keeps its working cultures in a tote in the fridge. As insurance it also holds 2-5 spawn bags of lion's mane or blue oyster for 4-6 weeks.
  • For carrying cultures on a trip, an insulated lunch box works. Cap n Stem also has ways of shipping cultures to growers abroad.

Our farm: the culture bank without a freezer

FARM NOTE This farm (Playa Negra, Costa Rica) has no -80 °C (-112 °F) freezer and will not buy one. Joseph's decision of 6 Nov 2026: all long-term storage is agar slants and sterile-water (Castellani) tubes. No cryovials. The brewery and yeast-bank route in Without a -80 °C freezer does not apply here. All 17 strains come from Cap n Stem, so Cap n Stem is also the fallback source if a line is lost. Where this section gives a number, the source is named in the chapter section it links to. Anything else is a farm choice (FARM NOTE) or still undecided (OPEN).

The method rests on the slant and sterile-water sections and on the test-and-expand line. The rule in the slant section is the starting point: keep both a slant and a water tube of every strain, so storage never depends on one method.

Procedure: banking a new strain at intake

Do this the week a strain arrives, before it goes into production.

  1. Log the strain with its code (two letters for the species plus a number, such as BO-01 for blue oyster), the source (Cap n Stem), the date and who received it. The culture as received is the master, P0. A plate made from it is P1. A slant or water tube carries the level of what it was made from.
  2. Plate the culture to a fresh dish. This is the first plate, P1. Let it grow only partway, as the water-tube procedure asks: not thick, not matted.
  3. From that one P1 plate, cut leading-edge squares and make the whole bank at once: 3-5 slants (making storage slants) and 3-5 water tubes (storing plugs in sterile water). Use one plate for the whole batch so every tube starts from the same material.
  4. Label every tube: strain code, tube type (S for slant, W for water), P-level, date banked, tube number. Example: BO-01 W3 P1 2026-11-09.
  5. Put the new tubes in the culture fridge (below). Move at least one slant and one water tube to the off-site copy (below).
  6. Run the test-and-expand line (below) on a tube from this bank before the strain feeds production.
  7. Enter every tube in the viability log (below).

CHECK Each strain has 3-5 slants and 3-5 water tubes, all labelled, all from one P1 plate, with at least one of each stored off site, and each is listed in the log.

Refresh rules

Item Rule Basis
Slants Replace within 6 months of banking. Slants 6-8 months old have been used without trouble, and one farm now refreshes them more often. This farm takes the shorter, safer end (Slants).
Water tubes Check every 6-12 months: pull one plug, plate it, record the days to cover. If it is healthy, the other tubes of that batch stay in the bank. Sterile-water lifetimes are anecdotal ("months to years"). The check turns the guess into your own data (Sterile-water storage, open questions).
Any strain, any storage Treat a tube more than 2 years from banking as suspect until a test fruiting proves it. The chapter's rule for old stock is 18-24 months for a vial and 2-3 years in the freezer (How often to refresh). Without cryo, take the shorter figure.
Refreshing Plate a healthy tube, grow it to the 1 cm stage, then make a new batch of slants and water tubes from that plate. Test it before the old batch is discarded. Re-banking, with slants and tubes in place of cryovials.

OPEN How many P-levels are too many? No source gives a ceiling for slant-and-tube banking. Until Cap n Stem answers, record the P-level on every tube, refresh from the lowest level alive, and reorder the strain from Cap n Stem if the only tubes left are several generations from the master. Ask Cap n Stem what ceiling they use.

The test-and-expand line from a tube

This is the chapter's test-and-expand line with a tube in place of a thawed vial.

  1. Take one slant or one water tube from the bank (two plugs if it is a water tube). Plate it onto two dishes: dish T (test) and dish E (expansion).
  2. Hold dish E back. Do not open it, subculture it or use it for anything else.
  3. Use dish T to inoculate one grain bag, then use that bag to inoculate about 4 substrate blocks of the normal recipe. Label the grain bag and blocks TEST with the strain code and date.
  4. Fruit the blocks. Record days to colonize, days to pin, form, and yield per block against the strain's own history.
  5. Pass: expand dish E for production. Fail: discard E and revive another tube from the bank.

When to run it:

  • At intake, for every new strain (step 6 of the intake procedure).
  • After every refresh, on one tube of the new batch.
  • Whenever a tube is more than 18-24 months old and you still want to use it.
  • Every month, for each strain in production, by reading the results of the real production lots, not by growing extra blocks. See Our farm: monthly strain check. This catches senescence before it reaches the line.

FARM NOTE Joseph's decision (6 Nov 2026): there is no separate monthly test line. A strain's health is read from the yield, form, days to pin and contamination of its normal production blocks, fed in from the farm's own records. The full test-and-expand line is kept for intake, refresh and old tubes.

The culture fridge

FARM NOTE Cultures live in one fridge that holds nothing else: no spawn, no food, no samples. Set it to 1-2 °C (34-36 °F). The off-site copy

FARM NOTE Keep a second set of at least one slant and one water tube of every strain somewhere other than the farm, in a fridge at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), such as a trusted grower's or a second building.
