Senescence and strain drift

Senescence is the ageing and decline of a culture line: slower, weaker or odd growth and poorer fruiting. Drift is a gradual change in how a strain behaves.

Signs of senescence

  • On plates: patches of unusually fuzzy growth with thicker, harder rhizomorphic lines growing out around them. One interpretation (speculative): the dikaryon's two nuclei are drifting apart, the fuzzy partner weakening and the rhizomorphic one taking over. In nature this is when a mon-di (Buller) pairing would happen (Fungal genetics basics).
  • After cryo revival, in oysters: irregular growth, patches of programmed cell death, browning or blackening.

RULE Learn the signs of senescence (fuzzy patches with hard rhizomorphic lines, irregular growth, browning). When you see them, refresh from your own bank or from a culture bank.

Species differences

  • Cordyceps militaris degenerates quickly (light, temperature and RNA-level pathways have been cited), especially through serial liquid-culture expansion. Published studies on its storage time, temperature and recovery have made growers more aware that dikaryotic strains do not last forever.

  • Lion's mane rarely senesces in one farm's experience; it fails through contamination or fruiting too early.

  • Cap n Stem's chestnut has never drifted, even before cryo.

  • Kings show no degradation; kings and chestnut are that farm's most consistent cultures.

  • Maitake is genetically stable on agar for long periods.

  • The toughest P. ostreatus strains never senesce, but they yield poorly.

  • Cordyceps: keep monokaryons (single-nucleus cultures) in separate stock. What growers call "senescence" in a mated Cordyceps liquid culture is really the culture falling back to a monokaryon. You can re-mate it by pairing it with the non-dominant monokaryon.

Drift and domestication

CASE Black oyster has changed. In early days on Master's Mix, white fuzz grew from the cut, formed amber droplets and receded, and the droplets became caps on king-oyster-like bumps (photographed by another grower). This no longer happens. Possible reasons: domestication, longer incubation, the switch to black bags, and repeated cryo and expansion cycles. One view is that long-domesticated strains either stabilize or fail in long storage; re-cloning also gave odd morphology.

  • Wild oyster clones show little stroma at first, but it rises with successive generations of the cell line. A Danish grower's wild red "basket" oyster now forms stroma heavily after long domestication.

  • Stroma usually appears in only 1-2 of several hundred bags from the same cell line. That points to a local stress response rather than a defective culture.

  • A study of wild cubensis found high genetic diversity (for example in New Zealand) compared with inbred domesticated lines. Heavily bred lines can be seen as productive but less stable.

  • Black pearl oyster is, in one grower's experience, more prone to odd mutations if incubation is sloppy.

  • A mutation-prone cubensis strain (Penis Envy) grew more evenly with a compacted, casing-like surface layer than in loose, through-spawned beds.

  • Speculative: shifts in which nucleus is "dominant" may explain odd growth labelled as senescence. The field has not defined dominance (the nucleus that drives the phenotype, versus one held for fruiting).

  • Do not assume the dominant nucleus is the faster grower; selection might favour something else, such as defence against bacteria. The recognition proteins involved are poorly known.

  • You can select cultures for traits other than yield, such as the longest shelf life, an unusual flavour or a striking look. A strongly violet oyster found by one breeder was later lost, which shows why unusual finds should be banked at once.

  • Wild clones are often more fragrant and flavourful than commercial strains, and selecting for yield slowly removes those qualities. A New Hampshire grower's cloned wild oyster made spawn that smelled and tasted better, but it yielded poorly and later contaminated.

  • Wild oyster clones are often unstable: "it smells so good... never fruits". A wild lion's mane (Hericium erinaceus) clone, by contrast, usually fruits in production much as it did in the wild.

  • Wild material can be surprisingly vigorous. A student found a wild Amanita (destroying angel, a deadly species) culture that grew faster than any commercial oyster culture he had been given.

Fungal genetics basics

AT A GLANCE One spore grows into a monokaryon (one nucleus type). Two compatible monokaryons fuse into a dikaryon (two nuclei per cell). Only the dikaryon fruits. Spores recombine; tissue keeps the phenotype.

  • A single spore grows into a monokaryon. Two compatible monokaryons fuse their hyphae (without the nuclei fusing) to form a dikaryon, with two distinct nuclei per cell. Only the dikaryon can form fruit bodies.
  • Monokaryons act as hermaphrodites: each can donate or accept a nucleus. If they are compatible they exchange and spread nuclei, and the resulting dikaryon seems locked in.
  • A dikaryon meeting a monokaryon can only donate. The monokaryon decides whether to accept one of the two nuclei. This is the di-mon or Buller phenomenon, described from papers on the honey mushroom (Armillaria). It makes a new strain without spores.
  • Spore-grown strains always recombine, so you never get a true copy of a phenotype you liked; tissue or mycelial propagation keeps it. Fungi are fairly stable genetically (a vague "1 in 10,000" mutation figure has been quoted). Breeding from monokaryons allows controlled crosses.
  • Some fungi are homothallic: one spore completes the life cycle, so a single spore landing on media can take over a bag. Heterothallic fungi need a compatible partner, but only before fruiting. Asci (spore sacs in some fungi) hold 8 spores (4 in some species). These points come from Neurospora, first described as a bread mould in French bakeries.
  • Ganoderma is heterothallic and tetrapolar (four mating types). A 1986 mating study (Adaskaveg and Gilbertson) found that G. lucidum and G. tsugae did not cross or form clamps, supporting their separation as species.

WARNING The Buller-phenomenon findings come from few papers and may not apply to all fungi.

A classroom sketch of the same idea shows two spores becoming "MON (+)" and "MON (-)" lines meeting at an "intersect (+,-)" that leads to "DI".

Mechanical dedikaryotization

Dedikaryotization splits a dikaryon back into its two monokaryons, so they can be used in new crosses (mon-di or di-mon). Mechanical methods (blending) are the simplest and most accessible. Protoplast-based methods (protoplast regeneration or fusion) need more lab capability.

Step Detail
Materials The dikaryon plate; several Erlenmeyer flasks or mason jars of liquid medium; a blender jar (mason jar on a blender base) with DI (deionized) or plain water
Medium 1% glucose + 1% peptone (w/v), for example 1 g of each per 100 mL, or 1.5 g of each per 150 mL
Sterilize Everything except the culture (flasks, blender jar, water); cool
Sample About a 0.5 cm cube from the leading edge (the apical growth zone)
Blend About 20-25 s for Pleurotus (shiitake trials pending), until it is flakes, not a chunk
Inoculate About 5 µL of homogenate per flask (optionally several 5 µL draws from different spots); swirl gently
Incubate Leave the flasks completely still, so each fragment grows into its own pellet; merged pellets can re-form a dikaryon
Pellets (oyster) Appear after about 3 days (elsewhere "about a week" to start forming); about 7-10 per flask
Pick Lift single pellets with a pipette and space them apart on a plate
Check Microscope for clamp connections. The goal (from one published protocol) is clamps on about 30% or fewer of septa; a dikaryon shows clamps everywhere.
Repeat Several cycles are usually needed

Procedure: mechanical dedikaryotization

  1. Mix the medium: 1% glucose + 1% peptone, for example 1.5 g of each in 150 mL water per flask.
  2. Sterilize the flasks, the blender jar and its water; let them cool.
  3. In the hood, cut a 0.5 cm cube from the leading edge of the dikaryon plate and drop it into the blender jar.
  4. Blend about 20-25 s (Pleurotus) until you see flakes, not a chunk. Do not blend longer: it kills cells.
  5. Add about 5 µL of homogenate to each flask and swirl gently.
  6. Leave the flasks completely still.
  7. After about 3 days to a week, lift 7-10 single pellets per flask with a pipette and space them apart on a plate.
  8. Check each colony under the microscope for clamps; keep those with clamps on 30% or fewer of septa.
  9. Repeat the cycle as needed; expect several.

CHECK A dikaryon shows clamps at every septum. A monokaryon shows none, or few that disappear over time.

  • Pellet centres stop growing while a halo grows outward; nutrient uptake is purely osmotic.

  • Clamps don't vanish at once. Some dikaryotic nuclei persist, one nucleus type often dominates the recovery, and getting both monokaryons is a matter of luck.

  • One protocol uses a very small amount of mycelium (heard as 1 µL into 100 mL). Colonies need repeated sectoring and clamp checks; some start with a few clamps that disappear over time. One speculation is that rupturing cells lets single nuclei escape.

  • Blending too long causes cell death.

  • Macerated mycelium put on agar or a nutrient source can set pins quickly (reported on Julian's podcast). One speculative reading is that maceration feels like a disaster to the fungus and triggers an "escape" pin set, comparable to morels fruiting after fires.

  • An agar slurry is effectively a first step of dedikaryotization (Agar slurry).

  • The kit in use: graduated 150-250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks; a stovetop pressure cooker on a hotplate; a mason jar on an Oster-type blender base in front of a hood; a flask of cloudy white homogenate; a plate with about 7 separate pellet colonies; pipetting onto a microscope slide. The end goal is two "MON" dishes joined by hyphae to a "DI" dish.

  • Hardier species such as blue oyster and shiitake tolerate "mass maceration": blending the mycelium. After blending, grow out the colonies and look for hyphae with no clamp connections; take each clampless extension forward to isolate a monokaryon. The full protocol starts from a half-centimetre cube cut from the leading edge of a culture.

Breeding

State of the field

  • 1935: Frank Kaufert studied the spore system of Pleurotus corticatus (now placed under P. dryinus). He found about five routes to spore production, including asexual spores on stressed mycelium, without understanding dikaryons. He also used wood-block culture.

  • 1968: Eugenio and Anderson compared compatible versus incompatible pairings using Kaufert's block method; compatible dikaryons yielded about 200 g more.

  • Around 1971, Paul Stamets and a colleague studied clamp connections with an electron microscope.

  • From the 1980s to 2010, reishi research focused on genetics, mating systems and markers.

  • Breeding of new phenotypes largely stopped in the late 1980s. Japan and China hold vast shiitake libraries, but long-term breeding programmes are rare. The industry needs to return to breeding.

  • A spawn-industry veteran has said (on the Mushroom Revival podcast) that there have been essentially no oyster breeding programmes since the late 1970s or early 1980s.

  • Small farms do breed. A California grower crosses blue oyster strains (for example 8801 with Lambert's 123) and trials the crosses in small grow tents.

  • Mossy Creek Mushrooms (Tennessee) breeds every week, mostly oysters. Its method is deliberately harsh at the start ("very abusive in the beginning"), so it selects aggressive, hardy strains from the outset.

  • For shiitake the same breeder wants a strain that is easier to produce, "can really take abuse" and finishes in 8 weeks. He rates strain 3790 an improvement on 3782, but neither is yet as good as he wants.

  • Colourful oysters (a neon blue that fades through other shades to white or green) that grow aggressively help with market displays and grow-kit sales. Distributors, however, care about only one or two traits.

Breeding ideas worth trying

These are proposals and speculation, not proven methods.

  • Extract monokaryons from your culture bank and remix them within a species group (blue oyster, yellow oyster, shiitake) to create new phenotypes and breeding programmes.
  • Julian already sells monokaryon cultures, so breeders can cross proven phenotypes instead of starting from spores. AI may one day predict mating outcomes from genomes.
  • Simple experiments: grow out each monokaryon of a strain and compare it with the dikaryon to guess which nucleus dominates; grow a block from one monokaryon and add the other late; put a monokaryon and a dikaryon on one plate and re-isolate the monokaryon (incompatible pairs form a clear line). Each step takes only 5-30 min, with 1-2 week waits.
  • Breeding against stroma: if one nucleus drives stroma, pair the better monokaryon with others and grow them in stroma-inducing conditions to see which lines avoid it. One Danish grower isolated about 20 wild oyster strains, all of which made stroma, and is running a dedikaryotization project.
  • Chestnut and nameko are both Pholiota. A "bridge" strain able to mate with each might combine chestnut's qualities with fewer of nameko's slimy traits: use spores of the bridge cross, split back to monokaryons and DNA-test for recombination. This is pure speculation needing hundreds of trials.
  • Could crossing breed out chestnut intolerance? It is described as all-or-nothing and "proven", with no source given.
  • Crossing black oyster (with nebrodensis ancestry adapted to limestone and high pH) with other oysters might relax its high-pH need for fruiting.
  • One grower is crossing black oyster monokaryons with other oysters.
  • Sporeless or low-spore strains (for example of golden oyster, which is invasive in places) are a planned topic. A near-sterile hybrid like black oyster may be ecologically safe, because it cannot cross within itself, only with wild species.
  • Claimed intergeneric fusions (oyster x lion's mane, lion's mane x reishi, reishi x shaggy mane, shaggy mane x hen of the woods) can form clamps but don't fruit. They might pass genes into later hybrid crosses (speculation).
  • Cordyceps: production and crosses are starting (single-cell isolation, storage of fast-degrading strains), with a Cordyceps militaris monokaryon project planned.
  • Reishi contains 400+ identified compounds, which argues for selecting strains on whole-spectrum chemistry rather than a single compound.

Case study: black oyster (Shimofuri Hiratake / Black Pearl)

AT A GLANCE Black oyster is almost certainly a multi-species hybrid made by a Japanese company through six rounds of crossing among P. ostreatus, P. nebrodensis and P. eryngii varieties. Its exact parentage is unresolved until a whole genome is sequenced.

  • Names used interchangeably: Black Pearl, Black King, Cosmic Queen, Shimofuri.
  • US history: a culture was brought back from Japan. Cap n Stem got it via Brooks Warden (then at Far West Fungi), with other growers also in the chain, probably around 2017. An "Aloha" strain was also called black oyster, and another version came from a North Carolina farm. It stayed "in the petri dish" in the US for a long time before anyone fruited it seriously.
  • Hokuto Corporation (a large Japanese mushroom company with a southern California plant) described it on its website as an eastern x western oyster hybrid (ostreatus x ostreatus). That account was repeated publicly in the US and now looks wrong.
  • Clues to a complex hybrid: the owner of Sprouted Mushrooms did Buller-style crosses of black oyster with kings and blues; spore crosses of black oyster produced only one mating pair and nothing new.
  • Young black pearl fruits look king-oyster-like before forming an oyster cluster, which is why some suspect king parentage.
  • Sequencing: a 2023 Facebook post by one grower reported sending "Black Pearl King" to ALVALAB (Spain) for ITS, TEF1 and RPB2 sequencing (three standard DNA barcode regions). The NCBI BLAST hits (database matches) were messy: ITS best about 65% to P. fuscosquamulosus (heard differently, unverified), ITS-forward to P. ostreatus, and TEF1 and RPB2 to P. eryngii at about 97% and 92%. A separate BLAST also hit P. eryngii var. ferulae.
  • A commenter pointed to an ostreatus x eryngii hybrid patent, which turned out to be Hokuto's. Patents are filed in each country where protection is wanted, which is why a Japanese company's patent appears in Canada. The document runs 29 pages and maps every cross.
  • The patent is Canadian Patent CA 2 878 902 C, "Novel species of Pleurotus sp. and method for producing same". Owner: Hokuto Corporation; inventors Ishikawa, Inatomi, Ouchi and Oku. PCT filed 2013-07-10, priority JP 2012-07-31, issued 2016-11-29. Its dendrogram (family-tree diagram) groups P. eryngii, NITE BP-1378, P. eryngii var. elaeoselini, NITE BP-1379(2), P. ostreatus, NITE BP-1379 and P. nebrodensis. The abstract describes interspecific crossing among P. eryngii, var. elaeoselini, var. tuoliensis, P. nebrodensis and P. ostreatus, carrying both eryngii and ostreatus genes.
Cross Parents (as read from the patent)
1 P. ostreatus x P. nebrodensis
2 P. eryngii (likely a Japanese commercial king) x P. eryngii var. elaeoselini
3 Cross 1 x cross 2
4 Cross 3 x P. ostreatus
5 Cross 4 x P. eryngii
6 Cross 5 x P. ostreatus; deposited strains NITE BP-1378/1379
  • Plain ostreatus x eryngii crosses can form a dikaryon but don't fruit. Hokuto bridged through nebrodensis first, single-spore isolated the fertile offspring, then crossed with eryngii lines.
  • Next steps wanted: a chemical dedikaryotization and a full genome of black oyster. Uploading a four-species, multi-cross hybrid to public databases muddies phylogenetic data meant for wild organisms.
  • Anyone holding wild clones of P. eryngii var. elaeoselini, var. ferulae, P. nebrodensis or Mediterranean oysters is encouraged to sequence them and share them, so the patent crosses can be repeated.

RANGE Black oyster parentage. Recommended reading: a multi-species hybrid involving P. eryngii varieties, P. nebrodensis and P. ostreatus, as the patent and sequencing indicate (still with some uncertainty about the exact parents). Other accounts: an eastern x western P. ostreatus hybrid (Hokuto's website; also given as European x Asian P. ostreatus), and king x blue.

DNA work

AT A GLANCE The workflow is: extract DNA with a kit, confirm it with PCR and a gel, then send it to an outside lab for sequencing. A gel shows that DNA is present; it does not identify the organism.

Why a farm does DNA work

  • Cap n Stem has studied stroma in Pleurotus grain spawn for about a year; many farms meet stroma as a problem they cannot beat. The plan: extract DNA, confirm it with PCR and a gel, then send it to an outside lab for partial or whole-genome sequencing.
  • The wider plan: whole-genome DNA from many stroma-affected and healthy Pleurotus (including the same cell line in neighbouring bags), to build a phylogenetic picture and look for an unstable gene cluster that activates under stress. Also stress a culture deliberately for comparison, and sequence black oyster to settle whether it is a blue x king hybrid. One lab worker (Gregor) leads extraction, and PCR machines are being bought.
  • Dr. Jason Slot (fungal evolution and horizontal gene transfer; credited with finding the psilocybin gene cluster using nanopore sequencing) agreed to analyse the data at a reasonable rate if the results are published openly. He specified the primers, the extraction methods, and sequencing via Novogene.
  • Influences: Alan Rockefeller's workflow of iNaturalist + DNA barcoding + GenBank; affordable pocket-sized Oxford Nanopore sequencers; the Hamilton Morris podcast; William Padilla-Brown; and people running PCR and gels from a car. Rockefeller is credited with building up GenBank's fungal sequences nearly single-handedly, and his work is revising the names and supposed toxicity of some species.
  • One community member's "Pholiota adiposa" sequenced as something slightly different, so the taxonomy of cultivated chestnut may shift. This book keeps calling it Pholiota adiposa while noting the name is disputed.
  • Extract from monokaryons when sequencing. A dikaryon carries two genomes, while a monokaryon gives one clean genome for scaffolding, and comparing two monokaryons can pinpoint differences (for example linked to stroma or heat sensitivity). Experts insist on this, though the full reasons are not well explained.
  • Modern identification tools include SCAR markers derived from ISSR fragments (example: an 882 bp fragment gave a stable SCAR primer pair producing a 773 bp species-specific band) and ERIC elements (127 bp imperfect palindromes first known from bacteria) used as fingerprint primers. Fungal DNA taxonomy is still developing.
  • A cheap, portable barcoding tool would let growers verify their strains; it is still a wish.
  • A microgravity project plans to compare flight and ground samples genetically, with scanning electron microscopy and chemistry, cautioning that denser mycelial networks may not be healthier ones.
  • A Boston researcher (unnamed) studies fungal evolution and horizontal gene transfer; the claim is that psilocybin production arose as a discrete evolutionary event.
  • Culture collecting is shifting toward DNA sequencing and digital phylogenetics.
  • Public sequence databases and culture collections contain many mislabelled or wrongly matched species. Even trusted sources make mistakes, mix up swabs or spore prints, or swap dishes. The only way to know 100% what you have is to have it sequenced.

DNA extraction (kit-based, QIAGEN DNeasy-style)

Volumes are in microlitres (µL; 1,000 µL = 1 mL).

Step Detail
Sample Let the agar culture air-dry/cool. Take a clump of fluffy aerial mycelium from the top into a collection tube and mash it against the wall; maximum 100 mg wet weight.
Lysis buffer 400 µL, added as two 200 µL draws with a 20-200 µL pipette; work fast
RNase A 4 µL; stir the tip in the liquid because it clings. Cap and vortex hard, washing liquid from the walls back down; a pellet remains.
Heat 10 min in a hot water bath on a float so the tube isn't submerged; invert a few times. The bath temperature was not stated; the standard kit value is 65 °C (149 °F).
P3 130 µL, vortex, 5 min on ice; a white precipitate forms at once
Spin 10,000 rpm for 10 min (12 min in one written version)
Shredder Pipette the lysate (not the pellet) onto a QIAshredder column; spin 5 min. About 450 µL is recoverable; 400 µL was taken.
Transfer Move the flow-through to a fresh tube without disturbing the pellet
AW1 1.5 x the volume (400 µL → 600 µL); mix at once by pipetting
Bind Load 650 µL onto the DNeasy mini spin column; 1 min at 7,500 rpm; discard the flow-through; repeat with the rest
AW2 500 µL; spin (speed not legible in the source); discard the flow-through
Elute Column in a fresh tube; 100 µL buffer AE; stand 5 min at room temperature; 1 min at 7,500 rpm. Can be repeated for more DNA.
Store Pipette (don't pour) into a labelled storage tube ("norm" for normal mycelium); fridge
  • Yield is about 100 µL of clear DNA solution. A gel uses only 2 µL, so one extraction supports many tests; build a sample library.
  • The bench: the mycelium is pulled apart into tubes to open up the cells; a small benchtop microcentrifuge with a digital display, a vortexer, glass beakers, 96-well tube racks and a stainless bench.

RANGE Uncertain points in this protocol. First spin: 10 min is recommended (12 min in one written version). AW1: 600 µL by the 1.5x rule (660 µL was also said once). Heat bath: use the kit's standard 65 °C (149 °F), since no temperature was stated. The lysis buffer was described as ethanol-based and evaporating; kit lysis buffers usually are not (unverified). Check your own kit's handbook.

PCR setup

PCR (polymerase chain reaction) copies one short stretch of DNA millions of times so it can be seen on a gel or sequenced.

Component Volume (25 µL reaction)
Water 9.5 µL
PCR master mix (polymerase, the four nucleotides, loading dye; used as supplied) 12.5 µL
Forward primer (5 µM working stock) 1 µL
Reverse primer (5 µM working stock) 1 µL
DNA extract 1 µL

A handwritten bench card for the same mix reads: "1 uL F+R = 2 uL / 12.5 uL Master / 1 uL DNA extract / 15.5 uL total / 9.5 uL water / running 25 uL PCR reaction".

Procedure: setting up a PCR

  1. Rehydrate the dried primers to a stock of about 100 µM, then dilute to a 5 µM working stock.
  2. Keep DNA and reagents on ice or refrigerated throughout; the longer they sit at room temperature, the more they degrade.
  3. Add in this order: water, master mix, primers, DNA. No tip change is needed while the tubes are still empty.
  4. Run the thermocycler. One farm uses a miniPCR (8 tubes, run from a phone app) with a saved protocol named for mycologist Alan Rockefeller; denaturation is at 95 °C (203 °F), and the lid preheats before cycling. The app shows the protocol name, the device (for example "mini8X-16004"), lid heating, and the sample temperature (for example 26.4 °C / 79.5 °F before the run).
  5. Store PCR products in the fridge; they keep about two weeks.
  • How it works: after heat denaturation separates the strands, the forward and reverse primers bind each strand and mark where the polymerase starts copying.
  • An example run: sample 1 = normal POCNS, 2 = stroma POCNS, 3 and 4 = the same pair for a second strain heard as "30, 15" (unverified). POCNS appears to be Cap n Stem's oyster strain code (a "POCNS-17 053124" label appears on a bag).

Gel electrophoresis

Purpose: an electric current through an agarose gel shows whether an extract contains DNA. It does not identify the organism; sequencing is outsourced.

Step Detail
Buffer TBE (Tris-borate-EDTA), both for casting the gel and as running buffer; it carries current and holds a stable pH without reacting with DNA
Melt agarose Agarose tablets in TBE heated above 100 °C (212 °F) on a magnetic stirring hotplate until clear (many people microwave it; agarose is very heat-stable)
Stain Cool below 50 °C (122 °F) before adding GelRed, or the stain degrades and loses fluorescence
Comb Remove slowly and evenly (the walls between wells are thin)
Orientation Wells at the negative end; DNA runs toward positive
Buffer depth Cover gel and wells with TBE (1.5-2 mL, about 1-2 mm over the wells; the figure is approximate), so a slightly misplaced tip still drops the sample into the well
Loading Use the middle wells for a better view; don't blow out the last air bubble, which can push sample out
Run About 20-30 min, until the fluorescence is about mid-gel

TIP Cool the gel below 50 °C (122 °F) before adding GelRed; this is standard practice.

CASE A run of four POCNS samples gave a single clear band in all four lanes: intact DNA was present. The bands then faded and streaked, because the isolates were two months old. Reading the gel: degraded DNA moves as a band and then fades, while a contaminated sample shows a strong band followed by long streaks down the lane. The gel showed four orange bands near the top, one per lane, fading and smearing in later images; no ladder (size-marker) lane was run. Lesson: run a gel before paying for sequencing, and use fresh extracts.

History of culture storage

  • Dehydration was the first preservation method. Apart from deep freezing, refrigeration is the main alternative, and it only slows degradation.

  • 1949: Mary E. Stebbins (as heard) showed cultures could be kept under mineral oil.

  • Liquid nitrogen storage started around the 1970s. Before then, strains were serially subcultured on agar and eventually degraded.

  • A long-running deep-freeze study of mushroom mycelium (about 35 years, with recoveries every 2-3 years) recovered one sample after 29-30 years. The study is not named here (unverified).

  • Culture collecting is now shifting toward DNA sequencing and digital phylogenetics (DNA work).

  • A Japanese shiitake master has kept his mother culture for 33-35 years without cryo storage, by moving it between different agar recipes and liquid culture. Sylvan, a large spawn company, also avoids cryo because it is easy to do badly. Developing its two patented strains took Sylvan about 20 years.

Key rules

  1. Bank every strain you rely on as a frozen snapshot close to the original isolate, and always expand from that snapshot rather than from the last plate.
  2. Prepare cryo grain by ringing hydrated rye berries around a fresh culture on agar; bank as soon as the berries are colonized through, before they turn to mush.
  3. Use about 3 mL of 10% v/v glycerol per 5 mL vial, keep the grains fully submerged, and store at -80 °C (-112 °F). If you don't have a freezer, ask a brewery or yeast bank.
  4. Thaw vials fast in a water bath at about 30 °C (86 °F) and plate the carrier in the centre of a fresh plate; give each toothpick its own slant.
  5. Before releasing a revived or old vial, run a test line (one grain bag, about 4 fruiting blocks) and expand only from the held-back half if it passes.
  6. Check banked strains every 6-12 months and treat anything past 2-3 years in the freezer as suspect until a test fruiting proves it.
  7. For species that don't survive cryo (pink and golden oyster), or when you have no freezer, store leading-edge agar plugs in sterile water at about 1 °C (34 °F) with the cap slightly loose and parafilmed.
  8. Keep spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), not 6 °C (42 °F), and use G2 within 2-3 weeks of refrigeration; watch lion's mane for fruiting in the fridge.
  9. Learn the signs of senescence (fuzzy patches with hard rhizomorphic lines, irregular growth, browning) and refresh from your bank or a culture bank when you see them.
  10. When dedikaryotizing, blend briefly (about 20-25 s), keep flasks still, pick separate pellets, check for clamps, and expect several cycles.
  11. Run a gel before paying for sequencing to confirm the extract holds intact DNA, and use fresh extracts, because two-month-old DNA smears.
  12. Our farm: no cryo. Bank every strain as 3-5 slants and 3-5 water tubes from one P1 plate at intake, keep an off-site copy, test before use, and log every tube. See Our farm.

Open questions

  • Glycerol strength differs between protocols (5% versus 10%), and recommended refresh intervals range from 6 months to a decade.
  • No freezing rate, vial labelling scheme, or slant incubation conditions after thawing have been given.
  • Lifetimes for sterile-water storage and slants are anecdotal ("years", "6-8 months").
  • The dedikaryotization protocol has been verified only for Pleurotus; shiitake trials were pending, and the blend time for other genera is unknown.
  • Most explanations of senescence, nucleus dominance and maceration-induced pinning are speculation without cited data.
  • PCR primer identities, the thermocycler program beyond 95 °C (203 °F) denaturation, and the DNA extraction bath temperature were not stated; no ladder was run on the gel.
  • Black oyster parentage remains unresolved pending whole-genome sequencing.

chapters.html:
Grain Spawn

AT A GLANCE This chapter takes you from an agar plate to finished, chilled bags of grain spawn: choosing and buying grain, getting water into it, sterilizing it, growing a grain master (G1), expanding it into production spawn (G2), judging when spawn is ready, storing and shipping it, and preventing stroma and other spawn faults. The numbers used most:

  • Grain: clean, whole USDA Grade 1, preferably organic.
  • Moisture: as much as the grain holds without bursting: upper 40s % for rye (millet a little lower, since it tops out at 45-47%), about 55% for oats, 42-46% for maitake.
  • Sterilize, never pasteurize: the grain at the centre of the bag at 121 °C (250 °F) or more for 35 min or more, in an autoclave (a pressure steam chamber).
  • Expansion: one 4 lb (1.8 kg) master makes about 12 six-pound (2.7 kg) G2 bags; one G2 bag spawns about 20 ten-pound (4.5 kg) blocks.
  • Incubate cool and dim: About 17-18 °C (63-64 °F), cooler than blocks.
  • Store cold: 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) as soon as spawn is firm, before it pins (starts forming tiny mushrooms), buckles or forms stroma; about 2 weeks, 3 at most.

Most of the methods here are the house practice of Cap n Stem, a Maine farm that makes spawn, cultures and blocks at scale. Smaller farms' methods are given alongside where they differ.

What spawn is and why it matters

AT A GLANCE Spawn is a carrier. It moves living mycelium from the lab into the substrate. Because every later stage grows from it, any fault in spawn multiplies. Always fully sterilize it.

Spawn is grain (or another carrier) fully grown through with the mycelium of the mushroom you want to grow. Its main job is to carry the organism to the next stage. The food it brings into the substrate is a secondary bonus.

Almost any carrier works as long as it carries the organism. Corn, soil-like spawn and synthetic spawn (Amycel makes one) have all been used. Grain is the standard because it is easy to sterilize and gives many small inoculation points.

A short history. In 1905 B.M. Duggar showed that oyster spawn could be made on bean pods, leaves and manure. His work was published as a USDA bulletin from the University of Missouri. In 1932 James W. Sinden of Penn State patented steam-sterilized grain spawn, after testing which grains and moisture levels survive autoclaving. See Chapter 2 for more history.

The words used in this chapter

Term Meaning
G1, grain master, GM A 4 lb (about 1.8 kg) bag of sterile grain inoculated from an agar plate.
G2 A 6 lb (about 2.7 kg) bag of sterile grain inoculated from a G1. It is both the farm's own production spawn and the spawn sold to customers.
Knock The farm word for the whole inoculation job: adding spawn or culture to a batch of sterile bags (see Chapter 11).
Inoculate, colonize To inoculate is to add living culture to a bag; the mycelium then colonizes (grows through) it.
Autoclave A pressure steam chamber that sterilizes bags. A pressure cooker or canner is a small one.
Filter patch The breathable panel on a spawn bag that lets gas out but keeps microbes out.
Pins, primordia The first tiny mushroom buds. Spawn that pins in the bag is past its best.
Brick, popcorning, buckling Signs of over-mature spawn: knitted into a solid block, or bumpy knots forming on the bag surface before fruiting.
Shake Breaking up and mixing the grain inside a sealed bag so mycelium spreads from many points.
Stroma A dense, hot, swollen mass of the fungus's own cells that ruins spawn; see Stroma.

RULE No G3 spawn, and never transfer substrate to substrate.

WHY A G1 step saves work. Going straight from agar to G2 would mean cutting agar for every bag and coming back to re-shake each one. A G1 is poured into about 12 G2 bags and each is shaken once, with no revisit.

WARNING Never merely pasteurize spawn. It sits at the top of the expansion pyramid, so any bacteria that survive multiply through every later step. Fully sterilize it, even if you only have a small vessel.

Errors multiply downstream

One agar plate feeds 6-12 masters. One grower puts the loss from a single bad plate at upwards of 240 spawn bags, and the blocks made from those bags number in the thousands.

Example: 6 masters from one plate × 12 G2 bags each = 72 G2 bags. 72 G2 bags × 20 blocks each = 1,440 blocks. At 12 masters per plate the same plate reaches 144 G2 bags and 2,880 blocks. A plate-stage error cascades enormously.

Stroma multiplies roughly tenfold at each expansion, which is why G1 masters are screened especially carefully.

The expansion pyramid

AT A GLANCE Plate → 6-12 masters (about 6 at four agar cuts per bag, up to 12 at two) → about 12 G2 bags per master → about 20 blocks per G2 bag. Plan with these numbers.

Step Standard Range and limits
Plate to G1, 2 agar cuts per bag up to about 12 masters per plate —
Plate to G1, 4 cuts per bag (slow strains, or when rushed) about 6 masters per plate 6-8 per plate; Cap n Stem uses 6
G1 (4 lb, 1.8 kg) to G2 (6 lb, 2.7 kg) 12 G2 bags never fewer than 6 (too much inoculum, uneven ages); never more than 24 (overstretched, slow)
G2 (6 lb) to blocks 20 blocks of 10 lb (4.5 kg), about 0.3 lb (136 g) spawn per block, about 3% see Chapter 11 for spawn rates

The 1 master to 12 G2 ratio is used for every species at Cap n Stem and is repeated across at least six of their species descriptions.

RANGE Standard: 12 G2 bags per master. Context: on millet about 20 works, because its many small grains give many inoculation points. Other figures in use:

  • About 20 G2 per master (4 masters to 80 G2), and 12-20 G2 per master.
  • High Country Fungi, a small farm, feeds one 4 lb grain master from 1 agar plate and makes about 20 G2 bags from it.
  • Masters per plate: up to 12 is the usual figure; about 4 masters per dish on a slower test-and-expand line; one unconfirmed quote of "up to 30-some".
  • A typical expansion tree runs 1 dish → 4 dishes → 4 masters each → 80 G2 → 1,600 substrate blocks.

Test bags and the test-and-expand line

Test grain bags are made routinely, one plate to one master, to confirm that a strain is not senescing (losing vigour with age). Stage times, healthy fruit bodies and yields are checked against expectations, so the information given to customers comes from the farm's own grows.

Procedure: test-and-expand from a stored vial

  1. Thaw a stored culture vial (see Chapter 8).
  2. Split the carrier onto two fresh agar plates (see Chapter 7): a test dish and a held-back expansion dish.
  3. Use the test dish to inoculate one grain bag.
  4. Use that grain bag to inoculate about 4 substrate blocks of your normal recipe, and fruit them to harvest.
  5. Only if the test passes, use the expansion dish for production masters.

Always run this test for a vial that has been stored 18-24 months or longer.

CHECK Stage times, fruit-body shape and yield from the test bags match what you expect for that strain.

Choosing grain

AT A GLANCE Rye is the forgiving standard. Millet gives the most inoculation points but is hard to hydrate. Oats are the easiest to hydrate and suit lion's mane. Sorghum sits between millet and rye. Whatever you choose, stay with it and log it: changing grain changes everything downstream.

Grain Strengths Weaknesses Most moisture it holds after cooking
Rye (grouped with wheat and barley) Long-standing standard; forgiving; easy to hydrate to a good level and hard to over- or under-shoot; little contamination; ideal kernel size; middling metabolic heat; takes liquid culture well (popular for cubensis) More open voids between kernels, so fuzzy patches can appear; a "hotter" medium than wood-based substrate low 50s %
Wheat, barley Starchy; hydrate easily Glutinous: overcooked they turn goopy, raising stroma and "hot pocket" risk; Cap n Stem dislikes wheat and finds rye works better —
Oats Lowest barrier to entry; easiest to hydrate; hold a lot of water; gluten-free; useful to balance moisture in multi-grain mixes; dense white mycelium for lion's mane Big kernels, so few inoculation points and slower runs; airy, bulky bags need more shelf space; tend to sweat water off; above about 55% water pooled in the bags about 60% after autoclaving; house setting about 55%
Millet By far the most inoculation points, so faster colonization or less spawn; nutritionally complex (higher protein and minerals, high calcium, fatty acids); preferred for comb tooth masters Hull makes it fickle to hydrate without bursting; cold soaks stall in the upper 20s %; rich, so heat can spike fast; often desiccated with glyphosate if conventional about 45-47%
Sorghum (milo) Between millet and rye: easier to hydrate than millet, smaller than oats and a bit smaller than rye, round, bursts less in the autoclave; outpaced other grains for chestnut High in sugar and starch and prone to bursting; attacked by insects far faster than other grains; pricier and less available similar to millet, or a couple of points higher
Brown rice Temperature and pressure line up almost at once in the autoclave, so a simple cycle works Dries fast in an over-pressurized lab; on a knock day of about 700 bags the last racks congealed into bricks —
Buckwheat and others Used with added wood or coconut husk in space-research ground trials — —

Ease of hydration, easiest to hardest: oats, rye, wheat, sorghum, millet. Starchy grains (rye, wheat, oats, rice) take up much more water than millet or sorghum. This matters most with low-tech hydration such as a cold soak, or adding water before autoclaving.

Other growers' choices. High Country Fungi makes all its spawn on white millet. Catawba Mushrooms suggests trying sorghum-sudangrass as a grain.

TIP It is a myth that you need many different grains. Millet alone works well.

House recipes and grain by species

Cap n Stem's standard for all species: 3 parts rye to 1 part sorghum (milo), plus gypsum and calcium carbonate to buffer pH and reduce clumping. The exception is lion's mane, which now goes on oats.

A second version of the recipe uses certified organic millet or sorghum (currently sorghum, chosen by availability) plus rye. Rice, oats and many other grains have been trialled.

RANGE Recommended: 3 rye : 1 sorghum. A wheat-and-sorghum mix (with rye also mentioned), cooked in two big kettles, with the milo formerly soaked overnight, has also been used at the same farm, even though that farm dislikes wheat and finds rye works better than wheat.

Species Grain choice Why
Comb tooth Pure millet preferred for masters; 3 rye : 1 sorghum also works Millet keeps it in spreading mode, holds together and fruits later. Rye/milo is slightly slower and shows fruit bodies earlier. Final fruit and yield are the same.
Lion's mane Oats beat rye Oats hold more moisture (about 56%) and give dense, white mycelium, almost like an oyster bag. Oats were also "recently showing success" more generally.
Chestnut Milo Over about six crops milo outpaced the farm's other grains (early data). NMC traditionally used winter rye.
Maitake Any, if moisture is right Grain type matters less than moisture, solid sterilization and a clean incubation space.

Millet's many inoculation points let you use less spawn, or colonize faster at the same rate. At 0.3 lb (136 g) of spawn per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, millet runs a couple of days faster than pure rye.

RULE Changing grain means re-checking incubation temperature, CO2, filter patch type and bag size.

WARNING Switching grain source is the most common farm problem a large spawn maker sees. It can change fruit-body formation drastically. For pioppino this is "rule number one" (per one North Carolina grower).

  • Use the grain you can source reliably, at good quality and price. Sylvan, a large spawn company, uses rye because wheat is hard for it to get; an Australian farm uses wheat; millet is used where machines need a small, round grain. Over a whole run, the difference between grains is perhaps one day of colonization.

WARNING Be careful starting with milo (sorghum). One spawn maker said, "I've never had more issues than when I tried to use milo." He now uses milo and rye together, hydrated to "max potential", about 43% moisture.

Buying and storing raw grain

AT A GLANCE Buy USDA Grade 1, whole, clean, organic grain from a supplier who can tell you its grade. Supply chain matters more than price. Log each truckload against the last.

Don't treat any grain or method as dogma. Results depend on grain source, grade, age, organic versus conventional, and cooking equipment. The same grain varies by origin and year, and a new crop can differ, for example in protein.

Grade. Buy USDA Grade 1. Each commodity grain is graded, roughly from grade 1 down through grades 3-5 to livestock feed, on cleanliness and the share of intact kernels. Feed stores often cannot tell you the grade. Broken grain (for example cracked millet) cooks unevenly and leaches starch and germ into the mix.

Bad sources are common.

  • A tote of millet from a small Pennsylvania broker, full of broken grain, gnats, live grubs, other grains and plant debris.
  • Feed-store 50 lb (23 kg) bags with bugs, corn and rat droppings.
  • Totes of millet with insects and mould clumps.
  • A super sack of sorghum full of bugs.
  • Local Maine grain, early on, that was about 50% bugs and debris.

TIP Ask suppliers about cleaning and grade, and ask experienced growers for their sources.

Organic. Use organic grain. Conventional millet and oats are often desiccated with glyphosate before harvest, and conventional rye in wet Maine may get fungicide. Residues can cause patchy, odd colonization and failure to fruit, and supplier assurances about early application are hard to verify. Cap n Stem uses only organic grain.

Insects. Sorghum is attacked by gnats and larvae far faster than other grains, even in dry, climate-controlled super sacks on racking. Churn through it quickly. Long storage of truckloads needs protection; silos are the goal.

Supply and price.

Grain Where it grows (US) Price notes
Sorghum mostly Kentucky, Missouri and the lower Midwest pricier
Millet mostly eastern Colorado drought-driven price spikes, about 70 ¢/lb (about US$1.54/kg) one year
Rye, oats across the northern states —

RULE Stay flexible across grains. Supply chain matters more than price; don't buy the cheapest grain.

Totes concentrate damage at the end. When a 1-ton tote is drained from the bottom, the lighter damaged kernels rise and all come out at the end, so problems concentrate on the last day of a tote.

CASE In one problem batch the lot, age and hydration records all looked normal. The grain spawn production manager spotted the cause: the end of a bottom-drained tote, where the light, damaged kernels collect. Lesson: records are not enough; look at the grain itself.

Cleaning local grain. Small growers using local grain can buy or build a grain cleaner (a vacuum plus sieves, a few hundred dollars). The vacuum lifts light debris and the heavy kernels fall.

Incoming moisture. If you don't know how wet your dry grain is, assume about 10% (range about 7-15%). Mills can test and guarantee it, and it changes with age and storage humidity.

Oats and rancidity. Food-grade oats are usually heat-stabilized against rancidity. Non-stabilized whole oats are cheaper and fine if used within a couple of months; rancidity is mainly a problem once oats are rolled or cracked.

Procedure: setting a grain baseline

  1. Run small, careful test batches of a new grain and take notes.
  2. Record the result as your baseline (cook time, moisture, colonization speed).
  3. Log each new truckload against the last one.
  4. Keep that baseline until the shipment runs out, then repeat for the next.

CHECK Judge the grain by downstream results: vigorous colonization, substrate performance and mushrooms.

Moisture: the number that matters most

AT A GLANCE Get grain to the highest moisture it can hold without bursting, and make it even from kernel to kernel. Target the upper 40s % for rye; millet tops out at about 45-47%, so take it as close to that as it goes without bursting. Too wet is the more common mistake.

Why moisture matters

The goal is to get grain to the highest moisture it can hold, given a standard sterilization. Wet grain rides out drying during colonization, resists contamination, and carries even moisture and food into the substrate.

Grain can only hold so much water. Past that, kernels burst. Blanket rules such as "50%+ grain" or "never exceed X% or you get bacteria" are oversimplified: the grain's holding capacity is the real limit.

Problem What happens
Too dry Weak, slow growth and more contamination.
Too wet (the more common error) Mushy, burst grain and standing water that breed contaminants.
Burst kernels Burst grain releases free sugar and starch, which is effectively agar. It feeds any bacterium or spore, and it drives stroma because mycelium grows too fast there.
Uneven moisture One dry "sour patch" grain can make lion's mane stop colonizing and pin.

Evenness pays. Cap n Stem tuned its ingredients, process and autoclave cycle to a stable moisture of about 46% through all the grain, and got much denser, whiter mycelium.

What too dry looks like, by species:

  • Lion's mane: at low moisture (low 40s %) growth was slow, unhappy and permanently wispy, with more contamination and auto-fruiting even before full colonization.
  • Any species: very dry spawn (20-30%) may stall or rush to fruit.
  • Maitake: needs higher moisture than most people achieve. At correct moisture, master-to-G2 runs to dense white in 4-5 weeks; slightly too dry, it can take 9-10 weeks and be less vigorous.
  • King oyster: orange metabolites on spawn or substrate show the mycelium straining to break down something hard with too little water (dry clumps, dense kernels). Aim for even moisture through the whole medium.
  • Chestnut: sensitive to dry grain. Uncolonized or under-colonized kernels, especially dried-out ones, grow Trichoderma, because filter patches are not impermeable.

Leave headroom. Excess water may separate as liquid in the bag and later reabsorb. Fungi also exude water (guttation), very visibly in lion's mane. Do not aim for the absolute maximum; leave room for the changes autoclaving and incubation cause.

WARNING Grain at 50% moisture or less loses water quickly if the bag filter is left open to strong airflow. Fold the bag top over the filter (bag folding) and keep incubation airflow gentle.

Moisture targets

Grain or context Target Notes
Rye and millet, Cap n Stem production standard upper 40s %, just under 50% Millet holds only about 45-47%, so for millet this means as close to its limit as it goes without bursting
Tuned house grain (lion's mane focus) about 46%, uniform —
All grain, kettle method 40-50% by weight above 40% means not too dry; avoid bursting
Oats about 55% (house); about 56% for lion's mane above about 55% water pooled in bags
Oats, a published comparison 40% vs 50% 50% is aggressive but possible because the hull is thin
Maitake grain spawn 42-46%, absolute (includes the grain's own moisture and any sawdust) a working whiteboard reads "Grain Spawn MC = 42-46%"
Grain in general up to about 50% Dries out fast if the bag is left open or room airflow is strong
Too dry low 40s % (lion's mane); 20-30% (any) wispy, slow, auto-fruiting

RANGE Recommended: upper 40s % for rye, as close to 45-47% as millet will go, about 55% for oats, 42-46% for maitake. The full span in use is 40-50% for all grain cooked in a kettle, about 46% for a tuned house blend, and 40-50% for oats. Choose by grain: millet holds only about 45-47%, rye the low 50s %, and oats about 60%, so set each target a few points under what that grain can hold.

Measuring moisture

By weight. Weigh the dry grain, cook it, drain it and reweigh it. Some growers call a 40% weight gain "40% hydrated". That is a weight-gain figure, not wet-basis moisture % (water as a share of total wet weight). Sources often do not say which of the two they mean, so ask.

Worked example (arithmetic). Wet-basis moisture % = water in the grain ÷ total weight × 100. Take 10 lb (4.5 kg) of dry grain at the default incoming moisture of about 10%: it holds 1 lb of water and 9 lb of dry matter.

  • A 40% weight gain brings it to 14 lb, holding 5 lb of water: 5 ÷ 14 = about 36% wet basis.
  • To reach 48% wet basis, the 9 lb of dry matter must be 52% of the total, so the total is 9 ÷ 0.52 = about 17.3 lb: a weight gain of about 73%.

Squeeze test. Hydrated wheat or rye kernels give and then turn to jelly. Under-hydrated millet stays rock-hard. Properly hydrated grain is intact but slightly soft and gelatinous inside, with a little dry starch visible when you break a kernel.

Allow for the autoclave. Autoclaving is a second cooking phase, so work back from the result you want after the autoclave. Pressure sterilization adds water: spawn bags gained about 0.1-0.2 lb (45-90 g) each in test bags. So don't hydrate right to the burst limit.

RULE Cook for maximum hydration but stop short of bursting. Companies push hydration hard, and there is a point of no return, especially with richer grains.

Hydrating grain

AT A GLANCE Simmering in a kettle is the production standard: fast, controllable and self-cleaning. Soaking is simple but slow, uneven and prone to fermenting. Soak-then-boil gives the most water in hard grains like millet. Dry bagging is easy but stratifies.

Method How it works Good Bad
Kettle boiling (simmering) — recommended Grain simmered in a kettle of boiling water, then drained Much faster, easier to control and self-cleaning; separate rinsing did not help and wasted water and time Laborious, needs full attention, and is dangerous: spawn staff at one farm have burns
Cold soak Grain soaked in water in a barrel, drum, bucket or IBC Simple Grain:water ratio matters; unstirred grain settles and absorbs less; rye, oats and wheat can turn to mush; millet only reaches the upper 20s %
Hot soak Water at about 71-82 °C (160-180 °F) Higher moisture than a cold soak Temperature drops fast on contact with a big mass of cold grain (maybe to about 27 °C, 80 °F); hold it with a jacketed vessel or heaters, and stir or aerate
Soak then boil Soak first, then kettle-cook Highest moisture in hard grains like millet Intensive; Cap n Stem does it some of the time because, as a spawn company, every vigour edge matters; for their own use only they might simply grow on oats
Dry bagging Dry grain plus water in the bag; hydration forced during autoclaving Easy Tends to stratify: soggy bottom, dry or undercooked top

Soaking problems.

  • Millet in a cold barrel or IBC soak only reaches the upper 20s %. The dry core then pops like popcorn when heated, a sign of under-hydrated millet.
  • Over-soaking (for example in 5 gal, 19 L, buckets or 55 gal, 208 L, drums) causes germination "tails". Spilled millet even sprouts in floor cracks. Timing matters.
  • Rinsing matters most for soaking, because the grain sits in a broth of its own released material.
  • Long soaks, or drained grain left sitting, start fermenting (sugars to alcohols) and lose nutrition. Even after sterilization this can give irregular, splotchy colonization.

WHY The long-standing claim that soaking germinates bacterial endospores so they are easier to kill does not hold: sterilization kills them anyway (credited to a forum grower known as Roger Rabbit).

Dry bagging in practice. A well-known YouTube grower promoted dry bagging for years. Some people dry-bag millet with a Fenrir filler; Cap n Stem doubts it works well and dislikes pressure-forcing water into grain. Some cordyceps growers use it for rice-based media. Cap n Stem does not recommend shortcut no-soak hydration methods.

RULE Judge your process by downstream results: vigorous colonization, substrate performance and mushrooms. If it works with your grain and equipment, refine it rather than reinvent it.

Procedure: kettle-cooking grain

This is the Cap n Stem routine in jacketed steam kettles. Barrels of raw grain go into the kettles.

  1. Fill the kettle from an on-demand water heater at about 85 °C (185 °F) so it boils sooner.
  2. Bring it to a rolling boil (about 2 minutes in a jacketed kettle).
  3. Add the grain only once the water is at a rolling boil, like pasta. A jacketed kettle keeps boiling after about 200 lb (91 kg) of cold grain goes in. Use a false bottom or stir to avoid scorching.
  4. Rye: boil 6 minutes, then turn off the heat and steep 12 minutes. Milo: steep about 20 minutes in boiled water.
  5. Whatever your timing, cut the heat a little early, because grain keeps cooking while it drains. One grower cuts at 16 minutes of a planned 20.
  6. Drain at once. Draining steams off surface moisture. Don't leave grain sitting in a hot jacketed kettle (jacket at about 35 psi, 2.4 bar, steam): it dries quickly and starch sticks to the walls.
  7. Check kernels with the squeeze test.

CHECK Kernels are intact, "al dente", soft and gelatinous inside, with no free water outside them and no burst kernels.

RANGE Recommended for rye: 6 min boil + 12 min off-heat steep. A farm-tour account of the same kettles gives about 11 minutes or less of cooking, depending on grain and source. Either way, test each lot to find when kernels burst. Boil time is adjusted by a few minutes every time the rye supplier changes (3-4 suppliers so far). A set of 84 spawn bags takes two kettle boils of about 20-30 minutes each, plus 15-20 minutes of bagging.

TIP On-demand water heaters that pre-heat kettle water wear out; plan to replace them.

A typical spawn kitchen has green Uline barrels under the steam-jacketed kettle's outlet to catch cooked grain, and blue drums and a yellow bucket to move grain around.

Small-farm cooking setups

Both small farms consulted favour forced hydration: cooking grain until it is hydrated inside but dry on the surface.

  • Electric pressure cookers (High Country Fungi). Four large MegaChef electric pressure cookers, each making 2 bags (6 lb, 2.7 kg) of spawn, with a little gypsum. The grain is mixed in a drywall mixing tub, then bagged and sterilized.

  • Brewing pot on a propane burner (recommended by Catawba Mushrooms). A 30 gal (114 L) Megapot (Northern Brewer) with a false bottom on a two-burner propane stand (Bayou Classic SP40). It cooks 50-75 lb (23-34 kg) of dry grain per load; once hydrated, that fills 18-30 bags of 4.5 lb (2.0 kg). After the boil, spread the grain on a "grain table" with a big fan to drive off steam. The process is shown at mushroomvideos.com (US$8.99). These are US products; in Costa Rica, look for a large stainless pot and an LPG burner locally, or import them.

  • Soak-in-bag millet (a home-grower method). Put 4.25 lb (1.9 kg) of millet and 1 L of water in a filter-patch bag, soak 24 h, massage, then sterilize. This is a form of dry bagging, so expect some stratification.

  • A West Coast farm kettle-cooks its grain in water inside the autoclave and then bags it.

Procedure: cooking millet in electric pressure cookers

This is High Country Fungi's method. It is simple and close to set-and-forget, and it scales by adding cookers.

  1. Give each cooker its own 15 A circuit. Anything with a heating element needs its own circuit; two cookers probably can't share one.
  2. Put about 3.6 kg (8 lb) of white millet and 1.8 kg (4 lb) of water in each pot. With millet arriving at 11-12% moisture, this lands at roughly 40% moisture, the level this farm wants for its spawn (drier than the upper-40s standard in Moisture targets). A light sprinkle of sawdust pellets on top soaks up leftover water; it is optional, and shows as brown flecks on the millet.
  3. Close the lids. The cookers take about 10-12 min to reach pressure.
  4. Cook 12-15 min at pressure, usually 13 min (the display reads 13). Add a minute when the room is warmer and drier, because room conditions shift the result. Err towards a slight undercook; the aim is no free water left in the pot.
  5. Stand by when the timer ends. The cookers drop into keep-warm, which keeps heating the base and scorches the bottom layer, so switch each one off straight away.
  6. Leave the lids on and cool for at least 1 h, about 1.5 h in a warm room: cool enough to handle safely, but not cold.
  7. Open and check: a few burst kernels are normal, but many burst kernels (especially in millet) mean the grain was overcooked.
  8. Tip all the cookers into one large drywall mixing basin and mix so the moisture is even. Bag and sterilize straight away (the autoclave run).

CHECK A whole batch, sterilizer run included, takes about 4-5 h from start to finish. One farm runs it 2-3 times a week for 230-270 kg (500-600 lb) of grain a week.

TIP The same forced hydration works in a large sterilizer: put the grain and water in the insert, latch it and run about 0.7 bar (10 psi) for about 13 min, which is roughly what the cookers do. Big steam kettles also work (kettle-cooking). Overnight soaks followed by a long low simmer work too, but take more labour.

WARNING Millet is harder to cook well than any other grain. If you can get millet and dial it in, it is excellent; if not, start with an easier grain such as rye or oats.

Additives

AT A GLANCE Calcium carbonate and gypsum help, in tiny amounts: about 0.15% of total wet weight for the two together (about 4 g in a 6 lb bag), and never more than 1%. A little sawdust helps maitake.

Calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and calcium sulfate (gypsum, CaSO4) soak up excess moisture, improve texture and stop loose starch from clumping. Clumped starch otherwise leads to unhealthy mycelium, stroma or bacteria. Cap n Stem once used large amounts and now uses much less. A dash of sawdust also helps.

RULE Use additives very conservatively, starting under 1%. Calcium carbonate, gypsum or sawdust can glob together with loose starch into dense masses. Cap n Stem's current CaCO3 + CaSO4 total is about 0.15% of total wet weight (water included).

Example: a 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 bag at 0.15% holds about 0.009 lb (about 4 g) of calcium additives in total.

Sawdust in grain.

  • Sawdust in millet spawn gives visibly quicker, healthier early colonization for maitake, but large amounts give no sweeping gains. Cap n Stem disagrees with media voices who push a lot of sawdust in grain.
  • Maitake recipe: about 6% red oak sawdust or crumbles, measured by recipe, not counting water (whiteboard note "6% saw[dust]"). One large maitake producer uses up to about 10% with raw sawdust. Sawdust holds moisture, suits an oak-loving species, and its fine particles bridge between kernels for a slow grower.
  • One maitake grower finds sawdust spawn faster than grain spawn for maitake, and it pins sooner, though the overall growth rate is similar. Maitake strongly prefers wood.
  • Space-research ground trials tested added woods and coconut husk as extra food, against grain alone.

Mixing and bagging

AT A GLANCE Mix gently for 5-10 minutes, no more, check the mix, then bag by volume and check each G2 bag at 6 lb (2.7 kg).

WARNING Grain needs only a few minutes in a mixer to blend grains, calcium, wood or coir. Running the helix continuously grinds grain into chaff; this took Cap n Stem a long time to learn. Over-mixing in a helix also collects broken material into "pizza crust" clumps.

Procedure: mixing and bagging grain

  1. Lift the hot grain in barrels to the top of the mixer.
  2. Spread the grains, gypsum and any powder across the mixer. Use a gentle mixer (helix or paddle); aggressive mixing smashes grain into paste.
  3. Run 5-10 minutes, no more.
  4. Pull a bucket sample to check that the mix is even, and remove clumps. Uneven mixing gives patchy colonization.
  5. Discharge into a pneumatic bagger (Chapter 6), or a sliding fixed-volume doser about the size of a drinks can, set for bag size and grain type. It can be trimmed, for example by a quarter pound (113 g).
  6. Check each G2 bag on a scale for 6 lb (2.7 kg).
  7. Fold the filled bags and load them on autoclave racks (see Sterilizing grain).

CHECK Every G2 bag weighs 6 lb.

WHY Spawn weight matters more than block weight. Expansion rates assume a fixed amount of spawn per bag, so G2 bags are held at about 6 lb. Volumetric dosing works for grain only because the grain was hydrated evenly beforehand.

Housekeeping. A layer of chaff builds up inside the mixer, which is a nuisance. Grain and starch make mixer cleaning a big job. See Chapter 6 for mixers and baggers.

Sterilizing grain

AT A GLANCE Pressure-sterilize every spawn bag: grain at the centre of the coldest bag at 121 °C (250 °F) or more for 35 min or more. Start the clock when the logger in that bag reaches 121 °C. Use vacuum pulses or a good air purge, log a test bag in the coldest spot every run, and use the shortest cycle that works so the grain does not caramelize. See Chapter 12 for steam equipment and cycle theory.

Parameter Value Conditions
Recommended standard core 121 °C (250 °F) or above for 35 min or more Lab practice is often 5-15 min, but grain has a high bioburden (load of microbes) and a dense thermal mass.
Cap n Stem cycle 3-4 pre-vacuum pulses to about −10 inHg (−34 kPa), each refilled with steam, then 124 °C (255 °F) for about 35 min Primus vacuum autoclave; deliberately longer than the textbook 15-20 min above 121 °C
Boiler for the spawn autoclave stays at about 50 psi (3.4 bar) all week; delivers 45-50 psi (3.1-3.4 bar) to the autoclave head about US$100,000 high-pressure boiler in a shipping container
Water gained in sterilization about 0.1-0.2 lb (45-90 g) per spawn bag measured on test bags
Datalogger interval 15 s for spawn cycles substrate pasteurization can be logged more sparsely
Caramelization threshold reactions start at 121 °C (250 °F) sterilize for the minimum viable time

Keep the cycle short but sure. Aim for the minimum effective sterilization time; some farms' grain comes out toasted or black. Vacuum pulses bring temperature and pressure into line before the peak, which limits Maillard reactions and caramelization. Gravity cycles (no vacuum) need long holds above 121 °C (250 °F). Steam injection and vacuum cycling also add moisture to the grain, to a level Cap n Stem finds useful.

TIP On a stovetop or canning-style pressure unit you can imitate vacuum pulses by cracking the vent and closing it again to purge air. One commercial kit approximates this.

Procedure: an autoclave run for spawn

  1. Load the folded bags on racks. In a vacuum autoclave, leave enough vertical space between shelves for even vacuum and steam saturation, so every bag reaches the same temperature.
  2. Seal a datalogger in a test bag and place it in the hardest-to-heat spot (for example low on a rack), ideally with loggers in several spots. If your cycle ends with a vacuum "dry cycle", which dries bags most at the top of the rack, log there too.
  3. Set the logger to record every 15 s.
  4. Run the cycle: core 121 °C (250 °F) or more for 35 min or more (Cap n Stem: 3-4 vacuum pulses, then 124 °C, 255 °F, for about 35 min).
  5. Unload through the autoclave's second door (a pass-through autoclave opens on both sides) straight into a HEPA-pressurized clean room. With a single-door unit, move the bags straight to your cleanest HEPA-fed space to cool (Chapter 4).
  6. A suited worker pulls the run's test bag on the cool-down side. Check the autoclave printout, then the logger, before the next run is loaded.
  7. If in doubt, rerun the grain through a full cycle. Expect it to come out darker, because more time above 121 °C caramelizes grain.

CHECK The logger in the coldest spot shows the core at or above 121 °C (250 °F) for at least 35 min.

WARNING Unlike pasteurization, a finished pressure cycle cannot simply be re-entered. Once it ends, the only fix for a doubtful run is a full rerun.

Cap n Stem runs several autoclave cycles a day.

After the autoclave: clean unloading and cool-down

Sterilized grain is axenic (free of all other life) and an "open buffet" until it is sealed and inoculated. Unload it through the autoclave's second door straight into a HEPA-pressurized clean room. Cap n Stem's spawn lab uses full-body PPE.

A separate cool-down room matters when the autoclave runs all day while staff inoculate, because bags come out at 66-121 °C (150-250 °F). With one run a day you can cool and knock in the same room. Cap n Stem's room order is:

  1. Flow-hood room (highest pressure).
  2. An empty, very clean cool-down room, where autoclaved grain cools overnight.
  3. The inoculation room.

See Chapter 4 for lab layout and pressure.

Shortcuts to avoid, and filter-patch cautions

  • Tyvek patches. According to a patent Cap n Stem cites, Tyvek should not go above about 120 °C (248 °F), yet sterilization runs at 121 °C (250 °F) or more. This may make Tyvek a questionable filter patch for grain; it is still under investigation (see Chapter 11).

  • Tyvek sleeves. Inserting a flat Tyvek sleeve over the grain, between the gussets, before folding does not filter cooling air in a steamer. It might make some sense in an autoclave, where bags suck in during pressure changes. A bag maker also dismisses the practice, and Cap n Stem used to do it.

  • Ultra-pasteurized grain. Selling non-sterilized ("ultra-pasteurized") grain as master spawn is shady practice. It may be acceptable for your own use.

  • Pre-cooked rice pouches. The "Uncle Ben's 90-second rice" method uses pre-sterilized commercial pouches. It defies sterile practice yet works for hobbyists; it is a useful challenge to dogma but not a production method.

  • Why bags burst in the pressure cooker. Steam takes up far more space than water. When it vents through the filter patch, the patch is overwhelmed by steam rushing out and then air rushing back in. The Tyvek sleeve was invented to solve this: the bag is left unsealed, folded like an accordion, inside a Tyvek sleeve, so steam escapes out of the top and the sleeve pulls tight as it cools. It is labour-intensive, fine for a hobbyist but not for 50,000 bags a day.

  • In vacuum-cycle autoclaves the filter patch must touch the grain, or the bag explodes. Cap n Stem had bags made with the patch set lower for this reason.

  • Early growers made grain spawn in mason jars without filters. The lids were turned upside down so steam could vent during sterilizing; on cooling they sat tight enough to keep contaminants out without cracking the jar. Every jar or bag draws in room air as it cools, so cooling in dirty air causes losses.

Inoculating grain masters (G1)

AT A GLANCE Two about 1 cm squares of agar from the leading edge per 4 lb master, one on the front face and one on the back; four for slow strains or when rushed. Work in front of HEPA filters, bag opening toward the filter.

Cut squares of about 1 × 1 cm from the leading edge of the agar colony, where cell division is most active.

Situation Agar squares per 4 lb (1.8 kg) master Placement
Standard, all species 2 one against the front face, one against the back, so growth is visible
Slow strains, or when rushed 4 front, back and both sides
Pioppino (between slow and fast) typically 2, sometimes 4 plates used at about 2-3 weeks old
Single test masters 2 pieces about three times the normal size one on each face, about halfway down the bag, for faster, even spread

Procedure: inoculating a grain master

  1. Work in the clean room in front of a HEPA filter wall.
  2. Spray the outside of the grain bag with alcohol.
  3. Open the bag with its mouth angled slightly toward the HEPA filter, so clean air flows across the opening.
  4. Sterilize the scalpel (Chapter 7) and cool the hot blade on the centre of the plate.
  5. Cut about 1 × 1 cm squares from the leading edge.
  6. Drop in 2 squares (one against the front face, one against the back), or 4 for slow strains.
  7. Seal the bag (bag sealers) with the open end still facing the filter.
  8. Label it with the species, generation, date, strain and bag number.
  9. Fold the bag and send it to incubation.

CHECK Within about 1-1.5 weeks a semicircle of growth spreads from each square, visible through the bag face.

In practice a row of unsealed rye/milo bags sits open toward the filter while the agar goes in, then each is sealed. A 4 lb master is noticeably smaller than a 6 lb G2 bag.

Labelling. A good label carries species, generation, date (MMDDYY), strain code and bag number, for example "Comb Tooth G1 121323-HCFF-2". Shorter labels such as "B-BO #2" with a date "8/12" are also used.

WHY Cap n Stem does culture work in its best flow hood, and spawns in an FFU-pressurized clean room in front of another bank of FFUs, giving double HEPA filtration, because early mistakes multiply. See Chapter 4.

Liquid culture instead of agar. Inject 20 mL of liquid culture (LC) per 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain bag through a self-healing injection port. This dose was chosen as an industry standard for fast colonization (it is the volume of one common LC syringe). For a 4 lb (1.8 kg) master no dose is given; scaling by weight gives about 13 mL. Aerated LC started slightly slower on grain than plain LC; overall colonization time was about the same. See Chapter 7 for making LC.

Growing out the master

AT A GLANCE Leave the master unshaken about 1-1.5 weeks, shake once the colonized circle covers about half a bag face, then allow 0.5-1.5 weeks more: fully grown about 2 weeks after inoculation. Use it or chill it by week 3.

Leave the master unshaken for about 1-1.5 weeks while a patch (a semicircle from each cutting) establishes. Shake it when the colonized circle covers about half a bag face. Then allow about 0.5-1.5 weeks more to full colonization: around 2 weeks in total.

WARNING Don't leave a master about 2 weeks unshaken. It mats densely around the cutting while other areas stay uncolonized, giving uneven spawn.

Species What to expect from a G1
Chestnut Easily disturbed. Shaking or thermal shock too early (for example re-shaking soon after the agar cutting) often does not recover and leads to odd growth, cell death and contamination. Let it establish; vigour increases with age.
Lion's mane Almost invisible growth in week 1. About a week after the shake the bag is fully colonized but still wispy, with some firmness when squeezed.
Black oyster At 18-21 °C (65-70 °F), about a week after the shake the master is fully white and firm. Oysters tolerate another 1-2 weeks at room temperature before refrigeration or use.

RULE Refrigerate masters at 2-3 weeks (firm, white, metabolites present) if they are for spawning or for customers; otherwise they keep growing.

Shaking at scale. Cap n Stem re-shakes hundreds of grain masters a week, each once it reaches a set amount of growth. Music is fine during shaking as long as staff keep count and don't double-shake or skip bags.

Heat from masters. G1 bags (started from an agar wedge) make no heat at first, but later produce nearly as much heat per pound as heavily spawned bags. Rolling racks let you keep G1 grain somewhere warmer until it starts making heat, then roll it somewhere cooler. See Incubating spawn.

Expanding to G2

AT A GLANCE One master into 12 sterile 6 lb bags, broken up thoroughly and spread evenly; shake straight away. G2 runs faster than G1.

Procedure: the G2 knock

  1. Lay out 12 sterile 6 lb (2.7 kg) bags in front of the HEPA wall and open them.
  2. Break up the master thoroughly by squeezing and kneading it through the closed bag before you open it, so no concentrated mass of inoculum grows out and makes disproportionate heat.
  3. Pour the master roughly evenly into the 12 bags, by eye. A handful per bag is enough if the bags are shaken properly.
  4. Seal the bags.
  5. Shake each bag right away to spread the inoculum through the grain. G2 has no establishment lag.
  6. Space the bags evenly on incubation racks (see Incubating spawn).

CHECK Inoculum is spread evenly with no big lumps. Each bag gets about 1/12 of the master, never less than 1/24 or more than 1/6.

Chestnut masters break up far more easily than matting species such as oyster, reishi and turkey tail.

G2 runs faster than G1 because it starts from colonized grain.

In a typical spawn room, gowned workers line grain bags up in rows on wire racks; shiitake grain racks can fill whole incubation bays.

G2 timelines by species

These times were measured at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). In a cooler 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) spawn room, expect them to run a little longer.

Black oyster (black pearl) firm by day 7 at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F); spawnable or shippable at the end of week 1; normally held another week, then refrigerated white wisps for the first about 4 days, then a dense brick
