High Country Fungi's G2 millet spawn is ready in about 10 days.

Lion's mane grain is deliberately incubated longer than usual at Cap n Stem, for more robust, reliable spawn. Many growers ship it at the first sign of density or primordia.

TIP "Super spawn." A West Virginia farm makes its G1 with about 30% hydrated sawdust or pellets mixed into the grain, in 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags. Hydrate the sawdust or pellets with hot water so they don't clump. It colonizes faster and more evenly than straight grain and "shaved usually about a week to week and a half off incubation for all species", without running hotter.

  • The same farm keeps quart grain masters of many species ready, since a pound of grain is cheap to throw away, and plates the last kernels from each spawn bag to test it.

Incubating spawn

AT A GLANCE Grain makes far more heat than substrate, so run the spawn room cooler than the block room: about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F). Space bags widely, keep it dim, and watch the top shelves, which run hottest. See Chapter 13 for incubation rooms in general.

Grain is a "hotter" medium than wood-based substrate: it produces much more internal heat per volume, so it should incubate cooler than blocks.

Setting Value Notes
Spawn room ambient (recommended) about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) blocks run at about 19 °C (66 °F)
Spawn room ambient About 16-18 °C (low-to-mid 60s °F), below 19 °C (66 °F) —
Grain ambient for stroma prevention about 18 °C (65 °F) blocks about 19 °C (66 °F)
Grain incubation room 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) the temperature at which the species timelines in this chapter were measured

RANGE Recommended: about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) for spawn. The full range in use runs from about 16-18 °C (the low-to-mid 60s °F) through about 18 °C (65 °F) for stroma prevention up to 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) in grain incubation rooms. Run cooler for rich grain, aggressive oysters and densely packed racks; the stroma risk rises with heat.

Cooling equipment. Holding these temperatures needed refrigerant-coil (Heatcraft-type) cooling rather than standard HVAC, and an independent air conditioner for the spawn room. Positive pressure flushes air out constantly, which makes it harder. See Chapter 5.

Air pattern. In a positive-pressure HEPA spawn room, supply air high and let it leave low, so cold air sinks against the spawn heat. Positive pressure raises air exchange but traps heat, and the filter fans add heat, so over-pressurized spawn rooms run hotter than expected.

All Cap n Stem spawn incubates inside the lab, so lab temperature control also governs its spawn schedules.

Heat inside the bag and on the rack

Peak heat comes at the end of colonization, about day 11 for oyster spawn. Rich grain such as millet can spike very fast.

Vertical stratification. Same-strain, same-day bags can look completely different by shelf: on top shelves they are dense, hard, swollen with liquid and maybe starting stroma, while bottom bags are still patchy with no metabolite colour. The difference can be dramatic: one extreme example was about 27 °C (80 °F) at the top against 10 °C (50 °F) at the bottom. It happens even when air flows fairly evenly in one direction: the bottom shelf still runs colder than the 6th and 7th shelves. Keep a close eye on the top shelves.

TIP To see what is happening, seal a datalogger or thermocouple inside a bag at inoculation and watch the internal temperature surge, then fall.

RULE Space grain bags evenly and widely. Spawn bags usually have a more restrictive filter, which builds more CO2 and heat, so spacing matters even more than for blocks.

CO2, bag folding and light

CO2. Elevated CO2 keeps mycelium vegetative and delays pinning; fresh oxygen pushes it toward fruiting. Higher CO2 widens the window for catching spawn just past full coverage.

Folding. Folding the top of a grain bag over its filter patch restricts gas exchange, so more growth stays vegetative and the grain at the top doesn't dry out. Light, temperature and CO2 are the three controls you have over spawn in the bag.

Light. Early incubation of nearly all species goes best dim or dark, including cordyceps; black bags help. Keep light near zero for lion's mane spawn, which pins on light before the mycelium is fully dense. Avoid strong light and big temperature swings to prevent in-bag pinning or buckling, for example in shiitake spawn. Black pearl grain is the exception: light or dark storage made no difference to it, unlike lion's mane, which pins far more in light.

RANGE Recommended: dim, indirect light in spawn rooms. Motion-sensor lighting has given mixed results:

  • A sudden bright flash from motion-sensor lights was too strong a trigger in one trial, so that room went to dim, indirect light; red lighting was also considered.
  • Motion-sensor lights that shut off after 10-15 s have worked well elsewhere.
  • After constant lights made lion's mane pin early, one farm switched to motion-sensor lighting that is dim most of the time.

The common thread: keep light low and brief.

Reading when spawn is ready

AT A GLANCE Use spawn just past full coverage: firm and slightly densified, but not mature, pinning or bricked. Each species looks different at that point.

Teach staff the three colonization phases:

  1. Jump-off (the most sensitive phase): mycelium leaves the inoculum and starts into the new grain.
  2. Exploration: white and fuzzy.
  3. Consolidation or maturation: dense, digesting, preparing to fruit.

RULE Use spawn just past exploration, when it has slightly densified but is not mature. Old spawn jumps off more slowly.

TIP Once other people knock and shake spawn, train them to judge these stages by eye and by squeeze.

Species Ready spawn looks like Too early or too late
King oyster evenly colonized, just past full coverage Used or refrigerated too early, it may die or perform weakly. Left 0.5-1 week past colonization it becomes a solid brick with some stroma (less than other oysters). Left too long it turns leathery and slow to leap onto substrate.
Chestnut fully white, grains joined into a block that has some squish It never becomes a hard brick like oyster, because it stays thread-like rather than matting.
Black pearl oyster firm; forms at most a weak skin that breaks up easily —
Blue oyster firm brick Left long, it forms fleshy, rubbery chunks.
Pioppino soft and fluffy; never knits as hard as shiitake or oyster spawn. When metabolites are visible and growth starts creeping up the bag, it is ready for cold storage —

Squeeze a bag to judge it: ready spawn of firm-knitting species holds together as a firm brick, while under-grown spawn stays loose.

Metabolites are normal. Yellow or orange secondary metabolites on older grain are normal for shiitake, chestnut and pioppino; the amount varies with incubation temperature. Chestnut shows clear water droplets about a week after the yellow ones, which is also normal.

Pioppino fluff. On grain, pioppino fluff is less pronounced because grain is nutrient-dense. A lack of fluff on blocks, not on grain, is the warning sign.

Auto-fruiting in spawn bags

AT A GLANCE Catch spawn at firmness, before it fruits. Never sell spawn with fruit on it.

RULE Catch bags at firmness, before they fruit, and never sell spawn that is auto-fruiting. Cap n Stem never ships spawn with any fruit; buckled or slightly brown spawn without fruit is used in-house.

Species Auto-fruiting behaviour
Shiitake (and most strains) Popcorning or buckling on spawn bags signals approaching fruiting. Once the culture switches to fruiting it does not go back to vigorous spreading.
Pioppino May pin small in the bag, and is probably the one species where some in-bag pinning can be tolerated (unconfirmed).
Lion's mane Starts fruiting whenever conditions get unhappy. Small Hericium primordia on spawn tend to reabsorb into the mycelium if the fruit mass is not large, so some auto-fruiting is tolerated; heavy auto-fruiting makes spawn slow to re-establish.
Comb tooth Only auto-fruits on grain once fully colonized. It costs about half a week more turnaround but stays in spawn mode, which extract companies may value.
Black pearl oyster Rarely auto-fruits; it goes to stroma first.
Other oyster strains Pin (form tiny mushroom buds) on the top and bottom of old grain bags.

Storing and shipping spawn

AT A GLANCE Chill spawn to 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) as soon as it is firm. Use it within about 2 weeks (3 at most). Pre-chill before shipping, and ship fast.

Item Value
Cold room temperature about 2 °C (35 °F), just above freezing to avoid ice damage
Fridge for stored spawn must hold 1-2 °C (34-36 °F); a month at about 6 °C (42 °F) gives a massive quality drop
Refrigerated G2, general definitely good for 2 weeks; 3 weeks pushes the limit "for any mushroom"
Lion's mane spawn no more than about 2 weeks in cold storage; it still tries to fruit, so monitor it
Comb tooth G2 for later sale stop at about 2 weeks (firm, some white, before fruiting) and refrigerate
Black oyster masters about a month in cold storage, with rising risk of stroma and hardening; inspect them; beyond a month is a no-go
Chestnut spawn holds up very well cold; the least worry for orders meant to last about 2 months (which Cap n Stem discourages)

RULE Move spawn to cold before it popcorns. Metabolism continues slowly in the cold.

WARNING Time alone causes stroma. Some varieties form stroma just from sitting too long, even when healthy. In split-batch trials, the portion used on time gave healthy, high yields and the portion left to sit formed stroma. Healthy spawn can also develop stroma during long or hot shipping or storage.

Shipping

Temperature is the variable that always bites when shipping spawn, especially in summer.

  • Cap n Stem uses many 40 ft (12 m) refrigerated containers, plus home-built cold rooms (which are less even), to pre-chill spawn.
  • Packed, active spawn heats itself, so chill it first and ship fast.
  • In a box test, spawn with gel packs in an insulated box, left out over a weekend, held temperature remarkably well.
  • Gel packs first chill, then buffer, then give out, so heat stress usually comes at the end of transit.
  • Spawn shipped by air goes through pressure swings, so bag choice matters (see Chapter 11).

TIP A simple quality-control hold: split each grain batch into two lots, test one, and ship nothing until testing is complete. One grower does this routinely.

  • Surplus blocks are a different problem for each species. Pioppino blocks "will store for six months" in a refrigerated container, but "everything else will auto-fruit even at 34 degrees" (1 °C). Block makers therefore try never to over- or under-produce.

  • Spawn and substrate are "highly metabolically active", so they make their own heat in the box. Cap n Stem will not ship pallets without refrigeration: it uses refrigerated LTL freight (less-than-truckload, a shared truck), costing US$150-2,000 depending on distance. Small orders of 1-40 boxes go the same day by airline cargo, still with ice packs and insulated boxes in summer.

  • Cap n Stem will not ship spawn without insulation and cold packs. In summer, shipping can cost more than the spawn itself, and a box can still arrive hot and spoiled. One Florida grower who had stopped driving 1.5 hours to collect his spawn was considering driving again for the hot months.

  • When a farm reports bacteria "in the spawn", the cause is often heat in transport. Cold shipping fixes it, but farms that scale fast often panic and ask for refunds rather than pay a little more for shipping. Customers who insist on cheap, unchilled shipping lose the spawn and everything it was mixed into.

  • Bags sealed at sea level balloon when sent by air, because aircraft holds and cabins are pressurized only to the equivalent of about 2,300 m (7,500 ft) altitude.

Stroma

AT A GLANCE Stroma is the fungus's own stress growth: dense, hot, swollen lumps, almost always in oyster grain spawn. It cannot be cut out and spreads to every bag made from affected spawn. Prevent it with whole grain, no bursting, low additives, broken-up inoculum, cool incubation and good timing. Screen masters hardest.

What stroma is

"Stroma" simply means a mass of fungal cells. The term is used loosely, published research mostly ends with "cause unclear", and there is little scientific documentation; most knowledge is growers' experience.

What it is not.

  • It is not monotub "overlay" (as described on the Shroomery forum) or Agaricus "blob mutants".
  • Older growers called it "Mycogone". Mycogone is actually a genus of real Hypocreales contaminants that can look similar. True stroma is a genetic or epigenetic response of the cultivated fungus itself.
  • It is distinct from healthy "mycelial consolidation", a secondary dense layer that can look odd but is fine. Stroma swells rapidly into flabby, balloon-like growths.
  • John Donahue's shiitake book uses "stroma" for early primordial knots. Shiitake has also been seen forming small white heads that stall, which may be a related predisposition.

Why it is so serious. It is called "mushroom cancer" or a tumour: it cannot be cut out, and any small amount spreads into every bag inoculated from the affected spawn, as Trichoderma would. Even apparently clean parts of the bag carry it. It gives unhealthy mycelium, fewer and deformed fruits, and unpredictable behaviour. It is not airborne and does not spread through the air; it ruins the affected material.

What it feels like. Stroma tissue is dense outside, weak and mushy inside, and very hot: a broken-up stroma bag from a cooler felt about 38 °C (100 °F), much hotter than the healthy mycelium next to it.

It may be virus-linked. This is still unresolved, and textbooks tend to dismiss it as a spawn problem.

Where it shows up

  • In grain spawn, about 99% of the time. It almost never appears on agar and rarely in substrate blocks. It is linked to heat from digesting rich grain.
  • In blocks, stroma comes from the spawn nine times out of ten (unless the mix is badly uneven). It can be seen forming within about 5 days of inoculation and worsens daily.
  • Shape: in grain bags it radiates from a centre and is more circular. In blocks it appears as harder, less circular pouches, because it arrives in a clump of affected grain.
  • Species: at Cap n Stem it is almost entirely an oyster problem: P. ostreatus types (the house blue) most, then black oyster, plus a small, delicate oyster strain (name unconfirmed). Pleurotus showed the lowest tolerance.
  • Black pearl in blocks: very dense, often amber- or orange-tinted white circular patches that predict poor yield and misshapen fruit.
  • Frequency: it usually appears in only 1-2 of several hundred bags from the same cell line, which suggests a local stress response rather than a defective culture. It has been seen on millet, rye and straight sorghum, and less on the sorghum mix (small sample).
  • Genetics: wild oyster clones form less stroma at first, but incidence rises with successive generations; a Danish grower's wild red oyster clone now forms it heavily. Cap n Stem keeps its stroma-prone house blue because its 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) yields underpin customers' businesses.
  • On agar it is very rare. When seen, blame plate age, heat or poorly mixed media (for example undissolved malt extract).

Many farms meet stroma as a "contamination" they cannot beat. Cap n Stem has studied it in Pleurotus grain for about a year, with DNA extraction, PCR and gel checks, and outside sequencing planned. See Chapter 8 for DNA work.

Causes

The best working explanation is a stress response. Mushy or burst grain and loose starch form dense clumps that are hard to colonize. Metabolism spikes there, producing excess heat and CO2, and that combination triggers stroma.

Triggers seen in practice:

  • Big temperature spikes with rich grain.
  • Free starch from over-hydrated grain leaching into residual water.
  • Aggressive species such as oyster.
  • Heat or stress in black pearl oyster.
  • Time or high ambient temperature alone, in some varieties, even with perfect grain.

CASE A batch of bags with a leached, greasy polymer residue (a rainbow sheen, slippery, and so bad the lab could not seal them) produced stroma in every affected bag, across many species. The bag supplier was Unicorn, during an ownership change. Published papers also link polymers to stroma. Lesson: when stroma appears across species at once, suspect the bags.

CASE A recent outbreak was traced, by examining the stroma colonies, to burst sorghum from an older, moth-damaged lot, while the rye kernels' interiors were intact. Lesson: damaged grain bursts, and burst grain feeds stroma.

WHY Growers ask these fungi to digest much richer, protein-heavy media than the wood they evolved on, so mis-set variables readily cause problems.

Prevention

  1. Buy Grade 1, mostly whole, intact grain (see Buying grain).
  2. Cook for maximum hydration but stop short of bursting. Cook grain intact and "al dente", with no free water outside the kernels. More water is not better.
  3. Keep additives (CaCO3, gypsum, sawdust) very low, under 1%; Cap n Stem's total is about 0.15% of wet weight.
  4. Break up inoculum thoroughly so it is evenly distributed.
  5. Control ambient temperature, especially for big, rich grain bags of aggressive blue oyster packed together: about 18 °C (65 °F) for grain. The critical variable is the internal temperature at peak metabolism near the end of colonization. Avoid heat spikes.
  6. Watch the time: move spawn on to inoculation or into the fridge at the right moment. Don't leave fully colonized masters sitting for 2 weeks.

Screening for stroma

Packing managers screen out stroma bags; small spots can swell into huge masses within days. G1 masters are low-volume and are screened carefully.

Procedure: checking spawn for stroma

  1. Before using any spawn bag, inspect it for hard, discoloured spots. A stroma spot never reverts to growing mycelium.
  2. Press on any dense spot. Rock-hard and lumpy means stroma. Soft, or just yellowing where you pressed, is normal. True stroma appears in older dense zones, not newly colonized ones.
  3. Remember the look-alikes: harmless dense, pillowy splotches are normal in black pearl grain, and dense white pioppino patches can look like stroma but stay soft.
  4. If a lot has shown stroma anywhere, break open suspect bags from it. Stroma can form in the core of a bag (a "golf ball") while the outside looks clean; a lab manager found it this way.
  5. Discard any bag with stroma, and every bag made from it.

CHECK A slit block or broken-open bag with stroma shows a whitish, swollen, rubbery lump; affected grain shows white, lumpy masses.

Stroma is Cap n Stem's one persistent biological problem. Screening relies on human judgement, and occasionally a few hundred bags are tossed. The farm refuses to accept a loss of about 3% as normal. Grain spawn will always need hands-on care: it is an artisanal process built on a commodity.

Other spawn problems

AT A GLANCE If many blocks from one spawn bag or lot fail the same way during incubation, suspect the spawn. If the trouble shows only at fruiting, look elsewhere first, especially at water. See Chapter 16 for contamination in general and Chapter 19 for symptom look-ups.

Symptom Likely cause What to do

In the spawn maker's experience the outlier is "always water" (an untreated well, or even city water). This is a strong claim: rose comb is also commonly linked to chemical fumes. Maitake is hard. Maitake grain spawn is harder to make than most: growth slows fast if the medium is even slightly off. Spawn bought in about 2015-16 arrived brown with sparse growth, apparently from liquid inoculation.

WARNING Spilled grain wrecks HEPA filters. Grain splashed into the bottom edge of a HEPA filter, and bags rammed into the frame, rupture filters, and a trapped millet seed becomes a mould source. Vacuum spilled grain out; never pick at it with a knife or blow it with compressed air. Fit an angle-iron bumper along the table. See Chapter 4.

Making versus buying spawn

AT A GLANCE Making spawn costs at least a day of labour a week; buying it costs roughly US$80-160 a week for a small farm. A middle route is to buy masters and make only G2.

Option Cost Notes
Make all your own spawn at least about 1-1.25 days of labour per week With a canner, one spawn run is over a day of labour each week.
Buy all spawn in roughly US$80-160 per week
Buy grain masters (or LC) from a spawn lab and make only bulk spawn one run a week, for example a month's spawn for one variety the middle option

How much spawn you need. For 100 blocks of 10 lb (4.5 kg) a week at a 1:20 ratio (one spawn bag per 20 blocks), you need about 5 spawn bags a week. The source used 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags; with the 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 standard, 5 bags still cover 100 blocks.

Small equipment does not scale well: see Sterilizer options. If you buy, keep to a small number of trusted spawn suppliers; one grower recommends no more than two. See Chapter 22 for costing.

What other farms decided.

  • A New Hampshire farm makes no spawn at all, after losing one bag in four when it tried. It buys spawn on winter rye and millet.
  • A Tallahassee farm found switching to Cap n Stem spawn "a huge change". It had been running too many things at once and getting more contamination than it should, and its consistency went "way higher". Making your own spawn does make cloning and trying new strains easier, and small growers may feel it saves money or makes them "more real", but for this farm it was holding the business back.
  • A Jacksonville grower made half his spawn and bought half for a few years, then decided spawn-making wasted time and money in his setup: "this is not a lab, this is an efficiency". He bought ready-colonized cocoa-coir bags at first, then about 100 blocks a week from a grower in Georgia, and finally made all his own blocks from bought spawn.
  • A California farm started with bought G2 spawn, then bought an autoclave to expand its own G2 from bought masters. That removed shipping waits and the need to juggle three calendars (spawn, substrate and mushrooms) around a supplier.
  • Even farms that make spawn need a backup supplier: when a Colorado farm's autoclave failed one summer, Cap n Stem supplied its spawn.

Bags a week 8 G2 + 4 masters = 12
Capacity of two 75X runs 10-12 bags
Spare bags none
Grain, cooked 8 × 6 lb + 4 × 4 lb = 64 lb (29 kg)
Pot loads (8 lb millet + 4 lb water makes 12 lb cooked) 5.3, so 6 pots: 3 in round A, 3 in round B

Result: the plan fits, but only with both runs full at 6 bags and nothing to spare. Spare masters and any second G2 bag for the small species (which would be 14 bags) do not fit in two runs.

OPEN Masters are 4 lb bags, smaller than the 6 lb G2 bags. Whether 7 or 8 bags go in one 75X run is not in any source. Measure it on the first run (stack count and the time to come up to 17 psi) and write the answer here. If it does not fit, a third short run, or a smaller G2 count, is the only way to make the spares. Six pots make 72 lb, 8 lb more than needed: bin the extra, or bag it as a spare master only if the run has room.

Monthly strain check

FARM NOTE Joseph's decision (6 Nov 2026): there are no separate monthly test bags. The check on genetic viability is the result of the real production fruiting, fed into the records for each strain. Once a month, for each strain in production, read the last four weeks of production lots against the strain's own history: days to colonize, days to pin, form, yield per block, and contamination rate by lot code (contamination targets). A strain that is slipping gets its slants and water tubes marked WATCH (viability log). The full test-and-expand line is still run at intake, after every refresh and for any tube older than 18-24 months.

The grain moisture log

Log moisture on every grain day. A run is worth nothing if you cannot say what the grain was.

Column What to write
Date and run e.g. 2026-11-11, round A
Grain lot Supplier, sack, date opened (baseline)
Dry grain Weight in lb or kg
Water added Weight
Cooked, drained weight Weight
Weight gain % (cooked − dry) ÷ dry × 100
Wet-basis moisture % Water ÷ total × 100 (see the worked example in Measuring moisture)
Squeeze test Hard, right or jelly
Burst kernels None, a few or many
Bag weight after autoclave Weight, to see what the autoclave adds (about 0.1-0.2 lb, 45-90 g, in tests)
Result later Days to colonize, stroma, contamination

Where the farm's recipe sits today, worked through the arithmetic in Measuring moisture, assuming millet comes in at about 11.5% moisture:

Water per 8 lb (3.6 kg) millet Wet-basis moisture Weight gain
4 lb (1.8 kg) about 41% about 50%
4.5 lb (2.0 kg) about 43% about 56%
4.9 lb (2.2 kg) about 45% about 61%
5.4 lb (2.4 kg) about 47% about 68%

FARM NOTE Start with 8 lb millet and 4 lb water per pot, which lands near 40% (the pot method used here). The target is as close to 45-47% as millet goes without bursting (Moisture targets). Move the water up in half-pound steps, one change at a time, only while kernels stay intact and spawn colonizes evenly; stop at the first sign of many burst kernels. Leave headroom for what the autoclave adds.

Key rules

  1. Buy USDA Grade 1, whole, clean, organic grain. Log every truckload against a baseline, and use sorghum quickly before insects get to it.
  2. Hydrate to the most the grain holds without bursting: upper 40s % for rye (millet just under its 45-47% limit), about 55% for oats, 42-46% for maitake. Allow for the water the autoclave adds.
  3. Kettle-cook to "al dente" with no free water; mix grain gently for only a few minutes; keep CaCO3 + gypsum around 0.15% of wet weight.
  4. Always pressure-sterilize spawn (grain at the centre of the coldest bag at 121 °C, 250 °F, or more for 35 min or longer); never just pasteurize it. Use vacuum pulses or a good purge to shorten the cycle, and log a test bag every run.
  5. Inoculate 4 lb (1.8 kg) masters with two about 1 cm leading-edge squares (four for slow strains). Leave them about 1-1.5 weeks, then shake.
  6. Expand one master into about 12 six-pound (2.7 kg) G2 bags (never fewer than 6 or more than 24). Break the master up thoroughly and weigh G2 bags accurately.
  7. Incubate spawn cooler than blocks (about 17-18 °C, 63-64 °F), space bags widely, keep light dim, and watch the top shelves for heat.
  8. Use or chill spawn just past full coverage, when firm but before it pins, buckles or bricks. Never sell spawn with fruit on it.
  9. Store spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) for about 2 weeks (3 at most); lion's mane no more than 2 weeks. Pre-chill spawn before shipping.
  10. Treat any stroma as untreatable. Screen G1 masters hardest, break open suspect bags from affected lots, and fix the causes: burst grain, heat and time.
  11. Our farm: four species a week means four masters and 3/3/1/1 G2 bags, a monthly strain check read from production results, and a grain moisture log every run. See Our farm.

Open questions

  • Expansion ratios. The G1 to G2 ratio is given as 12 in most sources and 20 in others, and plate yields range from 4 to "30-some" masters. The operative figures still need confirming.
  • The cause of stroma. A stress response, genetics, polymers and a virus have all been proposed; Cap n Stem's sequencing work has not yet reported results.
  • Filter patches. Whether Unicorn T (Tyvek) patches survive sterilization at 121 °C (250 °F) or more without damage, and whether A patches filter as well as T patches on spawn bags, is still being tested (see Chapter 11).
  • Units for hydration. Grain hydration is quoted both as wet-basis moisture % and as weight-gain %, and sources do not always say which; see Measuring moisture.
  • Lighting. Whether motion-sensor lights help or harm spawn rooms is unresolved.
  • Autoclave water. No figure is available for how much moisture the autoclave adds beyond the about 0.1-0.2 lb (45-90 g) per bag measured in tests.

chapters.html:
Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the fruiting substrate that goes into blocks: the sawdust base (raw dust, hardwood fuel pellets, combo pellets), the supplements that add nitrogen, recipes and ratios, moisture targets, how substrate is mixed and hydrated (from hand-mixing to dosing pellets and water straight into the bag), calcium additives, and recipes by species. The numbers people use most:

  • Master's Mix = 50:50 hardwood sawdust : soy hulls. It is the American default: hot, fast and high-yielding, but harder to manage.
  • Shiitake and maitake need far less supplement: about 20-30%.
  • Moisture at bagging: most blocks 61-63% total moisture; shiitake 64-65%; maitake 60-61%; above about 68% invites bacteria.
  • Count the water already in your inputs and measure honestly: about 7% in combo pellets, 7-15% in fuel pellets, up to 70-80% in raw oak dust.
  • Every bag the same: same moisture, even mix. Uneven mixes cause hot spots, bacteria and stroma.
  • Never more than 50% soy hulls.

Substrate is the food the mushroom grows on. In a commercial farm it is a mix of a woody base (usually hardwood sawdust) and a richer supplement, wetted to an exact moisture, packed into a filter bag, heat-treated, inoculated with spawn and left to colonize. What goes into the bag, and how evenly it is wetted and mixed, decides how fast the block colonizes, how hot it runs in incubation, and how much it yields. This chapter takes you from the ingredients to a bag of evenly hydrated substrate ready for the steam box. The bag itself, bagging machines and inoculation are in Chapter 11.

How substrate works: carbon, nitrogen and particle size

AT A GLANCE Wood supplies carbon; a supplement adds nitrogen for speed and yield. Finer base material needs less supplement. Density, strain and local supply all change the right recipe.

Carbon and nitrogen

  • You can grow on carbon-only media such as straight sawdust. Supplements raise the nitrogen content, which gives faster growth and higher yield.
  • Every ingredient carries both carbon and nitrogen, so calling one a "carbon" ingredient and another a "nitrogen" ingredient is shorthand. Sawdust has some nitrogen; hemp hurd and oats sit in between.
  • Balance a recipe for what you want most: speed, metabolic stability or yield.

The ratio of carbon to nitrogen in a mix is called the C:N ratio. A low C:N (more nitrogen) feeds the fungus faster but also makes the block run hotter and gives contaminants more to eat.

Group Ingredients
Carbon (the base) sawdust, straw, hemp hurd
Nitrogen (supplements) soy hulls, wheat middlings ("midds") or bran, millet, rice bran, beet pulp, and many more
  • Arid or poorer regions grow almost everything on straw plus rice bran; Spain is one example.
  • A starch source from a grain supplement is a needed part of a fruiting substrate. Historically that was oatmeal; in Cap n Stem's mixes it is the soy hulls.
  • These fungi evolved on wood, but growers ask them to digest much richer, protein-heavy media. That is why mis-set variables (moisture, mixing, temperature) so readily cause problems.

Particle size and density

Particle size governs how much supplement you need. Think "sand versus rocks": a finer base needs less supplement, a coarser one needs more.

  • Supplements differ in particle size and in how available their nutrients are to the fungus (bioavailability): wheat midds and soy differ on both. Combo pellets are ground to a chosen particle size.
  • Too-dense substrate is a problem. Fine, powdery soy or sawdust that isn't coarse enough gives uneven texture, a bag whose top differs from its bottom, and poor mixing. Straw can have similar issues.
  • Powdery wheat middlings pack like flour into a dense "cake" or "brick". The mycelium in it grows dense and cannot shed heat.
  • Species differ in the density they like. A side example from another crop: growers of mutation-prone Psilocybe cubensis strains (for example Penis Envy) found that compacting a casing-like layer over a spawn layer gave more uniform growth than loose, through-spawned beds.

Recipe, strain and supply

  • Not every strain likes a given recipe. A fragrant wild oyster strain grew through 50:50 but fruited poorly on it. Colonizing a substrate does not mean the strain will fruit on it.
  • Thinking only in terms of oysters misleads small farms. The rule to remember is "phenotype : substrate": match the recipe to the strain in front of you.
  • Treat recipes as non-static. Raw materials such as soy hulls and oak are limited and availability changes, so know your alternatives.

RULE If you are starting out, use Master's Mix or a wheat-bran-based recipe. Pick the cheapest, most available, proven and scalable material, not hard-to-get or hard-to-handle inputs. Coffee grounds are a poor commercial substrate; many have tried.

  • Substrate structure (particle size and wood quality) matters, and most books skip it. Copying another farm's recipe fails if your sawdust or pellets differ from theirs.
  • Bags are the method that works. A Houston grower first tried recycled cardboard and coffee grounds in 5-gallon buckets and biodegradable sacks with holes, with limited success: "you just have to do bags".

Wood: species and forms

AT A GLANCE Use a hardwood (red oak is the reference). Check the sawdust is pure: aromatic softwoods suppress mycelium unless kiln-dried or pelletized. Sawdust comes in three forms (raw dust, hardwood fuel pellets, combo pellets) that behave very differently.

Which wood

  • Cap n Stem uses red oak. In the US, red oak harvest is concentrated in a band down the middle of the country. In Belgium everything is grown on beech, the dominant local hardwood. Straw is available almost anywhere grain grows.
  • Red oak versus white oak: red oak is less dense, faster-growing, easier to get, and releases nutrients faster for quicker yield. White oak is denser and better for long-term shiitake on logs. John Donahue's book discusses oak cell structure.
  • Oak's complex cell structure holds a lot of water. Softwoods hold less, and alder holds less than oak. Oak is also dense and hard for steam to penetrate, more so when wet (see Chapter 12).
  • Oak is the safest wood for shiitake if you can get it reliably at a good price. Other hardwoods work: one farm uses alder, and Far West Fungi uses whatever hardwoods it can get.
  • Pioppino may prefer a soft hardwood such as poplar over dense oak or maple (a grower's suspicion, unconfirmed).

WARNING Check the species purity of your sawdust. Suppliers may mix in softwoods such as cedar without knowing it matters. Aromatic softwoods contain antifungal compounds that suppress mycelium to varying degrees.

Softwood is not always a problem once it has been processed:

  • Kiln-drying or pelletizing softwood (Douglas fir, pine) makes it a mostly harmless carbon source. Western growers use 100% Douglas fir pellet substrates even for temperamental species, including shiitake.

  • Raw kiln-dried softwood used alone yields somewhat less. For softwoods, aged fir or pelletized softwood works best.

  • A working theory (unproven): pelletizing (pressure and heat) drives out moisture and destroys the sap-based antifungal compounds of softwood, leaving a more inert, more bioavailable carbon. Pellets cost more but give consistency.

  • Eucalyptus works. Australia has no oak, and one Brisbane farm grows everything on eucalyptus (pellets at first, moving to sawdust). Japanese growers told them it would work, because eucalyptus oils are in the leaves, not the timber.

  • Pecan (a hickory relative) sawdust in central Texas was so fluffy that three bulk bags ("super sacks") weighed almost nothing, and collecting enough meant a 1.5-hour drive every week.

  • Fir pellets (about US$3 per 40 lb, 18 kg, bag) gave yields comparable to Master's Mix for one California grower.

WARNING Know exactly what wood is in scavenged sawdust. A Texas grower's dust-collector bag from a wood shop was cherry with ribbons of what he was "99% sure" was hemlock, and it ruined "so many grows". A little black walnut is also harmful.

The three forms of sawdust

Sawdust reaches a farm in three forms: raw dust, hardwood fuel pellets (HWFP) and combo pellets.

  • Raw dust comes either from sawmills (fresh, "green") or from furniture and flooring factories (kiln-dried). The two behave like different products.
  • Fresh dust is either used at once or composted and turned ("fermented").
  • Hardwood fuel pellets are about 80-90% hardwood and 10-20% softwood.
  • Combo pellets are sawdust and soy hulls milled and pelleted together, typically 50:50.

Raw sawdust

Raw dust is the cheapest-looking option and the hardest to run consistently.

  • Raw dust falls into fresh/green, aged and composted categories. Its moisture, tannin (especially in red oak), pH and C:N all vary.
  • That variation produces a "sine wave" of yields unless you compost and turn the pile completely, which is a lot of work with 33 tons (30 t) at a time. Shoulder seasons, when sap is low, show the swings most.
  • Raw piles swing in moisture and C:N: water sinks to the middle, the outside dries, and a 33-ton load heats strongly in the centre. Raw dust can sit at 70% moisture or more.
  • Turned or composted piles stabilize. Turning daily, as big Asian farms and older US farms do with outdoor piles, is the best way to work with raw dust. Composting also leaches tannins out over time.

CASE When Cap n Stem used raw, unturned oak dust in Maine (the pile froze outside), results went good, poor, good, poor, regardless of where in the pile the dust came from. Lesson: an unturned raw pile is not one material.

  • Ageing and fermenting change the wood. At the back of a 60,000 lb (27 t) pile, aged red oak dust suited shiitake while other species did poorly on it.
  • Raw amended substrate is not shelf-stable. In Southeast Asia and elsewhere, substrates are deliberately composted or fermented so microbes and enzymes start breaking the wood down before the fungus does.
  • A large Pennsylvania farm (probably in Kennett Square) kept big piles of red oak sawdust marked to test different ageing times. Cap n Stem never aged red oak; it used it as received, out of concern that stored sawdust would mould.
  • A New Hampshire grower (Eric) still fruits chestnut on raw dust. Raw-dust blocks give tighter clusters with bigger mushrooms; pellet blocks give a more even flush and higher total yield. The age of the sawdust also changes fruiting.

Raw dust is wet. Red oak usually arrives at about 70-80% moisture.

RULE Measure raw dust moisture every day with a real method (see the oven-dry test). The squeeze test only goes so far. Never assume raw dust is dry.

  • Raw dust can be so wet that you add almost no water and use dry supplements just to dry the mix out. With mill sawdust you may need to add dry ingredients in some seasons to reach the moisture target.

Storing raw dust.

  • Raw dust, pellets and loose supplements all carry microbial loads, driven mainly by exposure to moisture, so keep them dry. Piles that are not being composted must stay dry.
  • Properly hot-composted dust is effectively self-sanitized by heat: a test plating of hot compost onto agar grew nothing.
  • Raw dust storage is costly. A 33-ton moving-floor load occupies roughly 25 x 75 ft (7.6 x 22.9 m), with 50 x 75 ft (15.2 x 22.9 m) also quoted, and needs a tractor, labour and space. "Free" sawdust isn't free.
  • Before switching to pellets, Cap n Stem stored 30-60 tons (27-54 t) of raw dust delivered by walking-floor trailers. Moisture varied, chips had to be sifted out, and there was no room to age it, so it was used fast.
  • About 40 tons (36 t) of raw red oak was stored indoors on a concrete warehouse floor. Indoor storage is ideal only within the material's shelf life, and an open pile is exposed to any water that gets in.

CASE During a snowmelt flood, berms built from sifted-out oak chips to protect a stored pile failed, because wood floats. Lesson: plan raw-dust storage for water getting in, not just for rain falling on it.

  • Red oak versus white oak. Red oak has more tannins than white oak, and tannins drive composting in a sawdust pile.
  • Fresh versus aged dust. Raw sawdust from fresh logs is wet and prone to contamination. Sawdust aged "too far" gives shiitake blocks that colonize fully, brown and buckle, and then never fruit. Sterilizing old red oak leaches tannins into a brown liquid at the bottom of the bag. Use fresher or well-turned material.
  • Ageing piles. Piles left outdoors in rain and snow heat to "well over 120" °F (about 50 °C) at the core. Turn them so they don't go too far, and use them at the right point. Kentucky Shiitake Systems (KSS), which at its height made about 120,000 seven-pound shiitake logs a week (as recalled), turned its red-oak piles carefully to get uniform growth.
  • Handling raw material is expensive at scale. That is why Cap n Stem sells combo pellets: kiln-dried, hammer-milled hardwood with supplement already added, at about 7% moisture and shelf stable.

Case study: sifting chips out of raw dust

Cap n Stem's first sawdust was fine, solid red oak from a small local mill with no chips, but supply was limited and too costly. They switched to a large New Hampshire pallet maker.

The new dust contained chips that shiitake could not colonize: the dust arrived at about 70% moisture but the chips were bone-dry. Soaking the chips was rejected because the material would freeze in winter, so the chips had to be sifted out.

Sifter version Design Outcome
v1 Table with a 6 x 8 ft (1.8 x 2.4 m) frame holding a mesh screen; dust shovelled on Manual and slow
v2 Screen shaken by an old pump motor with an angle-iron linkage Loud, shook itself apart, bogged down; a fire hazard when it stalled. Don't ever do this.
v3 Flat conveyor with an RPC (reusable plastic) crate, later tilted so chips run off one end and dust falls into barrels The flat version just filled crates with chips
v4 Rotating trommel drum of rolled perforated steel with welded ribs, belt-driven on a stand, with guards Dust falls into barrels and chips exit the low end; only two barrels at a time instead of four

The finished v4 trommel is a steel drum on a wooden frame with roller supports and a belt drive; the dust slides down a chute beneath it into barrels.

  • A 33-ton load was sifted "one sift at a time". The barrels weighed 50-80 lb (23-36 kg), about 75 lb (34 kg) typical, and had to be lifted to the mixer that fed the bagger.
  • A winch hung about 22 ft (6.7 m) up kept failing when barrel handles broke, and lifting barrels by hand onto stepped platforms caused a back injury. See Chapter 18 for lifting safety.

WARNING Near miss: a cracked barrel on the winch tipped, a worker steadied it by hand, and the hook nearly caught his hand. Never put hands on a hoisted load, and retire damaged barrels.

  • Combo pellets ended the sifting. The old process took huge manual labour for a substrate that performed about half as well as the pellet substrate that replaced it. Changes in the supply chain had kept forcing the farm to buy extra mixers and sifting equipment.

Hardwood fuel pellets (HWFP)

Hardwood fuel pellets are the pellets sold for pellet stoves.

  • HWFP are typically 80-90% hardwood and 10-20% softwood; another estimate is 80%+ hardwood and under 10% softwood.
  • Softwood is added mainly because old, undersized pellet-mill motors and dies cannot push 100% hardwood without overheating and wearing the dies. The hardwood species vary by region (oak, poplar, cherry).
  • HWFP became popular through online forums (Shroomery, Facebook) because hobbyists couldn't source hardwood sawdust. The softwood share is not disclosed but usually does not matter.
  • Fuel pellets are highly compressed sawdust with a slick lignin skin, at about 11% moisture (range about 7-15%).
  • Using them straight is like using grain spawn that was never soaked or simmered, which is not advised (see Chapter 9).
  • In a side-by-side test with equal pellet weight and equal water, fuel pellets left pooled water, stayed pellet-shaped and needed much longer to absorb than combo pellets. Pure oak pellets also absorbed water slowly in a Japanese automatic bagger trial.
  • Several other growers also use fuel pellets with dry bagging.

WARNING Master's Mix made from HWFP plus soy hull pellets often hydrates unevenly. The two pellet types break down at different rates and stratify: light material rises and dense dust sinks (the "Lucky Charms effect"). That creates high-nitrogen hot spots even when the bag's average moisture hits target.

  • Prices (US, late 2020s). Hardwood fuel pellets can be found for about US$4-5 per 40 lb (18 kg) bag at farm stores, while some sellers charge about four times that before shipping. Soy hull pellets cost about US$18 a bag plus shipping. Certified organic pellets cost more.
  • In regions without hardwood forests, pellets can be hard to find: one central Texas grower paid US$9 a bag for the last 10 bags at a patio-and-fire shop. Delivery is a bigger problem than finding supplies, because full truckloads are almost impossible for a small farm; combine several part loads instead.

Combo pellets

A combo pellet is sawdust and supplement milled, mixed and pelleted together, so every pellet already carries the recipe.

  • What they are: pellets of 100% single-species red oak plus soy hulls, ground to a consistent particle size, brought to the same moisture, passed through 5-6 vortex or air mixing stages and pelletized, so each pellet matches the ratio within about 1%. Blends offered are 50:50 (Master's Mix) and 70:30 (a wheat-midds shiitake blend). They are shelf-stable.
  • How they are made: kiln-dry, hammer-mill everything to the same particle size, pre-mix and post-mix in vortex mixers, then press through pellet dies with the same consistency from batch start to end, which is hard to do well. Kiln drying is said to break down the woody layer and help several species.
  • Pellet mills already run soy hulls through their dies to clean and lubricate them, which made the combo idea easy to adopt. Other binders include starch.
  • Pelletizing works by friction heat and pressure through a perforated die. Home pellet mills need higher moisture to hold shape: a trial at about 70% moisture with 60-70% oak made pellets that moulded.
  • Commercial fuel and combo pellets are dried to about 7%, where nothing grows. That is drier than mill grain at 10-12%.
  • A Canadian container grower had been making combination pellets for about six years when Cap n Stem described the product (date unconfirmed), and Cap n Stem became their customer and partner.
  • Combo pellets are drier than fuel pellets and have less lignin sheen, so they break up more easily. Drier pellets absorb more water and hold more. Some fine powder in a sack is normal.

How they hydrate. Combo pellets hydrate and fluff within about 10 s of contact with water, and the block is ready right after dosing. In a side-by-side test they puffed up "like leavened bread", left no standing water even when the bag was tipped, and broke up like pure sawdust.

In that test three filter-patch bags were compared: combo pellets (light tan), fuel pellets (darker) and a competing pellet (darker and coarser). After watering, the fuel-pellet bag sat in pooled water and the combo-pellet bag was a swollen, uniform crumb.

  • Mixing raw dust with soy, or HWFP with soy pellets, takes far more processing and labour to make even. The labour saved is the main argument for paying the higher price of combo pellets.
  • One grower who switched said he would not go back to raw sawdust.

CASE Chestnut is the species that convinced Cap n Stem. On raw dust, going from 5 to 10 lb (2.3 to 4.5 kg) blocks raised yield only about 20%; another account says yield per block stayed the same at about 1-1.5 lb (0.45-0.7 kg). The first batch on combo pellets doubled yield or more on 10 lb blocks (target 2-3 lb, 0.9-1.4 kg, described as about 125% more).

  • Why pellets do better is not known. The working theory: pellet sawdust is kiln-dried and acts as a uniform, easily digested inert carbon (like "granola"), while raw dust varies.

Limits and storage.

  • Combo pellets are inflexible: the recipe is fixed at manufacture ("like working with metal instead of wood"). Master's Mix 50:50 has endured. Trial blends included wheat-midds blends, straw/soy and straw/"cocoa" (term unconfirmed), tested for whether they held moisture and stayed mould-free in storage.
  • Combo pellets may not be optimal for maitake and shiitake.
  • Store them indoors and dry, not outside like raw sawdust. Months in a humid building are fine. The longest-stored batch, about 6 years old, still gave consistent yields.
  • The same building that held about 30 tons (27 t) of raw sawdust floor to ceiling holds about 60 tons (54 t) of combo pellets in about 60 totes or super sacks (each about 45 in, 1.1 m, high). Pellets are also sold in 30 and 50 lb (14 and 23 kg) bags.
  • Pallets of about 7%-moisture pellets store far more substrate per square foot than 70%-moisture raw dust.
  • Rats love raw soy pellets and will bore through walls for grain, but they seem to ignore combo pellets: Cap n Stem has had no rodent-chewed sacks or pest-infested batches.
  • Even for combo pellets, keep more than one supplier: Cap n Stem has several.
  • One company launched a compressed "combo brick" of sawdust and soy, like a coco coir brick, as a new product.
  • The only other maker at scale named in the sources is Mushroom Media Online. It originally mixed separate soy pellets and hardwood fuel pellets rather than making a true co-milled pellet. In one side-by-side hydration test its pellets puffed fairly fast but left dry pellets on top, were crumbly, and contained stray white strands that looked like super-sack fibres. Judge any pellet by your own yield trials.

CASE Cap n Stem switched all its substrate to combo pellets. Before that, it sifted and mixed red oak sawdust by the truckload for 6,000-7,000 blocks a week, which took an enormous amount of labour. Now pellets gravity-feed from a bulk bag onto a conveyor and into a small hopper serving two to four Odin fillers (an auger plus a load cell). For a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block the auger stops at about 4.1-4.2 lb (1.9 kg) of pellets, and solenoid valves then spray in the calculated water. Moisture is identical from block to block even if the weight varies (9.8 lb is fine). Automated filling gives about twice the output with half the people.

Supplements

AT A GLANCE Soy hulls are the "hot" US supplement: never above 50%, never de-oiled soy meal. Wheat midds and bran are gentler and used for shiitake and maitake. Trial every new ingredient or supplier before switching, and keep several sources.

A supplement is the nitrogen-rich part of the recipe. It drives speed and yield, and it is also what makes a block run hot or go wrong.

Soy hulls

  • Soy hulls' C:N ratio is not much different from wheat midds, yet their nitrogen seems far more bioavailable. Soy therefore behaves "hot" while midds are gentle. The exact reason is unknown (see Open questions). This view comes from a Canadian pellet maker.
  • Soy hulls come uncrushed, crushed or pelletized; cottonseed hulls are similar.
Form Behaviour
Crushed (hammer-milled into about 6-7 shreds per hull) Hydrates quickly; the easiest form to mix
Pelletized Dense, very tough pellets; hot water helps break them down
Uncrushed Tough cups: hard to hydrate, less available to mycelium, hold less water, and can make anaerobic blocks, especially with pasteurization

RULE Never go above 50% soy hulls.

WARNING Soybean meal or soy cake (de-oiled soy) is much higher in nitrogen than hulls. Avoid it, or use it only with extreme care.

Supply.

  • Soy hulls are a US-specific input. Australia, most of Europe and Asia lack them as a waste stream. The US is a top soy exporter; a large Northwest mill had to be convinced to sell domestically, because about 90% of its revenue is exports.
  • Soy is about the second-largest North American crop and is mostly exported. Hulls mostly go to animal feed, so supply was high and prices low until recently.
  • Soy hull prices follow macroeconomics and the weather (good grazing seasons drop grain prices), not mushroom demand. Watch commodity prices and buy ahead of shortages.
  • Soy plus sawdust became a default after it appeared in Paul Stamets' Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms and after experimentation by several growers; soy hulls were easy to source.

RULE Build a supply chain and stick with it, but keep several sources for each ingredient.

  • Unground soybean hulls gave a New Hampshire grower about 2 lb (0.9 kg) of mushrooms per 5 lb (2.3 kg) block.

Wheat midds, bran and other supplements

  • Wheat midds (middlings) and bran are different ingredients. Midds are mill-floor scrapings and fines: variable, and sometimes very rich. Bran is the flaky milling fraction and is richer. Bran was once about five times the price of midds: about $50 a bag for bran against $10 for midds some years ago.
  • Variability in the older shiitake recipe came partly from midds sourcing, with "plan-C" suppliers whose nutrition varied.
  • Midds shortages pushed growers to try shiitake on soy (as is done in Asia), with mixed success, and to reduced-soy recipes.
  • Pretzel waste is used as a supplement. A Pennsylvania organic supplier (McGeary Organics) joked that people need to eat more pretzels to keep it available.
  • Use locally cheap ingredients, but trial them first. In Maine, beet pulp and oats are cheap (tried, not adopted); elsewhere rice bran is the local choice.
  • Molasses gives oysters readily available sugar. Smaller farms (for example Jordan at Texas Fungus) can run elaborate recipes with molasses and the like. Large crews with staff turnover cannot run complex recipes reliably and suit a simple standard mix.
  • Other supplements: hemp hurd, molasses, pea hulls.
  • The "goat mix" is credited to one farm and is based on straw pellets. Most fancy new mixes are combinations of pellets.
  • Coco coir is an inert carbon that needs added nutrients. Some legal psilocybin regulations restrict substrate ingredients, for example allowing coir but not others. Straw plus soy or straw plus midds is common for cubensis.
  • Cottonseed hulls or fermented straw are the only substrates said to compete with Master's Mix for oyster yield.

RULE Trial any new ingredient source against your current baseline before switching. A new midds supplier can be a different product under the same name.

  • When you can't get soy hulls. Soy hulls supply nitrogen, protein and fibre. Alternatives are other hulls with an outer husk (beet, cottonseed, oat), wheat bran or wheat middlings. Buckwheat flour (which contains no wheat) has been used. Oats work in ultra-pasteurized substrate, and grains such as sorghum, wheat, rye or millet can be ultra-pasteurized without too many bacterial problems. Fermented straw is another base. What you can source changes with the season and the rain. As Cap n Stem puts it: "We've limited ourselves in the States to this thing that we call combo pellets or masters mix, but it's not the only thing you can use... experiment with what's out there."
  • Local substitutes that worked. Before Master's Mix supplies reached him, a California grower used oak sawdust from a nearby sawmill (a truckload for about US$20), fir pellets, beet pulp shreds, wheat bran, cottonseed meal and trial amounts of alfalfa.
  • Beet pulp pellets are very hard to hydrate, even in warm water. Straw pellets absorb too much water and leave a dry top layer, so add something that holds water.

WARNING Cotton gin "trash" (sticks, fluff and immature seed) grew oysters for one Texas grower, but he was afraid to eat them because cotton fields have been treated with arsenic-type defoliants in the past, and he could not get heavy-metal testing done. Don't sell mushrooms from a waste stream you cannot test.

Recipes and ratios

AT A GLANCE Master's Mix (50:50) for oysters, pioppino, king oyster and chestnut. 70-80% wood : 20-30% bran or midds for shiitake and maitake. About 30-40% soy for lion's mane. Ratios are by weight.

The standard ratios

Recipe Ratio Use and notes
Master's Mix (recommended start) 50% hardwood (red oak) sawdust : 50% soy hulls The highest-yielding oyster substrate but the richest and most fickle. Cap n Stem uses it for nearly everything. "Very American": hot, fast, high-yielding, harder to manage.
Shiitake / maitake style 70-80% hardwood dust : 20-30% wheat bran or midds (or pretzel waste, rice bran, even soy) Slow species with long in-bag development; "European"-style lower supplementation
Combo pellet blends 50:50 and 70:30 70:30 is the wheat-midds shiitake blend
Lion's mane (leaner) soy reduced to about 30-40% A better range than full 50:50
Maitake 20-40% soy (lean towards 20-30%; one large maitake producer uses about 30%) Well below full 50:50 Master's Mix

A teaching sequence of whiteboards sums up the system: "50:50 sawdust : soy hulls"; then the C:N ratio; then "50% dust : 50% soy"; then "Dust (hardwood) 70-80% : Wheat/pretzel/midds/bran 20-30%".

RANGE Master's Mix standard: 50:50 sawdust : soy hulls by weight. Cap n Stem stays at 50:50 for simplicity and yield.

Context: hot or humid sites. Start leaner, at 60:40 sawdust : soy hulls (40% soy), and raise the soy only if incubation temperature and blotch stay under control. This is a difference of climate, not a disagreement about the recipe:

  • 60-65% hardwood : 35-40% soy hulls: Avery (see Chapter 26) started at 50:50 and moved gradually to this range because 50% soy raised their blotch and contamination rates.
  • 55:45 or 60:40 sawdust : soy hulls: the starting point Ryan (see Chapter 26) suggests for a hot, humid site; he reports about 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) of blue oyster (strain POCNS) from a 10 lb (4.5 kg) bag.

Other figures you will hear:

  • 43% soy: some growers tested it and got yields similar to 50%, but differences depend on cooking and inoculation.
  • Master's Mix has sometimes been misquoted as 70:30; 70:30 is the shiitake blend, and Master's Mix is 50:50.
  • Comb tooth: given as 50:50 soy hulls to sawdust, with 60:40 (soy hulls 40) also called ideal; the source wording is ambiguous (see Open questions).

Choose the lower soy end if your blotch or contamination rate rises, or if incubation runs warm (see Richness and heat).

  • European growers tend to use cereal- or grain-based, lower-supplement, gentler recipes. To foreign growers, US 10 lb blocks at 50% soy look CO2-rich and costly "turn and burn"; US farms prioritize speed, bigger fruit and consistent yields.

  • For reishi, Ryan supplements sawdust with 15% wheat bran.

  • Why US recipes are so rich. US growing runs "bigger, stronger, faster": high supplementation gives a huge, very fast first flush at some cost in quality. Growers in East Asia produce prettier shiitake (and dry about 98% of it), but US farms pay for air conditioning, heating, the building and expensive labour, so faster blocks and higher yields pay for themselves.

  • Master's Mix is not a fix-all. Most shiitake strains don't need nitrogen anywhere near that level ("you can deal with about 10% bran"), though some strains do well on higher nitrogen and denser substrate. It is all strain-driven. One Massachusetts grower's over-supplemented shiitake gave misshapen blobs in the first flush, then a normal second flush.

Shiitake and maitake: less is more.

  • Master's Mix is a poor fit mainly for shiitake (the biggest exception) and maitake. Maitake can grow on it, but with odd morphology and more mould.
  • Slow species suit low supplementation: shiitake, with its long browning cycle, and maitake, with its long in-bag development. Shiitake prefers a lower-nitrogen mix than oysters ("less is more").
  • Cap n Stem's shiitake mix is softer and less "hot", which lets the three metabolic phases (colonization, buckling, browning) proceed. These bags are folded, not shaken (see Chapter 11).
  • A typical shiitake recipe board for a 10 lb block in an XLS-A bag reads: raw sawdust with 20-30% wheat midds, oat or bran, or rice bran, and 70-80% hardwood dust, with a second column for the pellet version.
  • Some shiitake farms grow on Douglas fir pellets.
  • Maitake on 50:50 combo pellets succeeds only if blocks fully mature before opening. Over-rich maitake blocks give lots of metabolites, more mould, hot cores, and mould on the developing fruit as exudate wicks up. Poking drain holes just drips the liquid onto the bags below.
  • Avery grows maitake on loose, aged sawdust with 25% soy, incubated for about 8 weeks.

CASE Chestnut deforms when there is too much substrate per fruiting site. In 30-40 lb (14-18 kg) straw buckets with side holes, oysters fruited fine but chestnut produced one odd mushroom. Lesson: block size and the number of fruiting sites must suit the species (see Block sizes).

  • Tiger sawgill grows on ordinary hardwood sawdust with a little wheat bran, wetted until a hard squeeze gives just a little water. It fruits readily, and can contaminate other growers' blocks in a shared fruiting chamber.

CASE On Maui, two growers produced oysters on free sugar-cane bagasse (the fibre left after crushing cane) from the sugar mill. They packed it into 50 lb (23 kg) columns hung from bowline knots in a greenhouse, and got giant clusters. Two small rooms were framed inside the greenhouse on a linoleum floor, with white panda film (white-on-black plastic sheet) stapled between the studs. They started with about US$15,000, always sold out at their local market, and never paid themselves. The numbers in their plan were "so wrong": how many bags one person can process in a day, the spawn needed per bag, how much spawn two All American sterilizers can make and the energy to run them around the clock, the internal pasteurization temperature of 50 lb columns, and the temperature inside the columns while fruiting. Bagasse also carries sugars that feed contaminants.

Moisture

AT A GLANCE Bag most blocks at 61-63% total moisture; shiitake 64-65%; maitake 60-61%; comb tooth 61-62%. Above about 68% expect loose water and bacteria. Count the water already in the ingredients, dose by weight, and aim for every bag to be identical. Every 1% matters.

"Total moisture" means the weight of all the water in the bag (the water you add plus the water already in the ingredients) as a percentage of the bag's total weight. All targets in this book are total moisture on that basis.

Why moisture matters

  • Mycelial cells are about 70-80% water, and substrate needs about 60-70%.
  • Too wet invites anaerobic conditions, bacteria and blotch. Too dry stalls the mycelium and favours dry-tolerant contaminants such as Trichoderma (see Chapter 16).
  • 60-61% is like a forest floor at field capacity: fully hydrated, not pouring water.
  • The fruiting block supplies about 99% of the water the mushrooms need (see Chapter 14).
  • Every 1% matters.

Fruiting block (general) about 62-63% The block supplies about 99% of the water the fruit needs

That seems dry against the about 61% ideal, and they may measure moisture differently (unconfirmed). If you try the drier figure, check how it was measured first (see Open questions).

  • Aim for no moisture difference between the top and bottom of the bag, so colonization is even.

CHECK A bag at the right moisture, tipped on its side, leaks no water. Bags coming out of the steam box should be solid and even, not flaky.

CASE Shiitake strain behaviour at the moisture extremes. KOM shiitake (one grower's account) tolerates low moisture and still yields; kept too wet, it goes anaerobic with "popcorning" and browning on the top only, but still fruits, and the bacterial slime can be wiped off. Strain 3790 kept too wet gives sloshy blocks with buckling and browning only on the top half and little fruiting. Lesson: find each strain's moisture window by trial.

WARNING Shiitake is unforgiving about moisture. If block moisture is even about 5% off target, shiitake won't fruit, and you find out only about 10 weeks later. Low-nitrogen kits (some commercial kits use under a quarter pound of supplement per block) keep a long shelf life because they don't fruit until they are opened to air.

Counting the water already present

The single most common moisture mistake is forgetting that the dry ingredients are not dry.

  • Allow for the moisture already in the ingredients. Combo pellets rest at about 7%; pellets in general run 7-11%, and fuel pellets about 7-15%. Ignoring pellet moisture is a common error.
  • Hardwood fuel pellets are usually around 8% and soy hulls 10-12% (one grower's measurements).
  • Raw red oak dust arrives at about 70-80% (see Raw sawdust).
  • Measure your own inputs by oven-drying a sample, and ask manufacturers for the per-batch average moisture; it isn't printed on the bags.

Procedure: oven-dry moisture test

  1. Weigh out 100 g of the sawdust (or pellets, or supplement).
  2. Dry it in an oven on a low setting for 1 hour, stirring it as it dries.
  3. Weigh it again.
  4. The weight lost is the water. If 90 g is left, the material held 10% water.
  5. Use that figure when you calculate the water to add, aiming for 60-62% total water, counting the water already in the materials.

CHECK Repeat the test daily on raw dust, because its moisture swings from load to load and through the pile.

Procedure: calculating the water to add

This is plain arithmetic, using the measured moisture of your inputs.

  1. Weigh the dry ingredients going into the bag (for example 4.2 lb of combo pellets).
  2. Work out their dry matter: weight × (1 − their moisture). At 7%: 4.2 × 0.93 = 3.91 lb.
  3. Work out the total bag weight that gives your target: dry matter ÷ (1 − target). At 61%: 3.91 ÷ 0.39 = 10.0 lb.
  4. Water to add = total weight − weight of dry ingredients: 10.0 − 4.2 = 5.8 lb (2.6 kg, which is 2.6 L of water).
  5. Dose the water by weight or with a flow meter (1 g = 1 mL of water).

WHY If you treat the same 4.2 lb of pellets as bone-dry and add water for 61%, you add 6.6 lb instead of 5.8 lb, and the bag actually lands near 64%: about three points too wet, from one ignored number.

CASE A farm had trouble only with lion's mane, which is sensitive to hydration, and cut its moisture to about 56%. The real problem was that its sawdust arrived at about 70% moisture, not the amount of water it was adding. Lesson: check what is already in the inputs before changing the recipe; this was a case of changing the wrong variable.

Measuring and distributing water

  • The squeeze test asks two questions: does the mix hold together, and does water come out when you squeeze it hard?
  • "Hose it and squeeze-test" hydration, common on older Washington-era farms and still used today, leads to big losses, doesn't scale, and is easy to half-do on a bad day.

RULE Measure solids by weight and water by weight or flow meter (1 g = 1 mL of water). The aim is "twins, not sisters": every bag has the same moisture content, even if the total weight varies slightly. Block-to-block yield consistency comes from exact moisture.

  • After about a year of combo-pellet trials, blocks within about 2.5-3 lb (1.1-1.4 kg) of each other (for example 9 lb against 11 lb) yielded almost the same, provided the moisture was right for the strain.
  • Dosing dry pellets by volume is inaccurate, because pellet size, dust content and density vary. "10 lb" bags came out at about 8.7-9.0 lb, and 4.2-5.1 lb dry fills varied too, so a fixed volume of water gave widely varying moisture.
  • Even if the bag average hits target (for example 61%), the water may not be evenly spread.
  • Water-in to inoculation takes about 30 hours on a pellet system: bags watered at 8 am, steamed and cooled, inoculated around noon the next day. That time lets the water spread through the bag.
  • Pellets should fully absorb their water before steaming. If they take it up during steaming, the bags warp and balloon at the sides. Add the water fast, or evenly from the top down.
  • Substrate bags gain essentially no water during atmospheric steaming, because the patch is folded over and steam cannot exceed atmospheric saturation (see Chapter 12). Get the water right before the bag goes in.

WARNING Too much water for the materials pools at the bottom of the bag and goes anaerobic. The mycelium walls it off and bacteria take over (their endospores survive pasteurization). You see a hard line, a sloppy wet bottom, and a smell you can detect through the patch.

Water source

  • Water used to hydrate substrate that is then pasteurized or sterilized causes few problems; city water is fine.
  • Minerals, heavy metals or chlorine in the end product more likely come from the substrate than the water.
  • Exception: deep wells in drought areas can carry bacterial blooms and heavy mineral loads, though pH, moisture and C:N matter more than water quality.
  • If you already filter, soften or carbon-scrub water for the boiler, use the same water for substrate (see Chapter 17 for water quality).
  • PFAS ("forever chemicals") are fairly easy to filter out of water but very hard to remove from substrate or soil.
  • In one experiment, dry-sterilized or ultra-pasteurized pellets hydrated with UV-treated, unheated water plus spawn colonized cleanly with several Pleurotus species. The main difference was fruit colour, probably from the untreated mineral content (unconfirmed).
  • Heavy-metal concerns mainly trace to imported Chinese or other Asian cylindrical substrate logs. Their sawdust may come from any chipped wood, including recycled furniture, and some are chemically sterilized with formaldehyde (claims unconfirmed).

Mixing and hydrating

AT A GLANCE Two ways to get water into substrate: wet bagging (mix and hydrate in a mixer, then bag) or dry bagging (dose dry pellets into the bag by weight, then add water to the exact target). Dry bagging needs no mixer and no clean-out, and scaled one farm from about 30 to about 1,680 bags a morning.

Wet bagging and dry bagging

  • Wet bagging: a fully hydrated premix comes out of a mixer and is then bagged.

  • Dry bagging: dry pellets go into the bag, then water is added in the bag. The Fenrir filler, Eric Meyer and Mossy Creek all work this way.

  • Hydrating pellets with water in the bag, with no mixer, is what makes the Fenrir filler possible. Bagging uses load cells (electronic scales): pellets drop to a set weight, then water sprays in to the exact moisture target. The hardware is in Chapter 11.

  • An in-house filler of this kind can be set to any target moisture (about 20-100%) and accounts for the pellets' own moisture.

  • A Tallahassee farm learned dry bagging and Master's Mix in an early consultation, which also got it into a growers' network (CMGN); that "really opened up" the business.

Mixer practice (wet bagging)

  • Mix the dry ingredients first. When combining pellets with raw dry sawdust, hydrate the pellets first and then add the sawdust, so mixing takes a long time.

  • With soy pellets, dissolve or break them down before adding the sawdust (see the procedure below). Oak in combo pellets helps them break apart.

  • With pellets and measured water, dissolve additives (calcium, molasses, etc.) into the water source, for example dosing from an IBC tote the way a hydroponic system does.

  • The mixer or hopper chute must be smaller than the bagger's inlet, so all the substrate falls through and none spills past the frame or platen; a metal or plastic collar mounts to the top rim (see Chapter 11).

  • A typical wet-bagging line: a drum of material is tipped into a red ribbon mixer; inside, the ribbon agitator turns the pellets under a stream of water; a clear bag fills under the mixer's discharge chute.

  • Mixers have risen in price from about $8,000 (Cap n Stem's 2-yard mixer) to about $30,000. If money is short, spend it on a boiler instead; pellet systems can use cheap wooden hoppers.

  • Small-scale mixing. One grower scaled from mixing by hand in a bowl to one, then two, then three 3 cubic foot (85 L) cement mixers from a hardware store. Keep your hands out of a turning mixer: they are dangerous.

CASE A farm near St Louis mixed its substrate in a mortar mixer and dumped it into 200 gallon (750 L) black tubs. One person hand-scooped 150 bags in about 15 minutes, working along 10-12 folding tables. The mix was hardwood fuel pellets, corn gluten meal, soy or cotton meal, wheat middlings and rice hulls (before soy hulls were common), and it gave great yields of beech, maitake and king oyster. Two troughs with big rubber lids were fed by one sawdust steamer through copper pipe. The farm cased its kings with hydrated lime mixed into peat or coir, unpasteurized.

Procedure: mixing raw dust with soy hull pellets

This was Cap n Stem's method before combo pellets.

  1. Put the soy hull pellets in the mixer with almost all of the batch's water.
  2. Run the mixer about 20 minutes, until the pellets have broken down evenly. Hot water helps break dense soy pellets down.
  3. Add the sawdust.
  4. Top off with the little water that remains.

WHY If you add everything at once, the soy stays dry and the sawdust ends up too wet: the bag average may hit target, but the nitrogen and water are in different places.

WARNING Mixers trap old wet material. A chunk of wet combo-pellet mix stuck in a mixer turned foul. Clean daily to keep a steady state, and give key equipment an intensive clean weekly. Cleaning out after each mix wastes a lot of water and time, especially with raw inputs.

CASE A farm that alternated between a Fenrir filler and a mixer used near-boiling water in a mixer that had a grime layer (case relayed second-hand). The pellet mix came out much darker before cooking: a nutrient-rich cake that steam pasteurization could not fully handle. Lesson: a dirty mixer seeds the substrate before it ever reaches the steamer.

Case study: scaling block making from 30 to 1,680 bags

Cap n Stem went through five stages of block making. Each stage shows what limits output: lifting, mixing, bagging, then clean-out.
