Calcium additives and pH

AT A GLANCE Target substrate pH about 6.5. Gypsum (calcium sulfate dihydrate) buffers pH; lime (calcium carbonate) raises it. Farms add 1-4% calcium carbonate. Use pure products only.

  • Target substrate pH is about 6.5.
  • Calcium carbonate (lime) adjusts pH. Calcium sulfate (gypsum) buffers it and is fairly neutral, which is why most farms add gypsum rather than carbonate: soy shifts the pH during colonization. In short: calcium carbonate (lime) = pH adjust; calcium sulfate (gypsum) = pH buffer.
  • Studies suggest calcium carbonate raises yield, especially in oysters. Farms add anywhere from 1-4%. Too much can cause excess heat during colonization, or stickiness.
  • For cubensis substrates, one published reading says gypsum stabilizes pH as metabolites acidify the substrate, advises an initial pH of about 8, and says gypsum increases yields.
  • Pleurotus nebrodensis needs a very basic substrate, pH 8-11 (add calcium) (unconfirmed).
  • For a king oyster casing layer, peat moss is mixed with high-calcium, low-magnesium hydrated lime. For lime-pasteurizing straw, use low-magnesium hydrated lime.

WARNING Source pure calcium products. Agricultural lime may carry heavy metals or arsenic. For gypsum you want calcium sulfate dihydrate; don't use crushed drywall.

RANGE Calcium carbonate in fruiting substrate: 1-4%, added with care. Grain spawn is a different medium and uses far less: in grain, Cap n Stem keeps calcium carbonate plus gypsum to about 0.15% of wet weight and advises staying under 1% (see Chapter 9). The two figures are for different media, not a disagreement. No species-specific substrate figures are available (see Open questions).

Substrate richness and incubation heat

AT A GLANCE More nitrogen means more heat. If incubation runs hot, cut supplement richness before anything else.

  • Block size (5 against 10 lb) and recipe richness set the temperature regime in incubation: more nitrogen and supplement means more heat.
  • Farms whose incubation rooms reach about 22 °C (72 °F) in summer cut back from 50:50 to less soy, or none, using wheat middlings instead. They give up some yield to keep blocks healthy.
  • Denser substrate needs stronger cooling fans and slightly lower temperatures. Looser, less rich substrate tolerates 20-21 °C (68-69 °F) ambient.
  • Lean "European mix" substrate (exact meaning unconfirmed) spikes less in heat than rich media.
  • Nitrogen hot spots respire harder, producing more CO2 and heat, which pushes more gas through the patch and heats the block. An even mix is needed for even heat.
  • Very high spawn rates act as a strong supplement and make blocks run hot, especially in an already rich mix (see Spawn rate).

CASE Reduced-soy shiitake substrates can give excellent yield and speed but make "hot" blocks. A midday August swing from 19 to 21 °C (66 to 70 °F) sent one crop haywire: part of it white and inactive, part brown, part fruiting inside the bag at week 9. Squishy blocks signal heat stress and death of cells in the core, and will not fruit.

RULE If incubation runs hot, cut supplement richness before anything else.

  • The finer and more supplemented the substrate (wheat bran, rice bran and middlings all make it denser), "the more you should lean towards sterilization over pasteurization". Dense, rich blocks are where thermophilic (heat-loving) bacteria take off at warmer incubation temperatures. For shiitake, use a coarser sawdust so the mycelium can breathe.

What heat treatment does to substrate

The full pasteurization and sterilization cycles are in Chapter 12. These points are about what heat does to the substrate itself.

  • The longer substrate is exposed to steam or heat, the worse it becomes for mycelium. Aim for thorough but minimal treatment. Overcooked ("roasted") blocks are chemically altered and colonize poorly. Plotted as substrate quality against process time, the line only goes down.
  • At 121 °C (250 °F) caramelization and other reactions begin. Overcooking in big industrial autoclaves caramelizes substrate and hurts colonization and fruiting. A right-sized boiler keeps blocks from coming out charcoal-black; growers using "Bubba barrel" steamers for 15-24 h get compost-like substrate (see Chapter 12).
  • Dry-heat treatment in containers penetrates poorly, dries the substrate and can chemically alter grain or pellets (polymerization), lowering yields. Steam is preferred.

Heat changes substrate in stages. One run-log template marks these zones (see Chapter 12 for logging a run by temperature zone):

Block temperature What happens What to do
27-46 °C (80-115 °F) Primary fermentation of the supplement Start heating right after mixing
71-82 °C (160-180 °F) Onset of hemicellulose breakdown Keep climbing
82-93 °C (180-200 °F) Fastest Maillard browning and structural damage Cross this band as quickly as possible
93-96 °C (200-205 °F) The hold Hold here
above 96 °C (205 °F) Overprocessing Avoid

Substrate faults

AT A GLANCE Most substrate faults come from mixes that are too rich, too wet, unevenly mixed, or held too long before processing. Sour-smelling blocks go in the bin. Full diagnosis is in Chapter 16 and Chapter 19.

Sign Likely cause What to do
Heavy metabolite exudate in the bag (any species except shiitake, where it is normal) Media too rich, or under-sterilized or under-pasteurized; bacteria will then likely prevent fruiting entirely Reduce supplement; check the cook
Bacteria coming from the substrate Cook too short or too cool; the mix fermenting; the mix sat too long before processing or inoculation Check cook time and temperature, and the time from mixing to steaming and to inoculation
Sour smell (dirty socks, fermenting wine) Too-wet media favour anaerobes; the block is bacterially fouled Throw the block away
Stressed-looking mycelium and odd fruit, with no visible contamination Poor mix generating sugar alcohols that mushrooms struggle to use; this cuts yield and favours contamination Improve mixing
Sectoring, odd mycelium, wet spots, stroma, heavy exudate even with good steaming Poorly mixed or wrongly hydrated mix. Metabolites can also come from temperature swings or competitors. Fix mixing and dosing first
Stroma in a block A badly mixed ball of supplement (soy, wheat bran, canola), much as pockets of uncomposted manure cause hot spots in Agaricus beds Break supplement down fully before adding wood
Yellow liquid at the bottom of lion's mane bags Rich 50:50 mix. Working hypothesis: a too-hot core lets bacterial endospores germinate, conditions go wet and anaerobic, and the mycelium pumps out metabolites in defence. Use a leaner lion's mane mix
Slow heating in the steamer Air not pressed out of bags before steaming, which many people skip Press the air out before steaming
  • Clumpy super sacks of supplement were probably wet at some point. Don't use them.
  • Some microbial load is always present in substrate. The aim is a level your steaming reliably kills.

Fermentation before the cook

Fermentation is "the silent enemy" that even experienced growers overlook. Wet, mixed substrate starts to ferment if it sits before it is cooked, and rich mixes such as Master's Mix go fastest.

  • How fast mixed blocks ferment depends on the time of year, the climate in the mixing room and even the temperature of the mixing water.
  • Let it go a little too long before the cook and you get blocks that are worthless, or that take about 3 extra weeks to colonize.
  • If you make blocks faster than you can cook them, the first blocks made sit longest. When they are stacked, the oldest bags go in last, so load in the order the bags were made.
  • A sour "stank" smell outside the bag means fermentation has started. Set those bags aside and don't waste spawn on them.

Spent substrate: re-use and disposal

AT A GLANCE Every block becomes waste after its last flush, so plan where spent substrate goes before you start. Most farms give or trade it away as soil amendment or compost; a few re-use it.

Getting rid of it.

  • A New Hampshire farm trades over 75% of its spent substrate with a compost company, which also supplies it with wood. Picking mushrooms off the compost pile or trimming every scrap from a block costs more labour than it earns.
  • Cannabis and garden growers can ask mushroom farms for spent substrate as a soil amendment; otherwise it costs the farm money to dump.
  • In Washington state, a cannabis farmer collects spent blocks straight off the racks and composts them with a neighbour's cow manure and hay, using no fertilizer.
  • Rural farms pile it on their land; city farms truck it to park composting sites. Cap n Stem gives contaminated, surplus or auto-fruited blocks to a neighbour who uses them as fill (a trailer is dropped off and collected every few weeks), and gardeners take some in spring.

Selling it. A Washington farm sells compost at US$6 per cubic foot (about 28 L) at its farmers market and gets about 10 calls a week in spring. At US$30-35 per cubic yard (0.76 m³, a top price) and about 200 blocks per yard, after un-bagging, turning and loading "you're mostly breaking even".

WARNING Mass oyster fruiting on compost piles breeds flies. Keep spent-block piles away from the farm buildings.

Re-using it.

  • About half of one California grower's production runs on re-used spent substrate. Oyster blocks are chipped and kept in short, fat piles so they dry without composting, then re-amended with a little soy hull, re-bagged and steamed. He still gets about 2.5-3 lb per 10 lb block (1.1-1.4 kg per 4.5 kg). Spent kiln-dried media mainly needs its nitrogen and trace nutrients topped up.
  • A Massachusetts grower crumbled spent blocks and layered them with lime-pasteurized fresh straw in buckets, kept at 21-27 °C (70-80 °F), as a kind of spawn. The results were odd: clusters mixing old and young mushrooms, which he puts down to too little micropore tape over the hole, so oxygen triggered fruiting while the bucket was still colonizing. He uses these only for donated mushrooms, not for sale.

WHY Spent substrate carries a "burnt out" mycelial network and can behave like a contaminant. It works for some species if you stop and restart at the right stage.

A short history of block substrates

Background on how today's recipes came about. More fungal history is in Chapter 2.

Year Milestone
1917 Richard Falck grew oyster mushrooms outdoors in wartime Germany, in trenches of (probably treated) wheat straw and on hardwood stumps.
1929 Bessie E. Etter found that wood-rot fungi fruited in the lab only when wood (sawdust or ground wood) was present, plus cornmeal or oatmeal starch.
1958 Block, Tsao and Han fruited oyster within about two weeks on sterile sawdust fortified with oatmeal, in jars. This is seen as the US proof of block cultivation. Bags came in the 1970s-80s.
1963 Zakia Bano and Srivastava industrialized oyster growing in India on paddy straw, an abundant agricultural waste.
Later Soy plus sawdust became a default after Stamets' Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms (see Soy hulls).

Key rules

  1. Start from Master's Mix (50:50 hardwood : soy hulls) for oysters, pioppino, king oyster and chestnut. Drop to 20-30% supplement (wheat bran or midds) for shiitake and maitake, and about 30-40% soy for lion's mane.
  2. Never exceed 50% soy hulls, and avoid de-oiled soybean meal.
  3. Bag most blocks at 61-63% total moisture (shiitake 64-65%, maitake 60-61%). Anything above about 68% is asking for bacteria.
  4. Count the water already in your inputs: about 7% in combo pellets, 7-15% in fuel pellets, and up to 70-80% in raw oak dust. Measure it; don't guess.
  5. Dose solids and water by weight so every bag has the same moisture; dosing pellets by volume is inaccurate.
  6. Make the mix even: break soy pellets down with most of the water first, and avoid stratification of HWFP plus soy pellets.
  7. Let pellets absorb all their water before steaming, and press air out of the bags.
  8. Use pure gypsum (calcium sulfate dihydrate) as a pH buffer around pH 6.5. Add calcium carbonate at 1-4% only with care, and never use drywall or contaminated agricultural lime.
  9. Store dust, pellets and supplements dry and indoors; discard clumpy, once-wet supplement sacks.
  10. If incubation runs hot, cut supplement richness before anything else.
  11. Trial any new ingredient or supplier against your baseline before switching, and keep several suppliers for each ingredient.
  12. Clean mixers daily and deep-clean weekly; old wet material in a mixer turns foul.

Open questions

  • Why soy nitrogen behaves "hotter" than wheat midds at a similar C:N ratio is unexplained.
  • The mechanism behind combo pellets outperforming raw dust (kiln drying, particle size, homogeneity) is a theory only, and is not independently tested.
  • The comb tooth ratio (50:50 against 60:40 soy hulls : sawdust) is ambiguous in the source.
  • Calcium carbonate dosing for substrate (1-4%) has no species-specific figures or yield data from trials.
  • The 54-57% maitake moisture figure attributed to one large maitake producer may reflect a different measuring method; this is unresolved.
  • No figures exist here for the pH of Master's Mix before and after colonization.

chapters.html:
Bags, Filters and Inoculation

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the bag the block lives in and the lab steps that turn a cooled bag into an incubating block: bag makers and materials, filter-patch grades and what they do to gas exchange, fill and headspace, block sizes, baggers and load-cell fillers, then "knock, seal, shake" (spawning, sealing and mixing), spawn rates and the block temperature at the knock. The rules people use most:

  • Bag: polypropylene with a mid-grade patch (the Unicorn "A" / XLS-A type) suits most 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks. Leave headspace.
  • Test every bag lot and every seal. In a good lab, most leftover contamination comes from gussets, seals and patches.
  • Knock temperature: about room temperature; no hotter than about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F). 38 °C (100 °F) kills spawn.
  • Spawn rate: one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag per 20 ten-pound blocks, about 3%.
  • Shake: break the spawn up and shake it through the whole bag.

A commercial block is a filter-patch plastic bag holding wetted, heat-treated substrate mixed with spawn. The bag keeps contaminants out while letting the block breathe through a small filter window (the patch). This chapter starts with the bag (what it is made of, which patch, how full, how big), then how bags are filled, then the lab sequence that inoculates them: the knock (opening the bag and adding spawn), sealing, and shaking. Heat treatment between filling and the knock is in Chapter 12; what happens after the shake is in Chapter 13.

Why plastic bags

  • A biodegradable grow bag is hard to make, because the organism inside and the contaminants outside both want to eat it. A sensitive organism in an artificial environment needs a barrier.
  • Filter-patch bags are not truly hermetic, but they create a microclimate that is far easier to keep clean than open beds.
  • Fully compostable cup-style containers exist and work, but they must stay in-house: shipping, storage and specialized equipment make them hard to justify.

WHY Think of a colonized filter bag as a synthetic log: the plastic is the bark and the block is the heartwood. Cutting the bag is like scarring a log: local gas exchange (plus light) at the cut triggers pinning (see Chapter 14).

Bag makers

Maker What to know
Unicorn (US) The one US maker, used by most US and Canadian growers. Makes its filter membranes in-house, which helps batch consistency and protected supply during COVID.
A large Japanese maker Makes circular-patch bags in PE, PP and true black; runs its machines 24 hours a day (unconfirmed). Does not make its own membranes (unconfirmed).
SacO2 (Belgium, sister company of Mycelia) Known for zipper-patch bags and "microsacs". May make its own membranes.
Chinese makers Numerous, but quality and value are less consistent than the three specialists.

  • Very few major grow-bag makers exist.

  • Bag prices cannot fall much: the industry scales with more machines and people rather than with automation.

  • Unicorn's former owner would do small custom runs. New management asked for million-unit orders for a custom bag, so small growers have lost access to custom sizes.

  • Cap n Stem used to make all its spawn in SacO2 bags and switched to Unicorn after unspecified problems. It still keeps cultures in SacO2 microsacs (see Chapter 8).

  • Until recently, automatic baggers needed Japanese or Chinese bags, which open more reliably. Unicorn now makes machine-grade bags that open easily. Tariffs are a concern for imported bags.

  • Bag prices (US, mid 2020s). Unicorn XLSA bags rose from about 25 to 45 cents a bag. A New Hampshire farm pays 22-27 cents for Tough Pack bags made 24 km (15 miles) away, with no shipping cost.

  • Imported Japanese bags (available in the US through Far West Fungi) are very consistent and cost about the same delivered as US-made bags. Some US makers sell only in small batches.

  • Keep a stock of bags. A large supplier once had no 10 lb bags for two months.

Bag materials and thickness

AT A GLANCE Polypropylene (PP) is the standard: heat-tolerant, seals well, holds its shape. Polyethylene (PE) is cheaper and tougher in the cold but cannot be autoclaved. Unicorn bags are about 2.2 mil (small) or 3 mil (XL) thick. Test every lot.

Polypropylene (PP) Polyethylene (PE, including HDPE)
Use The dominant bag plastic The other option
Heat Higher heat tolerance Cannot take high temperatures; no retort (autoclave) use
Seals Tougher ultrasonic or heat seals around patches
Shape Holds shape through compression and steam cycles; more pliable, stays tight, nearly vacuum-sealed against the block More rigid, but holds a headspace poorly
Cold Becomes brittle and rips more easily: it stretches well, but once holed it lets go Durable and tough in the cold
Other Cheaper; noisy; foggier
  • PE is promoted by some (for example someone at the Japanese maker) as the material of the future.
  • PE (NMC-type) bags are tough to cut and shred open if overcut. Folded-over PE did not stick to the substrate, so chestnut pins got trapped and deformed inside the bag. With PE, a folded top cut gapes into a wound that dries the medium, giving slow, poor pin sets.
  • Bag formulations are secret. One sample bag that was tough enough to smack against a wall was lab-tested and contained an unidentified organic component.

CASE A batch of bags carried a leached, greasy polymer residue: a rainbow sheen, slippery to the touch, and the lab could not seal them. Every affected bag produced stroma, across many species. The supplier was Unicorn, during an ownership and pricing change. Lesson: inspect and test each new bag lot before it reaches production.

Thickness

  • Unicorn standard thicknesses are about 2.2 mil (56 µm) for smaller bags (14A, 3T and so on) and 3 mil (76 µm) for XL bags. Cap n Stem orders a custom 3T in 3 mil.
  • Thicker plastic matters if your sterilization cycle uses aggressive pressure changes, and for shipped spawn that gets thrown around. Sporadic rips during shaking add up to a real loss.
  • Unicorn has changed its plastic a lot, making substrate bags harder to seal. Bags have arrived too thin, too thick or the wrong size.

RULE Test every bag lot: thickness, size and sealing (see Bag failures and checks).

  • Bags and pre-vacuum autoclaves. Cap n Stem does not use Unicorn bags for spawn, because its pre-vacuum autoclave pulls the air out so fast that those bags deform or burst ("just blows up"). SaCO2-type bags are made differently and survive the cycle. The fast cycle is worth having because it limits caramelization of the grain. Unicorn bags are tough in an ordinary sterilizer: one user ran them at about 149 °C (300 °F) and 20 psi for half a day with no bursts.
  • Reliance on plastic is hard to escape in this industry.

Filter patches

AT A GLANCE The patch is the bag's lung. A tighter patch keeps CO2 higher (most species colonize faster and safer) and loses less water; a more open patch dries blocks and has raised contamination. Default: the Unicorn A patch (XLS-A bag) for substrate, T for spawn.

How patches are rated

  • There are two filter philosophies. Patch bags have a membrane with a rated pore size (micron-rated). Pillow or zipper bags have woven or non-woven random-mesh membranes that behave like a HEPA filter: no single pore size, but a measurable overall efficiency. SacO2 zipper bags use a non-woven "three matrix" membrane.
  • Pore size tells you what particle size can pass, not how much gas moves. The membrane industry measures air permeability in Gurley seconds: the time for a set volume of air to pass through a membrane under standard pressure. A higher Gurley number means a slower, less permeable membrane.
  • Tyvek passes much more air than an A patch despite its smaller pores, according to the membrane data (but see the uncertainty below).
  • PTFE (Teflon) is the base material of many filter membranes.
  • The Gurley and material data come from a patent by a long-time R&D person at a spawn company (probably Amycel). It covers polymer performance, deformation under pressure and heat, recommended pore sizes and three-layer patch adhesion. According to it, Tyvek should not go above about 120 °C (248 °F), yet sterilization normally runs at 121 °C (250 °F) or more.
  • The Unicorn system: choose the bag dimensions, the plastic thickness, and one of three standard patches (A, B, T), plus the patch size, which governs air movement.

Unicorn patch grades

Patch Pore size as stated Gas exchange Typical use
A (recommended default for substrate) about 0.5 micron (2.5x the T pore size) Middle of the road; restrictive to contaminants; far less drying than Tyvek Traditionally substrate. XLS-A is Cap n Stem's main production bag; right for maitake; Unicorn's old website said it was designed for shiitake.
B Much larger, "an order of magnitude": about 5 micron The most open Cubensis in practice; in-bag lion's mane fruiting; Unicorn's old website recommended it for oysters
T (Tyvek) about 0.2 micron Uncertain: see below The standard choice for spawn
  • The XL versions are sold as XLS-B, XLS-A and XLS-T.
  • Unicorn grades get more porous going up the letter stack: an A filter is tighter than a B.
  • Older B patches peeled off easily and fell off if they touched in the autoclave; the product has since changed.
  • The A/B/T variants matter less than people think, and an A bag holding 10 lb of substrate has enough headspace for species fruited inside the bag.

What is uncertain about patches

RANGE Standard: the A patch for substrate blocks and the T patch for spawn. Judge any patch by how evenly and cleanly your blocks colonize. Accounts differ on a few patch details, so check them against the manufacturer's specification:

  • Letter order. One account says T is the most restrictive and B the most permissive; all accounts agree that A sits in the middle.
  • Is Tyvek open or tight? One account says the T (Tyvek) patch has the finest filtration but much higher air flow than A, so grain and substrate dry out, especially in a bag with an inflated headspace. Other accounts describe Tyvek-patch bags (3T-type, and John Donahue's Northwest Mycological bags) as trapping CO2 and puffing up: fine for 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks but too restrictive for bigger bags, where the core would go anaerobic. Maitake guidance calls T "too little" gas exchange, and an early reishi culture stuck as antlers in bags with "very impervious" Tyvek-type clip patches.
  • Gurley values. One explanation says more Gurley means more filtration and that T has a higher Gurley value while also passing more air. In standard usage a higher Gurley-seconds number means less air permeability, so both cannot be true.
  • Spawn versus substrate patches. One account says substrate-bag patches are typically more restrictive than grain-bag patches, so substrate bags can build higher CO2 (not measured). Another says spawn bags generally use the more restrictive filter, building more CO2 and heat.
  • Is pore size enough? A "0.5 micron" rating alone is not enough to judge whether a filter keeps a bag sterile, even though 0.5 micron is smaller than almost all airborne cells and spores.

Choosing a patch

Two criteria matter: contamination performance in your own environment, and enough gas exchange to avoid hypoxia or a CO2 build-up that stunts mycelium.

  • Most species colonize faster and more safely at higher CO2, with a more restrictive patch.
  • High-exchange B bags may suit fast species fruited in the bag, such as cubensis or cordyceps. Slow ones like reishi would likely give stunted antlers from surface drying.
  • When Cap n Stem tried B-patch bags for a while, its contamination rate rose sharply, mostly Trichoderma.
  • B-patch bags gave far too much air exchange for chestnut and dried a crusty layer on block tops.
Use Patch Why
Most 10 lb substrate blocks A (XLS-A or equivalent) Shiitake discussion assumes XLS-A bags holding 10 lb blocks, the standard on most farms
Maitake A (Unicorn XLS-A or equivalent) B is too much exchange and T too little for healthy in-bag development
Pioppino A (XLS-A type) Does well
In-bag fruiting in general A The tighter patch lets the mushroom develop without turning goopy or pulling in bacteria
Lion's mane (high-yield strains) fruited in the bag B More air exchange, more fruit
Spawn T The standard; A-patch spawn bags are being tested to reduce drying, but whether A filters as well as T is unproven
Cubensis grain bags (1-2 lb, 0.45-0.9 kg, heavily inoculated) more open Fast respiration makes these bags CO2-rich and near-anaerobic, so they need more gas exchange than a 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg) gourmet block

  • A-patch spawn bags were sent cross-country to customers as a shipping test; results were not reported.

  • Spawn shipped by air goes through pressure swings. Non-woven matrix filters develop weak spots under this, while micron patch filters hold up better.

  • Bag problems can stay hidden in a very clean facility (Mycelia does fine with SacO2 bags in-house) and show up only under less ideal conditions such as shipping.

  • John Donahue's Tyvek-patch bags (now discontinued) held more CO2, lowering the air exchange needed in incubation; shiitake tolerates up to about 20,000 ppm CO2 in the bag. Open A patches give faster colonization and heavier fruit, but higher utility costs.

  • Any decent spawn bag works for maitake spawn, even Donahue's ballooning Tyvek bag.

  • Over a shiitake block's long incubation it loses water vapour through the patch; choose the filter rate with that in mind (see shiitake moisture).

  • Some patches are a random three-dimensional fibre mat rather than a Tyvek-type sheet with a known pore size, so "the air can go both ways". That lets contamination in when air exchange is high, and Cap n Stem doubts they suit spawn.

CASE A batch of "super greasy", slippery bags from one supplier gave stroma on chestnut, pioppino and lion's mane, which Cap n Stem had never seen on those species. It blames the bags.

Patches, heat, CO2 and contamination

  • The patch affects gas exchange and heat: 0.5 micron and 5 micron patches give very different exchange, and CO2 output also depends on room temperature. 10 lb blocks in XLS-A 0.5 micron bags breathe out a lot of CO2 (see Chapter 13).
  • Patches are not hermetic. Nothing is perfectly hydrophobic, and a wetted patch (in humid cooling rooms, or over hot about 60-62%-moisture substrate) becomes a direct conduit for mould drawn across by fans.
  • Uncolonized grain kernels, especially dried-out ones, grow Trichoderma, because patches are not impermeable.
  • Fold the top of grain bags over the filter patch to restrict gas exchange. This keeps more of the growth vegetative and prevents dry tops.
  • Early grow kits (small blocks of about 2-3 lb, 0.9-1.4 kg) got pin mould from an overly porous patch that let air out, combined with undercooked substrate. Pin moulds like oxygen (see Chapter 16).
  • An old training rule: never let filter patches touch each other in the autoclave.

RANGE Patch area, recommended: if the mycelium looks evenly healthy from top to bottom, the patch is big enough. Makers of large-patch and pillow bags (SacO2 brochures) say one small patch is not enough and that more patch area gives an even gas composition through the block.

  • The filter patch is the block's "window to reality". Gases move across it because of the difference in partial pressure on each side. Brands differ in how they behave once soaked with water or clogged with spores. Hard water sprayed for humidity in an incubation room can crust a patch with minerals until gas no longer moves through it.

Fill, headspace and bag shape

AT A GLANCE Fill substrate bags about one third to one half full and leave the rest as headspace. Fill spawn bags fuller, with little headspace.

  • A fill rule from one long-time grower: a block bag should be about one-third substrate and two-thirds headspace, which lets metabolic CO2 diffuse out through the patch.
  • XLS-A bags at about 9.8 lb (4.4 kg) fill are a little short of two-thirds headspace. One third to 50% fill is more realistic.
  • Some spawn makers (probably including Amycel and SacO2) fill bags fully with no headspace, which seems to suit spawn.
  • The trade-off: a headspace raises CO2 during incubation (good for substrate) but allows more water loss; no headspace gives more even O2 exchange and less drying (better for spawn).
  • The XL A-patch bag is about twice the size of the 5 lb A-patch bag, but people load anything from 5-6 lb to 12 lb (2.3-2.7 kg to 5.4 kg) into it.
  • Side gussets (folded side panels) give squarer blocks but more heat-sealed area, and the points where four plastic layers meet are weak. Many people open the gussets out and seal wide.
  • Folding a gusseted bag before autoclaving can produce a vacuum-tight seal as it cools. Some growers want this; Cap n Stem does not.
  • Getting bags to open fully is a major labour and automation problem; larger sizes open better.
  • Bags come clear or black, with square patches, circular membranes or zipper-style filters; a black bag under purple light shows a square patch with a circular membrane, labelled with its strain and date code (for example "POCNS-17 053124").

Black bags

  • Black bags block light, so the mycelium keeps maturing without pinning. That widens the holding window and lets pins form only at the cut. A 10 lb clear oyster bag colonized in 10-14 days pins immediately unless refrigerated; black bags extend that window.
  • Black bags have noticeably raised yields for several species. One estimated gain is about 0.15 lb (70 g) per block (a rough figure, unconfirmed), possibly more for dense species like lion's mane or maitake.
  • Clear bags are still useful for seeing contamination or stroma.
  • For chestnut, black bags help by limiting premature pinning, but they probably do not raise yield much.
  • Only the Japanese maker produces a truly opaque black bag. Unicorn's black version is poor and PE-only, which limits sterilization options.
  • Side-cutting maitake from black bags (a method credited to several growers, one of them in Texas) works if timed right: fully colonized, perhaps with early metabolite droplets, but before distinct lobes form on top. Maitake fruited from one grower's black bags looked far better than maitake from a clear bag at the Santa Cruz festival.
  • Switching to black bags for black oyster is one possible reason a strain's behaviour changed; consider bag colour when a strain suddenly behaves differently.

TIP Keep clear indicator bags, about 1 in 20 (19 black + 1 clear per 20 knocked), to judge colonization progress.

  • Black bags cost more and give about the same yield as clear bags: "if you can't grow it on a clear bag, don't put it in a black bag".

Block sizes

AT A GLANCE 10 lb (4.5 kg) is the norm and the practical maximum in PP bags with a small filter. 5 lb (2.3 kg) runs cooler and is far more forgiving if you cannot hold a steady incubation temperature. 12 lb (5.4 kg) blocks can't breathe and overheat.

Size What to expect
10 lb (4.5 kg) (the norm) The norm on most farms. Incubate ultra-pasteurized blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) ambient. Yields 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) depending on species. The practical maximum in PP bags with a small filter. "More than twice as hard" to manage as 5 lb.
5 lb (2.3 kg) Produces much less heat: at 20 °C (68 °F) ambient the core may be about 22 °C (71-72 °F), so it tolerates about 20-21 °C (the upper 60s to 70 °F), and grows much slower at 16 °C (60 °F). Far more forgiving if you cannot hold a steady incubation temperature. Tumbling mixes them better. Sterilized 5 lb blocks incubate at about 22 °C (72 °F).
1-2 lb (0.45-0.9 kg) cubensis grain bags Heavily inoculated; need more gas exchange
about 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) Early grow kits in cardboard crates
6-7 lb (2.7-3.2 kg) For chestnut, no more yield than 5 lb
11 lb (5.0 kg) One grower (Avery, see Chapter 26) runs 11 lb blocks and stresses that they must be kept cold, with incubation around 17 °C (62 °F).
12 lb (5.4 kg) Can't breathe, goes anaerobic and overheats (a core of about 32 °C, 90 °F, was mentioned). No extra efficiency for chestnut. Some builders still make them without higher yields; others ran 12 lb blocks earlier and still do.
  • Block size works in thresholds: for chestnut, 5 and 10 lb are the useful steps. Surface area and air exposure matter as well as weight.
  • Shape matters. Log or cylinder shapes shed heat better than a fat block with little surface area. Five 10 lb blocks deep on a shelf get very hot in the middle; 4-5 lb (1.8-2.3 kg) blocks stratify far less (see Chapter 13).
  • Switching from 5 lb to 10 lb blocks (on raw sawdust with soy hull, wheat midds and pea hulls) made each block cheaper per pound of mushroom: customers got over double the mushrooms per block, and a pallet holds 160-180 x 10 lb blocks instead of 320 x 5 lb blocks, so there is less handling.
  • Customers rarely complain about slight block weight variation, and blocks lose weight in incubation anyway. Block weights within about 5-6 lb or 10-12 lb barely affect yield (about 2-2.5 lb, 0.9-1.1 kg).
  • Stratified colonization (strong at the top, weak or anaerobic toward the bottom) is typical of 10-12 lb blocks not held long enough at the cook plateau. Raising cook temperatures fixed one farm's case (see Chapter 12).

CASE Moving shiitake strain 3782 from 5 lb to 10 lb ultra-pasteurized blocks with the same recipe produced tiny "paper pin" mushrooms and only moderate yield, which pushed farms toward strain 3790. One large producer is credited as the main pusher of 10 lb blocks. Lesson: a bigger block is a different growing environment, not just more of the same.

  • 10 lb blocks have become the norm for maitake mostly by habit (one grower uses 5 lb). Whether core heating in 10 lb blocks matters for maitake is unknown.
  • Raw-dust chestnut stayed on 5 lb blocks long after other species moved to 10 lb, because the larger block gave no more yield until combo pellets arrived (see Combo pellets).

RANGE Dry matter in a 10 lb block at about 60% moisture: 4 lb (1.8 kg). That follows from the arithmetic: 40% of 10 lb is 4 lb. A figure of about 3.3 lb (1.5 kg) has also been given; it would correspond to roughly 67% moisture. Use the arithmetic from Chapter 10 for your own target.

RULE Keep blocks at 10 lb or less in PP bags. Choose 5 lb if you cannot hold incubation temperature steady.

Choosing a block size for your farm

Pick one block size and stick to it; two bagging lines cost too much. Each size gives a different mushroom, so the right choice depends on your customers, your climate and your staff.

Choose 10 lb (4.5 kg) if Choose 5 lb (2.3 kg) if
You want the highest yield per block (Cap n Stem's preference) Staff carry blocks all day: 10 lb blocks have caused carpal tunnel and tendonitis
Customers want big, market-size oyster clusters, or food carts want the biggest caps You cannot give 10 lb blocks enough cooling and airflow
Summer fruiting is hot: 10 lb blocks hold up far better in a hot fruit room You ship blocks or need easy handling
You grow oyster or lion's mane ("fine for lion's mane and oyster") You grow shiitake (see the warning below)
  • The trade-off is a "teeter-totter": 10 lb blocks fruit better in heat but run hotter in incubation.
  • A Washington farm chose 5 lb for everything. Side-by-side tests gave "pretty decent yields" from a block that mimics a log's diameter with less core depth, and smaller blocks tolerate a wider range of incubation temperatures (it sterilizes its blocks). Its mushrooms fit the standard US 5 lb kraft mushroom flat, whereas large blocks give big mushrooms that may not fit a paper bag and whose cap edges break in the truck.
  • 10 lb blocks can give clusters too big to sell: "a four pound cluster of oysters, who is gonna buy this?" One large farm sells lion's mane in portions, because nobody pays US$30 for a 2 lb (0.9 kg) head. Smaller 5-7 lb blocks give a different, smaller mushroom.

WARNING Don't make 10 lb shiitake blocks. Shiitake fruits from the surface "like a Chia pet", so a 10 lb block has too little surface for its mass and throws "blob tops" and poor quality. A large California shiitake farm picks whole blocks without scissors; each picker can do about 1,400 lb (635 kg) of shiitake a day, against a weekly pick of about 15,000 lb (6,800 kg).

Filling bags: baggers and fillers

AT A GLANCE Wet bagging uses a mixer plus a volumetric bagger (fast per bag, but it stops for every mixer batch). Dry bagging uses load-cell fillers that weigh dry pellets into the bag and add the exact water: no mixer, no clean-out, and every bag the same moisture.

How the water and substrate get into the bag is covered in Chapter 10. This section covers the machines.

RULE Dose pellets and water by weight, not volume, so every bag gets the same moisture.

Volumetric pneumatic baggers (wet bagging)

The concept is the simplest way to move a fixed volume of material, with few moving parts. A shuttle driven by an air piston slides a tube back and forth across a polypropylene sheet: it fills the tube under the hopper, then carries it over a drop chute into the bag, giving consistent volumetric fills (John Donahue-style).

  • An earlier double-piston version with small, fast "pea-shooter" pistons at too high an air pressure was overcomplicated and disliked by staff.
  • A pneumatic bagger can fill a bag every 4-6 s but must stop for every mixer batch (100-200 bags), so the effective rate is lower.
  • A substrate mixer (about $13,000+) plus a pneumatic bagger (about $2,000) is the conventional wet-bagging route.
  • Grain is also bagged volumetrically (see Chapter 9).

Building one: Cap n Stem's DIY bagger.

  • Frame: 1.5 in (38 mm) stainless angle-iron tabs with 9/16 in (14 mm) holes, 1/2-13 threaded rod and nuts, about 1.5 in OD washers, and galvanized Unistrut (1-5/8 in, 41 mm) rails. Each leg joint is a "sandwich" of lock nut, washer, tab, washer, nut, so the frame can be raised, lowered or shortened.
  • Welding galvanized parts: grind the zinc coating off first (60-80 grit flap disc), because zinc fume is harmful. The frame was TIG-welded with 1/16 in (1.6 mm) mild-steel filler, with eye protection (see Chapter 18).
  • Holes: cut with an annular cutter on a mill, using cutting oil so the cutter keeps its temper. Clean the oil off with acetone or lacquer thinner.
  • Piston mount: a bottom cross-piece with a locating hole stops the lower platen sliding when the piston fires. Tack the piston, then fully weld it. The pistons came from Grainger (name as heard) or Fright Props.
  • Boards: 3/4 in (19 mm) HDPE; chutes 1/4 in (6 mm). Plywood or MDF could substitute, but MDF swells when wet unless sealed. A warped HDPE board can be softened in water at about 93 °C (200 °F) for a few minutes and over-corrected slightly, because HDPE has shape memory.
  • Chute fit: the mixer chute must be smaller than the bagger inlet so nothing spills past the platen.
  • The finished unit has a hopper on top, a horizontal piston driving the shuttle board above a still board, and a drop chute below; an isometric drawing of the frame shows the adjustable legs.

Load-cell fillers (dry bagging): Odin, Fenrir, Okta

A load cell is the weighing sensor in an electronic scale. Load-cell fillers weigh the dry material into each bag and then add the exact water to hit the moisture target.

  • Names: a small builder made the "Thor" bagger; a Canadian container grower built the "Odin"; Cap n Stem named its simplified version "Fenrir".
  • Odin: two hoppers with separate augers for 50% red oak sawdust and 50% soy hull, plus a scale, then water: three measurements per bag. It was slow, expensive to fabricate, sensitive to mismatched motor speeds and to non-pellet materials compacting, and its drops were too large for bags. Cap n Stem ran it for nearly a year.
  • Fenrir: pre-blended combo pellets allowed a single feed stream. A Fenrir kit is a controller, a load-cell scale and bag holder, and an auger trough with a water head; the customer builds the hopper (Cap n Stem's is wooden, about 8 ft high x 12 in wide, 2.4 m x 30 cm).
  • Mechanics: a motor turns an auger in a trough running from the hopper to a 3D-printed chute head over the bag. Water comes via PEX pipe to an on/off solenoid valve and out of a perforated nozzle in the head. The bag holder is shaped so the opened bag tucks around it. The STL (3D-print) files and Arduino code are open-source.
  • Electronics: 12 V DC supply, a stepper driver (speed set by DIP switches and voltage), separate water and load-cell boards, and a front "wheel" display controller from Seeed. Modes cover accuracy, dry-weight-only (pellet-only bags for dry sterilization or next-morning watering) and water-only.
  • Throughput: About 15 s per 10 lb bag (Odin about 20-24 s), so about 200-240 bags per hour per unit, with no stops for mixing or clean-up. The "Okta" has 8 heads (4 per side).
  • With four load-cell stations side by side (a row of funnel hoppers on a wooden frame, each with its own controller and a bag hanging beneath), one operator bags about as fast as a Japanese commercial bagger.
  • The working unit: a plywood controller box with a small screen, an aluminium bag-holder platform with fin guides, a black 3D-printed chute head, and a steel auger trough with blue PEX and a brass solenoid; the older black twin-hopper Odin and the tall plywood Okta hopper stand behind.
  • Prices: Fenrir about $1,340 shipped for one unit, topping out at about $2,000. Competing small-builder baggers are volumetric.

Procedure: one Fenrir fill cycle

  1. Hang the opened bag on the holder, tucked around it and centred.
  2. The auger runs and pellets fall into the bag until the target dry weight is reached; then the auger stops.
  3. The controller waits about 1.2 s for pellets still in the air to land.
  4. It computes the water: target total weight minus pellet weight, adjusted for the pellets' residual moisture.
  5. It opens the solenoid, then pulses the water to finish exactly on target.
  6. Remove the bag for folding. A learning algorithm compensates for in-air pellets over time.

CHECK The load cell is a 5 kg cell costing about $50, so bags over about 11 lb (5 kg) won't register. Never jam objects into the cell's gap. Mount cells to minimize tipping and centre the bag holder. Keep the auger outlet low and the water flow moderate so impact doesn't throw off the readings.

TIP When choosing between a Fenrir and a Thor bagger: the Fenrir only supports combo pellets, while the Thor depends on reliable water pressure, so check your water supply first. Ryan (see Chapter 26) feeds a Thor from auxiliary water tanks through a 7.5 gpm (about 28 L/min) pump so that bag filling never runs short of water. The suggested pump is a 7 gpm (26 L/min), 120 V, 5-chamber self-priming diaphragm pump.

Japanese automatic baggers and the Fenrir adapter

  • The base machine is a Japanese automatic bagger, imported via Far West Fungi and claimed to be the first and only 10 lb substrate bagger. It runs at 900 bags an hour: it picks up a bag, opens it, fills it (originally with compression, which was removed) and ejects it for folding and racking.
  • Running it stock with pre-hydrated mix needs two or three 2-4 cubic yard (1.5-3.1 m³) mixers with lifts feeding its rotating "cake pan" hopper: about $100k of mixers on top of a $40-80k bagger plus conveyors, about $200k in all. Farms balked.
  • The Fenrir head adapter (nicknamed the "Pelomatic") doses pellets by weight and water per bag, and needs only a conveyor to a small top hopper. It is claimed suitable for 400-900 bags an hour.
  • In the adapter, water comes from two solenoid-driven PVC tubes with flap valves that fill about 6.5 lb (2.9 kg) in 2-3 s; pellets drop from four augers into buckets on load cells, which rotate to keep pace. A clear bag held open in the carousel receives a few inches of dry pellets; on top of the bagger sit a black hopper, red pneumatic lines, a blue water line and a white feed hose.
  • The adapter removes the pneumatic shuttle that carried hydrated substrate (the main sensor trouble spot) and runs separately from the Japanese controller. The hopper level can be controlled with the bagger's existing laser sensor. It needs only a super sack over a boot plus an auger or flap conveyor. At the time of the source it needed 2-3 more weeks of programming.
  • Claimed labour gain: bagging reduced to about one person folding and swapping super sacks. Payback comes through speed and redeployed staff, amortized over 2-10 years. Tariffs are expected to raise Japanese bagger prices.
  • Japanese baggers are redundant, simple, sensor-based and pneumatic. They need compressed air, occasional lubrication of the slides and a 240 V three-phase supply, and rarely break.

WHY Manual bagging (standing under a bagger all day, packing, folding, racking) is heavy repetitive strain. Automation reduces injuries as well as labour (see Chapter 18).

The knock: setting up the lab

AT A GLANCE "Knock, seal, shake" is the mandatory lab sequence once heat-treated substrate has cooled. Keep HEPA air over the bags without a break from opening to sealing, work one row deep and within one bag length of the filter, and shake away from the clean air.

"Knock, seal, shake" is the mandatory lab sequence once bulk pasteurized or sterilized substrate has cooled: spawn the bag (the knock), seal it, mix the spawn through it, then send it to incubation.

The lab itself (clean-room design, flow hoods and FFUs, gowning) is covered in Chapter 4. These are the points specific to the knock.

  • Keep HEPA coverage continuous from opening to sealing, with no gap between the spawning and sealing stations. A gap works for a while, then bites you.
  • Air speed drops with distance from the filter: from about 120 near the filter to about 60 at 36 in (91 cm) (units not stated; feet per minute is the usual unit, unconfirmed). Keep the blocks, the spawn bag, the alcohol bottle and your hands close to the filter.
  • Don't work deeper than one bag length from the filter. With 12 in (30 cm) bags on a 36 in (91 cm) table, about 18 in (46 cm) is left.
  • Leave a margin between the spawn bag and the edge of the filtered zone (people quote 4, 6 or 12 in, 10, 15 or 30 cm); the edges are the most vulnerable.
  • Size the knock table only one row deep, so workers physically cannot stack blocks. One grower who opened about 400 bags at once on a deep table showed what not to do.
  • Order work from cleanest to dirtiest (for example knock first, mix substrate second); product flows from the cleanest rooms outward (see Chapter 3).
  • Cap n Stem spawns in an FFU-pressurized clean room in front of another bank of FFUs, giving double HEPA filtration.
  • Protect the filter face: a stainless angle iron along the table at the base of each filter keeps bags off it, and stray grain bounces off it.
  • Shake bags of sterile media or spawn away from the laminar flow, so you don't pump dirty air into the work zone. Single operators who fold, pinch and shake at the hood get away with it at small scale.
  • Inoculated bags placed straight onto the rack they will grow on speed up knock days.
  • A typical knock station: two workers at a stainless table in front of a wall of flow-hood filters, with racks of clear bags beside them; masked, gloved workers load the spawned bags onto a wire rack.

Cooling bags before the knock

  • Cooling bags in front of laminar flow dries them out. A separate HEPA cool-down room (fed by a pass-through autoclave, with racks, and bags folded over) is better, because no hands open bags there.
  • Don't cool pasteurized blocks inside the pasteurization vessel. Pull them out hot (with welding gloves) into the HEPA lab. Blocks become prone to contamination as they cool toward about 38 °C (100 °F), and hot blocks are less likely to pick up contaminants in transit than cool ones (see Chapter 16).
  • In summer, warm pasteurized blocks make the inoculation room hot. Provide cooling, but not with a unit inside the lab. Keep the lab at about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F), because staff in Tyvek suits overheat when knocking.

Block temperature at the knock

AT A GLANCE Knock at about room temperature. Working target 27-32 °C (80-90 °F). Over 32 °C (90 °F) is bad; 38 °C (100 °F) or more kills spawn. Knock promptly: pasteurized blocks ferment if left for days.

Guidance Value
Ideal About room temperature, provided the room isn't hot
Working target Bring blocks from about 96 °C (205 °F) to about 32 °C (90 °F), checked with an IR thermometer while squeezing the bag. By the time about 20 are open with cool spawn added, they are about 27 °C (80 °F). Aim for 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); over 32 °C (90 °F) is "no bueno".
Upper "empirical" number About 30 °C (86 °F); others quote figures of about 32-37 °C (the 90s °F)
Ultra-pasteurized blocks Cool below 38 °C (100 °F), preferably to room temperature, and inoculate swiftly. Sterilized blocks can wait longer. Treat "quasi-pressure" blocks like pasteurized ones.
Lethal Knocking at 38 °C (100 °F) or more kills spawn: no growth, a couple of nodules, or a weak surviving portion, often mistaken for contamination
  • A typical schedule: bags are pulled hot (about 9 pm), cool overnight in front of flow hoods in the lab, and are inoculated the next day. In one logged run, racks pulled at about 9:30 pm were cooled with about 18 °C (65 °F) air to 37 °C (99 °F) by 8 am and knocked at about 9:30 am.
  • On a pellet system, water-in to inoculation is about 30 hours (see Chapter 10).

WARNING Pasteurized blocks "expire". Surviving bacterial endospores germinate and the blocks ferment (sour smell) if left for days before inoculation. Symptoms of fermented blocks, or blocks inoculated too hot: the spawn dies, the bottom to middle of the bag goes bacterial, perhaps a little mould appears on top, and the target mycelium forms dense, walled-off, struggling colonies instead of fast, feathery growth.

  • How long cool-down takes. Cap n Stem pulls racks out of the steamer in the afternoon or evening and knocks the next morning or afternoon. In air at about 19 °C (66 °F), blocks fall below 38 °C (100 °F) in only about 10-12 hours, which is a fine temperature to inoculate.

WARNING Don't pull very wet, hot blocks straight into very cold air (walk-in cooler temperatures). So much condensation forms, wicking out of the top of the block, that the bags won't seal.

Spawn rate

AT A GLANCE One 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 spawn bag per 20 ten-pound blocks: about 0.3 lb (140 g) per block, about 3%. Stay within 12-30 blocks per spawn bag. Spawn more heavily for ultra-pasteurized substrate and slow or disturbance-sensitive species.

Spawn rate is the share of the fruiting substrate's mass made up by spawn. Grain nutrition matters somewhat, but the main benefit is many inoculation points: the fungus spends less energy exploring and more digesting, giving faster colonization and bigger yields. A recommended range of about 2-5% is a rough guide (unconfirmed).

Rate Meaning
1 x 6 lb G2 : 20 x 10 lb blocks (recommended) About 0.3 lb (140 g) of spawn per block, about 3% of wet weight. The house standard, used across oyster, black oyster, comb tooth, lion's mane, chestnut, shiitake, pioppino and maitake.
1:20 for 10 lb blocks; 1:40 for 5 lb blocks Both about 3%
About 2.5% For substrate blocks; conditions differ from grain
8 to 30 blocks per spawn bag The heavy end is used by some farms. Don't go beyond 30 for 10 lb blocks (vigour drops and incubation gets too long). Heavy spawning = hot and fast; light = "low and slow".
12-30 blocks per bag (lion's mane) Below 12 overloads an already rich substrate with grain supplement; above 30 raises mould risk
About 40 blocks per spawn bag "A teaspoon"; some farms stretch this far
One box of spawn = about 120 blocks At the 1:20 rate (equal to six 6 lb bags)
15 x 11 lb blocks per 6 lb bag of white millet spawn About 3.6% of block weight: a little heavier than 1:20. One grower's practice (Avery, see Chapter 26).
  • Sterilized substrate tolerates low spawn rates. Ultra-pasteurized substrate needs more, because time is not on your side.
  • Industry-standard spawn rates exist for real practical and scientific reasons, especially for less voracious species like king oyster. Low rates lengthen colonization and cut yields dramatically, and poor distribution (not shaking well) can stretch king oyster colonization to 3 weeks.
  • Very high spawn rates act as a stronger supplement than anything else and make blocks run hot, especially in a rich mix (see Chapter 10). Over-spawning lion's mane produces more heat and bacteria: dark, wet circular spots around each inoculation point.
  • Maitake hates disturbance, so raising the spawn rate at any step speeds its jump-off if contamination or schedule is a concern.
  • Millet's many inoculation points let you use less spawn, or colonize a couple of days faster at the same rate (see Chapter 9).
  • Expansion rates depend on a fixed amount of spawn per bag. Under-spawning or loose hand-spawning gives variable colonization.

WHY One bad G2 spawn bag ruins 20 blocks, or 60-80 lb (27-36 kg) of mushrooms. That is part of why spawn is treated as precious.

RULE Use one 6 lb spawn bag per 20 ten-pound blocks (about 3%). Stay within 12-30 blocks per bag. Spawn more heavily for ultra-pasteurized substrate and for slow or disturbance-sensitive species.

  • Spawn bags per block as insurance. Some farms knock only 10-20 blocks from each 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag. The aim is not speed: it means one bad spawn bag can't ruin many blocks. Stretching one spawn bag over 80 blocks spreads the cost but needs good quality controls.

Spawning methods

Procedure: hand-spawning a run of blocks

  1. Break up the 6 lb G2 grain spawn bag inside the bag so the kernels run free. Breaking spawn is fine.
  2. Soak the end of the spawn bag in isopropyl alcohol.
  3. Snip a small corner off.
  4. With 20 cooled blocks open in one row at the HEPA wall, pour a little grain straight from the spawn bag into each bag in sequence, until the one bag is spread across all 20. Some variation between bags is accepted (automatic spawners vary too).
  5. Seal each bag (see Sealing), then shake it (see Shaking), on a shake table.

CHECK Every bag in the run gets spawn, and the spawn bag is empty at the 20th block.

WARNING Never break up a block meant for fruiting: that damages the forming primordial mats. Only spawn is broken up.

  • Scooping spawn (for example a quarter cup per bag) is too prone to contamination at scale. Pouring straight from the broken-up spawn bag means fewer transfers.
  • Hand spawning is fastest at small and medium scale. Far West Fungi has 3 people in a corner (open bag, spawn, slide on), and its staff agree robots aren't better yet.
  • Cap n Stem tried John Donahue's volumetric pneumatic canister spawner fed from stainless hoppers. Each hopper needed sterilizing (peracetic acid and drying, and still only near-sterile), one bad spawn bag risked cross-contaminating many blocks, and it slowed the line. They sold it and went back to hand spawning.
  • A Japanese automatic spawner exists: a conveyor carries the bag, which is opened, spawned and closed; the machine has a hopper over the conveyor. Neither Cap n Stem nor Far West is convinced it beats a hand crew, and it is relatively slow unless you run several.
  • Through-spawning (mixing spawn through the whole bag) is used throughout, and is considered necessary for fast, robust colonization of ultra-pasteurized (not sterile) substrate. The downside is that more incubation cooling is needed. Top-spawning against through-spawning has not been compared here (see Open questions).
  • Labour is getting scarcer and pricier, and the repetitive motions are hard on bodies over about 30, so automation is expected.

RULE Pour broken-up spawn straight from the bag into each block; don't scoop, and never break up a block meant for fruiting.

Other ways to inoculate

  • Agar slurry: a fully colonized agar plate (agar included), macerated in sterile water, can replace grain spawn. Open sterile substrate bags (for example of brown sawdust-type substrate) in the hood, add about 45 mL per bag (earlier trials about 50 mL), seal, and shake very thoroughly. Even distribution of the fragments is the critical step. It is not proven to match grain-spawn yields, and not all species tolerate it (see Chapter 7).

  • Chestnut slurry bags showed nothing for about 2 weeks, then were suddenly fully colonized, so expect a long lag. Chestnut 5 lb blocks from slurry gave many small, very consistent clusters (about 20 caps) against bigger, robust clusters (about 5 caps) from normal spawn: a clear change in form.

  • Liquid culture into grain: 20 mL per 6 lb bag (see Chapter 9).

  • Under development: adding sterile pellets, water and spawn precisely into a pre-sterilized (for example gamma-irradiated) bag, so it mixes itself and just needs sealing and shelving, with no shake.

  • Speed at scale. A scoop table lets one worker scoop about 800 bags an hour, and two people can shake about 300 bags an hour. Saving two seconds a bag matters when you make thousands: one farm's line went from 200 to 300 bags an hour. A semi-automatic weighing auger bagger can injure a worker, so guard it.

Sealing

AT A GLANCE Bad seals are the biggest weak point of lab work. Use a properly set band or impulse sealer, let the seal cool before the bag drops, and pull-test seals: the film should tear before the seal.

Cap n Stem's sealing history shows the trade-offs of each method:

Stage Method Problems
1 Fold the bag top twice, fold the sides in, and cinch with a zip tie pulled tight by a zip-tie gun; airtight, so gas passes only through the filter (some growers still use this) Small headspace, so less CO2/O2 buffering; slowed and altered colonization
2 Handheld jaw impulse sealers Held down by hand; overheat after about 80 bags; PTFE strips break; burned hands
(tried by others) Electromagnetic clamp sealers (used early by North Spore) Appeared to give too little clamping pressure
3 Jaw sealer retrofitted with a pneumatic piston on a compressor (John Donahue's idea) A worker deliberately put his hand in at about 90 psi (6.2 bar) and crushed his fingers: don't. It allowed a vertical station with laminar flow across it, but cycle time per bag was the bottleneck.
4 Electromagnetic impulse sealer about 24 in (61 cm) wide (20-36 in, 51-91 cm, available) sealing two bags side by side Nearly doubled speed, but new hires misaligned bags (sealed two together, missed edges): the farm's first real training and SOP problem
5 (current) Bosch Doughboy 550 band sealer, the only band sealer worth buying in Cap n Stem's view; Syntegon's newer model is better but pricier and more complex
  • A band sealer carries bags through the sealing band and a ceramic cooling section, then drops them into a tumbler that acts mainly as a holding station, so bags don't pile up and pop. The seal must cool briefly before the bag drops.
  • An overheating impulse sealer burns micro-holes. The top seal made after inoculation is especially prone to this.
  • For grain masters (see Chapter 9): seal with the open end still facing the filter, then label, then fold.

WARNING A single Neurospora spore entering through a pin leak in a seal can sporulate and spread across the whole of a farm's block production. Bad seals are the biggest weak point of lab work.

Procedure: seal pull test

  1. Take a sealed bag from the current run.
  2. Pull the two sides of the bag apart across the seal.
  3. Pass: the film tears before the seal does. Fail: the seal peels open.
  4. On a fail, check for overlap, a thin or uneven element, too little amperage and poor compression: uneven seals cause pin leaks.

CHECK Squeeze each sealed A-patch bag hard: it should not let much air out. If XL A bags deflate when pressed, they are not sealed. B patches pass air fast, and that alone does not mean more Neurospora risk.

RULE Seal with a properly set band or impulse sealer and let the seal cool before handling. An overheated sealer makes pin holes.

TIP Press gently on the bag to leave a little air inside before sealing, and hold the bag lightly while the sealer closes. One Louisiana farm found this "night and day" for results.

Shaking

  • Technique: "cat paw" the bag (knead it through the plastic), flip it, and repeat, working the grain into all the gaps, then tamp it down. Some staff are "bad shakers"; check their bags.
  • More trapped air gives more headspace but makes a bag more likely to pop during the shake.
  • A tumbler can never fully mix a 10 lb block in an XLS-A bag. Bags leave the tumbler onto a table for a manual shake, which is a big labour cost.
  • With 5 lb bags, tumbling works better. One grower built a tall tumbler on John Donahue's idea: a culvert of the right length, pitch, speed and internal baffling mixes evenly enough that bags only need inspecting and shelving.
  • Bag shape matters: one crew finds a 5 lb block harder to mix than a 10 lb block, and narrow cylindrical 10T bags holding the same grain volume are very hard to shake.
  • Cap n Stem's shiitake blocks are folded rather than shaken; no further detail is available.
  • Check the seals while shaking. Not shaking properly, or not checking seals, is one of the technique faults that can contaminate a whole lot.

WARNING Poor shaking gives patchy colonization and grain clumps that generate excess heat; overheating in ultra-pasteurized substrate can kill the mycelium. Poor spawn distribution can stretch colonization to 3 weeks.

RULE Shake every bag thoroughly (cat paw, flip, tamp); tumblers alone don't fully mix 10 lb bags.

Bag failures and checks

AT A GLANCE Once process, training and equipment are good, most remaining mould comes from bag defects: gussets first, then seals and patches. Contamination that is sporadic across a batch but always at gussets or tops points to the bag, not the batch.

  • Once process, training and equipment are good, most remaining mould cases are bag manufacturing defects, and the gusset is the weakest point.
  • The biggest current complaints about bags are how seals are made, how patches are attached (ultrasonic against heat), seal width, gusset strength and plastic thickness.
  • Other failure points: heat seals too weak, or too hot so they create micro-perforations (especially the top seal made after inoculation), and patches with manufacturing defects.

CHECK Contamination that is sporadic across a batch but consistently located near the gussets or the tops of bags suggests a bag manufacturing problem, not the batch. A typical example: mould starting at a break in the bottom gusset while the spawn has colonized the rest of the bag (see Chapter 16).

CASE Cap n Stem's "Neurospora wars" at its first shop were caused by bag seals: first zip-tie and fold closures, then an impulse sealer that overheated and burned micro-holes, and Donahue bags of that era leaking at the side or bottom gussets (air came out when squeezed). Fixing the seals ended it.

  • Bags are not truly sealed while cooling. A bag sucked tight can still draw in contamination: tightness only shows that the pressure changed too fast, and the bag reopens as temperatures equalize. Polypropylene sticking to itself is usually the cause. Bags pulled in after a cycle are only a rough cue that steam displaced the air (see Chapter 12).
  • The claim that Unicorn bags "self-seal", so you can cook and cool them anywhere, is wrong: filters are not that tight, and one spore is enough.
  • The flat Tyvek sleeve that some older teaching folds into bags between the gussets does not filter cooling air in steamers, because the bag sides do not stay stuck together.
  • For blocks you fruit yourself (not sold), a small, contained Trichoderma patch in the corner of a sealed bag can still be fruited and yield well.

WHY Explain to staff why small things such as how bag folds are done matter. Small errors can damage the business.

RULE Test every new bag lot. Squeeze sealed bags (they should hold air), pull-test seals (the film should tear first), and watch for contamination clustered at gussets or tops.

  • Bags from one early supplier developed tiny holes at the gussets (the folded side panels), which caused contamination. Both farms that found this switched to Unicorn and SaCO2 bags.

Staff, routine and errors

  • SOP (standard operating procedure) examples: no talking while pouring or inoculating spawn; don't nest one bag inside another the wrong way. Some lab leads don't talk at all during inoculation.
  • Written SOPs and redundancy matter, because the owner eventually isn't the trainer.
  • Staff always look for shortcuts. Stacking blocks behind each other on the knock table to fit more is busy-ness that doesn't help.
  • Repetitive work induces a trance. Long chats or audiobooks during, say, 700 of 1,000 bags lead to errors when something changes (for example a switch to twice as many blocks per spawn bag) and to mislabelling. Music is fine for pure repetition if staff keep count.
  • Once systems are in place, production is easy: about 1.5 hours to make 100 blocks. Keep systems fixed rather than constantly experimenting.

RULE Write SOPs, keep the knock room quiet, and explain to staff why each fold and seal matters.

CASE A North Carolina grower can look at any block and say from her notebook when it was made, what is in it and its spawn date. When a problem shows up on one set of 50 blocks out of a run of about 600, she first rules out the steam run (she has objective records that it reached temperature), then traces the problem to the spawn used that day. She walks the building several times a day looking for problems.

Key rules

  1. Use polypropylene bags with a mid-grade patch (Unicorn A / XLS-A or equivalent) for most 10 lb blocks. Keep B patches for in-bag cubensis or lion's mane, and test before changing spawn-bag patches.
  2. Test every new bag lot. Squeeze sealed bags (they should hold air), pull-test seals (the film should tear first), and watch for contamination clustered at gussets or tops.
  3. Fill block bags to roughly one third to one half, and fill spawn bags fuller with little headspace.
  4. Keep blocks at 10 lb or less in PP bags; choose 5 lb if you cannot hold incubation temperature steady.
  5. Dose pellets and water by weight, not volume, so every bag gets the same moisture.
  6. Pull pasteurized bags hot into a HEPA-pressurized cool-down space, and knock at about room temperature: never over 32 °C (90 °F), and 38 °C (100 °F) kills spawn. Knock promptly, before pasteurized blocks ferment.
  7. Use one 6 lb spawn bag per 20 ten-pound blocks (about 3%); stay within 12-30 blocks per bag; spawn more heavily for ultra-pasteurized substrate and slow or disturbance-sensitive species.
  8. Pour broken-up spawn straight from the bag into each block; don't scoop, and never break up a block meant for fruiting.
  9. Keep HEPA coverage unbroken from opening to sealing, work one row deep within one bag length of the filter, and fit an angle-iron bumper.
  10. Seal with a properly set band or impulse sealer and let the seal cool before handling. An overheated sealer makes pin holes.
  11. Shake every bag thoroughly (cat paw, flip, tamp); tumblers alone don't fully mix 10 lb bags.
  12. Write SOPs, keep the knock room quiet, and explain to staff why each fold and seal matters.

Open questions

  • The order and real air permeability of the Unicorn A, B and T patches are reported inconsistently, as is whether Tyvek is the "open" or the "tight" patch. Manufacturer Gurley and pore data have not been checked.
  • Whether Tyvek patches are damaged by sterilization at 121 °C (250 °F) or more, as the cited patent implies, is still being investigated.
  • No in-bag CO2 measurements by patch type have been made.
  • The A-patch spawn-bag shipping trial has no reported results.
  • The black-bag yield gain (about 0.15 lb per block) is a rough estimate.
  • The dry matter in a 10 lb block is given as both about 3.3 lb and about 4 lb (see Block sizes).
  • Top-spawning against through-spawning has not been compared.

chapters.html:
Steam: Pasteurizing and Sterilizing

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers how substrate, grain and liquids are heat-treated with steam: the time and temperature standards, the equipment from pressure cookers and sauna steamers up to low-pressure boilers, vacuum autoclaves and high-pressure boilers, cycle types, the overnight "under pressure" middle method, loading, cool-down, boiler feed water, and proving each run with data loggers. The rules and numbers you will use most:

  1. Measure the core of the hardest-to-heat block, not the chamber air or the pressure gauge.
  2. Ultra-pasteurize substrate at a core of 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for at least 2-3 hours and no more than 4-6 hours.
  3. Sterilize spawn at a core of 121 °C (250 °F), 15 psi (1 bar), for about 35 minutes.
  4. Cook no longer than needed: every extra hour of heat degrades the medium.
  5. Pull blocks hot into a HEPA-pressurized room to cool. Most widespread contamination comes from bad cool-down, not bad cooking.
  6. Inoculate pasteurized blocks at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), as soon as they have cooled: the same day, or the next morning after an overnight cool-down.

Why we heat-treat, and why the core decides

Grain and sawdust arrive full of living moulds and bacteria. If you add spawn to them untreated, those organisms grow faster than the mushroom mycelium and take over the bag. Heat treatment kills them first, so the mushroom gets a head start.

Steam is the default kill method for blocks, grain and liquids. Dry or convection heat, formaldehyde and tyndallization (repeated gentle heating on several days) exist, but none of them is recommended here; see Alternatives to steam.

What counts is the temperature at the centre (the core) of the block that heats slowest, not the temperature of the air or steam around it. A chamber can read 100 °C while the middle of a dense block is still at 60 °C. Every number in this chapter is a core temperature unless it says otherwise.

The three treatments

AT A GLANCE Sterilization uses pressure and kills everything. Ultra-pasteurization uses unpressurized steam at 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) and kills fungi and active bacteria but not bacterial endospores. Classic pasteurization is cooler and is a different process.

Treatment Pressure Core temperature What survives Typical use
Sterilization about 15 psi (1 bar) 121 °C (250 °F) or above essentially nothing (prions excepted) grain spawn, liquids, shiitake and other sterilized blocks
Ultra-pasteurization none (vented) 93-100 °C (200-212 °F), held for hours heat-resistant endospores of thermophilic bacteria sawdust and pellet blocks for most species
Low-pressure "middle" 5-10 psi (0.3-0.7 bar) not stated some endospores rarely used; results unproven
Classic pasteurization none below about 82 °C (180 °F) beneficial bacteria (on purpose) straw, manure and other bulk substrates

Sterilization means pressurized steam killing essentially everything (prions excepted). The result is axenic: nothing else is alive in it. That makes a sterilized bag an "open buffet" for anything that lands on it afterwards, so sterilized media need the cleanest handling of all (see Cool-down and transfer).

Ultra-pasteurization is the term most farms use for unpressurized steam that brings the block core to 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) and holds it there for hours. It kills fungi and active (vegetative) bacteria, but not the heat-resistant endospores of thermophilic (heat-loving) bacteria. Those endospores remain in every block. They cause trouble only if conditions let them: substrate too wet, a core undercooked and then shaken, incubation too warm, or blocks left too long before inoculation.

Classic pasteurization is a different, cooler process. One reading puts it below about 82 °C (180 °F): it kills fungal spores but leaves beneficial bacteria alive, which suits bulk substrates such as straw and manure. The old pasteurization used for Psilocybe cubensis hobby growing, at 71-77 °C (160-170 °F), kills much but leaves much alive. The process in this book is ultra-pasteurization, not classic pasteurization.

WARNING A vented (unpressurized) vessel can never go above 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level. If it builds pressure, you are drifting toward sterilization in a vessel that may not be built for it. Never build makeshift pressure into containers that are not pressure-rated: it is dangerous.

The 5-10 psi middle ground. Steaming at 5-10 psi (0.3-0.7 bar) kills more than pasteurization but does not reliably kill all endospores. Results at these pressures have been called "mystical": there is no hard science or data behind them. The naming is comparable to dairy terms such as "high-temperature short-time" (HTST) pasteurization.

Pressure units. Autoclaves and boilers are measured in psi (pounds per square inch). The small pressure differences between clean rooms are measured in pascals (Pa); see Chapter 4.

Kill temperatures

Fungi are easy to kill with heat. Bacterial endospores are not. This difference is the whole reason ultra-pasteurization works.

Organism group Kill point Notes
Most moulds die by about 66 °C (150 °F)
Pin moulds, Neurospora, Trichoderma, Aspergillus spores about 66 °C (150 °F); about 71 °C (160 °F) kills essentially all fungi per-species thresholds are not certain
Most fungi above about 71 °C (160 °F) one loose remark put it as low as about 43 °C (110 °F)
Neurospora among the first fungal spores killed by steam
Bacterial endospores survive unpressurized steam need pressure (sterilization) to kill

RANGE Plan on about 71 °C (160 °F) as the point where essentially all fungi are dead. Stated thresholds run from about 66 °C (150 °F) for most moulds up to 71 °C (160 °F); one loose aside gave about 43 °C (110 °F), which is too low to rely on. The thresholds are stated loosely and have not been measured per species.

What this means in practice: because fungi die so easily, a batch contaminated by many fungal species at once is unlikely to be a cooking failure. In the same way, Neurospora in properly cooked spawn or substrate came in after the cook, during cool-down or handling. See Diagnosing a cook failure and Chapter 16.

Time-and-temperature standards

AT A GLANCE Ultra-pasteurize: core above 93 °C (200 °F) in the slowest block for at least 2-3 hours, at most 4-6 hours. Sterilize: core 121 °C (250 °F) at 15 psi for 35 minutes. Time and temperature trade off; measure the core and hold only as long as needed.

The table puts the recommended row for each treatment first. The other rows show the full range of practice and the conditions behind it.

Treatment Pressure Core temperature Hold at core temperature Conditions
Ultra-pasteurize substrate (recommended) none (under 1 psi) 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) 1-3 h general working standard
Ultra-pasteurize none above 93 °C (200 °F) in the hardest-to-heat block 2-3 h; never "24 h" unmeasured proved with a core logger
Ultra-pasteurize none above 93 °C (200 °F), still creeping up about 2 h; 3 h is overkill container with a strong boiler
Ultra-pasteurize (shipping container) none 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) about 3 h (sometimes 2), depending on load density Cap n Stem container runs
Ultra-pasteurize (barrel cart) none above 93 °C (200 °F) 2 h, maybe 3 sauna steamer on a barrel cart
Ultra-pasteurize (general) none up to 100 °C (212 °F) about 3 h
Ultra-pasteurize none about 100 °C (212 °F) in the hardest-to-heat block 2-4 h
Quasi-pressure ("quasi-sterilization") vessel brought to 15 psi, then steam off 93-100 °C (200-212 °F); maitake about 99 °C (210 °F) for set hours until the vessel falls back to 0 psi, often overnight see the overnight method
Low-pressure "middle" 5-10 psi (0.3-0.7 bar) not stated not stated unproven
Sterilize grain or substrate (recommended) 15 psi (1 bar) 121 °C (250 °F) or above 35 min or more (one grower uses 35-40 min)
Sterilize grain in a vacuum autoclave pulsed vacuum, then pressure 124 °C (255 °F) about 35 min see cycle types
Sterilize water jars about 15 psi not stated about 35 min
Laboratory glassware (for comparison) 15 psi 121 °C (250 °F) 5-15 min; literature on bioburden gives about 3-15 min not for mushroom media

RANGE Ultra-pasteurization hold: the core of the slowest block above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 hours and no more than 4-6 hours, proved by a logger. 2-3 hours is the common ground and the most common minimum. The full range: 1-3 h at 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) as a general standard; about 2 h, with 3 h called overkill, in a container fed by a strong boiler; about 3 h (sometimes 2) at 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) depending on load density; and 2-4 h at about 100 °C (212 °F). Longer holds of 4-6 h, the upper limit, appear on the temperature-zone log sheet and in slow barrel runs; see Logging a run by temperature zone.

Why mushroom media need 35 minutes, not 5-15. Lab glassware is sterile after 5-15 minutes at 121 °C. Grain and substrate carry a very high microbial load and form a dense thermal mass, so they get a longer margin. Engineers who build lab autoclaves see mushroom cycles as slow, because mushroom loads hold far more biomass than lab ware. A reference-book article shows graphs of vacuum cycles with a pre-pulse, a hold and a post-pulse.

RULE Follow published, empirical time-and-temperature standards, not forum opinion.

Forum rules such as "steam for at least 24 hours" or "15 psi for 90 minutes to 2 hours" are arbitrary misconceptions with no data behind them. Time and temperature trade off against each other. Measure the core, then hold 35 minutes for sterilization and at least 2-3 hours (at most 4-6) for ultra-pasteurization.

CASE Hold time versus total time. At Cap n Stem, blocks sit in loose steam for "about 10 hours", and loggers show they reach sterilizing temperature but do not hold it long. The same process is also described as 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) held for 3 hours, then immediate cooling. Both are true: the 10 hours is the total cycle time, and the 3 hours is the hold at the core. Always say which one you mean.

Cook no longer than needed

RULE The longer substrate is exposed to steam and heat, the lower its quality for mycelium. Aim for thorough but minimal treatment.
