  • Overcooked ("roasted") blocks are chemically altered and colonize poorly. At 121 °C (250 °F) caramelization and related reactions begin, so sterilize for the minimum time that still works.
  • Big industrial autoclaves that overcook (including some large farms) caramelize the substrate and hurt both colonization and fruiting. Some farms' grain spawn comes out toasted or black.
  • Bubba barrel users who run 15-24 h get compost-like substrate. A right-sized boiler keeps blocks from coming out charcoal-black.
  • Shorter pasteurization with more steam input and a clean cool-down is claimed to give better yields, healthier substrate and faster incubation.
  • Slow cooling in a closed vessel extends the effective treatment: the substrate keeps cooking after the steam is off (passive overcooking).

WHY A strong steam source gets the core up fast, so the total time at high temperature stays short. See Sizing the boiler to the vessel and the temperature-zone log, which shows where the damage happens.

Which treatment for which material

AT A GLANCE Spawn is always sterilized. Most substrate is ultra-pasteurized. Maitake does better under pressure; shiitake works either way.

Material Treatment Why or conditions
Spawn (all grain) always fully sterilize, even in a small vessel spawn sits at the top of the expansion pyramid, so any surviving bacteria multiply through every expansion
Substrate, most species ultra-pasteurize proven at scale; spawn is too precious to risk on sterilized blocks handled loosely
Oyster (Pleurotus) anything from sterile to non-sterile grows on sterile, pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized and even non-sterile substrate
Shiitake either method: sterilize or the overnight quasi-pressure cook, or ultra-pasteurize many growers find it does better under pressure; Cap n Stem ultra-pasteurizes it with good results. Trial both
Maitake quasi-pressure cook (best); full sterilization also works do not move maitake to ultra-pasteurization
Lion's mane pasteurization or ultra-pasteurization may suit it based on a reading of bacterial-community research

Spawn. Some well-known educators ultra-pasteurize grain. That may be acceptable for your own use, but selling non-sterilized grain as master spawn is shady. See Chapter 9.

Substrate. Cap n Stem ultra-pasteurizes thousands of blocks per week, and a whole run has essentially never failed. One reason substrate is not sterilized is that spawn is precious: one bad G2 spawn bag ruins 20 blocks, which is 60-80 lb (27-36 kg) of mushrooms.

Oyster. Lime- or steam-pasteurized straw with open-air inoculation is how many growers start.

Maitake. The quasi-cook under pressure gives the best results. One large producer ultra-pasteurizes some products in containers but does maitake only under pressure. Full sterilization also works, but then every downstream step must be cleaner. Ultra-pasteurized maitake, especially when moved to fruiting too early, can give young fruits that turn white and cauliflower-like instead of darkening. The likely cause is bacteria that survive without pressure. See Chapter 20.

Lion's mane. A paper on bacterial communities in wild versus cultivated Hericium erinaceus (Li et al., Scientia Horticulturae; reading unverified) has been read as a reason pasteurization or ultra-pasteurization may suit lion's mane.

The treatment also sets what comes after it:

Downstream setting Ultra-pasteurized Sterilized
Incubation temperature about 19 °C (66 °F) for 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks; warmer lets endospores activate, starting around 24 °C (75 °F) in the core about 22 °C (72 °F) for 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks
Spawn rate higher, because time is not on your side; through-spawning (mixing spawn through the whole bag) is considered necessary tolerates low spawn rates

See Chapter 13 for incubation and Chapter 11 for spawn rates.

CASE At its peak, a New Hampshire farm ran 2,200 bags a week of pasteurized substrate with 16 staff and lost about half of them to contamination. The contamination stopped when it switched to sterilizing 4-6 lb (1.8-2.7 kg) blocks. It now runs 300 bags every other day.

Alternatives to steam

Most farms that start with something else end up on steam. Lime and dry heat were tried before steam on one farm, and others have tried microwaving. These are amateur steps that all lead back to steam, which is the quickest and easiest way to pasteurize any non-grain substrate.

  • Lime. Use low-magnesium hydrated lime.
  • Dry heat in containers (used by some farms). Heat penetrates poorly, so higher temperatures are needed. Heat stratifies, so only the upper half of a container reaches temperature: bags go only from the halfway mark up (a 40 ft / 12 m container holds what a 20 ft / 6 m one would) and are flipped upside down. Dry heat dries the substrate and can chemically alter grain and pellets, lowering yields. Steam is preferred.
  • Pure heat without steam can make sense in BTU (energy) terms but penetrates much more slowly.
  • Chemicals. Some imported substrate logs are said to be sterilized chemically with formaldehyde (unconfirmed).

The pasteurize-versus-sterilize question is contentious among growers. One member of a grower group was removed from the group during an argument over sawdust.

How small farms started, and why they moved to steam. Most small farms began with a cheap low-heat method and outgrew it:

  • Lime-soaked straw (straw soaked in hydrated lime water, not cooked) grew oysters in buckets on a Florida porch, which surprised the grower given Florida's very high airborne bacterial load. He then made 50 lb (23 kg) cold-soaked straw logs before moving to blocks steamed in a 55 gallon (208 L) barrel.
  • Lime pasteurization "fails like 70% of the time", in the words of an Oregon grower who started with slow heat-pasteurized straw oysters, then lime, then 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks of brewery spent grain mixed by hand in a truck bed and cooked 200 at a time in a 55 gallon drum.
  • A Maine grower grew on county straw (about 6 US cents a pound) with lime pasteurization, then spent about four months treating straw with pool bleach plus peracetic acid, producing about 400 lb (180 kg) a week. Buckets were dropped because of the water used to wash them. Moving from straw to hardwood blocks changed how he judged the mushrooms as a chef.
  • A Memphis grower lime-pasteurized cotton gin waste (cottonseed hulls and burrs, a trailer load for US$20-50) and shredded straw in a barrel with a string trimmer. He later doubted it was safe to handle that material.
  • Hydrogen-peroxide-treated blocks "weren't great" for a Chicago farm, which moved to atmospheric steam sterilization.
  • A San Diego farm started with oysters on lime-pasteurized substrate in laundry baskets.
  • A California farm began with hardware-store straw pasteurized in a barrel over a propane burner on bricks, at "160-something degrees for about three hours" (about 71-75 °C), spawned into perforated plastic tubes hung from poles in a plastic-lined garage corner. Three tubes a weekend gave 2.3-4.5 kg (5-10 lb).

Heating a whole room. Before the internet, one grower stacked bagged raw substrate in his insulated grow room and ran propane or kerosene construction heaters, poked through holes in the wall from outside, overnight to heat the whole room to about 82 °C (180 °F). After about three days of cooling he inoculated the bags in the open with grain spawn, then incubated and fruited the batch in the same room. It worked, but only as a batch: you have to heat the whole room each time, so it cannot run a continuous cycle. Pennsylvania Agaricus houses do the same, steaming the whole room to about 99 °C (210 °F) between crops.

WARNING Don't bring outside contamination in. Material from another farm that had been left outside at about 27 °C (80 °F) was too contaminated for Cap n Stem to allow into its warehouse.

Steam equipment: from pressure cooker to boiler

AT A GLANCE Small farms start with pressure cookers, sauna steam generators and barrels. Production farms ultra-pasteurize in a shipping container fed by a low-pressure boiler, and sterilize spawn in an autoclave. Compare upfront cost, running cost, cycle time and maintenance before you buy; see Choosing a system.

Setup Typical cost Capacity per run Cycle Details
Pressure canner (All American 75X) not stated about 5-6 spawn bags several hours, watched Pressure cookers
Sauna steam generator(s) on a steam box about $130-160 per unit 3 units of 7 kW: about 500 five-lb (2.3 kg) or 250 ten-lb blocks about 16 h Sauna steam generators
Bubba barrel (electric element in a drum) about $1,000 to a couple of thousand about 80-100 ten-lb (4.5 kg) blocks 12-24 h Barrels
Barrel cart with an external sauna steamer not stated not stated 7-10 h total Barrels
Shipping container plus low-pressure boiler about $5k container plus $18-40k boiler about 1,000 blocks 8-10 h, can run overnight Containers, Low-pressure boilers
Electric pressure vessel (Blue Myco) about $7-10k maybe about 100 bags about 24 h Electric vessels
Electric autoclave about $30-40k (board range $10-35k) a couple of hundred blocks per day 18 h or more Electric vessels
Vacuum autoclave plus high-pressure boiler about $0.5 million spawn and substrate about 35 min hold plus pulses Vacuum autoclaves

Pressure cookers and tabletop units

A pressure cooker or canner is the entry point for sterilizing spawn, agar and liquids. An All American 75X pressure canner fits about 5-6 spawn bags. Making spawn this way takes half a day of grain prep, several hours of watched sterilization, half a day of cooling, and then knocking (inoculating the cooled bags): more than a day of labour per week.

Ten years ago, US practice assumed full sterilization in pressure cookers, a few 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags per load. Large autoclaves existed mostly in big facilities and colleges. A stovetop-style pressure cooker on an electric hotplate also works for sterilizing flasks of medium.

Tabletop units such as the All American 75X run gravity cycles, holding at 121 °C (250 °F), 15 psi (1 bar), or just above.

Procedure: sterilizing jars and bags in a pressure cooker

  1. Leave jar lids slightly loose and cover them with foil. Cover any lid filters with foil too, or sterilize filter assemblies separately in an empty, foil-covered jar.
  2. For aeration lids with internal tubes (hard to fit several to a small cooker), pop the tubes off, wrap them separately and sterilize them alongside.
  3. Load the cooker and heat it with the vent open. Vent vigorously before closing, so steam purges the air.
  4. Optional: mimic vacuum pulses by cracking the vent, then closing it again. A commercial kit for canning-style retorts approximates this; it shortens cycles and evens out heat-up.
  5. Bring the cooker to about 15 psi (1 bar) and hold about 35 minutes for water jars, and 121 °C (250 °F) for 35 minutes or more for grain.
  6. Let the cooker cool. Move jars to the flow hood and tighten the lids there. Fit filters and reassemble lid tubes at the hood.

CHECK Lids should open easily later. Over-tight lids on hot glass are hard to open and risk breaking the jar.

WARNING Never leave pressure cookers running unattended. One spawn producer (North Spore) once ran about 20 X75 pressure canners, some borrowed, on timers with nobody watching; experienced growers find that terrifying.

Sauna steam generators

A sauna steam generator is a mini boiler with an electric element, a toilet-style float valve for the water feed, a steam outlet, an overpressure relief valve and a controller. Newer units add drain and flush valves and a network cable for a controller. The element cycles and the float holds the water level, so steam comes in pulses, with a large output for the size. A typical unit is a small metal box about 12 x 7 x 17.5 in (30 x 18 x 44 cm) with a front panel, brass fittings and a sight glass.

Item Value Notes
Price about $130-160 from overseas sites (also seen at $120) barely changed over the years
Size to buy 7 kW sold in 7, 7.5, 9 and up to 12 kW; in a side-by-side test, higher kW gave no extra steam
Power typically 240 V breaker sizing differs between makers even for identical-looking units (some 50 A two-pole, others 30 A or 20 A); specs unconfirmed, so get an electrician
Timer 60-minute maximum must be reset every hour; the board can be rewired or daisy-chained to run indefinitely, until it burns out
Units per box 1 for a small proofer-style box; 3 for a bigger box
Lifespan about a week on hard water; about two years each on good water for one grower depends on water and treatment

CASE The one-hour timer. Because the controller stops after 60 minutes, someone has to reset it every hour for the whole run. A guest once slept at the farm to do it.

Reliability. Cheap eBay units kept breaking, sometimes overnight in the middle of a run; one grower ran 3-4 at once to cope. Another grower got about two years from each unit. These units keep heating, can overload circuits, and have caught fire at several farms, mostly through mistreatment.

Water decides lifespan. In Westbrook, Maine, with soft water, units lasted. After Cap n Stem moved to Gardiner, hard water scaled them and killed units within about a week (the elements shorted). See Water treatment.

RANGE Sauna-steamer capacity: three 7 kW units for one steam box of 500 five-lb (2.3 kg) blocks or 250 ten-lb (4.5 kg) blocks. In Westbrook, two 7.5 kW units ran one steam box of about 500 five-lb blocks per run; elsewhere three units did 500 five-lb blocks on a timeline of about 16 hours. Hardware cost was about $300; electricity cost much more. A 7 kW versus 9.5 kW difference has been suggested as a reason one grower's units lasted longer (unconfirmed), while a side-by-side test found no output gain above 7 kW. Capacity per unit and the link between kW and lifespan are anecdotal.

  • Retrofit for barrel owners. If you are tired of burning out the bottom elements of a barrel boiler, cut the element out and plumb a sauna steamer in, with a drain.
  • A popular build. The steamer-barrel setup is widely copied; one grower who publishes the design receives photos of other growers' builds every week.
  • Keep up the output. For ultra-pasteurization, what matters is a steam source that can keep up its output for long enough. Low-wattage generators on a barrel take much longer to reach temperature. Soften the feed water, or the elements scale up fast (Cap n Stem's advice).
  • Another option. One builder makes small boiler-style steam generators fed by carbonator pumps (power heard as "120 watt", unconfirmed). They are an alternative to 240 V sauna steamers.

WARNING Sauna steamers draw 7-9 kW each. If the plug and circuit are not sized for that load, "you would burn your whole electrical panel down". Have an electrician size the supply.

  • Running cost. A California farm's first site ran four 9 kW sauna steamers in a line to steam 250 blocks, and its electric bill was about US$3,000 a month. At the time nobody there knew how to buy a real steam boiler. One of the founders still uses a single 9 kW steamer to feed a home-built tunnel (with a floor drain and sand-filled cinder blocks) that holds 800-900 bags, steamed overnight and inoculated next morning.
  • Overriding the thermostat doesn't fix an undersized box. One grower rewired his sauna steamers (bypassing the built-in temperature cut-out with a contactor) so they ran for 36 hours, but the substrate usually never reached temperature and he "made so many bags of orange cotton candy": orange mould, probably Neurospora.

WHY When a basement grower scales up, buy a boiler. Doing 250 blocks in a day beats doing 30 a day in a small barrel with burned-out staff. "Do everything in bulk as best you can." The boiler pays for itself in time, and nobody stays satisfied at 1,000 lb (450 kg) a week.

Barrels

The double barrel. The "RR" double-barrel steamer was popularized on the Shroomery forum and is credited to a forum grower known as Roger Rabbit. A bottom 55 gal (208 L) drum acts as the boiler: steam is injected, or a little water is heated by a water-heater element and topped up by a float valve. It is plumbed into a second drum lying on its side above, which is loaded like an oven. It proved to many growers that atmospheric ("ultra") pasteurization works without a retort (a pressure-rated cooking vessel). In 2012 one grower fed his double barrel from a cheap steam generator instead.

Older and simpler setups.

  • Asian growers have long pasteurized in lined-up barrels with a little water, packed substrate, a small vent valve on top and a wood fire underneath, then hand-carted the substrate to the lab.
  • Low-tech DIY: two 55 gal (208 L) drums, one upright over an open propane flame as the boiler, steaming into a horizontal drum with two block shelves and an exhaust. One was built in Arizona. An electric element would be much slower. The legality and safety of an open flame are questionable.
  • A grower on the CMGN forum (possibly in Cambodia, growing milky mushrooms) stacked substrate in cheap RPC (reusable plastic) crates outdoors under a tarp tucked into the dirt, injected steam by rubber hose to about 93 °C (200 °F) for some hours, then carted it straight to a cool-down room. Other growers who started with low-tech setups include James Shoop and Cyrus Lester, who now uses a container (names unverified).

The Bubba barrel. A Bubba barrel is an electric drum with a 240 V element immersed in water at the bottom. It costs roughly $1,000 to a couple of thousand dollars, and prices are rising because they are trendy. One client's size held roughly 80 ten-lb (4.5 kg) blocks per run; another account gives about 100 ten-lb blocks per run. The cycle is long because a small element must boil a thin layer of water.

Barrel cycle time Conditions
about 15-16 h per run (start around dinner time) Bubba barrel, about 100 blocks
12-18 h, up to about 24 h to get bag cores above 93 °C (200 °F)
about 19-24 h per cook electric elements
15-24 h gives compost-like substrate
7-10 h total, similar electricity barrel cart with external sauna steam

Bubba barrel problems.

  • Reaching in to load and unload is a contamination vector.
  • Leaving blocks to cool inside, or wheeling barrels into the clean area, adds risk.
  • Dense cylindrical packing leaves inner blocks cold and outer ones overcooked; see Loading the vessel.
  • Do not cook grain in a Bubba barrel: the long electric cycles over-alter the medium.

RULE Check that the steam barrel has water before every run. Make it a line in your SOP (standard operating procedure).

The barrel cart (proposed upgrade). Flip a 55 gal (208 L) drum so the lid, fitted with casters, becomes a rolling base. On the base stands a central post, or a "tree" of welded or bolted pegs, holding the blocks. Slide the barrel down over it, clamp it, and connect a sauna steamer by a quick-connect hose: steam in one side, air and steam out the other. Hold above 93 °C (200 °F) for 2 hours (maybe 3), roll the cart into the lab, lift the barrel off and cool the blocks under HEPA air. Up to four barrels could run off one steam source.

A barrel workflow. At about 100 blocks per run, a week looks like this.

Day Work
1 Mix, load, clean, start the barrel around dinner time
2 Lab prep and spawn work
3 Knock (inoculate), shake and rack
Result about 100 blocks, or about 200 lb (91 kg) of mushrooms per week: under half of a 500 lb (227 kg) target

Running a large barrel: one grower's practice. Avery, who grows on Master's Mix (a sawdust and soy-hull blend; see Chapter 10), runs 110 and 130 gal (416 and 492 L) Bubba's-style barrels.

  • Run the barrel at 94 °C (201 °F) for about 17 hours. The goal is to bring the bags to 93 °C (200 °F) and hold them there for 4-5 hours, confirmed with a probe in the bags.
  • Start the barrel as soon as it is loaded, or the soy begins to ferment. Unload within 3 hours of the end of the cook.
  • The float valve's rubber gasket breaks down over time: replace it every 6-8 months. A 5 psi (0.3 bar) water feed is fine, but fit a pressure regulator, because too much pressure upsets the system.

Barrel lessons from other farms.

  • Heat stratifies in a barrel. Catawba Mushrooms (North Carolina) steams blocks in stainless barrels heated by a water-heater element at the bottom. The bottom blocks reach temperature first and end up cooking about 4-5 hours longer than the top blocks, which are the ones the run is timed on. This has been its biggest struggle.
  • A barrel system that works. A Kansas City farm connects several steamers to barrels with tri-clamp fittings. A run takes about 3.5 hours, so two runs fit an 8-hour day and the system is never left unwatched. The barrels are not moved to the lab: HEPA-filtered air is piped into each barrel through a tri-clamp and hose, and the barrels cool in place overnight, ready to inoculate the next day, with low contamination. The farm believes such a system could be sold for under US$15,000.
  • A backyard wine-barrel steamer. A California farm converted a large stainless wine barrel from a winery into a steamer, steaming 50 blocks once a week on a 220 V circuit run to the garage, venting out of the back door. The lab was a flow hood in the garage, and the farm bought spawn at about US$15 a bag rather than make it. Steaming 50 blocks every day would give about 350 lb (160 kg) a week.
  • The early growers' path. One Texas grower began with a barrel or two with a false bottom, then built a steam shed, which he calls "the worst idea in steaming".

WARNING Two barrel disasters to learn from.

  • A propane barrel steamer (two 55 gallon drums at about 3 psi, about 80 bags each stacked vertically) caught fire when it was left running unattended: insulation on the boiler ignited near the propane tank and the fire department came. The grower switched to electric. He also once cooked bags for 36 hours straight to beat contamination, which he calls "how to properly kill all of your spawn".
  • An electric barrel steamer (PID-controlled, run off a clothes-dryer socket, 36 bags per load) flooded on its first run. A cheap float valve stuck because mains water pressure overpowered the nylon float, the barrel filled to the top, and the element kept heating water that ran down the yard. An RV pressure regulator on the water inlet fixed it, but the first three runs all failed. A 5-bag electric All American also burned out its element after a leak.

Steam boxes and shipping containers

AT A GLANCE Steam in high at one end, exhaust low at the far corner, exhaust open the whole time. Load on wheeled racks. A 20 ft (6 m) container takes a 1.5 in (38 mm) inlet and a 2 in (51 mm) outlet.

Custom steam boxes with three sauna generators plumbed in were "not worth it" at Cap n Stem. If you can afford a boiler, buy one, and use a shipping container rather than building or welding a custom box. A container gives more control: steam in, stale air and steam out, and a circulating flow. One New Hampshire grower built a concrete steam bunker with fixed shelves, which other growers consider extreme.

Cap n Stem's steamer is a fabricated shipping container with a metal floor, steam fed in at the top, and the exhaust at the bottom at the far back. It is filled with wheeled racks whose shelves keep each block separate; workers roll a tall rack of spaced bags straight in. The racks are fabricated from stainless angle, have about 7 shelves and take Metro-rack shelves, so whole racks move from the chamber to the lab.

RULE Steam in high at one end, outlet low at the opposite corner.

WHY Steam rises and pushes the air down and out by gravity, giving even saturation. Injecting steam low causes turbulent, uneven steaming. The layout mimics old canning retorts. The last spot to heat is low near the front (the door end).

TIP For a 20 ft (6 m) container with a 1.5 in (38 mm) steam inlet, use a 2 in (51 mm) outlet and leave it open throughout. When the exhaust flow stays steady through the boiler's on/off cycling, the space is saturated.

  • Pass-through pasteurization (steam in, out of the exhaust) uses far more steam than any recirculating approach.
  • A container is not a sterile vessel. Containers with wooden floors (under metal planks), water troughs and leaky doors pull in dirty air as they cool. Do not cool blocks inside; see Cool-down and transfer.
  • Opening the doors acts as a purge. On a small steam box (about 250 ten-lb / 4.5 kg blocks) read with older type K thermocouple readouts, opening the doors to add a forgotten rack and closing them again made the temperature climb 17-22 °C (30-40 °F) faster than before. In a large container the door-opening effect shows up on the logger.
  • Because substrate only needs ultra-pasteurization, the unloading side outside the lab can be a "dirty" area, with bags going straight from the steamer into the lab.

CASE A Tallahassee farm's steamer, built by an employee in two or three weeks, has three insulated chambers with aluminium skins and doors strapped shut. Each chamber holds a rolling cart of about 200 blocks and is fed by its own small stainless boiler heated with a hardware-store water-heater element. It is plumbed so condensate pools and drains out of the bottom, and it "works really great".

RANGE Sauna steamers per box. Standard (Cap n Stem): two to three 7 kW sauna steamers per about 500 five-pound (2.3 kg) blocks in a tight, insulated box. Context: a Texas farm's first steam box was wood skinned with aluminium, leaky, with rope-and-winch doors. With about 500 blocks packed in, one steamer took a very long time to reach even 66 °C (150 °F), so three more were added. Four steamers running 17 hours made "the electrical bill... more than I could take home in a month" for the first eight months. The lesson is the box, not the steamers: seal and insulate it.

  • Sawdust blocks are a great insulator, so you can't just pack them tight and expect steam to reach the middle. Leave steam paths between blocks. One grower prefers a trough steamer and calls the vertically loaded box design a "cat killer".

Low-pressure boilers

AT A GLANCE A propane- or gas-fired low-pressure boiler feeding a shipping container is the standard production setup for ultra-pasteurization: about 1,000 blocks in an 8-10 hour run that can be left overnight. Set it to cut out at about 10 psi (0.7 bar).

Sioux Corporation of South Dakota makes propane-fired Scotch-marine low-pressure boilers that are used in other industries, such as soil pasteurizing and aggregate. They come skid-mounted and plug-and-play. One New Hampshire grower started the trend of using them on mushroom farms more than 10 years ago.

  • Licensing. These boilers run under 15 psi (1 bar), so generally no boiler-operator licence is needed, but check your state's rules.
  • Fuel. Fuel-fired boilers run on propane, natural gas or oil; electricity only runs the blowers. Natural-gas equipment can often be converted to propane by changing orifices and fittings (Cap n Stem did this on a steam kettle).
Model Output Price Capacity
SF-25 (also given as "SR-25") about 1.1 million BTU, or about 500,000 BTU and up (sources differ) about $30,000; a board shows "30-40K" a 20-40 ft (6-12 m) container; anywhere from one block up to about 6,000 blocks per batch; 1,000+ blocks
SF-11 (also given as "SR-11") about 0.5 million BTU, or about 250,000 BTU (sources differ) was about $18-20k, now likely $30-40k about a 10 ft (3 m) container (maximum about 20 ft / 6 m); about 500 blocks per run; run about 8-10 h

WARNING The BTU figures and model letters (SF or SR) for these two boilers differ between sources: SF-25 about 1.1 million or about 500,000 BTU; SF-11 about 0.5 million or about 250,000 BTU. Treat the specs as unconfirmed and check with the maker before you size anything.

One small farm runs an SF-11 with a container of about 10 ft (3 m). No autoclave big enough to take an SF-25's batch size is affordable.

How it cycles. The boiler fills, fires, sends steam to the container, cuts the burner at the set pressure, refills and fires again, continuously. No thermocouple feedback from the load to the boiler is involved.

Setting Value Notes
Boiler limit 15 psi (1 bar), or just under
Main maximum (cut-out) about 10 psi (0.7 bar) Honeywell spring pressure switches
Differential 5-7 psi (0.3-0.5 bar) pressure ebbs and flows; cranking settings up gives wide cycles. In one demonstration it cut off around 7 psi and restarted as pressure fell
Supply gate valve open 3 of 10 turns so the boiler cycles instead of being drained
Pipe run about 60 ft (18 m) to the container condensate comes out first, then a strong plume of steam
  • A low-pressure boiler as its own regulator. A Colorado farm at 2,500 m (8,200 ft) pairs a 1956 steel retort with an 18 hp low-pressure boiler that cuts out at 15 psi and back in at 14.5 psi. This avoids the regulator problems of feeding a vessel from a high-pressure boiler. In Colorado a low-pressure boiler needs no licensed operator, only a yearly firebox inspection (rules differ by place). The retort takes 250 ten-pound blocks a run; that is its "sweet spot", and the farm chooses not to cram more in.

NOTE Altitude lowers the boiling point. At 2,500 m (8,200 ft) water boils at about 91 °C (196 °F), so atmospheric steaming cannot reach pasteurizing temperatures there and a pressure vessel is needed.

Procedure: starting a low-pressure boiler

  1. Confirm the feed-water treatment is in place and the boiler fills with filtered, softened water; see Water treatment.
  2. Check the interlocks: manual-reset level switch, water-feeder level switch, adjustable pressure switch and manual-reset pressure switch.
  3. Open the propane supply.
  4. Turn the boiler switch 90 degrees.
  5. Open the gate valve to the container about 3 of its 10 turns. Expect condensate first, then steam.
  6. Leave the container exhaust open for the whole run.

CHECK The burner should cut out near the set maximum (about 10 psi) and restart as pressure falls, and the exhaust flow should stay steady through those cycles.

What the equipment looks like. A Sioux boiler is a horizontal steel drum with a red end plate, brass pressure switches and gauges on top, copper feed lines and a small boxed inline water-treatment cartridge. Cap n Stem's runs indoors all year with a chimney and has run about 7 years in that building.

Cost. A shipping container (about $5k) plus a low-pressure boiler ($18-40k) handles about 1,000 blocks in an 8-10 hour run that can be left overnight. An electric autoclave of $30-40k does a couple of hundred blocks per day. A boiler costs about half what an autoclave does. Mixer prices have risen from about $8,000 to about $30,000; if you must choose, spend on a boiler instead.

Pressure classes. Cap n Stem's rough US classes: low pressure under about 5 psi (0.3 bar), medium up to 15 psi (1 bar), high above 15 psi. US boiler codes usually treat steam boilers at 15 psi or less as "low pressure", so check local rules. Running a retort at 15-18 psi (1.0-1.2 bar) inside needs a boiler delivering roughly 21-40 psi (1.4-2.8 bar). Ultra-pasteurization needs only low-pressure steam.

CASE Have a backup plan for boiler failure. Cap n Stem's fire-tube boiler cracked its fire housing after a tube had been re-rolled too many times, and a new one took about six days. The rental boiler came with a 30-day minimum (about US$21,000) when they needed it for three days.

Electric pressure vessels and electric autoclaves

Electric pressure vessels. Blue Myco electric pressure vessels look like brewery fermentation tanks. They cost roughly $7-10k, run a cycle of about 24 h, and hold maybe about 100 bags. They are the cheapest entry route for sterilizing grain spawn, but not for substrate, where 15 psi is unnecessary. A volume of "10 to 30 litres" has been quoted, which could not hold 100 bags; it is probably mis-stated, so check the real volume with the maker.

WARNING Do not build DIY pressure vessels from 55 gal (208 L) drums.

Electric autoclaves. Single- and double-door electric autoclaves are sold by "Unicorn Lou" (probably Lou of Unicorn Bags, unconfirmed), and North Spore has used such units for years (unconfirmed).

Feature Typical value
Length about 10 ft (3 m)
Power 240 V, about 60 A
Price about $35k (a board range of $10-35k)
Cycle 18 h or more
Real pressure hovers at 12-14 psi (0.8-1.0 bar) rather than 15
Maintenance heating elements need frequent replacement

A common scale-up path is a larger autoclave (Unicorn, or probably Blue Myco) for block production. Electric heating can make sense if you have abundant amperage, high oil or gas prices, or only run once a week.

TIP Build "backups on backups". A Tennessee farm chose two more All American pressure canners, swapped on hot plates, over a US$14,000 310 L non-vacuum sterilizer (rated just under 15 psi, so sold as a boiler), because when one big system goes down you are stuck. It also spent about US$2,000 on pipework so its new boiler can back up the old one.

  • A small builder has designed a 9 kW boiler kit for trough steamers for about US$800. It fits on the same pallet as his bagging machine, "almost a farm in a box".

Vacuum autoclaves and high-pressure boilers

A vacuum autoclave pulls the air out of the chamber with a vacuum pump before and between steam pulses, so the load heats fast and evenly; see Cycle types.

Cap n Stem's spawn autoclave is a custom Primus bought on eBay for about $3k (retail about $250k), about $12k all-in once installed. The engineer who installed it, described as the only qualified Primus technician in the US Northeast, recommended MadgeTech loggers (see Loggers).

  • Primus units allow controlled ramp rates, a deep vacuum pre-pulse and a ramp to about 15-18 psi (1.0-1.2 bar). The controller reads, for example, "CYCLE COMPLETE JACKET 248.1F" (120.1 °C). The machine is a large double-door sterilizer with many radial door clamps.
  • The autoclave prints a paper record of each cycle on a ribbon. Staff and visitors find watching it engaging, which helps make good process visible.

High-pressure boilers. Big autoclaves need a high-pressure boiler. Cap n Stem first rented a 1950s unit; now they have a boiler of about $100,000 built into a shipping container so it can sit outside. It stays at about 50 psi (3.4 bar) all week and delivers 45-50 psi (3.1-3.4 bar) to the autoclave head.

  • An outdoor containerized boiler can freeze over winter weekends and must be protected. It is quiet compared with a Sioux low-pressure boiler; the loudest part is the sparge.
  • The sparge tank preheats feed water with runoff steam through copper coils to about 77-82 °C (170-180 °F); a pump then injects it into the bottom of the boiler. A blowdown separator and cooler handles the discharge. Preheating feed water is the main challenge at high pressure. A typical installation is a white jacketed boiler with a gauge and a blue feed pump, and a separate blue control panel, inside a red container.
  • The same steam can run a steam-jacketed kettle (jacket about 35 psi / 2.4 bar) for cooking grain. Grain left in it desiccates quickly; see Chapter 9.
Route Cost Suits
About 5-10 psi low-pressure autoclave plus low-pressure boiler $10-20k plus about $30k: about $50k substrate; probably not grain spawn
Vacuum autoclave plus high-pressure boiler $100-300k plus $150-300k: about $0.5 million spawn and substrate

TIP A high-pressure boiler can also run gravity cycles on a non-vacuum autoclave, but vacuum cannot easily be bolted on later. If you will ever want vacuum, buy it with the autoclave.

A little history. Autoclaves date from about the 1920s. In 1894 Costantin and Matruchot used steam sterilization for the first pure mushroom cultures on agar, and in 1932 James W. Sinden (Penn State) patented steam-sterilized grain spawn. See Chapter 2.

  • A pharmaceutical autoclave in use. A Detroit farm's 110 gallon (416 L) Italian top-loading autoclave does about 240 lb (110 kg) of substrate per run. A cycle takes a little under 3 hours: about 30 minutes up to temperature, about 1.5 hours' hold and about 30 minutes down, so four runs fit a relaxed day. Early on the owner ran it every 3 hours from Monday morning to Thursday morning without sleeping.
  • The same farm moved to bulk ultra-pasteurization with a Sioux boiler of about 500,000 BTU/h (about 146 kW). Any such boiler must be ASME-certified (built and stamped to the US pressure-vessel code) for safety. With a boiler, whole grow rooms can also be steamed clean between cycles.
  • Buy used. Cap n Stem bought a Primus sterilizer worth "a half a million, quarter million dollars" from a junkyard through eBay for about US$2,500, and it turned out pristine. Much of its early equipment cost about 5% of its value.
  • Why one farm chose an autoclave over a boiler and container. Catawba Mushrooms plans an autoclave rather than a Sioux boiler with a 20 ft container as the steam chamber, because an autoclave kills thermophiles. It wants to grow maitake at scale in the humid southeast US, where seasonal heat (the winter-to-spring change and summer) raises contamination pressure, and bulk soy arrives by rail nearby in bulk bags.

WARNING Autoclave buying advice from experienced growers: never buy a Chinese locking double-door autoclave, because the door may never unlock. Buy an old Reed or a used Japanese import.

Choosing a system

RULE Before buying, compare upfront cost, operating cost (utilities dominate at scale), cycle time and maintenance.

  • Do not scale by multiplying small equipment. 2,000 blocks would need about 20 Bubba barrels, and Cap n Stem struggled to make even half their blue oyster spawn with All American canners. It is better to wait and make one larger leap, to equipment that supplies two fruit rooms in one or two days, than to step up to a single Bubba barrel.

  • Buy a right-sized boiler and a shipping container before multiplying barrels or building custom steam boxes.

  • Automate. The old Westbrook farm's steam generator was not automated: someone had to be on site about every two hours overnight to work the valves.

  • Compare with data. Logged runs show dramatic differences between Bubba barrels, sauna-style steam barrels, autoclaves and boiler-fed containers. See Proving every run.

  • The middle ground. Between barrels or troughs and a retort or big boiler with a container sits a 10 ft (3 m) container with racks and an SU-SF11 steam generator. The next step up (an SF25) costs about US$30,000, plus a 20 or 40 ft container, racks, and a lab big enough to cool the whole load.

  • Steam generators that sit under the bags inside the vessel have had "meltdowns" mid-cycle (smoke, no flame). A separate steam source can be disconnected without ruining the batch.

WHY Steam generation (the boiler) is the most expensive thing new farms don't realize they need. Budget for it from the start.

Sizing the boiler to the vessel

There are two sizing questions: the boiler's output in BTU or horsepower, and the volume of steam it supplies relative to the vessel. Size the boiler to the chamber and to the block load.

CASE An upstate New York farm put a boiler the size of a window air conditioner on a huge autoclave. Outer blocks reached 121 °C (250 °F) hours before the centre, so the edges overcooked while the middle may have been undercooked. Size for a fast ramp and an even temperature through the load.

Remember the heat that leaves with the load. 2,000-5,000 bags per cycle leaving the steamer at 93 °C (200 °F) or more swing the receiving room from hot and humid to cool and dry while they cool. See Chapter 5 for cooling those rooms.

Cycle types

AT A GLANCE A cycle must first get the air out, then hold the load at temperature, then exhaust. Gravity cycles are simple but slow. Pre-vacuum cycles are fast and even. Liquid cycles exhaust gently.

Cycle How it works Strengths and weaknesses
Gravity purge the air with steam, ramp to the plateau, hold, cool passively simple infrastructure, but slow, and needs long holds above 121 °C (250 °F); gravity-style cycles spend most of their time flushing air. Tabletop units such as the All American 75X run gravity cycles, holding at 121 °C / 15 psi (1 bar) or just above
Pre-vacuum (pulsed vacuum) alternating steam pulses and increasingly deep vacuum pulls remove the air reaches an even temperature much faster; temperature and pressure correlate before peak temperature, which limits Maillard (browning) and caramelization reactions
Liquid like gravity, but with a slow, gentle exhaust avoids boil-over and broken glass

A pre-vacuum grain cycle (Cap n Stem). Repeated pre-vacuum pulses to about -10 inHg (about -34 kPa) with steam refills, 3-4 pulses in all, then 124 °C (255 °F) for about 35 minutes. Test bags show a slight water gain from the steam and are otherwise fine. See Chapter 9 for grain.

The figure above is drawn from a logged run (file "R15373 MultiChannel", 23 June 2021): three vacuum pulses, with pressure dipping to about 0.3-0.5 bar absolute between peaks of about 1.9-2.0 bar; temperature ramping from about 25 °C (77 °F) to a 121 °C (250 °F) plateau held roughly 45 minutes on the logger (the intended hold is about 35); then pressure dropping and temperature falling to about 60 °C (140 °F) over about 1.5 hours.

  • With a vacuum autoclave, leave enough vertical space between shelves for even vacuum exposure and steam saturation, so all bags reach the same temperature.
  • On old-style retorts without a vacuum pump, a few operators pull vacuum by hand. This is considered scary and hazardous.

Air is the enemy: pressure is not temperature

RULE Purge the air before you start timing a hold. Pressure without the matching saturated-steam temperature means air is still in the load.

  • 15 psi does not guarantee 121 °C (250 °F). Trapped air pockets register as pressure but resist heating. Purge the air first.
  • Pressure and temperature must correlate according to saturated-steam tables (pure steam at 15 psi gauge is 121 °C). A pressure spike without a matching temperature means air remains. In vacuum cycles the temperature creeps up while the pressure pulses swing harder; correlation usually arrives around the last pulse, and then the load holds at the plateau.
  • Bags pulled in ("sucked in") after a gravity or pasteurization cycle are a rough visual cue that steam displaced the air. It is not an exact test.
  • Press the air out of bags before steaming. Many people do not, and the trapped air hinders heating.

Run-to-run variation

No two runs are the same, so log every one (see Proving every run).

  • A pre-heated chamber behaves differently. Back-to-back runs reach temperature faster, which throws off precision. By the sixth run in a day you would need different settings (more vacuum pulses). This is true of manual 1960s retorts too.
  • Equipment drifts. Steam equipment never performs identically: sensors and parts age and the load matters. Log the core temperature every cycle so you see drift coming.
  • Grain type matters. Brown rice correlated temperature and pressure almost immediately, so a simple cycle was enough. But in an over-pressured lab it dried fast, and on a knock day of about 700 bags the last racks took hours longer because the grains congealed into bricks.
  • The dry cycle. The vacuum "dry cycle" at the end of an autoclave run desiccates bags most at the top of the rack.
  • A test bag every run. Cap n Stem runs several autoclave cycles a day. Each run's test bag is pulled on the cool-down side by a suited worker, passed out, checked before the next run is loaded, and then reset.

The overnight under-pressure method

AT A GLANCE Bring a pressure-rated vessel to 15 psi, shut the steam off once the block cores reach 93-100 °C (200-212 °F), and leave it sealed overnight until it is back to zero. It suits shiitake and maitake.

This middle method has no formal name; growers call it quasi-pressure, quasi-sterilization or a quasi-cook. It sits between ultra-pasteurization and full sterilization.

Procedure: quasi-pressure cook

  1. Load a pressure-rated vessel (a retort or autoclave). In a double-door vessel, load from the dirty side.
  2. Steam the vessel to 15 psi (1 bar) or more, from a boiler at about 40-45 psi (2.8-3.1 bar) head pressure.
  3. Watch a core thermocouple. When the blocks read 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) at the core, shut the boiler off. For maitake, aim for block internals at about 99 °C (210 °F) for a set number of hours.
  4. Leave the vessel sealed, often overnight, while the pressure decays slowly.
  5. Unload once the vessel is back to zero, on the clean side, into a HEPA room.
  6. Treat the blocks like pasteurized blocks and inoculate promptly.

CHECK The core log should show the blocks reached 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) before the steam was cut, and the vessel gauge should read zero before you open it.

A double-door setup is often sketched as: "Clean | 15 psi | 200-212 °F | 40 psi | Dirty", that is, the clean unloading side, the vessel at 15 psi, the core target of 93-100 °C, the boiler at 40 psi, and the dirty loading side.

Benefits claimed for the method.

  • Consistently productive shiitake blocks, with better yields and browning.
  • Less contamination; it kills far more bacteria than ultra-pasteurization.
  • It avoids overcooking raw inputs.
  • The vessel stays sterile while it cools.
  • Downstream handling can stay "semi-clean", like a pasteurization workflow.
  • It suits old canning retorts and weak boilers.
  • No 2 a.m. unloading.
  • Several farms run it as their default for all species.

RANGE No hold time has been set for this method. It is described both as "15 psi vessel, internal 93-100 °C (200-212 °F)" and, for maitake, as about 99 °C (210 °F) held "for a set number of hours". Neither gives a hold time.

How quasi-pressure blocks behave after unloading, and whether they carry less contamination risk after the cook, has not been tested.

Loading the vessel

AT A GLANCE Fill to no more than 2/3 to 80% of the vessel, on racks with gaps. Never a solid stack.

RULE Fill vessels to at most about 2/3 to 80% of chamber volume (blocks plus racks), and leave channels so steam penetrates.

  • Avoid solid stacked masses. They are common in cylindrical Bubba barrels and densely packed Blue Myco units. Spacing also speeds cooling and saves you knocking half-cool blocks.
  • Over-packing happens in barrels, autoclaves and steam boxes at scale. Stack with chimneys (every other block, in a brick pattern) so steam reaches every side.
  • In an over-packed barrel, inner blocks stay colder than outer ones: the outer and top blocks overcook while the inner ones harbour survivors.
  • Racks with shelves keep every block separate and leave air channels. Dense oak cell structure is hard for steam to penetrate, and worse when wet.
  • Hand-loading individual blocks is a contamination vector. Move blocks in racks or cages for frictionless transfer. Paul Stamets has made the same point.

Loading spawn bags. Fold the filled spawn bags and load them on autoclave racks. Never let filter patches touch each other in the autoclave; this is an old training rule. Older Unicorn B patches peeled and fell off if they touched in the autoclave; the product has since changed. See Chapter 11 for bags and filters.

Getting the substrate ready.

  • Pellets should fully absorb their water in the bag before steaming. If they take up water during steaming, the bags warp and balloon.

  • From water-in to inoculation takes about 30 hours (bags watered at 8 a.m., steamed and cooled, inoculated around noon the next day). This gives the water time to distribute through the bag.

  • A dirty mixer can defeat the cook. One farm alternated a Fender-type filling machine and a mixer (names unconfirmed), using near-boiling water in a mixer with a layer of grime. The pellet mix came out much darker before cooking: a nutrient-rich cake that steam pasteurization could not fully handle. See Chapter 10.

  • Each ultra-pasteurization run brings cleanup at both ends, so it pays to fit as much as you sensibly can into one run. An Oregon farm's practical limit is "the last 200 of 600 bags" in a day.

CASE An employee at the same farm loaded the steam shelf as full as possible "with no space", 28 five-pound blocks a shelf: one of the "bright ideas" that cause chaos. One summer its average losses were about 30%, which the owner traced to staff not following the SOPs (standard operating procedures). Now nobody changes a step without asking.

Bags and water uptake

  • Substrate bags gain essentially no water in atmospheric steaming, because the patch is folded over and steam cannot exceed atmospheric saturation.
  • Spawn bags under pressure gain about 0.1-0.2 lb (45-90 g) in sterilization, measured on test bags. So do not hydrate grain right to its burst limit. Autoclaving is a second cooking phase: work back from the result you want after the autoclave. See Chapter 9.
  • Steam injection plus vacuum cycling adds a useful amount of moisture to grain; the amount has not been measured.

Bag plastics.

  • Polypropylene (PP) is the dominant bag plastic. It tolerates more heat, keeps the seals around patches tough, and holds its shape through compression and steam.
  • Polyethylene (PE) cannot take high temperatures and cannot go in a retort. Unicorn's black bag is PE-only, which limits how it can be sterilized.
  • Thicker plastic matters if your cycle uses aggressive pressure changes, as a pulsed vacuum cycle does.
  • A cited patent says Tyvek should not go above about 120 °C (248 °F), yet sterilization runs at 121 °C (250 °F) or above. This may be why Tyvek patches are questionable for grain spawn; the question was still under investigation.

Bags as they cool.

  • Folding a gusseted bag before autoclaving can produce a vacuum-tight seal as it cools. Some growers want this; Cap n Stem does not.
  • Bags are not truly sealed while cooling. A bag sucked tight shows a pressure differential (the pressure changed too fast) and reopens as temperatures equalize; polypropylene sticking to itself is usually the cause.

RANGE Tyvek sleeves and "self-sealing" bags. An older teaching puts a flat Tyvek sleeve over the grain between the gussets before folding, supposedly to filter air as the bag cools. In a steamer it filters nothing; it may make some sense in an autoclave, where bags breathe under pressure change. A bag maker also dismisses the practice, and Cap n Stem used to do it. Separately, do not believe the claim that Unicorn bags "self-seal", so they can be cooked and cooled anywhere: filters are not that tight, and one spore is enough. Cool every bag in clean air.

Cool-down and transfer

AT A GLANCE Most widespread contamination comes from bad cool-down, not bad cooking. Pull blocks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, straight into a positive-pressure HEPA room. Never cool them in an unpressurized vessel, and never carry cool blocks through dirty air.

RULE Most widespread contamination comes from improper cool-down. Pull blocks hot into a positive-pressure HEPA room to cool; never cool them in an unpressurized vessel, and never carry cool blocks through dirty space.

A HEPA room is a room supplied with air through high-efficiency filters, kept at slightly higher pressure than its surroundings so that air only ever leaks out of it, never in. See Chapter 4.

The recommended method. Pull blocks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more after the hold (typically 96-99 °C / 205-210 °F), straight into a HEPA-filtered, positive-pressure room to cool. Wear welding gloves. Hot blocks kill much of what touches them and are less likely to pick up contaminants in transit than cool ones.

The alternative. Cool the blocks inside a vessel that is back-pressurized with HEPA air. Even then, carrying cool blocks through dirty space, or a long way, remains a risk.

WARNING Do not cool pasteurized blocks inside an unpressurized vessel. It sucks in air as it cools. Blocks become susceptible as they fall to about 38 °C and up (the 100s °F), and a wet, dirty container overnight will contaminate them. Cooling too long, or inside the vessel, also gives surviving bacteria time to multiply.

If the route must cross dirty space. Pull the blocks hot, let the steam pour out, and put them on racks sprayed with 70% isopropyl alcohol, in front of positive-pressure HEPA air. Even with hot handling through a dirty space you might lose about 5 of every 150 bags. See Chapter 16.

How clean the route must be.

  • Pasteurized blocks tolerate crossing a not-pristine area on the way to the HEPA lab: a clean, mopped, low-airflow "quasi-clean" space, often sketched as a small chamber marked "low air flow" and "clean". Some farms even move them outdoors briefly. With ultra-pasteurization, the steam room itself may stay relatively dirty, with blocks pulled through a small door onto a clean rack.
  • Sterilized media must exit a double-door autoclave straight into clean, HEPA-positive space, with a stricter process (full-body PPE in Cap n Stem's spawn lab) until the bags are sealed.
  • Neurospora growing outdoors near the route the blocks travel is a particular hazard. See Chapter 16.

RULE Never put a dropped block or rack back with the batch. Floor contact can contaminate everything.

WARNING Do not pull air through a HEPA filter by suction, for example with HEPA shop-vacs hooked to a steam box for cool-down. It seals poorly and contaminates everything. Filters must have air pushed through them, with gaskets all round.

Cooling times and inoculation temperature

Situation How fast it cools
Lab with plenty of cool filtered air (recommended) below 38 °C (100 °F) within hours, about half a day
Cap n Stem container run: racks pulled about 9:30 p.m. into air at about 18 °C (65 °F) 37 °C (99 °F) by 8 a.m.; knocked about 9:30 a.m.
Autoclaved grain bags cooled overnight in a dedicated clean cool-down room
Closed steam box (not recommended) drops slowly from 93 °C (200 °F) over about 8-10 h; some leave blocks 48 h
A customer's container cooled overnight in place (not recommended) about 10-27 °C (50-80 °F), then carried across dirty space

When to inoculate. Cool ultra-pasteurized blocks below 38 °C (100 °F) and inoculate swiftly. Below 32 °C (90 °F) is safe without a second thought; room temperature is preferred. Sterilized blocks can wait longer. Inoculate at about room temperature: about 30 °C (86 °F) is cited as an empirical upper limit, and others quote about 32-37 °C (the 90s °F). Too hot, and the spawn is killed or denatured on contact.

Procedure: cooling blocks to inoculation temperature

  1. Pull the racks from the steamer at about 96 °C (205 °F) into the HEPA cool-down room.
  2. Let them cool to about 32 °C (90 °F). Check with an IR (infrared) thermometer while squeezing the bag, so you read the substrate, not the plastic surface.
  3. Open about 20 bags at a time on the flow rack with cool spawn; by the time you work through them they are about 27 °C (80 °F).
  4. Inoculate at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F). Over 32 °C (90 °F) is "no bueno".
  5. Inoculate pasteurized blocks as soon as they have cooled (the same day, or the next morning after an overnight cool-down); do not let them sit for days.

CHECK Squeeze-and-read with the IR thermometer shows 32 °C (90 °F) or less before the first bag is opened.

RANGE Upper inoculation temperature: aim for 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), room temperature preferred. The range of practice runs from "room temperature preferred" and about 30 °C (86 °F) as an empirical limit, to a working window of 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), to "below 38 °C (100 °F)".

WARNING Pasteurized blocks have an expiry. Surviving endospores germinate, and blocks ferment (sour smell) if left days before inoculation.

The cool-down room. A separate cool-down room matters when the autoclave runs all day while staff inoculate: hot bags at 66-121 °C (150-250 °F) would overheat the workers. With one run a day you can cool and knock in the same room. Cooling in front of a laminar flow hood desiccates bags; a HEPA cool-down room with a pass-through autoclave is better. Room layout and HVAC details for cool-down rooms (plenum, exhausting the hot air, matching HEPA fan capacity) are in Chapter 4 and Chapter 5.

Cool-down failure cases

CASE The open window. One summer day at Cap n Stem, blocks sat in the steam unit until they were below about 66 °C (150 °F), then were carried past an open window to the lab about 10 ft (3 m) away. The racks pulled first, nearest the door and the window, went to Neurospora within about 2 days of inoculation; the back racks less. Lesson: pull hot, and never route cooling blocks past open air.

CASE The overnight container. A customer cooked in a shipping container, let it cool overnight in place to about 10-27 °C (50-80 °F), then carried the blocks across a dirty space: "an open invitation" to contamination.

CASE The compromised suction filter. A farm cooking 5-10 lb (2.3-4.5 kg) blocks in adapted Bubba barrels with sauna steamers pulled "HEPA" air into the barrels during cool-down to keep positive pressure. It worked at first, worsened slowly, then failed. The suck-through intake filter (likely 99.95-99.97% efficient or worse) was probably compromised.

CASE The days-long wait. On a Midwest farm, blocks colonized weakly ("wispy", "greasy"), and many species, even reishi, did not fruit. Hot blocks had sat 1-3 days before moving from the ultra-pasteurizer to the filtered cool-down room, giving thermophilic endospores a head start while the blocks drew in dirty air.

CASE Hot blocks through the snow. One grower switched to hauling hot blocks by Kubota tractor through the snow into their lab, and their problems went away. Growers with a separate steam building, for example about 400 ft (122 m) from the lab, face the same question: move the blocks while they are hot.

CASE Steam heat in the incubation room. Blocks leaving a Bubba barrel at about 93 °C (200 °F) into a space that was also incubating pushed local temperatures from a regulated 19 °C (66 °F) toward 66 °C (150 °F), badly disturbing the incubating blocks. Fix: separate steam from the lab and incubation, seal the concrete, line walls with coroplast, make the lab airtight, and vent steam and heat outside.

In summer, heat from warm pasteurized blocks overheats inoculation rooms. Provide cooling, but not with a cooling unit inside the lab itself. See Chapter 5.

Diagnosing a cook failure

AT A GLANCE Start with the method and the cool-down, not the ingredients. Pull the logger record first.

  1. Start with the production method (sterilized or ultra-pasteurized) and the cool-down speed, not the ingredients.
  2. The first thing to check when blocks go bad is the data-logging thermocouple record. See Proving every run.
Symptom Likely cause Notes
Contamination widespread but inconsistent: in patches through the batch, many types (bread moulds, forest moulds, bacteria); uneven colonization and yield steaming failure the classic cook-failure signature
Random moulds of different colours a few days after knocking air contamination, or insufficient steaming (organisms resident in the wood survived)
Many fungal species at once probably not the cook (fungi die easily); look at cool-down and handling see Kill temperatures
Uneven growth, outer blocks dried out overcooking, for example a barrel run 24 h; inner blocks may do fine not contamination
Stratified colonization: strong at the top, weak or anaerobic toward the bottom 10-12 lb (4.5-5.4 kg) blocks not held long enough at the plateau one farm that moved into a new facility fixed it by raising cook temperatures
Sporadic chunky spots over a colonization of about 2 weeks, not in every bag of the lot undercooked substrate, not bad spawn
Pin mould undercooking, dirty cool-down or bad seals, worsened by excess airflow in early grow kits it came from an overly coarse filter patch plus undercooked substrate
Heavy metabolite exudate (in species other than shiitake) media too rich, or undercooked bacteria are then likely to stop fruiting entirely
Pioppino mycelium on top flattens, goes glossy and slick, and will not pin there bad culture, cook or grain spawn
Mycelium killed in ultra-pasteurized substrate overheating from poor shaking
Splotchy colonization even after sterilization fermentation from long grain soaks see the RANGE below
  • If bacteria come from the substrate, check the cook time and temperature, whether the mix was fermenting, and how long it sat before processing and inoculation.
  • More microbes survive pasteurization than sterilization, so other errors (such as excess moisture) are punished harder on pasteurized substrate.
  • Lion's mane is an indicator species. A systemic problem (pasteurization, moisture, temperature, light, a mould source) may show only on lion's mane, while hardier species outcompete it.

RANGE Long grain soaks. A common claim is that long soaking germinates the endospores in grain so they are easier to kill. In practice it is not needed: sterilization kills them anyway, and a forum grower known as Roger Rabbit is credited with debunking the claim long ago. Long soaks instead start fermentation, which can give splotchy colonization even after sterilization. See Chapter 9.

For full contamination diagnosis, see Chapter 16 and Chapter 19.

CASE In August 2016 a New Hampshire farm had four catastrophic failures in one month. Its boiler failed two hours into pasteurization; two HVAC technicians couldn't fix it, and when a co-owner took it apart a 3.7 m (12 ft) flame shot across the room. 2,200 bags sat at 46 °C (114 °F) for two and a half days before the owner had to decide whether to re-run them. 5,000 bags had unsealed bottom gussets that blew out when shaken. That one month put the farm in a financial hole until 2019.

Proving every run: data logging

AT A GLANCE Put a thermocouple logger in the core of the slowest-heating block on every run, keep the files, and read the curve before you unload. A good logger costs a few hundred dollars; one bad run can sink a farm.

RULE Log core temperature every run with a thermocouple logger, and keep the files so you can spot drift.

Why log. Most farms keep few operational records, and start only when they become certified organic or after a disaster. Logs let you trace a failed sterilization days later instead of relying on memory. Temperature is the most important data point on a farm: in sterilization, incubation and shipping. Data answers the questions you set in advance ("did X reach temperature for long enough?") reliably.

  • Use core thermocouple loggers whenever you change equipment or process, and ideally on every run. Do not grow complacent with machinery: on slim margins, one bad run can sink a farm.
  • Without a good logger your data is junk. A couple of hundred dollars is worth it. Train staff and write SOPs.

CASE Before logging, Cap n Stem steamed two boxes separately out of distrust, so that if one failed they would save half. Logging showed exactly when each reached temperature, and the habit stopped.

Loggers

A thermocouple is a temperature sensor made of two joined wires; a logger records its readings over time. MadgeTech (New Hampshire) loggers are the most accurate and reliable that Cap n Stem has used; a planning board from an early design simply reads "Type K thermocouple datalogger, MADGETECH?".

Logger Use Price Notes
MadgeTech newer small pasteurization model / MicroTemp100 (recommended for substrate) atmospheric pasteurization about $200-300 slim probe, USB adapter; range about -34 to 100 °C (-30 to 212 °F)
MadgeTech stainless "bullet" wireless logger pasteurization cores about $500 waterproof with a gasket; free software; interval 10 s to hourly
MadgeTech PRTemp140 ("140") (recommended for autoclaves) autoclave cycles and liquids about $800-1,000; about $1,200 after a post-COVID redesign logs temperature and pressure together; survives vacuum cycles and submersion (placed in carboys for liquid cycles); interval 1 s to daily; in use since 2019
Cheap Amazon type K thermocouple logger budget option about $150 a frayed lead can read the junction where the wire crosses the steam-box wall, giving absurd readings (such as 500); probes break after about 10 uses

Software. The free MadgeTech 4 software works like this: select the device, right-click Stop, Download, then graph. You can zoom, select points, generate data tables and statistics, and save locally or to the cloud. Start a logger with Quick Start or Custom Start (interval, manual or automatic start, wrap-around). Logger software such as MadgeTech's can export readings to a spreadsheet, where the band times and F value can be calculated automatically instead of read off by hand.

Interval. Log every 15 s for spawn autoclave runs, which gives the detail needed for tuning. Substrate runs can be sparser; one example used 1 min. Program the logger by USB, unplug it, and place it in a test bag.

TIP Buy as many MadgeTech loggers as you can. Use them only for the cook, and take them out once the load has cooled (advice from Ryan, a consulting grower).

Loggers can also be sealed inside colonizing grain or substrate bags in incubation, and in fruiting blocks, to track internal temperatures. See Chapter 13.

Where to put the probe

RULE Put the probe in the hardest-to-heat spot: low on a rack, near the middle and bottom of the load. Ideally log several spots.

  • Even well-designed autoclaves stratify. The coldest spot is away from the natural air-then-steam flow, down low. In a container steamed high at the back, the last spot to heat is low near the front.
  • Where to put the probe depends on the loading: a dense Bubba barrel and open racks in a container need different interpretation.
  • Running two probes (back versus front of the container, bottom versus top of the autoclave) maps how the load varies with outside temperature and steam supply. A probe at the top of the autoclave rack shows where the dry cycle desiccates most.

Procedure: a logged container ultra-pasteurization run

  1. Start the logger (1-minute interval is enough for substrate).
  2. Insert the probe into a block on the first shelf near the doors (the low front, the last spot to heat), and mark that block with a Sharpie.
  3. Close the doors and start the steam; see Procedure: starting a low-pressure boiler.
  4. Wait for the core to pass 93 °C (200 °F), then hold above 93 °C for at least 2-3 hours, and no more than 4-6 hours.
  5. At the end, crack the doors, grab the marked block and close up again. Heat and steam are about 99% retained, because the blocks are at temperature.
  6. Read the data. If the core did not reach or hold temperature, close up and fire the boiler again.
  7. To unload: whoever pulls the racks shuts the steam, opens the doors, checks with a handheld IR thermometer that the blocks are above 93 °C (200 °F), then reviews the logger.
  8. Pull the racks hot into the HEPA cool-down room; see Cool-down and transfer.

CHECK The logger curve shows the marked block's core above 93 °C (200 °F) for the full hold, and the IR thermometer reads above 93 °C at the door.

A pressure cycle is different: unlike pasteurization, a finished pressure cycle cannot simply be re-entered. Check the autoclave printout first, then pull the logger to confirm. When a run looks suspicious, rerun the grain or redo the batch.

Example logged runs

Container pasteurization at Gardiner, Maine. Steam on about 11 a.m.; ramp starting about 12:20; block core at 93 °C (200 °F) just under 6 hours in; held above 93 °C for the target 2-3 hours; racks pulled about 9:25-9:30 p.m.; cooled with air at about 18 °C (65 °F) to 37 °C (99 °F) by 8 a.m.; knocked about 9:30 a.m. The logger was a MicroTemp100 at a 1-minute interval, read in MadgeTech 4: 6,229 readings over about 4 days 7 h 48 min from 21 September 2023. The curve ramps from about 27.5 °C (81.5 °F) to a plateau near 99 °C (210 °F), maximum 99.4 °C (210.96 °F), then decays over the following day to a minimum of 21.1 °C (70.02 °F).

A bullet logger in a block shows the hours above 93 °C (200 °F) directly: the "steam heating 200 °F" line on the graph is the one that matters.

CASE A boiler far bigger than the load gives repeatable runs. A New Hampshire farm's 25 hp boiler makes about 400 kg (880 lb) of steam an hour, which the owner explains as boiling 458 L (121 gallons) of water in 11 minutes. It could sterilize 2,700 kg (6,000 lb) of bags; he sterilizes 136 kg (300 lb). He ran probes six times, and the centre bag hit 110 °C (230 °F) internal at exactly 1 h 37 min each time, matching a heat-transfer formula a friend worked out from his data. He now runs no probes: steam on, and at 22 minutes he closes a valve most of the way. Within 22 minutes he knows whether the door seal will hold. (Cap n Stem's standard is still to log every run; see Proving every run.)

Failures caught by logging

CASE Scaled fire tubes. Blocks were not reaching 93 °C (200 °F); a handheld IR thermometer at the opened door confirmed it. The cause was boiler fire tubes encrusted with scale. After cleaning, runs returned to normal.

CASE The slow creep. Cap n Stem's Sioux boiler's fire tubes corroded and crusted, producing less heat and steam, so runs needed about 3 extra hours to reach temperature and hold 2 hours. The logged history revealed the slow creep in ramp time. Logs also show seasonal effects and leaks in steam lines.

Prevention more broadly: track contamination by season, check airflow and pressure, and recheck after any change (for example, an autoclave installed through a wall that left a gap).

Logging a run by temperature zone

AT A GLANCE Split each probe's heating curve into temperature bands and record the time spent in each. Ramp through the damaging bands as fast as possible, hold in the 93-96 °C (200-205 °F) band, and keep time above 96 °C (205 °F) under 3 hours.

A run log divides each probe's heating curve into temperature bands and records how long the substrate spends in each. The template in the project folder (mycowizards/templates/substrate-temperature-log.pdf) has one row per probe per run, with the date, the vessel and the probe location. Read it together with the probe placement rules: the probe in the slowest-heating block decides the run.

The bands, in the order the substrate passes through them. The labels in quotation marks are the sheet's own.

Band °C (°F) Sheet label What happens Target
1 ambient to 60 °C (140 °F) "Microbial activity / chemistry modification" native microbes are still alive and feeding on the supplement move through quickly
1a 27-46 °C (80-115 °F) "Primary fermentation" soy hulls and other supplements start to ferment and sour; this is why a loaded barrel must be started at once minimize time here
1b 46-60 °C (115-140 °F) "Microbial activity zone" heat-loving bacteria grow fastest under 1 hour
2 60-71 °C (140-160 °F) "Early biological and chemical activity" ("preconditioning") most moulds die around 66-71 °C (150-160 °F); see Kill temperatures ramp
3 71-82 °C (160-180 °F) "Hemicellulose hydrolysis onset" ("nutrients break down") the substrate itself starts to change chemically ramp quickly
4 82-93 °C (180-200 °F) "Highest chemical and structural damage" ("rapid Maillard reaction") the band where browning (Maillard) reactions do the most damage ramp as fast as possible
5 93-96 °C (200-205 °F) "Effective sterilization": the main working zone where the hold happens; it is ultra-pasteurization, not true sterilization, which needs 121 °C (250 °F) under pressure hold here
6 above 96 °C (205 °F) "Peak zone / overprocessing" extra quality loss for little extra kill under 3 hours

Ramp and penetration columns. The sheet records ramp times for 60-82 °C (140-180 °F), 82-93 °C (180-200 °F) and 93 °C (200 °F) to peak, under the label "inefficiencies / damage accumulation: fastest here wins". It also records the elapsed time to 71, 82 and 93 °C (160, 180 and 200 °F) as a "thermal penetration curve", showing how heat moves into the substrate. Comparing these across probe locations shows cold spots and whether the steam supply keeps up (see Sizing the boiler to the vessel).

Hold minimums ("killing time"). The sheet treats these as alternative ways to reach the same kill; lower temperatures need longer.

Core above Minimum hold
88 °C (190 °F) 6-8 hours
92 °C (198 °F) 4.5-5 hours
93 °C (200 °F) 4-6 hours
96 °C (205 °F) counted as overprocessing

Maximum temperature and lethality. Each run also logs the maximum temperature and an F (lethality) value, referenced to 97 °C (206 °F), with "6-8" marked ideal.

What an F value is (an explanation added here; it is not on the sheet). An F value adds up the killing effect of the whole curve as equivalent time at the reference temperature. For each logging interval, F = Δt × 10^((T − 97 °C) / z), summed over the run, where Δt is the interval in hours and T is the core reading; F is in hours. The sheet does not state z, the number of degrees that changes the kill rate tenfold. A common working value for bacterial spores is 10 °C (18 °F). With that value, an hour at 87 °C (188 °F) counts as only 0.1 hour at 97 °C, and an hour at 107 °C (224 °F) would count as 10. Readings far below the reference add almost nothing, so the hold dominates the total.

RANGE Hold length. Recommended: the slowest block's core above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 hours and no more than 4-6 hours, proved by a logger. Use the short end only with a fast-steaming boiler and a measured cold spot. The temperature-zone sheet's minimums are longer (4-6 h above 93 °C / 200 °F, 6-8 h above 88 °C / 190 °F), and so is one barrel grower's practice (bags held at 93 °C / 200 °F for 4-5 h in a 17-hour barrel run); most other figures put the hold at 1-3 h above 93 °C, with 3 h called overkill. The sheet also counts anything above 96 °C (205 °F) as overprocessing, while container runs at Cap n Stem hold 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for about 3 h, and 100 °C (212 °F) holds are also described. The shorter holds rely on a fast-steaming boiler and a well-measured cold spot. Log your own runs and compare yields and contamination before you settle on a hold.

Water treatment for boilers and steamers

AT A GLANCE Filter, soften and carbon-treat all boiler feed water, do regular blowdowns, and never feed distilled or RO water. This applies to a $120 sauna steamer as much as to a $100,000 boiler.

RULE Filter, soften and carbon-treat boiler feed water, do regular blowdowns, and never feed distilled or RO water.

Feed water must be treated: raw water, then carbon filter, then softener, then feed tank, then boiler. Scale ruins sensors and parts, lowers steam quality, and can cause failure or fire. A couple of thousand dollars of water treatment protects equipment meant to run for decades, and this applies even to small electric steamers.

The recommended incoming chain for all water entering the farm:

  1. A physical (particulate) filter, usually a washable cartridge. It can sit on either side of the other stages.
  2. A softener, if the water is hard. High-flow units are not expensive.
  3. A carbon (charcoal) scrubber.
  4. Then split: to production (the boiler, substrate water, and the solenoids on Fenrir filling machines), and to fruiting-room humidification, where RO (reverse osmosis) or steam is added.

The main purpose of this chain is to protect boilers, steam generators and pressure vessels, where heating drops the minerals out of the water. Problems arise when any stage fails.

WARNING Do not feed distilled or RO water to a steamer or boiler: it is corrosive to metal. Hard water scales. Soften and treat instead. This applies equally to a $120 sauna unit and to a $100,000 "Clear Fire" high-pressure boiler (probably the Cleaver-Brooks ClearFire, unconfirmed).

  • Inline treatment on Sioux boilers. Sioux boilers take an inline screw-cap housing on the feed line, holding a replaceable dissolving puck (like a urinal cake) that softens, treats and pH-balances the water. Cartridges last about 3-4 months at 5 days a week. Untreated feed water drives costs and problems "through the roof".
  • Blowdowns. A blowdown means briefly opening the pressurized bottom drain to flush out sediment. Blowdowns matter as much as water treatment. The part that wears out on Cap n Stem's boiler is the caps at the back, which is also water-related.
  • Hard versus soft water. Hard water in Gardiner killed sauna steamers within about a week; soft water in Westbrook let them run a long time. Scaled fire tubes caused slow ramps and failed runs (see Failures caught by logging).
  • Substrate water. Water used to hydrate substrate that is then cooked rarely causes problems; city water is fine. Minerals, heavy metals or chlorine in the product more likely come from the substrate itself. If you already treat water for the boiler, run the same water to the substrate.
  • An experiment with untreated water. Dry-sterilized or ultra-pasteurized pellets were hydrated with UV-treated (unheated) water plus spawn, then sealed. They colonized cleanly with several Pleurotus species. The main difference was fruit colour, probably caused by the untreated mineral content.
  • Steam humidity. A running boiler also makes steam humidification of fruiting rooms possible, and that steam is mineral-free; see Chapter 5.

See Chapter 17 for water quality in the rest of the farm.

Steam safety

WARNING Do not pressurize containers that are not built for pressure, and do not build DIY pressure vessels from 55 gal (208 L) drums.

  • Sauna steamers have caught fire at several farms and can overload circuits. Size breakers to the manufacturer's spec, with an electrician.
  • Unattended banks of pressure canners on timers, manual vacuum pulls on old retorts, and open propane flames under drums are all hazardous.
  • Handle hot blocks with welding gloves. Unloading a hot pasteurization trough outdoors is part of the job, and new hires often do not expect it.
  • Check the boiler interlocks (manual-reset level and pressure switches) as part of every start-up; see Procedure: starting a low-pressure boiler.

See Chapter 18 for farm safety in general.

What has gone wrong on real farms.

  • A steam box made of walk-in cooler panels blew a wall out 46 cm (18 in) with "just a whisker of pressure". Never let a box hold pressure: give it an open drain and vent.
  • A sterilizing room with 20 cm (8 in) concrete walls lost about 500,000 BTU an hour (about 146 kW), burned a lot of propane, and its bags took 72 hours to cool below 38 °C (100 °F). For two months the owner switched the boiler on and off by hand every five minutes all night, until a small Arduino controller took over.
  • An autoclave bought for "pennies on the dollar" turned out to have a 5 cm (2 in) hole in the bottom. Inspect used vessels before you rely on them.
  • Cap n Stem's Sioux boiler blew out at the back when a slow drip from a fire tube ate away the refractory lining; catching it early avoided a meltdown. Have boilers inspected. Several clandestine growers' sites have burned partly or fully.
  • Home-built double-barrel steamers often lack safety devices: "you're going to blow up your neighbour".

WARNING Farm fires are real. A Louisiana farm burned down about a year into building, with a founder inside; he suffered second- and third-degree burns over much of his body. Cap n Stem knows of four or five farm fires, usually from faulty wiring, all from "trying to jankily cook" substrate. If someone turns off the water line to a steamer, "the steamer is just gonna cook" until something burns. Fit low-water cut-outs and high-temperature limits, and never leave a home-built steamer unattended.

Key rules
