  1. Measure the core of the slowest-heating block, not the chamber air or the pressure gauge.
  2. Ultra-pasteurize substrate at 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) core for at least 2-3 hours and no more than 4-6 hours; longer only degrades it.
  3. Sterilize all spawn at 121 °C (250 °F) core for about 35 minutes; never only pasteurize spawn.
  4. Use pressure (sterilization or the overnight quasi-pressure cook) for maitake. For shiitake, pressure and ultra-pasteurization both work: trial both.
  5. Purge the air before timing a hold: pressure without the matching saturated-steam temperature means air is still in the load.
  6. Load to no more than 2/3-80% of the vessel, on racks with gaps; never a solid stack.
  7. Steam in high, exhaust low at the far end, exhaust open throughout (about a 2 in / 51 mm outlet for a 1.5 in / 38 mm inlet on a 20 ft / 6 m container).
  8. Pull blocks hot into a positive-pressure HEPA room to cool; never cool in an unpressurized vessel or carry cool blocks through dirty space.
  9. Inoculate pasteurized blocks at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F) as soon as they have cooled (the same day, or the next morning after an overnight cool-down); do not let them sit for days.
  10. Log core temperature every run with a thermocouple logger, and keep the files to spot drift.
  11. Filter, soften and carbon-treat boiler feed water, do regular blowdowns, and never feed distilled or RO water.
  12. Buy a right-sized boiler and a shipping container before multiplying barrels or building custom steam boxes.

Open questions

  • No hold time has been set for the quasi-pressure method, and its effect on contamination risk after the cook has not been tested.
  • The BTU ratings and model names of the Sioux boilers differ between sources (SF or SR; 1.1 million and 0.5 million BTU, or 500,000 and 250,000 BTU).
  • Results at 5-10 psi (0.3-0.7 bar) are unscientific; no data exists.
  • Fungal kill thresholds are stated only loosely, from 43 to 71 °C (110-160 °F).
  • Sauna-steamer capacity per unit varies between accounts, and the link between kW rating and lifespan is anecdotal.
  • The Blue Myco vessel volume ("10-30 litres" for about 100 bags) is inconsistent.
  • Whether Tyvek patches tolerate cycles at 121 °C (250 °F) and above was still under investigation.
  • The amount of water grain gains from vacuum steam injection has not been measured.
  • A planned comparison of how sterilized and pasteurized substrate mature, logged with in-bag loggers, has not yet been published.

chapters.html:
Incubation

Incubation is the stage after inoculation when bags sit on racks while the mycelium grows through the grain or substrate. This chapter covers where the incubation room sits, how to rack and space bags, how to remove the heat that colonizing blocks make, what CO2, temperature and light to hold, how long each species needs, and how to read problems in the bag.

AT A GLANCE The numbers used most:

  • Blocks: 19 °C (66 °F) measured at the bag surface, so the core stays under about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F).
  • Grain spawn: cooler, about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F).
  • Room CO2: a controlled band of about 1,500-3,000 ppm.
  • Spacing: two hand widths between bags, on every side and above (one hand width is the bare minimum).
  • Load: racks and blocks fill about 1/10 to 1/4 of the room's volume, and never more than half.
  • Stability beats precision: swings in temperature, light or air do more harm than a slightly wrong set point.
  • White is not ready for chestnut, shiitake and maitake.

Quick links

  • Set up: location · sizing · racks · spacing and loading · starting small
  • Control: heat · cooling · set points · stability · measuring · CO2 bands · light by species · humidity
  • Species: timings table · shiitake · chestnut · maitake · grain spawn · holding blocks
  • Problems: diagnosis · looks wrong but normal · tracing a bad batch · key rules

Terms used in this chapter

Term Meaning
ppm Parts per million: how CO2 in air is measured. Fresh outdoor air is roughly 400-500 ppm.
BTU/h British thermal units per hour, a rate of heat. 1 BTU/h is about 0.29 W; 12,000 BTU/h is one "ton" of cooling (about 3.5 kW).
Reefer / evaporator A walk-in-cooler style unit: the cold coil and fan hang inside the room; the condenser (which dumps the heat) sits outside.
HRV / ERV Heat (or energy) recovery ventilator: swaps stale room air for outside air while recovering most of the heat.
Positive / negative pressure More air pushed in than leaves (air leaks out, keeping dirt out), or the reverse (air leaks in, keeping the room's gases from escaping).
Knock Inoculate a bag with spawn and seal it.
G1, G2 / masters First and second generations of grain spawn (see Chapter 9).
Filter patch and headspace The breathing window on the bag, and the empty air space above the substrate.
Primordia (pins) Baby mushrooms.
Buckling, browning The normal blistering and then browning of a shiitake block's skin (see shiitake).
Stroma A tough, leathery mycelium mat that will not fruit well.
Endospores Heat-resistant bacterial spores that survive steaming.
Metabolites Liquids and pigments the mycelium gives off.

Why incubation matters

AT A GLANCE Incubation decides the crop. It needs a steady temperature, controlled CO2, the right light and humidity that simply stays out of the extremes.

Incubation is the most important room to control in block production. There are four controls: temperature, gas exchange (CO2 and oxygen), light (which can ruin a batch) and humidity (which only needs to stay out of the extremes).

Incubation is the one stage that truly needs a steady temperature. The mycelium makes its own heat, and that heat output rises and falls as it colonizes. A stable room lets the mycelium pass through those peaks. A fluctuating room gives erratic colonization, and this is worst with difficult species.

A useful picture: incubation is a slow fruiting room. The bags take care of humidity, light matters somewhat, and CO2 and heat are the two things you must manage.

WHY The mass of the mushroom comes from the substrate, not from the fruiting room. What happens in incubation sets the crop.

Some species depend on incubation more than others:

  • For shiitake, roughly half of the skill sits in incubation and half in fruiting. Shiitake is easy to fruit but hard to incubate.
  • For maitake, incubation is the longest and most critical phase. Do not rush it or disturb it.

RULE Full white colonization is not the finish line for chestnut, maitake and shiitake. They need further maturation (ripening) in the bag before they are ready to fruit.

Farms differ in how hard they push incubation. European producers publish longer incubation times and lower average yields than US farms. The European approach is gentler and slower (a "scientist" approach); the US approach is hot and fast (a "cowboy" approach). Neither is clearly better.

WHY "The most important part is the substrate and incubation. You can have the nicest growing room in the whole world, but if you have the worst incubation and substrate production, that is going to be complete garbage." The reverse, good blocks in a poor room, still grows "great". As one veteran grower puts it: "Everyone thinks it's all about the growing room. It's never about the growing room. It's always about the first half." Very good substrate can even resist blotch from a badly humidified fruit room.

What happens inside a colonizing bag

Staff need a shared vocabulary for the phases of colonization (the mycelium spreading through and digesting the substrate).

Phase What it looks like Notes
Jump-off Mycelium starts growing out of each spawn grain The most sensitive phase
Exploration White and fuzzy; spreading through the substrate
Consolidation (maturation) Dense; digesting the substrate and preparing to fruit

The phases matter because heat and CO2 output change with them. Output is low at first and peaks near the end of colonization, as the last patches close (see when the heat peaks).

Where the incubation room sits

AT A GLANCE Incubation is its own controlled zone. It holds racks and nothing else, it stays away from hot blocks and fruit-room air, and it never shares air with fruiting.

The four zones

A block farm runs as four zones. Each is an independent environment.

Zone What happens there How it is controlled See
1. Mix and steam Substrate mixing and steaming Unregulated except for worker comfort Chapter 10, Chapter 12
2. Cool-down and lab Blocks cool, then are inoculated Recirculated, cooled and HEPA filtered Chapter 11, Chapter 12
3. Incubation Bags colonize CO2-controlled (about 1,500-3,000 ppm) and cooled (19 °C, 66 °F at the bag), held constant This chapter
4. Fruiting Blocks produce mushrooms CO2, humidity and cooling regulated, but allowed to swing a little Chapter 14

Each room needs its own control if you want even air exchange in each. For the full farm layout, see Chapter 3.

One room, one function

RULE The incubation room holds racks and nothing else.

CASE A farm incubated its racks inside its lab and had constant contamination. Removing contaminated bags, and the foot traffic that came with it, carried spores onto the knock table (where bags are inoculated). Lesson: one room, one function.

  • Make the flow through the facility one way, with no backtracking. Walking through incubation to reach the lab drags contaminants along.
  • Keep hot blocks out of incubation. Blocks leave a steam barrel at about 93 °C (200 °F). Pulling them into a space that is also incubating can push nearby air from a regulated 19 °C (66 °F) toward 66 °C (150 °F), which badly upsets the incubating blocks.
  • Keep contaminated bags away from cooling blocks. Even a clean incubation room will have a few contaminated bags, for example Neurospora pushing through a torn bag or patch. Keeping those bags a few feet from blocks that are cooling for tomorrow's inoculation is a major contamination route.

A typical small-farm plan (a converted milk barn) puts the steam barrel in a small annex by the drain, a knock and cool-down area across the top of the building, and incubation filling the rest, with an attic plenum alongside.

Air direction between rooms

Air must flow from clean to dirty, and incubation air must never reach fruiting.

  • Incubation's surplus cooling may be pulled into the lab if it is strong enough, as long as the lab's substrate heat is exhausted. Lab heat must go to the mix and steam side or outside, never back into incubation.
  • At Cap n Stem (a large block and spawn farm in Maine, USA, that appears often in this book), the block incubation room's refrigeration also conditions the adjoining lab rooms (spawn cool-down and other incubation). Those rooms draw air from incubation and return it, while staying positively pressurized. This shared-air approach works for labs and incubation, but not for fruiting.
  • Another layout is one long building: an unconditioned mix area, then a narrow lab, then incubation. Cooling units recirculate inside incubation. HEPA units in the wall shared with the lab pull cool air from incubation into the lab and return it. High CO2 does not matter in the lab, and the lab gets free cooling for staff and for substrate cool-down (see the figure below).
  • An existing attic can serve as a cooled plenum (an air chamber) that feeds filtered, positively pressurized air down into the lab and incubation, with air leaving toward the dirty steam side. Insulate the walls and the plenum heavily.
  • An incubation room that is also a clean room needs its own ventilation for CO2 on top of its filtered supply.

RULE Never feed CO2-rich incubation air into fruit rooms, and never let fruit-room air (spores, humidity) reach incubation. Run two separate climate systems.

Lending incubation air to the lab is fine, but only while the incubation room still holds its own CO2 band; see the over-exchange case for what happens when it does not.

Which way each room should push air:

Room Pressure Why
Lab and spawn room Positive Filtered air leaks out, so dirt cannot leak in
Block incubation, recirculated with a CO2 exhaust Slightly negative CO2 cannot drift into clean areas (Erik's approach)
Block incubation fed from a filtered attic plenum Positive The other design in use: filtered air leaves toward the dirty steam side
Fruiting Its own separate system Its spores and humidity must never reach incubation

See Chapter 5 for fans, filters and pressure in detail.

CASE A farm's old fruit rooms were positively pressurized and pushed smells and spores into incubation. The same farm divided its old incubation with polypropylene curtain walls, which swayed and buckled as pressure changed. Lesson: separate fruiting and incubation air completely, and build solid walls.

Sizing the incubation room

AT A GLANCE Give incubation more floor than any other room: about twice the fruiting space, and three weeks of racks for a two-week species. Shiitake needs 5-10 times more.

  • Incubation needs more floor space than the lab. In one converted milk barn, about two thirds of the building went to incubation racks. Plan roughly twice as much incubation space as fruiting space.
  • Consulting clients who buy a building nearly always undersize incubation.
  • Shiitake needs roughly 5-10 times more incubation space than fast species for the same output, because its incubation runs about 6 to 14 weeks.
  • Cooling blocks in the same space as incubating ones makes incubation temperatures swing. Taking turns (one big knock, incubate everything, empty the room, repeat) avoids that only until demand grows, usually within weeks. Then you need at least one run a week and a separate cool-down space.

Procedure: size racks for a fast species

This applies to species with about a 2-week incubation (oysters, lion's mane).

  1. Count how many weeks a batch stays in incubation: about 2 weeks.
  2. Add one week, so you provide 3 weeks' worth of space. The newest batch then always has a rack to go to while the oldest batch is at two weeks.
  3. Work out blocks made per week. Example: one steam run of 80 blocks a week = 80 blocks per week.
  4. Multiply by the weeks of space: 80 x 3 = 240 block places.
  5. Divide by what one rack holds, with proper spacing: at 80 blocks per rack, 240 / 80 = 3 racks at least.
  6. Space the racks so they breathe; do not pack them into one hot mass.

For a slow species, use its own incubation time in step 1. A shiitake block that spends 12 weeks in incubation needs 13 weeks of space, which is why shiitake takes 5-10 times the room.

CHECK On the day the oldest batch leaves, the next batch must already have an empty rack waiting. If it does not, add rack space before adding production.

The building shell

The building shell matters as much as the equipment inside it.

  • Concrete, steel and brick act as heat sinks or heat sources. Untreated concrete adds heat in summer and draws heat out in winter; the radiant effect of surfaces is real.
  • Example: one farm's spawn incubation room backs onto an old brick wall that faces a neighbor's always-open loading dock, so outdoor extremes leak in. The farm keeps adding rigid foam insulation.
  • A black roof can reach about 66 °C (150 °F) on a 32 °C (90 °F) day, against about 38 °C (100 °F) for a white or reflective roof. Insulate the ceiling at least as well as the walls; hanging coolers cannot keep up under a hot roof. A lab built in Arizona with reflective panels stayed cool on 43 °C (110 °F) days.
  • Climate sets the difficulty. Coastal San Francisco Bay Area farms (Far West Fungi is the example) enjoy stable weather. Arizona, Texas, Florida, Nevada and Maine, with their hot or cold swings, need a plan. Do not assume the builder considered heat. Buffering incubation from outside walls and ducting the cooling in helps.

CHECK When planning or retrofitting the shell: insulate the ceiling at least as well as the walls; make the roof white or reflective; keep incubation off outside brick or concrete walls where you can; and do not assume the builder planned for heat.

TIP Colonizing blocks make heat, so you can trim room temperature with the exhaust outlet. Room too cool (a cold winter): close the outlet panel a little, so less warm air leaves. Room too warm (high summer): open it, and the room drops a couple of degrees within minutes.

See Chapter 5 for insulation, heat loads and cooling equipment in detail.

Spawn rooms and block rooms

AT A GLANCE Grain spawn incubates in a filtered, positive-pressure room, cooler than blocks, with no cooling units inside. Blocks with filter patches can incubate in unfiltered, recirculated air.

Spawn bags and substrate blocks incubate in different kinds of room.

Feature Spawn incubation room Block incubation room
Air Positive-pressure HEPA room, supply high and exit low, so cold air sinks and counters spawn heat Bags with filter patches do not need positive-pressure HEPA air; air can be unfiltered, which is fine for substrate
Cooling units Never inside the room: recirculating units collect whatever is in the room and contamination builds up over time Units sit in the room and recirculate, which is easier on the equipment
Temperature Cooler than blocks, about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F); needs its own air conditioning (see set points) About 19 °C (66 °F) at the bag surface
Spacing Wider: spawn bags generally carry a more restrictive filter, so they build more CO2 and heat Two hand widths (see spacing)

Points to know about spawn rooms:

  • Positive pressure raises the air exchange but also traps heat, and the filter fans themselves add heat. Over-pressurized spawn rooms run hotter than people expect.
  • Fan motors and friction through HEPA filters warm the air: 18 °C (64 °F) supply air can arrive at 19 °C (66 °F). At Cap n Stem, air pulled from the 19 °C (66 °F) block incubation room through a fan and HEPA filter into a spawn room arrived at 20-21 °C (68-70 °F).
  • Grain spawn ideally incubates cooler than blocks, which forced Cap n Stem to give its spawn room its own air conditioning. All Cap n Stem spawn incubates inside the lab, so lab temperature control also sets spawn growth schedules.
  • Example: because one farm's spawn room has near-unidirectional positive-pressure flow, it can pack spawn on mobile shelves with little vertical gap. Even so, the bottom shelf runs colder than the sixth and seventh shelves.
  • Example: a typical spawn incubation room has wire racks of grain bags along white walls, workers in white suits, and carts of boxed blocks at the far end.

Recommended spawn-room design

  1. Put filters in one wall with fans behind them, giving near-laminar flow (air moving in one even direction).
  2. Send the return air to a pre-conditioning (pre-filter) room, where it is cooled and filtered again, instead of bringing in fresh makeup air (outside air drawn in to replace what leaves).
  3. Brief your HVAC contractor with the figure below and these points:
    • the pre-conditioning room is a pre-filter space whose air comes back to the same point;
    • size that plenum and the pressure difference together;
    • the return must handle the positive pressure, or the fans overheat.

No target pressure difference or air-change rate is given in the sources; the HVAC designer has to set them for your room.

Our farm: where does spawn incubate?

FARM NOTE The textbook's rule is that grain spawn incubates cooler than blocks, at about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F), below 19 °C (66 °F), in a filtered positive-pressure room with no recirculating cooling unit inside (Spawn rooms and block rooms, set points). Lion's mane and black oyster spawn are the exception, at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). The farm's own set points are a lab at 18-19 °C under positive pressure and incubation air at about 18 °C with block cores kept to 21-22 °C or less.

What has to be housed, from the weekly spawn plan: about 8 grain masters and 16 G2 bags at once, plus test bags and any spares. That is roughly 24-30 bags on wide spacing, because spawn bags carry a more restrictive filter and build more CO2 and heat (spacing).

FARM NOTE Decided (Joseph, 6 Nov 2026): spawn incubates on a physical shelf in the incubation container. Air there is about 18 °C, which suits the 17-18 °C spawn target, but it is recirculated and unfiltered, and the textbook accepts that for filter-patch blocks, not for spawn bags. So on that shelf:

  • Keep spawn bags well apart (wider than block spacing, see spacing) and keep the bag filters unblocked.
  • Put a logger on the shelf and record the top-shelf temperature, which runs hottest (heat on the rack). Spawn above 19 °C (66 °F) is where stroma starts.
  • Keep lion's mane and black oyster spawn there too: their 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) range is the exception, and about 18 °C suits them.
  • Hold the shelf to the capacity above, about 24-30 bags.

OPEN Write the measured top-shelf and bottom-shelf temperatures here after the first two weeks, and say whether spawn stays clean in recirculated air. If contamination in masters or G2 passes 5% (targets), the fallback is a dedicated cool cabinet or room with filtered supply and no recirculating unit inside.

Racks

AT A GLANCE Pallet racking is cheapest per block; rolling racks save handling; any dense pack needs ventilation channels and cooling sized for the full load.

Rack type Typical size and capacity For Against
Pallet racking with slatted or strapped decks About 4 ft (1.2 m) deep, 10-12 ft (3.0-3.7 m) tall, 7-8 levels, 4 ft (1.2 m) aisles; a 10 ft (3.0 m) span holds about 10 bags per row (possibly 20; not confirmed) Cheapest per block (built from 2x4s and strapping); slatted decks let air move vertically and horizontally Wood decks can splinter; needs aisles
Pallet racks for shiitake (one large farm's setup) About 48 in (1.2 m) wide, about 10 ft (3.0 m) tall, about 5 blocks across, aisles on both sides with lights Air and light reach all sides Overstuffing lowers output
Tall stationary metal racks (imported) Built to use 20 ft (6.1 m) ceilings at one farm Consistent airflow and spacing, no splinters; a bag is handled once until fruiting or packing Need some work on arrival; said to add labor
Standard metro-style wire racks Hold only about 30% as many blocks in a tall room Easy to buy Waste height
Rolling racks About 7 wire shelves on casters; suit 8-9 ft (2.4-2.7 m) ceilings Fewer handlings; bags are placed on the rack they grow on (faster knock days); whole batches roll to fruiting or the cooler; grain can be staged warm and then rolled somewhere cool; aisles can be deleted for horizontal density No safe 20 ft (6.1 m) rolling racks exist; dense packs need ventilation channels; often the wrong size and shoved into corners
Danish or Dutch flower trolleys Packed densely Very high density Become one giant hot block without ventilation channels

TIP Choosing a rack: ceilings of 2.4-2.7 m (8-9 ft), or product that leaves the building (spawn, blocks for sale): rolling racks. Tall ceilings and product that stays: stationary racks or pallet racking, the cheapest per block. The labor claims for the two types overlap (stationary racks are said both to add labor and to mean a bag is handled only once), so do not choose on labor alone.

WARNING Do not roll shiitake racks around during incubation. Moving racks or bumping blocks can shock shiitake into pinning in the bag (see stability).

  • Permanent shelving packs more blocks into a room, but it only pays off if cooling is sized for the full possible load. Otherwise colonization times vary widely.
  • Rolling racks in use:
    • Keep G1 grain racks somewhere warmer until they start making heat, then roll them somewhere cooler.
    • Keep maitake dim to incubate, then roll it into bright light (about 3 weeks is one example) to trigger pinning.
    • Roll a thousand oyster blocks into the cooler before a long weekend.
  • For a spawn or block supplier, mobile racks are ideal: product leaves the building, each bag stays on the shelf it was knocked onto, and the rack rolls into the refrigerated truck or reefer for packing.
  • Do not cycle incubation racks through fruit rooms. The humid, caustic air rusts shelving, and stainless steel is very expensive.
  • Dense trolley packing is used at a European substrate company (name unconfirmed) and is credited to two growers, one of them Gary Mills at Mycopia (maitake; unconfirmed). It works only with ventilation channels left through the pack.

Typical setups on working farms: tall pallet racking with wooden slat decks and blocks packed side by side several rows deep with open aisles; a long aisle of green-framed pallet racking with slat decks, filter-patch blocks in rows with gaps between them and ducting overhead; cross-braced pallet racks 4 ft (1.2 m) deep and 12 ft (3.7 m) tall with a 4 ft (1.2 m) aisle; galvanized rolling racks with about seven wire shelves on orange casters; and wire racks packed with tall filter-patch bags.

Spacing and loading

AT A GLANCE Leave two hand widths between bags on every side and above. Fill a room to about 1/10 to 1/4 of its volume, and never more than half. Spread each week's batch across the shelves.

Space between bags

Pack as many bags as you can without hurting their metabolism or making the room uneven.

RANGE Standard: two hand widths between bags on all sides, including above (a hand width is roughly 8-10 cm, 3-4 in). The bare minimum is room to fit one hand between bags; close up toward it only once a logger shows the cores staying below 21-22 °C (70-72 °F). Spawn bags need even wider spacing because of their tighter filters.

  • Bags that touch at peak growth (two oyster bags, for example) make dead spots and local heat. The contact area stays sawdust-coloured and loosely colonized. This is often blamed on lack of light, but the cause is heat.
  • Even with a high room air exchange, touching blocks form hot junctions.
  • For shiitake, where two blocks touch, that patch will not buckle and will not fruit, because buckling maps where primordia (baby mushrooms) will form. Space every block so air reaches all sides; spacing breaks up heat pockets.
  • Overstuffed racks produce less than fewer, healthier blocks.

Example: a shelf 5 bags deep and 10 bags long, with a hand's width between bags, holds 50 bags. A rack of about 10 such shelves holds about 500 blocks, giving off about 1,000 BTU/h (about 290 W) per rack, and more in poorly ventilated pockets.

  • "Make smaller substrates and space them more apart": they stay cooler and get more air around them, so shiitake "buckle and brown nicely". Open-bottom (wire) shelves are fine.
  • A small incubation room in a hot city. A Houston farm's incubation room is 3.4 x 7.3 m (11 x 24 ft), with about 40 wire racks of 1.2 x 1.8 m (4 x 6 ft), NSF-rated (food-safe), each holding about 60 bags: close to 2,000 bags in all, cooled by a 2-ton (7 kW) air conditioner. Bags are kept "pretty spaced". Moving racks in and out is like a sliding-block puzzle: "not efficient", but efficiency was never the goal.

How full to load the room

RANGE Standard: racks and blocks take up about 1/10 to 1/4 of the room's volume, because overpacking dries things out and builds heat and CO2. This is Cap n Stem's rule for fruit rooms, applied with the same caution to incubation.

  • Ceiling for incubation: the load should never take more than about half of the room's cubic footage.
  • The older "one-third rule" for incubation and fruiting rooms (attributed to Paul Stamets' writing) is still widely quoted.
  • Context: tall, dense racks can go past these figures only when cooling and air movement are sized for the full load (see racks).

Worked example: a room 10 m x 6 m x 3 m high (33 x 20 x 10 ft) has 180 m³ (6,360 cu ft). The standard 1/10 to 1/4 is 18-45 m³ (640-1,590 cu ft) of racks and blocks; the half-room ceiling is 90 m³ (3,180 cu ft).

  • Packing rooms to make them "efficient" raises the CO2, humidity and temperature burden, slows growth and causes more bacterial trouble.
  • A new, large, lightly loaded room behaves differently, because each bag has more air. Bring it up to a steady load quickly and do not leave it unattended, or blocks overgrow or go patchy from too much oxygen.

CASE An upstate New York farm packed its incubation room solid and ran no fans. It is the standard warning example of what overloading does.

RULE Plan at least as much incubation space as fruiting space; 1:1 is the bare minimum, and most new growers plan less. Cap n Stem's advice: "if you're doing just oysters, try like four to one". New growers badly underestimate incubation space. You can squeeze in more blocks, but they overheat and come out poor quality. One Australian farm sublet space in the next building for extra incubation.

  • Colonizing blocks produce a lot of heat, so cooling them in a hot summer costs a lot.
  • Slow species take space. A rack of maitake sits for weeks without moving while the rest of the room turns over "10 times"; one California farm reckons that rack could instead have fruited about 500 lb (230 kg) of oysters. Chestnut takes a quarter of the same farm's incubation room.

Placing batches on the racks

  1. Do not put a whole day's or week's batch of one species in one block of shelving.
  2. Stagger weeks across shelves: week 1 of oyster on one shelf, week 2 above it, and continue the pattern on the next unit, so heat output is spread out. Avoid complete randomness; keep a pattern you can follow.
  3. Mix low-heat species (pioppino) with high-heat ones (oyster, chestnut).
  4. Keep aisles wide and do not move shelves. Bumping blocks or moving racks can shock shiitake into pinning.

CASE One winter a row filled entirely with pioppino ran cold (a faulty cooling unit added to the problem). Pioppino makes far less heat per pound and grows slowly. Mixing it with chestnut or oyster evens the room out.

  • Block size changes how heat stratifies on a shelf. Five 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks deep get very hot in the middle, while 4-5 lb (1.8-2.3 kg) blocks stratify far less. Fans barely reach a block that is insulated by its neighbors.
  • Rack centres run about a week behind rack edges when light, air and heat are uneven, and the top of a rack may buckle and brown faster. Once most shiitake blocks are about 90% brown, fruit them all; small differences wash out.

Heat: where it comes from and when it peaks

AT A GLANCE Colonizing blocks make heat. Richer recipes, more spawn, bigger blocks and finer substrate make more. Heat peaks near the end of colonization. Size cooling for about 6-10 BTU/h per 10 lb block until you have measured your own rooms.

What makes blocks hot

Factor Effect on heat
Block size 5 lb (2.3 kg) and 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks have different temperature regimes; bigger blocks run hotter
Recipe richness More nitrogen and more supplement mean more heat
Poor mixing Nitrogen hot spots respire harder and push out more gas and heat; the mix must be homogeneous for even heat production (see Chapter 10)
Spawn rate Very high spawn rates act as a strong supplement and make blocks run hot, especially in an already rich mix
Through-spawning Mixing spawn through the whole block, which is necessary for ultra-pasteurized substrate, needs more cooling capacity than top spawning
Poor shaking Grain clumps generate excess heat; in ultra-pasteurized substrate the overheating can kill the mycelium (see Chapter 11)
Too-fine substrate Powdery wheat middlings pack into a dense cake with dense mycelium that cannot shed heat
Grain versus wood Grain (rye) is a hotter medium than wood-based masters mix and makes much more heat per volume. Rich grain like millet can spike very fast; a leaner "European mix" (exact recipe unconfirmed) spikes less
Species Pioppino produces much less heat per pound than oyster or chestnut
Shape Logs and cylinders shed heat better than a fat block with little surface area
  • Heavy spawning gives hot, fast colonization; light spawning gives "low and slow". At the light end, do not stretch one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag over more than 30 ten-pound blocks (about 0.2 lb or 90 g, 2%, per block). The usual rate in this book is 3% (0.3 lb or 136 g per block, 20 blocks per bag).
  • Over-spawned lion's mane makes more heat and more bacteria.
  • G1 bags started from an agar wedge begin with no heat, but later produce nearly as much heat per pound as heavily spawned bags.

WARNING 10 lb (4.5 kg) is the practical maximum in polypropylene bags with a small filter. At 12 lb (5.4 kg), blocks cannot breathe, go anaerobic (run out of oxygen) and overheat, with core temperatures around 32 °C (90 °F). Some producers still make 12 lb bags, without higher yields.

CASE Before one farm installed rooftop cooling units, overheating blocks in summer were a serious problem. A partner once proposed coring a void in each block with a wine bottle to reduce internal heat. It was not adopted; better cooling was the answer.

CASE A Maine farm that bought its blocks switched part of its order from shiitake (about 8 weeks in the room) to lion's mane and chestnut. "All of a sudden my air conditioning problems went away", and space was freed too. As the owner put it, "if eight weeks of shiitake disappear, four weeks of lion's mane appear".

When the heat peaks

  • Peak heat output comes at the end of colonization: about day 11 for oyster spawn and day 11-12 for oyster blocks.
  • Output is low at first and spikes near the end, as the last patches close.
  • Blocks at different stages produce different amounts of heat and CO2. Heat is mainly an incubation problem; fully colonized blocks are past their hottest phase.
  • For shiitake, the initial spawn run to a fully white block is the hottest, highest-CO2 phase. Metabolic spikes come at the transitions, especially as the spawn run consolidates.
  • Heat, CO2 and metabolism feed each other: more CO2 means more heat, and more heat means more CO2. Design the layout around this. Too much heat plus too much CO2 cascades into bacterial and mold blooms.
  • A broken-up stroma bag (a bag where the mycelium has formed a tough, leathery mat) pulled from a cooler felt about 38 °C (100 °F), much hotter than the healthy mycelium next to it.
  • No peak day is recorded for other species. Put a logger in a bag to find your own.

RULE Run incubation as a rolling load, so total heat output stays steady. Fill-then-empty batch cycles, common on cubensis farms, never reach thermal equilibrium.

How much heat

Heat output is usually quoted in BTU per hour (BTU/h; 1 BTU/h is about 0.29 W). The figures in use differ, so the table converts each one to a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block.

Figure given Basis For a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block Use
About 1 BTU/h per pound of substrate Wet substrate About 10 BTU/h (2.9 W) Sizing (high end)
About 2 BTU/h per pound of dry substrate A 10 lb block holds about 3.3 lb (1.5 kg) of dry matter About 6 BTU/h (1.8 W) Sizing (low end)
About 3.5 BTU per 10 lb bag, quoted as "per pound of dry substrate" Units and basis unconfirmed About 3.5 BTU/h (1.0 W) (unconfirmed) Not for sizing
About 2 BTU/h while colonizing (low at first, spiking near the end) A 10 lb block held at the ideal core-to-surface differential About 2 BTU/h (0.6 W) Low-end estimate
About 1,000 BTU/h A rack of about 500 blocks About 2 BTU/h (0.6 W) Low-end estimate

RANGE For sizing cooling, use the higher figures: about 6-10 BTU/h (1.8-2.9 W) per 10 lb block, until you have measured your own rooms. Estimates differ by a factor of about five: about 2 BTU/h per block at the ideal differential, about 6 BTU/h from 2 BTU/h per dry pound, and about 10 BTU/h from 1 BTU/h per pound of substrate.

Worked example: 2,000 blocks x 10 BTU/h = 20,000 BTU/h, about 1.7 tons of cooling or 5.9 kW. Add the heat coming through the roof and walls and from fans and lights (see Chapter 5) before choosing a unit.

Scale makes the difference. Ten blocks are negligible, 200 are noticeable in a small room, and 20,000 are an order of magnitude more.

  • A 10 lb (4.5 kg) or larger block runs about 3 °C (5 °F) warmer at the centre than at the outside. The heat each block makes per hour, times the number of blocks in a room, means you don't need heating even in New England: "you're just cooling all the time".
  • The core-to-surface gap is "extraordinarily different" between block sizes: about 1 °C (2 °F) for a 5 lb block against 3 °C (5-6 °F) for a 10 lb block. The gap depends on the CO2 in the room, how rich the substrate is, the spawn rate and how densely the room is packed, which together set the blocks' metabolic rate.
  • In practice, incubation size has to be matched to the air handling, the set temperature, the blocks' metabolic rate, and a heat exchanger, ERV or HRV (energy or heat recovery ventilator) to remove CO2. "There's no way to get around forced cooling or forced heating."

Cooling and airflow

AT A GLANCE Incubation mostly needs cooling, not heating. Use walk-in-cooler evaporators mounted high, add circulation fans, and keep ducts and pipes away from the racks.

  • Most incubation rooms mainly need cooling, because colonizing bags are exothermic (they give off heat). Heating matters only for small rooms in long cold seasons.
  • Large rooms make so much heat that they need only cooling, even in New England. Example: a room of about 20,000 blocks held 19 °C (66 °F) through a roughly two-day power outage, at −18 °C (0 °F) outside, on block heat alone. The block count where heating stops being needed is not established.

Choosing cooling equipment

The preferred equipment is a walk-in-cooler style evaporator unit, often called a "reefer" unit. The evaporator (the cold coil and its fan) hangs inside the room; the condenser (the unit that dumps the heat outdoors) sits outside, for example on the roof. These units throw a lot of air a long way, blow out air at about 13 °C (55 °F), and can hold blocks at 19 °C (66 °F). Mounted high, they reduce the top-to-bottom temperature difference. Heatcraft and Chandler are two makers of these units in use on farms.

Equipment What it can do When to use it
Walk-in evaporator ("reefer") units with outdoor condensers Can be set anywhere from about 19 °C (66 °F) down to freezing; can go as low as 2 °C (35 °F); move enough air to solve airflow too. Units differ in coil size and depth, fan speed and refrigerant, which changes how much they dehumidify. The simplest affordable way to hold temperature Recommended for any commercial room, and needed for large incubation of 4,000-6,000 sq ft (370-560 m²)
Standard split HVAC unit Holds about 18-20 °C (65-68 °F) at best and prefers about 22 °C (72 °F); struggles on 38 °C (100 °F) days Not for large rooms; otherwise you end up adding many fans
Window or portable ducted AC unit Fine at very small scale Only with a couple of racks, and only if you do not cram the room

Cap n Stem's block incubation is held at 19 °C (66 °F) by four evaporators with roof condensers. The air is unfiltered, which is fine for substrate.

WARNING An overloaded room was cooled by one 7.5-ton (about 26 kW) unit for 4,500 sq ft (420 m²) of incubation. The results are described under vertical stratification.

Air movement

  • Incubation, unlike fruiting, needs lots of recirculating air. Example: with 15 ft (4.6 m) ceilings, stratification (layering of warm air over cool) can reach 16 °C (60 °F) at the bottom and 27 °C (80 °F) at the top. You then get bad blocks at the top and bottom, and acceptable ones only in the middle.
  • Oscillating or circulation fans help break up stratified pockets in dense incubation. Sealed bags will not dry out much if room CO2 is steady.
  • Mount evaporators high and use circulation fans (see vertical stratification).
  • The interiors of racks are always the hardest to ventilate. Too much airflow (lab-style gushing) seems to harm shiitake buckling. The goal is just enough movement for even temperature and CO2.

WARNING Keep pipes and ducts away from the racks. Cooling pipes drip condensation onto bags. Ducts radiate heat: one farm ran the duct of a 7.5-ton unit serving its spawn room (switching between heating and cooling with the seasons) down the middle of block incubation, and got row-to-row differences in temperature and growth until it found the cause.

WARNING If cooling fails, a dense incubation room becomes intolerably hot surprisingly fast. Have a backup way to move air in and out. Shiitake suffers first.

CASE On a spawn supplier's advice, one farm covered its maitake shelves with black plastic to block light. The plastic killed the airflow and the blocks failed. Lesson: never block airflow to control light.

Temperature

AT A GLANCE Hold 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at 19 °C (66 °F) measured on the outside of the bag; the core then sits about 2-3 °C (4-5 °F) warmer and must stay below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F). Run grain spawn cooler, at 17-18 °C (63-65 °F). Stability matters more than the exact number.

Why the bag surface is the reference

Measure at the bag surface, because that is what you can reach; the core is warmer, because the mycelium makes heat. The gap between the core and the bag surface is the core-to-surface differential.

Keep that gap as small as possible for even, clean growth. It widens with poor airflow and with too-fine substrate, so narrow it with more air movement, coarser substrate and wider spacing.

WHY Ultra-pasteurization holds substrate at up to 100 °C (212 °F) for about 3 hours. (The 93 °C, 200 °F, quoted earlier is the temperature of blocks as they leave the barrel, not the cook temperature.) It does not kill everything: steam kills active bacteria, but they quickly form heat-resistant spores (endospores), and the mycelium has to out-compete these survivors. In a warmer room the endospores wake up. This is why Cap n Stem holds 10 lb ultra-pasteurized shiitake incubation at 19 °C (66 °F).

The figure below sums up the ideal: a 10 lb filter-patch block cooked at 100 °C (212 °F) for 3 hours, 19 °C (66 °F) outside the bag, about 21 °C (69-70 °F) at the core, about 2 BTU/h of heat, room CO2 of 2,500-3,000 ppm and a 5,000 ppm limit.

The spring transition is hardest, because he is running the wood boiler and the air conditioners in the same week. For about eight weeks twice a year the systems aren't fighting the weather and "the mushrooms just do what they want".

Why the core temperature matters

Too hot:

  • If the core passes about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F), especially in 10 lb blocks, colonization suffers and problems such as blotch increase.
  • Above 19 °C (66 °F) ambient, black oyster cores overheat at peak metabolism, causing stroma, bacterial trouble and slower pin set after the bag is cut.
  • A temperature spike can compromise a block without visible signs. A severe spike can leave a block that colonizes and looks normal but never fruits. Even brief spikes can do permanent harm.
  • Shiitake strains 3790 and 3782 incubated too hot can buckle and brown normally and then fruit nothing ("duds").
  • Squishy blocks show heat stress and cell death in the core, and will not fruit.
  • Lion's mane on a rich 50/50 recipe gives more yellow liquid at the bag bottom. The working explanation: a hot core lets dormant bacterial endospores germinate, conditions turn wet and anaerobic, and the mycelium pumps out defensive metabolites.
  • Neurospora (an orange mold) is more common in warm, poorly regulated incubation. High-CO2 rooms tend to be hot.

Too cold:

  • Too cool slows colonization. Hotter rooms and bigger blocks speed up metabolism and heat output.
  • Cold corners measured at 14-16 °C (58-60 °F), against a 19 °C (66-67 °F) set point, slowed chestnut and pioppino by about a week.

Stability and swings

RULE Stability beats precision. Incubation stability (temperature, airflow and light) is the key.

WARNING Accidental shock (an AC failure, a temperature drop, bumping blocks, moving shelves) triggers pinning inside the bag in shiitake. Higher-nitrogen blocks and later stages are more prone, but it can happen as soon as buckling finishes. Top-shelf blocks that fall are known as "suicide blocks". Move triggered blocks promptly into fruiting or a cooler.

Vertical stratification

Warm air rises, so the top of a tall room runs hotter than the bottom.

  • Signs: same strain, same batch and same day, yet top-shelf bags are dense, hard, swollen with liquid and perhaps starting stroma, while bottom bags are still patchy with no metabolite colour. The top-to-bottom difference can be dramatic, for example 27 °C (80 °F) against 10 °C (50 °F).
  • Light and heat both stratify, so the top of the rack is brighter and hotter.
  • Fix: mount evaporators high to reduce the top-to-bottom difference, and use circulation fans.

CHECK Bags on the top and bottom shelves should read within a degree or two of each other. If they do not, add recirculation before changing the set point.

CASE An overloaded room (one 7.5-ton, about 26 kW, unit for 4,500 sq ft, 420 m²) browned shiitake well a third of the way up the racks and less well above that. At the top, single blocks showed every stage at once: smooth, buckled, fruiting and brown. Shiitake is hard to do well in 10 lb blocks.

Measuring temperature

Temperature is the data point that matters most in this work: in sterilization, in incubation and in shipping.

Procedure: log the temperature inside a bag

  1. When you open a bag to inoculate it, push a datalogger or thermocouple probe into the core of the substrate, then seal the bag as normal. (The bag has already been steamed, so the probe goes in at the knock.)
  2. Place a second logger outside the bag on the same shelf, to compare inside and outside readings.
  3. Place further loggers at several spots in the room (top, middle and bottom shelves; corners; near ducts) to check the room thermostats.
  4. Leave the bag logger in through the whole incubation to watch the internal temperature surge and fall. For shiitake, follow one block through its roughly three-month incubation and into fruiting; set the shortest logging interval the logger's memory allows for that long.
  5. Walk the room with a handheld infrared (IR) thermometer for spot checks between downloads. Readings vary, so keep a second instrument to cross-check any reading that looks wrong.

CHECK The core should stay below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F) at the peak, and different shelves should read within a degree or two of each other. If they do not, find the cause before changing anything else.

TIP MadgeTech data loggers are one brand in use; MadgeTech also makes humidity and gas loggers.

CASE In a room with uneven growth, staff first blamed the spawn. Loggers showed the cause was supplemental AC ducting, not the main cooling units. Lesson: log several spots in the room before blaming spawn or culture.

CASE A California grower began probing block cores during incubation instead of pointing an infrared gun at the bag surface, and it changed how he cools his rooms. When he moved from 5 lb to 10 lb blocks the room ran about 5-6 °C (10 °F) warmer. He now holds the room at about 20 °C (68 °F), which keeps the blocks at about 23 °C (74 °F) on average. Growers who say "we keep our rooms at 66" (19 °C) often forget how much heat 10 lb blocks make. An infrared thermometer reads only the surface.

CO2

AT A GLANCE Some CO2 is good in incubation: it keeps mycelium growing instead of pinning. Hold the room at about 1,500-3,000 ppm with a CO2-switched exhaust or heat recovery ventilator. Never let it pass 5,000 ppm where people work, and never let it drop to around 500 ppm.

What CO2 does

  • Elevated CO2, in the bag and to a degree in the room, keeps mycelium vegetative (growing, not fruiting) and delays pinning. Fresh oxygen pushes it toward fruiting.
  • For spawn, aim to catch the bag just past full coverage, as it starts to densify. Higher CO2 widens that window.
  • Most species colonize faster and more safely at higher CO2, with a more restrictive filter patch on the bag.
  • Mycelium breathes as people do. A crowded incubation room behaves like a packed dance party: more activity, more CO2 and more heat. CO2 matters little at hobby scale and dominates at commercial scale (a point made by Amanda of KM Mushrooms; name unconfirmed).

Controlling CO2

  • Use an exhaust or makeup-air fan, ideally an HRV (heat recovery ventilator) or ERV (energy recovery ventilator) that swaps room air with outside air while recovering heat, switched by a CO2 controller to hold about 1,500-3,500 ppm.
  • On grow-room controllers, "veg" mode (wide differential, high ppm) suits incubation, and "flower" mode (narrow differential, low ppm) suits fruiting.
  • Keep the swing fairly narrow: a band that is too wide drives metabolic heat.
  • Makeup air can come from a cooler, lower-CO2 part of the building instead of hot outdoor air.
  • For big rooms, recirculate through the reefer units and exhaust only occasionally, to hold 2,000-3,000 ppm.
  • Another approach (Erik Lomen of Cap n Stem): recirculate incubation air through the AC with no fresh-air intake. Let CO2 leave by leakage or by a CO2-controlled exhaust at around 3,000 ppm, and keep the room slightly negative so the gas never reaches clean areas (see Chapter 5).
  • Air-condition the incubation room and fit a CO2 monitor (advice from High Country Fungi).

WARNING Without an extraction system already in place, a cooling shortfall on the hottest days starts the heat-CO2 spiral and spoils blocks. In a power outage, CO2 climbs fast, because blocks keep respiring with no exhaust.

WARNING Do not lower CO2 by suddenly dropping the temperature. It shocks shiitake and can trigger pinning in the bag.

Procedure: set up CO2 control

  1. Fit a CO2 monitor in the room at mid-rack bag height, away from the exhaust and the cooling unit's outlet. In a tall room, a second monitor near the top racks shows any CO2 layering.
  2. Install an exhaust fan, or better an HRV/ERV, switched by a CO2 controller.
  3. Set the controller to switch on at 3,000 ppm and off at 1,500-2,500 ppm to start (lower off points mean fresher air and more fan time). Keep the band fairly narrow, and adjust later from your logs (other growers use on 3,500 / off 1,500).
  4. Draw makeup air from a cooler, lower-CO2 part of the building where you can.
  5. Never send incubation air to the fruit rooms. Do not use the incubation HVAC to condition other rooms if that drags incubation CO2 below its band (see the case below); a lab may borrow incubation air only while the incubation monitor still reads at least 1,500 ppm.

CHECK Over a full day the room reading should stay inside about 1,500-3,000 ppm, never fall toward 500 ppm and never pass 5,000 ppm.

Too much air exchange

CASE A consulting client used its incubation HVAC to condition other rooms, which held incubation at about 500 ppm. The result was patchy growth and splotchy, drying shiitake blocks. Too much exchange also drops humidity, so bags lose weight through the patch.

Grain (up to about 50% moisture) and substrate (in the 60s %) dry out quickly with too much exchange, unlike liquid culture.

CO2 and staff safety

WARNING The OSHA workplace limit (a US safety standard) is 5,000 ppm averaged over a shift. Spikes happen: one farm's incubation once ran at about 7,000 ppm. Monitor CO2 wherever people work, and never sleep in incubation. See Chapter 18.

CO2 was the likely cause, and there was no CO2 meter in that incubation room. Staff had also napped on the incubation scaffolding. Lesson: never sleep in incubation, and monitor CO2 wherever people work.

Bags, patches and headspace

AT A GLANCE The bag's filter patch and headspace set how much CO2 and heat stay in the bag. A tighter patch keeps more CO2 (faster, safer colonization) but more heat; a more open patch breathes more but dries the block. Bag details are in Chapter 11.

A filter patch is the breathing window on the bag. Its micron rating is the size of particle it stops: the smaller the number, the tighter the patch, and the more CO2 and heat it keeps in the bag. Choose bags on two criteria: how they perform against contamination in your environment, and enough gas exchange to avoid a CO2 build-up that stunts the mycelium.

10 lb blocks in XLS-A bags (name unconfirmed), 0.5 micron patch Breathe out a lot of CO2
Older Tyvek-patch bags (3T-type, and John Donahue's Northwest Mycological bags) Trap CO2 and puff up; fine for 5 lb blocks, but too much CO2 and heat for bigger bags, where the core would go anaerobic. They lowered air-exchange needs and are now discontinued
B-patch bags with chestnut Far too much air exchange; dried a crust on the block tops, so chestnut needs a tighter patch
  • Open A patches give faster colonization and heavier fruit than the old Tyvek bags, at a higher utility cost (more ventilation and cooling).
  • Headspace trade-off: a headspace (the empty air space above the substrate, a bag "plenum") raises CO2 during incubation, which is good for substrate, but allows more water loss. No headspace gives more even oxygen and less drying, which is better for spawn.
  • By volume, a block bag should be about one third substrate and two thirds headspace (a rule from John Donahue, a bag and spawn supplier). XLS-A bags filled to about 9.8 lb (4.4 kg) are a little short of that. Headspace lets CO2 diffuse out through the patch.
  • Zip-tied bags with a small headspace colonized more slowly and differently.
  • Blocks lose moisture through the patch during incubation. Bag at 61-62% moisture to reach about 60% at fruiting (see Chapter 10). Shiitake is made wetter, partly because of its long incubation.

TIP Choose by what you see. Dried crusts on block tops: use a tighter patch. Blocks overheating or going anaerobic: use a more open one. Whether spawn or substrate bags usually carry the tighter patch is stated both ways in the sources, so check the specification of the bags you actually buy; in-bag CO2 for different patches has not been measured.

Black bags

  • Black bags block light, so the mycelium keeps maturing without pinning. This widens the holding window and lets pins form only at the cut.
  • A 10 lb clear oyster bag colonized in 10-14 days will pin straight away unless refrigerated. Black bags extend that window.
  • Black bags have noticeably raised yields for several species. Clear bags remain useful for spotting contamination or stroma.

TIP In a black-bag batch, keep about one clear indicator bag in 20 to judge progress.

Light

AT A GLANCE Keep most species dim or dark in early incubation (black bags help). Shiitake and maitake are the exceptions: they need even light from the aisles. Chestnut and lion's mane must be kept away from bright light. Never put strong cold light close above the hot top shelf.

Light colour is given in kelvin (K): about 6,500 K is cold, bluish daylight white; about 1,500 K is a deep red-amber.

General rules

  • Early incubation of nearly all species, including cordyceps, goes best in dim light or darkness. Black bags help.
  • Oysters can go through every stage to fruiting readiness in darkness. Shiitake is the clearest case of a species that needs light cues.
  • Light can ruin a batch. The US and Canadian growing community has only recently started taking light seriously.
  • Chinese and Japanese practice uses warm light for incubation and cool light for fruiting, mimicking the seasons. Light colour can change mushroom colour, size, taste, texture and fruiting speed.

WARNING Strong, cold light (for example 6,500 K) close above the top rack, where bags are hottest at the patch, burns mycelium. Red-spectrum light around 1,500 K or lower is considered safe. The damage shows as dry, dead sawdust at the top of the block.

Laying out the lights

  • Hang lamps over the roughly 4 ft (1.2 m) aisles between rack rows, so the light is indirect and even. Point aisle lights inward toward the racks.
  • Light stratifies like heat: with ceiling lights above a rack, the top-shelf blocks get the most light and the most heat.
  • Spawn rooms: pitch dark would be best biologically (especially for lion's mane), but staff need to work. One idea for future spawn rooms is to copy the red-lit rodent rooms used at the Jackson Laboratory.

CHECK For light-needing species, if you cannot see into the centre of a rack well enough to spot contamination, there is not enough light.

Motion-sensor lighting works in some rooms and not others:

Room Lighting Why
Block incubation (general) Dim, indirect light most of the time; motion-sensor lights that switch off after 10-15 seconds where staff need to see Recommended default
Lion's mane blocks Dim most of the time, motion-sensor lights for work Constant lights made it pin more and earlier
Spawn incubation Dim, indirect light only; no motion-sensor flash A sudden bright flash proved too strong a trigger

RANGE Colour of light. Warm light for incubation is the traditional Asian practice. One farm uses 6,500 K all-spectrum lights in shiitake incubation, while Far East shiitake practice uses red-spectrum lights. No lux figures are available for any species.

Too little light shows as brown primordia only around the edge of the block top. Blue spectrum is often recommended to start in-bag primordia; red spectrum is suggested for fine control. Humidity

  • Incubation humidity only needs to avoid extremes; the bags handle it.
  • Excess air exchange lowers room humidity, and bags then lose weight through the patch.
  • There is no target RH (relative humidity) figure for incubation rooms; humidity control matters in fruiting (see Chapter 14).

RANGE Humidity in incubation. Standard (Cap n Stem): no humidifier in incubation. Cap n Stem's incubation runs at about 16-21 °C (60-70 °F) all year, even in the driest winter, without added humidity. Context: in an arid climate the air conditioner can dry an incubation room enough that some growers add humidity there. An Oregon grower humidifies because his cooling "is pulling water out. If there's no water to pull out, there's nothing to cool". What works in a dry place does not apply in a humid one such as Mississippi.

  • Block filter patches breathe, so the room's humidity slowly changes block moisture. A New Hampshire farm's incubation air runs at about 50-60% RH in summer and about 30% in winter, so it adjusts substrate moisture with the season. A 1% change in moisture shows up "on the back end" in yield.

Species timings and readiness

AT A GLANCE Oysters and lion's mane are ready in about 10-14 days; king oyster in 14-18; chestnut and pioppino about 3 weeks or more; shiitake 6-14 weeks; maitake's top is cut at about weeks 5-8 and it reaches harvest at about 8-12 weeks, plus about a week to finish. For chestnut, shiitake and maitake, white is not ready. Full species profiles are in Chapter 20 and growth numbers in Chapter 21.

Other working farms report these incubation times: black pearl oyster about 18 days at 18 °C (65 °F) in black bags; maitake about 8 weeks; chestnut about 5 weeks in incubation, then 3 weeks fruiting; golden, pink and blue oyster 9-10 days. See Chapter 26.

Blue oyster

Blue oyster colonizes a 10 lb clear bag in 10-14 days and pins at once unless chilled. Left too long, oysters consolidate into a thick mat and become slow and reluctant to fruit. Aggressive blue oyster in big, rich, packed grain bags is a stroma risk, so control the ambient temperature.

Black oyster (black pearl)

  • Fully colonized and fruitable in about 10 days with good temperature control, then an unusually long grace period before it pins in the bag. Cap n Stem ships it at 12-13 days.
  • Block mycelium starts light white and becomes fluffy and brick-dense, with some sheath on top, but much less rubbery than blue oyster.
  • In an agar liquid culture (ALC) trial, black oyster colonized in about 2 weeks, like chestnut. Blocks pulled at 2 weeks and at 3 weeks behaved differently, which suggests a maturation threshold. A block pulled early still matures, but it does so in the fruit room.
  • Longer incubation (2.5-3 weeks) plus side fruiting raised yields by an estimated 0.5-1 lb (0.2-0.5 kg) per block. The numbers were small, and drying of one face is a possible confound. Even so, an extra week can mean more income per run.
  • Black oysters can form puffs or mounds at the cut sites, with pins on them.

King oyster

  • Plan 14-18 days. On substrate it spreads from each spawn grain as dense, expanding circles. Early on these circles are separate, so a young king oyster block can look patchy like pioppino; that is normal. Left too long it forms a thin, shiny skin on all sides.
  • In typical incubation (elevated CO2, diffuse light), kings form a skin and pin only after that, which is best avoided. Freshly colonized blocks give the most even pin set.
  • Poor shaking can stretch colonization to 3 weeks. Low spawn rates lengthen it and cut yields sharply.

Lion's mane

  • One farm's house strain looks ghostly and wispy, as if contaminated, yet it is fully colonized in about 10 days, and the top quickly fills with primordia even where there is no spawn.
  • A one-week block is still fluffy and under-colonized; it ships the following week. Its bag's large patch and headspace give more gas exchange, so it colonizes lightly and fruits on top of the bag.
  • The mycelium stays faint in incubation and densifies only in fruiting, with light and oxygen.
  • Readiness cue: a marshmallowy pillow of aerial mycelium on the top surface where room light hits. Slack bags put primordia into the nooks of the bag.
  • Past 16-18 days the primordial mat on top complicates fruiting.
  • Its speed sits between the oysters and slow species like chestnut. It likes a steady temperature and should be kept from running hot, as with shiitake.

Comb tooth

Comb tooth colonizes much denser and firmer than lion's mane and digests substrate toward fruiting faster. A comb tooth block knocked two days later than a lion's mane block was further along.

Chestnut

Plan chestnut at 4-6 weeks unless space forces you to go earlier (3 weeks is the earliest). It is a good species to grow after blue oyster for learning that white does not mean ready, and ripening in the bag also keeps blocks safer from contamination than sitting in a fruiting room.

Week What you see
About 2 Full but faint colonization; blocks start to secrete yellow, orange and caramel metabolites and become pock-marked
3 Noticeably firm: the earliest point to fruit. White, with slight yellowing
4 A rust-coloured or orange-caramel band forms in the headspace, under the headspace line
3-6 Ripening to full maturity; blocks swell with caramel metabolites
  • Fruited at full white colonization, chestnut gives a lower yield (the substrate is explored but not digested) and a very slow pin. Ripening another 1-2 weeks or longer, until the block swells with caramel metabolites, gives faster pin set, faster harvest and more vigorous fruit.

RULE If incubation space is the bottleneck, fruit chestnut sooner. If the fruit room is the bottleneck, or neither is, let the blocks sit and ripen.

  • Ripened chestnut can wait without fruiting, so it works as a buffer crop to smooth out other species' peaks.
  • Chestnut is not weak, and it has clear temperature thresholds where its vigor jumps, but it is less tenacious than oyster, so expect somewhat higher contamination.
  • In short: 2-3 weeks to colonize fully and 3-6 weeks to ripen. A CO2 figure of "below 900 ppm" is also given for chestnut without saying which stage it is for. It is far below the incubation band, so it most likely applies to fruiting (see Chapter 14).
  • Agar-slurry inoculated chestnut bags showed nothing for about 2 weeks and then were suddenly fully colonized.

Pioppino

Pioppino colonizes blocks in splotches that look like bacteria or contamination but are not. It takes about 3 weeks for the colonies to join and consolidate. King oyster also starts in separate patches that join, at its own pace. Pioppino is shipped at about week 3; batches a week apart show the progression clearly.

Shiitake

AT A GLANCE Three phases: spawn run (about weeks 1-2), buckling (about weeks 3-5) and browning (about weeks 5-13). Hold 19 °C (66 °F), give even light and gentle air, never shock the blocks, and fruit at 75-80% brown or more.

Phase Weeks (10 lb block) What happens What it needs
1. Spawn run About 1-2 Colonization to a fully white block; safe from contamination after 2-3 weeks; the hottest, highest-CO2 phase Temperature
2. Buckling About 3-5 Surface cracks and blisters as a protective skin forms Temperature plus airflow
3. Browning About 5-13 The skin turns brown Temperature plus airflow plus light

Total time is 6 to 13-14 weeks depending on strain. All three phases need a steady 19 °C (66 °F); swings between 16 and 27 °C (60-80 °F) are what to avoid.

Buckling is the surface of the block cracking and blistering into bumps as the protective skin forms. Browning is that skin turning brown. To judge percent brown, look at the block through the bag and estimate how much of the surface area has turned brown.

RANGE Recommended: plan a 10 lb spawn run of about 2 weeks and use the table above. Other schedules in use, for other strains and recipes:

  • One grower: weeks 1-4 wispy colonization (the block still breaks if squeezed); weeks 4-8 densification, with some bumpy texture or browning at the end; weeks 8-12 buckling (some growers call this bumpy stage "popcorning"; it is not the swing fault of that name), with the substrate visibly shifting day to day, then browning over the whole bag and pins in weeks 11-12.
  • A shorter version: colonize weeks 1-4, bumpy pinning texture weeks 5-8, browning weeks 7-12.
  • Spawn run: 2-3 weeks; and 1-2 weeks against 2-3 weeks when held at 16 °C (60 °F).

Watch the blocks, not the calendar.

  • A block that colonizes, buckles and browns may still never fruit if one phase was disrupted.
  • Buckling is a stress response that forms a protective skin. In the wild the fungus colonizes dense, dark wood, not loose substrate in a clear bag.
  • The brown skin is only on the outside (the inside of a cut block is white). It is what lets shiitake fruit all over the block.
  • Do not fruit before 75-80% brown. Fruiting at 75-80% gives fewer, larger mushrooms. Leaving it well past fully brown (growers joke "120% brown") gives more, smaller mushrooms and sometimes a higher yield. Choose by your orders and target size.
  • Shipping stage versus too far: a de-bagged block ready to ship is brown and crumbly with sparse cap pins; a block covered in pins and stems has gone too far.
  • If you cannot hold steady temperatures, 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks are far more forgiving; a 10 lb block is "more than twice as hard".
  • Cap n Stem's 10 lb shiitake recipe (30% wheat, 70% red oak by weight, water only) is a softer, less hot mix that lets the three phases proceed. See Chapter 10.

Maitake

Weeks Stage
1-4 Colonization
4-6 "Spider eyes" appear: small moisture bubbles on a pillowy surface; the top turns wavy
4-8 Primordia build from the edges across the top as a raised, bumpy mass
5-8 Primordia rise toward the patch as "hands" (a fist-sized lump) that split into "fingers" (separate lobes): the fist-to-fingers stage

Timing varies from block to block, at 19-20 °C (66-68 °F).

  • Blocks knocked the same week do not synchronize: about half get there on time while others lag or lead, and there is no reliable induction step.
  • Some growers slope the substrate top and others (Far West Fungi, a California farm) keep it perfectly flat by compression, to influence where primordia form.
  • From week 4, check every block weekly. Cut the top off at the fist-to-fingers stage. Large farms give staff a measuring stick so everyone cuts at the same size. Too early gives thick, undifferentiated fronds; too late gives odd growth.
  • Side cutting a black bag (a slit in the side instead of cutting off the top) works if timed when the block is fully colonized, perhaps with early metabolite droplets, but before lobes form on top. This method is credited to a few growers and is not confirmed.
  • Shipping maitake blocks makes little sense, because the long incubation is easily upset by moving them, though some farms do it.

Beech, reishi and turkey tail

  • Beech: incubated with light for a long time. Stretching incubation to 6-8 weeks visibly gives denser, juicier mycelium.
  • Reishi: can stay in the bag for months to a year, growing layers against the bag wall and out of the patch. Antlers held for a year and then stripped can form proper caps within about a month.
  • Turkey tail: blocks left too long become extremely hard and difficult to break up.

Grain spawn incubation

Spawn production is covered in Chapter 9. These are the incubation timings that matter when planning the incubation room. Spawn rooms run at 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) unless the row says otherwise. "Masters" and G1/G2 are the grain generations; the "shake" is breaking up and mixing the grain partway through colonization; "firm" means the bag holds together as one block.

AT A GLANCE Most incubation problems are heat, CO2, light or swings. Look at where in the room and where in the bag the problem sits, log temperatures, and trace by lot before changing anything. The full symptom index is in Chapter 19; contaminants are covered in Chapter 16.

Things that look wrong but are normal

  • Pioppino's splotchy colonization, with uncolonized patches, is normal.
  • Ripening chestnut blocks turn golden-mustard. New staff often mistake this for Neurospora. Tell them apart: chestnut's colour is in the block itself and comes with caramel droplets; Neurospora is orange cobweb growth climbing into the headspace, then powdery orange spores.
  • Lion's mane blocks look ghostly and wispy while colonizing normally. But early lion's mane colonization is so faint that asexual Trichoderma (green mold) can hide in it, showing only as slightly denser matting and a slightly different off-white until it turns green.
  • Yellow secondary metabolites on older shiitake grain and on chestnut and pioppino spawn are normal. Chestnut grain also shows clear water droplets about a week after the yellow ones.

Diagnostic habits

  • Treat lion's mane as an indicator species. A systemic problem (pasteurization, moisture consistency, ambient temperature, lighting, a mold source) may show only on lion's mane while hardier species cope. Do not assume the culture is at fault.
  • Work backwards from data. With dozens of lots a day, knee-jerk changes (changing the incubation temperature, firing someone, swapping filters) waste money.
  • Remove infected bags from incubation immediately. There is nothing to salvage from Neurospora.

Procedure: trace a bad batch

  1. Note the lot, knock date, rack and shelf of every bad bag.
  2. Check whether the bad bags share a spawn lot or a substrate lot. Many failures from one lot point to that lot.
  3. Check the loggers and room readings for those shelves: temperature, CO2 and any swings.
  4. Check the cook records for the batch (Chapter 12).
  5. Change one thing at a time, and watch the next batches before changing another.

CASE One worker's habit of emptying contaminated bags outside let spores blow back into the building. Bag and bin them instead.

CASE A farm's "Neurospora wars" at its first shop ended only when it fixed its bag seals. The causes were zip ties, an overheating impulse sealer that burned micro-holes in the bags, and leaky gussets in the bags of that era. Check your own seals for holes against the light, and set the sealer as Chapter 11 describes.

  • Keep lot traceability (which batch, which spawn, which sawdust) and have data-driven conversations with your block supplier. Variation between sawdust piles changes results.
  • A holding room lets blocks wait and be moved ("birthed") into the fruit room only after they pin, so no fruit-room shelf time is wasted.

An incubation cycle, start to finish

  1. Before the knock, check that an empty rack is waiting (sizing).
  2. Place the new batch following your stagger pattern (placing batches), with two hand widths between bags.
  3. Every day, read the room's temperature and CO2 against the set points and CO2 band, and walk the room with an IR thermometer.
  4. Look over the bags as you walk. Pull any contaminated bag at once and bag and bin it.
  5. Watch each species for its readiness cue (species table), not just the calendar.
  6. Move ready blocks to fruiting (Chapter 14), the cooler (holding) or shipping (Chapter 15).

Starting small

A first incubation room needs little: a window or portable ducted air conditioner is fine with a couple of racks, as long as the room is not crammed. Add a CO2 monitor, a CO2-switched exhaust fan, and one logger in a bag. Move to walk-in evaporator units as the room grows.

Key rules

  1. Hold 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) measured on the bag surface, and keep cores below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F). Run grain spawn cooler, at about 17-18 °C (63-64 °F); black oyster and lion's mane spawn rooms run at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). Set points
  2. Use refrigeration-style evaporator units mounted high, plus circulation fans. Ordinary split HVAC rarely holds 19 °C (66 °F) in a loaded room. Cooling
  3. Size cooling for the full possible load, using the higher heat figures (about 6-10 BTU/h per 10 lb block) until you measure your own. Heat
  4. Leave two hand widths between bags on every side and above; never let blocks touch at peak growth. Spacing
  5. Fill the room to about 1/10 to 1/4 of its volume, never more than half, and run it as a rolling load rather than in fill-and-empty batches. Loading
  6. Stagger each week's batch across shelves, and mix low-heat species (pioppino) with high-heat ones. Placing
  7. Control room CO2 with a CO2-switched exhaust or HRV in a narrow band around 1,500-3,000 ppm; never above 5,000 ppm where people work. CO2
  8. Keep light dim for most species and nearly dark for lion's mane spawn. Give shiitake and maitake even light from the aisles, and keep chestnut away from bright, cold lamps. Light
  9. Stability beats precision: avoid temperature swings, shocks and moving racks, especially for shiitake and chestnut. Stability
  10. Put a logger inside a bag, and log several spots in the room, before blaming spawn or culture. Measuring
  11. Learn each species' readiness cue: white is not ready for chestnut, shiitake or maitake. Species
  12. Keep incubation a single-purpose room, away from hot blocks, cooling blocks and fruit-room air, and pull contaminated bags at once. Location

Open questions

  • Heat output per 10 lb block differs about fivefold between estimates (2, 6 or 10 BTU/h), and no measured data are available. Until you have your own logs, size cooling at 6-10 BTU/h per block.
  • CO2 band figures vary (1,500-3,000, 2,000-3,000, 2,500 ideal, a controller upper point of 3,500 or 4,000 ppm). In-bag CO2 for different patches has not been measured. Until then, start at on 3,000 / off 1,500-2,500 ppm, depending on how much CO2 you tolerate.
  • The order of the Unicorn filter letters (A, B, T) by restrictiveness is unconfirmed and should be checked against the manufacturer's specifications. Whether grain or substrate bags carry the tighter patch is also stated both ways. Until then, judge patches by the blocks (crusts mean too open; overheating means too tight).
  • Room fill: the standard is 1/10 to 1/4 of the room's volume, and never more than half for incubation; the one-third rule is the older rule of thumb. Until you know your rooms, stay inside the standard and log heat and CO2.
  • Motion-sensor lighting is both recommended and found to be too strong a trigger. No lux or light-intensity figures are available for any species. Until then, use the lighting table by room.
  • No target humidity figure is available for incubation rooms.
  • The core-to-surface temperature gap varies between about 2 and 5 °C (3 and 9 °F), depending on the block and the conditions.
  • Incubation room temperatures for king oyster, pioppino, lion's mane blocks and beech are not stated separately from the general 19 °C (66 °F) guidance. Until you have your own data, use 19 °C (66 °F) and log it.
