chapters.html:
Fruit Rooms and Fruiting

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers how to build and run a fruit room (layout, size, materials, drainage, airflow, humidification, temperature control, lighting, cleaning, container and tent setups) and the settings that make blocks fruit well: temperature, humidity, CO2 and fresh air, light, pinning triggers, timelines, flushes, and the shape faults that point back to each setting. The numbers used most:

  • Temperature: 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) for the staple species, about 16 °C (60 °F) as a typical target.
  • CO2: cycle about 450-900 ppm, never above 1,000 ppm; a typical controller setting is fan on at 900, off at 600 ppm.
  • Humidity: let it swing roughly 70% to 90% RH and back, not held saturated. Maitake is the exception (steady 90-93%).
  • Plenum (supply air): at or below about 450 ppm CO2 and lightly humidified to 40-50% RH.
  • Exhaust for a 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) room: 800-1000 CFM straight outside.
  • Time in the room: 2-3 weeks per block for most species.

The core rules: a fruit room is the dirtiest space on the farm, so pull conditioned air one way from a clean plenum and exhaust it outdoors under negative pressure; never recirculate fruit-room air through expensive equipment; automate CO2 before anything else; let humidity and CO2 breathe in a gentle cycle rather than holding the room saturated; and do not overpack. Much of the room advice here comes from working farms, chiefly Wild Fruitings in Augusta, Maine.

This chapter has two halves. Part A (The fruit room) is about building the room and its equipment. Part B (Running the crop) is about the settings, the triggers that make blocks fruit, the timelines and the faults. If you are standing in the room looking for one number, go straight to the species parameter table.

What the fruit room is for

Fruiting is the last stage of production. A fully colonized block arrives from incubation, it is opened or cut, and it produces mushrooms (the fruit bodies of the fungus). The room's job is to give the right signals and to keep the developing mushrooms healthy.

  • The block supplies about 99% of the water the fruit needs (for example a block at 63% moisture). The room's job is to allow evaporation alternating with condensation and humidification, so the fruit body forms properly.
  • Mushrooms draw water from the block (around 62% moisture). Caps that get soaked by the room lead to bacterial blotch and other problems.
  • Young primordia (the first tiny mushroom beginnings, also called pins) draw on the block, but developing fruit responds to the air. So sediment and microbes in humidifier water reach the fruit. Blotch and rose comb come from the humidity, not the block.
  • As farms scale, unexplained blotch and contamination often trace back to the fruit-room humidifier, not to the spawn or block supplier.
  • When blotch gets out of hand it is usually tied to the humidification method. The two factors to look at are where the air comes from and how it is filtered, and where the water comes from and how it is treated.
  • "Proper humidification" means a fine mist, in-line filtered water, no recirculation, and accurate measurement.
  • Fungal form depends heavily on environment: fruit bodies grown in the dark look bizarre.

WHY Fruiting is the one stage where CO2, humidity and cooling are all regulated, and where some swing is allowed; incubation is held constant. No air may pass into or out of fruiting from the other zones.

Part A. The fruit room

The facility: three spaces, one-way air

AT A GLANCE Three spaces: a cold room, a plenum that is also the work area, and the fruit rooms. Air flows one way: outside → plenum → fruit room → outside. Fruiting never shares air with incubation.

A fruiting facility needs three spaces:

Space What it does Key rules
Cold room (reefer or walk-in) Stores incoming blocks and fresh mushrooms Hold 1-4 °C (34-40 °F) and no warmer. Use a walk-in or a CoolBot room. Doesn't need to connect to the plenum; better kept out of the plenum and away from the fruit rooms, mainly because of spore load.
Plenum (also the work area) Harvesting, grading, packing (and dehydrating). Captures and conditions the fresh air that feeds the fruit rooms. Not an entrance, bathroom or office. Can sit in front of the rooms, above them, or in a separate building with ducting.
Fruit rooms Where blocks fruit Must connect to the plenum.

Fruit rooms generally have three parts: a heating/cooling unit, the plenum, and the room itself.

A generic layout

The simplest layout splits a rectangle in half. One half is the plenum. The other half is divided again into fruit rooms 1 and 2. Air comes in from the plenum side and leaves through the far outside wall. The example building is about 40 x 20 ft (12.2 x 6.1 m) with one internal dividing wall.

A worked version of this design is a 28 x 40 ft (8.5 x 12.2 m) building: the plenum holds a recirculating unit, fruit rooms 1 and 2 each exhaust through the far wall, and a walk-in cooler sits at one end (see the figure).

RANGE Example farm dimensions are approximate (given from memory). Wild Fruitings has been described as two fruit rooms of about 14 x 20 ft (4.3 x 6.1 m) with a plenum of about 20 x 28 ft (6.1 x 8.5 m). It has also been described as a 15 x 24 ft (4.6 x 7.3 m) open outbuilding with an 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m) cooler and two 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit rooms, with the outbuilding acting as the plenum.

Treat the fruit room as filthy

RULE Treat the fruit room as a filthy environment. The job is to protect the rest of the building from the fruit room more than to protect the fruit room from the building.

  • Fully separate fruiting from incubation. Incubation air holds far too much CO2 for fruiting, and fruiting air carries spores and humidity that would load incubation. Fruiting draws from outside (via its plenum) and exhausts outside, one way only.
  • Run two independent climate systems: one for production, incubation and lab cooling, and one for fruiting plus harvest, pack and grade. Air can recirculate within each system, but the two must never be combined. Cooled, CO2-rich incubation air must never feed a fruit room.
  • A single AC feeding a multi-zone plenum can serve several rooms with independent dampers, but fruiting cannot be on it. A shared-air arrangement that works for labs and incubation does not work for fruiting. See Chapter 5 for climate systems.
  • Plan roughly twice as much incubation space as fruiting space. See Chapter 3 for whole-farm planning.
  • Putting fruit rooms between the lab and incubation under one roof is common and workable, but not advisable.
  • Lab and fruit-room design are similar in principle. The fruit room is designed to stop CO2 and spore backflow; the lab is designed for filtration and linear airflow (Chapter 4).
  • Keep compost piles well away from air intakes.

CASE At one farm (Cascadia), intermittent Neurospora on fruiting blocks was traced to a compost mound near the fruit room's ducts. Lesson: what sits near your intakes ends up on your blocks.

Room size, capacity and loading

AT A GLANCE The reference room is 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) and produces about 500-600 lb (225-270 kg) a week when well run. Lay it out in weekly cohorts and do not pack it full.

Item Value Conditions
Reference room footprint 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) The "standard" farm fruit room; the 12 ft wall faces the plenum.
Output of a 12 x 24 room About 500-600 lb (225-270 kg) a week Well managed and rolling. More racks fit but unbalance the room.
Racks per row (12 x 24 room) Five 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) racks with 5 shelves, about a 20 ft (6.1 m) run Leaves room to manoeuvre.
Blocks per rack 50 (two rows of five 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks per shelf) 250 blocks per row of racks.
Facility with 2-3 fruit rooms About 1,000 lb (450 kg) a week Harvest and packing moved out of the rooms.
40 x 8 ft (12.2 x 2.4 m) shipping container Up to 13 racks (7 + 6), 650 blocks 2 ft 4 in (71 cm) aisle.
Two rooms with DIY mini-splits About 300 blocks per room About 18 kW of heat pump in total holds about 18 °C (65 °F); you need more for about 16 °C (60 °F).
High Country Fungi's 16 x 16 ft (4.9 x 4.9 m) room Peaks at about 600 lb (270 kg) a week One working farm's room.

Lay the room out in weekly cohorts

  • Blocks take 2-3 weeks to fruit out. So lay the room out as three rows for week 1, week 2 and week 3 cohorts and rotate them, so there are always blocks to harvest.
  • Keep spare space even for two-week species, in case one cohort isn't cleared before the next arrives.
  • Scheduling is like Tetris: know each variety's time to harvest so racks free up in time. In summer one small farm has to fit about 300 incoming blocks while about 300 spent blocks go to compost.
  • A fixed room is hard to scale, so plan around busy and slow seasons. See Chapter 22 for production planning.

Don't fill the room with unripe blocks

  • Don't fill fruit rooms with unripe blocks. Unripe chestnut sits 4-5 weeks before harvest, while ripened blocks need 2-3 weeks.
  • Decision rule for chestnut: if incubation space is the bottleneck, fruit sooner. If the fruit room is the bottleneck, or neither is, let the blocks ripen.
  • Ripened chestnut can wait without fruiting. That makes it a buffer crop for smoothing peaks and gaps in other species.
  • In the same way, a black oyster block pulled at 2 weeks still matures, but it does so in the fruit room. A 3-week block spends less fruit-room time before primordia.

Don't overpack

RULE Don't pack rooms to make them "efficient". Density raises CO2, the humidity load and the temperature-control burden. It slows growth and brings more bacterial problems.

A room that isn't packed full needs fewer air exchanges.

RANGE How full to load a room. Standard: blocks fill about 1/10 to 1/4 of the room's vertical cubic capacity, for healthier mushrooms, less heat and fewer air changes. Context: the reference 12 x 24 ft room above (five racks per row, 50 blocks per rack) is that room at full capacity, about 500-600 lb (225-270 kg) a week with its exhausts sized to match; watch CO2 and fruit form as you approach it. The older "one-third rule" (attributed to Stamets' writing) is still quoted. What fraction of its volume the full 12 x 24 ft layout fills was not stated, so check your own room with a datalogger as you load it.

CASE A Houston farm packs its 3.7 x 7.3 m (12 x 24 ft) fruiting room unusually densely by fruiting every block from the top. The layout is "like a library": 1.2 m (4 ft) deep racks along both long walls and an aisle of about 0.9 m (3 ft) down the middle, so racks can be swung out. Staff have to move carefully so as not to break off lion's mane.

WHY Small-farm layouts stop working at scale. Fruiting from the side as well adds about 0.25 lb (0.1 kg) per block, and over 3,000 blocks that is a lot of mushrooms. At scale, the layout has to follow yield and the labour of moving blocks, not the grower's favourite engineering.

Building the room: materials, drainage and power

AT A GLANCE Steel studs, Coroplast walls and flashing tape. Trapped floor drains go in first. Little electricity is needed, but seal every controller box against humidity.

Walls and framing

  • Framing: use steel studs. They are light, replaceable, movable and cleanable.
  • Wood studs wick water up from the humid floor, grow mould, and after some years become a contamination source that forces a tear-out. Hemlock and similar woods are possible but not advised.
  • Build with materials that won't rot: steel studs and Coroplast, or SIPs (structural insulated panels). One farm imported SIPs from China at about $2 per linear foot.
  • Wall skin: Coroplast (fluted plastic sheet) in 4 x 8 ft (1.2 x 2.4 m) sheets of about 2 lb (0.9 kg) each, which suit studs at 2 ft (61 cm) on centre. Fasten with stainless self-tapping screws.
  • COVID-era cost was about $8-11 a sheet. Sign shops sell it, and large sign companies may sell pallets cheaper.
  • FRP and other heavy plastic panels are heavy and hard to install. Contractors will want to add wood backing; refuse.
  • Seams: seal with 3M flashing tape. It is stretchy, rubbery, self-healing and very strong once stuck. Lumber yards stock it more reliably than hardware stores.
  • The same three materials (steel stud, Coroplast, flashing tape) also suit lab builds (Chapter 4).
  • Coroplast is easy to clean, and damaged sheets are simply swapped. The flutes can hold water and some mould, but far less than organic wall materials.
  • Expect to rebuild parts of any fruit room periodically.

Drainage first

RULE In a new build, drainage is the first priority. Fit a P-trap (a water seal) so sewer or septic air can't back up into the room. Otherwise bacteria (including blotch) and odours can enter.

  • Fruit rooms need floor drains, because standing water breeds bacterial blooms. Without a drain the water has to be vacuumed out by hand.
  • The plenum does not need drains.
  • Optional extras that speed up cleaning: slope the slab to a floor channel about 6 in (15 cm) deep, or dig a sump pit about 16 in (41 cm) deep with a sump pump, to collect wash and mist water.
  • Drainage and trapped drains are among the root causes to fix for blotch, together with water filtration, air filtration, negative pressure and humidifier design (Chapter 17).

Power, controllers and sensors

  • Fruit rooms need little electricity: lights, pumps, maybe a compressor for high-pressure misting. Standard 110-120 V service is usually enough. Consult an electrician.
  • Heating and cooling are the biggest power cost.
  • Seal controller and sensor boxes against humidity. Put silicone in the gland grooves, use cable glands or flex conduit, and tighten cover screws evenly. The controller boards are as sensitive as an Arduino.
  • Mount the wet/dry-bulb humidity sensor as far from the misting nozzle as possible, and keep it clean.

Racks and carts

  • Rolling racks (carts) are the most important fruiting tool. Roll a cart out to a harvest, grade and pack area; this keeps spores off workers and out of the plenum.
  • Keep one species per rack and dedicate each rack to one lot, so the whole rack is harvested, cleaned and reloaded together.
  • Consolidate stragglers that haven't fruited onto one rack. Rolling racks make this easy.
  • Fixed conduit racks lead to forgotten, overgrown clusters at the back (oversized pioppino is the classic example).
  • Don't cycle incubation racks through fruit rooms. Humid, caustic fruit rooms rust shelving, and stainless steel is very expensive.
  • Keep fruiting racks in the fruit room and never mix them with incubation racks, because humidity rusts them quickly (Cap n Stem's advice).
  • Black wire shelving about a year old showed only a little rust.
  • Use large casters. Racks with small casters are the ones that failed, at 2 am during a harvest.
  • For shiitake, slatted or strip shelves work better than flat shelves, because they leave fewer unbrowned contact patches that never fruit.

WARNING Loaded rolling racks have tipped over while being loaded or moved, for example at night while harvesting about 300 shiitake blocks (600-700 lb, 270-320 kg). Keep spare racks so rescued blocks have somewhere to go.

CASE Two real rooms. A small Maine farm's room has black wire rolling racks: grey and black oysters fruiting from bag tops on the top shelf, golden oysters in the middle, a rack of browned shiitake and a lower rack of bagged blocks. The grower said it was not the ideal layout at that moment. Wild Fruitings' room has wire shelves of side-cut blocks, a wall-mounted CO2 controller, a dial thermo-hygrometer and an exhaust fan high on the wall.

The plenum

AT A GLANCE The plenum is the clean, conditioned room that feeds air to the fruit rooms. Keep it at or below about 450 ppm CO2 and at 40-50% RH, give it its own fresh-air intake, and make it as big as you can.

  • A plenum is a separate space (a side room, a barn interior, a basement, an attic or the end of a shipping container) conditioned to roughly the fruit room's target temperature.
  • The fruit room draws makeup air from the plenum and exhausts outdoors, never back into the plenum and never into incubation: the air is full of spores.
  • The plenum's size isn't fixed, but its heating and cooling must keep up with the room's air-exchange rate.
  • The plenum's first job is to recirculate air through an AC system. When a fruit room calls for fresh air, that room's damper opens and its CO2-rich air goes outside.
  • The plenum can be anywhere, as long as conditioned air is ducted to the room. Examples: a whole barn as the plenum, with a temperature unit recirculating inside it and the fruit room inside the barn pulling air through a damper and exhausting outdoors. Or an AC in an attic ducted down a disused chimney to a basement fruit room.
  • If the plenum is in a separate building, duct the air across (over or under ground) and make the intake an active fan. A passive damper can't pull air through a long duct.

Plenum size

The plenum doesn't have to match the fruit room, but bigger is better. A small plenum needs more outside makeup air and therefore a bigger AC. A larger plenum saves money, even though some farms claim otherwise.

Plenum CO2

RULE The plenum must be at or below about 450 ppm CO2, because the fruit room can never get lower than its supply air.

  • A plenum can share space with a walk-in cooler or harvest area. But don't store CO2-producing blocks in it, and don't run heavy activity there.
  • Monitor plenum CO2 and give the plenum its own outside makeup air (fresh-air intake).
  • One safeguard is a about 250 CFM (about 425 m³/h) squirrel-cage fan on a CO2 controller to bring outside air into the plenum.
  • It is better to pressurize the plenum slightly positive than to depressurize it.
  • Wild Fruitings keeps a plenum window permanently cracked to hold CO2 down. A package unit with an economizer (a built-in fresh-air damper) does this better, but economizers don't fit evaporator-type units.

Plenum humidity

RULE Humidify the plenum lightly to about 40-50% RH with a small standing humidifier or a fine mister on low (a practice credited to an Australian grower).

WHY Otherwise the fruit rooms are fed very dry air. Jumping from near 0% RH in the supply to about 75% in the room causes heavy condensation on walls, rots the structure and lengthens humidifier run times. A 40-50% plenum makes the jump much smaller.

Negative pressure and one-way airflow

AT A GLANCE Pull air out of the fruit room with an exhaust fan; let plenum air in through a damper. The room sits at lower pressure than the rest of the building, so its spores, CO2 and humidity can only go outdoors.

  • Blowing air into a sealed room creates positive pressure. That air leaks out through cracks or loads the fan.
  • A positively pressured fruit room pushes CO2-, spore- and humidity-laden air into the plenum and ruins it. It is the same problem as recirculating HVAC (see the inset in the figure below).
  • Recommended: a negative-pressure room. An exhaust fan inside or just outside the room pulls air out to the outdoors. Makeup air enters from the plenum through a duct with a damper. The damper prevents backflow and stops the room being over-depressurized.
  • The intake can be a backdraft damper: it opens when air is pulled and closes to stop CO2-rich room air leaking back into the plenum.
  • "Negative" is relative: it means lower pressure than the surrounding facility.
  • Farms are tempted to recirculate for efficiency, but one-way airflow is what makes a room "rock solid".
  • Isopropyl foot baths at fruit-room doors make little difference. A clean plenum and consistent one-way airflow are what matter.

CASE One farm's old fruit rooms were positively pressurized. The walls bulged and boomed, and fruit-room smells and spores leaked into incubation. Lesson: push air out, never in.

RANGE Recommended: an active exhaust fan. It is the only good way to regulate CO2 and keep the room negative. The counter-argument is that the fan collects spores. A working grower agrees negative pressure "makes the most sense" but says it is the hardest arrangement on equipment, since spore-laden air passes through the fans. Opening a full shiitake room once released a spore cloud that coated a fan and seized it: keep a backup fan. Fans and ducts are the hardest parts to clean, and a noisy fan is often the first sign one is failing.

Sizing the exhaust and intake fans

AT A GLANCE For a 12 x 24 ft room, a CO2-controlled exhaust of up to about 1000 CFM, plus an optional about 500 CFM temperature exhaust. 1 CFM (cubic foot per minute) is about 1.7 m³/h.

Item Value Conditions
Exhaust, 12 x 24 ft room (recommended) about 1000 CFM maximum on a speed controller (rheostat), modulating about 400-1000 CFM with room load Switched on by the CO2 controller.
Exhaust, 12 x 24 ft room 800-1000 CFM blowing straight outside The intake on the 12 ft plenum wall can be a damper rather than a fan.
Second exhaust, for temperature about 500 CFM on a thermostat, with its own damper Alongside the 1000 CFM CO2 exhaust.
Shipping container, 8 ft (2.4 m) wide 1000 CFM variable-speed intake fan from the plenum; two 700 CFM CO2-controlled exhaust fans in the end wall Container reference layout.
Maitake room, 12 x 24 ft about 500 CFM running continuously (not 1000 CFM) Dedicated maitake room.
Plenum CO2 fan about 250 CFM squirrel cage Brings outside air into the plenum.

Two exhausts, placed at the far end

  • Two independent negative-pressure exhausts, one on CO2 and one on temperature, are preferred over a single fan wired to both a thermostat and a CO2 controller. Two fans are easier to wire, give redundancy and allow independent control.
  • A shared intake damper can open passively from the suction of either fan.
  • Place the exhaust at the back and the intake damper at the front, fed from the preconditioning plenum.
  • Two exhaust fans placed symmetrically either side of centre at the far end give more even, one-direction (not laminar) flow, and fewer hot or high-CO2 pockets, than one off-centre fan.

RANGE Exhaust height. Standard (Cap n Stem): intake from the plenum at the front, exhaust at the back, air moving one way through the room (see Negative pressure and one-way airflow). Context: in a long, narrow 40 ft shipping container, a Massachusetts farm found the low exhaust pulled all the humidifier fog down to the floor before it could spread. Moving the exhaust to the top of the far wall fixed it. In the first of its two container rooms the equipment had been laid out for plants; reordering the machines and putting them on timers also helped.

Air-exchange rate

  • Air-exchange rate = fan CFM ÷ room volume, the same calculation used for labs. It applies to a 12 x 24 x 10 ft (3.7 x 7.3 x 3 m) fruit room.
  • Worked example: the room volume is 12 × 24 × 10 = 2,880 cu ft (about 82 m³). A 1000 CFM fan moves 60,000 cu ft an hour, which is about 21 air changes per hour while it runs. At 400 CFM it is about 8 changes per hour.
  • To see airflow, some people push smoke through the room. An old joke tip from one farm was to smoke a cigarette in the fruit room: with good exchange you shouldn't see the smoke. Not advised.

Never recirculate inside the fruit room

RULE Never put recirculating HVAC, evaporators, heat exchangers you can't wash, or circulation fans inside the fruit room.

  • Don't put a conventional recirculating HVAC unit in a fruit room. Spores and humidity clog it fast; a $30,000 unit could be dead within about a month.
  • Don't rely on HEPA or pre-filtering to make recirculated fruit-room air acceptable.
  • A rough spore estimate: one mushroom releases on the order of a billion spores, so about 100 shiitake on one 10 lb (4.5 kg) block could mean about 100 billion spores.
  • One large farm puts refrigeration evaporators inside its fruit rooms, and spores clog the coils so badly that it strips them weekly. Use a plenum instead: fruiting doesn't need temperature control tight enough to justify risking expensive equipment.
  • One urban farm company put evaporative coolers inside fruit rooms recirculating the air. The cooling worked, but the equipment was constantly fouled and rebuilt.
  • HVAC contractors may over-engineer, and won't understand why you refuse to recirculate fruit-room air.

No oscillating or circulation fans

  • No oscillating or circulation fans in fruit rooms. That is a cannabis-grower habit. Use only the intake and exhaust, because mushrooms prefer still air between exchanges.
  • Avoid turbulence. In nature mushrooms form in still, sheltered spots. Growers coming from cannabis with many oscillating fans dry out and stress the fruit.
  • Aim for calm, consistent temperature, light and airflow, with gentle CO2 waves and no big peaks.
  • This is not a contradiction of incubation practice: circulation fans are recommended in dense substrate incubation, to break up stratified pockets. That is a different room with a different job (Chapter 13).

RANGE Recommended: no recirculation of fruit-room air through HVAC or filters; recirculation is acceptable only for clean plenum air. Inside the plenum, recirculation is the most efficient approach, and heat-pump heads "in your room" can be used where the room air is clean plenum air. Other practice: a published author recommends filtration and recirculation. A large Agaricus (button mushroom) farm, referred to here as KSS, grows excellent king oysters in rooms of about 80 x 80 x 25 ft (24 x 24 x 7.6 m). It uses a about 30-ton (about 105 kW) unit with a fresh-air damper feeding a perforated PVC manifold down the centre, mostly recirculated, and cleans about 11 return-duct filters daily.

Temperature equipment

AT A GLANCE Cooling is the hard part almost everywhere. Use walk-in-cooler-style evaporators in hot climates and heat pumps or mini-splits in temperate and cold ones. Put every unit in the plenum, not the fruit room, keep condensers outside, oversize, and build in redundancy. The settings themselves are in Temperature; equipment in general is in Chapter 5.

  • Cooling is the hard part almost everywhere, from Canada to El Paso.
  • In Maine both heating and cooling matter, but summer cooling has been the bigger problem for one small farm. Its winter heating keeps a base temperature at which cold-loving varieties still grow. It runs two heat pumps.

Cooling by climate

Climate Recommended equipment Notes
Hot Walk-in-cooler-style systems: an evaporator fan coil plus an outdoor condenser/compressor. Heatcraft is the preferred maker. Evaporator units cool to 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) more easily than a package unit cools to 20 °C (68 °F). That helps in Arizona, Florida and SoCal. With enough air exchange these systems can run without a heat source in mild climates, though fresh air must still come in.
True desert Evaporative coolers
Temperate and cold Heat pumps/mini-splits that heat and cool (Halcyon, Mitsubishi and many others)
  • Plenum cooling options: mini-splits (cheap and DIY-installable, but installers often botch them), Halcyon units, or reefer-style evaporators with outdoor condensers.
  • Budget option: MrCool DIY mini-split heat pumps. About 18 kW handles about 300 blocks per room in two rooms at about 18 °C (65 °F); you may need more for about 16 °C (60 °F).
  • Other options: one or two 9-18 kW heat pumps, a ducted recirculating package unit, or walk-in evaporators fed from an outside condenser.
  • Any cooling unit's condenser/compressor must be outside the building.
  • Example setups: a plenum with two wall units holding 10-16 °C (50-60 °F), an outside condenser, about 18 kW of heat pump and 300 blocks per fruit room; or, in a cold climate, the plenum held at 10 °C (50 °F) with intake heaters raising the air to 13 °C (55 °F) as it enters the rooms.
  • A used 20 or 40 ft (6.1 or 12.2 m) reefer container (about $9,000) comes with a 480 V refrigeration unit. With a step-down to 240 V on about a 40 A breaker it gives plenty of cooling, and it could be split into a cooled plenum and a walk-in.

Heating

WARNING Don't use propane "hot dog" greenhouse heaters. Unless properly vented they put CO2 into the space. Avoid any combustion heater that adds CO2.

TIP Cold-climate trick: put 120 V plug-in thermostatic heaters on the fruit-room intake, for example raising 10 °C (50 °F) plenum air to 13-16 °C (55-60 °F). Filter them so spores aren't baked onto the coils.

Sizing and redundancy

  • For two 12 x 24 ft rooms plus a about 24 x 24 ft (7.3 x 7.3 m) plenum, use two units for redundancy, about 3.5 tons (about 12 kW) of cooling in total.
  • Redundancy is a principle that applies throughout the farm.
  • Oversize the AC: for example, pay about $2,000 more for 10 tons instead of 7.5.
  • Spare no expense on air conditioning.
  • Keep backups of racks, fans and humidification. When one small farm's humidifier compressor broke, it limped along on a Hydrofogger, which doesn't do as well. Small farms have to weigh backup equipment against paying rent.

CASE The real limits of a small Maine farm. At −28 °C (−18 °F) outside, its heaters couldn't hold temperature; below about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) growth stalled, and some weeks it had nothing to sell to chefs. In summer, a too-warm room gave bad blotch (blue oysters came out tan and goopy). It controlled that by pulling as much AC as possible from the adjoining room. Lesson: reliable climate control means you still have mushrooms when competitors' crops fail, and you can take their orders.

Other temperature levers

  • Running the humidifier helps pull room temperature down for chestnut.
  • Steam humidification warms the room by about 0.5-1 °C (1-2 °F).

Energy recovery and container layouts

AT A GLANCE A fruit room throws away conditioned air all day. A washable Coroplast heat exchanger can recover some of that energy. The shipping container is a common, cheap fruit room with a small plenum at one end.

  • A conventional fruit room is an energy sink: it conditions fresh air, then dumps it outside full of CO2.
  • As one Canadian container grower puts it, a fruit room is about as efficient as a house in winter with the furnace blasting and all the windows open.
  • Energy is "near impossible to chase", because every extra air exchange adds cost, and hot-climate sizing gets expensive. Usually an HVAC specialist sizes it.

The container reference layout

  • A small plenum at the entrance holds a high-efficiency heat pump (or other temperature unit) and a CO2-controlled fresh-air damper fan.
  • A thermostat-controlled intake fan moves air from the plenum to the room through a fully gasketed door.
  • Two exhaust fans sit at the far end beyond the racks, with an optional exit door.
  • Insulating the whole container is mostly unnecessary; only the plenum really needs it, if anything.
  • In the reference plan the plenum is 4 ft 8 in (1.42 m) long, the intake fan is 1000 CFM (variable speed), the two exhausts are 700 CFM each on either side of an end door, and 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) racks run in two rows (see the figure).
  • Simpler version: wall off 4-6 ft (1.2-1.8 m) at one end of a 20 or 40 ft container as the plenum. The rest is fruit room. There is no room for a walk-in cooler, which has to sit outside.
  • A container farm can build a small plenum inside the container.
  • Containers are popular because they are cheap (a few thousand dollars) and modular. But a whole farm (lab, incubation, sterilizer) in one or two containers is capacity-limited.
  • In the same farm's container, about 3 m (10 ft) of the 12 m (40 ft) length was a conditioning room of about 3 x 2.4 m (10 x 8 ft). The intake fan meant to move air from the conditioning room into the grow space was wired to switch on by temperature, not all the time and not by CO2; it should have been tied to CO2. The grower prefers pulling fresh air in by exhaust over pushing it in with an intake fan, as a personal preference.

WARNING Packaged "cool ducting" fruiting air systems sold by some mushroom suppliers are not worth the money, in Cap n Stem's experience: "don't do it, man. It's not worth it... it's essentially ducting with a really overblown humidistat." The HEPA filter never worked, and "the whole thing is just so expensive". Build the plenum and ducting yourself.

The original heat-exchanger container and an adapted design

  • The original design: the heat exchanger is on the front of a 40 ft container. You walk through a 2 ft (0.6 m) door into a about 10 ft (3 m) plenum, leaving about 30 ft (9 m) of growing space. The plenum held a hot-water radiator from a boiler (for a cold Canadian climate) and a humidifier.
  • Conditioned humid air went into a full-length perforated duct along one side (perforations growing larger along the duct, end capped). A low-level perforated return duct on the other side went back through the exchanger.
  • Drawbacks: lots of ductwork that clogs with spores in humid air, and low-pressure humidification that degrades and is hard to keep clean.
  • The design only works with a hydrofogger in the plenum. The constant cross-draft exchanged the room air about every 6 minutes. With a plain humidifier at one point, the humidity stayed in a local "bubble" and the room stratified.
  • Adaptation for high-pressure fog (a Hart-type system) or a pull-up humidifier: take the CO2-rich return from the back of the room into the exchanger. Deliver fresh air through an elbow duct pointing down near the door, which sets up a rolling vortex down the room to the return.
  • Put the fog nozzle near the door so the moving air spreads humidity evenly. Feeding high-pressure misting through ducts gives uneven saturation.
  • In the adapted layout, the return duct runs along the ceiling from the far end back to the exchanger, and a fog nozzle by the door sprays into a looping vortex.
  • Retrofit of the reference layout: put the exchanger where the CO2-controlled fresh-air damper was, duct its fresh outlet into the plenum, remove the rear exhaust fans, and run a full return duct from the back of the room to the exchanger.
  • Not recommended: an example seen in Florida with the exchanger at the back and the plenum at the front. It created two very different climates at the two ends.

The Coroplast heat exchanger

  • The Coroplast heat exchanger is a stack of fluted sheets with alternate layers blocked, so exhaust and intake air trade heat without mixing.
  • It can be rinsed of spore gunk, whereas metal-fin exchangers foul.
  • Claimed heat recovery is about 85% (second-hand figure, unconfirmed).
  • Without an exchanger, you can simply duct in makeup air with a CO2 meter in the plenum and duct the exhaust out. It works, just less efficiently.

Humidification equipment

AT A GLANCE The humidifier is the most common source of blotch in a fruit room (why). Use a fine, non-recirculating mist from treated water. Keep ultrasonic units outside the room. First choice: a TAC misting system; the proven alternative is a Hart high-pressure air/water atomizer (Chapter 5). The humidity targets themselves are in Relative humidity.

Humidifier types compared

Type How it performs Notes
TAC misting (recommended first) A wall-mounted electric box that makes a fine, dry vapour (about 1 micron) with no compressor. High Country Fungi's first choice, ahead of Hart, because compressor burn-out is Hart's main failure. Details in Chapter 5.
High-pressure air/water atomizer (Hart Environmental): the proven alternative The best-proven option for fruit rooms; it has cleared blotch on several farms. A small mixing box with a 12 V solenoid fires a "dry fog" from a top corner when the controller calls. 1-2 heads per 12 x 24 ft room. Details below.
Steam humidification Makes sense where a boiler already runs. Carries essentially no minerals. A fine atomizer gives saturation without visible fog. Warms the room about 0.5-1 °C (1-2 °F).
Hydrofogger (hydrofogger.com; a float-fed ultrasonic unit from the cannabis trade) Efficient; little difference between sizes. Price rose from about $165 (mini) to about $450; at $600-700 you may as well buy high-pressure fog. Not overkill even for tent growers.
Aeromist-type compressor misting Built for about 10 min on/10 min off; fruit rooms run 10 on/2 off and burn out the compressor. 16 heads soak blocks. Seen to fail often.
Ultrasonic pond foggers (discs in a barrel or drum) Most correlated with blotch complaints. Inside the room they recirculate dirty air through a warm, wet vat and blow it over the crop. Coarse droplets defeat ordinary hygrometers.

WHY fine fog: Fine atomization gives a "dry fog" that evaporates instead of pooling the way ultrasonic water can. Finer fog raises the threshold at which condensation collects, and the room feels dry. Standing water always causes problems.

Ultrasonic units: keep them outside the room

RULE Ultrasonic units go outside the room. An untreated fogger is one of the biggest bacterial vectors and the usual cause of weekly "I have bacterial blotch" calls.

  1. Feed the unit with a about $2 float valve.
  2. Fit a coarse replaceable filter on its air intake.
  3. Dose the water with 150-250 ppm bleach (or ClO2, chlorine dioxide), for example via a peristaltic pump.
  4. If the drum must sit inside the room, duct its intake to outside air, so it pulls fresh air and pushes humid air into the room instead of recirculating room spores.

The fix in short, against blotch (Pseudomonas tolaasii): a drum fogger with a fan duct in and a fog duct out, and 150-250 ppm bleach (or ClO2) in the water. Lysol and peroxide were ruled out as fogger additives (but see the peroxide rescue).

Procedure: boxing in a Hydrofogger that sits inside the room

This is the advice given to a Vermont farm with a Hydrofogger inside the room.

  1. Box off a corner of the room with Coroplast, with a wall vent so the box draws air from outside the room.
  2. Put the Hydrofogger in the box. It has a 6-8 in (15-20 cm) collar: duct it up and out into the room, so the unit draws its air from the box.
  3. Optionally put a coarse filter on the box intake to keep bugs out.
  4. Make the unit easy to pull out and clean.
  5. Add bleach to the water if you clean daily.

CHECK The fog leaving the duct should come from outside air, not room air, and the drum should not collect grime faster than you clean it.

Case: two rooms side by side

CASE At Wild Fruitings, the ultrasonic room was so foggy the shelves were barely visible, and a hand in the stream got wet. In the Hart room it did not. In the fogger room, black oyster caps showed slight yellowing (an early blotch sign), and a block near the humidifier had died. Yellowing on oysters is a key sign of poor humidification. The ultrasonic dome collects grime and needs constant cleaning; that farm cleans it and doses bleach.

High-pressure atomizer (Hart system) details

  • Compressed air and filtered water meet in a drip-free mixing box inside the room, with screw-in heads of different spray patterns. The mist barely wets a hand.
  • Heads cost roughly $300 each (unconfirmed), plus a rotary compressor (about $300-500).
  • Nozzles come in two micron sizes. Clean clogged ones by soaking in vinegar, and swap in a spare.
  • Add an inline peristaltic dosing pump (about $50) for bleach or ClO2, and optionally a water softener.
  • Units have been reported running 8-10 years.
  • The compressor need not be big. A Kobalt 26 gal (98 L), about 4.5 SCFM (standard cubic feet per minute, about 7.6 m³/h) unit worked in a demonstration and is the suggested minimum. Size it to run 50% of the time or less; extra tank volume helps. Other growers size much larger (see Chapter 5), because an overworked compressor burns out.
  • Farms using it include New Hampshire Mushroom Co., Far West Fungi and others.
  • The nozzle droplet size is quoted at about 0.03 micron (unconfirmed).

CASE One farm had chronic blotch. It tried ClO2 and H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide) sprays; the blotch went away after a Hart system was installed.

The one exception: chestnut likes dense fog

Chestnut is the one species for which a Hydrofogger (dense, wet fog) is recommended over the usual approach of fine mist and HVAC-conditioned air. Successful growers (for example in New Hampshire) fog heavily, and nameko likes the same sticky, humid conditions.

Measuring and controlling humidity

  • Cheap digital controllers (Inkbird) fail within a couple of months.
  • The most accurate method is the old wet-bulb/dry-bulb sensor.
  • The Pola HP57 (confirm the model number with the supplier) is a combined temperature/humidity controller with a dry/wet-bulb sensor: a small hanging water vat with a wick tube. The oldest technology is the best here: it is more accurate and more cleanable than cheap electronic sensors.
  • Example: in one room the controller read about 66% RH with the door open and immediately called for humidity.
  • Mount the sensor as far from the misting nozzle as possible and keep it clean (sealing controllers).

RANGE Recommended: control the humidifier from an accurate RH controller (wet/dry bulb). Cycle timers (for example 30 min on/10 off) are an improper way to control RH: humidity runs very high and blotch worsens when temperature rises. Budget option, if you have no controller: a cycle timer on the fogger (for example 10 min on/20 s off in the driest season), checked frequently because the right setting changes with the seasons.

Water treatment for humidifiers

AT A GLANCE Treat every drop that goes into the humidifier. Filter it (physical, softener if hard, carbon), then add RO or steam for fruiting if you can, and dose 150-250 ppm bleach or ClO2. Use inline UV as a cheap first line. Full water treatment is in Chapter 17.

Treatment Dose or detail Notes
Bleach in fogger water (recommended) 150-250 ppm Standard on large industrial farms.
Bleach for fruit-room water treatment (other figure) about 150-200 ppm Never more than about 400 ppm, even for cleaning.
ClO2 (chlorine dioxide) Alternative to bleach Allowed under organic certification.
Dosing method Peristaltic pump ($30-200) into the fogger's small auto-fill line Work out the dose from the bottle label.
Inline UV Sized in gallons per hour The cheapest good first line; non-chemical.
RO (reverse osmosis) Wastes roughly 2 gal of reject water per 1 gal of product (unconfirmed) Optional, but the best solution for blotch and rose comb.
Steam Instead of RO Carries essentially no minerals.
  • Use multiple barriers: treat water before the auto-fill bucket, and filter or treat the intake air.
  • Dumping untreated city water into a humidifier invites blotch. The about $500 upgrade pays back quickly.
  • City water is usually OK. A shallow dug well carries a high microbial load compared with a about 200 ft (61 m) drilled well. Water is mainly a fruiting-room issue.
  • People resist RO or treated water as "stripping the good stuff", but untreated water carries more harmful than helpful content.
  • Humidifier water must also be filtered, because high-pressure nozzles, Hydrofoggers and ultrasonic discs all foul with sediment and minerals.
  • Beyond softening, carbon and particulate filtering, the two options for humidification water are RO or steam.
  • Even after filtration plus steam or RO, farms often still add bleach, peroxide or non-activated ClO2.

The full water chain

The full chain is: physical filter, then softener (if the water is hard), then carbon. Then the line splits: one branch goes to production; the other goes to fruiting, where RO or steam is added. Problems arise when any stage fails.

Rescue treatment: hydrogen peroxide

  • If blotch persists with good humidification, check the water source.
  • A New Jersey grower on a shallow dug well fixed blotch by injecting hydrogen peroxide or ClO2 into the line with a dosing pump.

Procedure: peroxide reservoir for a blotch outbreak

This recipe comes from a North Carolina grower. Use it intermittently, during the problem window, not year-round.

  1. Use a 10 gal (38 L) humidifier reservoir.
  2. Every 3 days, dump the reservoir and clean it.
  3. Refill with water plus 1.5 quarts (1.4 L) of 3% drugstore hydrogen peroxide. That gives roughly 0.1% H2O2.
  4. Continue through the blotch window, then stop.

CHECK Previously decimated blocks recovered within about two weeks.

WARNING Never spray 2.5-3% peroxide straight onto fruit.

RANGE Recommended: about 0.1% peroxide in humidifier water only as a short-term "get out of jail" treatment; it has been used successfully on about five farms. Water-treatment guidance also lists peroxide among normal humidifier additives. Earlier guidance crossed out peroxide (with Lysol, Pine-Sol and vinegar) as a no-go for fogger water, with no reason given. The dose thresholds quoted for harm are internally inconsistent (from "over about 1% harms" to a study figure of 0.025 = 2.5%), so check a primary source before using higher doses.

Lighting hardware

  • Use ordinary bright 6500 K full-spectrum (daylight) fixtures, not grow-light intensity. They also show the mushrooms' true colour.
  • Following Chinese and Japanese practice, use warm light for incubation and cool light for fruiting. This mimics the seasons and can change colour, size, taste, texture and fruiting speed.
  • Species-specific light needs are covered in Light as a fruiting signal.

WARNING Strong light is a hazard to some species. Bright 6500 K lamps close above the top rack burned the tops of chestnut blocks (dry, dead sawdust), while red light around 1500 K or lower would be safe. Under full-spectrum fruit-room lights, chestnut on top shelves dries and crusts, so keep it low or out of direct light.

CASE High Country Fungi (Avery) switched to blue-spectrum LEDs, combining 54 W blue strips at about 450 nm with 6500 K white. The strips are threaded through clear tubing to waterproof them. The 16 x 16 ft (4.9 x 4.9 m) room has 4 fixtures, each 4 ft (1.2 m) long with 4 strips. The grower's view: "Lighting is important."

Cleaning and hygiene

AT A GLANCE Clean the whole room between every load, spot-clean in between, and remove blotched fruit on sight. Bleach at about 250 ppm for spraying, never above about 400 ppm. Wear a respirator. More on cleaning agents in Chapter 16.

  • Clean fruit rooms far more than people expect, daily if possible. Rotate cleaning agents.
  • Big industrial growers clean every room top to bottom after each crop despite heavy automation, and small farms should too.
  • Bleach dosing: don't exceed about 400 ppm for cleaning. If you can easily smell it, it's too strong.
  • Maitake rooms: clean every single day, because the fruit easily picks up Trichoderma and other airborne contaminants.
  • One grower estimates that about 50% of farm time goes to cleaning.
  • Cleanliness protects the machinery as well as the crop.

WARNING A grower in Arizona used undiluted pharmaceutical-grade bleach and was injured. Dilute to the ppm figures above (Chapter 18).

Procedure: cleaning the room between loads

  1. Clear the room of the old cohort.
  2. Clean the racks: they get filthy from spore drop and Trichoderma.
  3. Spray the walls with about 250 ppm bleach, then power-wash or wipe them.
  4. Clean the floor (one small Maine farm uses mostly bleach on floors, sometimes alternating with vinegar) and push the water to the drain.
  5. Check every incoming block for green, blue or "rainbow" moulds before it goes in.
  6. Load the new blocks.

CHECK No standing water on the floor, no visible mould on racks or walls, and no contaminated block loaded. Between full cleans, the same Maine farm spot-cleans walls rather than doing them weekly.

RANGE Recommended: clean the whole room between every load and spot-clean in between; daily if possible. Daily cleaning is essential for maitake rooms; for other rooms it is ideal rather than mandatory. A working Maine farm cleans fully between loads and spot-cleans walls rather than weekly.

Spores, blotch and your lungs

  • Harvest on time, because overblown mushrooms lose shelf life and raise the spore load (Chapter 15).
  • Phenotype selection can reduce spore load. A "spore-less oyster" is near-mythical, though large spawn companies are said to be good at low-spore strains.
  • Remove blotched fruit on sight so it doesn't spread through the room.
  • Blotched mushrooms boxed and put in the cooler spread blotch to the others there.

WARNING Spore lung is a real risk. Wear a respirator or harvest outside the room. Wear a respirator while fruiting and harvesting shiitake. See Chapter 18.

  • Running a farm in the heat is mostly cleaning: "like working at a hotel" or as a janitor. The grow room probably needs scrubbing from top to bottom every week. It is hard work that hired staff tend to skip or do half-heartedly, and then problems pile up. New helpers often quit after a hot day of cleaning.

Mixed-species rooms and rack placement

AT A GLANCE Most species can share a room. Put light-lovers high and shiitake and chestnut low, never put lion's mane under shiitake, and give maitake its own room.

  • Most species can be fruited together in one room.
  • Ideal rack order, top to bottom: lion's mane on top. Yellow (golden) oysters toward the top, since they seem to respond better to light. Blue and black oysters middle to bottom. Chestnut and shiitake on the bottom. Top-fruiting maitake also goes on top.
  • Ideally, shiitake is kept fully separate from everything else.
  • Never put lion's mane below or near shiitake. Shiitake drips brown exudate that browns the white lion's mane.
  • When opening shiitake bags, leave a small rim of bag at the bottom to catch exudate, so it doesn't ruin the rack or the blocks below.
  • Rinse shiitake blocks before putting them in the room. No regular spraying is needed.
  • An all-purpose room kept cold can handle king oysters using the stripped-block method.
  • Top or side fruiting makes little difference to the crop; it matters mainly for airflow. Golden oyster is side-fruited, and top fruiting fits more blocks on a shelf.

Maitake needs its own room

  • Maitake needs its own room. It dislikes other species' spores, fast air exchange and humidity swings, and its regime uses equipment less efficiently than a mixed room.
  • That is hard at small scale; in tents, give maitake its own tent.
  • Maitake protocols are converging (about 90% of farms share the essentials). The main trick is that maitake does not fruit consistently alongside other species, especially in an overcrowded mixed room.

Mapping airflow with comb tooth

TIP Coral (comb) tooth shows you how air moves. It browns where airflow is too strong and goes "popcorny" where air is stagnant. Place a few on every shelf and tier to map the room. Where the back racks popcorn, put CO2-tolerant species such as king oyster there. Blue oyster likes fast air.

WARNING Mixed rooms work until they don't. An Ohio farm grew about 200 lb (90 kg) of king oysters a week "week after week", fruiting them alongside other mushrooms and even spraying them with a hose, without blotch. Then, "literally like someone flipped a light switch, they started blotching out". Kings are "highly susceptible to blotch" and one of the species "you don't like to grow with other mushrooms" because of the spore load. Many farms get away with fruiting "the gamut" together for a while, but "never get away with it forever", and then blame the spawn maker. That farm now plans dedicated rooms.

  • Heavy spore producers need their own room. On a Maine farm, shiitake rooms spored so heavily that chestnut racks moved into them "would just die". The only other species that did this was golden (yellow) oyster, whose purple-tinged spore cloud was so heavy that shiitake and goldens each needed their own room. Other species could be mixed; grey oysters and kings were grown together because they want the same temperature.
  • A New Hampshire farm runs about 12 species at once in six grow rooms, several species per room, all tied to one intake fan, so it has to balance them all: "it's stupid now, but it made sense financially".

WHY Sharing one room among many species "waters down the profitability" of the whole farm. Farms in China and Japan "do 95% of one thing and 5% of everything else". If you fruit six species in one room, "you're really going to be making most of your money from two of those varieties". In a less than ideal climate, "refine the ones that work the best in your local climate", using "a data-driven approach to determining which ones are actually making money" rather than keeping varieties for show. Pink and golden oyster "look good on the Insta" and "draw people into your booth", but they may not be your earners. Farms in one region can each specialize and cooperate on substrate, spawn and sales.

Room types: beyond the two American rooms

US farms tend to build only two kinds of grow room.

  • The shiitake room: "slightly higher CO2", "a little bit of condensing humidity", "generally low light".
  • The exotics room: for oyster, lion's mane or chestnut, run so they grow "without them getting excessively stemmy or losing their caps".

Farms in Asia add two more that Americans overlook, "the very cold grow room... and a very hot grow room", plus shade-cloth houses that use solar gain and seasonal farming. Asian farms pair technology-heavy rooms with such an "overflow" area. One Washington grower thinks a shade house used six months a year, flushed several times, with flies controlled "with a flow through methodology and with high velocity air", would be "really profitable" for "certain varieties that don't need as much active humidification or as much climate control".

Small-scale, home and alternative setups

  • Grow tents are harder than they look at scale: constant rag-cleaning of many tents, flexing frames, tipping over. Hobbyists are urged to move up to a proper room.
  • Example: Cactus Hat's owner went from a tent at home to a garage farm to a dedicated building.
  • Species that fruit well inside the closed bag (forming a healthy mat) need no fruit room when the product will be dried or extracted: lion's mane, reishi and maitake.
  • The bag's filter patch matters for in-bag fruiting (Chapter 11). Lion's mane does best with the more open "B" patch (about 5 micron). Maitake needs the tighter "A" patch (about 0.5 micron) so it develops without going goopy or pulling in bacteria.
  • For maitake in-bag development, XLS-A is right; B gives too much exchange and T too little.
  • Fast species such as cubensis or cordyceps may suit high-exchange (B) bags, while slow reishi would likely give stunted antlers from surface drying.
  • For a cubensis terrarium, judge perlite moisture by lifting the tub (dry perlite is almost weightless). A home RH of 50% or more is recommended.
  • Cave growing in France and other European countries produces beautiful king oysters, with big headroom, natural humidity and no engineered air exchange.

TIP The kitchen-counter test. If bought-in blocks all fail in your room, fruit one on your kitchen counter. If it does fine there, the problem is your environment, usually water or humidity.

  • Tents are harder than open space. A Florida farm's first fruiting chamber was a 1.2 x 2.4 m (4 x 8 ft) cannabis grow tent. It filled with CO2 and was harder to grow in than a bigger space. The growers tore it down and fruited in their open garage (sometimes with a humidifier running in the garage), and the mushrooms "did way better". A fruit room is a lung, not a cannabis grow room.
  • A university research group fruits in a converted deli fridge. An earlier study grew mushrooms in closed boxes to hold humidity, and poor CO2 control there likely caused odd, in-between fruit forms.

Part B. Running the crop

Part B covers the four room settings (temperature, CO2 and fresh air, humidity, light), then what makes a block start fruiting, how long each species takes, what yield to expect, and how to read faults in the mushrooms themselves. All the per-species numbers are collected in the species parameter table.

Temperature

AT A GLANCE 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) for the staple species (shiitake, oyster, lion's mane), about 16 °C (60 °F) as a typical target. Cooler gives denser, better-keeping fruit and less disease; warmer gives speed and more blotch.

Setting Value Conditions
Typical target (recommended) About 16 °C (60 °F) Species-dependent.
General range 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) Staple species: shiitake, oyster, lion's mane. Some species go higher and some lower; enoki and nebrodensis oyster are low-temperature outliers.
Small Maine mixed-species farm Ideal 16-18 °C (60-65 °F) A little outside that is fine; far outside gets messy.
High Country Fungi (Avery) Best 14-16 °C (58-60 °F); workable 17 °C (62 °F); highest you want 18 °C (65 °F) Above 18 °C (65 °F) gets rough.
Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan) 14-17 °C (58-62 °F)
Growth stalls Below about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) Seen on a Maine farm in deep winter.

RANGE Recommended: about 16 °C (60 °F). The full range for staples is 13-18 °C (55-65 °F). Choose the cool end (13-16 °C, 55-60 °F) for density, quality, shelf life and less contamination; choose the warm end (around 18 °C, 65 °F) for speed. Above 18 °C (65 °F) problems climb sharply.

Speed versus quality

  • Production speed responds non-linearly to temperature (a "log curve"). 13 °C (55 °F) is much slower than 18 °C (65 °F), so a swing of about 5-6 °C (10 °F) can move a delivery by about 5 days. Plan around customer deadlines.
  • The cool end gives denser tissue, potentially higher quality and less contamination. The warm end is for speed.
  • Colder-grown mushrooms keep longer, and you can speed up or delay a harvest by adjusting temperature.
  • Heat-CO2 feedback: more heat raises metabolism and CO2, which drives more heat. A packed room has to stay ahead of it.
  • Fully colonized blocks are past their hottest phase, so CO2 and heat output are much lower during fruiting than in incubation.

Heat brings disease

  • Blotch peaks in the heat of summer and the shoulder seasons. Blotch season is the change into warm, humid weather (Chapter 17).

  • Bacterial blotch and other fruit-room problems climb sharply in warmer conditions.

  • Chestnut blocks grow Trichoderma on top when the room is too hot.

  • Lion's mane gets more bacterial infection, and RH and fresh air are harder to balance, when too hot.

  • King oyster above 16 °C (60 °F) brings trouble with blotch, overlay and holding humidity.

  • Heat can ruin a room in a day. On a 35 °C (95 °F) day in Texas, a grower found a whole room of pinning blocks at 10 a.m. with "clusters falling on the floor".

  • Mushrooms recover quickly: after a heat wave "messed up a lot" of a California farm's crop, it rebounded in about two weeks, whereas a field farmer would have to wait until next year.

Temperature changes colour and form

  • One grower's first oyster strain, "Steel Blue", fruited almost pure white when too hot and deepest blue when cold.

  • Oysters that come out white whatever their strain usually point to a room that is too warm. The fix is to get the temperature down.

  • Cold black oysters look king-like (thick stems) but clustered. Warm ones look much more like ordinary blue oyster, though with fatter stems.

  • Cooler rooms give kings darker, granite-speckled caps.

  • Different strains (phenotypes) let you match what you grow to your temperature range. Black pearl kings "don't like the heat" and fail in a hot summer, and one California grower has failed to breed one that survives it. He reports warm-weather enoki pinning in his summer heat. Enoki is normally a cold-fruiting species (see the species table); a warm-pinning enoki would be a particular warm strain.

Cold air and condensation

  • Cold air holds less moisture, so humidification left unchanged condenses on the fruit. The mild result is mycelium growing out from the caps. Worse results are bacteria and even rose comb.
  • Use finer atomization (high-pressure fogging nozzles, see humidifier types) rather than large droplets.

TIP Pinning-room hack. Above about 18 °C (the mid-60s °F), black oyster pinning drops off steeply. In summer, start pins in the coolest space you have (a dedicated pinning room), even if it isn't the fruit room.

CO2 and fresh air

AT A GLANCE Automate CO2 first. Cycle the room between about 450 and 900 ppm with a narrow differential: exhaust on at about 900, off at about 600. Never above 1,000 ppm. The plenum must be at or below about 450 ppm.

FAE (fresh air exchange) is how CO2 is removed: the exhaust pulls CO2-rich room air out and plenum air replaces it. CO2 is measured in ppm (parts per million).

CO2 setpoints

The working targets across all sources fall between about 450 and 1,000 ppm.

Automate CO2 before anything else

RULE A fruit room without a CO2 meter is unacceptable. CO2 is the number-one thing to automate, and essential once you have several rooms or want a vacation.

  • Don't trust your senses ("I can feel it" farmers).
  • Running a fan constantly instead wastes conditioned plenum air when the room is half empty.
  • A CO2 controller switching the fresh-air fans is the one thing every fruit room should buy: it is easy and changes a lot. Fresh air in, straight exhaust out.
  • Blocks emit varying amounts of CO2, spores and exudate every day. You can't automate all of that, but you can control CO2.
  • Hardware: CO2Meter.com sells a mushroom-specific meter/controller that switches a fan between ppm setpoints; the same unit works for plenum and room. Price is about $230-300 ($300 in one quote, about $230-250 in another).
  • The controller uses cannabis terms: "veg" mode (wide differential, high ppm) is for incubation; "flower" mode (narrow differential, low ppm) is for fruiting.
  • Fast species (shiitake, lion's mane, chestnut, pioppino, oyster) don't have time to recover from high CO2, so control it tightly. Reishi can fruit for months and recovers.

CASE Without a CO2 controller, one small farm got deformed fruit, such as a single huge about 4 lb (1.8 kg) "washer" black oyster.

The "lung" cycle

The recommended way to run a fruit room is the "lung" cycle, not constant fresh air.

  1. The exhaust runs until CO2 reaches the low setpoint (for example 600 ppm).
  2. The fans stop. The room sits idle and fogs up ("inhale"): humidity spikes until the humidifier shuts off.
  3. CO2 rises to the high setpoint (for example 900 ppm).
  4. The exhaust restarts ("exhale"), pulling in conditioned plenum air, and humidity drops. Then the cycle repeats.
  • This ebb and flow of evaporation and condensation makes for healthier fruit. It beats constant air exchange, which strips the room and leaves RH flat around 80-85%.
  • For kings, use bigger intake and exhaust fans on a CO2 meter, pulling conditioned air. Nobody has been seen to succeed with kings under constant fresh air.
  • Run the exhaust from a CO2 controller, not continuously.
  • Put the CO2 sensor on the far wall, set at 600 / 900 ppm, switching the 1000 CFM exhaust.
  • Keep the cycle narrow. Too wide a differential (for example 1500 down to 600 ppm), or a fan outage, gives lion's mane "dreadlocks": uneven maturity, with part rushing to spine while another part is still primordial. The fruit recovers within about a day once fixed.

CASE Evidence for cycling. One farm's early king failures came from poor humidification and too much airflow, with 250 CFM fans running constantly before it had CO2 meters. A French Canadian grower had lion's mane problems under constant exchange; switching to cyclic CO2-triggered exchange removed all their blotch and malformed growth.

TIP For lion's mane in a big room, send fresh air along the floor. A New Jersey greenhouse farm's lion's mane was pink and poor. The advice it was given: lion's mane doesn't like moisture or airflow on it, so instead of "traditional HVAC", "send it down along the ground", because "CO2 falls"; raise the mushrooms up and fruit the more delicate varieties on the upper shelves.

CO2 inside bags

CO2 is heavier than air. In maitake bags, a slit down one or two sides lets CO2 spill out instead of pooling, and lets the mushroom push the bag open.

RANGE Recommended for small farms buying blocks: the cycled "lung" approach above. Other practice: some growers favour constant exhaust, and large growers criticize the lung concept; the cycled advice targets small farms buying blocks, not big farms with large AC systems. The maitake protocol is an exception: a about 500 CFM fan running continuously in a 12 x 24 ft room, plus steady 90-93% RH, because maitake dislikes fast exchange and humidity swings. KSS kings thrive under constant, barely perceptible, mostly recirculated airflow. No side-by-side data compare the two approaches.

Relative humidity

AT A GLANCE Let humidity breathe: roughly 70% up to 90% and back, in step with the CO2 cycle, with no water sitting on caps. Keep the floor dry. Maitake (steady 90-93%) and chestnut (very high, dense fog) are the exceptions. The equipment is in Humidification equipment.

Context RH target Notes
General swing (recommended) about 70% up to about 90% and back Not constant saturation.
General, cycling about 75-85%
High Country Fungi (Avery) Swings between about 78% and 90% "Misty forest, fog breathing".
Constant fresh air (avoid) Flat about 80-85%
Lion's mane Upper 80s to low 90s %, a bit lower than oysters Swings help.
Lion's mane (Wild Fruitings) "Standard" humid-room levels, cycled up and down Exact figures unconfirmed.
Chestnut, pinning 90-95%
Chestnut, after primordia 88-90%
Chestnut Very high, dense fog Hydrofogger (why).
Maitake Steady 90-93% High-pressure fog.
Reishi 85-95%
