Cycle humidity rather than saturate

  • A swing of roughly 70% to 90% and back mimics natural daily oscillations.
  • Constant over-humidity puts water droplets on caps, which causes malformations.
  • RH swings help lion's mane develop even spines and a smooth surface, without crater-like crenulations.
  • Lion's mane humidity is cycled to suppress Mycogone-type problems.
  • Holding 90% all the time is how you get blotch. The crop's weight comes from water in the block; misting only keeps the block surface hydrated. Keep the grow-room floor bone dry.
  • One working setting: misting 6 minutes on and 14-15 minutes off (High Country Fungi).
  • Stripped blocks lose more water, so raise humidity when you strip them. Blotch tends to stay where water sits.
  • In cold rooms, adjust humidification down or use finer atomization (Cold air and condensation).
  • Why one large Pennsylvania farm needs no humidifier for kings: a large mass of wet wood shelving and concrete releases water under constant airflow (plus steam sources). The same materials in a small room would not be enough.
  • Reishi: a 1943 humidity study found wet conditions favour chlamydospores (thick-walled resting spores). Below about 85% RH, Ganoderma pore tubes grow hyphae instead of a proper pore surface (details unconfirmed).

RANGE Recommended: a breathing swing of about 70-90% RH for most species; some growers prefer a narrower 75-85%. Maitake: steady 90-93%, because it dislikes humidity swings. Lion's mane has been described both as needing "constant high humidity" with tight, homogeneous control and as benefiting from swings; in practice, keep it high (upper 80s to low 90s %) with gentle swings.

  • Large rooms can stay humid without humidifiers. At a Kennett Square (Pennsylvania) sized gourmet farm, the "doubles" (concrete rooms about 18 x 18 x 7.6 m, 60 x 60 x 25 ft) have no humidifiers, "just air exchange and recirculation"; they are hosed down and steamed out between crops. The sheer mass of substrate at about 66% moisture keeps the room humid.

TIP If a humidifier breaks, you can hold humidity for a day or two by misting the blocks with a hose, wetting the floor and running fans, as one Washington farm did for two days.

Light as a fruiting signal

AT A GLANCE Light is a signal, not food. King oyster, nebrodensis, beech and maitake need a lot; lion's mane and shiitake need some; oysters can manage in the dark; chestnut is burned by strong light. Fixtures are in Lighting hardware.

  • Light is both a pinning trigger and a developmental cue for these non-Agaricus species. It works as a signal, not as photosynthesis.
  • Strongly light-triggered: king oyster, its Mediterranean relative nebrodensis, and beech/shimeji. Chestnut somewhat. Lion's mane to some extent.
Species Light need
King oyster Light matters a lot. Long hours of very bright, even light. Being bathed in light matters more than its direction.
Maitake Lots of light, about 6500 K or the coolest spectrum, kept on all the time. Strong floodlights in fruiting, and adequate light even in incubation.
Lion's mane Fairly light-triggered. No precise regime is needed, but solid ambient full-spectrum light improves pin set. Less light-dependent than maitake.
Black oyster Standard full-spectrum light is fine. Blue-spectrum LED is known to suit king oyster and probably helps black pearl, but isn't critical.
Golden oyster Place on upper shelves; they seem to respond more to light.
Pioppino Lights on once the pin carpet forms.
Shiitake The clearest case of a species needing light cues. Browning is light-driven: blocks kept dark barely brown, so expose all sides to some light.
Oysters Can go through every stage to fruiting readiness in darkness.
Chestnut Would be burned or set back by king/maitake-level light (warning).

King oyster and light

  • One large Pennsylvania farm runs long hours of very bright light. Even, intense light over each part of the substrate gives uniform round-capped kings; uneven light gives fluted, sideways, malformed caps (not yet tested in a controlled trial).
  • One grower built a light-and-cooling chamber that was lowered over racks of kings before they went to the fruit rooms, with intense light and heavy AC down to about 4 °C (40 °F).
  • Japanese farms and Mycopia run blue tube lights along rack rows.
  • Kings in typical incubation (elevated CO2, diffuse light) form a skin and only pin after it forms, which is best avoided. Light is a major induction factor.

Maitake and light

  • Maitake can incubate in a dim spot and then be rolled into bright light (about 3 weeks in, as an example) to trigger pinning.
  • In short, maitake fruiting needs high-pressure humidification, lots of light (6500 K or the coolest spectrum), slow air movement and 90-93% RH.

RANGE Chestnut and light. Chestnut is listed among species partly triggered by light, but it also wants less ambient light than most species and is burned by strong light. Read together: some light helps, intense light harms. Keep chestnut on low shelves, out of direct light.

When to move blocks to fruiting

AT A GLANCE Move a block when it shows its species' readiness cue, not by the calendar alone. Too early raises contamination risk and gives poor form; too late gives pins trapped inside the bag. How blocks get to this point is in Chapter 13.

Species Ready when Too early / too late
Shiitake At least 75-80% brown. Once most blocks in a rack are about 90% brown, fruit them all. Fruiting at 75-80% brown gives fewer, larger mushrooms; about "120% brown" gives more, smaller ones and sometimes more yield.
Lion's mane A pillow of marshmallowy aerial mycelium on top; the bag has shrunk tight against the block. Slack bags give primordia in nooks. Too late: primordia form inside the bag and fruit is malformed. Too early: contamination risk rises.
Chestnut Ripened 1-2+ weeks past full colonization, until it swells with caramel-coloured metabolites. Ripening gives a faster pin set and more vigorous fruit.
Black oyster About 3 weeks' incubation Shortens fruit-room time to primordia.
Maitake "Fist-to-fingers" stage of in-bag primordia. Inspect every block (one farm uses a ruler mark). Too early: thick, undifferentiated fronds and stalls. Too late: odd growth.
Pioppino Wild fluff on top, then amber exudate droplets, then a carpet of nodules that turn yellow/golden. See the RANGE in cutting methods.
King oyster Freshly colonized Don't hold long in a cooler before pinning.
Reishi antlers Antlers can be held in a bag even a year, then stripped Stripped antlers can form proper caps within about a month.

Triggering fruiting: cutting

AT A GLANCE Cutting the bag is the main fruiting trigger. Cut decisively into the mycelial mat, match the cut to the species, and never cut half-moons around pins that have already formed.

  • Cutting is the most direct fruiting trigger. It sits between "let it fruit when it wants" and temperature, humidity and light regimes.
  • Some growers (for example in Rochester, NY) have been reluctant to cut blocks for fear of hurting them.
  • A colonized filter bag is a synthetic log. Cutting or stripping it is like scarring a log: local fast gas exchange (plus light) triggers pinning.
  • The plastic is the bark and the block the heartwood. Light through a crack or wound in a tree signals "exposed, fruit now".

How to cut

  • Cut decisively. A cut creates a weak, oxygen-exposed spot that the mycelium regrows into.

  • Cut well into the block to scar the outer mycelial mat. Don't wait for pins and then cut around them; that is the pioppino method, since pioppino pins on top first.

  • Don't cut delicate half-moons around existing pins: that gives elongated, CO2-affected stems.

  • Deliberate disruption of the mycelium is the point (kinkake, the Japanese term; spelling unverified).

  • Uneven maturity inside a bag can cause premature pinning elsewhere in it.

  • In bottle growing, kinkake (scratching the surface) acts like casing, creating fresh surface, and the single opening for gas and light makes induction easier to control.

  • For big blue oyster clusters, one New Hampshire farm uses an H cut. Bags tamped into "TV" or "ski slope" shapes are hard to handle.

Bag plastic and colour

  • Bag plastic matters (Chapter 11). With PE (polyethylene) bags, a top cut folded over gapes into a wound that dries the medium on both sides, giving slow, poor pin sets or a deformed mushroom plus scattered pins inside the bag. PP (polypropylene) bags are more pliable and stay tight against the block.
  • PE bags are tough to cut and shred if over-cut, and folded-over PE didn't stick to the substrate, so pins got trapped and deformed.
  • Black bags block light, so the mycelium keeps maturing without pinning. That widens the holding window and lets pins form only at the cut.
  • A 10 lb (4.5 kg) clear oyster bag colonized in 10-14 days will pin immediately unless refrigerated; black bags extend that window.

Cutting methods by species

Species Method
Black oyster (recommended) Slit or cross-cut the long face about 1/4 in (6 mm) deep with a clean blade, for a dense, large cluster. Top-fruiting is not recommended.
Black oyster (trial) Top: cut off the very top, fold the sides down, leaving about 3-4 in (8-10 cm) of bag above the substrate, kept puffed open. Side fruiting did at least as well.
Lion's mane Open at the pillowy stage: a long shallow slit or an X across the top. Side slits or an X are also used, as for blue oyster.
Lion's mane (home vs farm) Home: top-fruit for one big flush plus smaller ones. Large farms: four side cuts for smaller, consistent fruit; multiple cuts for many small clusters (one farm once used a paddle studded with broadhead arrow tips).
Lion's mane (speed) Cutting off the top layer may fruit slightly faster.
Comb tooth Like lion's mane: fold the bag over and cut an X, a straight slit, or an H with side slits. It can also fruit from the uncut top.
Chestnut A razor-deep (about 1/8 in, 3 mm) slice across the top, with air pressed out and the wound kept tight; tolerates a slightly deeper cut than most. Or a cross or X on the broadest face. Fruit upright.
Maitake Cut the top off at the "fist-to-fingers" stage, plus a single slit down one or two sides. Don't cut the bag down to the block.
Maitake (black bags) Side-cut when fully colonized, perhaps with early metabolite droplets, before distinct lobes form on top (credited to a few growers; not confirmed).
Pioppino Traditionally snip the corners for air exchange; most farms cut the top off and let it fruit up to the top; some cut halfway. If pins appear at the sides, clip the bag top and use the top surface.
King oyster In-bag/collar pinning (cut the top off after pins, leaving a collar), a stripped block, or casing trays (King oyster methods). Fruit from the top centre, with no side growth.
Shiitake Strip the bag (optionally after 1-3 days of in-bag pinning), soak or shock, and flip the block 180 degrees (Shocks).
Reishi Strip or cut the bag to expose the antlers to fresh air.

RANGE Black oyster, top versus side. Recommended: side cuts (slit or cross on the long face), because the strain naturally clusters. Many growers top-fruit black oyster, some to imitate king oyster form. One trial found side fruiting at least as good as top fruiting, but the two rounds also differed in incubation time and the sample was small.

RANGE Pioppino opening time. Recommended: open at the fluff-and-amber-droplet stage. Pioppino traditionally fruits from a pin carpet on the block top, but by that point it is "a little too late", giving stringy, nutty results.

  • Lion's mane can be fruited on netted racks with the bag cut at both top and bottom. The bottom clusters can get "a little bit soggy" but still work; watch the humidity.

King oyster methods

King oyster gives three distinct fruiting methods. Pin "top fruiting" (letting pins form on top before opening) is best kept for fast pioppino.

Method How Results and risks
Stripped block (recommended for a cold all-purpose room; one grower's method) Put fully colonized bags in the fruit room. When clusters of pins appear (often from light exposure), cut the bag fully off and set the block on a shelf. Even pinning with scattered moderate-size mushrooms and no spots for water to pool. A good catch-all.
In-bag/collar pinning Pins form inside the bag (with a few cuts top or bottom), or the bag top is cut off after pins form, leaving a plastic collar to protect them. The hardest method, though people think it the safest; fine for tabletop growers.
Casing trays (one grower, since about 2013-14) Pack about 6 colonized blocks of one phenotype into a busboy tray with one crumbled block between them, let them knit, then case loosely about 3 in (8 cm) deep with peat moss mixed with high-calcium, low-magnesium hydrated lime (no pasteurization). Mushrooms come up one by one and look beautiful, but casing pulled up with each mushroom sends labour through the roof, and yield is poor.

Collar pinning in detail

  • Failure mode: humidity condenses inside the bag where warm substrate meets cooler incoming air, and the condensate floods the bag and kills the pins.
  • Workaround: make small slits (for example one under the filter patch) before opening. With high in-bag CO2 the blocks will pin in the bag.
  • Timing: freshly colonized blocks, not ones held long in a cooler, give an even pin set in the collar.
  • One large Pennsylvania farm cuts the bag off just below the filter once pins appear.
  • Top fruiting in a small room needs stiller air, which the collar helps provide.

Shocks and other triggers

AT A GLANCE Shiitake is the one species that reliably responds to physical shock: strip, soak about an hour (or cold-shock or slap), flip, and expect a burst of pins in about 5-7 days.

  • Shiitake is the one species that reliably responds to physical shock, within about a day. Left undisturbed, a block may not fruit for a long time. Temperature swings also trigger it.
  • It is the one species that, anecdotally, likes shock.
  • Shiitake is perhaps the easiest mushroom to fruit but the hardest to incubate, with skill split roughly 50/50 between incubation and fruiting handling.
  • The brown skin is what lets shiitake fruit from all over the block. Mushroom mass comes from the substrate, not the room.

Shiitake shock options

Option Detail
Straight into fruiting with no treatment The most common approach.
Water soak About an hour; also rehydrates blocks below the 65% moisture target.
Cold A cooler. Strain LE3790 likes cold: cold shock or refrigeration slows metabolism and delays pinning.
Physical slapping A physical shock.
  • Cold water and slapping are thermal and physical shocks that give a stronger, more synchronized pin set.
  • Refrigeration helps hold and shock blocks so fruiting can be staggered fortnightly.
  • Don't hold 3790 blocks too long in the cold, or the bag fills with malformed mushrooms.
  • Accidental shocks in incubation (AC failure, a temperature drop, bumped blocks, moved shelves) trigger pinning in the bag. Move triggered blocks promptly to fruiting or a cooler.
  • People have tried electrifying shiitake logs to shock-fruit them. Don't do this.

Procedure: stripping and shocking shiitake blocks

  1. Check readiness: at least 75-80% brown, or fruit the whole rack once most blocks are about 90% brown (readiness).
  2. Optional in-bag pinning: leave the bag on for 1-3 days of pinning to get fewer, bigger mushrooms (see below).
  3. Strip the bag. If you open bags rather than strip them fully, leave a small rim of bag at the bottom to catch exudate.
  4. Soak about an hour (or cold-shock or slap).
  5. Rinse the blocks before they go into the room.
  6. Flip each block 180 degrees so the wetter bottom is on top, for more even fruiting up the block (done at Cascadia).
  7. Set the block on a slatted or strip shelf, on a low rack.
  8. To halve a block, cut it top to bottom, not across, because water settles to the bottom and halves cut across would yield unevenly. Lay each half cut side down: a cut face never fruits (it has no skin).

CHECK Primordia within about 2 days; the flipped block is bursting with pins all around in about 5-7 days.

The in-bag pinning trick (shiitake)

  • Leaving the bag on lets CO2 build, so fewer pins form and, if well timed, mushrooms are bigger.
  • It's an old trick with strain 3782 for medium caps, also used with 3790, JC and KOM. It also shows up under-hydrated blocks.
  • Remove the bag after 1-3 days of pinning, or caps get bruised, flattened and bacteria-prone (puddling) and lose their surface hairs.

RANGE Which shock for which shiitake strain is anecdotal (one-block comparisons). JC fruited faster and harder when beaten than when cold-shocked, while 3790 responded better to a cooler. Recommended: try both on a few blocks of your own strain.

Other triggers

  • Nebrodensis fruits in the wild after hard frosts (frosty nights, days in the 10-15 °C (50s °F) range). One grower froze their blocks and they fruited large mushrooms, at low yield.
  • Chestnut incubation temperature swings (even 16 to 19 °C, 60 to 66 °F) trigger banded pinning in the bag.
  • Hericium (lion's mane and comb tooth) is easily triggered to abort colonization and pin by light, temperature swings or low moisture.
  • Speculatively, macerating mycelium may read to the fungus as a disaster and prompt an "escape" pin set.

Flushes and yield

AT A GLANCE Most commercial rooms take one flush per block (two for lion's mane). Oysters give about 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) per 10 lb block, kings and maitake about 2 lb (0.9 kg). More yield data are in Chapter 21.

Flushes

  • One farm (Wild Fruitings) runs every species for one flush except lion's mane, which gets two. A 2 lb (0.9 kg) first flush plus 1.5 lb (0.7 kg) second flush is "doing fine" (block size presumably 10 lb, 4.5 kg).
  • A compost customer reportedly got 11 flushes from lion's mane blocks. Whether late flushes (for example a 13th) still carry the beneficial compounds is an open question.
  • Maitake: second flushes are not recommended (they are uncommon with top-fruiting varieties).
  • High-yield blue oyster strains fruit about four times.
  • Spent lion's mane and oyster blocks used as garden mulch keep fruiting.
  • Stamets' book describes timing shiitake blocks to pin before they brown, then taking a second flush after browning.
  • Reishi can keep fruiting for months. Year-old bags can become mostly antler, with little of the 10 lb (4.5 kg) substrate left.

TIP Decide on a second flush block by block, by weight. A Massachusetts grower runs second flushes in the colder months. After the first harvest, a block weighing over 7.5 lb (3.4 kg) usually gives at least another pound (0.45 kg); under 7.5 lb it goes to compost, because keeping it is more risk than reward.

Yield figures

Species Yield Conditions
Oysters generally About 4 lb (1.8 kg) per block Compared with kings.
Blue oyster (house strain) 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) per block Block presumably 10 lb (4.5 kg).
Blue oyster (strain POCNS, Catawba Mushrooms) About 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) bag
Oyster 40 blocks gave about 80-100 lb (36-45 kg) Block size not stated.
Black oyster 2.58-2.87 lb (1.17-1.30 kg) per block, average about 2.7 lb (1.2 kg) Side-fruited, about 3 weeks' incubation.
King oyster About 2-2.25 lb (0.9-1.0 kg) per block With everything right.
Maitake About 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block Fronds or in-bag "blob".
Lion's mane 2 lb + 1.5 lb (0.9 + 0.7 kg) Two flushes.
Lion's mane, in-bag 50 blocks gave about 122 lb (55 kg) fresh Auto-fruited, for drying.
Whole room (High Country Fungi, 16 x 16 ft) Peaks at about 600 lb (270 kg) a week
Blue oyster, 11 lb (5 kg) block (High Country Fungi) At least 2.5-2.8 lb (1.1-1.3 kg), more when dialled in 2.5 lb (1.1 kg) is a good yield for most varieties; pioppino yields a little less. While learning, plan on about 2.25 lb (1.0 kg).

  • Kings are a craft crop and not worth it without cooling and air handling.

  • Harvesting a day late (caps upturning, spores dropping) visibly cost black oyster weight (Chapter 15).

  • Weight is not always yield. Lion's mane grown in filter-patch bags at high CO2 next to reishi "looks as though you're getting a heavier mushroom, but you're just getting more water weight", so harvesting later adds no real material. Reishi is the opposite: it builds denser layers that do add yield the longer it grows. Gilled mushrooms such as Flammulina (enoki) inflate a pre-formed primordium "like a balloon", while polypores such as maitake (hen of the woods) build new layers and can grow over debris.

Reading the mushrooms: shape and colour faults

AT A GLANCE The mushrooms tell you what the room is doing. Long stems and small caps mean CO2 is too high. Water-soaked, warty or rose-combed caps point to humidity or water quality. White oysters and goopy blotch point to heat. Full diagnosis by symptom is in Chapter 19.

Oysters and lion's mane are good indicators of room airflow. A good room gives short stems and flattening caps.

Air and CO2 faults

Symptom Species Likely cause and fix
Long stems, no caps ("cordyceps-like") Oyster High CO2.
Vase-shaped caps, long stems Oyster Poor airflow.
Stem elongation Black oyster CO2 not exhausted early enough: set the fan to come on in the 800s ppm.
Single huge about 4 lb (1.8 kg) "washer" fruit Black oyster No CO2 control.
Elongated stems at a cut Any Cutting half-moons around existing pins.
Coral-like, reaching fruit that cooks floppy Lion's mane High CO2 (for example fruiting in the bag with one corner open).
Same deformities as above Lion's mane Low fresh air/high CO2 from hot rooms or dense packing with blocks touching.
"Dreadlocks" (part spining, part still primordial) Lion's mane CO2 differential too wide, or a fan outage.
Bleached, crusty beige, flat caps King oyster Too much CO2 and not enough light.
Fluted, sideways, malformed caps King oyster Uneven light intensity across the substrate.
Antlers instead of caps Reishi High CO2 in the bag (perhaps 3,000-5,000 ppm with an A-style filter). Under about 1,000 ppm, or outdoors, reishi gives kidney-shaped caps.
Small, stuck antlers Reishi Very impervious Tyvek-type patches (high CO2).
Stem grows sideways, never caps Reishi (wild) CO2 and conditions shaping form.

Humidity and water faults

Symptom Species Likely cause and fix
Uneven spines: long and drooping on one side, a dense bald ball on the other Lion's mane RH too high (no evaporation off the fruit).
Crater-like crenulations Lion's mane Lack of RH swings (swings smooth the surface).
Popcorn/cauliflower-like formation Lion's mane Off or inconsistent conditions.
Pink or yellow tint on young fruit Lion's mane Room too dry. The fruit should start and finish white, yellowing slightly at maturity.
Warty caps King and black oyster Very high humidity (distinct from rose comb).
Mycelium growing out of caps; then bacteria and rose comb Black oyster Condensation in cold rooms; coarse droplets.
Rose comb (gill tissue on cap tops), odd colours, mushy deformities, poor texture Many Too little air exchange or no breathing cycle; constant over-humidity.
Rose comb Many Minerals and microbes in humidifier water.
Different fruit colour Pleurotus (oysters) Untreated mineral content of hydration water.
Fused mushrooms, small cap-on-cap Chestnut Excess humidity or condensation settling on caps. Usually circumstantial and not a warning sign, unlike in oysters.
Pins killed in the collar King oyster Condensate flooding the bag (collar pinning).
Bruised, flattened, hairless caps, puddling bacteria Shiitake Bag left on for more than 1-3 days of pinning.

Blotch and disease signs

Symptom Species Likely cause and fix
Yellowing caps Oyster Early blotch sign from poor humidification.
Tan, goopy fruit Blue oyster Blotch in a too-warm summer room.
Goopy golden/rusty lesions only at cut sites where water collects Oyster and others Room-borne blotch (the blocks colonized fine).
Black slime on stems Lion's mane Probably a different bacterium from classic blotch.
Bizarre deformed morphology Pleurotus Viruses: common and untreatable. Weakened crops are also more blotch-prone.
White, cauliflower-like young fruit instead of darkening Maitake Bacteria surviving ultra-pasteurization (Chapter 12), worse when moved to fruiting too early.
Mould on developing fruit as exudate wicks up Maitake Over-rich (50/50) blocks.
Poor yield, slow pins, malformed fruit Oyster, black oyster Stroma in the block.

Temperature, handling and block faults

Symptom Species Likely cause and fix
Caps flatten fast, stems wither and droop, bad smell Chestnut Too warm.
Oysters white whatever the strain Oyster Room too warm; get the temperature down.
Browned white fruit Lion's mane Shiitake exudate dripping from above.
Malformed fruit inside the bag Lion's mane Cut too late.
Single odd mushroom Chestnut Too much substrate per fruiting site (30-40 lb, 14-18 kg, straw buckets).
Deformed fruit plus scattered pins inside the bag Chestnut PE bag cut gaping and drying.
Petals desiccate and die Maitake Bag cut down too short (no protective collar).
Thick, undifferentiated fronds ("cultivated look") Maitake Cut too early. Rich media speed development so fronds don't fully differentiate.
Bag full of malformed mushrooms Shiitake 3790 Held cold too long.
Glossy, slick, flattened top that never pins; dry side pins Pioppino Bad culture, cook or spawn.
Drastic change in fruit form Pioppino Switching grain source: "rule number one" is not to switch (Chapter 9).
Many small consistent clusters versus few robust clusters Chestnut Agar-slurry versus normal inoculation (which method gave which is unclear in one account).

RANGE Cause of rose comb. Recommended: check both room management and water. Most rose comb, odd colours and mushy deformities come from too little air exchange or no breathing cycle; many "rose comb" problems are just poor room management. The opposite view is that the outlier is "always water" (almost every time): the same black oyster spawn lot gave heavy rose comb at a Rhode Island farm and excellent fruit in Kentucky. One grower's write-up proposes that fine mineral dust settling on caps disrupts local water gradients and polarity cues. In one case, ultrasonic discs in a tarped barrel that ran condensate back into the barrel concentrated particulates until every species except chestnut showed topside caps, including golden enoki. The molecular pathways are not established. No controlled comparison of these explanations has been made.

CASE Early black oyster form. On Master's Mix, after cutting, white fuzz like pin mould grew from the cut, formed amber droplets and receded; the droplets shrank to become caps as king-like bumps formed. This no longer happens with the domesticated strain. Japanese methods for this strain are very different, and Japanese growers (Hokuto) would likely be shocked by the huge, wild-looking black oysters US farms produce.

Fruiting parameters by species

AT A GLANCE One row per species: the numbers to set the room and handle the blocks. Full species cards are in Chapter 20, and stage-by-stage numbers in Chapter 21.

Temperatures are in °C with °F in brackets. Blank cells mean no figure is available.

Species Fruit temp RH CO2 / fresh air Light Initiation Time in room
General / mixed room 13-18 °C (55-65 °F); about 16 °C (60 °F) typical; 16-18 °C (60-65 °F) ideal on a Maine farm; growth stalls below about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) Cycle about 70-90% or about 75-85% 450-900 ppm cycle; 1000 max; on 900/off 600 6500 K daylight fixtures Cut or strip 2-3 weeks per block
Blue oyster In the staple 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) range; blotch worse when warm Standard humid room High CO2 gives long stems, no caps Can mature in darkness Slits or X on the sides Mid-speed
Black (pearl) oyster 10-18 °C (50-65 °F); ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F); about 10-12 °C (low 50s °F) for dense, slow fruit; pinning drops above about 18 °C (mid-60s °F) Standard; fine atomization in cold rooms Fan on at about 800-900 ppm Standard full spectrum; blue LED may help 1/4 in (6 mm) slit or cross-cut on the long face (or top) Pins about 5-7 days after cut; about 10-14 days to harvest
Golden oyster Upper shelves (responds to light)
King oyster 10-16 °C (50-60 °F); trouble above 16 °C (60 °F); no trustworthy pinning above about 17 °C (63 °F); 20 °C (68 °F) fails Relatively high, steady; raise when stripped CO2-controlled cycling, not constant fresh air Very bright, even, long hours; blue tubes in Japan Collar, stripped block, or casing tray; top centre
P. nebrodensis Low-temperature species; frost-triggered Strongly light-triggered Freeze blocks
Shiitake 3790: 10-16 °C (50-60 °F), call it 13 °C (55 °F); 3782: about 10-27 °C (50-80 °F) tolerated No regular spraying; rinse blocks In-bag CO2 trick for 1-3 days Needed for browning Strip, soak/cold/slap; flip 180 degrees Pins about 2 days; about 6-8 days from strip
Lion's mane 13-18 °C (55-65 °F); HeCNS sweet spot about 16 °C (60 °F); POW tolerates warmer Upper 80s to low 90s %; swings help On 800-900, off 450-700 ppm; narrow differential Fairly light-triggered; full spectrum improves pin set Slit or X on top, or side cuts 14-20 days at about 16-17 °C (low 60s °F)
Comb tooth Prefers about 19-21 °C (upper 60s °F); tolerates 10-15 °C (the 50s °F) As lion's mane X, slit, H; or uncut top Slow start; 5-7 days fractalizing
Chestnut Pin at 10 °C to about 17 °C (50 °F to the low 60s °F), ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F); finish at about 16-17 °C (low 60s °F); up to about 18 °C (65 °F) OK; 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) poor or no pins 90-95% pinning; 88-90% after; heavy fog (Hydrofogger) Below about 900 ppm Keep from strong light Razor-deep cross/X on the broad face; upright 7-10 days to pins + 7-12 days; 2-3 weeks if ripened
Maitake Across 16-21 °C (the 60s °F); some strains to about 24 °C (75 °F); Shogun more warmth-tolerant than 9827 Steady 90-93%, high-pressure fog <1,000 ppm; about 500 CFM continuous slow air Lots, 6500 K, always on Top off at fist-to-fingers + side slit 7-10 days
Pioppino 18-24 °C (65-75 °F); tolerates about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F); warmer = faster Lights on once the carpet forms Cut top off Fast
Reishi 85-95% Antlers above about 1,000 ppm (in-bag 3000-5000); caps below about 1,000 ppm Strip bag for caps Months
Nameko Sticky, very humid, like chestnut
Enoki Below the 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) general range
Beech/shimeji Strongly light-triggered

Key rules

  1. Build three spaces: a cold room, a clean conditioned plenum that is also the work area, and fruit rooms. Fruit-room air goes one way, from plenum to outdoors, and never back (facility).
  2. Keep fruit rooms negative: a CO2-controlled exhaust pulls air out and a backdraft damper admits plenum air. Add a second, thermostat-controlled exhaust for temperature (negative pressure).
  3. Never put recirculating HVAC, evaporators, heat exchangers you can't wash, or circulation fans inside the fruit room (no recirculation).
  4. Automate CO2 before anything else. Cycle roughly 450-900 ppm with a narrow differential, and keep the plenum at or below about 450 ppm (CO2).
  5. Let the room breathe: humidity swinging roughly 70-90% with the exhaust cycle, and no water sitting on caps. Maitake is the exception and wants a steady 90-93% (humidity).
  6. Humidify with a fine, non-recirculating mist from treated water (bleach or ClO2, UV, RO or steam). Keep ultrasonic units outside the room (humidifiers, water).
  7. Build with steel studs, Coroplast and flashing tape, and put trapped floor drains in first (building).
  8. Run 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) for the staples: cooler for density and less disease, warmer for speed. Plan on a delivery shift of about 5 days per 5-6 °C (10 °F) (temperature).
  9. Don't overpack. Rotate weekly cohorts on rolling racks, one species and one lot per rack (loading).
  10. Cut decisively into the mycelial mat, and match the cut to the species. Never cut half-moons around existing pins (cutting).
  11. Place lion's mane and golden oysters high, shiitake and chestnut low, never lion's mane under shiitake, and give maitake its own room (mixed rooms).
  12. Clean between every load and remove blotched fruit on sight. Wear a respirator, or roll carts out to harvest (cleaning).

Open questions

  • Loading density: the standard is 1/10-1/4 of the room's volume. The 500-600 lb (225-270 kg) a week from a 12 x 24 ft room is that room's full capacity, but what fraction of the room that layout fills was not stated (Don't overpack).
  • Humidity figures for lion's mane at Wild Fruitings are unconfirmed. No species-specific RH figures exist here for blue, golden or pink oyster, shiitake or pioppino.
  • Pink oyster, golden oyster, nameko, enoki, beech and cordyceps: fruiting temperatures, CO2 and timelines are largely missing.
  • Constant versus cycled fresh air is argued from anecdote (a large Pennsylvania farm, a French Canadian grower, early king failures). No side-by-side data exist, and the recommended maitake protocol itself runs continuous slow air (the lung cycle).
  • Peroxide dose limits for humidifier water are quoted inconsistently and from an unnamed study. Verify against a primary source (peroxide).
  • Rose comb is attributed to air exchange or to water minerals. No controlled comparison exists (faults).
  • The black oyster timeline (4-5 versus 10-14 days from pin to harvest) needs checking by trial.
  • Atomizer droplet sizes: the Hart nozzle figure (about 0.03 micron) and the steam atomizer figure (about 0.3 micron) are unconfirmed.

chapters.html:
Harvest, Storage and Preservation

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers when to pick, how to pack and chill the crop, how blocks and spawn travel through the cold chain, and how surplus is dried or turned into powders and tinctures.

  • Pick on time, not late. A late harvest trades shelf life and quality for weight.
  • Cooler at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer. Get mushrooms into it promptly.
  • Keep spores and blotched fruit out of the cooler and the packing area.
  • Blocks below 27 °C (80 °F) in transit; spawn stored at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F).
  • Dry surplus at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) with steady airflow: expect about 10% of fresh weight in 24-48 h.
  • Wear a respirator when harvesting, especially shiitake and reishi.

The chapter follows the crop in the order it moves: safety first, then the decision to pick, the people and racks that do it, the packing table, the cooler, the truck, and finally the drying room for whatever cannot be sold fresh. The fruit room itself, and how to get blocks to fruit, is covered in Chapter 14.

Words used here: a block is a bag of colonized substrate ready to fruit; spawn is colonized grain used to inoculate blocks; a flush is one wave of mushrooms from a block; the cooler is any cold store (a walk-in, a CoolBot room or a refrigerated shipping container, called a reefer); the plenum is the clean, conditioned work room in front of the fruit rooms.

Temperatures at a glance

What Target Limit or warning Section
Fresh mushrooms in the cooler 2 °C (36 °F) 1-4 °C (34-40 °F); no warmer Cooler
Colonized blocks in storage 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) Black pearl oyster 1 °C (34 °F), and it still pins in time Holding blocks
Blocks in transit Refrigerated Substrate never above 27 °C (80 °F) Blocks in transit
Spawn in storage 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) A month at 6 °C (42 °F) badly hurts quality Spawn
Drying closet 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) 38 °C (100 °F) is too hot Drying

Why harvest timing decides profit

A mushroom is the fruit of the fungus. Once it is ready, it keeps growing, flattens, and starts to drop spores. Every hour past the right moment costs you shelf life, and spores dropped in the room load the air, the racks and your lungs.

  • Harvest on time. Overblown mushrooms have a shorter shelf life and raise the spore load in the room.
  • The most common harvest mistake on commercial farms is picking too late. Late shiitake gain weight, but their quality and shelf life are terrible.
  • Give up some yield for shelf life. One day late badly cuts the storage life of chestnut.
  • Clusters on one block do not mature together, so expect to pick the same block more than once.

WHY A late pick can add weight or cost it. Late shiitake gain weight while their quality is ruined; black oyster harvested one day late, with caps turning up and spores dropping, visibly lost weight. Either way, a late harvest is a mistake.

CASE A large bottle-growing farm (Mycopia) grew chestnut as one of its first bottle species. Its customers complained about poor shelf life, because the mushrooms were picked too late. Lesson: a late pick shows up later as shelf-life complaints from buyers.

TIP One small farm harvests as young as possible, before the mushrooms drop spores (sporulation), for the longest shelf life, and aims to sell within 24 hours of harvest. It picks lion's mane as soon as the spines appear, while they are still short. Another grower sells enoki at harvest, because it goes bad within about 3 days.

  • "More pounds, smaller caps. Bigger caps, less yield, less pounds." This holds for Agaricus and shiitake: letting caps grow bigger costs total weight, but bigger mushrooms are "more robust and don't bruise easily". Decide which your buyers pay for.

Harvesting safely

RULE Wear a respirator rated for fine particles whenever you harvest, especially shiitake and reishi, and whenever the room air is hazy with spores. No specific type is named in the sources; see Chapter 18 for choosing one.

WARNING Spore lung, an allergic lung illness from breathing mushroom spores, is real. After about a week of harvesting shiitake strain 3782, several staff on one farm got spore lung; it was compared to years of chain smoking packed into minutes. Wear a respirator while fruiting and harvesting, or harvest outside the room.

  • One farm always harvested reishi outdoors, because its spores are so heavy.

TIP Shiitake juice from opening hundreds of blocks a day stains like walnut ink. Wear old clothes: one harvester wore cheap white "sacrifice" t-shirts (6 for $6) and stripped blocks next to a drain.

Harvest cues by species

AT A GLANCE Shiitake: pick while the cap rim is still curled. Chestnut and oysters: before caps flatten. Lion's mane: while the spines are still short and even, before they lengthen, droop and swell. Maitake: when fronds have formed after the primordia tops darken.

The table gives what to look for, how long it usually takes, and the signs that you are already late. "Pins" are the first tiny mushrooms; "stripping" a shiitake block means taking the bag off it. For each species' full growing profile see Chapter 20, and for the room conditions behind these timings see Chapter 14.

Species Pick when Time to harvest Signs you are late
Shiitake The cap rim is still slightly curled or crinkled around the stem and the veil (the thin skin joining cap rim to stem) is just cracking About 6-8 days from stripping the block; pins appear within a couple of days Flat, saucer-shaped caps with very thin skin that soak up water and rot quickly
Black oyster Before the caps flatten or over-expand About 4-5 days after pinning in one trial; about 10-14 days from pins to harvest in another account Caps turning up, spores dropping
Chestnut Gills still partly covered, before caps flatten too far Recognisable baby mushrooms take 7-10 days from cutting the bag, then 7-12 more days of development. A whole block fully fruits in about 2-3 weeks. In the fruit room: 2-3 weeks if the blocks were ripened first, 4-5 weeks if not If the room is too warm, caps flatten fast, stems wither, and the mushrooms droop and smell bad
Lion's mane Commercially, well before full maturity, while the spines are still short and growing evenly 14-20 days in a room at about 16-17 °C (low 60s °F); fruiting inside the bag takes about 1.5-2 weeks Spines long and drooping, dropping spores and swelling with water. Pink or yellow tints mostly mean the room is too dry: the fruit should start and finish white, a little yellower when mature
Comb tooth At the end of the fractalization (branching) phase, when the branching has finished About 5-7 days of fractalization Mature fruit droops and turns spongy and cauliflower-like
Maitake When fronds have formed, after the tops of the primordia (the first knobs of a fruit body) darken About 7-10 days in the fruit room if the bag was cut on time; the whole cycle from knock to harvest is about 13 weeks If the bag is cut too early, the fruit stalls and becomes one of the slowest things in the room
Pioppino Just before the cap breaks away from the stem edge and flattens About 1.5-2 days from pin carpet; warmer is faster Not recorded
Reishi (antler form) When the antlers are ready to be "scalped" (cut off level with the block) When fruited inside the bag, 3-4 months for the antlers to reach the top of the bag Not recorded

TIP For black oyster, plan on 10-14 days from pins to harvest; 4-5 days was the best case in one trial. The 5-15 days quoted for the fruit-room stage in general applies to fast species, not to chestnut.

How to pick (twist or cut, whole cluster or single fruit, how much stem to leave) is not described in the sources; see Open questions. After the pick, flush counts and spent blocks are covered in Chapter 14.

Shiitake details

  • If shiitake pin inside the bag, remove the bag within 1-3 days of pinning. Otherwise the caps get bruised and flattened, become prone to bacteria ("puddling": water pooling and rotting on the cap), and lose their surface hairs.
  • A good flush goes from a block covered in small, light-capped pins to a dense flush of mature caps.

Maitake: the cut sets the harvest

  • When you cut the bag top decides the harvest quality. Cut it at the "fist-to-fingers" stage, when the fist-sized lump of primordia on top starts splitting into finger-like lobes (see Chapter 13). Too early gives thick, undifferentiated fronds with a "cultivated look"; too late gives odd growth.
  • Big farms give staff a marked ruler to hold against each block, so every worker cuts at the same stage.

CHECK After cutting, the tops of the developing primordia should darken considerably. If they do not darken, something is wrong: check the cut timing, light and humidity against Chapter 14.

Strain and handling notes

A strain is a named line of one species, bought from a culture or spawn supplier (see Chapter 8).

  • The lion's mane strain HeCNS gives dense, heavy fruit with short spines that do not droop. This makes it easier to handle and it holds up better after harvest.
  • One farm fruits black oyster blocks on wire shelving with the bag tops folded open. Ready clusters are dense and grey-brown, with long white stems.

Planning harvest labour and room schedules

AT A GLANCE Match harvest crew to crop size, keep one species and one lot per rack, and lay the fruit room out in weekly cohorts so something is always ready. A swing of about 5-6 °C (10 °F) in room temperature can move a delivery by about five days.

Size the crew to the crop

CASE In the run-up to a Christmas sales boom, one grower harvested hundreds of pounds of shiitake alone in an 8-hour day. By the time they finished, the buttons in the first rows were already opening again. In a similar case, a grower harvesting a whole shiitake room alone over a holiday bumper crop found the last mushrooms going over before they were done. Lesson: harvest capacity must match crop size, and fruiting work suits people who enjoy it.

  • Weekly labour example: one farm harvested on four days and graded and packed on two other days. Batching the work so that harvest, grading and packing all happen on the same two days, by the same people, can remove a whole position. No crew-size figures are recorded.
  • One way to plan this is a Sunday-to-Saturday chart with one lane per person: substrate, harvest, grade/pack, and deliveries/market.
  • Living on site lets one Houston grower harvest up to five times a day (early morning, after dinner, at 9 pm) to pick every cluster at its peak.

Temperature sets the delivery date

  • Fruiting speed responds to temperature along a curve. At 13 °C (55 °F) fruiting is much slower than at 18 °C (65 °F), so a swing of about 5-6 °C (10 °F) can shift delivery by about five days. Plan harvests around customer deadlines. Room targets are in Chapter 14.
  • Shiitake and pioppino are fast, oysters are in the middle and chestnut is slowest. Overall, the fruit-room stage takes about 5 to 15 days, and in deep winter chestnut can take two months.

CASE In very cold weather, -28 °C (-18 °F) outside, one farm's heaters could not hold room temperature. Growth slowed to a stop somewhere between 13 and 16 °C (55-60 °F), and some weeks there was nothing to sell to chefs. Lesson: size heating for the coldest week, or expect gaps in supply. See Chapter 5 for heating.

Rack and room scheduling

  • Scheduling a small fruit room is like Tetris. Know each variety's time to harvest so racks free up in time. In summer, one small farm has to fit about 300 incoming blocks while about 300 spent blocks go to compost (the period is not stated).
  • Keep one species and one lot per rack, so a whole rack is harvested, cleaned and reloaded together. Consolidate stragglers onto one rack.
  • Fixed racks (not on wheels) lead to forgotten, overgrown clusters at the back. Oversized pioppino is the typical example.
  • Lay a fruit room out as three rows, for week 1, week 2 and week 3 cohorts, so there are always harvestable blocks. Blocks take 2-3 weeks to fruit out. Leave slack even for 2-week species, in case one cohort is not cleared before the next arrives. Slower species, such as unripened chestnut at 4-5 weeks, need more rows.
  • A balanced maitake room loads new blocks and harvests about every 5 days, with a room rotation of about 7-10 days. Second flushes (a flush is one wave of mushrooms from a block) of maitake are not recommended.

Getting the crop out of the room

  • Rolling racks or carts are the most important fruiting tool. Roll them out to a separate harvest, grade and pack area, so spores stay off you and out of the plenum.
  • The plenum is where harvesting, grading, packing and dehydrating happen. It is not an entrance, a bathroom or an office.
  • Harvest, packing and grading belong on the same cooled and filtered air system as the fruit rooms, kept separate from the incubation and lab system. See Chapter 5.
  • Fully clean walls, floors and racks before loading new blocks. Racks get dirty from spore drop and Trichoderma (green mould).

CASE Racks fail at bad moments. Rolling racks have tipped over while being loaded or moved, for example at night while harvesting about 300 shiitake blocks (600-700 lb, 270-320 kg) grown for Cap n Stem. The racks that failed, at 2 a.m. during harvest, were the ones with small casters. Lesson: use racks with large casters, and keep spare racks so rescued blocks have somewhere to go. No safe load limit per rack is recorded.

  • The photos online of full "walls" of mushrooms are usually harvest racks wheeled into the grow room. Catawba Mushrooms (North Carolina) doesn't harvest inside the grow room; it wheels the racks out.

Handling by species

  • Lion's mane tissue is soft, full of water and bruises easily. Handle it carefully.
  • Antler reishi is scalped off the blocks into large bins, and the antlers are then broken off. This is laborious: hardened material behaves like a mix of cement and styrofoam and is hard to cut with saws or snips. No more worker-friendly method has been found yet.

Shaping the harvest for the market

How you open and time a block changes the size and number of the mushrooms. Decide by your orders. Cutting methods are covered in Chapter 14.

  • For retail clamshells of mixed species, many small lion's mane clusters beat one big "brain". Several cuts per block give many small fruits that do not all come at once. Example: one farm used a spiked paddle to make many openings at once.
  • Large farms make four side cuts on lion's mane for smaller, more consistent fruit suited to small packaging. Home growers often fruit from the top for one big flush followed by smaller ones.
  • Fruiting shiitake when 75-80% of the block surface is brown gives fewer, larger mushrooms; letting blocks brown further gives more, smaller ones. Choose by orders and target size.
  • Leaving shiitake to pin inside the bag gives fewer pins and, if timed well, bigger mushrooms. This is an old trick with strain 3782 for medium caps. Strip the bag within 1-3 days of pinning (see Shiitake details).

Blotched and diseased fruit at harvest

Bacterial blotch shows as discoloured, often slimy patches on the caps. Its causes and prevention are covered in Chapter 17.

RULE Pull blotched fruit on sight. Never box blotched mushrooms into the cooler, and never sell bleach-sprayed fruit.

  • Remove blotched fruit as soon as you see it, so it does not recycle through the room. Even with clean air, treated water and fine misting, it will appear now and then.
  • Spraying affected fruit with dilute bleach is a quick defence against spread, but sprayed mushrooms cannot be sold: discard them and fix the source. Room cleaning strengths are in Chapter 17. Infected young fruit often aborts before maturing.
  • Blotched mushrooms boxed and put in the cooler spread blotch to the other mushrooms in the cooler.
  • At one farm where over half the crop was shiitake, blotch was barely noticed. It was handled by picking off blotched oyster pieces, or not packing them.
  • Blocks affected by stroma (a hard crust of mycelium on the block surface; see Chapter 16) give poor yields, slow pinning and malformed fruit that is not sellable, though it might be used for powder (see Powders).

Grading and packing

AT A GLANCE Pack into breathable boxes lined with butcher paper, stamp a best-by date 7 days from harvest, and chill at once. Pack to the buyer's specification; turn off-grade pieces into seconds (cheaper, imperfect product), powder or dried product rather than compost.

Grades and buyer specifications

No grading scheme (size classes, defects) is recorded in the sources; grade to what each buyer asks for.

  • Japan recognizes about 30 shiitake grades. Strain 3790 was long a top choice there for grade A fruit; it does best when the substrate is not over-supplemented and the blocks are incubated and fruited on time.
  • Comb tooth ships as large, white, coral-like heads packed in cardboard boxes.
  • Some maitake clients want uncut "blobs" grown in the bag, which are much simpler to produce.
  • Some cooks find the blobs taste better and slice them like king oyster, into slices that look like marbled rye bread. Others prefer shredded fronds with a pulled-pork texture.
  • Reishi antlers are weighed on a bench scale (for example a Torrey) and packed to each client's specification in vacuum-sealed bags.

Procedure: vacuum-sealing reishi antlers

  1. Weigh the antlers to the client's specification.
  2. Adjust the vacuum sealer's settings on a test bag before the run, then seal each bag. (Bag size and settings are not recorded.)
  3. Check every bag by eye and by hand for antler punctures before boxing.

CHECK A good bag stays tight against the antlers. A loose or soft bag has lost its vacuum, usually where an antler tip has pierced it: repack it.

Procedure: packing fresh mushrooms for wholesale and retail

WHY One small farm adopted this method after oysters kept in a domestic chest fridge turned waterlogged, split and yellow. Breathable boxes and a cold commercial fridge fixed it.

  1. Use breathable, wax-coated corrugated produce boxes.
  2. Line the bottom of each box with butcher paper.
  3. Pack the mushrooms, then lay a strip of butcher paper on top. Punch holes in the paper if more airflow is needed.
  4. For retail, pack into perforated cardboard punnets (from a produce-packaging supplier) and wrap them in butcher paper.
  5. Hand-stamp a best-by date 7 days from harvest. This farm uses 7 days for all its product; short-lived species such as enoki (about 3 days) need a shorter date.
  6. Put the boxes straight into a commercial fridge at 2 °C (36 °F). See The cooler.

CHECK Mushrooms that turn waterlogged, split or yellow in storage (as oysters did in a domestic chest fridge) mean the packing or the fridge needs fixing: use breathable boxes with butcher paper and a commercial fridge at 2 °C (36 °F).

Box weights and box sizes are not recorded.

TIP Keep the packing table organized, for example with a cut-down box to hold scissors, markers and stickers.

Selling notes

More on pricing and selling is in Chapter 22.

Selling to chefs

  • For chefs: a pound (0.45 kg) of lion's mane is about a softball-sized piece.

  • Chefs who cut lion's mane into steaks are left with offcuts. Suggest crab-cake-style patties or a salad topping as an upcharge, and pass ideas from one account to new ones as a sales tool.

  • Culinary ideas to share: king oyster sliced thin on a mandoline and seared like bacon; black oyster sliced lengthwise into planks and pan-seared. Black oyster's appeal is a big, king-like stem with a softer, oyster-like texture. Selling at markets

  • At farmers' markets, brown paper bags are poor for small sales, while bags with handles suit large ones. Pre-weighing captures full value but costs time.

  • Transport to market in big coolers or insulated delivery bags with ice packs.

  • At slow markets, fill the display baskets but sell from the boxes until they run out, then sell from the display.

  • Overproduction (cancelled orders, or blocks that fruit on their own or pin from the sides) usually ends up composted or sold as soup mushrooms or seconds. Drying is the alternative; see Drying surplus.

CASE Pick straight into the box you will sell in. A large Pennsylvania farm writes the next day's "pick set" every afternoon (about 2-3:30 pm): a text to each farm division listing what to pick into which box, in priority order (customer A's branded boxes, then customer B's, then plastic trays for retail packs, then generic 5 lb cases). Mushrooms shouldn't be moved from box to box. "Someone's doing the labour at some point": either at the farm or at the packing house.

CASE A film-wrapping machine (heated pad, automatic stickers and date labels) took a Maine farm from hand-wrapping about 4,000 punnets ("tills") in a late night to about 4,000 in an hour. The crew changed from three fillers per wrapper to two fillers feeding the machine, at about seven punnets a minute per line. A COVID-era grant paid for it when a supermarket chain suddenly wanted only packaged mushrooms. The owner calls automation the best thing he did: the same good staff, doing more valuable work.

The cooler

AT A GLANCE Hold the cooler at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer, and above freezing to avoid ice damage. Size it for at least two pallets of blocks plus the fresh crop, about 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m) for a two-room farm; more is better. Make it easy to clean, because spores get everywhere.

Where the cooler fits

  • A fruiting facility needs three spaces: a cooler, a plenum and the fruit rooms.
  • Cooling is one of the most important things on the farm: coolers for outgoing pallets, for spawn before use, and for blocks waiting to be packed for shipping. DIY or improvised coolers are fine.
  • The plenum can share space with a walk-in cooler or the harvest area, but do not store CO2-producing blocks there, and do not run heavy activity in it.
  • In a shipping-container farm there is no room inside for a walk-in, so it must sit outside.
  • In the example 28 x 40 ft (8.5 x 12.2 m) building below, the walk-in cooler sits next to the plenum and two fruit rooms. See Chapter 3 for whole-farm layout.

Temperature

  • Recommended: about 2 °C (36 °F); acceptable 1-4 °C (34-40 °F), no warmer. A walk-in or a CoolBot room both work. The cooler stores incoming blocks and fresh mushrooms.
  • One small farm stores boxed mushrooms in a commercial fridge at 2 °C (36 °F). A CoolBot room (an ordinary insulated room cooled by a household air conditioner with a CoolBot controller) is an option, but it is less dependable than a purpose-built unit.
  • Humidity: no target for the cooler is recorded.
  • Refrigerate chestnut promptly and sell it quickly to keep its looks.
  • Fresh mushrooms can sit in refrigeration for a fairly long time before drying, so owning a reefer or walk-in makes drying easier to schedule.

RULE Whatever cooler you use, make it easy to clean and take apart, because spores get everywhere.

WARNING Walk-in evaporators only recirculate the air inside; they bring in no fresh air. In a space full of spores their fins and coils clog with spores, even if the mushrooms are picked early. Keep the cooler away from spore-laden air and clean the coils.

  • Stop the cooler drying the crop. Cold-room (reefer) units "have a propensity to dry out vegetables", and mushrooms, about 90% water, lose weight fast. Fit more evaporator and condenser capacity than the bare minimum and run it less, with a lower fan speed, so less air moves over the mushrooms. Add an insulated floor and strip curtains on the door so warm air doesn't rush in every time it opens. Done right, shelf life goes from a day to one or two weeks, depending on species.

Size and cost

  • For two fruit rooms of about 14 x 20 ft (4.3 x 6.1 m) in a 28 x 40 ft (8.5 x 12.2 m) building, block storage alone needs about two pallets, about 8 x 4 ft (2.4 x 1.2 m) of floor. With fresh mushrooms too, plan on about 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m), and more if you buy blocks less often than weekly. More cooler space is better.
  • Wild Fruitings, a Maine farm used as an example throughout these chapters, has a cooler of about 8 x 8 ft (2.4 x 2.4 m).
Cooler option Cost Notes
Used 20 or 40 ft (6.1 or 12.2 m) reefer container About $9,000 Plenty of cooling, and it could be split into a cooled plenum and a walk-in. Its refrigeration unit runs on 480 V, so it needs an electrician and a step-down transformer to 240 V (on about a 40 A breaker)
New walk-in cooler About $15,000-40,000; up to $200,000 for large installations
DIY or improvised cooler, CoolBot room Not stated DIY or improvised coolers are fine. Make any cooler easy to clean and take apart
  • Size the walk-in for more than the week's crop. A Texas farm sized its cooler for about 200 lb (90 kg) of mushrooms a week with "a little extra room", not knowing that farms also keep backup blocks in the cooler; the space "gets eaten up so fast".

Keeping quality by species

Only enoki has a shelf life in days in the sources (about 3 days); for the rest the table gives relative keeping quality. As a working figure, one small farm stamps a best-by date 7 days from harvest on its fresh product (see packing).

Species Keeping quality
King oyster Stores very well; long shelf life
Black oyster Fairly good if harvested before the caps flatten; less than king oyster, but a good wholesale mushroom
Lion's mane (HeCNS) Dense fruit holds up after harvest, but the soft tissue bruises easily
Chestnut Short. Harvest before the caps flatten, chill and sell quickly; one day late sharply cuts storage life
Shiitake Flat, late-picked caps rot quickly; late picking makes shelf life terrible
Enoki Goes bad within about 3 days; sell at harvest
Pioppino, comb tooth, maitake, reishi (fresh) Not recorded
Dried mushrooms (any species) About 7 years if sealed and kept very dry (claimed; see Packaging dried product)
  • Learn the shelf life of your own crop in your own cooler. A New Hampshire grower knows his king oysters last exactly 14 days in his cooler (depending on the time of year). Others work only from pick timing. Fruiting is the hardest part of the business because you have about seven days to sell each harvest.

The cold chain for blocks and spawn

AT A GLANCE Shipping blocks and spawn uses the same cold chain as fresh mushrooms. Keep block substrate below 27 °C (80 °F) in transit. Store spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), not 6 °C (42 °F). Pre-chill, vent the cartons, leave air channels in the pallet, and ship fast.

Temperature is the variable that always bites when shipping spawn, blocks, cultures or fresh mushrooms, especially in summer. Spawn is grain colonized by mycelium, used to inoculate substrate (see Chapter 9); a block is a bag of colonized substrate ready to fruit (see Chapter 13).

Blocks in transit

RULE Do not let block substrate go above 27 °C (80 °F) in transit. Summer freight in an unrefrigerated truck, at 38-49 °C (100-120 °F), is not acceptable. Refrigerated shipping makes blocks last much longer.

If you ship blocks:

  • Block shipping cartons are perforated for refrigerated freight, and pallets are stacked with air channels down the middle so the blocks hold temperature. Shipping blocks in boxes without vent holes, as some big companies new to block sales do, is a mistake.

  • A typical shipping pallet is strapped cardboard block cartons with round vent holes.

  • Packed pallets wait in refrigerated shipping containers for truck pickup. Local pickups are packed in Gaylord bins (large pallet-sized cardboard boxes). Some customers have their own packing requirements. If you buy blocks:

  • If you buy blocks by LTL (less-than-truckload) refrigerated or dry freight, the site road must take an 18-wheeler, or deliveries will not come.

  • Maitake blocks travel and store badly: farms that buy them and refrigerate or truck them have problems, because maitake's development is easily upset.

Block size Blocks per pallet Freight per pallet Freight per block
10 lb (4.5 kg) About 150-200, typically 160-180 About $500-1,000, up to about $1,600 About $3-6, up to about $10
5 lb (2.3 kg) About 320 Same About $1.50-3, up to about $5

Freight at these prices can make buying blocks from a distant farm uneconomic.

Holding blocks cold

  • Colonized chestnut blocks keep at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) more or less indefinitely before pinning (not formally tested).
  • Black pearl oyster blocks hold several weeks at 1 °C (34 °F), but eventually pin even then.

Spawn storage and shipping

  • Store spawn in a good fridge at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F). A month at 6 °C (42 °F) causes a big drop in quality.
  • Cap n Stem's reefers run at about 2 °C (36 °F), just above freezing, to avoid ice damage. The farm pre-cools spawn in many 40 ft (12.2 m) refrigerated containers, plus home-built cold rooms, which hold a less even temperature.
  • Pre-chill the spawn in the cooler at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) before packing, because packed, active spawn heats itself, then ship fast.
  • Healthy spawn can develop stroma (a tough, leathery mycelium mat) during long or hot shipping or storage, which is another reason to keep it cold and ship it fast.

CASE In a box test, spawn packed with gel packs in an insulated box and left out over a weekend held its temperature remarkably well. Gel packs work in three phases: first they chill, then they buffer, then they give out. So heat stress usually comes at the end of transit. Lesson: pre-chill the spawn and ship fast so the parcel arrives before the packs give out.

RANGE Cold storage life of spawn (G2 is the second grain generation; masters the first):

Spawn Plan on Limit
Refrigerated G2 spawn (recommended figure) About 2 weeks 3 weeks is pushing it for any mushroom
Black oyster masters and spawn About a month
Chestnut spawn Holds for orders meant to last about 2 months Orders planned that far ahead are generally discouraged

See also: storing cultures (agar plugs in sterile water) and DIY flow hoods are in Chapter 8.

Growing for drying: fruiting in the bag

If the product will be dried or extracted, you can let blocks fruit inside the closed bag. This needs no fruit room.

  • Species that fruit well inside the closed bag and form a healthy mat: lion's mane, reishi and maitake.
  • If only mass matters (for extracts or tinctures), lion's mane can be left to fruit untended in the bag, like reishi antlers. For market fruit, cut the bag.
  • One grower leaves in-bag lion's mane until it fills the headspace (the empty space above the substrate), breaks it off, folds the top back and lets it fruit again.
  • The filter patch is the breathing window on the bag; A, B and T are a bag maker's codes for patches of different tightness. High-yield lion's mane strains do best with the more open B patch: more gas exchange, more fruit. Maitake needs the tighter A patch so it develops without turning goopy or drawing in bacteria. Beyond that, the choice of patch matters less than people think, and a 10 lb (4.5 kg) A bag has enough headspace for in-bag fruiters. See Chapter 11 for bags and filters.
Species Time to leave in the bag Notes
Lion's mane About a month For mass only, untended
Maitake 2-3 months at most After that it gets "sad and soupy"
Reishi 3-4 months for antlers to reach the top of the bag; can stay up to a year Woody, so it keeps

Drying surplus

AT A GLANCE A clean closet, a dehumidifier with an auto-drain, mesh racks and a little filtered fresh air dry surplus mushrooms at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) in 24-48 h. Expect about 10% of the fresh weight as dry product. Size the batch by the dehumidifier's capacity in pints per day.

Why dry

  • Dehydration rescues surplus that would otherwise be composted or sold as seconds.

  • In one trial, about 50 surplus lion's mane blocks (and 50 maitake blocks) from a cancelled order were left to fruit inside their bags, then dried with home dehumidifiers. The aim was the lowest-impact method that works at home scale, instead of forced hot air or a contract freeze-drying service.

  • The same dehumidifier method is used commercially on larger farms of other species, so it can scale.

  • "You're growing a funny shape of water." About 3 lb (1.4 kg) of fully hydrated mushrooms dries to about a quarter pound (110 g).

How drying works

  • Drying needs four things: heat, airflow, a clean space, and somewhere for the removed water to go.
  • Mushrooms are mostly water: up to about 95%, and about 89-90% in the lion's mane trial below (dry product was 10-11% of fresh weight). Ganoderma (reishi) is nearer 80%.
  • Reishi barely needs a drying process: being woody, it dries on its own.
  • A dehumidifier is a small air conditioner that dumps its heat back into the same room: it gives off heat while it removes water. That heat helps drying, but it can also overheat a closed space (see the temperature row below).

Building a dehumidifier drying room

Dehumidifiers are rated in pints per day (PPD): how much water they can pull out of the air in a day (1 US pint is about 0.47 L). As a rough sizing rule worked from the trial below (about 109 lb of water removed from 122 lb of fresh lion's mane in 48 h by two home units), allow about 1 PPD of capacity for each 1 lb (0.45 kg) of fresh mushrooms you want to dry per day. Closet size and shelf spacing are not recorded.

Item Recommended Details and conditions
Chamber A closet lined with Coroplast (corrugated plastic sheet) and cleaned thoroughly Needs one electrical outlet
Drainage A dehumidifier with an auto-drain Run the clear tubing outlet to a barrel outside the closet or to a floor drain
Racks Frames about 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) with 10-12 shelves Shelves of heat-tolerant polypropylene composite mesh (sold for cannabis curing), fixed with stainless screws
Dehumidifier, better option A ceiling-mounted, attic-style unit at about 100-130 pints per day (PPD), about 47-62 L/day, for around $500 Spend a bit more for capacity
Dehumidifier, basic Store-bought home units remove about 20-40 PPD (about 9-19 L/day) Capacity sets batch size
Temperature 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) A shut closet reached about 38 °C (100 °F), which was judged too hot
Air Door cracked open, with a small fan near the bottom pulling air in Filter the makeup (incoming) air if possible. Pull more air in if the source room is dry; pull less, and circulate more with an exhaust path, if it is humid

WARNING Improvised wooden drying boxes heated by a hot plate with a fan are a fire hazard. A plugged-in dehumidifier is the safer choice.

Procedure: drying mushrooms in a dehumidifier closet

  1. Clean the lined closet thoroughly before each batch.
  2. Check the dehumidifier's auto-drain tubing runs to the barrel or floor drain.
  3. Cut the mushrooms into slabs, leaving pieces a little thicker rather than thinner (no thickness is recorded; see the TIP). The sources describe slabs for lion's mane only.
  4. Lay the slabs one layer deep on the mesh shelves.
  5. Load no more than the dehumidifier's capacity can handle (about 1 lb, 0.45 kg, of fresh mushrooms per day for each pint per day).
  6. Crack the door and run a small fan near the bottom to pull air in; filter that air if you can.
  7. Hold the closet at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), read on a thermometer at middle-shelf height. If it climbs toward 38 °C (100 °F), let in more air.
  8. Dry for 24-48 h. If pieces are still soft at 48 h, keep drying and check the airflow.
  9. Pack the dried pieces in an airtight bag or jar the same day (see Packaging dried product).

CHECK Finished pieces have shrunk and turned golden-brown, and they crumble in the hand.

TIP Pieces left a little thicker dried more robustly: the structure holds together and reabsorbs moisture more slowly. Experiment with thickness for your species.

Lion's mane fruited inside the bag comes out as a large, dense, cauliflower-like mass shaped like the bag top; it is cut into white slabs for drying.

Results and timing

Measure Value Conditions
Dry as share of fresh About 10-11% Lion's mane, dehumidifier drying
Fresh yield About 122 lb (55 kg); 122-130 lb (55-59 kg) quoted 50 lion's mane blocks fruited inside the bag
Dry yield About 13-14 lb (5.9-6.4 kg); 13.3 lb (6.0 kg) quoted Same 50 blocks
Dry yield per block About 0.27 lb (about 120 g) Same trial
Drying time, typical dehumidifier 24-48 h
Drying time in the trial About 48 h Two home dehumidifiers
Large freeze dryer, for comparison About 48-72 h Freeze drying freezes the mushrooms and pulls the water off as vapour under vacuum

Powders

  • Dried reishi nubs and less marketable pieces (said to be just as potent; unconfirmed) are ground in a small industrial blender into a fine brown powder, nicknamed "mummy powder".
  • Stroma-affected fruit that cannot be sold might be used for powder (see above).
  • Turn off-grade pieces into powder or extract rather than composting them.

Value-added products

AT A GLANCE If you grow enough to fill every order, you will always have surplus. Plan products that use it from the start, and find out the licensing rules before you make anything for sale.

CASE A New Hampshire farm planned surplus products from the start: mushroom jerky (first from wild maitake, later oyster and shiitake), then frozen lion's mane pot pies, mushroom patties, soups and a chestnut chili. Old or broken chestnut mushrooms went into mushroom powder, "which I don't really make money on".

  • Licensing. The state's home-kitchen rules did not cover jerky, so the food-safety office stopped him and he needed a licensed commercial kitchen. It took years, his retirement savings plus a loan, and construction took twice as long as expected.
  • Prices. Jerky wholesales at US$6 a bag (button-mushroom jerky sells at US$5).
  • Packaging. The minimum print run for packages was 10,000 bags, which took over a year to use up.
  • Outlets. The products are in about 12-15 co-op and independent grocery stores. Big grocers need vendor applications and brokers.
  • Shelf-stable products add resilience. When COVID shut fresh sales, a Chicago farm began building extraction products (starting with a reishi extraction run). Dried, powdered, salt and jerky products all have room to grow alongside more farmers markets.

Tinctures and extracts

  • Extraction has to break reishi's tough, double-walled structure (spores and cell walls) to reach the compounds.
  • Wild reishi is hard to process. One grower's first tincture from wild reishi broke blenders and needed soaking, boiling and a double extraction (one extraction in alcohol and a second in hot water, then combined).
  • Even blocks that never fruit can be made into mycelium tinctures (made from the mycelium rather than the mushroom). Some commercial products use lion's mane mycelium grown on rice or oats.
  • Supplement and extract companies increasingly use comb tooth, possibly because its spawn stays in a stable spreading mode (pure mycelium rather than fruit).
  • Historically, wild reishi was a prized status item, partly because the dried fruit bodies keep a long time.

Procedure: simple home reishi tincture

  1. Fill a mason jar with dried reishi, broken or sliced into small pieces.
  2. Nearly fill the jar with clear grain alcohol of 70-90% alcohol by volume (140-180 US proof); high-proof moonshine works.
  3. Shake daily for one lunar cycle, about 4 weeks.
  4. Strain through cheesecloth.
  5. Simmer the strained liquid in a pot of water (about half a gallon, 1.9 L) for about 2 hours, until much reduced. The source does not say whether the liquid is mixed into the water or heated in its jar in a water bath; mixing it in drives off most of the alcohol.
  6. Cool and bottle.

WHY This method combines the alcohol and water steps in one sequence, rather than running two separate extractions.

WARNING High-proof alcohol vapour is flammable. Simmer with good ventilation and away from open flames.

The finished tincture is dark. The typical use quoted is 1-3 drops at a time, in a drink or straight, a couple of times a day.

The health claims made for reishi tincture are as dubious as they are endless, and this book does not endorse any of them. Selling tinctures brings labelling and legal rules; see Chapter 22.

CASE One farm makes about US$40,000 a year from tinctures, out of about US$375,000 gross. For bottling it suggests a peristaltic-pump bottle filler and a bottle labeller. See Chapter 22 for value-added products.

How two commercial makers extract.

  • Ultrasonic extraction (Colorado). A probe (horn) is inserted into jars of solvent and mushroom material, in batches up to 10 L. Collapsing bubbles (cavitation) break down the chitin in the cell walls. The makers describe it as greener: less solvent, far less power, no heat, and it can run in an ice bath. They keep the whole process cold, using freeze dryers rather than heat to concentrate extracts, because high-heat, high-pressure extraction may degrade some compounds.
  • Three-part extraction (Feral Fungi). Every mushroom goes through an organic alcohol extraction in custom-made Soxhlet extractors (glassware that cycles solvent through the material), a hot-water extraction (a boil), and an ash step: the spent mushrooms are burned to a fine white ash, and its mineral salts are leached out in distilled water for 8-12 hours and filtered. Mushrooms are "really stubborn to burn" compared with plants. In 2016 the maker struggled to source even 10 lb (4.5 kg) of dried lion's mane.

Packaging dried product

  • Dried mushrooms sealed and kept very dry are claimed to be shelf stable for about 7 years; no basis for the figure is recorded.
  • Polypropylene (PP) turns brittle in the cold and rips easily. This showed up when dried mushrooms were vacuum-packed in spare filterless PP grow bags: the bag stretches well, but once it has a hole it gives way. Use bags made for vacuum sealing instead.
  • Container types, oxygen absorbers and labelling for dried product are not recorded.
  • Reishi antler bags are vacuum-sealed and checked by hand for punctures before boxing (see the sealing procedure).

Key rules

  1. Pick on time: shiitake while the cap rim is still curled, chestnut and oysters before the caps flatten, lion's mane while the spines are still short. Cues
  2. Plan harvest crew for your biggest flush; do not rely on one person. Crew
  3. Keep one species and one lot per rack, and roll whole racks out to a separate harvest, grade and pack area. Use racks with large casters and keep spares. Moving
  4. Wear a respirator when harvesting, especially shiitake and reishi. Safety
  5. Pull blotched fruit on sight; never box blotched mushrooms into the cooler or sell bleach-sprayed fruit. Blotch
  6. Chill fresh mushrooms promptly at 1-4 °C (34-40 °F); chestnut in particular has a short life. Keep the cooler easy to clean and its coils free of spores. Cooler
  7. Keep blocks under 27 °C (80 °F) in transit; use vented cartons, air channels in pallets, and pre-chilled spawn with gel packs. Cold chain
  8. Store spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), not 6 °C (42 °F), and ship it fast. Spawn
  9. Dry surplus at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) with a dehumidifier sized in pints per day, an auto-drain and some fresh air. Drying
  10. Expect dried product to weigh about 10% of the fresh weight after 24-48 h. Results
  11. Seal dried product well, in bags made for vacuum sealing rather than cold, brittle polypropylene. Packaging
  12. Turn off-grade pieces into powder or extract rather than composting them. Powders

Open questions

  • No fresh shelf life in days is recorded for any species, and no cooler humidity target is stated.
  • Fresh packaging materials (clamshells, boxes, films) are mentioned only in passing; no packaging specifications are recorded beyond one farm's boxes, butcher paper and punnets.
  • No harvest cue is recorded for king oyster.
  • Black oyster pin-to-harvest time is recorded as 4-5 days in one account and 10-14 days in another.
  • Freeze-drying appears only as a comparison (48-72 h). Freezing fresh mushrooms, pickling and other preservation methods are not covered by the sources.
  • The 7-year shelf life for dried mushrooms is a claim without a stated basis.
  • Spawn cold-storage life varies between about 2 weeks, a month and 2 months depending on species and account (see the RANGE above).
  • Is there a more worker-friendly way to break reishi antlers off the scalped mass? None has been found.
  • How to pick each species (twist or cut, how much stem to leave), how many people a harvest needs, any grading scheme, the box weights, the slab thickness for drying and a safe load per rolling rack are not recorded.
