Contamination: Diagnosis and Prevention

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the competitor organisms that ruin spawn and substrate (Trichoderma, Neurospora, pin moulds, bacteria and others), how to read the pattern of an outbreak to find its source, and the process faults that cause most of them. Contamination is a symptom of a process fault, not bad luck. Read the distribution of the problem before you change anything, change one variable at a time, and suspect the cool-down, the lab air and the bag seals before you blame the cook or the culture. The rules and numbers used most:

  • Many colours of mould means air; all the blocks from one spawn bag means spawn; mould at gussets and seals means bags; patchy across a batch means the cook.
  • Move blocks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, straight into a positive-pressure HEPA room to cool.
  • Inoculate at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.
  • Incubate big blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) so the core stays under about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F).
  • Above about 62-68% moisture expect bacteria; too dry invites Trichoderma.
  • A steady loss of 5% or more is your whole profit margin. Do not accept it.

Stroma looks like a contaminant but is a stress response of the crop itself; it is covered in Chapter 17, together with bacterial blotch on fruit bodies (blotch). For a quick symptom look-up across the whole process, use Chapter 19.

How to think about contamination

AT A GLANCE Expect a few wipe-outs. Diagnose from data, one variable at a time, starting with the process and the cool-down. Small random losses are normal; a steady rate is not.

Contamination means another organism growing in your spawn or substrate faster than your crop. Some microbes are always present in raw inputs. The aim is to keep their numbers at a level your steaming reliably kills.

  • Expect substrate contamination to wipe you out a few times. The core skill is systematic diagnosis. Do not grab the first idea, and do not change several variables at once: that destroys your ability to find the cause. Causes are often multifactorial.
  • Work backwards with data. At the scale of a large farm (about 50 lots a day, thousands of bags), knee-jerk changes such as moving the incubation temperature, firing someone or swapping filters waste money. For example, sporadic Trichoderma traced to one spawn bag might come from a short cook or one or two bad grains.
  • A problem that persists for months is not a gradual "influx" of spores. Something in the process is causing it. Chasing it with more fungicide becomes an arms race. Trace the process instead.
  • Look first at the process (above all), then at entryways, then at how infected material is stored and disposed of.
  • Start with the production method (sterilized or ultra-pasteurized) and the cool-down speed, not with the ingredient list.
  • Observe before you buy parts. Find the path of least resistance for contamination (where positive pressure or recirculated air is coming from) before you replace a flowhood filter.
  • Talk problems through with other growers, but treat a single story with caution. Several matching stories build confidence.
  • Growers who have not farmed other crops tend to over-worry. One bad block in 50 is not a crisis; make more blocks.
  • But do not accept a steady loss as normal. A 5% contamination rate is roughly an entire profit margin in agriculture. A farm that tolerates a fixed 25% rate should diagnose its technique, filters and room instead.
  • Once process, training and equipment are good, most of the mould cases that remain are bag manufacturing defects (bags and seals).

Three questions sort most outbreaks: is it sporadic, is it confined to discrete chunks of production, and is it one organism? The diagnosis table in this chapter, and the look-up chapter Chapter 19, build on them.

Procedure: diagnosing an outbreak

  1. Do not change anything yet. Note which lots, bags, rooms and days are affected.
  2. Answer the three questions: sporadic or widespread, confined to discrete chunks of production or not, one organism or many.
  3. Match the pattern against the pattern table to find the most likely source.
  4. Pull the temperature logs for the cooks involved before anything else: did the core of the hardest-to-heat block stay above 93 °C (200 °F) long enough?
  5. Check the production method and the cool-down: how long blocks waited, how fast they cooled, and through what air.
  6. Check air paths: where positive pressure and any recirculated air come from, before replacing filters.
  7. Run the cool-down air test and plate-test the filters if the pattern points to air.
  8. Change one variable, keep records, and watch the next lots.

CHECK The contamination rate on the following lots falls, and stays down when you track it by season.

The competitors: what you will see

Trichoderma (green mould)

Trichoderma is the green mould. It is pervasive and always in the background, more so than Neurospora.

Appearance

  • It sporulates green. Before it sporulates, its asexual phase can hide inside faint early colonization, especially on lion's mane. It shows only as slightly denser matting and a slightly different off-white, very hard to tell from the crop until it turns green.
  • Inside blocks: if you cut open a run of about 40 chestnut blocks and find green inside all of them, the substrate is at fault.
  • In fruit rooms, racks get "gnarly" from spore drop and Trichoderma. Clean racks, walls and floors before you load new blocks, then watch each block for green, blue or "rainbow" moulds.

Causes and conditions

  • Trichoderma seems to tolerate wider moisture and temperature ranges than cultivated species (growers' observation, not measured), so it thrives in substrate that is too dry.
  • Uncolonized or under-colonized grain kernels grow Trichoderma, especially if they have dried out, because filter patches are not airtight. This has been seen with chestnut grain.
  • Wispy mycelium such as lion's mane is like a net with large holes. Dry media and loose colonization let Trichoderma in.
  • Too many blocks per spawn bag raises the risk. Lion's mane runs 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag; the acceptable range is about 12-30, and above 30 the mould risk climbs.
  • Using B-patch bags for a while sharply raised one farm's contamination rate, mostly Trichoderma (filter patches).
  • Chestnut blocks fruited too hot get Trichoderma blooming on top.
  • Maitake fruit picks up Trichoderma and other airborne contaminants easily. One farm cleans its maitake room every day, which it does not insist on for other rooms.
  • Pioppino is the first species to show Trichoderma: it is a slow, wispy grower and probably prefers soft hardwood such as poplar to dense oak or maple. Pioppino attracts much more green mould than maitake.
  • Case: a novel, aggressive mould variant (Trichoderma or Aspergillus; details half-remembered) appeared at about the same time at button-mushroom compost sites on several continents, including the Netherlands and the UK. One explanation offered, as speculation, is the agricultural use of Trichoderma since the 1950s. The lesson drawn: pathogens evolve toward their hosts.

What to do

  • A small, contained Trichoderma patch in a corner of a sealed bag can still be fruited and yield well, for blocks you fruit yourself (not for sale).
  • A bit of Trichoderma on the bottom of a fruiting block will not invade the fruit bodies. It is far less serious than blotch.
  • Unlike Neurospora bags, Trichoderma blocks may have something to recover.

Neurospora (orange bread mould)

Appearance and biology

  • Neurospora grows by long, narrow leading hyphae ("feelers") that explore fast, with denser growth behind. The speed quoted is 3-5 mm per hour, said to be the "land-speed record" for mycelial growth, fast enough nearly to watch.
  • Under the microscope the feeler hyphae branch out across the field ahead of the denser growth.
  • In production it shows as fast, cobweb-like filaments (it can be mistaken for cobweb mould). They darken and work up the bag toward the headspace, then turn crisp and orange and burst into masses of powdery spores. It reproduces asexually as powdery orange puffs of conidia (asexual spores) near the top of colonized blocks.
  • Some strains are homothallic (a single spore completes the life cycle), so one spore landing on media can take over a bag. Heterothallic strains need a compatible partner only for sexual fruiting. Its asci (spore sacs) hold 8 spores (4 in some species). It was first described as a bread mould in French bakeries.
  • In a sealed 5-10 lb (2.3-4.5 kg) bag it can explode over a weekend: knocked Friday, ruined Monday.
  • In nature it is found on tree bark and as an early colonizer at the edges of burn zones. A link with morels has been suggested without evidence.
  • It has beneficial uses: oncom (an Indonesian fermented soybean or press-cake food), a fermented cassava drink in Brazil, possibly Roquefort cheese production (unconfirmed), and use as a laboratory model organism since the 1920s.
  • It is not reported as harmful to people, apart from the general risk of breathing in huge spore loads (Chapter 18).

Lookalikes

  • Ripening chestnut blocks turn golden-mustard. New staff who have been warned about Neurospora often mistake this colour for it.
  • Fast, orange chicken-of-the-woods mycelium has been mistaken for Neurospora.

Causes

  • Neurospora spores are among the first fungal spores killed by steam. A properly cooked bag is not the source; exposure after the cook is. It is easy to kill with heat: roughly 66 °C (150 °F) is given as a rough figure, and another account gives a garbled figure near 60 °C (140 °F).
  • It is more common in warm weather and in warm, poorly regulated incubation (high-CO2 rooms tend to run hot). It shows up in summer about as often as Trichoderma does the rest of the year. As a rough guide it was said to take off above about 18 °C (65 °F); this was a passing remark, not a measured threshold.
  • Bad bag seals are the classic entry point. One spore through a pin leak can sporulate and spread across a whole block production. Bad seals are the biggest weak point of lab work; one farm now sees Neurospora only when a seal is bad.
  • Neurospora can establish and grow on a wet filter, and has been seen growing on the back of filters.
  • Neurospora growing outside along the route blocks travel is a particular hazard.
  • Even a perfectly clean incubation room will have some contaminated blocks, for example Neurospora pushing through a torn bag or patch. Keeping them a few feet from blocks that are cooling for next-day inoculation is a major vector.
  • With the process right, Neurospora should be as rare as other harmless bread moulds.

What to do

  • Remove infected bags from incubation immediately. Do not try to salvage them. Bag them and bin them. Never cut them open or compost them near the facility.
  • Make prompt removal of contaminated bags from the building a written procedure. Case: contaminated bags left in a warehouse over a weekend covered that part of the building in spores by Monday. In summer one farm's compost pile glows orange with it.
  • Keep compost piles as far as possible from air intakes.
  • Prevention routine: track contamination numbers by season, have a way to check airflow and pressure, change pre-filters and filters, clean ducts, and recheck after any building change. Example: an autoclave knocked through a wall left a gap.
  • Sporicides. Products sold as Spore Killer 1, 2 and 3 (SK1-SK3) are successive generations of one product line. Most strains respond to SK1 and SK2; the common bread-mould species is said to resist those and need SK3 (reported, unverified). A spray treats the symptom: if Neurospora keeps coming back, fix the process that lets it in.

WARNING Neurospora can persist on a farm for a year or more. Wheat bran that ended up in a Detroit farm's work area left traces of Neurospora that kept reappearing for at least a year; the grower calls it "an absolute farm killer". A revived farm in Wyoming that had stood empty had a "Neurospora nightmare" on its very first grow, even after cleaning the ducts, replacing the filters and pulling out the air handlers.

Pin moulds and other bread moulds

  • Pin moulds, Neurospora, Trichoderma and Aspergillus are pervasive but easy to kill with heat. This is why ultra-pasteurization works.
  • Pin moulds look like the familiar fuzz on old bread and fruit; some moulds form yellow-green powdery colonies.
  • Pin moulds grow extremely fast and like oxygen.
  • Causes: undercooking, a dirty cool-down or bad seals, made worse by excess airflow. Case: one farm's early grow kits (small 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) blocks in cardboard crates) got pin mould because the bags had an overly porous filter patch and the substrate was undercooked. After fixing both they never saw it again.
  • Lookalike: early black oyster blocks on Master's Mix grew white fuzz like aerial mycelium or pin mould from the cut, which formed amber droplets and then became the caps. This no longer happens with the domesticated strain.

Bacteria in spawn and substrate

Why bacteria survive

  • Steam kills active bacterial cells, but bacteria quickly form heat-resistant endospores; fungi do not.
  • Ultra-pasteurization (about 100 °C (212 °F) for some hours) is not sterilization. Bacterial endospores remain in every block and only cause trouble if conditions allow: too wet, a core undercooked and then shaken, or too warm.
  • Most moulds die by about 66 °C (150 °F). Higher temperatures kill everything except endospores, which need pressure (Chapter 12).
  • More microbes survive pasteurization than sterilization, so other errors such as excess moisture are punished harder on pasteurized substrate.

Appearance

  • General sign: a milky or viscous film. On shiitake blocks it shows as a moist, viscous film on the outside of the block, like frost on the inside of the bag.
  • A sour smell (dirty socks, fermenting wine), sometimes detectable through the patch.
  • Water pooled at the bottom goes anaerobic (airless). The mycelium walls it off with a hard line above a sloppy, wet bottom (see the bag figure).
  • Stratified colonization: strong at the top, weak or anaerobic toward the bottom of the block.
  • Yellow liquid at the bag bottom, more with rich 50:50 lion's mane blocks. Working explanation: a core or room that is too hot lets dormant endospores germinate, conditions go wet and anaerobic, and the mycelium pumps out defensive metabolites. It is also seen during fruiting.
  • Over-spawning lion's mane makes more heat and more bacteria: dark, wet circular spots around each inoculation point.
  • Fermented blocks, or blocks inoculated too hot: the spawn dies, the bottom to middle of the bag goes "gnarly" with bacteria, perhaps with a little mould on top, and the crop mycelium forms dense, walled-off, struggling colonies instead of fast, feathery, rope-like (rhizomorphic) growth.
  • Heavy metabolite formation in a bag (except shiitake, which makes them normally) signals media that is too rich or under-cooked. Bacteria are then likely to stop fruiting entirely.
  • Blocks colonize weakly, wispy or "greasy", and many species (even reishi) do not fruit.
  • Too-wet shiitake of strain KOM goes anaerobic, with popcorning and browning only on top, but still fruits, and the bacterial slime can be scraped off. Overly wet 3790 shiitake gives sloshy blocks that buckle and brown only on the top half and fruit poorly.

Causes

  • Heat. Incubate ultra-pasteurized shiitake blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F). Thermophilic (heat-loving) endospores start to take hold around 24 °C (75 °F), and 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks run about 2-3 °C (4-5 °F) hotter in the core than at the surface, so a 21 °C (70 °F) room means about 24 °C (75 °F) inside. Block cores above about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F), especially in 10 lb blocks, bring poor colonization and problems such as blotch. For 10 lb black oyster blocks the rule is also about 19 °C (66 °F) ambient; otherwise peak metabolism overheats the core, bringing stroma, bacteria and slower pinning (Chapter 13).
  • Heat plus CO2. Too much heat and too much CO2 feed each other, encouraging bacteria and mould blooms.
  • Too much water. Above about 68% moisture expect loose water and bacteria. Too-wet media favours anaerobic organisms (hydration).
  • Cook too short. 10-12 lb (4.5-5.4 kg) blocks not held long enough at the plateau give the stratified pattern.
  • Slow cooling. Cooling too long, or inside the vessel, gives surviving bacteria a head start (cool-down).
  • Waiting to inoculate. Pasteurized blocks have an expiry. If they are left days before inoculation, endospores germinate and the blocks ferment (sour smell).
  • A fermenting mix, or a mix left sitting before processing.
  • Over-rich media (for example 50:50 for maitake) gives heavy metabolites, more mould and hot cores.

What to do

  • If the bacteria came from the substrate, check the cook time and temperature, whether the mix was fermenting, and how long it sat before processing and before inoculation.
  • Throw sour-smelling blocks away.

Moulds of many colours ("rainbow" contamination)

  • A "rainbow" of different contaminants (green, grey, pin mould, white, even bacteria) points to air "nine or ten times out of ten", not to a bad cook. Spores get into bags as they cool even if the bags seem sealed, and they colonize fresh substrate faster than the spawn.
  • Random moulds of different colours everywhere a few days after knocking point to air contamination, or to steaming that was too light to kill organisms living in the wood.
  • Recurring green, brown, black or orange moulds usually point to bad filtration or negative pressure. If pressure is known to be good, inspect the filters for breaks near the bottom (lab air).

Contaminated wild clones on agar

  • Old or damaged specimens bring contaminants onto the plate. Worst case seen: an older maitake with surface mould, held unrefrigerated for a couple of days in transit. One cut was overrun by mould and the plate was dead.
  • The most common case is lots of bacteria and other growth around the tissue. Example: shrimp of the woods (Entoloma abortivum), which already involves two different fungi.
  • Optionally, isolate each separate organism on the plate (for example two bacteria and a mould) to map what the mushroom was living with.
  • From early jar work: once mycelium fully covers the top of a jar, the jar can be opened and the mycelium largely defends itself.
  • Cloning technique is covered in Chapter 7.

Reading the pattern: where did it come from?

AT A GLANCE The spread of a problem across bags, lots and time is your main diagnostic tool. Map it before you act.

Tests that help

Tests that help you confirm a suspected source:

Procedure: cool-down air test

  1. Before cooking, seal some extra bags completely. Optionally put a data logger inside one to confirm the temperature it reached.
  2. Cook and cool them with the batch.
  3. Incubate them unopened.
  4. If they grow contaminants, the air drawn in during cooling is contaminated.

CHECK Sealed test bags stay clean while the normally handled bags from the same run go bad: the cook was good, and the cool-down air is the problem.

  • Temperature logs first. When blocks go bad, check the data-logging thermocouples before anything else. A small bullet logger in a block shows the hours above 93 °C (200 °F). Do not grow complacent with machinery: one bad run can sink a farm with slim margins. Monitoring hardware is covered in Chapter 5.
  • Plate and particle tests of filters. Expose agar plates at several positions in front of the filter, or use a cheap particle counter. Farms resist suspecting their own filter, so test anyway (Chapter 4).
  • Gel check on DNA samples. In DNA work on stroma, a contaminated sample shows a strong band followed by long streaks down the whole lane, whereas old, degraded DNA shows a band that fades (Chapter 8).

Prevention, step by step through the process

AT A GLANCE Most contamination enters at a few points: raw materials, uneven hydration, a short or uneven cook, a slow or dirty cool-down, lab air, technique, bag seals, and hot incubation. Each section below gives the faults and the fixes for one step.

Raw materials and water

  • The hardest problems to fix are changes in raw material and bad water. City water is usually fine. A shallow dug well has a high microbial load compared with a drilled well of about 200 ft (61 m). Water is mainly a fruit-room issue (Chapter 17).
  • Exception: deep wells in drought areas can carry bacterial blooms and heavy mineral loads that affect substrate, though pH, moisture and the carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio matter more. An inline UV filter is mainly worthwhile for deep wells; for city water it is extra insurance.
  • Raw sawdust, pellets and loose nitrogen supplements (hulls, mids) carry microbial loads driven mainly by how much moisture they have been exposed to. Store them dry. Properly hot-composted sawdust is effectively self-sanitized by heat: one farm's plating of "nasty" hot compost grew nothing.
  • Clumpy super sacks of supplement were probably wet at some point. Do not use them.
  • Check that sawdust is the species you ordered. Suppliers may mix in softwoods such as cedar, whose aromatic compounds suppress mycelium (Chapter 10).
  • Much grain is poor: totes of millet with insects and mould clumps, a super sack of sorghum full of bugs. Ask experienced growers for good sources.
  • Conventional millet and oats are often desiccated with glyphosate before harvest, and conventional rye in wet Maine may get fungicide. Residues can cause patchy colonization and failure to fruit, and suppliers' assurances may not be verifiable. Cap n Stem uses only organic grain.
  • Mixers trap old wet material: a chunk of wet combo-pellet mix stuck in one farm's mixer turned foul. Clean daily, with an intensive weekly clean of key equipment. Grain and starch make mixer cleaning a big job.
  • Case (relayed by someone who works for an equipment maker; unconfirmed): a farm alternating between a filler and a mixer used near-boiling water in a mixer coated with grime. The pellet mix came out much darker before cooking, a nutrient-rich cake that steam pasteurization could not fully handle.

Hydration and mixing

  • "Hose it and squeeze-test" hydration, common since the early Washington-era farms, causes large losses, does not scale, and is easy to half-do on a bad day (Chapter 10).
  • Poorly mixed or wrongly hydrated substrate causes sectoring, odd mycelium, wet spots, stroma and heavy metabolite exudate, even with good steaming. Metabolites also come from temperature swings in incubation or from competitors.
  • Above about 62% moisture, Hericium (lion's mane) blocks pool water at the bottom. Aim for no moisture difference between top and bottom.
  • Too dry stalls the mycelium and favours dry-tolerant contaminants like Trichoderma. Too wet invites anaerobic bacteria.
  • Change the right variable. Case: a farm with trouble only on lion's mane cut its moisture to about 56%, but the real problem was sawdust arriving at about 70% moisture.
  • Grain that is too dry gives weak, slow growth and more contamination risk. Grain that is too wet (more common) gives mushy burst grain and standing water that breed contaminants. Grain at low moisture (low 40s %) gives permanently wispy growth, more contamination and early auto-fruiting (lion's mane) (Chapter 9).
  • Burst grain releases free sugar and starch, effectively agar, feeding any bacterium or spore.
  • Long soaks, or drained grain left sitting, start fermenting (sugars turn to alcohols). Even after sterilization this can give irregular, splotchy colonization.

RANGE Sugar in liquid culture: Cap n Stem settled on 0.5% sugar after testing 0.5-8%, and reports markedly less contamination. Common practice is 2-4% sugar, and some growers use 1%. The link between lower sugar and less contamination is one farm's experience, not a measured study (Chapter 7).

Cooking

  • Core rule: the core of the hardest-to-heat block above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 hours (at most 4-6), measured, rather than 24 hours unmeasured. Full cook parameters are in Chapter 12.
  • In an over-packed barrel the inner blocks stay colder, outer and top blocks overcook, and the inner ones harbour survivors.
  • An unpressurized vessel sucks in air as it cools, which brings lots of contamination.
  • Bags are not truly sealed while cooling. A bag sucked tight can still draw in contamination. Tightness only shows a pressure difference (pressure changed too fast), and the bag reopens as temperatures even out.
  • Contamination by many fungal species at once is unlikely to be a cook failure, because moulds die easily. Look at the cool-down air first.
  • Most farms ultra-pasteurize blocks: up to 100 °C (212 °F) for about 3 hours, then cool and inoculate. The mycelium must then out-compete the survivors, so keep the temperature difference between core and surface small for even, clean growth.
  • Spawn should always be fully sterilized. Selling grain spawn that was only ultra-pasteurized as master spawn is dishonest; it is acceptable, perhaps, for your own use.

RANGE Kill temperatures without pressure. Working value: most moulds die by about 66 °C (150 °F). Other figures: spores die around 66 °C (150 °F) and about 71 °C (160 °F) kills essentially all fungi (species thresholds unknown); most fungi die above about 71 °C (160 °F), with one loose figure of about 43 °C (110 °F) (unconfirmed); Neurospora is killed easily, with a figure near 60 °C (140 °F) (unconfirmed). All agree that bacterial endospores survive without pressure.

Cool-down: the biggest single source

AT A GLANCE Most widespread contamination comes from the cool-down. Move blocks while they are still at 93 °C (200 °F) or more into a positive-pressure HEPA room, and never let them cool slowly in a dirty space.

  • Most widespread contamination comes from improper cool-down.
  • There are two acceptable methods: (1) move blocks out while still very hot, 96-99 °C (205-210 °F), straight into a HEPA-filtered, positive-pressure room to cool; or (2) cool them inside a vessel back-pressurized with HEPA air, though moving the cooled blocks through dirty space afterwards is still a risk.
  • Recommended: after a 3-hour hold, move blocks at 93 °C (200 °F) or more straight into the positive-pressure lab, wearing welding gloves. Hot blocks pick up fewer contaminants in transit than room-temperature ones. Even with hot handling through a dirty space you might lose only about 5 of 150 bags.
  • Blocks become susceptible as they cool toward about 38 °C (100 °F) and the temperatures just above it. A wet, dirty container overnight will contaminate them.
  • A closed steam box falls from 93 °C (200 °F) slowly, over about 8-10 hours (some farms let blocks sit 48 hours). In a lab with plenty of cool filtered air, blocks drop below 38 °C (100 °F) within hours. Slow cooling also overcooks.
  • In warm climates, cooling bags outside a clean room is worse: warm outside air is pulled in more aggressively.
  • Shipping containers with wooden floors under metal planks, water troughs and leaky doors pull in dirty air as they cool. They are not sterile vessels; once the blocks drop below lethal temperature, cooling there is "an open buffet".
  • Pulling air through a HEPA filter (for example HEPA shop-vacs hooked to a steam box) seals poorly and contaminates everything. Laminar flow means pushing air through a gasketed filter.
  • Reaching into Bubba barrels to load and unload them is a contamination vector. Leaving blocks to cool inside them, or wheeling barrels into the clean area, adds risk.
  • Never put dropped blocks or racks back with the batch; floor contact can contaminate everything.
  • Hand-loading individual blocks is a contamination vector because tired or careless staff eventually slip. Move blocks in racks or cages (a point credited to Paul Stamets).
  • Keep cool-down separate from incubation. Blocks at about 93 °C (200 °F) pulled into a room that is also incubating can push local temperatures from 19 °C (66 °F) toward 66 °C (150 °F) and badly disturb the incubating blocks.

RANGE Where to cool pasteurized blocks. Recommended: move them hot into a positive-pressure HEPA room and cool them there. Cooling inside the vessel is acceptable only if the chamber is positively pressurized with HEPA air, and moving the cooled blocks a long way afterwards is still a risk. The strictest practice is never to cool pasteurized blocks in the vessel at all. A claim that Unicorn bags "self-seal", so they can be cooked and cooled anywhere, is false: one spore is enough.

Procedure: hot transfer to cool-down

  1. Finish the hold: the core of the hardest-to-heat block above 93 °C (200 °F) for the full hold (about 3 hours) (Chapter 12).
  2. Put on welding gloves.
  3. Open the vessel and move blocks at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, in racks or cages, straight into the positive-pressure HEPA room. Do not wait.
  4. Leave behind any block or rack that touches the floor.
  5. Let blocks cool in front of the filtered air until they are below 38 °C (100 °F), which takes a few hours.
  6. Inoculate promptly once they reach 27-32 °C (80-90 °F) (inoculation).

CHECK Run the cool-down air test now and then; the sealed bags should stay clean.

Lab air and filters

  • Never put a recirculating AC, heat pump, mini-split or recirculating fan inside a clean room or cool-down room, even temporarily. Its coil and filter collect what people shed and blow it back around unfiltered. Contamination builds over a grace period, then flourishes. In a small closet lab, an internal AC fights the flowhood (Chapter 4).
  • Ceiling ducts blowing conditioned air down onto flowhoods cause endless contamination, unless the duct connects to the back of a filter.
  • Do not put recirculating cooling units inside a spawn incubation room. Tell the HVAC contractor that the pre-conditioning room is a pre-filter space whose air returns to the same point.
  • Cheap hardware-store "HEPA" filters are not lab filters: 99.999997% is very different from 99.7-99.9%. Target removal of particles down to 0.3 micron.
  • The most abused part of a mini-pleat HEPA filter is the bottom edge at table level, where grain splashes into the face and bags get rammed into the frame. Vacuum grain out; never pick at it with a knife.
  • A HEPA filter that is switched off passively soaks up humidity, moisture from cooling blocks and spores from contaminated blocks. On restart it can compromise the knock table. Keep filters running, at low speed if needed.
  • Filter patches are not airtight. A wetted patch (a humid cooling room, hot substrate at 60-62% moisture) becomes a conduit for mould pulled across by fans.
  • One room, one function: keep inoculation away from other work. Case: a farm incubating racks inside its lab kept getting contamination, because removing bad bags and constant traffic spread spores to the knock table.
  • No floor drains, sinks or faucets in clean rooms. Epoxy-coat concrete floors, because mould grows in bare concrete.
  • Filter and lab design are covered in detail in Chapter 4 and Chapter 5.

Inoculation technique and handling

  • Technique alone can contaminate a whole lot: skin shedding, holding the spawn bag outside the laminar flow, fingers in bags, not shaking, not checking seals (Chapter 11).
  • Scooping spawn (say a quarter cup per bag) is too contamination-prone at scale. Pour a little grain directly from the broken-up spawn bag into each bag in turn, and accept some variation between bags.
  • Case: one farm tried a volumetric pneumatic spawner fed from stainless hoppers. Each hopper needed sterilizing (peracetic acid, then drying, and even then only near-sterile), and one bad spawn bag risked cross-contaminating many. It also slowed them down, so they sold it and went back to hand spawning.
  • Knocking at 38 °C (100 °F) or more kills the spawn: no growth, a couple of nodules, or a weak surviving portion. It is often mistaken for contamination, and happens with under-trained staff. Aim for 27-32 °C (80-90 °F).
  • Poor shaking gives patchy colonization and grain clumps that generate excess heat. Overheating in ultra-pasteurized substrate can kill the mycelium.
  • Adding bought liquid culture to an aerated LC vessel through a luer barb creates a weak point where dirty air can flow back when the pump is on a timer. Prefer agar or syringe inoculation in the hood, and keep filters dry.
  • Chestnut mycelium is easily disturbed. Shaking or thermal shock too early (for example reshaking a G1 soon after the agar transfer) often leads to unhealthy growth, cell death and contamination.
  • Spawn quality control at one producer: split each grain batch in two, test one part, and ship nothing until testing is complete (Chapter 9).

Bags and seals

  • Seal test: when you pull a seal apart, the bag film should tear before the seal does. Uneven seals (overlap, a thin versus thick element, too little current, poor compression) cause pin leaks.
  • Squeeze test: a properly sealed A-patch bag should let little air out when squeezed hard. If XL A-patch bags deflate when pressed, they are not sealed. B patches pass air quickly, which by itself does not mean more Neurospora risk.
  • The gusset (the folded side or bottom panel of the bag) is the weakest point. A typical failure: mould starting at a break in the bottom gusset while spawn has colonized most of the rest of the bag.
  • Other failure points: heat seals that are too weak, or too hot and making micro-perforations (especially the top seal made after inoculation), and filter patches with manufacturing defects.
  • Unicorn has changed its plastic often, making substrate bags harder to seal, and bags arrive too thin, too thick or the wrong size. Test bags; they can sink you (Chapter 11).
  • Bag problems can stay hidden in a very clean facility (the spawn maker Mycelia does fine with SacO2 bags in-house) and appear only in less ideal conditions, such as shipping.
  • A batch of greasy, residue-coated bags caused stroma rather than mould (stroma cases).
  • An older teaching puts a flat Tyvek sleeve inside the bag before folding, to filter air as it cools. It does not work in steamers, because the bag sides do not stay stuck together.

Procedure: testing a new bag lot

  1. Seal several bags on your sealer as you would in production.
  2. Pull each seal apart by hand: the film must tear before the seal gives.
  3. Squeeze sealed A-patch bags hard: little air should escape; if they deflate, they are not sealed.
  4. Inspect the gussets and filter patches for breaks and defects.
  5. Repeat for every new bag lot.

CHECK Over the following weeks, no contamination clusters at gussets or top seals (pattern table).

Incubation

  • Keep blocks apart by two hand widths; touching blocks create local heat (Chapter 13).
  • Running cooling pipes through racks would rain condensation onto bags.
  • Case: using the incubation HVAC to condition other rooms dropped incubation CO2 to about 500 ppm at one farm. Shiitake blocks grew patchy and dried out, and bags lost weight through the patch.
  • A shiitake block that colonizes, buckles and browns may still never fruit if one of its three phases was disrupted. The main shiitake incubation failures are duds and anaerobic bacteria, mostly from heat. One experienced grower traces their early failures to inconsistent temperatures and uneven light.

Fruit room and disposal

  • Fruit rooms need floor drainage. Standing water breeds bacterial blooms and otherwise has to be vacuumed out. The plenum does not need drains (Chapter 14).
  • Coroplast walls are easy to clean, and damaged sheets are swapped out. The flutes can trap water and some mould, but far less than organic wall materials. Expect to rebuild parts of any fruit room periodically.
  • The cooler end of a species' fruiting range gives denser tissue and potentially less contamination; the warm end is for speed.
  • Recirculating ultrasonic humidifiers inside the room spread spores and bacteria (humidifiers).
  • Open-bed growers (for example long button-mushroom beds) struggle most: lots of exposed air and traffic, and a 30 m (100 ft) bed cannot be binned, so they resort to chemicals. Filter-patch bags are not airtight, but they create a microclimate that is far easier to keep clean.

Case files: how real problems were traced

AT A GLANCE In almost every case the first suspect (the spawn, the cook, a staff member) was wrong, and the root cause was a seal, an air path, a waiting time or a stored pile of material.

These case files show how each problem was traced.

Case What happened Root cause found Fix
"Neurospora wars", Cap n Stem's first Westbrook shop Incubation racks overrun; infected bags dumped outside were pulled into the air inlets, making it worse Bag seals: zip-tie and fold closures, then an overheating impulse sealer that burned micro-holes, and bags of that era leaking at the gussets Fixing the seals ended it
Cascadia Intermittent Neurospora on fruiting blocks Compost mound too close to the fruit-room ducts Move compost away from intakes
The open window One summer day blocks cooled in the steam unit to below about 66 °C (150 °F), then were carried past an open window to the lab about 3 m (10 ft) away; the racks nearest the window went to Neurospora within about 2 days of inoculation Exposure during the cool-down transfer Move blocks hot into filtered space
A very large spawn customer Months of Neurospora; wanted to cancel orders and blamed the spawn Bags cooked in a shipping container, cooled overnight there to 10-27 °C (50-80 °F), then moved across dirty space. After switching to moving hot blocks, clogged pre-filters killed the lab's positive pressure Trace the process; maintain filters
Farm in a new facility Stratified colonization in big blocks Too short a hold at cook temperature Raised cook temperatures
Same farm, lab Rising rate of every kind of fungal contaminant despite a wall of recirculating flowhoods A ceiling "overpressure" duct fed by a fan sucking air through a weak roof filter (labelled 99.95-99.97%) Mini-pleat HEPA at the duct with the fan blowing through it, well gasketed
Barrel farm 5-10 lb (2.3-4.5 kg) blocks in modified barrels with sauna steamers, cooled while drawing "HEPA" air in; worked, then slowly failed Intake filter (suck-through, likely 99.95-99.97% or worse) compromised Replace with proper blow-through filtration
Midwest farm Weak, wispy, "greasy" colonization; many species, even reishi, would not fruit Hot blocks sat 1-3 days before going to the cool-down room; endospores got a head start while blocks pulled in dirty air Immediate transfer to filtered cool-down
New Jersey farm Lab problems Partly cheap hardware-store "HEPA" filters Lab-grade filters
Knock-table filter Contamination rose and forced overproduction Spilled grain built up at the HEPA base (cleaning standards decayed as training was passed on), and staff slammed blocks into the filter until it cracked New filter; an angle-iron stop at the table edge; a vacuum kept to hand
Arizona grower Persistent lab contamination A photo of the lab showed an AC with a return duct in the lab, recirculating contaminants from people traffic. Growers in this position tend to change steam time, mix or spawn supplier instead Remove recirculation from the lab
Grower hauling hot blocks Contamination problems Cooling blocks, then moving them cold Hauled hot blocks by Kubota through snow into the lab; the problems went away
Early grow kits Pin mould Porous patch plus undercooked substrate Tighter patch, longer cook
Warehouse weekend One Neurospora bag left over a weekend spread spores across that part of the building Contaminated material left indoors Remove contaminated bags promptly (written procedure)
Worker emptying bags outside Spores blew back into the facility Disposal near the building Bag and bin; never open bags near the facility
The flood Snowmelt came through the walls toward about 40 tons (36 t) of raw red oak sawdust stored on the warehouse floor; berms of wood chips floated away Storage of a big open pile exposed to water Two years later the flooded corner still held mouldy chip piles stuffed into old equipment, a contamination reservoir until cleared
Lion's mane-only farm Trouble only on lion's mane; the farm cut moisture to about 56% Sawdust arriving at about 70% moisture Measure incoming moisture
Wild-mould outbreak (Neurospora) A mushroom company is said to have shut down because of Neurospora Not known None recorded
  • After the flood, the crew moved from raw sawdust to combo pellets and say they would not go back.
  • Bag-batch and grain-batch stories that produced stroma (a greasy Unicorn bag lot, moth-damaged sorghum, the end of a grain tote) are in stroma cases.

Species susceptibility

Species Contamination tendency
Oyster (blue) Most tenacious; the reference for "all else equal"
Chestnut Not weak, but less tenacious than oyster: noticeably higher contamination rates, more prone to mould on grain, sensitive to dry grain and early disturbance
Maitake More contamination-prone at every step, because after any disturbance (breaking spawn, cutting agar) it takes 1-2 weeks to recover visibly, leaving media exposed. Needs a clean space and verified cooks; raising the spawn rate speeds the jump-off. Once going, about as fast as chestnut, pioppino and beech
Pioppino First to show Trichoderma; attracts more green mould than maitake
Lion's mane Indicator species for systemic faults; wispy growth lets Trichoderma in; over-spawning and heat bring bacteria
Comb tooth One grower has seen no blotch, Trichoderma or odd growth
Shiitake Can look fine through browning and still fail late from an undercook; bacteria from heat

Species details are in Chapter 20.

Our farm: contamination targets

FARM NOTE The farm's target is below 5% contamination at every stage: agar plates, grain masters, G2 spawn, and substrate blocks. The chapter's reason is that a steady 5% loss is roughly a whole profit margin, and a steady rate is never normal (How to think about contamination, the hidden cost).

Why per stage: losses multiply. Four stages that each lose 5% leave only about 81% of what you started (0.95 × 0.95 × 0.95 × 0.95), so a farm that "only loses 5% a stage" has lost about 19% overall. Three stages at 5% lose about 14%.

Stage What counts as contaminated Count against Target
Agar plates Any mould or bacterial colony; a discarded plate Plates poured and inoculated that week below 5%
Grain masters (G1) Any mould, bacteria, wet or sour smell, or stroma that forces a discard Masters inoculated in the lot below 5%
G2 spawn Same as masters G2 bags inoculated in the lot below 5%
Substrate blocks Any contaminated block found before or at harvest (green, orange, patch, bacterial) Blocks inoculated in the lot below 5%

How to count: write down every contaminated unit by lot code (the species letter plus the knock date) on the day it is found, and divide by the number of units made in that lot. Keep one row per lot per stage. Roll up a four-week figure for each stage.

Reading What to do
One lot above 5%, rest fine Read the pattern in the diagnosis table: one lot means a batch problem (cook, hydration, one bad bag lot).
A stage above 5% over the four-week roll-up Treat as a steady loss. Start the diagnosis procedure: work backwards from the logs, change one variable at a time.
A stage at or below about 2% Normal. One bad block in 50 is not a crisis.
Any Neurospora Remove at once, bag and take off site (waste route).

OPEN The sources give no measured contamination rates for any farm beyond "5% is a margin" (open questions), so 5% is a ceiling, not a proven goal. After about three months of counted data, replace it with the farm's own number for each stage.

Key rules

  1. Read the pattern before acting: many colours means air, one spawn bag's children means spawn, gussets and seals mean bags, patchy across a batch means the cook.
  2. Change one variable at a time and keep data; work backwards from the logs.
  3. Move blocks hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, straight into a positive-pressure HEPA room to cool; never let them cool slowly in a dirty space or wait for days.
  4. Inoculate promptly once blocks reach about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above.
  5. Keep recirculating AC units, heat pumps and fans out of labs and cool-down rooms.
  6. Test every bag lot with the pull-apart seal test and the squeeze test, and watch the gussets.
  7. Hydrate evenly. Above about 62-68% moisture expect bacteria; too dry invites Trichoderma.
  8. Incubate big blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) so the core stays under about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F).
  9. Remove Neurospora bags at once, bag them and take them off site; keep compost away from intakes.
  10. Do not accept a steady loss of 5% or more as normal; it is your margin.
  11. Treat lion's mane trouble as an early warning for the whole process.
  12. Our farm: aim below 5% at every stage (plates, masters, G2, blocks), counted by lot code. See Our farm.

Open questions

  • Cobweb mould, wet bubble, Penicillium and other named contaminants are not described in the sources beyond passing mentions; Aspergillus is only named.
  • Kill temperatures for individual mould species are stated loosely and inconsistently, from 43 °C to 71 °C (110-160 °F).
  • No measured contamination-rate data across process changes are available, apart from "5% is a margin" and anecdotes.
