chapters.html:
Diseases, Pests and Water Quality

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers problems that attack the crop itself rather than the substrate: bacterial blotch, rose comb and other malformations, viruses, stroma, insects and rodents, and the water and humidification systems that drive most fruit-room disease. Blotch and rose comb usually come from the room, not the spawn: dirty or recirculated air, untreated humidifier water, coarse fog and standing water. The rules and numbers used most:

  • When blotch appears only at fruiting, look at the room, the humidifier and the water, not the spawn supplier.
  • Treat humidifier water: particulate filter, softener, carbon, then RO or steam if you can, plus a light bleach or chlorine dioxide dose of about 150-250 ppm.
  • Swing humidity between about 70% and 90% rather than holding it saturated.
  • Keep susceptible species cool: king oyster 10-16 °C (50-60 °F), lion's mane about 16 °C (60 °F).
  • Pull blotched fruit on sight and never box it with good fruit.
  • In an outbreak, rotate strains and consider short-term peroxide dosing near 0.1%.
  • Treat stroma as a grain-spawn problem, and keep grain and blocks at about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F).

Fix the humidifier and the water first, keep rooms cool, swing humidity rather than holding it saturated, pull sick fruit at once, and rotate strains during an outbreak. Peroxide dosing can rescue a room, but the dose figures in circulation are inconsistent (peroxide). Contamination of spawn and substrate by moulds and bacteria is in Chapter 16; fruit-room design is in Chapter 14.

Bacterial blotch

AT A GLANCE Blotch is a waterborne bacterial disease of fruit bodies. It is the most common cause of crop loss on mushroom farms. It comes mostly from the fruit room (humidifier, water, standing water, warmth), not from the spawn. Pull sick fruit, fix the water and humidifier, keep the room cool.

What it is

  • Bacterial blotch is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas tolaasii. It is not a fungus and makes no spores.
  • "Blotch" is used loosely for a broad group of bacteria. P. tolaasii is the best-studied and most damaging. Because they all attack weak tissue under poor conditions, they can be treated the same way. Black slime on lion's mane stems is probably a different bacterium.
  • It is the most common and costly source of crop loss on mushroom farms worldwide. It hits button mushrooms most, then Pleurotus (oysters).
  • Button farms suffer most because of insects, water and huge, continuous beds without bags.
  • Blotch moves with water in the fruit room; any droplet can carry it. In practical terms, treat it as waterborne rather than airborne.
  • Blotch is more serious than other fruit-room contaminants. A little Trichoderma on the bottom of a block will not invade the fruit (Chapter 16).
  • It can wipe out whole farms. Some rooms have become unable to grow blue oysters at all.
  • The stakes: 40 oyster blocks that could yield 80-100 lb (36-45 kg) can be lost.

RANGE How much crop blotch destroys. The often-repeated "about 90% of crop failures are blotch" is not a measured figure; it means "if you have a crop loss, it is probably blotch". An extension page (Penn State or University of Pennsylvania, unconfirmed which) puts losses at about 15% of Pennsylvania crops, and another figure is about 20% of button mushrooms lost each year. All these figures are recalled loosely (unconfirmed).

Signs

Sign Species or context
Slight yellowing in caps, the early sign. Yellowing on oysters is a key indicator of poor humidification Black oyster near an ultrasonic fogger
Small yellow-brown discoloured caps scattered among healthy black oysters Black oyster in a fogger room
Tan, goopy blue oysters Blue oyster in a room that got too warm
Goopy golden or rusty lesions at cut sites where fruit emerges and water collects, after normal colonization Any species; this localization means the room is the source
First marks on caps, streaking on stems King oyster
Symptoms at the base of clusters where aborts begin, in the centre pin of a budding cluster, or abortive pins Oyster
Infected young fruits often abort before maturing Any
Blotch staying at points where water sits King oyster after stripping
Young fruits turn white with a cauliflower-like bacterial look instead of darkening Ultra-pasteurized maitake, especially bags put to fruit too early; blamed on bacteria not killed without pressure

Room or substrate?

Separating a room problem from a substrate problem is the key diagnostic task.

  • Blotch can originate in the substrate, but most growers who see it now get it in the fruit room.
  • Blotch tends not to show at once. It parasitizes fruit tissue once fruits start to form.
  • Problems hitting many blocks from one spawn lot during incubation point to the spawn or the substrate. Blotch that appears only at fruiting is not the spawn or block supplier's fault (pattern table).
  • In a room, blotch hits everything susceptible at once and leaves the rest untouched.
  • As farms scale, unexplained blotch and contamination often trace to the fruit-room humidifier, not to the spawn or block supplier.
  • Onset can be immediate or a year into fruiting, depending on water quality, construction, drainage and timing.
  • Cap n Stem's own first blotch was on king oysters, before they used soy in their substrate. Note whether a mix is soy-supplemented when diagnosing bacteria: it is an important distinction.

Procedure: kitchen-counter test

  1. If bought-in blocks all fail in your fruit room, take one block from the same batch out of the room.
  2. Fruit it on a kitchen counter, away from your humidifier and room air.
  3. Compare it with the blocks in the room.

CHECK If the counter block does fine, the problem is your environment, usually the water or the humidification.

Conditions that drive blotch

  • Warmth. Blotch season is the change into warm, humid weather, when growers' calls about it pile up; it peaks in summer heat and in the shoulder seasons. A published study links blotch to temperature, with some Pleurotus species worse at certain times of year. Blotch and other fruit-room problems climb sharply in warmer conditions with black oyster. Case: one small farm controlled it in summer by pulling in as much air conditioning from the adjoining room as possible.
  • Species temperature limits. Hericium (lion's mane) does poorly when too hot, with more bacterial infection; HeCNS does best at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F), with a sweet spot of about 16 °C (60 °F). King oyster does best at 10-16 °C (50-60 °F); above 16 °C (60 °F) expect blotch trouble (Chapter 14).
  • Wet caps. Constant over-humidity puts droplets on caps, and soaked caps lead to blotch. Run humidity as a swing, roughly 70% up to 90% and back, not constant saturation.
  • Cold air with unchanged humidification. Cold air holds less moisture, so humidity output that was right in summer condenses on fruit in cold weather. Mild cases give mycelium growing from caps; worse ones give bacteria and even rose comb. Use finer atomization, such as high-pressure fogging nozzles.
  • Timer-run foggers. Cycle timers (for example 30 minutes on, 10 off) are an improper way to control humidity. Humidity runs very high, and blotch worsens when the temperature rises.
  • Air exchange pattern. Case: a French-Canadian grower had lion's mane problems with constant air exchange. Switching to cyclic, CO2-triggered exchange removed all their blotch and malformed growth.
  • Standing water and drains. Standing water always causes problems. Fruit rooms need floor drains with P-traps so sewer or septic air cannot back up and bring in bacteria, including blotch.
  • Packing density. Packing rooms full raises CO2, humidity and the temperature-control burden, and brings more bacterial problems.
  • Slow-fruiting species spend longer exposed. Lion's mane is slower to fruit than oyster, which exposes it to blotch and other fruit-room problems.
  • The root causes. Peroxide is a treatment, not a fix. The root causes are water filtration, air filtration, drainage, trapped drains, negative pressure (what the room pulls in) and the humidifier design. When blotch gets out of hand it is usually tied to humidification: where the air comes from and how it is filtered, and where the water comes from and how it is treated.
  • Bacteria can never be fully eliminated. Design to keep the bacterial load low, because past a threshold even the best humidifier will not save you.
  • Advice from working farms: High Country Fungi (Avery) linked blotch to holding 90% RH constantly and to substrate with 50% soy, and cut soy to 35-40%. Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan) pulls any block showing condensation or blotch immediately (Chapter 26).

Susceptible species and strains

  • Pleurotus is hit most, especially blue oysters and kings. Heavily bred strains seem to suffer more (anecdotal).

  • King oyster is hard to grow without contamination, blotch and fly problems. Black oyster "saved the day" for many farms as an alternative from around 2018-2020.

  • More domesticated, long-established commercial lines may be less resilient (speculation). Very aggressive strains also seem more prone (observation, no data).

  • Shiitake is resistant, perhaps because it produces many secondary metabolites that are largely antibacterial. At a farm where over half of fruiting was shiitake, blotch was barely noticed and was handled by picking off, or not packing, blotched oyster pieces. Less oyster volume means less room for blotch to build.

  • Chestnut: bacterial blotch is not a direct problem, despite fogging.

  • Comb tooth: one grower has seen no blotch.

  • Blotch may hit one king oyster strain and not another. If it hits strain "3044", try "POCNS", "3015" or "King Blue" (strain codes unconfirmed).

  • Running one set of genetics year after year eventually gets it targeted, so rotate strains occasionally even with good practice. Blotch types may be specific to particular strains, much as shiitake strains 3782, 3790 and JC differ (Chapter 8).

  • Flies bring blotch. Catawba Mushrooms (North Carolina) had one blotch outbreak, cleared in about two weeks, but it devastated its fluffy blue oyster strains of the POCNS type, which are very blotch-prone.

Handling an outbreak

  • Remove affected fruit on sight so it does not recycle through the room. Even with clean air, treated water and fine atomization it will appear occasionally.
  • Do not box blotched mushrooms: in the cooler they spread it to other mushrooms (Chapter 15).
  • Triage by strain rotation: switch to different strains ("confuse the pathogen") to stop losses at once, even at a lower yield, while you fix the structural causes. Use peroxide in the humidifier as a first "get out of jail" card, then fix the rest.
  • Case: a New York farm sprayed a heavily blotched oyster block with bleach solutions at various strengths. The blotch died back and mushrooms grew around it. The die-back was attributed to the spray, not to chance.
  • Spraying affected fruit with dilute bleach is a quick defence, but do not sell bleach-sprayed mushrooms: discard them and fix the source.
  • Do not spray 2.5-3% peroxide straight onto fruit bodies; it damages them.
  • Do not spray vinegar or rice water on mushrooms.
  • Walking through every variable with an outside person helps a grower find the cause; growers tend to fixate on one variable.
  • A network of small farms and diverse supply chains is more resilient: a large centralized operation hit by blotch loses orders of magnitude more.

Procedure: blotch outbreak response

  1. Pull every blotched fruit and any block with condensation or blotch at once; do not pack or box them.
  2. Switch the affected rooms to different strains to stop the losses, even at lower yield.
  3. As a short-term rescue, dose the humidifier water with peroxide at about 0.1% (dosing).
  4. Lower the room temperature toward the cool end of the species range.
  5. Check and fix the root causes, one at a time: humidifier design, water treatment, drains and traps, standing water, negative pressure and intake air filtration.
  6. Stop peroxide dosing once the problem window is over.

CHECK New flushes come up without yellowing caps or goopy lesions at the cut sites.

Humidifiers: the main disease vector

AT A GLANCE "Proper humidification" means a fine mist, inline filtered water, no recirculation of room air, and accurate measurement. Ultrasonic foggers inside the room are the worst choice; fine dry mist (TAC misting first, or Hart high-pressure fog) and steam are the best.

Designs ranked

Design Verdict Why
TAC misting (electric, no compressor, about 1 micron dry vapour) First choice of High Country Fungi Avoids Hart's main failure, compressor burn-out; see Chapter 5
High-pressure fine fog (Hart Environmental mixing box with compressed air and filtered water) Proven; the best option for fruit rooms Fine atomization raises the threshold at which condensation collects; the room feels dry, and the mist barely wets a hand
Steam humidification Very good where a boiler runs constantly Steam carries essentially no minerals; helps with blotch and rose comb
Ultrasonic units moved outside the room, or ducted to outside air Acceptable Draws fresh air and pushes humidified air in, instead of recirculating room spores (the same logic as no recirculating AC in a lab)
Aeromist-style compressor and misting heads Mixed Designed for about 10 minutes on, 10 off; in fruit rooms people run 10 on, 2 off and burn out compressors, and 16 heads soak blocks; they have been seen to fail often
Pond fogger: floating ultrasonic units in a 55 gal (208 L) drum, fan duct in, fog duct out Most linked to blotch complaints Coarse droplets, recirculation, untreated water. An untreated fogger is one of the biggest bacterial vectors and behind the weekly "I have blotch" calls
Ultrasonic unit or fogger drum inside the room Worst Recirculates room air (spores, dirt) through a warm water vat and bubble dome and blows it over the crop; the dome collects grime and needs constant cleaning
  • In a room with an ultrasonic fogger the fog can be so dense that the oyster shelves are barely visible and a hand held in the stream gets wet; in a room with high-pressure mist the hand stays dry.
  • Ordinary hygrometers cannot read coarse fog from ultrasonic units accurately.
  • "Proper humidification" means fine mist, inline filtered water, no recirculation, and accurate measurement (Chapter 14).
  • Feed ultrasonic units with a cheap (about $2) float valve, and put a coarse, replaceable filter on the air intake.
  • Hydrofogger prices rose from about $165 (mini) to about $450. At $600-700 you may as well buy a high-pressure fog unit, which is not overkill even for tent growers. Dumping untreated city water into a humidifier is asking for blotch; the roughly $500 upgrade pays back quickly.
  • Case: one farm had chronic blotch and tried biocide sprays (chlorine dioxide, peroxide). After it installed a Hart high-pressure system, the blotch went away.
  • Steam humidification: a pressure-rated copper line runs from a constantly running boiler (even a low-pressure one) to a very fine atomizer (about 0.3 micron, unconfirmed). It gives saturation without visible fog and warms the room about 0.5-1 °C (1-2 °F). Some large farms in very dry climates use it.
  • Hart system parts, pressures and costs, and humidity controllers, are in Chapter 14 and Chapter 5.

Procedure: moving an in-room fogger out of the airstream

This was the advice to a Vermont farm with a Hydrofogger inside its room.

  1. Box off a corner of the room with Coroplast, with a vent through the outside wall into the box.
  2. Put the Hydrofogger in the box and duct its outlet (it has a 6-8 in (15-20 cm) collar) into the room, so it draws air from the box and blows humidity into the room.
  3. Optionally fit a coarse filter on the box intake to keep bugs out.
  4. Make the unit easy to pull out, and clean it thoroughly; add bleach to the water if you clean daily.

CHECK The fogger no longer pulls room air; the room air stays clear and caps stay dry.

Water quality

Why water quality reaches the fruit

  • Young primordia (the first pinheads) draw water from the block, but developing fruits respond to the humidity in the air. Sediment and microbes in humidifier water therefore affect them: blotch and rose comb come from the humidity, not from the block.
  • Water used to hydrate substrate that is then cooked rarely causes problems; city water is fine there.
  • Water quality is mainly a fruit-room issue. City water is usually fine for most uses. A shallow dug well has a high microbial load compared with a drilled well of about 200 ft (61 m).
  • People resist reverse osmosis (RO) or treated water as "stripping the good stuff", but untreated water carries more harm than benefit.
  • Deep wells in drought areas can carry bacterial blooms and heavy mineral loads.

The water treatment chain

  • All incoming water gets a physical (particulate) filter, then a softener if the water is hard, then a carbon scrub. It then splits: one line to production (boiler, substrate hydration, solenoids on the filling machines), and one to fruiting, where RO or steam is added. Problems arise when any stage fails: softener skipped, poor filter, broken RO, steam spitting water onto fruit. In short: physical, soften, carbon, then RO or steam.
  • Humidifier water must be filtered: high-pressure misting nozzles, Hydrofoggers and vats with ultrasonic discs all foul with sediment and minerals. Carbon filtering and softening also protect nozzles.
  • Beyond softening, carbon and particulate filtering, the two options for humidifier water are RO or steam.
  • RO wastes water (roughly 2 gallons of reject per gallon produced, unconfirmed), and the reject is mineral-rich. It is still the best, if somewhat wasteful, answer to blotch and rose comb.
  • Inline UV treatment is the cheapest good first line for fogger water. It is non-chemical, so it is not equivalent to bleach, and it is sized by gallons per hour. RO is optional. UV is mainly worthwhile for deep wells; on city water it is extra insurance.
  • Use multiple barriers: treat water before the fogger's auto-fill bucket, and filter or treat the intake air.
  • A simple layout: the water line feeds the fogger through an inline UV unit sized in gallons per hour (GPH), with a peristaltic pump dosing disinfectant.
  • Even after filtration plus steam or RO, farms often still add bleach, peroxide or non-activated chlorine dioxide to the humidifier.
  • Boiler feed-water treatment (protecting equipment rather than the crop) is covered in Chapter 12 and Chapter 18.
  • Example chain for a shallow, mineral-rich coastal well, worked out with Cap n Stem: a 1000 micron spin-down filter, then 100 and 50 micron filters, sediment filters, an iron filter, carbon and UV. A softener follows for boiler feed, and the misting system has its own DI/RO unit.

Disinfecting humidifier water

AT A GLANCE A light dose of bleach (about 150-250 ppm) or chlorine dioxide in humidifier water is standard prevention. Peroxide at about 0.1% is a short-term rescue during an outbreak. Never use household cleaners.

Agent Dose Use and notes
Bleach 150-250 ppm in the fogger water vat Standard on large industrial farms; dosed by a peristaltic pump
Bleach About 150-200 ppm Alternative figure for fruit-room water treatment
Chlorine dioxide (ClO2) Not given Alternative to bleach that can be used under organic certification
Hydrogen peroxide 1.5 quarts (1.4 L) of 3% drugstore peroxide in a 10 gallon (38 L) reservoir, about 0.1% H2O2 One North Carolina grower's recipe; reservoir dumped and cleaned every 3 days; about 0.1% is the working ideal
Hydrogen peroxide Injected into the line by a dosing pump A New Jersey grower on a shallow dug well fixed persistent blotch this way
Lysol, Pine-Sol, vinegar Do not use People try these in fogger water
  • Peristaltic dosing pumps (like an IV pump) cost about $30-200. Dose into the fogger's small auto-fill line, and compute the dose from the bleach label.
  • In short: a drum fogger gets 150-250 ppm bleach (or ClO2), never household cleaners; a high-pressure system adds a peristaltic dosing loop for bleach or ClO2.
  • Lightly disinfecting humidifier water with bleach is common industry prevention.
  • Chlorine at low ppm has not been seen to carry into the fruit.

RANGE Bleach in humidifier water: 150-250 ppm (also given as 150-200 ppm). Note that 200-400 ppm equals 0.02-0.04%, not "2-4%"; a conversion of "2-4%" to "200-400 ppm" is wrong by a factor of 100. A statement that bleach "turns into a biocide" at about 20% is garbled: bleach is biocidal at ppm levels, and cleaning bleach should not exceed about 400 ppm (Chapter 18). A claim that chlorine smells stronger at low concentration and that the smell disappears above a saturation point is unconfirmed.

Hydrogen peroxide: how it works and its limits

  • Peroxide does not sterilize or keep surfaces clean, because it breaks down quickly to water and oxygen. It kills bacteria, viruses and moulds on contact. Do not confuse it with isopropyl alcohol or bleach.
  • How it works: catalase, an enzyme present in nearly all organisms, splits peroxide into water and oxygen, and the reactive species formed destroy lipids and DNA. Bacteria, with thin barriers, suffer more than fungal hyphae, and human cells are better protected still.
  • Its useful window is narrow, unlike bleach or isopropyl: somewhere between about 0.1% and 1% it starts damaging mycelium. Fruit bodies probably tolerate a little more than mycelium on plates; stay conservative.
  • A published study (not identified) tested about 16-17 Pleurotus strains (pink, yellow, tropical, through P. eryngii) across temperatures and peroxide concentrations for the onset of cell death.
  • Case: a small grower in North Carolina who had never had blotch got a bad outbreak. Dosing peroxide into the humidifier water cleared the decimated blocks within about two weeks.
  • About five farms have used dosing at about 0.1% successfully. Peroxide costs more than bleach but is used at much lower volume.
  • Peroxide is widely used in food processing (for example dairy and cheese), approved roughly in the 1940s-50s (unconfirmed).
  • Use it intermittently during the problem window (for example the warmest months), not year-round. The effects of chronic use are unknown and probably bad. Growers are asked to share data.
  • Farm-grade 30% peroxide burns skin badly (Chapter 18).

RANGE Peroxide in humidifier water. Recommended: about 0.1% H2O2, short-term, during an outbreak (1.5 quarts (1.4 L) of 3% peroxide in 10 gallons (38 L) gives roughly 0.1%). It is the first rescue step in recent practice and is listed among accepted humidifier treatments; older guidance ruled peroxide out for fogger water alongside Lysol, with no reason given. The damage thresholds in circulation are inconsistent: "over about 1% harms mycelium"; "one fifth or one sixth of a percent"; a study's upper level quoted as "0.025, which is 2.5%" (0.025 as a fraction is 2.5%); and the study's ideal quoted as "0.001", called 0.1% (0.001 as a fraction is 0.1%; 0.001% would be a hundred times lower). Check the original study before relying on any threshold.

Rose comb

  • Rose comb is gill tissue forming on the tops of caps: the mushroom is "gravitationally confused". It is distinct from the warty caps that king and black oysters get in very high humidity.
  • Room management: most rose comb, odd colours, mushy deformities and poor texture can come from too little air exchange or no breathing cycle, and from over-humidity putting droplets on caps. Many "rose comb" problems are simply poor room management.
  • Condensation on fruit in cold weather can lead to bacteria and even rose comb (conditions).
  • Water: case: the same black oyster G2 spawn lot (one grain master makes 12-20 G2 bags) went to a Rhode Island farm, which got heavy rose comb and blamed the spawn, and to a Kentucky farm, which got excellent fruit. When one farm is the outlier, the cause is "always water" (about 9.9 times in 10), from an untreated well or even city water.
  • Steam humidification and RO are the best fixes for rose comb, because they deliver mineral-free moisture.
  • Mineral dust hypothesis: one grower wrote a four-page paper, partly developed with ChatGPT and other AI tools and not peer reviewed. It argues that fine mineral dust (calcium carbonate, silica) settling on caps may cause micro-damage and alter local water gradients, polarity cues and pH, so that topside gills could be an environmental response rather than a genetic one. It says explicitly that the molecular pathways are not established.
  • Case from the same grower: ultrasonic discs in a barrel under a tarp that ran condensate back into the barrel concentrated particulates. Rose comb became so bad that every species except chestnut had inverted or topside caps, including golden enoki.

RANGE Causes of rose comb. Fix first: the humidifier water (RO or steam) and the room's breathing cycle, since both are cheap to check. Explanations in use: humidity and air-exchange management; and water quality (minerals and microbes) as the dominant cause. Neither has been tested against the other.

Other malformations and what they signal

Malformation Cause
Fused mushrooms, a small cap growing on a cap (chestnut) Excess humidity or condensation on caps; common and circumstantial on chestnut, not a warning sign as it would be on oysters
Mycelium growing out from caps Mild condensation in cold weather
Warty caps on king and black oyster Very high humidity
Long stems, no caps, "cordyceps-like" oysters High CO2
Bleached, crusty beige, flat king oyster caps Too much CO2 and not enough light
Lion's mane deformities Low air exchange, high CO2, hot rooms, dense packing
Bizarre deformed oyster shapes Possibly a virus (viruses)
Comb tooth patch that fails to branch out (fractalize) Occasional; cause unknown

A cap with condensation droplets on it can grow a small secondary cap from the spot where water sits. The full list of fruiting shape problems, with their room causes, is in Chapter 14 and Chapter 19.

Viruses

  • A whole group of viruses attacks Pleurotus, showing as bizarre, deformed growth. Virus infection is common and essentially untreatable, and virus-weakened crops are more prone to blotch.

  • A virus outbreak in South Korea wiped out a large share of a year's oyster crop. It has been linked to centralized distribution of a few strains (for example "PO 775", unconfirmed) across the country.

  • Horizontal gene transfer has been floated as a speculative mechanism; neither viruses nor gene transfer have been shown to cause stroma.

  • Sending cultures between farms can spread viruses, insects or mites, and a culture "sometimes... is not what it says it is". Track where each culture came from (who kept it before you), and use genetic testing, which is getting cheaper.

Stroma

AT A GLANCE Stroma is hard, dense, hot, swelling growth of the crop's own mycelium. It is not airborne and does not spread through the air, but it ruins the bag and multiplies through every expansion. About 99% of the time it starts in grain spawn. Prevent it with whole grain, no burst kernels, light additives, well broken-up inoculum, about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F) incubation and spawn used on time.

Stroma looks like a contaminant but is the cultivated fungus itself reacting badly. For one large farm it is the one persistent biological problem.

What it is and is not

  • "Stroma" literally means a mass of fungal cells, good or bad. The word is used loosely, and published research mostly ends with "cause unclear".
  • It is poorly understood, with little scientific documentation; most knowledge is grower anecdote.
  • The best working view is that it is a genetic or epigenetic response of the crop itself, not an airborne contaminant. It does not spread through the air; it ruins the affected material.
  • Do not confuse it with "overlay" on monotubs; with Agaricus bed "blob mutants" that go crusty brown; or with mycelial consolidation, a healthy secondary dense layer (peelable from a plate) that can look odd. True stroma swells quickly into flabby, balloon-like growths.
  • Older growers called it "Mycogone". Mycogone is actually a genus of real contaminants in the Hypocreales, and some ascomycete contaminants grow in globular, crusty forms that resemble stroma. Hypocrealean contaminants have caused regional outbreaks in the past (France is named).
  • John Donahue's shiitake book uses "stroma" for early primordial knots. Some shiitake strains (on straw, or on poorly pasteurized or very dry substrate) form little white heads that stall or half-form mushrooms; this may be a related genetic tendency. It is also seen in cubensis and cordyceps.
  • A virus cause has been suggested; the question remains open. Textbooks dismiss stroma as a spawn problem. Researchers in an EU project on stroma and in Hungary have been named as possible contacts.

Appearance

  • In grain bags it radiates from a centre and is more circular. In substrate blocks it shows as hardened, less circular pouches, because it arrives in a clump of affected grain.
  • In black pearl blocks: very dense, often amber- or orange-tinted white circular patches, which predict poor yield and misshapen fruit.
  • Poke test on black pearl grain: harmless dense, pillowy splotches are normal. If a patch is not rock-hard (or just yellows when poked), it is fine. True stroma is hard and appears in older, dense zones, not newly colonized ones. A stroma spot never reverts to growing mycelium.
  • Pioppino grain patches may look like stroma but stay soft and fluffy.
  • Stroma tissue is dense outside, weak and mushy inside, and very hot. A broken-up stroma bag taken from a cooler felt about 38 °C (100 °F), much hotter than the healthy mycelium beside it, and it stays hot while active.
  • It can form in the core of a bag (a "golf ball" inside) while the outside looks clean. One lab manager found it by breaking open bags from a lot that showed stroma on others.
  • Small spots can swell to huge masses within days.
  • Signs of heat stratification in a rack: top-shelf bags dense, hard, swollen with liquid and possibly starting stroma, while bottom bags of the same batch are still patchy (Chapter 13).
  • Cut open with a razor, an affected block shows a whitish, swollen, rubbery lump in the substrate; affected grain bags carry dense, white-to-cream, lumpy masses.
  • Clear bags help you see stroma and contamination, even though black bags raise yields for several species.

Where it starts and how it spreads

  • About 99% of the time it starts in grain spawn. It almost never starts on agar and rarely in substrate blocks (possible with environmental triggers).
  • On agar it is very rare. When it is seen, blame plate age, heat or poorly mixed media (for example undissolved malt extract). Properly prepared agar and liquid culture essentially never show it. Overgrown oyster plates that mat and yellow may form stroma if not refrigerated (Chapter 7).
  • It is occasionally seen in G1 masters, which are low-volume and screened carefully because they sit at the top of the expansion pyramid.
  • It behaves like "mushroom cancer", a tumour: each expansion multiplies it roughly tenfold, it cannot be cut out, and any small amount spreads through every bag inoculated from it, even from apparently clean parts of the bag.
  • In blocks it comes from the spawn nine times in ten (unless the mix is badly uneven). It can be seen forming within about 5 days of inoculation and worsens daily.
  • Healthy spawn can develop stroma during long or hot shipping or storage. Cold-stored masters keep about a month, with rising risk of stroma, hardening and overlay; beyond a month do not use them (Chapter 8).
  • It usually appears in only 1-2 of several hundred bags from the same cell line, which suggests a local stress response rather than a defective culture. It has been seen on millet, rye and straight sorghum, and less on one farm's sorghum mix (small sample).

Effects

  • Unhealthy mycelium, fewer and deformed fruits, unpredictable behaviour.
  • Fruiting affected blocks gives poor yields (vigour diverted into stroma), slow pinning and malformed fruit. The fruit is not sellable, though it may be usable for powder (Chapter 15).
  • Pin set after cutting is slower.

Causes: the working model

  • Stroma is a stress response. Mushy or burst grain and loose starch form dense clumps that are hard to colonize. The mycelium's metabolism spikes there, producing excess heat and CO2, and that combination triggers stroma.
  • Contributing factors: heat from digesting rich grain; big temperature spikes with rich grain; free starch from over-hydrated grain leaching into residual water; and aggressive species such as oyster.
  • Burst grain releases sugar and starch that act like agar and make the mycelium grow too fast.
  • Wheat and barley go goopy when overcooked, raising the risk of stroma ("hot pockets"). Over-mixing grain in a helix mixer collects broken material into "pizza crust" clumps (Chapter 9).
  • Even perfect grain forms stroma in some varieties from too much time or too high a temperature.
  • In blocks, a badly mixed ball of supplement (soy, wheat bran, canola) could trigger it, like pockets of uncomposted manure in Agaricus beds, which make hot spots with similar disc-shaped growths. Poorly mixed or wrongly hydrated substrate can cause stroma (Chapter 16).
  • Growers ask these fungi to digest far richer, protein-heavy media than wood, so variables that are set wrong readily cause problems.
  • King oyster spawn left 0.5-1 week past full colonization consolidates into a solid brick with some stroma (less than other oysters). Black pearl forms stroma when too hot or stressed, and rarely fruits on its own on grain, going to stroma first. Do not leave fully colonized masters sitting for two weeks.
  • In 10 lb (4.5 kg) black oyster blocks, ambient temperatures above 19 °C (66 °F) overheat the core at peak metabolism, causing stroma.

Species and genetics

  • In one large farm's production, stroma is almost entirely an oyster problem: most of all P. ostreatus types (its house blue), then black oyster, and a small, dainty oyster strain (name unclear) despite its low vigour. Oysters have the lowest tolerance.
  • Wild oyster clones show less stroma at first, but incidence rises with successive generations of the cell line. A Danish grower's wild red oyster clone now forms stroma heavily after long domestication. Another grower isolated about 20 wild oyster strains, and all made stroma.
  • The same farm keeps its stroma-sensitive house blue because its 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) yields underpin its customers' businesses.
  • Research under way: the farm has studied stroma in Pleurotus spawn for about a year. The plan is DNA extraction, PCR and a gel to confirm DNA, then outside whole-genome sequencing of many affected and healthy Pleurotus (including the same cell line in adjacent bags), looking for an unstable gene cluster switched on by stress. Dr. Jason Slot agreed to analyse the data on condition it is published openly. The first gel showed intact DNA in all four lanes (normal and stroma POCNS, and the same pair for a second strain) (Chapter 8).
  • Breeding idea: if one nucleus triggers stroma, pair the better monokaryon (single-nucleus strain) with others and grow the results under stroma-inducing conditions to find lines that avoid it.

Case files

  • Greasy bag batch. A batch of cultivation bags with a leached, greasy polymer residue (rainbow sheen, slippery, the lab could not seal them) produced stroma in every affected bag, across many species, not just oysters. The supplier was Unicorn, during an ownership and pricing transition. Published papers also link polymers to stroma.
  • Moth-damaged sorghum. An outbreak was traced, by examining stroma colonies and finding burst sorghum inside them but intact rye, to older, moth-damaged sorghum. Sorghum is high in sugar and starch and prone to bursting.
  • The end of the tote. When a one-ton tote of grain drains from the bottom, lighter damaged kernels rise and all come out at the end, concentrating problems on the last day. Lot, age and hydration records all looked normal. The grain spawn production manager spotted it.
  • Split-batch trial. The part of a batch used on time gave healthy, high yields; the part left to sit formed stroma.

CASE A Texas farm's first 500 blocks for a large customer showed stroma: "hard, almost yellowed patches of growth". The grower put it down either to over-pasteurizing or to an incubation room that was too warm, "which in Texas... is going to be the issue. It always has been the issue." Stroma substantially cuts growth and yield (it is terrible for Agaricus farms) and it spreads: crush a stroma block into 100 clean blocks and they come out ten times worse, generation after generation. Heat and other stresses bring it on, which is why clean culture storage (cryo) matters.

Prevention

Procedure: preventing stroma in grain spawn

  1. Buy whole grain. Grade 1 (USDA-style grading), mostly whole and intact. Broken grain (for example cracked millet) cooks unevenly and leaches starch.
  2. Hydrate to just short of bursting. Maximize hydration but stop before the point of no return, especially with rich grains. Autoclaving is a second cooking phase, so work back from the result after the autoclave. Cook grain intact, "al dente", with no free water outside the kernels (Chapter 9).
  3. Go easy on additives. Calcium carbonate, gypsum, sawdust and the like can glob with loose starch; start under 1%. One farm's current calcium carbonate plus calcium sulfate total is about 0.15% of total wet weight.
  4. Break up the inoculum thoroughly, so there are no concentrated masses that make disproportionate heat.
  5. Control ambient temperature: About 19 °C (66 °F) for blocks and about 18 °C (65 °F) for grain. The critical variable is the internal temperature at peak metabolism near the end of colonization. Space grain bags evenly.
  6. Watch the clock. Move spawn to inoculation or to the fridge at the right time.
  7. Screen. Packing managers screen out stroma bags; break open suspect bags from affected lots; inspect grain for hard, discoloured spots before use.
  8. Clean your grain. Small growers using local grain can buy or build a grain cleaner (a vacuum plus sieves).

CHECK Opened bags from each lot show no hard, hot, discoloured lumps, including in the core.

  • At medium scale, screening relies on human judgement, and occasionally a few hundred bags are thrown out. Do not accept about 3% loss as a cost of business.

RANGE Calcium additives. In grain spawn: under 1%, with about 0.15% total (CaCO3 plus CaSO4) in one farm's practice. The 1-4% calcium carbonate range often given applies to block substrate, a different medium (Chapter 10).

Insects and rodents

  • King oyster is hard to grow without fly problems, among others.

  • One small farm has had no major insect infestation, only strays coming in through the open door.

  • A coarse filter on a humidifier box intake keeps bugs out (fogger box).

  • Insects are one reason button farms suffer most from blotch.

  • Grain: sorghum is attacked by insects (gnats, larvae) far faster than other grains, even in dry, climate-controlled super-sack storage. Turn it over quickly; silos would help. Case: a millet tote from a small broker arrived full of broken grain, gnats, live grubs, other grains and plant debris; feed-store bags often had bugs, corn and rat droppings; early local Maine grain was about 50% bugs and debris. Ask suppliers about cleaning and grade.

  • Rats love raw soy pellets and will bore through warehouse walls for grain; pest control is an ongoing war.

  • Combo pellets (sawdust mixed with soy hulls) are ignored by rats, unlike pure soy hull pellets; one farm reports no rodent-chewed sacks or pest-infested batches. Pellets must still be stored indoors and dry.

  • Case: fungus gnats wiped out the POCNS blue oyster at Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan). The response: tape every gap, fit magnetic bug screens on every opening, and hang sticky traps everywhere, about 8 per room or one on every shelf. Keep compost away from entrances.

  • The biology and control of fungus gnats, phorid flies and mites are not covered by the sources beyond the practical gnat control above (open questions).

  • Imported logs and blocks can carry hitchhiking pests in shipping containers. Some overseas producers use formaldehyde as a cheap sterilant, and many do not use autoclaves.

Spore load as a room problem

  • Fruit-room spore load clogs ductwork in humid air, and makes low-pressure humidification degrade and hard to keep clean.
  • A commercial heat exchanger would clog within hours and cannot be flushed; a Coroplast stack can be washed (Chapter 5).
  • Walk-in cooler evaporators only recirculate. In a spore-laden space their fins and coils clog even if mushrooms are picked early. Keep the cooler out of the plenum and away from fruit rooms.
  • Opening a full shiitake room released a spore cloud that coated and broke a fan; keep a backup fan. Maitake may do the same (unconfirmed).
  • Harvest on time: overblown mushrooms shed more spores.
  • The health effects of spores are in Chapter 18.

Cleaning fruit rooms

  • Isopropyl foot baths at fruit-room doors make little difference; a clean plenum and consistent one-way airflow matter.
  • Clean fruiting rooms far more than people think, daily if possible. Rotate cleaning agents: spray about 250 ppm bleach, power-wash or wipe walls, and push the water to the drain.
  • One small farm mostly bleaches floors, sometimes alternating with vinegar, and spot-cleans walls rather than cleaning them weekly.
  • Clean the room fully (walls, floors, racks) before loading new blocks.
  • The ultrasonic dome on in-room units collects grime and needs constant cleaning and bleach.

Procedure: turning a fruit room round between loads

  1. Remove all blocks, debris and any blotched fruit.
  2. Spray walls, racks and floors with about 250 ppm bleach (rotate with another agent from time to time).
  3. Power-wash or wipe the walls, and push the water to the trapped drain; leave no standing water.
  4. Clean any humidifier dome or vat and refill with treated water.
  5. Load the new blocks only once the room is fully clean.

CHECK No standing water on the floor, and no visible mould on rack corners or wall flutes.

Key rules

  1. When blotch appears only at fruiting, look at the room, the humidifier and the water, not the spawn supplier.
  2. Get humidifiers out of the room or ducted to outside air; never recirculate room air through a water vat.
  3. Treat humidifier water: particulate filter, softener, carbon, then RO or steam if you can, plus a light bleach or ClO2 dose (about 150-250 ppm).
  4. Use fine atomization and a humidity controller, not foggers on timers; swing humidity (about 70-90%) rather than holding it saturated.
  5. Keep susceptible species cool (kings 10-16 °C (50-60 °F), lion's mane about 16 °C (60 °F)); blotch climbs with heat.
  6. Provide trapped floor drains and never leave standing water.
  7. Pull blotched fruit on sight and never box it with good fruit.
  8. In an outbreak, rotate strains and consider short-term peroxide dosing near 0.1%, but verify the thresholds and do not use it year-round.
  9. Treat stroma as a grain-spawn problem: whole grain, no bursting, light additives, broken-up inoculum, about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F) and spawn used on time.
  10. Store grain and pellets dry, and turn grain stock over fast to keep insects and rats out.

Open questions

  • Flies, fungus gnats and mites are barely covered; no identification or control guidance is available beyond sealing, screens and sticky traps.
  • Peroxide thresholds and the cited Pleurotus study need checking against the original paper.
  • Whether peroxide belongs in fogger water at all is not settled; the 0.1% short-term rescue rests on a handful of farms.
  • The cause of stroma is unknown; the genome-sequencing project had not reported results.
  • The possible causes of rose comb (humidity management, water minerals) have not been tested against each other.
  • Virus diagnosis and control are not covered beyond "common and untreatable".

Safety

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the hazards to people on a mushroom farm: breathing in spores, CO2 build-up, steam and pressure equipment, electrical and fire risks, open flames, chemicals, heavy lifting and repetitive work, and a few food-safety points. Most of it comes from near misses and injuries on working farms. The rules used most:

  • Wear a respirator when harvesting or working among spore-dropping fruit.
  • Put a CO2 meter wherever people work, stay under 5,000 ppm, and never sleep in incubation.
  • Never build pressure into a vessel not rated for it, and never leave pressure equipment running unattended.
  • Get an electrician for 240 V steam equipment.
  • Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners; keep cleaning bleach at or below about 400 ppm.
  • Design manual lifting out of the work.

Spores and breathing

  • Spore lung (a lung reaction to breathing in large amounts of mushroom spores) is real. Case: harvesting shiitake strain 3782 for about a week gave several staff at one farm spore lung, likened to years of chain-smoking compressed into minutes; respirators were not emphasized there at the time. Wear a respirator while fruiting and harvesting.
  • The same farm always harvested reishi outdoors because its spore load is so heavy.
  • Rolling racks are the most important fruiting tool partly for this reason: roll carts out to a harvest, grading and packing area, which keeps spores off workers and out of the plenum. Wear a respirator or harvest outside the room (Chapter 15).
  • Harvest on time: overblown mushrooms raise the spore load as well as shortening shelf life.
  • Opening a full shiitake room can release a visible spore cloud. Spores once coated and broke a fan; maitake may be similar (unconfirmed).
  • Low-spore strains reduce the spore load. A truly "spore-less oyster" is near-mythical, though big spawn companies are said to be good at low-spore strains.
  • Neurospora is not reported as harmful to people beyond the general risk of breathing in huge spore loads (Chapter 16).
  • Myth: the popular theory that deaths after the opening of Tutankhamun's tomb were caused by black mould is not established fact.
  • Masks in the lab protect the product, not the worker: face masks are used, and an N95 is overkill for that purpose. That judgement is about contamination control, not about protection from spores in fruit rooms (Chapter 4).

WARNING No respirator type or rating has been specified for spore protection in the sources (open questions). Choose one rated for fine particles and get advice from a safety supplier.

Carbon dioxide

AT A GLANCE Blocks breathe out CO2 all the time. Incubation rooms run at 1,500-3,500 ppm; the workplace limit is 5,000 ppm. Measure it wherever people work.

Level What it means
5,000 ppm US OSHA workplace exposure limit (time-weighted average); stay below it
1,500-3,500 ppm Incubation control band. Start with the exhaust fan on at about 3,000 and off at 1,500-2,500, depending on how much CO2 you are willing to tolerate; the widest band suggested is on at 3,500, off at 1,500. Keep well under 5,000 (Chapter 13)
About 450 ppm Outdoor baseline, used for lion's mane exhaust control
About 7,000 ppm Reached once at the old site of Cap n Stem, a large block and spawn farm in Maine
10,000 ppm The range where some organisms' cells die

  • Case, sleeping in incubation: a staffer slept overnight on a couch in the incubation room (the warmest place) and had sleep paralysis with a loud, buzzing "presence". A colleague blamed CO2; there was no CO2 meter in incubation. Staff at the old farm also napped on the incubation scaffolding. Lesson: never sleep in incubation, and monitor CO2 where people work.

  • During a power outage CO2 climbs fast, because blocks keep respiring with no exhaust.

  • Do not heat fruit rooms with propane "hot dog" greenhouse heaters: they put combustion CO2 into the space unless properly vented and controlled.

  • A recommended CO2 meter: a CO2Meter.com grow-room controller (model RAD-0501), about $230-250, which tolerates humidity and spores and reads high ranges (Chapter 5).

  • Workplace CO2 limits trace back to brewing-industry studies of the 1950s-70s, in which staff breathed about 20,000 ppm through eight-hour shifts. High CO2 in incubation feels "smothering"; think about what your staff breathe.

Pressure and unattended operation

  • Do not build makeshift pressure into containers not designed for it. Unpressurized steam tops out at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level, and that is the design limit of such vessels (Chapter 12).
  • Case: North Spore once ran about 20 X75 pressure canners (some borrowed) on timers, unattended. Experienced growers find this terrifying.
  • Manual vacuum pulls on old-style retorts are rare and risky; few growers do them.
  • Equipment that is not automated needs people on site at night. Cap n Stem's old Westbrook steam generator needed someone about every two hours overnight to work the valves, and a sauna-steamer controller with a 60-minute maximum timer needed resetting every hour (a guest slept at the farm to do it).
  • 15 psi (1 bar, 103 kPa) does not guarantee 121 °C (250 °F): trapped air reads as pressure but resists heating. Purge the air first by letting steam vent strongly before closing a pressure cooker.
  • Over-tight lids on hot glass jars from a pressure cooker are hard to open and risk breakage. Sterilize with lids slightly loose and foil-covered, then tighten them in the hood (Chapter 7).

Procedure: running a pressure cooker safely

  1. Load jars with lids slightly loose and covered with foil.
  2. Heat with the vent open and let steam vent strongly to purge the air before you close it.
  3. Only then bring it up to 15 psi (1 bar), aiming for 121 °C (250 °F).
  4. Stay with it: never leave it running unattended on a timer.
  5. Let it cool, then tighten the lids in the flowhood.

CHECK A thermometer or logger in the load reads 121 °C (250 °F), not just the gauge reading 15 psi.

Boilers: safety features and settings

Item Value or practice
Low-pressure boiler limit (Sioux SF-25, propane, about 1.1 million BTU) 15 psi (1 bar) or just under
One farm's operating setting Main maximum about 10 psi (0.7 bar) with a 5-7 psi (0.3-0.5 bar) differential, so pressure ebbs and flows; cranking settings up causes wide cycles
Interlocks on start-up Manual-reset low-water switch, water-feeder level switch, adjustable pressure switch, manual-reset pressure switch
Start-up sequence Filtered water fills the boiler, open the propane, turn the switch
High-pressure boiler for autoclaves About 50 psi (3.4 bar) all week, 45-50 psi (3.1-3.4 bar) delivered to the autoclave head; containerized outdoors
Sauna steam generator Has an overpressure relief valve; newer units add drain and flush valves
Indoor fuel-fired boiler Needs a chimney
  • Blowdowns (briefly opening the pressurized bottom drain to flush out sediment) are as important as water treatment.
  • Treat boiler and steam-generator feed water (carbon filter, softener, feed tank). Scale ruins sensors and parts and can cause failure or fire; this applies even to small electric steamers. Do not feed distilled or RO water, which is corrosive to metal (Chapter 17).
  • Case: scale on the fire tubes showed up as blocks failing to reach 93 °C (200 °F); the logs revealed a slow creep in ramp time. Boiler maintenance is both a safety and a process issue.
  • An outdoor containerized boiler can freeze over winter weekends; protect it.
  • Opening the steam valve first discharges condensate water, then a strong plume of steam. On one farm the steam travels about 18 m (60 ft) to the steaming container.

Procedure: low-pressure boiler start-up

  1. Check that every interlock is in place and reset: manual-reset low-water switch, water-feeder level switch, adjustable pressure switch, manual-reset pressure switch.
  2. Let filtered (treated) water fill the boiler.
  3. Open the propane.
  4. Turn the switch on.
  5. Run at a maximum of about 10 psi (0.7 bar) with a 5-7 psi (0.3-0.5 bar) differential, always below the 15 psi (1 bar) limit.
  6. Open the steam valve slowly and stand clear: condensate comes out first, then a strong plume of steam.

CHECK Ramp time to temperature in the logs is not creeping up; if it is, look for scale and do a blowdown.

Hot blocks and boiling

  • Blocks pulled hot, at 93 °C (200 °F) or more, for cool-down are handled with welding gloves (Chapter 16).
  • Boiling grain is laborious, needs full attention and is dangerous; spawn staff on one farm have burns (Chapter 9).

Electrical and fire

  • Sauna steam generators typically run on 240 V. Breaker sizes vary by manufacturer even when units look identical: some need a 50 A two-pole breaker, others 30 A or 20 A. Get an electrician.
  • These units keep heating and can overload circuits. They have caught fire at several farms, mostly through mistreatment.
  • Their controller board can be rewired to run indefinitely instead of stopping at 60 minutes, "until it burns out". Do not defeat the timer.
  • Hard water scaled units and shorted their elements within about a week after a move.
  • DIY flowhoods carry electrocution and fire risk (rheostat wiring, flame tests indoors) (Chapter 6).
  • Case: a home-built sawdust sifter shaken by an old pump motor was loud, shook itself apart, bogged down, and became a fire hazard when it stalled: "don't ever do this".
  • Improvised wooden drying boxes with a hot plate and a fan are a fire hazard, compared with a plugged-in dehumidifier (Chapter 15).
  • Coroplast is not structural, and it is flammable and melts: in a fire, get out. Building codes (for example in Canada) may restrict its use.
  • A malfunctioning filling machine is "nine times out of ten" a loose wire. Keep terminals tight, with the correct strip length and no frayed or exposed copper touching neighbours. Re-tighten all the rear terminals, because once a machine is wall-mounted that side is rarely seen.
  • Japanese automatic baggers need a 240 V three-phase supply.
  • Humidity controllers and sensor boxes in fruit rooms must be sealed against moisture (silicone in gland grooves, cable glands, evenly tightened covers). A proper install grounds to a metal box. Check the real wiring diagram rather than relying on anyone's verbal description.
  • People electrify shiitake logs to shock them into fruiting. Don't.

CASE A Texas farm's building had panels like "layers on an ice cream cone" (a main panel, a sub-panel and two panels buried in a wall), and "you can only run one thing at a time". A cheap electrician pulled about ten 10-gauge wires through a 13 mm (½ in) conduit about 30 m (100 ft) long. The conduit wore a pinhole at a bend, a second electrician was alarmed, and the owner kept a box fan blowing on the breaker box because it got so hot it kept tripping. An infrared thermometer would have shown the conduit at "well over 100" °F (38 °C). The load was three sauna steamers on one PID controller with three solid-state relays, plus a second control box for the grow room fans, air conditioners and humidifier. Hire a qualified electrician and have the supply sized for your real load.

WARNING Fire codes apply to mushroom farms. One farm scaled to "1,000 to 2,000 pounds a week" and was then "shut down for lack of safety... by the fire marshals": it had not installed sprinklers in the grow rooms "because they had electrical outlets and power cords and stuff running all over". "Water and electricity, it's the blight of a lot of mushroom farmers."

Open flame and combustion

  • A low-tech DIY pasteurizer uses one upright 55 gal (208 L) drum over an open propane flame as a boiler, steaming into a second drum on its side; one was built in Arizona. Its legality and safety with an open flame are questionable.
  • Asian growers have long pasteurized in barrels over a wood fire, with a small vent valve on top.
  • Propane greenhouse heaters in fruit rooms add CO2 unless vented (CO2).
  • The lighter-flame trick shows airflow at a flowhood but says nothing about contamination; incense smoke or ribbons are alternatives.
  • An infrared tool sterilizer (Bacti-Zapper style) replaces an open flame for tweezers; cool the tip on agar or in 70% isopropyl at a cool-down station. In early days, soft-handled tools burned up in an alcohol lamp.
  • Grind zinc (galvanized) coating off before welding (60-80 grit flap disc), because zinc fume and dust are harmful to breathe. Wear eye protection.

Chemicals

Chemical Hazard or limit
Bleach plus ammonia-based cleaners Never mix. It gives off a toxic gas. Someone got sick doing this
Bleach for cleaning Do not exceed about 400 ppm; if you can easily smell it, it is too strong. A grower in Arizona used undiluted pharmaceutical-grade bleach and was injured
Bleach in humidifier water About 150-250 ppm (Chapter 17)
Farm-grade 30% hydrogen peroxide Burns skin badly; one grower has diluted it to 10-20% for cleaning hydroponic trays
2.5-3% peroxide Do not spray straight onto mushrooms
Peracetic acid Used to sterilize stainless spawn hoppers
Quaternary ammonium ("quats") Common in Europe; stays active in a bucket all day
Disinfectant smells Cause nausea in some lab hires

RANGE Bleach strength. Working values: about 150-250 ppm in humidifier water and no more than about 400 ppm for cleaning. A statement that bleach "turns into a biocide" at about 20% is wrong, and so is a conversion of "2-4%" to "200-400 ppm" (it is off by a factor of 100: 200-400 ppm is 0.02-0.04%). Use the ppm figures.

Contaminants in inputs and products

  • Buy pure calcium products. Agricultural lime may carry heavy metals or arsenic. For gypsum use calcium sulfate dihydrate, not crushed drywall (Chapter 10).
  • Reishi can accumulate heavy metals (lead, cadmium, mercury) from its substrate.
  • Heavy-metal concerns are said to trace mainly to imported Asian shiitake-type substrate logs, whose sawdust may come from any chipped wood, including recycled furniture, some of which are chemically sterilized with formaldehyde before shipping (unconfirmed).
  • Minerals, heavy metals or chlorine in the finished mushroom are more likely to come from the substrate than from hydration water.
  • PFAS ("forever chemicals") are relatively easy to filter out of water but very hard to remove from substrate or soil.
  • Conventional grain may carry glyphosate or fungicide residues; Cap n Stem uses organic grain (Chapter 16).

Manual handling, machines and ergonomics

  • Case: barrels of sawdust (about 23-36 kg (50-80 lb), typically about 34 kg (75 lb)) had to be raised to the mixer. A winch hung about 6.7 m (22 ft) up kept failing because barrel handles broke. The crew mostly lifted barrels by hand onto stepped platforms, which caused a back injury, and later used a forklift once space was cleared. Carrying barrels upstairs injured another worker's back.
  • Near miss: a cracked barrel on the winch tipped. A worker steadied it by hand, the barrel collapsed and the hook cinched, nearly catching their hand. Work stopped for the day. Lessons: never put hands on a hoisted load, and retire damaged barrels.
  • Case: a jaw sealer retrofitted with a pneumatic piston on a compressor crushed a grower's fingers when they deliberately put a hand in at about 90 psi (6.2 bar). Don't.
  • During a flood, a forklift hydroplaned driving through deep water; in the chaos the manager sent most staff home.
  • No safe rolling racks of about 6 m (20 ft) exist.
  • Manual bagging (standing under a bagger all day, packing, folding, racking) is heavy repetitive strain; automation reduces injuries (Chapter 6).
  • Moving blocks in racks or cages instead of hand-loading each one reduces handling (and contamination).
  • Tyvek suits raise body temperature about 6 °C (10 °F) above the room. Above the mid-20s °C (mid-70s °F), work inside a suit is miserable, so one farm keeps its lab at about 18-19 °C (65-66 °F).
  • Clean-room work strains some people: headaches from lighting, nausea from disinfectant smells, discomfort with white walls, constant white noise and suit confinement; fans and lights never stop. A chronic injury complicated one hire. Paid test days help match people to roles (Chapter 22).
  • Repetitive work induces a trance. Long chats or audiobooks during long runs lead to errors when something changes.

WARNING Don't use an open-door clothes dryer to tumble or shake bags. A worker's arm got caught and twisted in one, and a dryer may have caused a fire that burned down a mushroom farm in Massachusetts.

  • Ergonomics is part of safety: choose block sizes staff can carry all day, and design harvest areas that limit spore exposure.

Food safety and customers

  • Some people react to chestnut mushrooms with vomiting and diarrhoea; a former Alabama grower and their partner are both affected. Chestnut still ranks among the top five species for many farms.
  • Do not sell bleach-sprayed mushrooms (Chapter 17).
  • "Taste it, spit if bitter" is not reliable safety advice for wild mushrooms. Jack-o'-lanterns have been mixed up with chanterelles.

RANGE Chestnut intolerance. Treat it as an individual reaction that some customers have. Individual cases of digestive distress are reported; a claim that people either tolerate chestnut completely or get very sick, called "100% proven", has no source.

Allergies. Some people are allergic to particular species. A chef in Orlando became ill from golden oysters (a rare allergy) and would not put them on the menu. Two Alabama growers who took the chestnut culture from Cap n Stem were both badly allergic to it. Chefs drive the restaurant market: if you scare a chef you lose the client, so be ready to explain why your product is safe.

Grain questions. Customers with allergies ask whether mushrooms are grain-free. Grain spawn used for blocks is not an ingredient of the finished mushroom, but one Louisiana farm found the question hard to answer; prepare a clear answer in advance.

Medicinal products. A nurse and grower was told by an oncology pharmacologist not to use reishi during chemotherapy, because it affects blood clotting and blood pressure (and, she says, can be toxic at some doses). She is also wary of Amanita gummies and tinctures of unknown origin. Don't make medical claims for your products.

Wild mushrooms. Some food laws have no category for wild mushrooms at all. In New Hampshire an inspector made a chef throw out US$400 of matsutake. Foragers have tried to sell misidentified, toxic mushrooms to farms; never resell wild mushrooms you cannot identify with certainty.

Audits and inspectors. Regulation "really comes down to your customer". Larger buyers require third-party food-safety audits (one Pennsylvania farm uses Primus), which can go as far as proof of insurance from your box supplier. A tiny farm selling at a market needs far less. Inspectors and certifiers often don't understand mushroom farms and have to be educated.

WARNING Clean drains every day. A big button-mushroom grower abandoned a whole bottle-growing system after Listeria was found in a floor drain (not in the product).

Organic certification (US). US organic rules for mushroom substrate allow non-organic materials in some cases, through exemptions and composted inputs, and producers have argued that organic substrate materials are not available all year and that substitutions cause "detrimental yield drops". Some big farms became certified organic "overnight", while Cap n Stem paid extra to use organic inputs. Organic certifiers also apply the standards differently: one large producer moved back to its earlier certifier after another rejected it for something it had done for years. "If you're a new farm and you want to be certified organic, just know you're playing with something that is unfair."

Key rules

  1. Wear a respirator when harvesting, especially shiitake and reishi; where possible, roll racks out to harvest elsewhere.
  2. Put a CO2 meter wherever people work, stay under 5,000 ppm, and never sleep or nap in incubation.
  3. Never build pressure into a vessel not rated for it, and never run pressure canners unattended.
  4. Keep boiler interlocks working, do regular blowdowns, and treat feed water.
  5. Have an electrician size circuits for 240 V steam generators; do not defeat their timers.
  6. Do not heat fruit rooms with unvented propane heaters; keep open flames out of labs.
  7. Never mix bleach and ammonia cleaners; keep cleaning bleach at or below about 400 ppm.
  8. Handle 30% peroxide with skin protection, and never spray strong peroxide on food.
  9. Never put hands on a hoisted load; retire damaged barrels; use forklifts or automation instead of hand lifting.
  10. Keep fingers out of pneumatic sealers and machines.
  11. Buy pure calcium products and clean inputs to keep heavy metals out of the crop.

Open questions

  • No respirator type or rating is specified for spore protection.
  • Lockout and tagout, hearing protection, slip hazards on wet fruit-room floors, and confined-space entry into containers are not covered by the sources.
  • Pressure-vessel inspection, relief-valve testing and certification requirements are not covered.
  • The OSHA CO2 figure is given only as a time-weighted limit; short-term limits are not covered.
  • Chestnut intolerance is reported only anecdotally.
