chapters.html:
Troubleshooting by Symptom

AT A GLANCE Find what you can see, at the stage you see it, and read across: likely cause, what to check first, the fix, and where the full explanation is. Four habits solve most problems. (1) Pull the cook logger record before anything else. (2) Map the problem across bags, lots and days before you act. (3) Change one thing at a time. (4) If a problem shows only at fruiting, suspect the fruit room and its water, not the spawn.

How to use this chapter

  • Each table covers one stage of production, in process order: plates, grain spawn, the cook and cool-down, colonizing blocks, fruiting and water and humidifiers.
  • Check Things that look wrong but are normal before you throw anything away.
  • Words used here: knock (inoculating blocks with spawn), stroma, exudate, metabolites, endospores, gusset, headspace, filter patch, ultra-pasteurization, blotch, rose comb and ppm. "Sectoring" means the mycelium grows in uneven wedges instead of one even front. "Buckling" is the bumpy, blistered stage a shiitake block goes through before it browns.
  • Each row ends with a link to the section that explains the cause and the fix in full. This chapter is a finder, not the full story.

Plates and cultures

What you see Likely cause Check first Fix Details
Yellowing plate, or yellow metabolite droplets Plate past its peak Plate age Do not use; discard Plates past their peak
Plate older than 3 months Aged culture Date on the plate Discard (house rule on one farm); keep each line fresh Plates past their peak
Fluff clusters, centre fluffing up to the lid, small fruit bodies on agar Plate past peak but still alive Is the edge still clean white growth? Still usable; on lion's mane, cut from the outer edge away from the primordia Plates past their peak
Overgrown oyster plate matting and yellowing Left too long unrefrigerated Plate age and storage Transfer earlier or refrigerate; it may form stroma The 1 cm rule
Tough leathery crust on agar Stroma (very rare on agar): plate age, heat, or poorly mixed media such as undissolved malt lumps How the media was mixed Mix agar evenly; do not reuse old plates Stroma versus consolidation
A dense secondary layer that peels off the plate Mycelial consolidation: healthy - Nothing; peel off the skin on king oyster to reach fresh tissue Stroma versus consolidation
Different moulds on settle plates in front of the hood Hood or filter leaking Plate and particle test across the filter face Inspect the filter's bottom edge for breaks; replace Chapter 4

Grain spawn

What you see Likely cause Check first Fix Details
Green on dry or uncolonized kernels Dry grain colonizing slowly Grain moisture Hydrate grain fully and evenly Moisture
Irregular, splotchy colonization even after sterilization Grain fermented during a long soak, or drained grain left standing Soak time; time from draining to the cooker Shorter soak; process promptly. Long soaks are not needed to kill endospores Hydrating grain
Patchy, odd colonization and failure to fruit Pesticide or fungicide residue on conventional grain Grain source Use organic grain Buying grain
A whole lot contaminated Technique: shedding from hands, spawn bag held outside the laminar flow, fingers in bags Watch the knock Retrain on sterile technique Inoculating a grain master
Maitake spawn brown with sparse growth Medium even slightly off, or liquid inoculation Moisture and sterilization records Fix moisture and sterilization Other spawn problems
Mould in chestnut grain Chestnut is a little less tenacious than oyster Moisture; full colonization Keep grain moist and fully colonized Other spawn problems
Hard, dense, hot lumps in grain or blocks Stroma (not a contaminant) Spawn age and incubation heat Screen spawn; see the stroma section Stroma in spawn, Stroma
Dense, pillowy splotches in black pearl grain that are not rock-hard Normal Squeeze: true stroma is hard Nothing Normal
Spawn bags rip during shaking Thin plastic Bag gauge Use thicker bags Chapter 11
Spawn is a solid, leathery brick and slow to leap onto substrate Spawn left too long past colonization Spawn age Use spawn just past full coverage Reading when spawn is ready

The cook and cool-down

RULE When blocks go bad, pull the data-logging thermocouple record first. Start with the method (sterilized or ultra-pasteurized) and the cool-down, not the ingredients.

What you see Likely cause Check first Fix Details
Contamination in patches through the batch, many types (bread moulds, forest moulds, bacteria); uneven colonization and yield Steaming failure Logger record for the run Fix the cook Diagnosing a cook failure
Many colours of mould a few days after knocking Dirty air during cool-down or in the lab, or undercooked wood Cool-down air path; run a sealed-bag test Cool hot blocks in front of positive-pressure HEPA Cool-down
Strong colonization at the top, weak or anaerobic at the bottom of big blocks 10-12 lb (4.5-5.4 kg) blocks not held long enough at the plateau Core temperature log Raise the cook temperature or extend the hold Standards
Sporadic chunky spots appearing over about 2 weeks in some bags of a lot Undercooked substrate, not the spawn Cook data Longer or hotter cook Diagnosing a cook failure
Pin mould Undercooking, dirty cool-down, porous patch or bad seals, made worse by excess airflow Cook log, patch grade, seals Longer cook; tighter patch Filter patches
Outer blocks in a barrel dried and growing poorly, inner ones fine Overcooking (for example a 24 h barrel run) Cook length Shorter cook; this is not contamination Cook no longer than needed
Mycelium dead in ultra-pasteurized substrate Overheating from poor shaking Shaking after spawning Shake thoroughly Shaking
Weak, wispy, "greasy" colonization; many species (even reishi) fail to fruit Hot blocks waited 1-3 days before reaching a filtered cool-down room Time from cooker to cool-down room Move hot blocks straight into a clean cool-down room Cool-down
Spawn dies, block bottom "gnarly", crop grows in walled-off colonies Block fermented before inoculation, or knocked too hot Time and temperature at the knock Inoculate promptly at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F) Block temperature at the knock
Spawn never grows, or only a few nodules Spawn killed by knocking at 38 °C (100 °F) or more Block temperature at the knock Cool further before knocking Block temperature at the knock
Milky or viscous film, frost-like inside the bag Bacteria Cook, cool-down time, incubation temperature Fix whichever failed Bacteria
Heavy metabolite exudate (species other than shiitake) Media too rich, or undercooked; bacteria may then stop fruiting Recipe and cook log Leaner mix or a better cook Diagnosing a cook failure

Colonizing blocks

First read the pattern: where the problem sits across bags, lots and days usually names the source.

Pattern Most likely source Details
All the blocks (say 20) from one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag turn green That spawn bag Other spawn problems
Many blocks from one spawn lot fail during incubation Spawn or substrate supplier; trace by lot Reading the pattern
Sporadic across a batch, always near the gussets or the top seal Bag defect or bad seal; test seals, change bag lot Bag failures
Sporadic infiltration across a whole lot Technique, damaged filters or irregular airflow Reading the pattern
Systemic, across everything Equipment: the cook or cool-down air; rarely a working flowhood unless it has a bad break Reading the pattern
Recurring green, brown, black or orange moulds over months Bad lab filtration or negative pressure; check the filter's bottom edge Lab air
Only lion's mane has problems A systemic fault (pasteurization, moisture, temperature, light, a mould source) that hardier species cope with; do not assume the culture Diagnostic habits
What you see Likely cause Check first Fix Details
Green sporulation inside many blocks of one substrate run Substrate fault: cook, moisture or mix Cook logs, hydration, mix Test with sealed bags Diagnosis table
Orange cobweb growth working up to the headspace, then powdery orange spores Neurospora, usually through bad seals or torn bags; worse in warm rooms Seals and bag integrity Remove infected bags at once; bag and bin them; never open or compost them near the facility Neurospora
Hard line over a sloppy wet bottom, sour smell Too much water pooled; anaerobic bacteria Hydration Less water; even out hydration Hydration and mixing
Dark wet spots around every inoculation point Over-spawning and extra heat Spawn rate Lower the spawn rate Spawn rate
Bags "perspiring" heavily early in colonization Predicts contamination within 1-2 weeks (seen on lion's mane and blue oyster) - Watch and remove Diagnosing problems in the bag
Patchy, splotchy, drying blocks; bags losing weight CO2 too low (about 500 ppm) from too much air exchange Incubation CO2 Hold CO2 in the incubation band; separate incubation HVAC CO2 bands
Blocks overgrow or go patchy in a new, lightly loaded room Too much air per bag Room load Bring the room to a steady load quickly How full to load the room
Top-shelf bags dense and swollen (maybe stroma); bottom bags patchy Vertical heat stratification Temperatures top and bottom More recirculation, evaporators mounted high, stagger batches Stratification
Row-to-row differences; cold corridors next to hot ones Ducts radiating heat, or supplemental AC ducting Log several spots Log temperatures before blaming spawn Measuring temperature
Sawdust-coloured, loosely colonized patch where blocks touch; shiitake that won't buckle there Local heat at contact points Bag spacing Two hand widths between bags Space between bags
Dry, dead, crusted top on top-shelf blocks (especially chestnut) Strong cold light (6500 K) close above hot top shelves, or too open a patch Light position Chestnut low and away from lights; red light; tighter patch Light
Popcorning or blistering; shiitake skin slops off when stripped Temperature swings (even 3 °C, 5 °F) Temperature log Hold a steady temperature Stability and swings
Shiitake buckles and browns but never fruits ("duds") Incubation too hot, or one phase disrupted Core temperature 19 °C (66 °F) room air; keep the core at or below about 23 °C (74 °F) Set points
Shiitake surface contamination after browning and buckling Insufficient cook; shiitake can look fine and fail late Cook log Fix the cook Reading the pattern
Squishy blocks Heat stress and core cell death Core temperature Discard; fix the cooling Heat
Yellow liquid at the bottom of lion's mane bags Hot core on a rich 50/50 mix waking endospores Core temperature; recipe Leaner mix (soy about 30-40%), cooler incubation Diagnosing problems in the bag
Heavy exudate, sectoring, wet spots Poor mixing or hydration, temperature swings, competitors Mix and room log Homogeneous mix; stable room Diagnosing problems in the bag
Stroma visible within about 5 days of inoculation Usually (nine times in ten) the spawn; also heat at peak metabolism Spawn lot; ambient temperature Check the spawn; control the ambient Stroma
Mixed crop in one batch (white, brown and fruiting at week 9) Swings with a hot, reduced-soy recipe Room log Leaner recipe or tighter control Diagnosing problems in the bag
Pinning in the bag during incubation Shock (AC failure, bumping, moved racks), light (lion's mane), swings (chestnut), too long in clear bags (oyster) What changed in the room Wide aisles, fixed shelves, dim light, black bags; move triggered blocks to fruiting or the cooler Diagnosing problems in the bag
Shiny skin or thick sheath; slow, reluctant to fruit Held too long (oyster, king oyster) Block age Fruit on time or refrigerate Holding colonized blocks
Glossy, slick, flat pioppino top that never pins; dry side pins Bad culture, cook or spawn Trace culture, cook and spawn Fix upstream Diagnosis table

Fruiting

RULE A problem that appears only at fruiting is the fruit room's, not the spawn's or the block supplier's. Test with the kitchen-counter test: if a block from the same batch fruits fine on a counter, the room (usually its water or humidifier) is the cause.

Shape faults: air, CO2 and light

What you see Species Likely cause Fix Details
Long stems, small or no caps ("cordyceps-like") Oyster High CO2 More fresh air; automate CO2 CO2 setpoints
Vase-shaped caps, long stems Oyster Poor airflow Fix airflow Fans
Stem elongation Black oyster CO2 not exhausted early enough Turn the exhaust fan on when CO2 reaches about 800-900 ppm CO2 setpoints
Coral-like reaching fruit that cooks floppy Lion's mane High CO2, hot room, dense packing, blocks touching More air exchange; space blocks Air and CO2 faults
"Dreadlocks": part spined, part still primordial Lion's mane CO2 differential too wide, or a fan outage Narrow the CO2 band; check fans The lung cycle
Bleached, crusty beige, flat caps King oyster Too much CO2, not enough light More air and light King oyster and light
Fluted, sideways, malformed caps King oyster Uneven light across the substrate Even out the light King oyster and light
Antlers instead of caps Reishi High CO2 in the bag (perhaps 3,000-5,000 ppm); kidney-shaped caps form under about 1,000 ppm Choose the patch for the form you want Air and CO2 faults
Elongated stems at a cut Any Half-moon cuts around existing pins Cut before pins form How to cut

Humidity, water and condensation

What you see Species Likely cause Fix Details
Gill tissue on cap tops (rose comb), odd colours, mushy deformities Many Too little air exchange or no breathing cycle; constant over-humidity; minerals and microbes in humidifier water Check the breathing cycle and the water; RO or steam humidification Rose comb
Warty caps (not rose comb) King and black oyster Very high humidity Lower RH Relative humidity
Mycelium growing out of caps, then bacteria and rose comb Black oyster Condensation in cold rooms; coarse droplets Stop condensation Cold air and condensation
Small cap growing on a cap, fused mushrooms Chestnut Excess humidity or condensation on caps; usually harmless on chestnut Usually nothing Malformations
Long drooping spines on one side, bald ball on the other Lion's mane RH too high Lower RH Humidity faults
Crater-like crenulations Lion's mane No RH swings Cycle humidity Humidity faults
Pink or yellow tint on young fruit Lion's mane Room too dry Raise RH; fruit should start and finish white Humidity faults
Pins killed in the collar King oyster Condensate flooding the bag See collar pinning Collar pinning
Bruised, flattened, hairless caps, puddling bacteria Shiitake Bag left on more than 1-3 days of pinning Strip sooner Shiitake shock
Different fruit colour Oysters Untreated minerals in hydration water Treat the water Water treatment

Disease signs

What you see Species Likely cause Fix Details
Slight yellowing of caps Oyster, black oyster Early blotch, poor humidification Check humidifier and water Blotch signs
Tan, goopy fruit Blue oyster Blotch in a too-warm room Cool the room Conditions that drive blotch
Goopy golden or rusty lesions only at cut sites where water collects, after normal colonization Any Room-borne blotch Handle as a room outbreak Handling an outbreak
Aborting pins, symptoms at cluster bases Oyster Blotch Handle as a room outbreak Blotch signs
Black slime on stems Lion's mane Probably a different bacterium from classic blotch Clean and check water Blotch and disease signs
White, cauliflower-like young fruit instead of darkening Maitake Bacteria surviving ultra-pasteurization; worse when moved to fruit too early Wait longer before fruiting; consider sterilizing Blotch signs
Bizarre deformed shapes Oysters Virus: common and untreatable Replace the culture line Viruses
Poor yield, slow pins, malformed fruit Oyster, black oyster Stroma in the block Screen spawn Stroma
Green mould blooming on top of fruiting chestnut Chestnut Fruit room too warm Cool the room Diagnosis table
Mould on developing fruit as exudate wicks up Maitake Over-rich (50/50) blocks Leaner mix Blotch and disease signs

Temperature, cutting and handling

What you see Species Likely cause Fix Details
White oysters whatever the strain Oyster Room too warm Bring the temperature down Temperature changes colour
Caps flatten fast, stems wither and droop, bad smell Chestnut Too warm Cool the room Temperature faults
Browned white fruit Lion's mane Shiitake exudate dripping from above Don't rack lion's mane below shiitake Mixed-species rooms
Malformed fruit inside the bag Lion's mane Cut too late Cut on time When to move blocks
Deformed fruit plus scattered pins inside the bag Chestnut PE bag cut gaping and drying Cut smaller Cutting methods
Petals dry out and die Maitake Bag cut too short (no protective collar) Leave a collar Cutting methods
Thick, undifferentiated fronds Maitake Cut too early Cut later Cutting methods
Bag full of malformed mushrooms Shiitake (strain 3790) Held cold too long Shorter cold hold Shiitake shock
Drastic change in fruit form Pioppino Switched grain source Don't switch grain Chapter 9

Water and humidifiers

What you see Likely cause Check first Fix Details
Bought-in blocks fail in your room but fruit on a kitchen counter Your environment, usually water or humidification Kitchen-counter test Treat the water; fix the humidifier Water quality
Same spawn lot: rose comb on one farm, good fruit on another The outlier farm's water (in experience, almost always the water: about 99 times in 100) Compare farms Treat the water before blaming spawn Rose comb
Unexplained blotch and contamination as the farm scales The fruit-room humidifier Humidifier type and water See humidifier ranking Humidifiers
Blotch outbreak in the room Room source Water and humidifier Peroxide reservoir rescue treatment Peroxide procedure

Things that look wrong but are normal

What you see What it is
Golden-mustard chestnut blocks Normal ripening; often mistaken for Neurospora
Ghostly, wispy lion's mane blocks Normal; fully colonized in about 10 days. But Trichoderma can hide in it: watch for denser matting
Splotchy pioppino (and king oyster) blocks Normal; colonies join after about 3 weeks
Dense white patches on pioppino grain Normal; pioppino never knits as hard as oyster
Yellow or orange metabolites on older shiitake, chestnut and pioppino grain; clear droplets on chestnut a week later Normal
Cobweb-like aerial mycelium at a cut, then amber droplets Normal black oyster pinning
A peelable dense layer on a plate Mycelial consolidation, healthy
A small, contained Trichoderma patch in the corner of a sealed block you fruit yourself Can still be fruited and yield well (do not sell it)

Key rules

  1. Pull the cook logger record before anything else.
  2. Map the problem across bags, lots and days; the pattern names the source.
  3. Many blocks from one spawn lot failing during incubation means spawn or substrate; trouble only at fruiting means the room.
  4. A "rainbow" of moulds usually means dirty air at cool-down or in the lab; check the cook log too, because undercooked wood can give the same picture.
  5. Treat lion's mane as your early warning for systemic faults.
  6. Remove Neurospora bags at once and bin them sealed.
  7. Change one variable at a time; knee-jerk changes waste money.
  8. Check the "normal" table before discarding anything.
