chapters.html:
Species Profiles

AT A GLANCE One card per cultivated species, always in the same order: overview, strains, culture and spawn, substrate, incubation, fruiting, harvest and yield, problems, tips. The numbers and rules used most:

  • Incubate 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) room temperature for nearly every species. Block cores run several degrees hotter, and heat spikes cause duds, stroma and bacteria.
  • Spawn rate: one 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain spawn bag per twenty 10 lb blocks for most species.
  • "Fully white" is not "ready" for shiitake, maitake, chestnut and black oyster. Give them their ripening time: shiitake to 75-80% brown, maitake to the fist-to-fingers stage, chestnut to the caramel ring.
  • Fruit cold-lovers cold: black oyster, king oyster and chestnut pin best at about 10-17 °C (the 50s to low 60s °F). Pioppino and maitake tolerate warmer rooms.
  • Run CO2-triggered exhaust with a narrow band, roughly 450-900 ppm.
  • Harvest before caps flatten.

How to use this chapter

Each species has a card. The cards follow the same order, so you can jump straight to "Fruiting" or "Problems" for any species. Use the comparison table to find a number fast, then go to the card for the context behind it.

Most numbers here come from Cap n Stem, a Maine farm that sells spawn, blocks and cultures. Its house system is a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block of 50:50 red oak sawdust and soybean hulls, called "Master's Mix", spawned at one 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain spawn bag per twenty blocks and incubated near 19 °C (66 °F). The exact numbers for each species and stage are tabulated in Chapter 21. This chapter gives the context: why a species behaves as it does and what goes wrong.

A few terms appear on every card:

  • Master's Mix: the 50:50 mix of hardwood (red oak) sawdust and soybean hulls described above, usually made from "combo pellets" (pre-blended pellets that are hydrated before cooking). See Chapter 10 and the glossary.
  • Block: a filter-patch bag of cooked substrate that is inoculated with spawn and grows into one fruiting unit. "Knocking" a block means inoculating it. See Chapter 11.
  • G1 / master and G2: grain spawn generations. A G1 "master" bag is inoculated from an agar plate; each master inoculates several G2 bags; G2 inoculates the blocks. See Chapter 9 and the glossary.
  • Ultra-pasteurization: steaming substrate at just under boiling for several hours, instead of pressure sterilizing it. See Chapter 12.
  • Stroma: dense, hot, rubbery masses of mycelium that never fruit properly. Mostly an oyster problem; see the oyster stroma section.
  • Pins / primordia: the first tiny mushroom bodies. A flush is one wave of mushrooms from a block.
  • Auto-fruiting: mushrooms forming inside a spawn or block bag before you want them.

The house system behind the numbers

Setting Value Conditions
Block 10 lb (4.5 kg) of Master's Mix: 50:50 red oak sawdust and soybean hulls Most species; shiitake and maitake need a leaner mix
Spawn rate One 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 grain bag per 20 blocks (about 3% spawn) Other farms use 8-30 blocks per bag; above 30, vigor drops and incubation drags
Incubation room About 19 °C (66 °F) ambient 10 lb ultra-pasteurized blocks; sterilized 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks about 22 °C (72 °F)
Agar to master Two 1 cm agar squares per 4 lb (1.8 kg) master bag, or four for slow strains or for speed Up to 12 masters per plate at two squares
Master to G2 One master into 12 G2 bags of 6 lb (2.7 kg) Never fewer than 6 or more than 24

The broad patterns across species:

  • Fast oysters tolerate almost anything.
  • Slow species (shiitake, maitake, chestnut) must be incubated well past "fully white".
  • Cold-loving species (black oyster, king oyster, chestnut, lion's mane) pin poorly above about 17-18 °C (the low-to-mid 60s °F).
  • Shiitake and maitake want a leaner substrate than Master's Mix. Oysters, chestnut, pioppino and king oyster thrive on Master's Mix; lion's mane may do better with soy cut to 30-40%.

Species at a glance

Species Incubation of a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block Fruiting temperature Light Yield per 10 lb block
Blue oyster 10-14 days; pins at once unless refrigerated 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) Can run fully dark until fruiting 2-4 lb (0.9-1.8 kg); plan on 2 lb (0.9 kg)
Black oyster About 10 days; safe window to 3 weeks; an extra week adds yield 10-18 °C (50-65 °F), ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) Standard full spectrum 2.58-2.87 lb (1.17-1.30 kg) in one trial
King oyster 14-18 days (10-21) 10-16 °C (50-60 °F); no reliable pinning above about 17 °C (63 °F) Bright and even; strongly light-triggered About 2-2.25 lb (0.9-1.0 kg)
Lion's mane About 12 days (10-18) 13-18 °C (55-65 °F), sweet spot about 16 °C (60 °F) Dim in incubation; solid full spectrum to fruit About 2 lb then 1.5 lb (0.9 then 0.7 kg) over two flushes
Comb tooth Denser and faster than lion's mane Prefers 19-21 °C (upper 60s °F); tolerates 10-15 °C (the 50s °F) As lion's mane No figure recorded
Shiitake 6-14 weeks (about 12 at Cap n Stem); fruit at 75-80% brown LE3790 happiest 10-16 °C (50-60 °F); 3782 fruits at 10-27 °C (50-80 °F) Needed in incubation to brown 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg)
Maitake 8-12 weeks to harvest, plus about 1 week; cut at fist-to-fingers Anywhere in 16-21 °C (the 60s °F) More than usual in incubation; lots to fruit About 2 lb (0.9 kg), one flush
Chestnut 2-3 weeks, then 1-2 weeks or more of ripening Pins at 10 °C to about 16 °C (50 °F to the very low 60s °F); ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F); poor at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) Keep dim: the most light-sensitive species in incubation 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) target on 10 lb pellet blocks
Pioppino About 3 weeks 18-24 °C (65-75 °F); tolerates 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) Lights on once the pin carpet forms "Very high" (no figure)
Reishi Months to a year in the bag Needs 85-95% RH; CO2 decides antler or cap Not recorded Not recorded

Where each species goes in a mixed fruit room

In a mixed fruit room, rack position matters because light, temperature and dripping differ from top to bottom.

Rack position Species Why
Top Golden oyster, lion's mane, maitake Golden oyster and lion's mane respond more to light; maitake is hard to fruit in a mixed room
Middle to bottom Blue oyster, black oyster Standard placement
Low (ideally a separate room) Shiitake Never above lion's mane: shiitake drips brown exudate that stains white fruit
Bottom Chestnut Standard placement

Speed in the fruit room also differs. Shiitake and pioppino are fastest, oysters are in the middle and chestnut is slowest; overall the range is about 5-15 days.

Oyster: blue oyster and the Pleurotus group

AT A GLANCE The easiest and most forgiving crop, and the yield base of most farms. Key numbers for blue oyster on 10 lb (4.5 kg) Master's Mix blocks:

  • Grain spawn finished in about 10-12 days.
  • Blocks colonize in about 10-14 days at about 19 °C (66 °F) and pin at once unless refrigerated.
  • Fruit at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F), middle to bottom of the rack.
  • Plan on about 2 lb (0.9 kg) per block; good strains give 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg).
  • Main problems: stroma (starts in grain), bacterial blotch in warm rooms, viruses.

Overview

  • Oyster mushrooms are the genus Pleurotus. Its species (P. ostreatus, P. djamor, P. citrinopileatus, P. eryngii and others) share essentially the same growth biology and differ mainly in colour and preferred temperature, which is why many papers and farms simply write "Pleurotus sp.".
  • Oysters, together with Psilocybe cubensis, are the easiest mushrooms to grow. They colonize almost anything, which explains their popularity.
  • Pleurotus grows on sterilized, pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized and even non-sterile substrate. Many growers start with lime- or steam-pasteurized straw inoculated in open air.
  • Oysters can go through every stage up to fruiting readiness in complete darkness, unlike light-dependent species such as shiitake.
  • Beyond food, oysters are used for mycoremediation (for example oil spills), filtration and biomaterials.

A short history of oyster cultivation

Dedicated oyster farms only appeared in the late 1970s and 1980s, when commercial growing became established in the US and Europe. The milestones before that (see Chapter 2 for the wider history of mushroom science):

Year Milestone
1775 First scientific description, by von Jacquin, as Agaricus ostreatus, found on rotting trunks (especially walnut) in November-December
1871 Paul Kummer erects the genus Pleurotus
1905 B.M. Duggar shows that P. ostreatus spawn can be made, in a USDA bulletin from the University of Missouri (it is sometimes misremembered as a "patent" or as from Minnesota). The bulletin's table lists "Pleurotus ostreatus: beans, leaves, manure: rapid growth".
1917 Richard Falck grows oysters outdoors as German wartime food, using a trench method with wheat straw plus stump inoculation. In his stump method, saw cuts are made from three sides to the centre, spawn is pushed in, and a disc is placed on top.
1958 Block, Tsao and Han fruit P. ostreatus in about two weeks on sterile sawdust plus oatmeal, and get an unusually high 1.2 lb (0.54 kg) from non-sterile composted balsa
1963 Bano and Srivastava industrialize paddy-straw oyster growing in India, in large field plots, using Pleurotus flabellatus (a pink oyster now placed in P. djamor) and P. sajor-caju
1968 Eugenio and Anderson find that compatible (mated) pairings yield about 200 g more than incompatible ones

Strains

  • POCNS is Cap n Stem's house blue oyster code; batch labels read like "POCNS-17". The farm keeps it despite its sensitivity to stroma, because its 3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) yields underpin its customers' businesses. Small, dainty strains do not pay the same.
  • 3015 is a second strain used in Cap n Stem's stroma DNA work. When blotch targets one strain, 3044, 3015, POCNS and King Blue are offered as swaps.
  • JB is an old, very robust strain used by Far West Fungi and recently acquired by Cap n Stem. Robust P. ostreatus strains that never senesce (lose vigor with age) tend to be the poorest yielders, with small mushrooms.
  • Steel Blue was the first strain grown by Cap n Stem's co-founder. Its fruit was nearly pure white when too hot and deep blue when cold. Yields were weak on lime-soaked straw in drilled buckets.
  • High-yield blue strains are nicknamed "home wreckers". Commercial growers cannot compete without yield.
  • A small, dainty oyster strain (name unclear) still forms stroma despite its low vigor.
  • Wild clones do not escape stroma. A Danish grower's wild red "basket" oyster now forms stroma heavily after long domestication. Another grower isolated about 20 wild oyster strains and all made stroma. A fragrant wild oyster found by a third grower colonized 50:50 substrate but fruited poorly.
  • PO 775 is named as the narrow strain base behind the Korean virus disaster described under problems.

Culture and spawn

For general culture technique see Chapter 7; for grain spawn see Chapter 9.

  • Agar. Revive oysters on PDYA (potato dextrose yeast agar). In the 3-5 days a fresh plate sits in the flow hood, an oyster may already show a couple of inches (about 5 cm) of growth.
  • Transfers. Oyster mycelium is fluffy and aerial, so an inoculation loop works well. Flatter mycelium such as lion's mane and shiitake suits cut agar chunks instead.
  • Old plates. Overgrown oyster plates mat, turn yellow and may form stroma if they are not refrigerated.
  • Cryo revival. Some oysters revived from cryo storage showed irregular growth, patches of programmed cell death and browning or blackening, partly because of an earlier poor cryo routine. Kings and chestnut did not do this. See Chapter 8.
  • Grain timing. Pleurotus grain is typically finished in about 10-12 days. Blue oyster grain shows dense, popcorn-like spots before turning opaque white around day 7.
  • Holding. Once the master is fully white, oysters tolerate another 1-2 weeks at room temperature before refrigeration or use.
  • Over-aged grain. Blue oyster grain left too long forms fleshy, rubbery chunks, and old oyster grain bags tend to pin on the top or bottom. Oyster spawn mats into a hard brick that is harder to break up than chestnut.
  • Heat peak. Heat output peaks at the end of colonization: about day 11 for oyster spawn and day 11-12 for oyster blocks. Rich grain such as millet can spike very fast.
  • Breeding work. Mechanical de-dikaryotization (turning a normal two-nucleus culture back into single-nucleus cultures for breeding) works for Pleurotus: blend a 0.5 cm cube cut from the leading edge for 20-25 seconds. Pellets appear after about 3 days (about a week to start, by another account), with roughly 7-10 colonies per flask. See Chapter 8.
  • Agar slurry fails. Inoculating bags with a blended plate poured straight in failed on four oyster strains, giving only scattered fuzzy spots.
  • Bag filters. Unicorn historically recommended its more open B patch for vigorous oysters (and the tighter A patch for slow shiitake). See Chapter 11.

Substrate

  • Master's Mix (50:50 red oak sawdust to soybean hulls) is the highest-yielding oyster substrate, but also the richest and most fickle. Only cottonseed hulls or fermented straw compete with it. The ratio is 50:50; a "70:30" figure sometimes quoted for it is a slip.
  • A 50:50 mix works for oysters, pioppino and almost everything else.
  • Calcium carbonate at 1-4% is reported to raise yield, especially for oysters. Too much can cause excess heat during colonization or a sticky substrate.
  • Molasses gives oysters readily available sugar. Small farms can run elaborate recipes like this; large crews with staff turnover cannot.
  • Straw systems work. Steel Blue was grown in drilled buckets of lime-soaked straw. Oysters fruited fine from 30-40 lb (14-18 kg) straw buckets with side holes, where chestnut failed.
  • Experiment: dry-sterilized or ultra-pasteurized pellets hydrated with UV-treated, unheated water colonized cleanly with several Pleurotus species. The main difference was fruit colour, probably from the untreated minerals in the water.
  • Not every strain likes a given recipe, and colonizing a substrate does not guarantee fruiting on it. "Oyster-centric" thinking misleads small farms about other species.

Incubation

See Chapter 13 for incubation rooms in general.

Setting Value Conditions
Room temperature, 10 lb (4.5 kg) ultra-pasteurized blocks About 19 °C (66 °F) House standard
Room temperature, 5 lb (2.3 kg) sterilized blocks About 22 °C (72 °F)
Room temperature, aggressive blue oyster grain About 18 °C (65 °F) Big, rich, tightly packed grain bags
Time to colonize, 10 lb clear bag About 10-14 days Pins immediately unless refrigerated; black bags extend the window
Spacing A hand's width between bags Bags touching at peak growth create dead spots
  • For aggressive blue oyster in big, rich, tightly packed bags, control the ambient temperature. What matters is the internal temperature at peak metabolism, near the end of colonization.
  • Left too long, oyster blocks "consolidate": a thick mat or sheath forms and the block becomes slow and reluctant to fruit.
  • Stagger weekly batches of a species across shelves so their heat output is spread out.
  • Freshly inoculated bags that "perspire" heavily early in colonization, like bags at the fruiting stage, will probably contaminate within a week or two. This has been seen on blue oyster and lion's mane.
  • Rolling racks let a farm push a thousand oyster blocks into the cooler at once before a long weekend.

Fruiting

See Chapter 14 for fruit-room design and control.

  • Temperature. Staple species (oyster, shiitake, lion's mane) fruit at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F). At 13 °C (55 °F) fruit grows slower and denser; at 18 °C (65 °F), faster.
  • Colour. In some strains fruit colour tracks temperature. Steel Blue came out near white when hot and deep blue when cold.
  • Opening the bag. Blue oysters are cut with side slits or X cuts.
  • CO2. High CO2 gives long stems with no caps ("cordyceps-like").
  • Airflow gauge. Oysters are good indicators of room airflow: short stems and flattening caps (not vase-shaped ones) mean a good room.
  • Speed. Oysters sit in the middle for fruit-room speed: shiitake and pioppino are fastest and chestnut slowest, overall about 5-15 days.
  • Rack placement. Blue and black oysters go middle to bottom of the rack (see rack placement).
  • Humidity. Example of a heavily fogged room: in one fogger room the fog was so dense that shelves of large oyster bags were barely visible. Yellowing caps are a key indicator of poor humidification.
  • Spent blocks. Spent oyster blocks used as garden mulch keep fruiting.

Harvest, yield and shelf life

RANGE Plan on about 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block for a mixed farm; this is a conservative planning figure. Reported yields run from 2 to 4 lb per block, and the block size is not always stated.

Yield Conditions
About 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb block Conservative planning figure for a mixed farm
2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) per 10 lb block Depending on species
80-100 lb (36-45 kg) from 40 blocks, about 2-2.5 lb (0.9-1.1 kg) per block Block size not stated
3-4 lb (1.4-1.8 kg) per block House blue (POCNS) at Cap n Stem
About 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) per 10 lb bag POCNS blue oyster at Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan), where blue oyster is 70% of farm income
About 4 lb (1.8 kg) per block "Other oysters", contrasted with king oyster
  • Scale changes what loss means: one large farm discarded about 11,000 lb (5,000 kg) of oysters after overproducing. Match production to sales (see Chapter 22).

Problems

For diagnosis and treatment in general, see Chapter 16 (contamination) and Chapter 17 (diseases).

Bacterial blotch.

  • Bacterial blotch hits Pleurotus hardest, especially blue oysters and kings. Heavily bred strains seem to suffer more (anecdotal). Blotch is called the most costly crop loss worldwide after button mushrooms.
  • Warm rooms drive blotch. One summer, blue oysters came out tan and goopy until extra air conditioning was pulled from an adjoining room. Some Pleurotus species get more blotch at certain times of year.
  • Early signs: the centre pin of a budding cluster, the base of clusters where aborted pins begin, or the aborted pins themselves.
  • Fused caps on oysters are a warning sign (unlike on chestnut).
  • Controls: 150-250 ppm bleach in the humidifier water. A New York farm sprayed a blotched oyster block with bleach and the blotch died back while mushrooms grew around it. A farm growing mostly shiitake, with less oyster volume, barely noticed blotch. Switch strains when blotch targets one.

Viruses. A whole clade of viruses attacks Pleurotus, causing bizarre deformed fruit. They are common and essentially untreatable, and virus-weakened crops are more prone to blotch. The Korean oyster industry was wiped out for a while (unconfirmed), which is linked to a few strains (the "PO 775" base) being distributed nationwide. The lesson: a narrow strain base is a risk.

Stroma

Stroma are dense, hot, rubbery masses of mycelium. In Cap n Stem's production it is almost entirely an oyster problem: worst in P. ostreatus types, then black oyster. It is one of the most persistent problems on an oyster farm.

  • Where it starts. About 99% of the time it starts in the grain spawn. It spreads with every expansion and cannot be cut out.
  • Triggers. Heat spikes in rich grain, burst grain and free starch, aggressive species, additives clumping with starch, clumped inoculum, time and heat. One batch of bags with a greasy polymer residue caused stroma across many species, with Pleurotus the least tolerant.
  • Prevention. Use whole grade-1 grain, hydrate it short of bursting, use additives sparingly (Cap n Stem's calcium carbonate plus gypsum total is about 0.15% of wet weight), break up the inoculum, control temperature and move spawn on time. See Chapter 9.
  • Wild clones. Wild clones show less stroma at first, but incidence rises over successive generations.
  • Research. A DNA sequencing project with Dr. Jason Slot is underway, looking for a stress-activated gene region.

Spores. Selecting phenotypes reduces spore load. A truly "spore-less" oyster is near-mythical, though big spawn companies are good at low-spore strains. Spore load matters for staff health (see Chapter 18).

Tips

  • Use a CO2 controller on the fruit-room exhaust, and watch stem length and cap shape as your airflow gauge.
  • Do not leave colonized oyster blocks or spawn to sit. Refrigerate or fruit them promptly, because they consolidate or pin.
  • Mix slow, cool-running species (pioppino) into incubation rows with oyster or chestnut so heat evens out.
  • Mark data-logger test bags unmistakably. One crew lost a logger inside a batch of mostly oyster blocks.

Black oyster (black pearl)

AT A GLANCE A vigorous hybrid oyster with a big king-like stem, now a standard crop on many farms. Key numbers:

  • Blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) are fruitable in about 10 days, with a safe window of about 10 days to 3 weeks; an extra week of incubation is cheap insurance for yield.
  • Fruit at 10-18 °C (50-65 °F), ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F); above about 18 °C (mid-60s °F) pinning drops steeply.
  • Exhaust fan triggered at about 800-900 ppm CO2.
  • Fine high-pressure mist, not coarse fog.
  • 2.58-2.87 lb (1.17-1.30 kg) per block in a side-fruited trial.

Overview

  • Names. Black Pearl, Black King, Black Pearl King, Cosmic Queen and Shimofuri (Hiratake) are used interchangeably; it is jokingly called "a patented strain".
  • Origin. The best-supported origin is Hokuto Corporation's "Shimofuri Hiratake" and a Hokuto interspecific-hybrid patent (Canadian patent CA 2,878,902, issued 2016) that crosses P. ostreatus, P. nebrodensis and P. eryngii varieties. Hokuto's website called it an eastern × western ostreatus hybrid, and others have claimed king × blue; Cap n Stem once repeated the website description publicly and now thinks it was wrong.
  • The patent. Its front page reads "Novel species of Pleurotus sp. and method for producing same", Hokuto Corporation, issued 2016-11-29. It includes a dendrogram (family-tree diagram) grouping P. eryngii, P. eryngii var. elaeoselini, P. ostreatus and P. nebrodensis with the deposited strains NITE BP-1378 and BP-1379.
  • Crossing scheme claimed in the patent. (1) ostreatus × nebrodensis; (2) eryngii × eryngii var. elaeoselini; (3) cross 1 × cross 2; then repeated back-crosses to ostreatus and eryngii. Plain ostreatus × eryngii crosses form a dikaryon (a mated, two-nucleus culture) but do not fruit, so nebrodensis served as a bridge.
  • Other evidence. A 2023 sequencing post online gave messy BLAST hits to P. ostreatus and P. eryngii (about 92-97% on the TEF1 and RPB2 genes). Spore crosses of black oyster gave only one mating pair.
  • Other accounts. It is also described as a Japanese breeding project crossing European and Asian P. ostreatus, with suspected king parentage because young fruit look king-like; other growers say they are unsure of the exact parentage.

RANGE Three accounts of the parentage exist: European × Asian P. ostreatus (as reported from the Hokuto website), king × blue, and a multi-species ostreatus / nebrodensis / eryngii hybrid per the Hokuto patent. The patent reading is the best supported; whole-genome sequencing is planned.

  • US history. Cap n Stem received it around 2017 through a contact then at Far West Fungi. An "Aloha" strain and another version from North Carolina were also sold as black oyster. It took off about 2018-2020 and "saved the day" for farms as an easier alternative to king oyster.

  • Appeal. A massive king-like stem with a softer, somewhat rubbery oyster texture, and vigorous growth even in poorly controlled conditions. A good way to serve it: slice lengthwise into planks, pan-sear, and serve on a baguette.

  • Changing behavior. In the early days on Master's Mix, white fuzz from the cut formed amber drops that became caps. This no longer happens; possible reasons are domestication, longer incubation, black bags and repeated cryo and expansion cycles.

  • Ecology. Because it is a hybrid that cannot cross within itself, it may be ecologically safer than sporing wild-type strains.

  • Where black pearl came from. The oyster many farms grow as a "king oyster x blue oyster cross" (black oyster or black pearl) originated with Hokuto Kinoko, a Japanese company with a site in California. It crossed a European oyster with a king oyster variety (P. eryngii var. nebrodensis), crossed two other king oyster varieties, and after about 11 crosses found a way to mate P. ostreatus with P. eryngii. The method is covered by a process patent filed under a name unlike its market name (see Chapter 2).

  • Crosses generally work between strains whose DNA is about 97-99% similar, and rarely below 98.5%.

Culture and spawn

Step Method and numbers Notes
Cryo storage Rye berries colonized just past the grain; 5-10 grains in a about 5 mL vial with about 3 mL of 10% v/v glycerol; frozen at −80 °C (−112 °F) See Chapter 8
Revival On PDYA; 3-5 days in the flow hood at about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), then sealed and moved to 18-21 °C (65-70 °F)
G1 master Two 1 cm squares per 4 lb (1.8 kg) bag (up to 12 masters per plate), or four squares (about 6 per plate) for speed; shake at about 1-1.5 weeks; fully white and firm about a week later Unshaken for two weeks, it mats around the cutting and leaves other areas bare
G2 One master into 12 × 6 lb (2.7 kg) bags (never under 6 or over 24); grain room 18-21 °C (65-70 °F); firm and spawnable by day 7, normally held to about day 14, then refrigerated
Cold storage Cold-stored masters keep about a month Stroma and overlay risk rise with time
  • A healthy plate shows thick, clearly visible white threads growing out evenly and staying tight to the agar until the edge. Fluffed-up old plates are still usable, but not once they yellow. House rule: no plate older than 3 months.
  • Grain behavior. It forms at most a weak skin that breaks up easily, and it rarely auto-fruits (it goes to stroma first). Harmless dense, pillowy splotches are normal: if a poke finds the spot soft, it is fine. Storing grain in light or dark made no difference.
  • Liquid culture. Aerated liquid culture (ALC) and plain liquid culture into 6 lb masters: ALC started slightly slower on grain, but overall colonization was the same. See Chapter 7.

Substrate and spawn rate

  • The house standard is one 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 per twenty 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks, about 3%. Other farms use 8-30 blocks per bag; beyond 30 blocks per bag, vigor drops and incubation drags.
  • An idea (speculation): the nebrodensis lineage may make black oyster dependent on high pH to fruit, and crossing it with other oysters might relax that.

Incubation

  • Timing. At about 19 °C (66 °F) ambient, a 10 lb block is fully colonized and fruitable in about 10 days, with an unusually long grace period (about 10 days to 3 weeks) before it pins in the bag. Cap n Stem ships blocks at 12-13 days.
  • Temperature. Warmer than 19 °C (66 °F) risks overheated cores, stroma, bacteria and slower pinning. Black oyster is more prone to odd behavior if incubation is sloppy, so watch ambient temperature closely.
  • Maturation. In a liquid-culture trial, blocks were fully colonized in about 2 weeks but heavier after 2.5-3 weeks, which suggests a maturation threshold. A block pulled early matures in the fruit room instead.

RANGE Fruitable at about 10 days, with a safe window to 3 weeks; one trial found 2 weeks to colonize and better weights at 2.5-3 weeks. Both agree an extra week does no harm and may add yield.

  • What it looks like. Block mycelium looks like other P. ostreatus (white, then brick-dense) but with a much less rubbery top sheath than blue oyster. Black oysters can form puffs or mounds at cut sites with pins on them.
  • Cold holding. Colonized blocks hold several weeks at 1 °C (34 °F), but as a cold-loving strain they will eventually pin even at that temperature.

Fruiting

Setting Value Conditions
Temperature, ideal 13-16 °C (55-60 °F)
Temperature, range About 10-18 °C (50-65 °F); 10-12 °C (low 50s °F) for dense, slow, high-quality fruit Above about 18 °C (mid-60s °F) pinning drops steeply
CO2 Exhaust fan triggered at about 800-900 ppm Avoids stem elongation
Humidity Fine, high-pressure atomization Not coarse fog
Light Standard full spectrum Blue LED suits king oyster and probably helps, but is not critical
  • Cutting. Cut a slit or cross about 1/4 in (6 mm) deep on the long face of the block for a dense, large cluster. Some growers top-fruit to mimic the king form, but this is not recommended because the strain naturally clusters.
  • Top vs side. In one trial, round 1 was top-fruited (top cut off, sides folded down to leave 3-4 in (8-10 cm) of bag above the substrate) and round 2 side-fruited. Side fruiting did at least as well, though incubation time also differed and the numbers were small. A typical side-fruited room has blocks on wire shelving with the bag tops folded open and dense grey-brown clusters with long white stems.
  • Pinning sequence. Cobweb-like aerial mycelium puffs from the cut, amber droplets appear at about 5-7 days, then primordia form. It is slower to pin than most oysters.
  • Summer hack. Initiate pins in the coolest room available.
  • Shape. Cold-grown fruit look king-like (thick stems) but clustered; warm-grown fruit look more like blue oyster with fatter stems.
  • Humidity in cold rooms. Cold air holds less water, so unchanged humidification condenses on the fruit, leading to mycelium growing from the caps, then bacteria and rose comb. Use fine high-pressure atomization.
  • Without CO2 control. One farm with no CO2 controller got a single huge, roughly 4 lb (1.8 kg) "washer" black oyster.
  • Temperament. It is temperamental in the fruit room; farms often call for help when it stops performing.

Harvest, yield and shelf life

  • Time to harvest. About 10-14 days from pins to harvest, similar to cold oysters. In a liquid-culture trial at a partner farm, fruit developed fast and were ready about 4-5 days after pinning.

RANGE Pin to harvest is about 10-14 days in the standard profile and about 4-5 days in one partner-farm trial, where pinning itself "took a while". The two figures probably measure from different "pinning" points. Plan on 10-14 days from the first sign of pinning.

  • Trial weights. Side-fruited blocks after about 3 weeks of incubation gave 2.58-2.87 lb (1.17-1.30 kg) per block, very consistently. Aerated and plain liquid culture effectively tied: 13.54 vs 13.68 lb (6.14 vs 6.21 kg) per five blocks. Longer incubation plus side fruiting was estimated to add 0.5-1 lb (0.2-0.45 kg) per block over round 1.
  • Pick on time. Harvesting a day late (caps upturning, spores dropping) visibly costs weight.
  • Shelf life. Fairly good if picked before caps flatten; less than king oyster, but a good wholesale mushroom.

Problems

  • Stroma. Second only to blue oyster in Cap n Stem's production. In grain it is hard and appears in older, dense zones. In blocks it shows as very dense, often amber-tinted circular patches that predict poor yield and misshapen fruit. Too much heat or stress triggers it. See oyster stroma.
  • Blotch. Blotch climbs sharply in warm rooms. With an ultrasonic fogger on a 30 min on / 10 min off timer, clusters showed slight cap yellowing and a block near the humidifier succumbed.
  • Rose comb. One G2 lot gave heavy rose comb (lumpy, deformed cap growth) in Rhode Island and excellent fruit in Kentucky. Water quality is blamed almost every time (about 99 times in 100), which is a strong claim; fumes are blamed in other cases (see Chapter 17). Warty caps in very high humidity are a different symptom.

RULE Treat black pearl as a one-flush strain. It grows fast and is tenacious, but don't keep blocks in the room after the first harvest: harvest damage plus water sitting on top leaves a big area of exposed substrate that contaminants are waiting for. If a problem shows up first in one strain, check the whole room and your raw materials, because it can point to a wider problem.

Tips

  • Give it an extra week of incubation: it is cheap insurance for yield.
  • Keep the fruit room at 10-15 °C (the 50s °F) and use fine mist, not coarse fog.
  • Inspect grain for hard, discolored spots before spawning; a stroma spot never reverts.

King oyster (Pleurotus eryngii)

AT A GLANCE A craft crop: excellent shelf life and strong demand, but hard to fruit well. Key numbers:

  • Plan 14-18 days to full colonization; move blocks to fruit as soon as they are colonized.
  • Substrate moisture 62-63% total.
  • Fruit at 10-16 °C (50-60 °F); no trustworthy accounts of good pinning above about 17 °C (63 °F).
  • Bright, even light and cyclic CO2-triggered exhaust.
  • Expect about 2-2.25 lb (0.9-1.0 kg) per block, not the about 4 lb (1.8 kg) of other oysters.

Overview

  • Wild P. eryngii varieties are mostly Mediterranean and North African, associated with carrot-family plants such as giant fennel. King oyster is weakly parasitic on them rather than a pure decomposer.
  • It is huge in Europe and East Asia, grown with slow, "low-and-slow" traditional methods. Trialling many European and Asian strains on Master's Mix would probably turn up a high performer.
  • It is a craft crop, not a "meal ticket": not worth growing without cooling and air handling. It is hard to grow without contamination, blotch and fly problems, which is why black oyster replaced it on many farms.
  • In the kitchen: slice thin on a mandoline and sear like bacon. The texture is rubbery but the flavor excellent. It is a favorite oyster of Cap n Stem's growers, and some prefer it to chestnut.
  • It sells "like hotcakes": there are not enough quality kings on the market, and a uniform, steak-like single mushroom is less intimidating to buyers than clusters.

Strains

  • Conch: from Mushrooms Naturally, popularized on CMGN (an online growers' network); the US standard, still grown more than 2603. It auto-fruits in incubation even in rough conditions, and those deformed fruits usually do not regrow.
  • Mycelia 2603: a messed-up, soggy block left on a countertop lost its first malformed fruits but regrew good ones days later.
  • Siberia: obtained by trade, given to North Spore, since lost.

RANGE Which of Conch and 2603 is more forgiving is unclear. With an excellent process, Conch is judged superior.

  • Kings and chestnut are Cap n Stem's most consistent cultures: no cell-line degradation in cryo or refrigeration, and no odd growth on agar.

Culture and spawn

  • On grain, king mycelium spreads evenly and smoothly and is easy to read. It is less vigorous than blue oyster.
  • Spawn timing is critical. Left 0.5-1 week past full colonization, it consolidates into a brick with some stroma (less than other oysters). Pulled too early, it may die or perform weakly. Too late, it turns leathery and is slow to leap to the substrate.
  • Agar plates left too long form a secondary skin that can be peeled off to reach fresh tissue underneath.
  • At lab and spawn level kings are forgiving, but they expose any off variable (such as moisture) because they need a well-regulated metabolic rate, like maitake and pioppino.

Substrate

  • Before soy-based Master's Mix, kings were hard to fruit consistently. A richer substrate colonizes evenly.
  • Kings like relatively high moisture: 62-63% total in a pellet mix. Wetter blocks leak more liquid into the bag.
  • Orange metabolites (coloured liquid) on king substrate or spawn signal mycelium straining against dry clumps or dense kernels. Aim for homogeneous moisture.
  • Low spawn rates lengthen colonization and dramatically cut yield in less voracious species like kings. Stick to industry-standard rates and shake the spawn into the substrate thoroughly.

Incubation

  • Plan 14-18 days to full colonization. Some blocks finish in 10; three weeks is the outside, often caused by poor spawn distribution.
  • Colonization spreads as dense, expanding circles from each grain. Like pioppino, it looks patchy before the circles join.
  • Blocks left too long form a thin, shiny skin on all sides. In typical incubation (high CO2, diffuse light), pins come only after the skin forms, which is best avoided. Freshly colonized blocks, not ones held long in a cooler, give an even pin set.

Fruiting

Fruiting is the hard part.

Setting Value Conditions
Temperature 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) ideal Above 16 °C (60 °F) expect blotch, overlay and humidity trouble; no trustworthy accounts of good pinning above about 17 °C (63 °F). Cooler rooms give darker, granite-speckled caps
Light Bright, deep and even Strongly light-triggered
Humidity Relatively high and steady Raise it when blocks are stripped, because they lose more water
Air exchange Enough to keep air clean, not rapid; exhaust run in cycles from a CO2 controller Not continuous

Opening systems.

  • Common systems: pins form inside the bag after a few cuts at the top or bottom, or the top is cut off after pins form, leaving a plastic collar.
  • Fruit from the top centre. Unlike pioppino, side growth is unwanted.
  • Collar failure. Condensation forms where warm substrate meets cooler incoming air and runs down into the pins, flooding them. Workaround: make small slits (for example under the patch) before opening. The collar is the hardest method, though many think it the safest.

Light. King oyster is strongly light-triggered, like its cousin P. nebrodensis and like beech (shimeji). One large Agaricus farm uses long, very bright lights; Japanese farms and Mycopia run blue tube lights along the rows. Depth and evenness of light matter more than its direction. Even, intense light gives uniform round caps; uneven light gives fluted, sideways caps.

CO2. Run the exhaust from a CO2 controller in cycles, not continuously. Bleached, crusty, flat beige caps mean too much CO2 and too little light.

RANGE Recommended: cyclic, CO2-triggered air exchange. It works like a "lung" of evaporation and condensation; constant fresh-air exchange strips the room and leaves RH flat at around 80-85%, and no grower is known to have succeeded with kings under constant fresh-air exchange. Many other growers run constant exhaust instead.

Other proven methods.

  • Big-room method: one large Agaricus farm grows kings in big Agaricus rooms with heavy insulation and a large HVAC unit feeding a perforated duct, giving barely perceptible, mostly recirculated air. There is no active humidifier (wet wood and concrete supply moisture) and no blotch. The bag is cut off just below the filter once pins appear.

  • Stripped-block method: fully colonized bags go into the room; when pin clusters appear, the bag is removed entirely and the block set on a shelf. This gives scattered, moderate mushrooms and no water pooling. A good catch-all for a cold, all-purpose room.

  • Tray method: about six colonized blocks of one phenotype packed into a busboy tray, with one crumbled block between them, cased about 3 in (7.5 cm) deep with peat and high-calcium, low-magnesium hydrated lime. It gives beautiful single mushrooms but needs high labor and yields poorly.

  • Light-and-cooling chamber: before Cap n Stem had a fruit room, a chamber with intense light and air conditioning down to about 4 °C (40 °F) was lowered over racks of kings (no controlled trial).

  • Caves: cave growing in France and elsewhere gives beautiful kings: headroom, natural humidity, no engineered air exchange.

  • Bottles: bottle growing with surface scratching (kinkake) gives one opening for gas and light, which makes induction easier.

  • Kings need to be "super wet, but dry": very high humidity with zero condensation. A tiny change in the room and kings are "freaked out till the end". One New Hampshire grower sometimes lowers the humidity in a king room even when it already reads dry.

Harvest, yield and shelf life

  • Even with everything right, expect about 2-2.25 lb (0.9-1.0 kg) per block (block size not stated, presumably 10 lb / 4.5 kg), not the about 4 lb (1.8 kg) of other oysters. Mycopia, which grows in bottles, treats a third of a pound (about 0.15 kg) per bottle as a good crop.
  • Long shelf life: kings store very well.

Problems

  • Blotch. Cap n Stem's own first blotch was on kings, before soy entered their substrate. Watch cap tops and streaking stems. Blotch stays where water sits on stripped blocks. One strain may be hit and not another. See Chapter 17.

  • Over-ventilation. Early failures came from poor humidification and too much airflow: 250 CFM (425 m³/h) fans running constantly, with no CO2 meters.

  • Warty caps appear in very high humidity; this is distinct from rose comb.

  • Kings don't suit straw. A New York farm's early king attempts on straw logs in a basement went badly; Cap n Stem knows only one grower who grew kings on straw logs, and he moved to cottonseed hulls. The same farm learned much of its king technique from Korean videos online, by watching the farm equipment in the background.

Tips

  • Fruit cold (10-15 °C, the 50s °F), bright and evenly lit, with cyclic CO2 control.
  • Move blocks to fruit as soon as they are colonized; do not let them skin over.
  • Shake spawn into the substrate thoroughly and keep spawn rates at standard levels.

Pink and golden oyster (P. djamor, P. citrinopileatus)

AT A GLANCE Little detailed data exists for these two. Treat them like other oysters, but store cultures in sterile water (they do not survive cryo), and put golden oyster at the top of the rack.

Detailed growing data for these species is thin.

  • They share Pleurotus biology and differ mainly in colour and temperature preference.
  • History. In 1963 Bano and Srivastava used Pleurotus flabellatus (a pink oyster now placed in P. djamor) and P. sajor-caju on paddy straw in large Indian field plots.
  • Culture storage. Pink and yellow (golden) oyster do not survive cryo. Sterile-water storage of agar plugs is the best option for them (see Chapter 8).
  • Light and rack position. Golden oysters seem to respond more to light and go toward the top of the rack. In practice they are often seen on the middle shelf of a mixed room (not the ideal), beside comb tooth. Golden primordia look coral-like on the blocks.
  • Opening. Golden oyster is side-fruited at Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan).
  • Strains. High Country Fungi (Avery) grows Cap n Stem's house pink and gold strains and calls gold "anti-cancer"; that health claim is unproven.
  • Invasiveness. Golden oyster is invasive in places; work on sporeless or low-spore strains is planned.
  • Breeding. Yellow oyster is one of the species clusters (with blue oyster and shiitake) whose monokaryons (single-nucleus cultures) Cap n Stem encourages growers to remix into new breeding lines.
  • Peroxide tolerance. A cited study (unnamed) tested about 16-17 Pleurotus strains, including pink and yellow, for hydrogen peroxide tolerance. The onset of cell death was quoted at 0.025 and an ideal dose near 0.001, as fractions; the conversions given for these were inconsistent, so treat the numbers as unconfirmed.

Growing in the heat: start with pinks. A Memphis grower's first space was a passive solar greenhouse he "couldn't keep below like 90 or 80" (27-32 °C), yet he was "cranking oysters out of it". Asked about shiitake at those temperatures, Cap n Stem's answer was "I don't know if you really want to grow shiitake right now". It has this talk with new customers every week: people in hot places see photos and assume they can grow anything, but controlling temperature, humidity and air exchange in heat needs "a substantial capital investment". The short answer is "grow some pinks, man".

  • Golden (yellow) oyster is "a fast, warm one", and it is now found growing wild in many places, which one grower takes as a sign of warming climates.
  • The drawback is shelf life. Pinks and goldens "look pretty, but they don't hold up in the pan", and old pinks smell bad in the bin. One market seller used them mostly for display and steered customers to blue and king oysters, which "hold up nice".
  • A Pennsylvania grower started with golden oysters on straw, grown from liquid culture with his own spawn.

Lion's mane (Hericium erinaceus)

AT A GLANCE Grown on nearly every farm, but fickle: it reacts first to any farm-wide fault. Key numbers:

  • Grain moisture uniform at about 46% (oats about 56%); one dry kernel can make it stop and pin.
  • Spawn rate 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 (acceptable 12-30).
  • Block incubation about 12 days (workable 10-18); keep spawn and blocks dim and temperature steady.
  • Fruit at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F), sweet spot about 16 °C (60 °F) for HeCNS; RH upper 80s to low 90s %.
  • Exhaust on above about 800 ppm, off at about 450 ppm.
  • Two flushes: about 2 lb then 1.5 lb (0.9 then 0.7 kg).

Overview

  • Lion's mane is grown for flavor, gourmet and medicinal appeal and eye-catching looks. Nearly every farm grows it, and its total cycle time can approach that of oysters. It is fickle and needs consistent attention.

  • Hericium species differ mainly in shape; lion's mane and comb tooth are treated nearly identically in culture. Three wild northern Hericium are H. erinaceus (lion's mane), H. americanum (bear's head) and H. coralloides (comb tooth).

  • An indicator species. A farm-wide problem (pasteurization, moisture consistency, temperature, light, a mold source) may show only on lion's mane while hardier species out-compete it. Do not blame the culture first.

  • In the wild it is rare in cold Maine and more common in Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut, growing in tree knots and wounds. It has been seen growing together with bear's head.

  • Medicinal notes (growers' lay understanding, not established findings): two classes of small compounds (probably hericenones and erinacines) are said to cross the blood-brain barrier and support nerve-growth-related activity. Whether late flushes keep these compounds is an open question.

  • Business uses. It is very popular in Tampa / St Pete, where one grower helped launch food trucks selling vegan "wings" and sandwiches. Chefs' offcuts can become crab-cake-style patties. A lion's mane coffee was sold as a side product. Free trial samples are the main sales tactic. A pound (0.45 kg) is roughly a softball-sized piece. See Chapter 22.

  • Even blocks that do not fruit can be made into mycelium tinctures.

  • A New Hampshire farm takes its lion's mane (strain "129") from lab to picking in 19 days, at "almost 100%" biological efficiency, all year round. The grower says he found the method by accident, when he thought he had made a mistake, and that no book describes it.

  • Lion's mane is a West Virginia farm's biggest earner, because of its shelf life and because it dries well.

Strains

Strain Origin Behavior
HeCNS (the Leighton Banks strain) A wild clone gifted to Cap n Stem (Sagadahoc County, Maine, is referenced); claimed to be one of the two most widely grown US strains; sold under many names (for example "Tree Beard") because spawn companies rename strains Compact pom-pom fruit with tiny spines; multiple decent flushes; holds up to handling and cold storage; the new benchmark for wholesale yield; prefers slightly cooler conditions than Pow
Pow / HePow The other heavy-hitting commercial strain Tolerates slightly warmer conditions; good wholesale yield but less dense, spinier fruit
"Lion's Pride" / HELP Thought to be a Leighton isolate naturalized in the US South Tolerates heat and humidity; a forgiving "fail-safe" strain, but lower fruit quality at Cap n Stem
129 (Northwest Mycological) Cap n Stem's first strain Tough and less fickle; lower yield
9514 (Mycelia) Similar to 129
  • A strain map of the main commercial lines groups Leighton (HeCNS), Pow and HELP as the three to know.
  • A "house CNS blue" strain (name unclear) also appears in comb tooth work.
  • Lion's mane cultures rarely senesce. Failures are contamination or fruiting too early. A wild isolate found on a beach colonized Master's Mix but would not fruit.

Culture

  • Cryo. Rye grains colonized just past the berry, about 3 mL of 10% v/v glycerol per vial, stored at −80 °C (−112 °F), thawed in a 30 °C (86 °F) water bath. Comfortable for about 2-3 years. One crew at the same farm uses 5% glycerol.

RANGE Cryoprotectant: 10% v/v glycerol is used most often (lion's mane, black oyster, chestnut); 5% is also used at the same farm (lion's mane, shiitake). Storage: 2-3 years is reported as comfortable for lion's mane, while general advice elsewhere is to refresh cultures every 6-12 months. See Chapter 8.

  • Carrier quality. Thin, delicate Hericium mycelium needs well-hydrated, fully colonized rye carriers. Poor revival usually traces back to how the sample was prepared.
  • Agar. Use malt yeast agar for all Hericium. Activated charcoal (or blue dye) in the agar makes the faint, nearly transparent mycelium visible. Hold plates up to the light.
  • Plate timing. Plates reach the edge in about 1.5-2 weeks after a lag. Fresh plates sit 3-5 days in the flow hood at about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), then move to 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). Agar should run warmer than grain or blocks, because small plates do not self-heat; about 21 °C (70 °F) is noted as ideal, with 18 °C (65 °F) and 20 °C (68 °F) also noted for agar (unconfirmed which applies).
  • Fruiting on plates. Lion's mane often tries to fruit on the plate; such plates are still usable if you cut from the outer edge. Left too long on agar or in liquid culture it forms fruit bodies, even pushing past the plate film. An aged plate looks covered in fluff clusters with small fruit bodies forming.
  • Liquid culture. Many growers use liquid culture for lion's mane (it thrives and darkens the broth); Cap n Stem sticks with agar.

Spawn

  • Grain type. Lion's mane is the exception to the house mix of 3 rye : 1 sorghum. Oats hold more water and give dense white mycelium, "almost like an oyster bag".
  • Grain moisture. Oats at about 56%, or grain tuned to a stable about 46% from kernel to kernel. Low-40s % is too dry: slow, wispy growth, more contamination and more auto-fruiting. One dry kernel can make it stop and pin.

RANGE Target grain moisture: about 56% on oats, or a stable about 46% throughout (the grain type may differ between the two); oats near 60% with 55% used is also reported (see Chapter 9). Uniform hydration matters more than the exact number.

  • G1. A 4 lb (1.8 kg) bag with two 1 cm squares (four if rushed). Week 1 shows nearly nothing. Shake when the colony covers about half a face. It is fully colonized but wispy about a week later (about 2 weeks total).
  • G2. One master into 12 × 6 lb (2.7 kg) bags; 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) for 1.5-2 weeks, nearly as fast as oysters. Ship or refrigerate at about 2 weeks.
  • Longer incubation. Cap n Stem deliberately incubates lion's mane grain longer than many growers, who ship at the first sign of density or primordia.
  • Cold storage. Spawn still tries to fruit in cold storage: keep it no more than about 2 weeks and monitor it. Small Hericium primordia melt back into the mycelium, but heavy auto-fruiting makes spawn slow to re-establish.
  • Bag top. Folding the bag top over the filter patch keeps growth vegetative and stops dry tops.
  • Light. Lion's mane pins on light before the mycelium is fully dense, so keep spawn near dark and blocks dim. Constant lights in spawn incubation made it pin earlier. Motion-sensor lights were tried, but a sudden bright flash is also a strong trigger, so the compromise is dim, indirect light.

Substrate

  • Recipe. Commercially grown on Master's Mix (50:50) in 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks for yield, but margins are finer. Dropping soy to about 30-40% is suggested as a better range: rich mixes give yellow liquid and inconsistent fruit, while leaner ones colonize slower but more vigorously. Farms with unstable incubation might use a shiitake-style wheat bran / rice bran mix.
  • Moisture. Above about 62%, water pools at the bottom of the block. One farm cut moisture to about 56% without benefit, because the real problem was sawdust arriving at about 70% moisture. Lion's mane is hydration-sensitive.
  • Spawn rate. 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2, about 0.3 lb (0.14 kg) of grain per block; acceptable 12-30. Below 12 blocks per bag overloads an already rich substrate; above 30 raises mold risk. Over-spawning adds heat and bacteria (dark wet spots around the inoculation points).
  • Pasteurization. A paper on bacterial communities in wild versus cultivated H. erinaceus suggests pasteurization (rather than sterilization) may suit lion's mane (one grower's reading).

Incubation

  • Appearance. Block colonization looks ghostly and faint, like a slight opaque discoloration.

RANGE Plan 12 days before shipping, workable 10-18 days. Blocks have also been fully colonized in about 10 days, and in another case were still under-colonized at one week and shipped the following week (about 2 weeks).

  • Speed and temperature. Speed sits between oysters and slower species like chestnut. It likes steady temperature; keep mycelial temperatures from running high.

  • Easily triggered. Light, temperature swings or low moisture easily make it abort colonization and pin.

  • Ready cue. A marshmallowy pillow of aerial mycelium forms on top where room light hits. A bag shrunk tight against the block (a "synthetic log") also signals readiness.

  • Top fruiting. It tends to colonize lightly and fruit on top of the bag, because a large patch and headspace give more gas exchange.

  • Yellow liquid. A fully colonized white block may have yellow liquid pooled at the bag bottom (see problems).

  • Perspiring bags. Bags that perspire heavily early in colonization predict contamination.

  • With super spawn (see Chapter 9) and a good strain, a West Virginia grower cuts his lion's mane bags on day 10, and "at the end of week three with lions, if my grow room temperatures are right, I'm harvesting". His favourite strain is ready every 10-12 days "like clockwork", makes few metabolites, doesn't pin early, pins on top, and is pure white, not bitter and keeps well.

Fruiting

Setting Value Conditions
Temperature 13-18 °C (55-65 °F); sweet spot about 16 °C (60 °F) for HeCNS Too hot means more bacteria and a harder RH / fresh-air balance
Relative humidity Upper 80s to low 90s % A little lower than oysters; too high gives uneven spines; swings help even spine development
CO2, recommended Exhaust on above about 800 ppm, off at about 450 ppm
CO2, alternative On at 900, off at 600-700 ppm Used at one customer farm
Light Solid ambient full-spectrum light Improves pin set; less light-dependent than maitake
Rack Top of the rack, above (never below) shiitake Shiitake drips brown exudate that stains the white fruit

RANGE CO2 band: 800 ppm on / 450 ppm off recommended; 900 on / 600-700 off also works. Both keep the swing to a few hundred ppm. A 1,500-to-600 ppm band, or a fan outage, gives "dreadlocks" (uneven maturity), which recover within about a day once fixed.

  • When and how to cut. Pull blocks at the pillowy stage and make a long shallow slit or X across the top; side slits are also used. Cut well into the block to scar the outer mat. Unlike pioppino, do not wait for pins and cut around them. Cutting too late gives malformed fruit inside the bag; too early raises contamination risk.
  • Cut layout. Large farms use four side cuts for smaller, consistent fruit that suits packaging. Home growers top-fruit for one big flush plus smaller ones. A paddle studded with arrow tips was once used to "spank" blocks for many small fruits.
  • High CO2 (for example fruiting in a bag with only one corner open) gives coral-like, reaching fruit that cooks floppy.
  • Odd shapes. Popcorn- or cauliflower-like forms come from off or inconsistent conditions. Pink or yellow tints on young fruit mostly mean the room is too dry.
  • In-bag fruiting for drying or extracts. Blocks take about 1 month to auto-fruit in the bag; bags with the more open B patch gave more fruit. Harvest after 1.5-2 weeks, or break the fruit off and let it go again.
  • A working room. A typical lion's mane room has side-cut blocks, a wall-mounted CO2 controller and an exhaust fan. A good HeCNS (Leighton) block carries several large, compact pom-poms.

Harvest, yield and shelf life

  • Time. Slow in the fruit room: 14-20 days to harvest in rooms at about 16-17 °C (low 60s °F). The cue is even spine elongation. Commercially it is picked well before full maturity.
  • Flushes. One customer farm flushes every species once except lion's mane, which gets two: about 2 lb then 1.5 lb (0.9 then 0.7 kg), block size presumably 10 lb (4.5 kg). Years ago, pre-soy 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks gave about 0.5 lb (0.23 kg). A compost customer got 11 flushes (unconfirmed).
  • In-bag yield. 50 auto-fruited blocks gave about 122 lb (55 kg) fresh and about 13.3 lb (6.0 kg) dry: about 0.27 lb (0.12 kg) dry per block, 10-11% of fresh weight.
  • Quality. HeCNS fruit is dense, with short, non-drooping spines, and holds up post-harvest, but the tissue is water-laden and bruises easily.

Problems

  • Hidden Trichoderma. Trichoderma (green mold) hides in the faint early colonization as slightly denser matting in a different off-white, until it sporulates green. Wispy mycelium in dry media is "a net with big holes". See Chapter 16.

  • Yellow liquid at the bag bottom with rich 50:50 substrate. Working hypothesis: hot cores wake bacterial endospores, followed by wet anaerobic conditions and defensive metabolites.

  • Blotch. Slow fruiting exposes it to blotch. Black slime on stems is probably a different bacterium. One grower's blotch and malformation vanished when they switched from constant to cyclic, CO2-triggered air exchange.

  • Agar slurry inoculation failed.

  • "Bridging". Lion's mane sometimes pulls away from the block, forming a bridge, and a 1.4 kg (3 lb) head can fall off. In outdoor autumn trials it began "once the relative humidity dropped and you started to get that big day-night cycle"; the grower thinks it is temperature-driven. Comb tooth and bear's head "want to hold on" with a big trunk into the cut. He prefers top fruiting to side cuts.

Tips

  • Keep spawn and blocks dim and temperature steady: light and swings make it pin early.
  • Cut at the pillowy stage, decisively and into the mat.
  • For mixed retail clamshells, many small clusters beat one big "brain".

Comb tooth (Hericium coralloides)

AT A GLANCE Handled like lion's mane, but denser, better-behaved as spawn and more tolerant of warmth. Key numbers: Master's Mix at 61-62% final moisture, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain bag per twenty 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks, fruit preferably at about 19-21 °C (upper 60s °F).

Overview

  • Comb tooth behaves like lion's mane but colonizes denser and auto-fruits later, so it is better behaved as spawn.
  • Form. It grows out as a column, then branches repeatedly like Romanesco cauliflower, with teeth hanging underneath. The heads are dense, central and cloud-like; spinier and less "tentacled" than lion's mane.
  • Season. Wild season is August-October in the northern hemisphere; it fruits better in warm months.
  • Market. Supplement and extract companies increasingly use it, possibly because its spawn stays vegetative. Cap n Stem produces little so far; markets for wild-type shapes are still being worked out. It sells as a crab-cake substitute.

Strains

  • HcFF, originally a wild collection from Denmark. It is stable, very vigorous and high-yielding, with high-quality fruit, and keeps producing in warmer, varied conditions where lion's mane strains taper off. More farms are adopting it.
  • Label grain bags with species, generation, date, strain code and bag number, for example "Comb Tooth G1 121323-HCFF-2".

Culture and spawn

  • Agar. Malt yeast agar is preferred. Growth is visible in about 3 days; a full plate takes about 2-2.5 weeks (3-3.5 weeks if cool). The mycelium is faint and wispy with cord-like veins. Plates go to the fridge or into production at about 1 cm from the edge.
  • Grain master. 3 rye : 1 sorghum, or pure millet (preferred, because it keeps spreading and fruits later). Two 1 cm cuttings; leave 1-1.5 weeks, shake, then 1-1.5 weeks more.
  • G2. One master to twelve 6 lb (2.7 kg) bags; no lag; about 2-2.5 weeks. Stop at about 2 weeks if refrigerating. Do not sell spawn that is auto-fruiting. It only auto-fruits once fully colonized, about half a week later than lion's mane.
  • Grain moisture. Uniform moisture (about 46%) matters as much as for lion's mane.

Substrate

  • Recipe. It needs balanced carbon and nitrogen: straight combo pellets, 50:50 soy hulls to sawdust (60:40 is also called ideal; the wording was ambiguous).
  • Moisture. Target 61-62% final moisture, allowing for the roughly 7% moisture already in the pellets. Above about 62%, water pools in Hericium blocks.
  • Spawn rate. 1:20, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain bag per twenty 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks.
  • Watering rig. Cap n Stem hydrates pellets on an in-house rig: a row of bag stations on load cells, with solenoid water lines filling dry pellets to a weight target. See Chapter 10.

Incubation

  • It is much denser and firmer than lion's mane: a block knocked 2 days later was further colonized than a lion's mane block.
  • Incubation room fans blow air at about 18 °C (64-65 °F) to hold block exteriors at 19 °C (66 °F).

Fruiting, harvest and problems

  • Opening. Handled like lion's mane: fold the bag over and cut an X, straight slit or H; or leave it in the bag to fruit from the top uncut. Slow to start, then it "combs out" fast.
  • Temperature. Prefers 19-21 °C (upper 60s °F); tolerates 10-15 °C (the 50s °F).
  • Airflow indicator. Comb tooth browns in too much air and goes popcorny in stagnant air. See Chapter 14.
  • Harvest. "Fractalization" (the branching phase) lasts about 5-7 days. Mature fruit droops and turns spongy and cauliflower-like, so pick before that.
  • Room layout. Blocks lie on their sides on wire shelving, often beside golden oysters; harvested heads are large, white and coral-like, packed in boxes.
  • Problems. One grower has seen no blotch, Trichoderma or odd growth; an occasional patch fails to fractalize. It is hardy, dependable and liked by retail and wholesale customers.

Shiitake (Lentinula edodes)

AT A GLANCE The easiest mushroom to fruit and the hardest to incubate. Key numbers for a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block:

  • Lean substrate: 70-80% hardwood sawdust, 20-30% wheat bran or midds; moisture 64-65%.
  • Spawn rate 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 (about 2.5% spawn).
  • Incubate at about 19 °C (66 °F) room air; keep cores at or below about 23 °C (74 °F).
  • About 12 weeks (6-14 depending on strain) through three phases: spawn run, buckling, browning; light is required.
  • Fruit at 75-80% brown or more; harvest about 6-8 days after stripping the bag.
  • Yield 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg) per block. Wear a respirator when harvesting.

Overview

  • Shiitake is the easiest mushroom to fruit and the hardest to incubate: roughly half the skill is incubation and half is fruiting and handling.
  • It has one of the longest incubations (about 6-14 weeks) but fruits within about a week once triggered. It needs roughly 5-10 times the incubation space of fast species for the same output. Plan the incubation room accordingly (see Chapter 3).
  • Scale. Historically it is big: easily 50% or more of production at Cascadia Mushrooms, and over half of fruiting at another farm.
  • History. Shiitake on logs is often cited as the earliest cultivated mushroom. Folk stories tell of beating spore-laden logs beside fresh ones (half-joke oral history). A Maine log grower is said to have sold about $40,000 at one fair weekend (unconfirmed).
  • Market. Markets flooded with cheap imported shiitake push some growers toward niche species.
  • Reading. John Donahue's out-of-print Shiitake Growers Handbook (about 1988-89) is rated a top-five cultivation read. Stamets' Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms covers pinning before browning, then second-flushing after browning. See Chapter 23.
  • Grades. Japan grades shiitake into about 30 grades (also quoted as about 40).

Shiitake is a hard crop for small farms.

  • An Oregon farm quit growing shiitake and now buys it in: "It's a lot of space, a lot of time, a lot of cooling. I want nothing to do with it anymore." It plans to simplify like "all the old farmers": grow one or two things well and sell the same thing every week.
  • A Washington farm's business was started, and its first profits paid, by shiitake strain 3782, but "shiitake is now the least profitable" of its eight species in today's market. Early on it sold shiitake at US$3.50 a pint at markets before learning that others got about US$20 a pound.
  • A West Virginia farm's high-yield strain gives about 3.5 lb (1.6 kg) a block but takes about six weeks to colonize plus about three weeks in the grow room. Limited incubation space is "my biggest weak point... that's why I don't grow shiitake", even though wholesale is US$12-14 a pound and demand is high. Shiitake at scale needs "a lot of incubation space" and "dialed in heating and air conditioning control and lighting".

Strains

Strain Origin Behavior

3782 Mycelia; a cousin of 3790 A "revolution" around 2013-14 (1+ lb / 0.45 kg from a 5 lb / 2.3 kg raw oak and bran block); a forgiving "training wheels" strain, tolerant of moisture and heat; fruits from about 10 °C to 27 °C (50-80 °F); carpets of many small, thin caps; suits farms running around 29 °C (85 °F). On 10 lb ultra-pasteurized blocks it gave tiny "paper pins" and only moderate yield, which pushed farms to 3790
321 John Donahue / Northwest Mycological; Cascadia's strain Average 12-week colonization; very pretty gourmet fruit; low yield; still in use
"Straw" Said to come from Aloha Medicinals Common in the late 2000s; occasional 1 lb (0.45 kg) flushes from a 5 lb block, but thousands of blocks with none; one grower is breeding from it again
