  • Mycelia offers about nine shiitake strains and has been trying a 3782 × 3790 cross (results doubtful).

  • In short: 3782 gives small, plentiful mushrooms at moderate yield; 3790 gives fewer, medium-large mushrooms, also rated moderate yield on a side-by-side comparison.

  • Hot-weather strains are touchy. The warm-fruiting strains (3782 and 3790) are very sensitive: a temperature change of just 1-3 °C (2-5 °F) gives big differences in mushroom shape, or no fruiting at all. A Washington grower let 3790 get too hot in incubation and saw exactly this, and an Oregon grower found 3782 and 3790 "buckled" heavily in his incubation.

  • NMC 321 gives beautiful, high-quality mushrooms but low and inconsistent yields: 0.5-0.75 lb (0.2-0.35 kg) a block for one Washington grower, sometimes over-pinning, and poor yield after 12-14 weeks for another. A third Oregon grower got about a pound a block, and it kept about three weeks.

  • 3782 gives far higher yields but thin, fleshy mushrooms with poorer shelf life; one grower's customers asked him to call when he had "the normal ones".

  • KOM "is literally the [best]... cold weather, warm weather, too dry, too wet, not enough light. It doesn't matter, it just grows mushrooms." Even a set soaked too wet, with the bottom half rotted, browned on top and fruited. It is available from Cap n Stem.

  • A small-fruited shiitake strain from John Holliday (not Shiitake 75) "made lots of mushrooms" and covered the blocks.

NOTE Shiitake mycelium on agar plates can look like cobweb mould. Don't throw a plate out on looks alone.

Culture

  • Agar. Mycelium on agar is faint and loose. Charcoal malt yeast agar gives contrast. Malt suits slow strains because its nutrients release slowly.
  • Plate timing. A plate fills in about 3-4 weeks (as little as 3), faster at 25-27 °C (high 70s to 80 °F). Transfer at about 1 cm from the edge. A white inner secondary ring that later browns marks an ageing plate.
  • Storage. Sterile-water storage of agar plugs kept shiitake "pretty stable" over months. Glycerol above about 25-30% is reported in the literature to kill shiitake cells. See Chapter 8.
  • What does not work yet. Slurry inoculation gave only scattered fuzzy spots; de-dikaryotization trials for shiitake were still pending.

Spawn

  • Expansion. Slow strains get four agar cuttings per 4 lb (1.8 kg) master, so 6-8 masters per plate. Each master goes to 12 G2 bags, each G2 to 20 blocks.
  • G2 timing. 3-4 weeks: white dots by day 4-5, threads over the bag by 1.5-2 weeks, then it densifies. Yellow metabolites on older grain are normal. Finished spawn holds together as a firm brick when squeezed.
  • Auto-fruiting. Popcorning or buckling on spawn means it is heading toward fruiting. Once shiitake switches to fruiting it will not return to spreading, so spawn with fruit is never shipped. Store finished spawn at about 2 °C (35 °F) before it popcorns.
  • Conditions. Avoid strong light and big temperature swings in spawn incubation.

Substrate

  • Supplementation. Shiitake needs less supplement than most species: 20-30% wheat bran or midds (rice bran elsewhere) and 70-80% hardwood sawdust. Over-supplementing gives lower yield, uneven browning and unreliable pinning: "less is more". This is one of the most consistent rules for shiitake.
  • Cap n Stem 10 lb (4.5 kg) block. 70% red oak sawdust, 30% wheat (ground wheat, midds or bran), water only; mixed by folding, not shaking. The old 5 lb (2.3 kg) recipe was about 25% wheat midds and 75% raw red oak, ultra-pasteurized. Combo pellets come in a 70:30 wheat-midds blend for shiitake.
  • Soy. Master's Mix is a poor fit. Soy-based mixes work only at drastically reduced levels. Midds shortages pushed growers to try soy, with mixed success. Reduced-soy blocks can give amazing yield and speed but run "hot".

RANGE Recommended: hardwood sawdust with 20-30% wheat midds or bran. Combo pellets may not be optimal for shiitake, yet growers in the western US run 100% Douglas fir pellet substrates even for shiitake without problems, and some farms use fir pellets.

  • Wood. Oak is safest ("shiitake" means oak mushroom); alder and mixed hardwoods are also used. Red oak is less dense and releases nutrients faster than white oak, which suits long-term logs. Aged sawdust from the back of a pile suited shiitake while other species did poorly on it.
  • Raw sawdust varies (fresh, aged or composted; moisture, tannin, pH, C:N ratio), producing a "sine wave" of yields that is worst in the shoulder seasons. Wood chips had to be sifted out because shiitake could not colonize hard, dry chips. See Chapter 10.
  • Moisture. 64-65% total for shiitake, versus 62-63% for most species. Above about 68%, expect free water and bacteria. Red oak can arrive at 70-80% moisture. A wetter block offsets drying through the patch over the long incubation.
  • Cooking. Two methods work for shiitake. Many growers find it does better under pressure, sterilized or by a "quasi-pressure" middle method that gives consistently productive blocks and better browning: bring the vessel to 15 psi (1 bar / 103 kPa) with block cores at 93-100 °C (200-212 °F), shut the steam off, and leave it sealed overnight or until the pressure falls. Cap n Stem ultra-pasteurizes instead, at 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for 3 hours (a cycle of about 10 hours in total), with good results. Overcooking in big autoclaves caramelizes the substrate. See Chapter 12.

RANGE Cooking: both methods are in use, so trial both on a few blocks. Many growers get better shiitake from sterilization or the quasi-pressure method; ultra-pasteurization at 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) held for 3 hours works well at Cap n Stem. Blocks are described as sitting in loose steam for "about 10 hours", which is most likely the total cycle time rather than the hold.

  • Block size and bag. 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks in XLS-A bags are the farm standard (some run 12 lb / 5.4 kg). 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks are far more forgiving if incubation temperature is unsteady. Unicorn's A patch was designed for slow shiitake.
  • Spawn rate. 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2; the substrate gets only about 2.5% spawn.

Incubation

Shiitake incubation has three phases: the spawn run to a white block, buckling (also called popcorning), and browning.

Phase 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, standard guide 10 lb block, Cap n Stem 5 lb (2.3 kg) block What drives it
Spawn run to white Weeks 1-2 (2-3 also quoted) Weeks 1-4 wispy colonization Weeks 1-2 Temperature; the hottest, highest-CO2 phase
Densification / buckling Weeks 3-5 Weeks 4-8 densification Weeks 3-4 Temperature and airflow
Browning Weeks 5-13 Weeks 8-12 popcorn, buckling and browning; pins in weeks 11-12 Weeks 5-8 (to 10) Temperature, airflow and light
Total 6-14 weeks depending on strain About 12 weeks; a data-logger example ran about 3 months

Another version used at Cap n Stem: colonize weeks 1-4, popcorn weeks 5-8, brown weeks 7-12.

RANGE For a 10 lb block, plan on about 12 weeks. The spawn run is quoted as 1-2 weeks, 2-3 weeks, or weeks 1-4; buckling as weeks 3-5, 4-8 or 5-8. The differences come mostly from strain and from where one phase is said to end.

Temperature.

Setting Value Conditions
Room, 10 lb blocks About 19 °C (66 °F) The consistent recommendation
Room, 5 lb blocks About 20-21 °C (upper 60s to 70 °F) 5 lb blocks tolerate it
Core temperature limit At or below about 23 °C (74 °F) Above about 24 °C (75 °F), thermophilic bacterial endospores that survived ultra-pasteurization take hold
Core above room 2-3 °C (4-6 °F) hotter, and up to 4-5 °C (8-9 °F) at metabolic spikes Measure with a data logger inside a block

CO2.

  • Room CO2 ideal about 2,500 ppm, maximum 5,000 ppm. CO2 inside the bag is much higher; shiitake tolerates up to about 20,000 ppm inside Tyvek-patch bags.
  • A farm whose incubation CO2 sat at about 500 ppm (its HVAC was shared with other rooms) got patchy, splotchy, desiccated blocks.
  • Temperature, metabolism and CO2 feed each other. Correcting high CO2 by dropping the temperature shocks the block and can trigger in-bag pinning.

Light. Light drives buckling and browning; blocks kept dark barely brown. Use 6,500 K all-spectrum light (Far East practice uses red). If you cannot see into the centre of a rack well enough to spot contamination, there is not enough light. Place lights in the aisles, pointing inward.

Buckling. Buckling is a stress response that forms a protective skin. The brown, leathery skin is only on the outside (the inside stays white), and it is what lets shiitake fruit from all over the block. Where blocks touch, the patch neither buckles nor fruits, so space every block.

Airflow and racks.

  • Too much airflow (lab-like gushing) seems to harm buckling. Give gentle air on all sides of every block.
  • The interior of racks is hardest to ventilate; rack centres run about a week behind the edges. Once most blocks are about 90% brown, fruit them all.
  • Racks about 48 in (1.2 m) wide and 10 ft (3 m) tall, about 5 blocks across, with lit aisles on both sides. Overstuffing lowers output. An overloaded room (one 7.5-ton (26 kW) unit for 4,500 sq ft (418 m²)) browned well only a third of the way up.

Shocks. Accidental shocks (AC failure, a temperature drop, bumping blocks, moving shelves) trigger in-bag pinning; move triggered blocks promptly to fruiting or to a cooler. Shiitake suffers first if the HVAC fails.

Readiness.

  • Fruit at 75-80% brown at minimum. 75-80% gives fewer, larger mushrooms; leaving blocks to "120% brown" gives more, smaller ones and sometimes more weight.

  • Blocks ready to ship are fully brown and crumbly, perhaps with a few cap-only pins. Blocks already forming stems are pickup-only.

  • Side by side, a ready block is brown and crumbly with sparse cap pins; a late one is covered in pins and stems.

  • Light drives popcorning. Shiitake blocks tucked in a dark corner browned and popcorned (formed the bumpy surface that precedes browning) only on their lit sides; the back stayed white. Light is "the sole reason popcorning even happens", and it is rarely discussed.

  • A temperature spike two months into incubation makes shiitake pin early inside the bag.

TIP Some growers grow 10 lb (4.5 kg) shiitake blocks and cut them in half once browned, laying each half cut face down, for roughly twice the yield.

Fruiting

CASE Shiitake from imported logs. A Maine farm fruited Chinese shiitake logs that arrived frozen solid in winter. A pallet holds about 700 logs (1,400 when double-stacked) of about 3 lb (1.4 kg) each, and first cost about US$300 (about US$1.35 a log at the time). The first trial yielded only 0.75 lb (0.34 kg) a log. After much trial with thawing and soaking, the farm went from 1.6-1.7 lb (0.73-0.77 kg) a log in 11 days to 1.3-1.4 lb (0.6-0.64 kg) in about 4 days, averaged over 1,500-2,000 logs a day. If it didn't pick 2,000 lb (900 kg) of shiitake in a morning, it asked what had gone wrong the week before.

  • Earlier, its 5 lb (2.3 kg) Cap n Stem blocks were soaked for about two flushes, and strain 3782 gave about 1.5 lb per 4-5 lb block (0.7 kg per 1.8-2.3 kg).
  • Shiitake had to be cut with scissors, which gave staff carpal tunnel, and blocks were "spanked" (slapped) to trigger fruiting.
  • Logs from a Pennsylvania producer browned outside the bag, so there was no bag waste, but they had to be soaked; the farm built a soaking system from IBC totes (1,000 L plastic tanks) lifted by hydraulics.
  • Soaking for extra flushes isn't worth it at scale. A Washington farm was designed for shiitake only: 800 blocks a week, three flushes each over a 12-week fruiting period with soaking between flushes, so its fruiting room was huge compared with incubation. It ran the three-soak cycle once and never again: once you have a mixer and a retort, it is better to make new blocks than soak old ones for "three more mushrooms".

Procedure: fruiting a shiitake block

  1. Check the block is at least 75-80% brown.
  2. Trigger it, within about a day, by one of: moving it straight into fruiting (most common), cold (a cooler), a one-hour water soak (which also rehydrates dry blocks), or physical slapping.
  3. Rinse the block before it goes into the room.
  4. Strip the bag, leaving a rim of bag at the bottom to catch exudate, and flip the block 180 degrees so the wetter bottom is on top.
  5. Set it on slatted shelves, low on the rack, never above lion's mane. Do not spray it regularly.
  6. Expect pins within about 2 days and bursting at 5-7 days; harvest about 6-8 days after stripping.

CHECK Pins develop in stages: white bumps, then brown dots, then separating stems. Dense flushes of caps across the whole block mean the incubation worked.

  • Shock response. Shiitake is the one species that reliably responds to shock, within about a day.

RANGE Strain responses to shock differ (anecdotal): JC fruits harder when beaten, while 3790 responds better to a cooler at Cap n Stem. Separately, cold shock or refrigeration is said to delay 3790 pinning, and holding blocks too long gives malformed fruit in the bag.

  • In-bag pinning trick. Leave the bag on so CO2 builds and fewer, bigger mushrooms form. Remove it after 1-3 days, or caps bruise and puddle.
  • Halving blocks. When cutting blocks in half, cut from top to bottom and lay the cut face down.
  • Speed. Shiitake is fast in the fruit room (with pioppino). Keep it low on racks, ideally fully separate, never above lion's mane.
  • Staggering. Refrigeration lets block sellers hold blocks and stagger fruiting.

Harvest, yield and shelf life

  • Yield. 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block. Strain 3782 gave 1+ lb (0.45 kg) from 5 lb (2.3 kg) raw oak blocks; "Straw" about 1 lb (0.45 kg) on rare blocks.
  • Most common mistake: picking too late. Flat, "broad" caps add weight but collapse quality and shelf life. Pick while the cap rim is still curled.
  • Staffing. Harvest capacity must match the crop. Solo holiday harvests ended with the first rows already opening.
  • Clothing. Juice from stripped blocks stains like walnut ink: wear cheap shirts and work by a drain.

Problems

Symptom Cause Fix

  • Imported logs. Imported Asian substrate logs may carry heavy metals or formaldehyde (unconfirmed).

Tips

  • Hold incubation at 19 °C (66 °F) with steady light and gentle air on all sides of every block.
  • Keep supplementation lean and moisture at 64-65%.
  • Use data loggers inside a block to see real core temperatures across the 3-month run.

Maitake (Grifola frondosa, hen of the woods)

AT A GLANCE Treat maitake as seriously as shiitake: 8-12 weeks to harvest plus about a week, most of it undisturbed incubation, then a dedicated fruit room. Key numbers:

  • Grain spawn at 42-46% moisture with about 6% red oak sawdust.
  • Substrate lean (20-30% supplement) at 60-61% moisture (61% ideal); cooked by the quasi-pressure method, not ultra-pasteurized.
  • Incubate at 19 °C (66 °F), 20 °C (68 °F) maximum; never disturb; cut at the fist-to-fingers stage.
  • Fruit room: its own room, 90-93% RH, lots of 6,500 K light, slow steady air, CO2 below about 1,000 ppm.
  • About 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, one flush.

Overview

  • Maitake went from a rarely grown "white whale" to a widespread small-farm crop in about two years; specific maitake strains are among Cap n Stem's top three spawn sellers. Before that, farms bought it in from large producers.

  • Treat it with the seriousness of shiitake: 8-12 weeks to harvest plus about a week to finish, so learning cycles are slow. Unlike shiitake, it is unforgiving of a botched block, and its phases are less visible than shiitake browning.

  • Protocols are converging (about 90% of farms share the essentials). The main trick is that it does not fruit consistently alongside other species in a crowded mixed room. Growers still disagree strongly on timing.

  • It is naturally a warmer-weather, fall-fruiting species; wild heads reach about 30 lb (14 kg).

  • Shipping blocks to other farms makes little sense given the long, disturbance-sensitive incubation, though some suppliers do it. The bottle-growing industry has moved away from maitake (unconfirmed).

  • Farms to follow: Shogun (a Canadian maitake-only farm) and Woodbloom produce at large scale. Several experienced maitake growers share their methods openly; see Chapter 23.

  • A gap in the market. Few small growers can grow maitake well: "if you're good at something other people aren't, I can pay the electric bill with that". An Ohio farm restarted with 10 maitake blocks a week, raised it to about 40, and only then planned to expand, because "you never have full control, only a little".

  • A Tallahassee farm grows maitake and chestnut at much larger scale, roughly on par with its oyster and lion's mane, so its chef mixes contain mushrooms chefs are excited about rather than "oysters with a half pound of pioppinos in the corner".

  • It takes years to learn. An Oregon farm had "great success and then a lot of issues" with maitake: contamination, yield, recipe changes, people inoculating the wrong thing, black bags used on the oyster mix, and "undersized cooling, not understanding how much humidity that we needed to properly run like our cooling in every space". Like shiitake, it took years to learn its stages. In one strain trial only 2 of 100 blocks fruited; the rest dried out during the browning stage.

  • Catawba Mushrooms (North Carolina) also struggles with maitake: it moved blocks to fruiting too early, and CO2 in incubation was too high.

Strains

  • Mycelia 9827: the most significant strain now, very forgiving, and credited with the boom; Cap n Stem's second most popular strain. All the advice on this card assumes 9827.

  • Shogun: tolerates warmer fruiting than 9827; held in cryo and being expanded.

  • 494 (an old Northwest Mycological strain): inconsistent and behaves differently; other NMC numbers performed badly. An "Oakshire" strain is untested.

  • Import caution. Cultures were once hand-carried from Mycelia without phytosanitary papers on advice from a Mycelia contact; this was an illegal import, so do not copy it. About half of the strains brought back were excellent.

  • Strains differ a lot in speed and flavour. A Detroit farm grows a maitake strain from Mycelia on straight 50:50 combo pellets; the Shogun strain is slower.

  • Strain 494 (from John Donahue, sold through Northspore) is grown by very few farms. A North Carolina grower using it averages 3.5-4 lb (1.6-1.8 kg) of maitake a block. She dislikes "GF6" (possibly the strain sold as "Shogun"), which grows thin and brittle. She learned maitake by studying how it grows in the wild, after finding many published papers unreliable.

  • Prices (US). One large maitake producer runs fruiting for 100-105 days and sells wholesale at about US$9-10 a pound, aiming for US$3-4; another sells bagged maitake at about US$5-7 a pound.

CHECK Weigh blocks you buy. Blocks sold as "10 lb" often weigh under 9 lb (4.1 kg) when checked.

Culture and spawn

  • Agar. MEA (malt extract agar) gives more dynamic rhizomorphic (rope-like) growth than PDA; malt suits slow strains. Maitake stores well in cryo, stays genetically stable, and grows slowly on everything.
  • Cloning wild maitake. Tissue can sit quiet for a week before hyphae appear, so do not bin quiet plates early. Old, moldy or unrefrigerated specimens give dead plates. See Chapter 7.
  • Grain moisture is everything. Grain spawn is harder than for most species, and growth drops fast if the medium is even slightly off. Target 42-46% absolute grain moisture (including the grain's inherent moisture and the sawdust). At that moisture, master to G2 runs dense white in 4-5 weeks; slightly dry, it stretches to 9-10 weeks. Grain type matters less than moisture.
  • Sawdust in the grain. Add about 6% red oak sawdust to the grain (one experienced grower uses up to about 10%). Sawdust in millet speeds early colonization, and sawdust spawn pins sooner than grain spawn (unconfirmed), but large amounts give no sweeping gains.
  • Disturbance. After any disturbance (cutting agar, breaking up spawn) it takes 1-2 weeks to visibly recover, leaving exposed media. That, not weakness, is why it contaminates more. Once going, it is about as fast as chestnut, pioppino and beech. Contaminated maitake spawn bags were rare at Cap n Stem.

Substrate

  • Recipe. Lean supplementation like shiitake: 70-80% hardwood, 20-30% bran or midds. Cap n Stem prefers 20-30% supplement; one experienced grower uses about 30% soy; a 35% soy mix and a 20-40% range are also used.
  • Too rich. A full 50:50 combo works but is too rich: heavy metabolites, more mold, hot cores, mold on developing fruit and undifferentiated fronds. Master's Mix is a poor fit (odd shapes and more mold), and combo pellets may not be optimal.
  • Moisture. 60-61%, with 61% ideal; a 1% difference matters. About 63% on rich media becomes a pool of metabolites.

RANGE Substrate moisture: 61% recommended (60-61%). One experienced grower runs 54-57% (method unclear). A couple of percent above the standard about 62% has also been suggested for slow species like maitake.

  • Cooking. A "quasi-cook" gives the best results: bring the vessel to 15 psi (1 bar / 103 kPa), cut the steam and hold, with cores at about 99 °C (210 °F) for set hours, and unload at 0 psi. Avoid moving maitake to ultra-pasteurization: ultra-pasteurized blocks, especially when fruited early, give white, cauliflower-like bacterial fruit instead of darkening. See Chapter 12.
  • Block and bag. 10 lb (4.5 kg) is the norm, mostly by habit; one grower uses 5 lb (2.3 kg). Use Unicorn XLS-A bags: the B patch is too open and the T too tight. The tighter A patch also matters for in-bag fruiting.
  • Spawn rate. About 20 blocks per 6 lb (2.7 kg) bag (unit unconfirmed). Raise the rate to speed the jump-off.

Incubation

  • This is the longest and most critical phase: do not rush or disturb it. Full white colonization is not the finish line. Hold 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at 19 °C (66 °F), 20 °C (68 °F) maximum.
Weeks What you see
1-4 Colonization
4-6 "Spider eyes": moisture bubbles on a pillowy top
4-8 Primordia build across the top
5-8 Primordia rise toward the patch as "fists" that split into "fingers": time to cut
  • Blocks knocked the same week will not stay in sync; check each one.
  • Light. Give noticeably more light than usual incubation (not floodlights). Too little light shows as brown primordia only around the edge. Blue light is often recommended for in-bag primordia; red-spectrum light is suggested elsewhere for sensitive control.

RANGE Recommended: adequate light throughout incubation. Some growers incubate dim and then roll maitake into bright light (about 3 weeks, as an example) to trigger pinning. Covering shelves in black plastic once killed airflow and the blocks failed. Spectrum suggestions differ (red versus blue).

  • Top shape. Some growers slope the substrate top; others compress it flat (Far West Fungi).

Fruiting

Procedure: opening a maitake block

  1. Check every block individually for the fist-to-fingers stage; on a scale farm give staff a ruler mark for how high the primordia should be.
  2. Cut the bag top off, but not down to the block top: the remaining bag is a protective microclimate.
  3. Slit one or two sides of the bag so the mushroom can push out and CO2 can spill out.
  4. Move the block into the maitake room (see the settings below).

CHECK Healthy blocks show the tops of the primordia darkening considerably after cutting; fronds then form fast and harvest follows in 7-10 days. A block cut too early stalls and becomes one of the slowest crops in the room.

  • Black bags. Side-cutting black bags also works if timed when the block is fully colonized and before lobes form. Maitake from black bags looked far better than from clear bags at a festival display.
Setting Value Conditions
Room Its own room It dislikes other species' spores, fast air exchange and humidity swings
Relative humidity Steady 90-93% High-pressure humidification
Light Lots of light, 6,500 K or the coolest spectrum available, always on
Air movement Slow and steady: for example a about 500 CFM (850 m³/h) fan running continuously in a 12 × 24 ft (3.7 × 7.3 m) room
CO2 Below about 1,000 ppm Slow air leaves it slightly high
Temperature Anywhere in 16-21 °C (the 60s °F) One grower runs some strains to about 24 °C (75 °F); Shogun is more warmth-tolerant than 9827
  • Mixed rooms. In a mixed room maitake is hard to fruit and goes on top of the rack.
  • In-bag fruiting for drying. In-bag auto-fruiting works for about 2-3 months before the block turns "sad and soupy".

Harvest, yield and shelf life

  • Yield. About 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, whether sold as fronds or left as a "blob" in the bag. Black bags add about 0.15 lb (68 g) (a rough number).
  • Flushes. One flush; second flushes are not recommended. Room rotation is about 7-10 days, with loading and harvesting about every 5 days.
  • Product form. Some clients want blobs: simpler, said by some to taste better, and they slice like king oyster. Others prefer shredded fronds.

Problems

  • Over-rich or wrongly hydrated blocks: pools of metabolites, mold, hot cores, mold wicking onto the fruit.
  • White, cauliflower-like bacterial fruit after ultra-pasteurization.
  • Trichoderma and airborne contaminants on the fruit: clean the maitake room every day.
  • Spores: possibly heavy spore loads (unconfirmed); wear a mask.

Tips

  • Get grain moisture right (42-46%) and add a little oak sawdust.
  • Give it a dedicated, bright, humid, slow-air room.
  • Never disturb incubating blocks; cut at fist-to-fingers.

Chestnut (Pholiota adiposa)

AT A GLANCE Stable and easy in the lab, but it must ripen well past full colonization, stay out of strong light, be cut decisively, and fruit cold and foggy. Key numbers:

  • Incubate at about 19 °C (66 °F) with no swings; full but faint at about 2 weeks, firm at 3, then ripen 1-2+ weeks more until the caramel ring forms.
  • Pin at 10 °C to about 16 °C (50 °F to the very low 60s °F); 90-95% RH to pin, 88-90% after primordia; CO2 below about 900 ppm.
  • Slowest of the mixed species: 2-3 weeks in the fruit room for ripened blocks.
  • Short shelf life: pick while the gills are still semi-covered.

Overview

  • Name. It is sold as Pholiota adiposa, but the binomial is disputed; one community member's sample sequenced as something slightly different.

  • Core message. Stable and easy in the lab, but it must be ripened well past full colonization, kept out of strong light, cut decisively, and fruited cold and foggy.

  • Importance. A top-five species for Cap n Stem and "very high yielding"; rated 10-11 out of 10 for business importance, though only 6 out of 10 to eat by one grower.

  • Marketing. It photographs very well (speckled, scaly caps), which is good for markets and social media, and smells sweet like maple syrup while growing.

  • Digestion. Some people get digestive (GI) distress from it. One claim says tolerance is all-or-nothing, presented as "100% proven" without a source (unconfirmed).

  • Relatives. It is related to nameko (both Pholiota); wild relatives taste better than cultivated ones.

  • A buffer crop. It is a winter variety, fruitable year-round at lower yield. Ripened blocks can sit without fruiting, so it works as a buffer crop.

  • Chestnut is the least loved of the common species: "nobody loves chestnuts... I don't know why we grow them anymore", as Cap n Stem puts it.

WARNING Several people have reported severe digestive reactions to chestnut, for example after a first large, half-cooked serving. Customers who react to one mushroom may avoid all mushrooms afterwards. A West Virginia grower is phasing chestnut out for this reason, even though it fruited best of all his species during a rose-comb outbreak. Cook it fully and tell customers to.

Strains

  • PA CNS. Lineage: John Donahue (Northwest Mycological Consultants, NMC) to New Hampshire Mushroom Co. to Cap n Stem; now distributed worldwide. Many Pholiota give only odd one-off fruits; this strain gives full commercial flushes.
  • A second account describes the culture as cloned from a market sample bought at a Portland, Maine bakery and market, then shared widely.

RANGE The strain's origin is told two ways: through NMC and New Hampshire Mushroom Co., or as a clone of a Portland market sample. These may be different cultures or two parts of one story.

  • Stability. Exceptionally stable: it never drifted, even before cryo storage, and plain agar storage is fine. Kings and chestnut are Cap n Stem's most consistent cultures.

  • The chestnut strain most US growers have is one Cap n Stem took from New Hampshire Mushroom Company and sent out on about a thousand plates; it doesn't think anyone has bred new chestnut strains. Strains are often bought, renamed and resold; genetic markers could prove where a cultivar came from.

Culture and spawn

Step Method and numbers Notes
Cryo 10% v/v glycerol, one fully colonized rye kernel per vial (rye beat sorghum), −80 °C (−112 °F) Stable about 3 years; thaw at 30 °C (86 °F)
Agar Grows fast on PDA / PDYA, and equally well on MYA and PYA; thick enough to see on clear plates Reaches the edge in about 1.5-2 weeks; refrigerate at 1 cm from the edge
G1 master Two cuttings per 4 lb (1.8 kg) master (12 masters per plate); leave about a week, shake at 1-1.5 weeks; full in about 2 weeks Refrigerate at 2-3 weeks
G2 12 × 6 lb (2.7 kg) bags per master Above about 19-20 °C (67-68 °F) it finishes in about 2 weeks; cooler than that, about 3 weeks
Cold storage Refrigerated G2 is definitely good for 2 weeks; 3 weeks pushes it Spawn holds very well cold, even for 2-month orders
  • What normal looks like. Thready, wispy mycelium with grains staying separate. Yellow metabolite droplets by 2 weeks and clear droplets a week later are all normal. Finished spawn is white with some squish, never a hard brick.
  • Grain choice. Milo (sorghum) outpaced other grains over about six crops (early data). NMC used winter rye. Wheat is disliked.
  • Sensitivity. Slightly less tenacious than oyster on grain, and sensitive to dry kernels, which grow Trichoderma. It is easily disturbed: shaking or thermal shock too early often does not recover.
  • Agar slurry works for chestnut only. Pouring a blended plate into bags gave no visible growth for about 2 weeks, then sudden full colonization. Fruit form changed: many small, consistent clusters of about 20 caps versus bigger clusters of about 5, though which method gave which form is unclear.

Substrate

  • House recipe. Master's Mix in 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at 61-62% moisture, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 per 20 blocks (rate partly unclear).
  • Raw sawdust vs pellets. On raw sawdust, going from 5 lb (2.3 kg) to 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks gave the same yield per block, or only about 20% more, so chestnut stayed on 5 lb raw-dust blocks. Combo pellets doubled yield or more on 10 lb blocks (target 2-3 lb / 0.9-1.4 kg, "over 3" hoped for; described as about 125% more). This result convinced Cap n Stem to switch to combo pellets.

RANGE Moving raw-dust blocks from 5 lb to 10 lb gave no gain per block in one account and about +20% in another. Either way, combo pellets are the bigger lever.

  • Raw dust vs pellets, quality. Raw dust gives tighter clusters with bigger mushrooms; pellets give a more even flush and more total weight.

  • Block size works in steps. 6-7 lb (2.7-3.2 kg) is no better than 5 lb, and 12 lb (5.4 kg) no better than 10 lb. Too much substrate per fruiting site deforms the fruit: 30-40 lb (14-18 kg) straw buckets gave one odd mushroom.

  • Bags. Polypropylene stays tight to the block. Tough polyethylene bags gape at the cuts and dry the wound. B patches give far too much air exchange and crust the top. Black bags limit premature pinning but may not raise yield; knock 19 black bags plus 1 clear one as an indicator. See Chapter 11.

  • Substrate makes a big difference. Kiln-dried combo pellets gave up to 3 lb per 10 lb block (1.4 kg per 4.5 kg), against about 1.25-2 lb on raw oak.

  • Over-cooked blocks made from pure oak pellets (the bottom blocks in a stratified barrel) gave Catawba Mushrooms 2-3 months of poor chestnut that sat an extra 1-2 weeks before fruiting. The grower suspects the long cook broke down tannins and hemicellulose; this has not been tested.

Incubation

  • Temperature. About 19 °C (66 °F); the house figure is a joke-precise 66.66 °F (19.3 °C). Chestnut is not fussy, but temperature swings (even 16-19 °C / 60-66 °F) or overheating trigger pins and banded growth. Cold corners at 14-16 °C (58-60 °F) in a 19 °C (66-67 °F) room slowed colonization.
  • Colonization. Full but faint at about 2 weeks, noticeably firm at 3 weeks (the earliest viable fruiting). A dense white block at about 2.5-3 weeks is also reported.
  • Ripening. Give an extra 1-2 weeks or more, until the block swells with caramel-coloured metabolites and a rust-coloured ring forms in the headspace. Ripening gives faster, more reliable pin sets and more vigorous fruit; allow 3-6 weeks in total to ripen fully. Ripening blocks turn golden-mustard, which new staff mistake for Neurospora (an orange mold).

RULE If incubation space is your bottleneck, fruit sooner. If fruit-room space is the bottleneck, or neither is, let blocks ripen.

  • Light. The most light-sensitive species in incubation. Strong or cold full-spectrum light (for example 6,500 K close above the top rack) fries and dries the top. Keep blocks low; red light at or below about 1,500 K is safer. This is a consistent finding.
  • Cold holding. Colonized blocks refrigerate very well at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F), more or less indefinitely (not formally tested).
  • Temperature spikes. A severe temperature spike can leave a normal-looking block that never fruits.

CASE A New Hampshire farm used to incubate chestnut for 55-60 days on wheat midds. When the radiant heating failed, the room reached 29 °C (85 °F); the grower opened the windows to outside air at 4 °C (40 °F), and 1,500 bags pinned within 18 hours. The farm now incubates for about 40 days. Cold gives needle-thin stems, and shelf life is about 5 days. Spent chestnut blocks in compost drums gave another 9 kg (20 lb) over 60 days.

Fruiting

  • Cut deep. Once a Florida farm learned to cut deep into the substrate and let chestnut fruit from within, it got "amazing yields" and good shelf life when harvested on time.

Procedure: opening a chestnut block

  1. Confirm the block is ripe (caramel metabolites, rust ring in the headspace).
  2. Stand the block upright.
  3. Cut a cross or X on the broadest face, or a razor-deep slice about 1/8-1/4 in (3-6 mm) deep across the top, then press the air out. Chestnut tolerates a slightly deeper cut than most species.
  4. Do not cut half-moons around existing pins.
  5. Place it on a bottom shelf in a cold, foggy room (settings below).

CHECK Hyphal knots appear along the cut, then recognizable baby mushrooms in about 7-10 days, then 7-12 more days to harvest.

Setting Value Conditions
Temperature, pinning 10 °C to about 16 °C (50 °F to the very low 60s °F); ideal about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) Acceptable to about 18 °C (65 °F); poor or no pinning at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F)
Temperature, after primordia About 16-17 °C (low 60s °F) Too hot gives Trichoderma blooming on block tops
RH, pinning 90-95% The one species for which a hydrofogger's dense wet fog is recommended
RH, after primordia 88-90%
CO2 Below about 900 ppm
Rack Bottom shelves
  • Time in the room. Ripened blocks need 2-3 weeks of fruit-room time, unripe ones 4-5 weeks, and up to two months in a cold winter room. It is the slowest of the mixed species.

Harvest and shelf life

  • Short shelf life. Harvest while the gills are still semi-covered and before caps flatten. One day late sharply cuts storage life. Chill and sell quickly. Clusters do not mature in sync. Trade some yield for shelf life. See Chapter 15.
  • Case: Mycopia had poor shelf life with chestnut because it harvested too late.

Problems

  • Contamination. Less tenacious than oyster: expect higher contamination rates. A run of about 40 blocks all with internal Trichoderma points to the substrate, not the room.
  • Fused caps or cap-on-cap growth from condensation are circumstantial, not a warning sign. Blotch is not a direct problem despite the fogging. Chestnut was the one species unaffected by rose comb in a case with a badly set-up ultrasonic humidifier.
  • Patience. New growers mistake slow pinning for failure.

Tips

  • Ripen in the bag, keep in low light, cut decisively, fruit cold and very humid.
  • Mix chestnut into incubation rows with slower, cooler species to even out heat.

Pioppino (Agrocybe aegerita, black poplar mushroom)

AT A GLANCE Tough, forgiving and fast in the fruit room, and happy warmer than most species. Key numbers:

  • Grain: 3-4 weeks; blocks: about 3 weeks for colonies to join.
  • Fruit at 18-24 °C (65-75 °F); it tolerates about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), and warmer is faster.
  • Ready sign: fluff, then amber droplets. Open at the droplets; a full pin carpet is a little late. From the carpet to harvest is only about 1.5-2 days.
  • Keep incubation at or below about 18 °C (65 °F), or the top fluff won't form.
  • Watch for Trichoderma: it is the first of the common species to show it.

Overview

  • Fast and warm-loving in the fruit room, tough and forgiving. It grows well on Master's Mix, but its ideal conditions are fundamentally different from an oyster's.
  • Like kings and maitake, it shows up any variable that is off, because it needs a steady metabolic rate.
  • Grain source matters. Switching grain supplier can change how fruit bodies form dramatically; one grower calls this "rule number one" for pioppino.

Strains

  • AACN (Cap n Stem's house code) is a wild strain that came through another grower. It may not be true A. aegerita but a close relative. It yields very well.

Culture and spawn

Step Method and numbers Notes
Agar Fluffy, cottony, white radial growth; fills a plate in about 2-3 weeks Transfer or refrigerate at 1 cm from the edge. Past the edge it only gets fluffier; it never forms a tough mat.
G1 master 2 cuttings (sometimes 4) per 4 lb (1.8 kg) master; between slow and fast strains
G2 Each master to 12 × 6 lb (2.7 kg) grain bags (6 is also quoted)
Grain incubation About 3-4 weeks
  • What normal looks like. The grain doesn't densify until the colonies meet. Dense white patches can look like stroma but stay soft when poked. Yellow-orange metabolites from week 2 are harmless; together with growth creeping up the bag, they mean it is ready. A typical bag shows a dense white band above darker, less-colonized grain.
  • It may auto-fruit small pins in the grain bag, and it is probably the one species where you can get away with that (unconfirmed).

Substrate and incubation

  • Recipe. Master's Mix 50:50 from combo pellets, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag per 20 blocks (block size quoted as 20 lb, most likely meaning 10 lb, 4.5 kg). One grower suspects it prefers soft hardwoods such as poplar over oak and maple.
  • Bags. XLS-A-type patch bags work well.
  • Colonization. Splotchy, with patches that look like contamination but aren't. Colonies take about 3 weeks to join. Blocks ship at about week 3, when fully colonized and "pillowy" on top.
  • Keep it cool. The top fluff that signals a healthy block forms only if the block is not incubated warmer than about 18 °C (65 °F) or held too long.
  • Heat. It makes little heat and grows slowly. A row of pioppino ran cold in winter, and cold spots added about a week. Mix its rows with oyster or chestnut to even out the heat (Chapter 13).

Fruiting

  • When it is ready: wild fluff on top, then amber droplets of exudate on the fluff. The droplets are the giveaway that the block is about to pin. If you wait for the carpet of nodules on top (they turn golden), you are a little late and the fruit comes out stringy and gnarly. Don't be afraid of the fluff. Ready blocks show exudate droplets on the plastic and golden-yellow early pin nodules.
  • Opening: the traditional way is to snip the corners of the bag for air exchange, put it in the fruit room and watch the pins form. Some farms cut halfway down; most cut the top off and let it fruit up to the top. If golden pins form at the sides, clip the top rather than cutting there. Pioppino pins on top first and is cut around, unlike lion's mane, which is cut into the block. Top fruiting suits a fast species like pioppino.
  • Settings: 18-24 °C (65-75 °F); it tolerates about 27-29 °C (80-85 °F), and warmer is faster. Lights on once the carpet forms.
  • Speed: fast in the fruit room, similar to shiitake. Once the pin carpet changes, it is ready in about 1.5-2 days. Racks that get forgotten give oversized pioppino.
  • Side fluff. Pioppino also grows fluff along the sides of the bag. For shiitake, some oysters, king oyster and maitake, side growth is unwanted: mushrooms form there and fall off.

RANGE When to open. Recommended: open at the fluff-and-amber-droplet stage, by snipping the corners or cutting the top. Letting a full carpet of pins form first is the traditional method, but it is a little too late and gives stringy, nutty fruit.

Harvest

  • Harvest just before the cap breaks away from the edge of the stem and flattens.
  • In hot weather pack it in bigger boxes rather than small ones to protect the fruit.
  • One farm's yield is about 2.5 lb (1.1 kg) for most varieties from an 11 lb (5 kg) block, with pioppino a little less (Chapter 14).

Problems

  • It is the first of the common species to show Trichoderma (a slow, wispy grower), and it attracts far more green mould than maitake.
  • A bad culture, cook or spawn shows as a flat, glossy, slick top that never pins, with poor, dry side pins. A lack of fluff is a warning sign.

Reishi (Ganoderma lingzhi / lucidum)

AT A GLANCE A medicinal, not a culinary, species. Its shape is set by CO2: antlers in high CO2, kidney-shaped caps in fresh air. Key numbers:

  • In-bag antlers take 3-4 months to reach the bag top and can keep growing for up to a year.
  • Antlers form in high in-bag CO2 (perhaps 3,000-5,000 ppm); caps form below about 1,000 ppm.
  • Fruiting RH 85-95%.
  • About 80% water, so it barely needs drying.
  • Wear a respirator at harvest: spore loads are heavy.

Overview

  • Names and history. Lingzhi in Chinese, reishi in Japanese. Its history is murky because ancient texts lump many fungi and herbs together. The "7,000 years of use" claim rests on Ganoderma spores found at archaeological sites, which don't prove use. It is listed as a top-class herb in the Shennong Bencao Jing; of the six coloured "zhi" in that text, only the red one clearly matches modern Ganoderma.
  • Naming. First described as Boletus lucidus (Curtis, 1781), later placed in Polyporus and Fomes; Karsten created the genus Ganoderma in 1881. G. lucidum and G. tsugae did not cross in a 1986 mating study. Ganoderma is heterothallic and tetrapolar (see Chapter 8).
  • Cultivation history. The first full artificial cultivation, with a spore-bearing cap, was by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in the early 1970s; earlier lab attempts produced only antlers.
  • Medicinal evidence points to immune modulation rather than direct anti-tumour action, and many studies are small, in vitro or in animals. Over 400 compounds have been found. Triterpene and polysaccharide content varies strongly by species: polysaccharides 1.1-5.8% and triterpenes 0-7.8% (unconfirmed figures).
  • Market. Reishi is a favourite of the alternative-health market, its "pumpkin spice latte". Antlers and tinctures sell; some of the circulating health stories are deliberate parody, so don't repeat claims you can't source.
  • Eating and materials. Not much of an edible, though trimmed outer flesh has been described as having a foie-gras texture. Mycelium materials (leather, packaging) favour Ganoderma's tough, skin-like mat.

Strains

  • Cap n Stem's Ganoderma lingzhi strain came from John Donahue, who got it from European contacts in the 1980s. It is said to be high in certain triterpenes (anecdotal).
  • A wild Maine Ganoderma rescued on gentamicin agar was not robust and was dropped. Another grower grows a kidney-shaped isolate said to come from upstate New York.

Spawn, substrate and incubation

  • Reishi is a matting species: its spawn doesn't break up as easily as chestnut's.
  • Logs or bags. Short, well-hydrated logs colonize and fruit faster than long ones. Bags are much faster, but logs give sturdier fruit with more active compounds and predictable fruiting spots.
  • Supplement. One farm adds 15% wheat bran to reishi sawdust.
  • Bags can sit for months to a year, growing layers against the wall and out through the patch.
  • Cool-down matters even here. Even reishi failed to fruit at a farm where hot blocks sat 1-3 days before going into a filtered cool-down room (Chapter 4).

Fruiting

Setting Value Notes
CO2 for antlers High in-bag CO2, perhaps 3,000-5,000 ppm with an A-style filter
CO2 for caps Below about 1,000 ppm, or outdoors: the kidney-shaped cap forms Stripping the bag brings caps back (about a month for year-old antlers).
Humidity 85-95% RH Below about 85% the pore surface may not develop properly (from an unclear account of an old study).
In-bag fruiting time 3-4 months for antlers to reach the bag top; up to a year possible It can keep fruiting for months until a 10 lb (4.5 kg) bag is mostly antler.
  • Bag patches. Very airtight Tyvek clip-patch bags kept a Donahue culture stuck as small antlers. Very open B patches would probably stunt antlers by drying the surface.
  • Opened bags of in-bag antlers are the normal sight on a reishi farm.
  • In the wild, a reishi growing from a buried root has to push a stem up through the soil before it caps; one grew sideways all season without a cap.
  • Spore release peaks around midnight (a 1963 study).

Harvest and processing

  • Antlers are "scalped" from the blocks into bins and broken apart. This is hard work, because dried material behaves like cement and styrofoam. Weigh and vacuum-seal to the client's spec and check every bag for punctures. Nubs are ground to powder, which is said to be just as potent. See Chapter 15.
  • Reishi is about 80% water (most mushrooms are about 95%) and barely needs drying.
  • Tincture: cover dried reishi with 70-90% grain alcohol, shake daily for about a lunar cycle, and strain. Then simmer it in about half a gallon (1.9 L) of water for about 2 hours until reduced. Extraction has to break down tough, double-walled structures. The full procedure is in Chapter 15.

Problems and safety

  • Spore loads are heavy. One farm always harvested reishi outdoors; wear a respirator.
  • Reishi can take up heavy metals from its substrate, so know what your sawdust is.

Cordyceps (Cordyceps militaris)

Cordyceps comes up only in passing; no full growing parameters are available.

  • It degenerates quickly (light, temperature and RNA-level pathways are cited), especially through serial liquid-culture expansion. Preserve good cultures early (Chapter 8).
  • Cap n Stem is starting cordyceps production and breeding (single-cell isolation and storage of fast-degrading strains), with a planned monokaryon project.
  • Early incubation goes best in dim light or none; black bags help.
  • Fast species like cordyceps may suit fruiting inside high-exchange (B patch) bags.
  • Some cordyceps growers dry-bag rice-based media with a Fenrir-type filler (Chapter 6).
  • Stalled white heads that look like stroma also show up with cordyceps.
  • Like maitake, it needs a species-specific process, refined by many small growers sharing openly.
  • Cordyceps cultures have flown in spaceflight trial vials (a 15 mL tube labelled "Cordyceps #3").
  • Myth: the "Last of Us" idea of cordyceps adapting to human body heat is scientifically silly.

Psilocybe cubensis

This species comes up only in asides, mostly in the context of legal cultivation, and no full parameters are available.

  • Along with oysters, it is the easiest mushroom to grow. Cultivated cubensis can't simply be released into the wild and thrive.
  • Grain bags: growers often use 1-2 lb (0.45-0.9 kg) of grain per bag with heavy inoculation. Fast respiration makes the bags CO2-rich and close to anaerobic, so they need more gas exchange. In practice the Unicorn B patch is used only for cubensis.
  • Rye takes liquid culture well and is popular for cubensis. Rhizomorphic growth, prized by these growers, is not necessarily a sign of health.
  • Substrate: straw plus soy, or straw plus midds, is common. Some legal programmes restrict ingredients (for example, coco coir is allowed). One recommendation is gypsum to steady the pH (initial pH about 8) and raise yield.
  • Mutation-prone strains such as Penis Envy grew more evenly with a compacted, casing-like surface over the spawn layer than in loose, through-spawned beds.
  • Filling a room then emptying it all at once (common on cubensis farms) never reaches thermal balance; run a rolling load instead (Chapter 13).
  • Fruiting in high-exchange B bags may suit it. Home growers judge perlite moisture by the weight of the tub and keep home RH at 50% or more.
  • Several legal farms dry with dehumidifiers.
  • Genetics: wild populations are highly diverse, while domesticated lines are inbred. Dr. Jason Slot is credited with finding the psilocybin gene cluster. Mycelium holds far less active compound than fruit bodies, and spores hold none, which is why spore syringes were legal.
  • Agar-slurry inoculation is worth trying (Chapter 7), and aerated-culture lids of the Myco-op style are popular with cubensis growers.

Other species

Species What growers need to know
Beech / shimeji (Hypsizygus) Strongly light-triggered; incubated with light for a long time, and stretching incubation to 6-8 weeks gives denser, juicier mycelium. Once going it grows at about maitake's pace. Imports keep its price very low in some markets.
Enoki (including golden enoki) A low-temperature species, below the usual 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) fruiting range. Cheap imports flood some markets. Golden enoki got inverted caps in one case of rose-comb deformity. Sell it at harvest: it degrades within about 3 days.
Nameko A Pholiota relative of chestnut that likes the same sticky, humid conditions. Crossing the two to combine traits is pure speculation.
Pleurotus nebrodensis An endangered relative of king oyster from limestone and volcanic soils (Sicily to Afghanistan). Growers report it needs substrate pH 8-11 (add calcium) and frost to trigger fruiting; strongly light-triggered; a low-temperature oddball with low yield, more a curiosity than a crop. Cap n Stem had just released a culture, and Mycopia grows it.
Tremella (snow fungus) A wetter species that might take higher substrate moisture, perhaps about 63-65%. A single-product grower can build a business on it.
Turkey tail (Trametes versicolor) A matting species: blocks left too long become extremely hard. It has flown in spaceflight trial vials.
Bear's head (H. americanum) A wild autumn Hericium, less leggy than comb tooth; once seen growing with lion's mane.
Button mushroom (Agaricus) Hit hardest by blotch, because of insects, water and huge open beds; Pennsylvania farms lose roughly 15-20% a year (a loose recollection).
Morel Resisted indoor cultivation for over 100 years. Cultivated morels taste different from wild burn-site morels.
Chicken of the woods Cloned cleanly from a fresh specimen. Its fast orange mycelium has been mistaken for Neurospora (Chapter 16).
Shrimp of the woods (Entoloma abortivum) Hard to clone, because the tissue already involves two fungi plus bacteria.
Chaga A sterile mycelial mass on birch.
Lactarius indigo Found wild and delicious, but not yet cultivable.
Wild-only species Birch polypore (carried by Ötzi the iceman), tinder fungus (for carrying fire), chanterelle (spread, in a story about Frank Herbert, by pouring blended fruit at the base of trees), and Massospora (a cicada pathogen; see Chapter 2).
  • Hericium americanum (bear's head) from Cap n Stem grew downward almost like a cylinder, about 40 cm (16 in) long, like a sea sponge, on high racks. Detroit chefs freeze-dry it, coat it in oil and air-fry it; its open structure lets oil and marinade move through, unlike lion's mane.
  • Pheasant's back (dryad's saddle): one Tennessee breeder has cloned 26 wild strains and thinks it could be a good cultivated mushroom, but it must be sold very fresh and is slow (10-14 days in liquid culture before stirring).

Key rules

  1. Incubate 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) ambient for nearly every species. Cores run several degrees hotter, and heat spikes cause duds, stroma and bacteria.
  2. "Fully white" is not "ready" for shiitake, maitake, chestnut and black oyster. Give them their ripening time: shiitake 75-80% brown, maitake fist-to-fingers, chestnut with its caramel ring.
  3. Keep shiitake and maitake on lean substrate (20-30% supplement). Oysters, chestnut, pioppino and king oyster thrive on Master's Mix; lion's mane may do better at 30-40% soy.
  4. Fruit cold-lovers cold: black oyster, king oyster and chestnut pin best at 10-17 °C (the 50s to low 60s °F). Pioppino and maitake tolerate warmer rooms.
  5. Match light to species: shiitake and maitake need light in incubation, chestnut and lion's mane want it dim, and kings and maitake want bright fruit rooms.
  6. Use CO2-triggered exhaust with a narrow band (roughly 450-900 ppm). High CO2 means long stems, flat pale caps or coral-like lion's mane.
  7. Hydrate evenly: one dry kernel or wet pocket triggers pinning, stroma or bacteria, especially in Hericium and maitake grain.
  8. Move spawn and colonized blocks on time: oysters consolidate or pin, lion's mane auto-fruits, kings skin over.
  9. Harvest before caps flatten; late chestnut and shiitake lose shelf life fast for a small weight gain.
  10. Give maitake its own room, and keep lion's mane above shiitake, never below.
  11. Wear a respirator when harvesting shiitake and reishi.

Open questions

  • Pink and golden oyster have no dedicated profile: no substrate, temperature or yield figures beyond rack placement and their intolerance of cryo storage.
  • No full blue oyster parameter sheet exists to match the black oyster and lion's mane profiles, and oyster yield figures range from about 2 to 4 lb (0.9-1.8 kg) per block with unclear block sizes.
  • Glycerol strength for cryo storage (5% vs 10%) is inconsistent within the same farm.
  • Black oyster's parentage awaits whole-genome sequencing, and the causes of stroma await a DNA study.
  • Cordyceps and cubensis come up only in passing, with no growing parameters.
  • Chestnut's strain origin is told two ways (NMC lineage vs a Portland market clone).

chapters.html:
Growth Metrics by Species

AT A GLANCE This chapter is the number book. It gives, for each species and each stage, the substrate recipe and moisture, spawn rate, incubation temperature and time, fruiting temperature, humidity, CO2 and light, time to pins and harvest, flushes, yield, block size, shelf life and storage temperature. Start from the house baseline and change only what a species needs. The numbers people reach for most:

  • Baseline block: 10 lb (4.5 kg) of Master's Mix (50% red oak sawdust, 50% soybean hulls) at about 62% moisture.
  • Spawn rate: one 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 spawn bag per twenty 10 lb blocks, about 3%.
  • Incubation: 19 °C (66 °F) room air; keep block cores below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F).
  • Fruiting: 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) for the staple species; CO2 exhaust on at about 900 ppm, off at about 600 ppm, never above 1,000 ppm.
  • Plan on 2 lb (0.9 kg) of mushrooms per 10 lb block unless a species figure below is better established.
  • Store colonized blocks and spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F).

How to use this chapter

Every species grows on the same basic system: a substrate block is mixed, heat-treated, inoculated with grain spawn, incubated until the mycelium fills it, then moved to a fruit room to produce mushrooms. The numbers change from species to species, but most of them change only a little. So this chapter works in three layers:

  1. The house baseline: the default numbers for a standard block. Use them whenever a species section says nothing about a setting. The baseline comes from one working farm, Cap n Stem: a 10 lb block, 50:50 Master's Mix at roughly 61-63% moisture, one 6 lb spawn bag per twenty blocks (about 3%) and about 19 °C (66 °F) incubation. Each species then moves away from that baseline where it has to.
  2. Species comparison at a glance: four short tables and charts that put the species side by side, one stage at a time.
  3. Species by species: a full table per species, in production order (culture, spawn, substrate, incubation, fruiting, harvest), starting with oyster.

How the numbers are presented:

  • Where growers report different figures, the chapter gives a recommended value first, then every reported figure with its conditions in a RANGE callout. Figures are never averaged.
  • Temperatures are given in °C first with °F in brackets. Most source figures were measured in °F, so the °F figure is the original and the °C figure is a conversion.
  • Yields in pounds (lb) are fresh weight per block unless the table says otherwise.
  • "Not stated" means no grower gave a figure for that setting and species. Use the house baseline there.

For how to do each stage, see the process chapters: substrate, bags and inoculation, steam, incubation, fruiting and harvest. For the story, strains and tips behind each species, see Species Profiles. For every setting where sources differ across the whole book, see Settings and Their Ranges.

Procedure: setting up a species from the baseline

  1. Start from the house baseline: 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, about 3% spawn, about 19 °C (66 °F) incubation.
  2. Read the species table and change only the settings it gives: usually moisture, supplement level, incubation time, fruiting temperature and light.
  3. Where the species table gives several figures, run a small trial: a few blocks at each figure, with a datalogger in the room and in a block core. Do not simply pick the midpoint.
  4. Record days to full colonization, days to pins, days to harvest and fresh weight per block for each trial group.
  5. Adopt the setting that gave the best yield and quality, then repeat it on a full run before you change anything else.

CHECK After the first full run, compare your yield per block with the planning figure of about 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb block and with the species figure in the yield table.

The house baseline

AT A GLANCE 10 lb (4.5 kg) block of 50:50 Master's Mix at about 62% moisture; one 6 lb G2 bag per twenty blocks (about 3%); ultra-pasteurize with the slowest core above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h; knock at a core of 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); incubate at 19 °C (66 °F); fruit at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) with CO2 cycled between about 600 and 900 ppm; plan 2 lb (0.9 kg) per block.

These are the numbers to assume for any species whose table is silent on a setting.

Substrate and block

Parameter Value Conditions
Recipe Master's Mix: 50% hardwood (red oak) sawdust, 50% soybean hulls. Never more than 50% soy. Often bought ready-mixed as combo pellets.
Moisture (recommended) About 62% General hydration target. See the RANGE below.
pH and calcium pH about 6.5; calcium carbonate (CaCO3) at 1-4% is reported to help Especially oysters.
Residual moisture already in the inputs Combo pellets about 7%; hardwood fuel pellets 7-15%; pellets in general 7-11%; grain from the mill 10-12% (assume about 10%, range 7-15%) Count this water in the water calculation, or the block ends up too wet.
Block size 10 lb (4.5 kg); XLS-A bags filled to about 9.8 lb (4.4 kg) Fill rule: about one-third substrate, two-thirds headspace.
Block size limit 10 lb is the practical maximum in polypropylene bags with small filters; a 12 lb (5.4 kg) block goes anaerobic (runs out of oxygen); 9-11 lb blocks yield the same if the moisture is right
Block size (early practice) 5 lb (2.3 kg) bags Used in the early days of mixer-based production.

RANGE Substrate moisture. Recommended: about 62%. Reported figures:

  • 62-63% for a typical sawdust block.
  • 61-62% in the bag, falling to about 60% by fruiting; test 61-65% for each strain.
  • About 61% in a worked example.

Species that need a different figure (shiitake, Hericium, maitake) are listed in the moisture comparison.

WHY A pellet or grain input is never bone dry. If you calculate added water as though it were, a 62% target turns into 64-65% in the bag, which is too wet for several species.

Mixing, hydration and the water calculation are covered in Chapter 10; bags and fill in Chapter 11.

Spawn

Spawn is grain fully colonized by mycelium, used to inoculate the next stage. A G1 or "master" bag is made from an agar culture; G2 bags are made from G1 and go into substrate blocks.

Parameter Value Conditions
Spawn rate (10 lb blocks), recommended One 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 bag per twenty 10 lb blocks: about 3%, or about 0.3 lb (140 g) of grain per block Range used on farms: 8-30 blocks per bag; an older guideline is 2-5%.
Spawn rate (5 lb blocks) 1:40 Compared with about 1:20 (about 3%) for 10 lb blocks.
Spawn expansion, recommended One 4 lb (1.8 kg) G1 master to 12 × 6 lb G2 bags Range 6-24 G2 per master.
Spawn expansion (alternative) One 4 lb G1 to about 20 G2 bags
Spawn generations G2 goes into about twenty 10 lb blocks; no G3 is made
Liquid culture (LC) 20 mL LC per 6 lb grain master; 0.5% sugar (tested 0.5-8%; 2-4% is the common figure); culture cycle 10-12 days, 14 days maximum
Grain recipe 3 parts rye : 1 part sorghum (milo), plus gypsum and calcium carbonate; used for every species except lion's mane Rye boiled 6 min then steeped 12 min; milo steeped 20 min.
Grain moisture 40-50% Checked by weight.
Grain moisture by grain Millet: maximum about 45-47%. Rye: low 50s %. Oats: about 60% (55% used). Sorghum: similar to millet or a little higher. House standard: upper 40s % for rye and millet.
Grain additives Calcium carbonate (CaCO3) plus calcium sulfate (CaSO4, gypsum) at about 0.15% of total wet weight; keep under 1% Helps prevent stroma.

How to make and run spawn is in Chapter 9; agar and liquid culture are in Chapter 7.

Heat treatment and inoculation

Parameter Value Conditions
Grain sterilization Vacuum autoclave: pre-vacuum to -10 inHg (-34 kPa) three or four times, then 124 °C (255 °F) for 35 min
Sterilization (blocks or grain) Core at least 121 °C (250 °F) for at least 35 min
Ultra-pasteurization, recommended Slowest core above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h; Cap n Stem containers hold 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for 2-3 h Total cycle with a barrel steam cart 7-10 h.
Inoculation (knock) temperature, recommended Knock at a block core of about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F) At 38 °C (100 °F) or above, the spawn dies.
Water to inoculation About 30 h: watered, steamed, cooled, knocked the next day

RANGE Ultra-pasteurization (steam at normal pressure, no pressure vessel needed). Recommended: hold the hardest-to-heat core above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 h and no more than 4-6 h, proved by a logger. Reported figures:

  • 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for 2-3 h in Cap n Stem's container steamers.
  • Up to 100 °C (212 °F) for about 3 h.
  • Core 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for 1-3 h, with no pressure.
  • Hardest-to-heat core above 93 °C (200 °F) for 2-3 h, logged with a datalogger.

RANGE Inoculation temperature for ultra-pasteurized blocks. Recommended: knock at a core of about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); at 38 °C (100 °F) or above, the spawn dies. Reported figures:

  • Below 38 °C (100 °F), best below 32 °C (90 °F).
  • About room temperature, with about 30 °C (86 °F) as the upper figure found by experience.

WARNING Spawn knocked into a block core at 38 °C (100 °F) or above dies. Measure the core, not the bag surface.

Steam methods and run logs are in Chapter 12.

Incubation

Incubation is the stage where the mycelium grows through the block in the dark or in dim light. Blocks give off heat and CO2 while they grow, so the room must remove both.

Parameter Value Conditions
Block incubation temperature, recommended 19 °C (66 °F) measured at the outside of the bag; block core then runs about 21 °C (69-70 °F) 10 lb blocks. Loose or lean mixes can take up to 20-21 °C (68-69 °F) room air; about 22 °C (72 °F) is too hot.
Block core limit Room about 19 °C (66 °F) ambient; core must stay below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F) 10 lb blocks.
Sterilized 5 lb blocks About 22 °C (72 °F) Ultra-pasteurized 10 lb blocks stay at about 19 °C (66 °F).
Grain spawn incubation About 16-18 °C (low-to-mid 60s °F), cooler than substrate at 19 °C (66 °F)
Room CO2, recommended 1,500-3,000 ppm: exhaust fan on at about 3,000 ppm, off at 1,500-2,500 ppm depending on how much CO2 you are willing to tolerate; one source runs 2,000-3,000 ppm (off at 2,000-2,500) 5,000 ppm is the OSHA reference limit for workers.
Stroma onset Visible on blocks within about 5 days of inoculation Stroma is a tough, leathery mycelium skin.

RANGE Grain spawn incubation temperature. Recommended: 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) room air. Also reported: 18-21 °C (65-70 °F). Either way, spawn runs a little cooler than blocks.

RANGE Incubation room CO2. Recommended: exhaust on at about 3,000 ppm, off at 1,500-2,500 ppm depending on how much CO2 you are willing to tolerate. Reported figures:

  • 2,000-3,000 ppm (exhaust on at about 3,000, off at about 2,000-2,500).
  • 1,500-3,000 ppm.
  • At or below 2,500-3,000 ppm, with a heat-recovery ventilator (HRV) band of 1,500-3,500 ppm; 500 ppm is too low.

RANGE Heat given off by incubating blocks. No single figure is established; the reported figures differ up to five-fold, so none is averaged here.

  • About 2 BTU/h (0.6 W) per 10 lb block.
  • About 1 BTU/h per lb of substrate (0.29 W per lb).
  • About 2 BTU/h per lb of dry substrate, which is about 6 BTU/h (1.8 W) per 10 lb block.

Measure your own room with dataloggers before sizing cooling on any one of them. Cooling sizing is in Chapter 5.

RANGE How full to load an incubation room. Standard: about one-tenth to one-quarter of the room volume (the same figure applies to fruit rooms), with two hand widths between blocks. Context:

  • Never fill past about 50%.
  • The common one-third rule is the older rule of thumb.

All three figures are listed so you recognize them when other growers quote them.

Running the incubation room is covered in Chapter 13.

Fruiting

Fruiting is the stage where a colonized block is opened and moved to a fruit room with fresh air, high humidity and light, so it produces mushrooms. The plenum is the duct or chamber that delivers conditioned air into the room.

Parameter Value Conditions
Fruiting temperature, recommended Start at 16 °C (60 °F); best 14-17 °C (58-62 °F); 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) is the working range for the staple species (shiitake, oyster, lion's mane), with 18 °C (65 °F) the ceiling 13 °C (55 °F) gives slower, denser mushrooms; 18 °C (65 °F) gives faster growth.
Relative humidity (RH), recommended Cycle between 75% and 85%; plenum air 40-50%
Room CO2, recommended 600-1,000 ppm: exhaust fan on at 900 ppm, off at 600 ppm
Plenum supply CO2 At or below about 450 ppm
Light Bright 6500 K full-spectrum daylight light; warm light for incubation, cool light for fruiting
Humidifier water treatment 150-250 ppm bleach or chlorine dioxide (ClO2). During blotch outbreaks, about 0.1% hydrogen peroxide (H2O2): 1.5 qt (1.4 L) of 3% H2O2 per 10 gal (38 L) of water, changed every 3 days
Fruit-room water bleach About 150-200 ppm; up to about 400 ppm for cleaning
Time in the fruit room, recommended 2-3 weeks per block; plan the room as 3 weekly cohorts
Time in the fruit room by species About 5-15 days depending on species

RANGE Fruiting temperature. Recommended: start at 16 °C (60 °F), best 14-17 °C (58-62 °F), within the 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) working range for the staple species; treat 18 °C (65 °F) as the ceiling. Reported figures:

  • About 16 °C (60 °F) as the typical target, depending on species.
  • 16-18 °C (60-65 °F) ideal; growth stops below about 13-16 °C (55-60 °F). Maine mixed-species farm.

Species-by-species fruiting temperatures are compared in the fruiting table.

RANGE Fruiting humidity. Recommended: swing from about 70% up to about 90% and back, rather than holding the room saturated. Some growers prefer a narrower cycle of 75-85% RH, still not constant.

RANGE Fruiting CO2. Recommended: exhaust on at 900 ppm, off at 600 ppm. Also reported: cycle between about 450 and 900 ppm, with 1,000 ppm the absolute maximum; outdoor air is about 410-420 ppm.

WHY The room cannot get lower than the air you feed it. Outdoor air is about 410-420 ppm, so the plenum supply has to stay at or below about 450 ppm for the room to swing down to its lower set point.

Yield

Parameter Value Conditions
Yield for planning, recommended About 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb block Conservative. 250 blocks a week gives about 500 lb (227 kg) a week from a 12 × 24 ft (3.7 × 7.3 m) fruit room.
Yield by species 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) per 10 lb block depending on species
Room output A 12 × 24 ft (3.7 × 7.3 m) room gives about 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week at full rolling capacity

Fruit-room design and climate are in Chapter 14 and Chapter 5; yields and pricing for business planning are in Chapter 22.

Storage, transport, drying and cultures

Parameter Value Conditions
Cooler for blocks and fresh mushrooms 1-4 °C (34-40 °F)
Spawn storage 1-2 °C (34-36 °F); at 6 °C (42 °F) quality drops sharply Cap n Stem keeps spawn in a refrigerated trailer (reefer) at 2 °C (35 °F).
Transport Substrate never above 27 °C (80 °F); ship by refrigerated freight; pre-chill spawn before shipping and pack it with gel packs
Drying 24-48 h at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) with dehumidifiers
Dried shelf life About 7 years, sealed and dry
Culture storage (cryo), recommended -80 °C freezer; 10% v/v glycerol, about 3 mL per vial, colonized grain fully submerged; thaw in water at about 30 °C (86 °F)
Water storage of agar plugs Sterile water, cap left 1/8 turn loose, wrapped in parafilm, stored at 1 °C (34 °F)

RANGE Cryoprotectant strength and storage life. Recommended: 10% glycerol, the figure used in most accounts. Also reported: 5% glycerol, from the same farm in other accounts. Storage life: 2-3 years is comfortable , but another practice refreshes stored cultures every 6-12 months. The question is not settled (see open questions).

Storage methods are in Chapter 8; harvest, cooling and drying in Chapter 15.

Labour and cost

Parameter Value Conditions
Labour, cost and price About 1.5 h to make 100 blocks once systems are set up; under $3 per block to make; about $60 gross farmers-market retail per block One grower.

The full business numbers are in Chapter 22.

  • Moisture 54-57% (one experienced grower; method unclear).
  • "A couple of percent more" water than standard for slow species such as maitake (a suggestion).

Chestnut (Pholiota adiposa, as the strain is named)

AT A GLANCE Master's Mix or combo pellets at 61-62% in 10 lb blocks; steady 19 °C (66-67 °F) incubation in low light; 2.5-3 weeks to colonize plus 1-2 weeks or more to ripen; shallow top cut; fruit at 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) in dense fog (90-95% RH to pin); 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) per pellet block; very short shelf life.

RANGE Chestnut time in the fruit room. Recommended: 2-3 weeks if the block was ripened; 4-5 weeks if it was not. The slowest of the mixed species: about 2 months in deep winter if the room is cold.

RANGE Chestnut yield. Recommended target: 2-3 lb (0.9-1.4 kg) or more from a 10 lb pellet block, more than double the raw-sawdust figure (described as about 125% more). Reported figures:

  • About 1-1.5 lb (0.45-0.68 kg) on a 5 lb raw-sawdust block; a 10 lb raw-sawdust block gave the same.
  • Going from 5 to 10 lb raw-sawdust blocks raised yield only about 20%; combo pellets doubled it or more.
  • Historically, a New Hampshire farm grew small blocks of about 4.5-5 lb (2.0-2.3 kg) with fairly small yields.

Pioppino (Agrocybe / Cyclocybe aegerita)

AT A GLANCE Master's Mix 50:50; slow, cool-running incubation of about 3 weeks; fruit warm, 18-24 °C (65-75 °F); turn the lights on once the pin carpet forms.

Reishi (Ganoderma)

AT A GLANCE Reishi is grown for drying, not fresh sale. CO2 controls its shape: high CO2 in the bag gives antlers, low CO2 gives kidney-shaped caps. Expect months, not weeks.

Parameter Value Conditions
Strain Ganoderma lingzhi obtained via John Donahue (1980s, European origin)
Substrate Short logs colonize faster than long ones; logs give better fruit bodies than bags
Bags 10 lb bags can turn mostly into antlers over a year

Species Parameter Value

What goes wrong: the numbers behind common failures

AT A GLANCE Most failures in this chapter come from four things: blocks too big or too wet, heat (at the knock, in the core, in the fruit room), CO2 out of its band, and light at the wrong stage. For a full symptom-by-symptom guide, see Troubleshooting by Symptom.

What you see Cause The number to respect
Block core goes sour and anaerobic Block too big for the bag filter 12 lb (5.4 kg) blocks go anaerobic; stay at 10 lb (4.5 kg) or less in small-filter bags.
Spawn dies after the knock Block core too hot at inoculation At 38 °C (100 °F) or above, spawn dies; knock at about 27-32 °C (80-90 °F).
Leathery stroma skin on blocks Aggressive strain run warm Shows within about 5 days of inoculation; keep blue oyster blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) and grain at about 18 °C (65 °F); keep grain calcium additives at about 0.15%, under 1%.
Heat-loving bacteria in shiitake blocks Core too hot Thermophiles take hold at about 24 °C (75 °F) core; keep it at or below about 23 °C (74 °F).
Patchy, dried-out shiitake blocks Too much fresh air in incubation Room at about 500 ppm CO2.
Water pooling at the bottom of lion's mane blocks Substrate too wet Keep at or below about 62%.
Slow maitake grain spawn Grain slightly too dry 9-10 weeks instead of 4-5 weeks master to G2.
Lion's mane blocks pin in the incubation room Too much light during incubation Keep blocks dim and spawn near dark.
Burned chestnut mycelium on top shelves Bright light too close 6500 K light close above burns it; keep chestnut off the top shelves.
Chestnut pins early in incubation Temperature swings Swings between 16 and 19 °C (60-66 °F) trigger pins.
Long oyster stems with no caps CO2 too high in the fruit room Keep CO2 cycling below 1,000 ppm.
Pale, flat king oyster caps CO2 too high Run exhaust on a CO2 controller.
One huge "washer" black oyster of about 4 lb (1.8 kg) No CO2 control Control CO2; exhaust on at about 800-900 ppm.
Early king oyster crop failures 250 CFM (425 m³/h) fans run constantly, no CO2 meter Cycle on a CO2 controller instead.
Yellowing caps and blotch on black oyster Ultrasonic fogger on a 30/10-minute timer Use a fine high-pressure mist.
Green Trichoderma on chestnut block tops Fruit room too hot Fruit at 13-16 °C (55-60 °F), no higher than about 18 °C (65 °F).
Chestnut blocks do not pin Room at 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) Poor or no pinning in that range.
Short chestnut shelf life Picked late One day late sharply cuts storage life.
Spawn loses quality in storage Cooler too warm At 6 °C (42 °F) quality drops sharply; store at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F).

Key rules

  1. Start every species from the house baseline (10 lb block, about 3% spawn, about 19 °C (66 °F) incubation) and change only what the species table says.
  2. Raise moisture for shiitake (64-65%) and king oyster (62-63%); hold Hericium (lion's mane, comb tooth) at or below about 62% and maitake at 60-61%.
  3. Cut supplementation to 20-30% for shiitake and maitake; consider 30-40% soy for lion's mane.
  4. Keep block cores below about 21-22 °C (70-72 °F) for most species and at or below about 23 °C (74 °F) for shiitake; 10 lb blocks run 2-5 °C (4-9 °F) above room air.
  5. Budget incubation time by species: about 10-14 days for oysters and lion's mane, 2-3 weeks for king oyster and pioppino, 3-6 weeks for chestnut, about 12 weeks for shiitake and 8-12 weeks to harvest for maitake.
  6. Fruit black oyster, king oyster and chestnut at about 10-17 °C (the 50s to low 60s °F); lion's mane at 13-18 °C (55-65 °F); maitake at 16-21 °C (the 60s °F); pioppino at 18-24 °C (65-75 °F).
  7. Keep fruiting CO2 under about 900-1,000 ppm with a narrow band; maitake tolerates "slightly high" CO2 with slow air, and reishi antlers need high CO2 in the bag.
  8. Plan yield at about 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb block unless a species figure is better established (shiitake 3-5 lb, black oyster about 2.7 lb, chestnut on pellets 2-3 lb).
  9. Store colonized blocks and spawn at 1-2 °C (34-36 °F); chestnut blocks keep near indefinitely, black oyster blocks only weeks, lion's mane spawn about 2 weeks.
  10. When figures differ and you can't tell which context fits yours, test on a few blocks with a datalogger rather than picking a midpoint.

Open questions

  • No numeric RH or CO2 targets exist for oyster, pioppino, comb tooth or shiitake fruiting; the house defaults are the only guide.
  • Shelf life is described only in words for every species; no storage days are given.
  • Flush counts are stated only for lion's mane (2) and maitake (1).
  • The block size behind several yield figures (oyster, king oyster, lion's mane) is not stated.
  • Heat output per block differs up to five-fold between reports (see incubation).
  • Cryo glycerol strength (5% or 10%) and storage life (6-12 months or 2-3 years) are unresolved.
  • Pink and golden oyster, cordyceps and cubensis lack nearly all growth settings.
