chapters.html:
Running the Business

AT A GLANCE This chapter covers the money side of a mushroom farm: choosing a business model, what blocks and equipment really cost, planning capacity, labour and staff, buying and shipping, selling, and using yields and records as business numbers. A few rules come up again and again: treat cultivation as three separate businesses and start with one, cost your own labour honestly, size incubation generously, build redundancy and a diverse supply chain, and keep records so you can find the cause when something fails. The numbers people use most:

  • Plan on about 2 lb (0.9 kg) of mushrooms per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block; many growers get 3 lb (1.4 kg).
  • One 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room runs at about 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week on a rolling basis, from about 250 new blocks a week in three weekly cohorts.
  • Give incubation about twice the fruiting space, and 3-4 times for slow species.
  • A home-made block costs about $2.50-3 in materials. Count your labour and the real cost climbs toward the $8.50-9 bought-in price until you make about 2,000-5,000 blocks a week.
  • A 5% contamination rate is about a whole profit margin.
  • Spawn rate for planning: 1 bag of spawn per 20 blocks (about 3%).

Why the business side decides who survives

Many mushroom farms start and many die. The survivors are the ones who do not quit, and who grow on materials and methods that experienced growers recommend rather than reinventing them.

Small-business failure figures are often quoted loosely: about 50% fail in year one, 75% within five years and 98% within ten (unconfirmed). Beware beginner's luck, and do not assume quality holds when you scale up by 1x-5x.

RULE Design from the ideal and work backward. The default should be to justify every corner you cut, not to hunt for corners to cut. Start-ups that look for the cheapest possible proof of concept end up fighting uphill.

Hobby or profit?

The first question to ask yourself, and the first question a consultant asks a would-be farmer, is "hobby or profit?". Most people cannot answer it.

  • The move from hobby to profit is hard. "Save the world" goals, such as avoiding plastic bags, can distract you from building a viable business.

  • Experienced consultants dislike paid consults for complete beginners. They ask clients to email detailed questions first (some send about 40 pages), then hold a focused one-hour call. Build base knowledge or do a bootcamp first; in-person teaching works best.

  • Start on a proven commercial substrate. Coffee grounds are a poor commercial substrate. Use masters mix or a wheat-bran recipe, and choose the cheapest, most available, proven and scalable material. See Chapter 10.

  • Mushroom farming isn't for people trying to make money: there are better uses of capital and time. You can make some money, but it is precarious and a lifestyle, so do it on your own terms. Inflation and labour shortages looked set to stay (as of late 2021).

  • Most mushroom farmers, or their partners, keep a second job; you can't just make the leap unless someone funds it.

  • Many people in the industry burn out fast; the cycle of contamination, sales swings and growth is a "whirlwind".

  • From 2020 to 2024 many people "watched the YouTube videos... sink all your money into it... and don't ask enough questions". Mushrooms have "no shelf stability", so accept some waste rather than sell subpar product.

  • Farms "pop up... so game in one direction" but "haven't spent enough time with the organism and understanding its actual relationship to you and the environment you're putting it in, and then they go belly up". Failure is "largely... some dumb mistake that created too much of a financial burden". The cure is inviting experienced people in.

  • Revenue is not profit. "We could do $5 million and make a hundred thousand": most revenue goes back into the business. Cap n Stem may turn over millions of dollars a year, but its net is "barely enough to sustain its growth". One grower who wants to pay staff a good wage grows carefully because current revenue can't carry it yet. Ask whether you are in the black or the red, not how many accounts you have won.

  • You can't stay in the middle. A tiny diversified farm (mostly vegetables, with some shiitake logs and oysters on straw) can work, but a dedicated mushroom farm has to scale. Two Maine growers, below 340 kg (750 lb) a week, planned to hire at least one employee and quit their jobs at about 450 kg (1,000 lb) a week. Small New England farms run about 500-700 blocks a week; once you pass about 1,000 lb a week you must choose between quitting your job and hiring.

  • One North Carolina grower maxed out her basement at about 90 kg (200 lb), likely per week, before building a warehouse.

  • Stay independent if you can. A Houston grower drew plans for a 465 m² (5,000 ft²) building and spent money on it, then stopped: it would have locked him into management and debt with all the risk on him. He refused outside finance.

Learning from other growers

  • The Commercial Mushroom Growers Facebook group can be blunt to the point of mean. Its real lesson is that experienced farms all share the same problems and all solve them differently, so absorb many methods and adapt them.

  • Talk problems through with other growers, but never treat a single anecdote as gospel. Several matching stories build confidence.

  • More growers' advice is collected in Chapter 26, and the forums, books and people worth knowing are in Chapter 23.

  • About 70% of consulting is "giving people permission". Ask what "a living" means to someone before judging whether a space can make one.

  • Ask first: "do you want to grow for hobby or for profit?" It stumps most people. Cap n Stem consults only after a detailed written list of questions. Get basic knowledge before paying for a consultation; beginners do better with a hands-on boot camp or mentorship.

  • One experienced consultant asked clients to list and rank every question in advance, did not allow recording, and first checked whether the client could realistically do it before taking their money.

  • Learn every step. Think for yourself, and learn every step from agar, cloning and spawn to making and properly steaming blocks before you scale. Growers who only buy and fruit blocks ("fruiters") lack the skills to diagnose problems. Most block-buying farms go on to make their own, and later stop. Expect the farm to take over your relationships and your time.

  • Showing other farmers round your farm lowers suspicion, so you can talk, innovate and work together. Specialty mushrooms (oyster, lion's mane, chestnut, pioppino) are still a small, young industry.

  • The real value of conferences and festivals is meeting people face to face; impressions formed online are often wrong.

Choosing a business model

Three businesses in one

Mushroom cultivation is really three businesses, each with different tools, space and filtration needs:

  1. Culture preservation and spawn. Keeping strains alive on agar, slants or in a freezer and expanding them onto grain (spawn). See Chapter 7, Chapter 8 and Chapter 9.
  2. Fruiting substrate. Mixing, bagging, heat-treating and inoculating blocks. See Chapter 10 to Chapter 13.
  3. Fruiting and fresh sales. Growing the mushrooms out and selling them. See Chapter 14 and Chapter 15.

People tend to drift toward lab work or toward fruiting and selling, depending on their personality. For a start-up, fresh mushrooms are much easier to sell than cultures or spawn, and many new spawn-only companies lack credibility.

RULE Start with one model you can run alone, without hiring.

Fruiting is the easiest stage of the chain to keep decentralized (many small, local farms), then block production, then spawn. The spawn industry is consolidating: Sylvan is buying companies worldwide, Amycel protects its strains in a patent-like way, and a decade ago Paul Stamets required a waiver before he would sell spawn.

  • Specialize. Cap n Stem's view is that "specialization is the only real pathway forward" in the US. Most spawn and substrate producers "made the mistake of continuing to fruit mushrooms"; Cap n Stem stopped fruiting and now sells only substrate and spawn. It works to automate and keep costs down so that farms buying from it "somewhere in the middle of the line" can still run a successful business.
  • A New York farm's advice is the same: you can fruit, or make blocks, or do it all, but you can't do it all and grow as fast as you want. Most specialty growers started in a tent in a basement, so don't be embarrassed by a small start, and talk to other growers, because nothing is standardized yet.
  • "Picks and shovels" businesses (equipment makers and substrate companies) are doing very well, which is why one industry commentator chose media rather than competing with the growers he interviews.
  • Grow kits are a fragile business. During the pandemic a Tallahassee farm made about 1,400 blocks a week at peak as grow kits for another company, while fruiting only about 200 lb (90 kg) of mushrooms, mostly sold locally. When the kit business fell away it pivoted hard to fresh mushrooms, about six times more. Kit sales depend on social-media advertising that can be cut off at any time.

Spore-to-store: doing every stage yourself

"Spore-to-store" means one farm does every stage, from culture to sale. Historically most new farms chose it out of ego and an illusion of frugality, because they did not value their own time.

Spore-to-store can still work long-term in two situations:

  • The farm is small, lean and single-variety, and aims at a fixed steady state, for example being the region's best grower of one mushroom.
  • The farm is remote and has no reliable suppliers.

Growers of a single niche product, such as snow fungus, also suit spore-to-store.

CASE A Japanese log-shiitake grower in Maine started in the 1970s and was still growing in their 80s. From time to time they got sawdust spawn from a family business in Japan, expanded it, inoculated a few batches of logs, fruited them in a greenhouse and sold at the Common Ground Fair, taking about $40,000 in a weekend, including deep-fried shiitake (unconfirmed). Lesson: a lean, single-product operation can do well without a big lab.

Buying in instead of making everything

Most start-up farms that ask for consulting help buy blocks in and fruit them out. Unless you make your own blocks, you need a block supplier. Block suppliers named in the US include Cap n Stem, Earth Angel and Far West Fungi, among others. Find one near you. See Chapter 23.

  • Fruit bought-in blocks. Buying blocks frees a small farm to focus on fruiting skill and on customers (chefs, wholesalers, being visible). That builds market demand before you make a big equipment leap.
  • Fruiting-only can pay well. One block producer (Cap n Stem) says many farms that buy its blocks and simply fruit and sell them make a better living than it does, so a small fruiting-only farm makes sense.
  • Hybrid. Make about 100 blocks a week yourself and buy the other about 150 (one pallet) from a block producer such as Cap n Stem or Far West Fungi, to reach about 500 lb (227 kg) a week. This beats doubling your barrel runs until they become a full-time job.
  • Make bulk spawn only. Buy grain masters (or liquid culture) from a spawn lab and make only the bulk spawn, for example one run a week that produces a month of spawn for one variety.
  • Buy plates. Cap n Stem buys its agar plates and slants from Tip of the Cap instead of pouring hundreds a week in-house. At about $1 per plate, staff time is better spent elsewhere. It first tried Northeast Laboratories, which did not understand mushroom needs, and early on it poured its own.

RULE Culture upkeep takes about the same time at any scale: five varieties means five culture lines to keep fresh. Consider making spawn for only your one or two main varieties and buying the rest. Do not make spawn for a species you also buy in as blocks.

Farms rely on each other's specialties. One Florida grower (Cactus Hat) buys spawn from only two suppliers, Cap n Stem and another large spawn and block maker, and also uses a lot of that maker's Master's Mix.

TIP Reselling is normal. Buy in other specialists' mushrooms (for example another farm's maitake), or have them shipped by Southwest Airlines cargo if you are near a hub, to widen your range with less labour.

CASE A Maine "mushroom farm" bought Kennett Square mushrooms through a produce distributor and simply repackaged them for farmers markets. Reselling becomes normal as you scale, because crops fail.

WARNING Shipping maitake blocks to other farms makes little sense, because maitake has a long incubation that is sensitive to disturbance. It is done anyway, and farms that buy maitake blocks in and then refrigerate and truck them have problems. See Chapter 20.

RULE Learn the stages in this order: master fruiting (on bought blocks) first, then block making, then spawn, then cultures. One Florida farm sold its first 20 or so crops of pink oysters on pasteurized straw to chefs before harvest, and learned fruiting before making anything itself. When it later stopped fruiting, it handed its restaurant clients to a nearby farm.

Farms that buy their blocks.

  • Buying blocks let a Maine farm focus on fruiting: it could build a fruit room for US$3,000-4,000 by Friday, take blocks on Monday and be producing by the next Friday. It paid about US$5.75 a block early on; 5 lb (2.3 kg) shiitake logs from a Pennsylvania supplier were about US$4.25-4.50 (Cap n Stem's were 25 cents more), and 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks about US$8.50. At its best the farm grew 12,000-14,000 lb (5,400-6,400 kg) a week and sold it all, picking about 800 lb (360 kg) of lion's mane a week, with weekend days of 1,000-2,000 lb.
  • A New Hampshire grower made his own blocks briefly, but it took so much time that buying was "a no brainer" for his setup; he fruited only Cap n Stem blocks for over three years.
  • A Washington farm fruits blocks bought from regional block makers, because making its own is "crazy expensive" in time and money. At just under 100 lb (45 kg) a week it sells to restaurants, a natural food store and farmers markets, and plans to make it a full-time family income.
  • A Kansas City farm began by buying ready-to-fruit blocks to grow a large volume quickly, win customers and prove the market, and then built its own production. A large local farm doing about 1,500 lb (680 kg) a week for restaurants had closed during the pandemic, leaving a gap.
  • Don't import blocks from overseas. A Massachusetts grower was advised to import fruiting blocks from Vietnam and refused: transport time, carbon footprint, and no relationship or recourse if they failed. He buys from Cap n Stem, about 2.5 hours away.

CASE When the farm that bought a New Hampshire grower's whole output (50-70 lb, 23-32 kg, a week) suddenly stopped buying, he had 32 kg (70 lb) of oysters a week coming from blocks already ordered. One introduction led to six chefs, who became customers the same day.

Buying mushrooms in (brokering). Big farms buy in a share of their mushrooms to supply steadily; some even import shiitake and logs. A Detroit grower's view is that you are better off growing your own and asking a nearby farm for honest help when you are short, because brokered product varies in quality. A Colorado farm covers crop failures and bad weeks by buying wild mushrooms (it holds the state's wild-mushroom identification certification) from pickers across the country, for example 70 kg (150 lb) of lobster mushrooms; customers who come for morels buy the rest of their order too. Work with nearby competitors: the customer wants what they want.

TIP Focus on one strain first. A California farm tells new farms not to spread into jerky, tinctures and supplements at the start. In Cap n Stem's consultations, 90% of the questions it asks are "how are you going to sell these?"

Case study: from hobby to full-time farm

AT A GLANCE One Florida grower's path from home tent to a dedicated farm building, and the lessons in it: count the numbers early, get debt-free before you quit your job, and sell before you scale.

  • Start. Cactus Hat's founder started around 2013-2014, learning from the Shroomery forum after failed attempts at the lion's mane their partner wanted. Their path ran from a tent at home, to a garage farm, to a dedicated building on a 5-acre (2 ha) property in Brooksville, Florida.
  • Name. The farm's name is a local nickname for the Lutz area of north Tampa. The founder wishes they had chosen a bigger, more scalable name, but locals remember it and the farm has had buy-out offers. Service matters more than the name.
  • Selling. The founder started at a couple of farmers markets, turned out to be a natural salesperson, and moved on to restaurants.
  • Burn-out. The founder ran the farm alongside a 24-hours-on, 48-off firefighter-paramedic job. When mandatory overtime raised their shifts from about 10 to about 15 a month, while they also served about 12 restaurant accounts ordering around 40 lb (18 kg) a week (unclear whether per account or in total), they burned out.
  • Money. For about three years the founder never looked at the numbers, had no LLC and drew no pay. Getting debt-free apart from the house (the Dave Ramsey approach) and cutting living costs made it possible to quit. The last fire shift was 8 February 2022.
  • A buy-out turned down. The founder turned down a buy-out with profit sharing from a shipping-container vertical-farm company. The reasons: the non-compete and NDA terms, not wanting bosses again, and the fact that lab, incubation and sterilizer would have had to fit in 1-2 containers, which limits output unless spawn and blocks are outsourced.
  • Plans. At the new site: mostly fresh sales to larger accounts, plus a moderately priced one-to-one bootcamp with one student per session.
  • Side product. A lion's mane coffee, processed in a friend's commercial kitchen.

The farm's sales methods are in Selling to chefs and markets.

Costs and margins

AT A GLANCE Count labour, including your own, or your costings are wrong. The big costs at scale are labour and utilities (mostly heating and cooling), then rent. Contamination is the hidden cost that eats margins. Prices for equipment and inputs are in the price list.

What a block really costs

A block costs under about $3 in materials when input prices are good. At farmers market prices one block may gross about $60, but that ignores overhead, admin, labour and unsold product. The business is profitable, but less so than people expect, so start bookkeeping (for example in QuickBooks) early.

Growers often say they make blocks for about $2.50, against about $8.50-9 to buy them in. Once labour, including the owner's time, is costed, the true cost per block climbs toward the bought-in price and stays near it until about 2,000-5,000 blocks a week. Adding up material costs is not real costing. Drawn as a curve (an illustration, not measured data), the cost per block rises from $2.50 toward a plateau near $9 and dips only slightly at large scale.

RANGE Cost of a home-made block. Materials: about $2.50-3 a block (one small farm puts it under about $3 when input prices are good; about $2.50 is commonly quoted). Count your labour and the real cost climbs toward the $8.50-9 bought-in price until you make about 2,000-5,000 blocks a week. That curve is the source's own illustration, not a measured cost.

RULE Cost your own labour. A $2.50 materials block is not a $2.50 block until you make thousands a week.

  • Labour, not materials. "I don't care what material costs are, I care what labour costs are." A Tennessee farm plans every process around what its crew of 3-4 people can do.
  • What new growers miss. A Tampa grower's block costs under US$3 to make "when things are good", and at farmers-market prices each block brings in about US$60. That is all new growers see. They don't count overhead, admin, unsold product that dries out and is given away or dehydrated, and labour. Doing his own bookkeeping showed him the farm is profitable, "but not nearly as profitable as people hope". Scale cuts both ways: one large Pennsylvania farm once threw away about 5,000 kg (11,000 lb) of overproduced oysters.

Where the money goes

  • At scale the biggest costs are labour and utilities, then rent if it is unfavourable.
  • Power needs are small apart from heating and cooling, which are the biggest energy cost.
  • Energy is almost impossible to chase down in a mushroom facility. Each extra air exchange adds cost, and sizing for a hot climate (a Texas summer) is expensive. An HVAC specialist usually does the sizing. See Chapter 5.
  • Small inefficiencies (propane, water) do not matter at small scale but matter as you grow. Bulk buying by the pallet, and equipment that saves about 15%, become worthwhile.
  • Making your own spawn costs at least about 1-1.25 days of labour a week, compared with roughly $80-160 a week to buy it in.
  • Culture preservation costs a lot in dishes, agar, slants, bags and labour. Many growers neglect it and notice only when cultures senesce (age and weaken). See Chapter 8.
  • Cryo storage (deep-freezing cultures) is cost-inefficient unless your culture use justifies it. Cap n Stem offers to store other people's cultures in its freezers, and does not sell those cultures unless asked.
  • Bag prices cannot fall much: the bag industry relies on more machines and people rather than on scalable automation.
  • Custom bag sizes are getting harder to get. A former owner of Unicorn, the US grow-bag maker, would do small custom runs; the new management asked for million-unit orders for a custom petri-dish bag, so small growers lose access to custom sizes. See Chapter 11.

Contamination is the hidden cost

RULE A 5% contamination rate is roughly a whole profit margin in agriculture. Do not accept it as "not bad".

One HEPA filter costing $850 and lasting ten years works out to about $80 a year. Contamination costs far more, so a farm that tolerates a fixed 25% contamination rate should diagnose its technique, filter and room instead of living with it. One lab (Cap n Stem's) has not replaced a HEPA in 2.5 years; replacements happen only after damage. See Chapter 4 and Chapter 16.

Small spends that pay back

  • Water treatment. Untreated city water in the humidifier invites bacterial blotch. The about $500 water-treatment upgrade pays back fast in yield and quality. See Chapter 17.
  • Peroxide instead of bleach. Peroxide costs more than bleach but is used at a much lower volume. About five farms have successfully used roughly 0.1% dosing made from drugstore-strength peroxide. See Chapter 17.
  • Heat exchanger. Coroplast sheets cost about $9 each. In a hypothetical example, a Coroplast heat exchanger cut a $1,000-a-month air-conditioning bill to about $200. The saving is a worked example, not a measurement, and the about 85% exchanger efficiency behind it is hearsay. See Chapter 5.

Financing and start-up capital

AT A GLANCE Everything costs more and takes longer than planned. Budget about four times your estimate, at least double the time, and three months of operating cash. Banks rarely lend to mushroom farms, so most growers start small with their own money and grow from sales.

RULE "Figure out how much you think it's going to cost and multiply by four", and at least double the time. Add a "TIM cost" ("the things I missed"): staff not showing up, storms, a pandemic. Another grower's version: "everything costs two times as much and takes three times as long", and no new business makes money until about its third year.

  • Margins in the food chain are thin. Grocery and restaurant margins are 1-5%, so a mushroom farm can't live on a 1% margin; price for a real profit.
  • Cooling is the shock. Proper cold rooms and cooling are a large share of start-up capital: farms in consultation are shocked at "a hundred grand". Old "how to make money growing mushrooms" guides never mentioned heating and cooling costs. One Australian farm's first small cold room was so important that it is still running, barely standing, after being moved.

Cash flow

A farm that buys blocks waits a long time to be paid for each one.

Step Time
Order and pay for blocks about two months before they arrive
Fruit them 6-13 days (call it two weeks)
Sell the crop about another week
Restaurant pays on 30-day terms about four weeks later
Total from paying for a block to being paid for its mushrooms 8-12 weeks, with eight weeks of block bills in a row
  • Keep at least three months of operating capital. A block maker carries its costs for 2-12 weeks before a block even leaves.
  • Seasonal farms. A Colorado farm shuts production every winter (snow, dead winter sales, and a chance to rest and rebuild). It ramps up in March-April and is "in the hole" until June, when members of its community-supported agriculture scheme (CSA, customers who pay in advance for a season of produce) pay up front, bringing in about 30% or more of the year's revenue at once. It has looked at government farm operating loans to cover the restart.

Where the money came from

  • Government loan, slow growth. A Washington grower borrowed about US$600,000 through a USDA beginning-farmer loan in 2009 (about US$300,000 for equipment and US$300,000 for land and buildings), then struggled with repayments because building out alone took a long time. He overbuilt on purpose, so he would not jump from 100 to 600 lb (45 to 270 kg) a week overnight, and grew slowly to about 680 kg (1,500 lb) in a good week. Start small and grow, like the frog in slowly warming water; a sudden US$10 million farm isn't ready.
  • A bank loan that fell through. A California farm was approved for a US$500,000 SBA (Small Business Administration) loan, but after it signed the lease the bank's underwriters pulled it, after 40 days of paperwork and a book-length business plan. It now keeps 6-8 funding options open at once, and would put the house on the line.
  • Own savings only. A Jacksonville grower grows only with money he has, avoiding loans. His landlord takes a percentage of sales instead of a fixed rent, which is ideal for a start-up.
  • Build cheaply. A California farm was built in the late 1980s for about US$150,000, with very low overhead: one founder built the control panels and wired the CO2 sensors himself, and did everything but the concrete. Find people who can do things (a backhoe owner, a welder) to keep build costs down, because "mushroom farming isn't super profitable" at the start. Past a certain scale you do have to pay (that farm paid for a pit to hold three Primus autoclaves). Banks don't lend to mushroom farms, and investors complicate things.
  • Buy an existing business. Rather than start cold, a California grower bought a burned-out young grower's small operation, mainly for its places in good farmers markets (run by a body that interviews growers on their methods and prefers organic) and two wholesale accounts. She bought a house with a garage and yard as a safety net, rather than borrowing for a warehouse. At about 55 kg (120 lb) a week, organic certification isn't worth paying for.
  • Workshops as capital. An Australian farm's mushroom masterclasses paid for its mixer and still sell out in three cities. Grow kits saved it when COVID shut restaurants (its best week ever was followed by a dead week). It also sells spawn and substrate, because Australia lacks supply.
  • Debt as a tool. Two Maine growers, helped by a parent with hospital-finance experience, budgeted to pay themselves and keep savings as a "war chest for the winters". When their delivery van died they planned a business loan or credit line for a reliable one, which also builds a credit record for a business that has none. Debt is a tool if what you buy keeps you producing: a 5-10 year loan becomes just another bill, but plan what you will do if you go into the red, and remember that easy investor money may dry up in a recession.
  • Other starts. A Texas farm was funded from one founder's poker winnings; a business lawyer offered US$4,000 for 35% of the company, and the founders didn't pay themselves. A New Hampshire grower costed a farm building on his land at about US$400,000 and dropped it; he started small and grew without a backer.
  • Fast, funded growth. A venture-backed New York company's Austin farm took 30 days to lease and 30 days to build out, and sold out at once; it then opened two warehouses with 25-30 staff, and was building a 3,300 m² (36,000 ft²) farm in Los Angeles. All its mushrooms go out in compostable cardboard, everyone is paid a living wage, and spent substrate goes to compost and land-remediation projects.

Choosing steam equipment on cost

How steam systems work is covered in Chapter 12. This section is about the money.

RULE Before buying a steam system, compare upfront cost, operating cost (utilities dominate at scale), cycle time and maintenance.

  • An electric autoclave makes sense if you have plenty of amperage, face high oil or gas prices, or run only once a week. The US spawn company North Spore is said to have used electric autoclaves for years.
  • A about $5k shipping container plus an $18-40k low-pressure boiler handles about 1,000 blocks in an 8-10 h run that can be left overnight. A about $30-40k electric autoclave does a couple of hundred blocks a day.
  • Custom steam boxes with three steam generators plumbed in were "not worth it" for one block producer (Cap n Stem). If you can afford a boiler, buy one, because a shipping container gives more control than DIY boxes.
  • Mixer prices have risen sharply, so spend the money on a boiler instead. Pellet systems can use cheap wooden hoppers instead of a mixer.

WHY Substrate is pasteurized rather than sterilized partly because spawn is precious: one bad G2 spawn bag ruins 20 blocks, or 60-80 lb (27-36 kg) of mushrooms.

CHECK A well-run ultra-pasteurization system is reliable at scale. Cap n Stem ultra-pasteurizes thousands of blocks a week and has essentially never had a whole run fail.

Planning capacity

AT A GLANCE Plan the farm backwards from one fruit room. A 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) room takes about 250 new blocks a week and gives about 500 lb (227 kg) a week. Incubation needs about twice that space. Run at least one production run a week, and scale in one decisive leap rather than by adding small equipment. The physical layout is covered in Chapter 3 and fruit-room design in Chapter 14.

Sizing a farm around a fruit room

  • Reference room. A 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room, well run, tops out at roughly 500-600 lb (227-272 kg) a week on a rolling basis. You can cram in more racks, but the room gets too dense and falls out of balance.
  • Racks. A 12 x 24 ft room fits five 2 x 4 ft (0.6 x 1.2 m) five-shelf racks per row, a run of about 20 ft (6 m). Each shelf holds two rows of five 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks, so one rack holds 50 blocks and one row of racks holds 250.
  • Yield. Assume about 2 lb (0.9 kg) of mushrooms per 10 lb block. This is deliberately conservative, since many growers get 3 lb (1.4 kg). So 250 blocks a week gives about 500 lb (227 kg) a week.
  • Cohorts. Blocks spend 2-3 weeks in the fruit room, so plan three weekly cohorts: one row of five racks per week, labelled Week 1, Week 2 and Week 3, each row holding 250 blocks for about 500 lb (227 kg) of mushrooms.
  • Bigger sites. With 2-3 fruit rooms, and harvest, grading and packing moved to another space, a site like Wild Fruitings' (a Maine fruiting farm) could do about 1,000 lb (454 kg) a week.
  • Containers. A 40 x 8 ft (12.2 x 2.4 m) shipping-container fruit room holds thirteen 2 x 4 ft racks, or 650 blocks. See Chapter 14.
  • Typical buyer. A typical small-farm customer of a block producer buys one pallet of about 140 blocks a week. That would be one mix a week if they made their own.

Procedure: size a farm from a weekly sales target

  1. Set the weekly target in pounds of mushrooms, for example 500 lb (227 kg).
  2. Divide by a planning yield of 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block to get new blocks per week: 500 lb needs 250 blocks a week.
  3. Multiply by 3 for the fruit room, because blocks spend 2-3 weeks fruiting: 750 block places, which is one 12 x 24 ft room with three rows of five racks.
  4. Give incubation about twice the fruiting space, with at least three weeks of capacity for fast species and 3-4 times the fruiting space for slow ones. See Incubation space.
  5. Work out spawn at 1 spawn bag per 20 blocks (about 3%): 100 blocks need about five 5 lb (2.3 kg) spawn bags a week, so 250 blocks need about 12-13.
  6. Choose block-making and steam equipment that can supply the week's blocks in one or two days, or plan to buy part of the blocks in (one pallet is about 140-200 blocks).
  7. Schedule the week by task lanes and assign people to them. See Scheduling the week.

CHECK If your fruit room is packed tighter than 250 blocks per row of five racks, or holds blocks that are not ready to fruit, it will fall out of balance. Keep unripe blocks in incubation.

RANGE How full to pack a room. Standard: blocks fill about 1/10-1/4 of the room's volume, for CO2 control. Context: the 12 x 24 ft reference above (250 blocks per row, three rows, 500-600 lb a week) is that room at full capacity with its exhaust sized for the load. For incubation, never fill past about 50%. The older one-third rule (attributed to Paul Stamets) is still quoted. What fraction of its volume the reference room fills was not stated, so log CO2 and heat as you load your own. See Chapter 13.

Planning for time and seasons

  • Small-space scheduling is like Tetris: know each variety's time to harvest so racks free up in time. One small farm must fit about 300 incoming blocks while about 300 spent blocks go to compost each week in summer. Plan for slow and busy seasons.
  • Unripe chestnut blocks sit in the fruit room 4-5 weeks before harvest, while ripened blocks need only 2-3 weeks. Do not clog fruit rooms with unripe blocks.
  • Ripened chestnut blocks can sit without fruiting, so chestnut works as a buffer crop that smooths the peaks and troughs of other species.
  • Fruiting speed responds non-linearly to temperature: 13 °C (55 °F) is much slower than 18 °C (65 °F), so a swing of about 5-6 °C (10 °F) can shift delivery by about 5 days. Plan around customer deadlines.
  • Reliable climate control means you have mushrooms when competitors' crops fail, so you can take their orders.

Incubation space

RULE Give incubation roughly twice as much space as fruiting, and 3-4 times as much for slow species.

  • For fast species with about two weeks of incubation, provide three weeks of incubation space. At 80 blocks per Bubba barrel run and 80 blocks per rack, that means at least three racks, spaced so they can breathe.
  • Shiitake incubation runs from about 6 weeks at the fast extreme to 14 weeks, depending on strain. So shiitake needs roughly 5-10 times more incubation space for the same output as a fast species; a fast species gives the same mushrooms from about 20% of that space.
  • Owners who buy buildings nearly always undersize incubation, and ignore the sun's path and the roof colour. One farm owner regrets building incubation too small.
  • Do not pack an incubation room solid with no fans or airflow, as one upstate New York farm did. See Chapter 13.
  • Climate matters. Coastal San Francisco Bay Area farms such as Far West Fungi are very stable, but inland and extreme climates (Arizona, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Maine's swings) need a plan for heat and cold. Do not trust a building's builder to have considered heat.

CASE An Oregon grower's blocks first lived in his living room; grant funding then bought more shipping containers. He planned four fruiting and two incubation containers "because we're doing a lot of oysters back then". When he switched to slow species during the pandemic he found "I need a lot more space to incubate because this isn't oyster town. It's not one to one. Can't just turn and burn them", so a third container became incubation. He adapted hundreds of wire shelves on castors: "casters are the game", from the steam box through to fruiting.

Batch versus rolling production

RULE Plan for at least one production run every week, with cooling and incubation in separate spaces. A plan that shares one room and takes turns (one knock, incubate everything, empty the room, repeat) works only until the first new customer needs more, usually within weeks.

A small farm's week with one Bubba barrel, for about 100 blocks of 10 lb (4.5 kg):

Day Work
Day 1 Mix, load and clean, then start the barrel around dinner time; it runs about 15-16 h
Day 2 Lab prep and spawn work
Day 3 Knock, shake and rack the blocks
Result about 100 blocks, about 200 lb (91 kg) of mushrooms a week: less than half of a 500 lb (227 kg) target
  • You cannot scale by multiplying small equipment: 2,000 blocks a week would need about 20 Bubba barrels. Cap n Stem struggled to make even half its blue oyster spawn with All American pressure canners.
  • It is better to wait and make one larger leap, to equipment that can supply two fruit rooms in a day or two, than to step up to a single Bubba barrel.
  • Demand is lumpy. Big orders appear and vanish (for example, a school customer closing for the summer), which forces decisions about buying in versus producing.
  • Cancelled orders and overproduction (auto-fruiting or side-pinning blocks) usually end up composted or sold as soup mushrooms or seconds. Drying is the alternative, and owning a reefer or walk-in cooler makes drying easier to schedule. See Chapter 15.
  • Scale changes what a loss means: a large farm once discarded about 11,000 lb (5,000 kg) of oysters after overproducing.
  • Small tweaks pay. An extra week of incubation for black oyster can mean more income per production run.

  • "It only takes an hour and a half to do 100 blocks" once the systems are in place, and spawn is easy too, says a Tampa grower. The trick is not to keep changing or over-analysing systems once they work: build the lab, set the filters and the sealer, then leave them alone.

Spawn expansion: capacity and risk

Spawn multiplies at every step, so each culture plate carries a lot of future income, and a lot of risk. The steps are explained in Chapter 9.

  • For 100 x 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks at 1:20 (about 3% spawn; 1:40 for 5 lb (2.3 kg) blocks) you need about five 5 lb spawn bags a week.
  • Expansion from one held-back dish. The dish is expanded to about 4 dishes. Each dish gives about 4 grain masters of 4 lb (1.8 kg), so 16 masters in all. Each master gives about 20 G2 bags, so four masters give 80 G2 bags, and one 80-bag G2 run can inoculate about 1,600 substrate bags at 20 blocks per G2 bag.
  • Lion's mane chain. One vial (about 5-6 carriers) feeds slants; about 8 plates per slant; up to 30-some G1 masters per plate; 12 G2 bags per G1; and 20 blocks per G2. The quoted total is about 480 masters per vial; the spoken and written numbers for this chain do not fully agree.
  • One plate. One plate feeds 6-12 G1 masters, so a bad plate could ruin "upwards of 240 bags" (as stated; the full chain maths gives a far larger number).
  • One vial. A single cryovial can lead to about 60,000 lb (27,000 kg) of mushrooms. Showing staff this connects their role to the whole farm.

CHECK Do the multiplication yourself. 72 G2 bags x 20 blocks = 1,440 blocks, roughly 4,300-7,200 lb (1,950-3,270 kg) of mushrooms at 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg) per block. (This example has been miscalculated as "288 blocks, about 700 lb".) The point stands: plate errors cascade.

Planning for surplus and buffers

RULE "Figure out what you're going to do with your extra product because you're always going to have extra product." Make your own line (jerky, dried, powder) or partner with a company that does. Don't sell cheap to dump surplus. A shipping container converts easily into a dehydrator ("some type of heating element and a fan").

  • Grow most of it, buy the rest. A Kennett Square saying: "grow 80 or 90% of what you need and buy the rest." You can usually buy the gap cheaply, though sometimes the extra 10% costs more. One Pennsylvania farm used to be "the 10%" for the big farms, selling everything the same day, farm to farm, because its cooler was very small.
  • Don't plan blocks from today's sales. Today's sales are not the sales three weeks from now. Cut back today and you are short later, "chasing your tail".
  • Keep spare blocks. For weekly standing orders, a North Carolina grower always makes extra blocks and keeps some "on ice" in the walk-in, so one failed rack (for example a lion's mane batch gone wrong) doesn't mean a missed order. Cap n Stem "is always building a buffer to sort of bail farms out": in one week three farms needed hundreds of blocks of one variety because something failed on their end or a big customer changed its order.
  • Plan for sudden big demand. A buyer wanting 450 kg (1,000 lb) of shiitake a week can't be served when shiitake takes 60-odd days to incubate. Maitake ("hens") is the species growers chase, but most buyers don't know what to do with it.
  • Track waste. A Massachusetts farm wasted up to 66% of its mushrooms (unsold) for a period one winter. The grower built a calculator (blocks, pounds, cost and sale price, with a built-in 25% food-waste line) to show the farm should cut production until sales caught up. Donating excess to a community free fridge, with a receipt for the donation, avoids waste.
  • Seasons differ by place. A large California farm's busiest time is summer, while nearby farms and Japan are slow then because there is "way more produce on the market". A German farm's mushroom sales "go to like nothing" for two or three months in white-asparagus and strawberry season. The same California farm also brokers about 70 varieties a year, including button and portobello, because buyers want one supplier.

Yields as business numbers

AT A GLANCE Plan on 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block, whatever you hope for. Species differ a lot: shiitake can give 3-5 lb, king oyster only about 2. Full species-by-species numbers are in Chapter 21.
