  • Bigger blocks pay. Moving from 5 lb (2.3 kg) to 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks, on raw sawdust with soy hulls, wheat midds and pea hulls, raised yield, so each block was cheaper per pound of mushrooms. Customers got more than double the mushrooms per block, and pallets carry 160-180 large blocks instead of 320 small ones, which means less handling.
  • Strain yield underpins customers' income. Cap n Stem keeps its high-yield house blue oyster strain despite its stroma sensitivity, because customers' businesses depend on its yields. Small, dainty strains do not pay the same.
  • King oyster is a craft crop. Kings will not yield like other oysters even when everything is right. They are a craft crop, not a meal ticket, and not worth growing without cooling and air handling.
  • Bottle farms work on different numbers. Mycopia, a bottle grower, counts a third of a pound (150 g) as a fast, easy crop. Bottle-tray economics per square metre leave you chasing other farms' prices, and bag growing is preferred over bottles for that reason.
  • European versus US style. European producers (for example on the Mycelia and Sylvan websites) list longer incubation and lower average yields. That reflects a gentle, scientist-style approach versus the hot US "cowboy" approach; neither is better. The US style uses master's mix with 50% soybean hulls in 10 lb blocks. Foreign growers see this as costly, CO2-rich "turn and burn", but US farms prioritize speed, bigger fruits and consistent yields.
  • Chestnut is a business staple. Chestnut rates 10-11 out of 10 for business importance (lots of spawn and blocks are sold worldwide) but only 6 out of 10 to eat. It is a very high-yielding, reliable commercial mainstay, though no yield figures were given.

RANGE Chestnut yield on raw sawdust in 10 lb versus 5 lb blocks. Expect combo pellets to double chestnut yield or more compared with raw sawdust; this is agreed. On raw sawdust, one account found 10 lb blocks gave the same yield as 5 lb blocks (about 1-1.5 lb, 0.45-0.7 kg), while another found yield rose by about 20%.

Supply chain

AT A GLANCE Keep several suppliers for every ingredient, watch commodity prices, value reliable supply over low price, and never buy the cheapest grain. Suppliers are listed in Chapter 23.

Raw materials

  • Treat recipes as living documents. Raw materials such as soy hulls and oak are limited and their availability changes, so know your alternatives. See Chapter 10.
  • Soy is roughly the second-largest North American crop and is mostly exported, and soy hulls mostly go to animal feed. Their price follows macroeconomics and weather, not mushroom demand, so watch commodity prices and buy ahead of shortages.
  • Build a supply chain and stick with it, but keep several sources per ingredient. Even Cap n Stem's combo pellets have multiple suppliers.
  • Grain: sorghum is pricier and less available (grown in Kentucky, Missouri and the lower Midwest). Millet comes mostly from eastern Colorado and spikes in price during droughts. Rye and oats grow across the northern states. Stay flexible, value supply over price, and do not buy the cheapest grain. See Chapter 9.
  • Sorghum is attacked by insects faster than other grains, so storing truckloads long-term needs protection.
  • Grain spawn will always need hands-on human care. Parts can be automated, but it is an artisanal process that depends on a commodity.

CASE Early grain sourcing at one Maine spawn lab: a tote of millet from a small Pennsylvania broker arrived full of broken grain, gnats and grubs; feed-store bags often held bugs, corn and rat droppings; and locally sourced Maine grain was about 50% bugs and debris. Lesson: ask suppliers about cleaning and grade before you buy.

CASE Cap n Stem's first sawdust supplier was a small local operator near Damariscotta/Jefferson, Maine. Supply was limited and costly, so it switched to a large New Hampshire pallet maker.

  • Freight is a big hidden cost. A full truckload of substrate from Missouri to Maine cost US$1,200-2,800 before COVID and about US$5,000-5,400 in 2021.
  • Buy in bulk, or club together. Bulk suppliers want full truckloads (18-33 tonnes) and silos. Small farms club together on orders (for example five pallets) to get a price break and share a drop-off point.
  • To get supplement or pellets under about US$500 a ton delivered (in 2,000 lb, 900 kg, bulk bags), buy by the truckload from the biggest mills. Local mills made wheat-bran pellets for one Washington farm, so the bran moves in an auger and stores compactly. A 4 cubic yard (3 m³) commercial mixer now costs about US$80,000; a home-built pellet mixer cost about US$1,400. Target 61-66% moisture.

Combo pellets

Combo pellets are ready-made sawdust-and-soy-hull pellets that you only add water to. See Chapter 10.

  • Combo pellets (from any maker) are 100% red oak plus soy hulls, ground, moisture-matched, passed through 5-6 air-mixing stages and pelletized, with each pellet within about 1% of the target ratio. Blends are 50:50 (Master's Mix) and 70:30. They are shelf stable.

  • Combo pellets hydrate within about 10 s. Mixing raw sawdust and soy takes much more labour, which offsets the pellets' higher price.

  • Combo pellets ended sifting sawdust at Cap n Stem. The old process took huge manual labour for a substrate "half as good" as today's. One grower would not go back to raw sawdust after using combo pellets.

  • Large crews with staff turnover cannot manage complex recipes reliably, so a simple standard mix suits them. Smaller farms, such as Jordan's at Texas Fungus, can run elaborate recipes.

  • Makers: Top Shelf Fungi began making combination pellets about six years before this account was given, and Cap n Stem became its customer and partner. Mushroom Media Online is the other maker at scale; it originally just mixed separate soy pellets and fuel pellets. Another company launched a compressed sawdust-soy "combo brick".

  • Customers rarely complain about slight variation in block weight, and blocks also lose weight in incubation.

  • Many US farms' combo pellets come from Canada, because it is cheaper than US mills. A 25% tariff raises substrate cost, and imported equipment may cost about 30% more; each farm must decide whether to absorb the increase or pass it on.

  • Some suppliers sell sterilized dry substrate that the farm hydrates itself, which halves the shipping weight. Filter patches let air back in, though, so shelf life depends on the sterilization cycle; the method is still being worked out.

Decentralization protects the industry

  • Networks of many smaller farms, and diverse supply chains (grain, sawdust, pellets), protect the industry. A large centralized operation hit by bacterial blotch loses orders of magnitude more.
  • The Korean oyster industry was wiped out for a while by a virus (unconfirmed), which has been linked to centralized distribution of a few strains (for example the "PO 775" strain base).

Shipping and logistics

WARNING Temperature is the variable that always bites when shipping spawn, blocks, cultures or fresh mushrooms, especially in summer.

  • Shipping blocks by pallet costs about $500-1,000 (up to about $1,600) for about 150-200 blocks (160 typical). That can kill the buy-in model for distant farms, for example in Nebraska.
  • If blocks come by LTL (less-than-truckload) refrigerated or dry freight, the site road must take an 18-wheeler. See Chapter 3.
  • Block shipping cartons are perforated for refrigerated freight, and pallets are stacked with air channels down the middle so blocks hold temperature.
  • Big companies entering block sales often ship in boxes without vent holes. This is a mistake: blocks need ventilated cartons.
  • Customers have packing preferences. One Vermont customer farm has particular requirements, local pickups are packed in Gaylord bins, and packed pallets wait in refrigerated containers for the truck.
  • Pre-chill spawn in reefers before shipping, because packed, active spawn self-heats. Gel packs first chill, then buffer, then give out, so heat stress usually hits at the end of transit. Ship fast. See Chapter 15.
  • Ship shiitake blocks at this stage: fully brown and "popcorned" (bumpy), with a few cap-only pins at most and no stems. Blocks with pins and stems everywhere go only to customers who pick up.
  • To refrigerate G2 spawn for later sale, stop it at about two weeks. Do not sell spawn that is auto-fruiting.
  • Comb tooth spawn takes about half a week longer than lion's mane but stays in spawn mode (it does not rush to fruit). Supplement and extract companies increasingly use it.

TIP Label every bag the same way. One spawn lab's grain-bag label reads "Maine Cap N' Stem Mushroom Co / Comb Tooth G1 121323-HCFF-2": species, generation, date (MMDDYY), strain code, bag number.

  • Shipping blocks or spawn long distances isn't feasible for a small farm: heat and cold in transit, and losing five blocks is a lot.
  • Share delivery runs. For years a Philadelphia-area mushroom farm shared delivery days with a microgreens grower: one day each, carrying each other's product. Chefs liked it, because they want fewer vendors and the same delivery person on the same day. At the kitchen back door "you're number 22 this hour... get in and get out". Cap n Stem once shared a van with a tortilla maker, and a big Kennett Square distributor carries exactly mushrooms plus microgreens.
  • An online local farm hub (pick list on Tuesday, deliveries or hub pickup Wednesday-Thursday) kept one California farm's sales going in the pandemic. Petri dishes and a fruiting block on the market table start conversations.

Selling

AT A GLANCE Sell before you scale. Win restaurant accounts with free samples and dish ideas, raise prices before adding accounts, be honest when quality is off, and never oversell medicinal claims. Packing and grading are in Chapter 15.

Selling to chefs and markets

Many growers start at a couple of farmers markets and move on to restaurants, as one Florida farm did once its founder turned out to be a natural salesperson.

  • Ask yourself, as a would-be farmer, whether you have ever sold anything.
  • Approach chefs outside dinner service, deliver early when kitchens open, and wear consistent branded clothing so you are recognized.
  • The main sales tactic: give a new account free lion's mane to trial, with a concrete example of another restaurant's dish.
  • Learn what chefs do and pass it on. For example, lion's mane offcuts left from cutting steaks can become crab-cake-style patties or a salad topping sold as an upcharge.
  • Rule of thumb for chefs: a pound (450 g) of lion's mane is about a softball-sized piece.
  • Lion's mane is very popular in Tampa/St Petersburg, Florida. One farm there has helped 3-4 people launch food trucks around it, for example selling vegan "boneless wings".
  • Be honest, discount when quality is off, and communicate. One grower has never lost an account over a missed order or odd-looking lion's mane.
  • Trade mushrooms with local businesses for goods or food: barter is underrated.

How growers won restaurant accounts.

  • Ask for a standing order. A New Hampshire grower's pitch to each new chef: "tell me this is what I want every week and then I can grow that for you." If a chef only orders week by week, you can't know what to grow. Once a chef has a standing order they never need to call again unless they change it. Many new farms let chefs keep changing orders and then had to keep changing their block orders.
  • Make an appointment. Approach chefs by phone or appointment and bring product; don't cold-knock on the kitchen door, and never turn up unannounced, least of all an hour before Saturday service. The product must work with the chef's food cost.
  • Bring the farm to them. A New York grower walked into restaurants just before opening, the chef's worst time, carrying a fruiting block. When told the chef was busy, he set the block on the counter; staff crowded round and the chef had to come and talk. The same company got a 1.1 kg (2.5 lb) king oyster onto a Michelin-starred menu. A Jacksonville grower simply walks in with a box of mushrooms.
  • Carry ideas between chefs. Posting the dishes chefs made with your mushrooms gets other chefs wanting to make them. Carrying a menu concept (not a dish) from one chef to another can open several accounts. Show a chef what others are making and give some lion's mane free to try.
  • Know the uses. Lion's mane is "everywhere" in Tampa and St Petersburg because of the vegan scene: three or four food trucks started on lion's mane (vegan boneless wings, a vegan chicken sandwich). Cutting it into sandwich shapes leaves end pieces, which chefs shred into crab cakes or put on salads. Knowing these details helps you sell to new accounts.
  • Respect other growers. Set prices from your own costs and plan, not 25-50 cents under another grower's list. Before pitching a restaurant, ask whether it already works with another mushroom farmer; one customer chose a grower because she asked. Don't take a distributor's existing customers. Treat customers as partners whose profit depends on you showing up every week with consistent quality and quantity. About 95% of that grower's business now comes to her.
  • Chefs give you "one mulligan". Miss a delivery once and they forgive it; miss twice and they never buy again, because their menu depends on you. That is why many chefs buy everything from one food-service rep. To break in, prove consistency and variety. A California farm designed its building as a showroom with windows, so chefs and front-of-house staff could tour it (about an hour), and that "blew our business up".
  • Word of mouth. At the same farm, demand came from chefs talking to each other. About 30 restaurants verbally asked to be put on a waiting list (5-18 kg, 10-40 lb, each) for when it expanded, which was still a risk since nothing was signed. It now supplies over 125 restaurants a week, with zero debt.

How restaurant businesses grew.

  • A Memphis grower's first restaurant customer bought 4.5-9 kg (10-20 lb) of oysters a week; his goal was only to replace his income as a waiter. Four or five years of samples and visits built a market that hadn't existed. At one point he grew about 135 kg (300 lb) a week in his back yard with one full-time worker and his mother part-time on sales and admin.
  • Each city has a rough limit on what its fashionable restaurants will buy, after which you must look beyond restaurants. Before growing a species, find out what people near you need: what restaurants buy, what other farms grow, what substrate you can get locally. "Exactly where you are is going to determine your success or failure more than anything else."
  • In a small college town there weren't enough restaurant sales, so a Tallahassee grower drove more than two hours to farmers markets in Gainesville; he later had 30-40 chefs. Early sales were often co-ops and natural food stores taking three pounds a week (about US$30). He also supplied about 50 blocks a week to another farm.
  • A Texas farm's first chef ordered 23-32 kg (50-70 lb) of mushrooms a week in total and said "text me on Monday what you'll have for the week, I'll just buy it all"; the farm could supply about 7 kg (15 lb).
  • When a Vermont farm grew about 6 kg (14 lb) a week in a 0.6 x 1.2 m (2 x 4 ft) tent, a chef offered to take 16-18 kg (35-40 lb) a week, flexible week to week ("if you have to give me less one week, it's cool"), which gave the growers the confidence to expand.
  • A Philadelphia-area farm chose restaurants over farmers markets early on: with young children, a day driving to, setting up and staffing a market earned less than a few extra restaurant clients on a delivery run with a cheque in the post. Ten years on, every local market has new mushroom growers, though the city's restaurant scene is big enough that local growers don't really compete.
  • Lion's mane sales grow with teaching. A Massachusetts grower's customers who tried a quarter-pound box and followed his cooking directions came back for a pound a week, and regulars keep sales steady even on rainy market days. Restaurants were slower: chefs didn't know how to put it on the menu, pricing was unclear, and sampling visits took a lot of driving. In the city he would have had to charge about US$26 a pound for lion's mane.

CASE COVID showed how fast restaurant sales can vanish.

  • A New Hampshire grower was selling about 680 kg (1,500 lb) a week to over 70 restaurants when they closed. Weeks of blocks were already growing, so he made pot pies and sold through a local farm hub's home-delivery service. He is now at 35-40 restaurants plus farm stores and home delivery, close to his old volume. To keep customers he cut US$2 a pound on every species except shiitake, and had not raised prices back despite rising costs.
  • A Texas farm had every wholesale order cancelled on one Monday. Outdoor farmers markets carried it, and the 2021 national shortage of oyster and shiitake was a boon. Its local distributor understood "this is a living thing", paid every week rather than on 30- or 60-day terms, and promoted the farm.
  • A Washington farm emptied incubation into fruiting and sold about 1,800 half-pound bags of shiitake through a large Seattle CSA. At its first market years earlier it had sold out 4.5 kg (10 lb) in a day, when only 1 in 100 people had heard of lion's mane.
  • Florida was "a mushroom wasteland" apart from white buttons and five-day-old oysters, which shows how much room a fresh local grower can have.
  • One grower keeps orders on paper with a call list; others use a spreadsheet, since there is no special software. He likes knowing every client personally, and is wary of big grocery accounts that will drop you if you can't supply 230 kg (500 lb).

Farmers markets

AT A GLANCE Markets bring good cash on a good day, but they cost a full day of work, need shade and cooling, and small rural markets can't carry a farm. Pick big, established markets, talk to the other mushroom sellers, and be ready to answer the same questions all day.

  • Choose bigger markets. Two Maine growers' early markets earned as little as about US$50 for three hours. They dropped those, moved to bigger, established markets that already had a following and wanted mushrooms, and doubled their number of markets rather than doing one every day. Another farm took in about US$2,000 at a single market day. Markets carry more cash than they did years ago, but they are a lot of work, and some farms quit markets for a few wholesale accounts.
  • Small rural markets with many vendors can't carry a farm: one grower selling chaga and mushrooms at small rural markets once made US$300 in a week for 65 hours' work.
  • Several mushroom growers can share a market. "There are eight strawberry vendors at every farmers market I do, and they all sell out"; two or three mushroom growers can share one too. When four growers at one Tennessee market brought the same mushrooms, things changed once they told each other their plans: some moved to shiitake, some to wild mushrooms, some to other species, and those became the best money days. Kill a new competitor with kindness: tell them what you'll bring next week.
  • Answer the questions. The top questions at markets are: what is it, is it edible, will it make me trip, how do I cook it, and what does it taste like. Make a list of answers. Some customers think lion's mane is psychedelic; misinformation is constant. People ask for recipes; "just cook them like a mushroom". Tourists often say they have never seen lion's mane.
  • Seasons. Summer markets are flooded with fruit and vegetables, so mushrooms are less exciting; in winter (root vegetables and kale) mushrooms stand out.
  • At their first Oregon markets, customers asked only for foraged chanterelles, porcini and lobster mushrooms, so one grower foraged about 23 kg (50 lb) of chanterelles a week to bring. Restaurants were the early buyers of cultivated mushrooms, and chefs wanted oysters rather than shiitake, which they had had for years.
  • One Kansas City farm also sells 5 lb grow kits through garden and hydroponic stores and online.

WARNING Mushrooms lose weight fast in the sun. At his first market in summer heat, one grower brought 9 kg (20 lb), sold about 2.3 kg (5 lb) and came home with about 4.5 kg (10 lb): about 2.3 kg had evaporated. He now uses two coolers (about 2.7 kg, 6 lb, of boxed mushrooms each) plus a box with ice packs underneath, wrapped in pallet film, under the table, and moves heat-exposed stock to the dehydrator. Another grower hangs burlap for shade and uses reflective foil. Better still, buy a refrigerated van or a cooler on wheels; a plugged-in van is also a backup fridge.

WARNING Markets are long hours. A Colorado grower dropped a poor Saturday market to avoid burnout, after six to eight months a year of seven-day weeks starting at 4-5 am. Hire one or two seasonal helpers, though training is hard because so much of the work is intuition. "Fail forward": it's a marathon.

Selling direct when markets close.

  • When farmers markets closed in 2020, a New Hampshire farm ran a "pop-up market" in its car park (no table fee, 1-7 pm, a few vendors) and sold far more than expected. A local food alliance went from 30 home deliveries a week to over 1,000 in four weeks, because its online ordering already existed.
  • A Detroit farm's five-hour driveway sale (fire pit, music, a social-media video) did better than any farmers market and better than a day of restaurant deliveries. A restaurant is a middleman; selling direct brings more take-home money for less fuel.

RULE Don't stop production, even for a week. A gap "boomerangs" three to five weeks later, when you have nothing to sell.

Grocery, distributors and wholesale

AT A GLANCE One wholesale drop can replace twenty restaurant stops, but wholesale pays less, demands insurance and strict delivery, and can drop you without warning. Wholesale-only farms need very large volume to break even.

WHY Retail-focused companies make most of their profit on retail. "If you are focusing only on wholesale to distributors, that's hard to make profit getting $4 a pound on oysters... You gotta go 10,000 pounds a week to even break even." Cap n Stem's first consulting question is "how are you gonna sell it?" With no answer, don't grow fast.

  • One stop instead of twenty. A Maine farm found one delivery to a food distributor (a pallet dropped at the depot) replaced about 20 restaurant stops. In Kennett Square, packers buy mushrooms, put any farm's label on them and deliver on 30-day terms, so some "farms" are mostly distributors.
  • Distributors take a cut. A Louisiana farm, with restaurants about 90% of its business, was asked by a distributor for 20-25% of the sale price plus all its restaurant accounts, and higher prices. It refused, sells direct and hand-delivers every order, which builds feedback and relationships. When it did sell through others, it raised prices, because quality control passed out of its hands. The same farm reads restaurant traffic (hotel bookings, events coming to town) to plan production.
  • Supermarkets can be hard. A New Hampshire farm was in about 185 Whole Foods stores until it pulled its product: no contract, orders that stopped and started, long delivery drives, and product left in a wicker basket at about 20 °C (68 °F). Customers blame the farmer for bad-looking mushrooms, not the store. Whole Foods is cut-throat: a pallet off on weight or temperature is rejected and you buy it back.
  • Produce buyers matter more than shelf space. A Texas grocery chain put mushrooms unrefrigerated in the middle of the produce section, against the grower's advice, because they sell fast enough that quality doesn't suffer. Data showed mushroom buyers were the chain's biggest-spending customers. Austin buyers wanted whole golden oyster clusters (three per 5 lb case), because customers take a whole one home for the grill, unlike New Yorkers with small fridges.
  • Remote farms struggle with wholesale. A grower far from any city sold to his local grocery store, but the big chains would only buy through their wholesaler, which required US$1 million of insurance and delivery to its dock by 5 am daily. After cutting his price for the wholesaler and driving 3.5 hours each way, "I wasn't making any money". Farmers markets sold out, but they were weekly and all on the same day, so a one-person farm could do only one.
  • Big accounts can vanish in a week. A Houston farm supplied a company holding the contract for a large Texas grocery chain, plus a large restaurant chain, both through knowing the right people; when they said "we don't need them this week" he was left with 230 kg (500 lb) of lion's mane and nowhere to send it.
  • The 80/20 rule. A small share of customers gives most of the volume with little trouble; the many small ones cause most of the work. A Pennsylvania farm's sales staff manage 125 customers. From its early website, of every 100 callers about 20 came to buy, 10 came back a second week, and one or two became long-term customers. It stopped selling spawn because small orders jammed the sales office, and tried a US$500 minimum.
  • Buying blocks is a business choice too. For a buyer, a US$20 box of mushrooms resold for US$25 is a success, and so is a block that produces US$25-30 of mushrooms, with more work. Each step back down the chain (blocks, then spawn, then raw materials) adds margin but also more chance of failure. Farms that went vertical in recent years often come back to buying blocks; there is a scale below which making your own doesn't pay.
  • Grow the pie before fighting over it. One large Pennsylvania farm's plan to grow demand is to put specialty mushrooms "centre of the plate", with a picture of a meal on the package at an affordable price: "we need to grow the pie before we fight over it." Some market sellers buy its boxes and resell at up to 100% markup; that is fine if it's honest, and it cuts days off distribution.
  • Educate customers. The market data says specialty mushrooms barely exist, because supply was never there to measure demand. Cook a golden oyster in salt and oil in front of people: about 20% of those who "didn't like mushrooms" changed their minds for one New York company. Shelf-stable products let people try a species before buying it fresh.
  • Mini farms in stores. The same company put fruiting cabinets in stores and restaurants; one in a supermarket grew about 18-36 kg (40-80 lb) a week in a small footprint, sometimes with blocks already pinned before going in. Demand outran the cabinets, so it began supplying from a central farm too.
  • Home delivery. When New York shut down, the company sold from a van via an online form with a 2.3 kg (5 lb) minimum per delivery. Many repeat customers bought 5 lb a week, some eating about 18 kg (40 lb) in a summer, against a US average of about 0.9 kg (2 lb) per person per year (perhaps 4.5-14 kg, 10-30 lb, in China). It gave mushrooms and blocks free to people who had no money, especially food-service workers. One block, given 2-3 flushes at home, can feed a household for a week or two (2.3-3.2 kg, 5-7 lb, or more).
  • Catawba Mushrooms (North Carolina) sells at six farmers markets every Saturday and runs two refrigerated delivery vehicles. Its output grew from 180 to 360 to 450 and now 450-545 kg (400, 800, 1,000 and 1,000-1,200 lb) a week, but it is "not very profitable" yet; equipment is the bottleneck.

Imports and competition

AT A GLANCE Imported shiitake logs set the US wholesale price for shiitake. Selling more than a few hundred pounds of shiitake puts you in a global market. Oysters are also falling in bulk price, which is why growers look to other species.

  • Scale of imports. In 2024, 3,583 shipping containers of shiitake logs, labelled "mushroom spawn", entered the US (public customs data). One block maker estimates that is about 42,000 tonnes (93 million lb) of shiitake, roughly US$400 million wholesale and US$700 million retail. Early imported logs sold for under US$1 each, which shut down large Pennsylvania substrate producers: a block that costs about US$5 to make can't compete with US$1. Some overseas firms now produce in the US (one Washington site has about 18,600 m², 200,000 ft², of fruiting space).
  • Landed cost. Chinese shiitake logs landed in New Jersey at about US$1.70 each and fell to US$1.25-1.50 (sometimes delivered to the farm). A container cost US$6,000-7,000 and held 12,000-14,000 logs, so about 50 cents of each log's price was shipping. The logs take 90-100 days to grow abroad and fruit in about 7 days in the US, yet are sold as "product of USA". Organic certification of overseas suppliers relies on third-party audits that are hard to check.
  • All the large US shiitake farms grow on imported blocks; one supplier makes millions a year, and they are "legit, awesome" blocks that compete on both price and quality. Buyers' loyalty is to the lowest price. Shipping losses (refrigeration failures, freezing) still happen.
  • When imports stopped. When shipping stopped in 2021, shiitake vanished and the wholesale price rose from about US$3.60 to US$5.65 a pound. Imports had already driven US shiitake block makers out of business; one large Pennsylvania farm stopped and restarted. Most farms bank on shiitake plus a little oyster, and Cap n Stem had to limit shiitake to about a pallet per farm.
  • In October 2021 that Pennsylvania farm told small farms it could no longer supply blocks or fresh mushrooms. Fresh mushrooms paid better than blocks; during the years of cheap imported logs and labour shortages it had rented out grow rooms; and Kennett Square wholesale shiitake was about US$5.50 a pound, after being a loss leader for most of Kennett's history. At its height it made about 80,000 five-pound blocks a week (about 36,000-73,000 kg, 80,000-160,000 lb, of mushrooms). It cut costs "to the bone" to keep about 100 people employed.

RULE Never sell fresh mushrooms in competition with your own block customers.

  • Shiitake is the import most competitive with US growers. Selling more than a few hundred pounds locally puts you in a global market, and a few US farms produce 450-4,500 kg (1,000-10,000 lb) a week.
  • "Why are so many farms figuring out maitake now?" Partly because "oysters have dropped in bulk prices", so growers look for something different.
  • An investor-backed outdoor shiitake log farm was selling at about US$10 a pound.
  • Large Asian markets in France carry "epic amounts of dehydrated lion's mane", graded shiitake and many dried mushrooms; dried cordyceps are "everywhere and they're dirt cheap".
  • Prices can collapse when a market floods: on the US West Coast, prices for one legal-market mushroom product fell from about US$1,500 a pound to about US$70 or less in roughly two years.

Pricing

  • Early prices are often guesses: one Maine farm started at $8/lb (about $17.60/kg) in Portland, Maine, simply by picking a number.

  • Raise prices before adding accounts. Some accounts respect a firm list price even if it is high, while younger restaurants need hand-holding and can grow into excellent accounts.

  • In the late 2000s one grower sold "Straw"-strain shiitake at about $8/lb, including to a Chinese restaurant that thought it was log-grown.

  • Let sales data correct your intuition. QuickBooks reports often show that a "hot" species is over-weighted in your head, and production records explain sales dips to lenders and partners.

  • Don't sell cheap at markets. Don't sell at US$4-6 a pound at a farmers market; sell at US$15, and people will pay for fresh. A New Hampshire farm charges US$16 a pound (it was US$12 eight years earlier). Customers don't weigh a US$5 clamshell. Show market customers the unit price of pre-sliced supermarket shiitake: US$3.48 a pack is US$29 a pound.

  • Charge what you need. One California grower priced at US$15 a pound wholesale to restaurants, and chefs laughed, because it was twice the food-service price; his partner had been charging US$8 because food service was US$6, and nobody would buy at US$10. Three restaurants still took all of the first grower's 23 kg (50 lb) a week. Cap n Stem's advice was to charge what you need to be profitable, since every area is different.

  • Pricing new accounts. Some accounts respect a clear price, even a high one; some want a simple price list; young, unsure accounts need hand-holding ("this is what a pound looks like, about the size of a softball") and grow into loyal big accounts. Cap n Stem started at US$8 a pound because it made up a number, then raised prices once it saw chefs didn't care much. A Tampa grower who delivers early in the morning has never lost an account over a missed order or a poor batch, because he is honest and discounts it. While still a firefighter he had 12 accounts ordering about 18 kg (40 lb) a week each.

  • Wild prices swing: in a heavy chanterelle year in Maine, foraged chanterelles fell to about US$4 a pound.

  • Don't chase imported prices. A Colorado farm stopped trying to match the price of Pennsylvania and California product flown into Denver, because its production costs are different. Restaurants now pay it cash on delivery, at about US$4 a pound below retail, with nothing extra.

What to grow for market

Species details are in Chapter 20.

  • Avoid commodity species where imports flood the market. Where markets are flooded by Chinese imports or by large Chinese-owned Latin American farms, shiitake, beech and enoki sell for almost nothing; grow niche species that locals do not know. Example: a relative of one grower starting a farm in Brazil.
  • King oyster sells "like hotcakes", and there are not enough quality kings on the market. A uniform, steak-like mushroom intimidates customers less than clusters do. But kings are hard to grow (see Yields).
  • Black oyster "saved the day" for many farms as an alternative to king oyster, which is hard to grow. It took off around 2018-2020. It is temperamental in the fruit room, and farms often call for help when it stops performing.
  • Lion's mane is delicious, gourmet plus medicinal, eye-catching, and has a cycle close to oysters. Nearly every farm grows it, but it is fickle.
  • Maitake went from a rarely grown "white whale" to a widespread small-farm crop in about two years, and specific maitake strains are among the top three spawn sellers at one large spawn lab (Cap n Stem). Shogun (Canada) is a highly automated maitake-only farm linked to a big Japanese maitake farm, with about $5M of funding, and Woodbloom (Canada) now produces at very large scale. Some maitake clients want uncut "blobs" grown in the bag, which is much simpler. The bottle-culture industry has moved away from maitake because of its sensitive fruiting stage (unconfirmed).
  • Chestnut photographs very well and draws market and social-media attention. Harvest it on time: Mycopia grew chestnut as one of its first bottle species, and customers had problems because it was harvested too late and shelf life was poor.
  • Shiitake was easily 50% or more of production at Cascadia Mushrooms (at that time).
  • Comb tooth markets, and selling wild-type phenotypes, are still being worked out.

Two working farms' line-ups (see Chapter 26):

Farm What it grows and how it sells
Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan) Recommended focus: oysters (Italian, blue, golden, pink and black pearl), lion's mane, coral tooth and pioppino. Blue oyster is 70% of the farm's income.
High Country Fungi (Avery) Blue oyster; golden oyster; chestnut (5 weeks incubation, 3 weeks fruiting); pioppino, sold as "the Italian pasta mushroom"; lion's mane; comb or coral tooth, sold for crab cakes; and black pearl, which has king-trumpet texture, plates nicely and shreds like pulled pork.
  • Keep the list short. Small growers often try 10 strains or varieties, but "you can never get good at something if you don't do something"; the longer you're in it, the shorter your list and the better you get. New block customers order "50 pink and 75 gold", thinking pinks are easy to sell, then can't sell them and try to cancel blocks already made.
  • A Chicago farm keeps a tight list on purpose: blue oyster, black oyster and lion's mane grown "really well consistently", because chefs can make many dishes from each; it adds chestnut and is starting maitake to keep chefs excited. Find the customers, grow the mushrooms, and line those two up; the simpler the better.
  • "Don't grow what you can't sell." Outside the markets that value branding, mushrooms are a commodity.
  • Golden oysters. Farms sell "every colour of oyster in one bread box", and Cap n Stem questions who cares. "There's something about a gold oyster that everybody loves... except for chefs": shelf life is poor, so chefs must use them quickly, while retail customers are drawn to the yellow "like bees" to flowers. Fresh goldens have a particular candy-like smell. Packaging, mixes and presentation are the next thing small farms must work out.
  • Space decides the list. A Jacksonville farm grows mostly oysters and lion's mane because its space is tiny and chestnut sits on the shelf for four weeks. Customers who ask for something different often order just 1.4 kg (3 lb), which isn't worth growing or driving for; he would like a 4.5 kg (10 lb) minimum per delivery.
  • Quality wins the best buyers. A Houston grower harvests young, never ships blown-out or cracked caps, and donates whatever isn't premium. That put him in the city's top restaurants, which are the most loyal and consistent buyers, because once they find reliable top quality they keep coming back.
  • In the US "everybody grows an oyster and a pink oyster and a yellow oyster". In Japan mushrooms are grocery food, so one US block maker is moving toward grocery-friendly products such as beech mushroom (bunashimeji), shiitake and maitake.

Other products, and honesty about health claims

  • Blocks that do not fruit can still be made into mycelium tinctures. Stamets-type products use lion's mane mycelium grown on rice or oats. See Chapter 15.
  • Tinctures earn one small farm about US$40k of roughly US$375k gross revenue.
  • Reishi is the "pumpkin spice latte" of the fringe health world. It sells to clients, and a reishi tincture sells at farmers markets.
  • Reishi antlers are weighed and vacuum-packed to the client's specification, and each bag is checked for punctures before boxing.
  • Mycelium materials (leather alternatives, packaging) are a growth area, and reishi leads because it forms a tough, skin-like mat.
  • Stroma-affected blocks give unsellable fruit, at best usable for powder.

RULE Be honest about medicinal claims. The evidence is mostly in vitro (lab dish) and unproven. When customers ask on behalf of a sick relative, say so honestly and suggest a supplement at most. Experienced growers strongly criticize health-claim marketing such as Paul Stamets'; a story sometimes told about Stamets' mother is unconfirmed.

  • Never claim that mushrooms cure disease. When callers ask whether mushrooms can cure a relative's illness, one Tampa grower explains gently that none of it is proven (most tests are in the lab dish, not in people) and that growers aren't doctors, without crushing their hope.
  • One supplement company grew from making tinctures for personal health, to foraged turkey tail and reishi, to partnering with farms for raw material, choosing cordyceps because few others made it.

Tours, workshops and other income

  • Tours sell mushrooms. New Hampshire Mushroom Company runs tours every Sunday, some for 50 people, and nearly every visitor buys mushrooms afterwards; most of its direct retail moved from markets to tours.
  • Paid public tours. A California farm charges a flat fee, cash only, and schedules tours on weekdays around production; about half of callers want weekends, and it steers them to Monday or Friday. Visitors spend about US$20-30 each at the merchandise table, and tours add about US$1,000-1,500 in sales a week.
  • Wild mushrooms and insurance. The same farm forages and sells wild chanterelles (a couple of hundred pounds a week in season). A customer once claimed jack-o'-lantern mushroom poisoning; it turned out to be COVID. The farm carries product, liability (US$1.5 million) and property insurance.

Labour

AT A GLANCE Labour is the biggest cost you control. It does not scale linearly, so every scale-up step must add speed, not people. Fix your systems, then stop experimenting.

  • Staffing rule of thumb: about one dedicated person per 180 kg (400 lb) of mushrooms a week. A one-person farm at 545 kg (1,200 lb) a week doesn't work. There is a big gap between a person who harvests 90 kg (200 lb) a day and one who harvests 32 kg (70 lb), and one person in a crew is usually the "motor".

  • Automation changes the ratio. A large California farm aimed for about 1,800 kg (4,000 lb) a week with about four employees: its Japanese-style automatic bagger picks up a bag, opens it, fills and compresses it, punches two holes and ejects it, and with tray loading one person can bag about 4,000 a day.

  • Labour is the limit on growth. One early grower found that whenever he hired, he couldn't really afford the pay, and if the hire didn't work out he lost both the wages and the product, so he stopped hiring and stayed small. "You can't go commercial unless you can have employees." At about US$6 a pound (shiitake was about US$3 a pound national average then), you make money by volume and work ten times as hard. Running the business, with worries about power cuts and the rest, gave him high blood pressure; he made more money as a union electrician.

  • Australian wages are about AUD 26-28 an hour, so every hire must fit the business model. Mixing by hand gave one Australian grower pins and needles in her arms; a mixer changed everything.

  • Labour does not scale linearly: a three-person, three-hour job is far more than nine hours for one person. Owners should not stay the irreplaceable fastest worker if they plan to grow.

  • Each step up in scale must speed up the mix without adding labour, because extra staff erode profitability. Automation should leave just an on/off button.

  • Labour is getting scarcer and pricier, and repetitive motions are hard on bodies over about 30, so expect to automate.

  • Manual bagging is heavy repetitive strain, and automation reduces employee injury. A Japanese bagger with a Fenrir adapter claims to cut bagging to about one person. Payback comes through speed and redeploying staff, amortized over 2-10 years. Tariffs will raise Japanese bagger prices.

  • At small and medium scale, hand spawning is fastest. Far West Fungi has three people in a corner doing it, and robots are not yet better.

  • A wider impulse sealer nearly doubled sealing speed at one farm, but new hires misaligned bags. That was its first real training and SOP problem. See Chapter 11.

  • One grower estimates about 50% of farm time goes to cleaning (another guessed, as a joke, 43%).

  • Early on, Cap n Stem's founders worked 6-7 days a week, and exhaustion cost them days.

  • Harvest capacity must match crop size. A solo eight-hour pre-Christmas shiitake harvest ended with the first rows already opening again. See Chapter 15.

  • Once systems are right, production is easy, so keep systems fixed rather than constantly experimenting.

Scheduling the week

  • Map tasks across the week, Sunday to Saturday: for example substrate on three days, harvest on four, grading and packing on two, and deliveries on three plus a market. Each lane can become a person, and consolidating lanes can remove a whole position. Drawn as a weekly chart, that is four lanes (S S S, H H H H, G.P. G.P., and D D D M), each numbered as one person.
  • Keep the week simple. One grower ran one fixed day for bulk spawn and one for all deliveries. Avoid hopping between tasks daily.
  • A small farm can give each weekday one job: for example steam on Monday, cool-down and inoculation on Tuesday, spawn prep on Wednesday, agar and genetics on Thursday, and sales on Friday and Saturday. One small farm runs a single lab day each week. See Chapter 26.
  • Plan a day hour by hour for each person, including who is away selling, before fixing the farm layout. See Chapter 3.
  • A flexible anchor customer helps. One New Hampshire grower has a customer who takes about 36 kg (80 lb) a week and accepts any mix (all shiitake, or four species), which absorbs a cancelled 9 kg (20 lb) lion's mane order or an extra 14 kg (30 lb) chestnut request. Every day he prints the next day's pack sheet, checks the walk-in with his grower, and shuffles stock between accounts; some customers won't take a delivery missing one of their species. Orders go out four days a week and are packed the day before.

Hiring

  • New staff expect a romantic grow room, but the job means lifting 50 lb (23 kg) sacks overhead, unloading hot troughs and spending hours at an inoculation table. Many lose interest within 1-2 months.
  • Some hires fail in the lab for sensory reasons: lighting headaches, nausea from disinfectants, white walls and suits, or slowly building anxiety. See Chapter 4.
  • Hiring for "culture fit" did not predict who could tolerate lab work, and hiring instinct is usually wrong.
  • Interview tactic: talk the lab up as if it were a BSL-4 (top biosafety level) lab and watch whether the candidate frays.
  • Paid test days are strongly recommended. Walk the candidate through the whole job, then ask honestly whether they could do it.
  • In the lab, watch body language: engaged and energized, or eager to leave.
  • Match temperament to role. Market-booth staff need patience, while bag folders and knockers need tolerance for repetition.
  • Horizontal flow hoods let untrained staff work with essentially no problems, which helps when hiring.

CASE One Florida farm hired a seasonal worker purely for their calm phone manner, after rejecting about 20 others. Their small organizing habits added real value. Lesson: hire for temperament, not only for experience.

RANGE Hiring experienced lab staff. Hire for calm, steady temperament first, and be wary of hires who arrive overconfident because they already worked in a spawn lab. Some of one spawn lab's best lab staff came from Walmart and warehouse jobs; the same lab has also hired an experienced lab worker successfully, and has hired someone from a working lab and praised calm, steady people. Experience is a plus only when it comes without overconfidence.

  • Show the real job. In Florida the job means lifting 23 kg (50 lb) sacks overhead, unloading a 93 °C (200 °F) steam trough outside in the heat, and hours at an inoculation table that hurts your shoulders. New hires see the whole cycle within a month, and some lose interest. One farm's best seasonal worker lives in a van and leaves when it gets too hot. If an employee makes a mistake, treat it as a training failure, and write SOPs.

Procedure: run a paid test day

  1. Pay the candidate for a full day.
  2. Talk the lab up as a high-containment lab before they enter, and watch whether they fray.
  3. Walk them through the whole job, including the heavy and repetitive parts (50 lb (23 kg) sacks, hot troughs, hours at the inoculation table).
  4. Watch their body language in the lab: engaged and energized, or eager to leave.
  5. At the end, ask honestly whether they could do this job.

CHECK Many new hires lose interest within 1-2 months; if a test-day hire is still engaged after two months, the test worked.

Training, SOPs and team culture

  • Staff mistakes are training failures. (The recommended book is Extreme Ownership by Jocko Willink.) Example SOP points: no talking while pouring spawn, never nest bags the wrong way, and check the steam barrel has water. Written SOPs matter because the owner eventually stops being the trainer.
  • Small lapses, such as popping into the lab ungowned to grab a phone, become habits. Balance speed with technique and explain the why.
  • A 1980s cleanroom design manual (section 3.3, "Attitudinal Factors") lists the risks: white garments create anonymity, assembly-line repetition harms task identity, prescriptive training worsens attitude, and operators cannot see product quality, so work becomes ritual. Its remedies are whole-process training, rotating staff through tasks, and communication systems.
  • Named leads own critical areas (for example one the autoclave and boiler, one the crops), but decisions are collaborative.
  • One lab deliberately avoids employee ID numbers and cameras, to avoid a surveillance culture.
  • Music and media are a trade-off. People need to talk and bond, and an always-headphones hire can become isolated. Mixing crews can alternate between phone weeks and chattier weeks.
  • Leaders step in when a bad micro-culture forms, using humour and silliness.
  • Stressing why repetition matters keeps people engaged. Explain why small things like bag folds matter.
  • Owners should still do floor work at times. One owner spent six hours on the hood when half the staff were out and found it a relief.
  • Farming is siloed (lab, fruiting, mixing), so connect each role to the whole, for example by showing how much one cryovial produces.
  • Slim margins push people into panic fixes that then persist. Keep thinking strategically under pressure.
  • Ask lots of questions, because when the boss is away you will be the one welding the improvised kit.
  • Graphs and data give technical staff ownership. Standards slip over years, and data catches that where SOPs alone do not.

CASE Before a nine-week trip, the owners of an Australian farm wrote process documents and flowcharts for breakdowns (autoclave, mixer gearbox, cold room), named a lab manager, a site manager and a dispatch lead, stocked spare parts, and used a team messaging app. The one part they didn't stock, the mixer gearbox, failed. The team still grew output while they were away. Cap n Stem asks its staff for one email summary a day.

  • Delegate. A family business keeps too much in the family's heads. Delegate payables, receivables, logistics, estimates and projections. One large Pennsylvania farm closes only on Christmas Day; harvesting runs every day.
  • When an employee underperforms, one Houston grower's first question is "what am I doing wrong?" He prefers creative fixes to firing people, though he calls that a double-edged sword.
  • Keep staff long enough that the owners can build the business: a Texas farm carries more staff than similar farms, with many staying two years or more, so nobody is "indentured to this farm". Every new hire took on more than expected and freed the owners for owner work.

Records, redundancy and risk

AT A GLANCE Log every run and every culture, change one variable at a time when things go wrong, and build spare capacity into the things that keep crops alive. How to diagnose contamination is in Chapter 16.

Keep records

  • Most farms keep few records and start only when they become certified organic or after a disaster. Data lets you trace a failure days later.

  • Keep trademark and name-and-date records too; trademark disputes happen in this industry (for example between two sellers of grow bags).

  • Track every culture vial, test and expansion in a spreadsheet, database or Gantt chart. See Chapter 8.

  • Log every pasteurization run, as Cap n Stem does. Without a good logger your data is junk, and a couple of hundred dollars is worth it. See Chapter 12.

  • When customers call with failing blocks, the first question is whether they tracked their temperatures.

  • Track harvest yields mainly to check that your systems are working: dips and bumps in yield tell you how the systems are performing.

  • Get a financial person involved early. Cap n Stem only stabilized (at 25 full-time staff) once one was; one early grower was always behind on his bookkeeping.

  • A farm of about 300 blocks a week asking about big business software (SAP) should "just get QuickBooks online"; SAP costs at least US$30,000 a year.

  • Get paid. A Colorado farm offered 30-day terms to established restaurants and 15-day terms to new ones, but some paid 45 days late or more, so US$30,000-40,000 was owed at once. After the pandemic it moved its focus to CSAs and farmers markets, and restaurants now pay cash on delivery. Block sellers get burned by buyers who can't or won't pay; most don't mean to cheat, but "an invoice only says they owe you money". New, unknown buyers shouldn't expect credit terms, because your electric company only wants its money. One Ohio block maker has written off losses (for example US$3,000) rather than chase them in small-claims court.

Diagnose before you change anything

  • Work backwards with data. With about 50 lots a day, knee-jerk changes (changing incubation temperature, firing someone, swapping filters) waste money.
  • Expect substrate contamination to wipe you out a few times. The core skill is systematic diagnosis, changing one variable at a time.
  • Growers get fixated on one variable. Walking through every variable, one by one, is what finds the cause.
  • Specialist consultants (Cap n Stem among them) offer contamination troubleshooting to farms and keep a backlog of case studies. See Chapter 23.
  • Keep perspective: when a new grower agonizes over one bad block in 50, the answer is to make more blocks.
  • But do not accept a steady loss as a cost of business. Stroma is Cap n Stem's one persistent biological problem, and it refuses to accept about 3% loss from it.
  • Do not trust a seller's claim that a filter "should work as a HEPA", and do not bet the business on an unknown filter. Farms resist suspecting their own filter, so test it anyway. See Chapter 4.

CASE A large spawn customer wanted to cancel orders after months of Neurospora contamination. The cause was in the process, and adding more fungicide is an arms race. One mushroom company is said to have shut down because of Neurospora (unconfirmed). See Chapter 16.

Build in redundancy

  • Oversize air conditioning for redundancy (for example 10 tons instead of 7.5 tons, for about $2,000 more). See Chapter 14.
  • Keep backup racks, fans and humidification, weighed against the rent for the space they take.
  • During a bacterial blotch outbreak, rotate to different strains to stop the losses at once, even at lower yield, while you fix the structural causes. See Chapter 17.
  • Hand-loading individual blocks is a contamination route. Move blocks in racks or cages.

CASE During a flood at one farm, a forklift hydroplaned through deep water, and the chaos led the manager to send most staff home. Lesson: have a plan for floods and site emergencies before you need one. See Chapter 18.

RULE "Consistency is king." If you can't produce consistently you will struggle to make money, and redundancy is the key to consistency. Watch your systems fail before you fix them, so you see exactly where they fail.

  • Spread your customers. For a while one major customer took about 80% of what a California farm grew, then stopped ordering for over a year with no warning: "it nearly killed us". It now spreads its sales so no single loss sinks it. Bulk ingredient buyers take many samples and a lot of hand-holding, then suddenly order 2,000 kg ("feast or famine").
  • One lost week can wipe out six. A chef orders 7 kg (16 lb) a week and then doesn't want them; a distributor orders 113 kg (250 lb) a week and skips a week. That one lost week can wipe out six weeks of gains, because the mushrooms are too old to sell the next week.
  • Don't bet everything on one crop. A buyer once said he was spending his last dollar on a supplier's blocks; the supplier's answer: "a couple times a year we have some duds".
  • Shocks pass. At the start of COVID about 80% of a large Pennsylvania farm's sales disappeared for a few weeks (a skip full of dumped mushrooms made the papers). It cut production hard, and by October 2020 revenue was above pre-COVID levels; for two to three years it couldn't keep up. Grocery stores first stocked only essentials, then specialty mushrooms sold well. It now feels a wider economic pullback.
  • Partnerships. "Don't go 50/50 if you're ever going to have a partner, because if you don't agree, then you're going to stand still." One Maui partnership split over whether to raise money and grow. A Memphis farm is four family members (the owner's mother runs payroll, spreadsheets and customers from 20 years managing plumbing companies), and the owner won't hire couples again.
  • Protect your name. A California farm paid a lawyer about US$2,000 for a trademark search and found that a large UK company already held a US mark on a similar product name (applied for in 2020, granted in April 2021). Fighting it would cost US$30,000-40,000, so the farm will change the name eventually. Amazon's brand registry needs a registered trademark, so trademark early.
  • Don't rely on one social platform. Instagram removed Cap n Stem's main account without warning; cultivator pages can be taken down.
  • Ask mushroom people. General business-development consultants promised one California grower help, then billed her and asked whether she'd heard of Paul Stamets and whether mushroom farming counts as vertical farming for grants. What she actually needed was "an affordable HVAC person", or how to build an HVAC system herself. Rely on mushroom people, not general business people.

Strains, breeding and the future market

Strain work is covered in Chapter 8; strain names and codes are listed in Chapter 23.

  • This is a young industry: dedicated oyster farms date only from about the late 1970s-1980s.
  • Strains once moved only by trade. There was no middle tier of spawn sellers between industrial spawn makers and hobbyists.
  • Breeding of new phenotypes (new visible types) largely stopped around the late 1980s, and the industry needs to return to it.
  • One aim is to get growers to extract monokaryons (single-nucleus strains) from their culture banks and remix them into new phenotypes. One breeder already sells monokaryon cultures.
  • Cap n Stem plans formal breeding and will give its strains memorable names. Its JC shiitake was cloned in 2018 from log-grown shiitake.
  • The KOM shiitake strain is expected to become a flagship strain within 1-3 years.
  • Spawn companies rename strains: the Leighton Banks lion's mane is sold under many names, and Cap n Stem sells it as "HeCNS". Ask for lineage, not a name.
  • A cheap, portable DNA barcoding tool to verify strains would help growers; none exists yet.
  • Replicating the patented black oyster crosses needs sequenced wild clones of P. eryngii varieties, P. nebrodensis or Mediterranean oysters; growers who hold such clones are asked to share them.
  • Species-specific processes, refined by many small growers sharing openly (as with maitake and cordyceps), are how the industry advances. Strains should not be hoarded.
  • Strains mailed out years ago by one breeder now fruit at farms across the country.
  • Cap n Stem is designing a new facility in Lewiston, Maine, from a clean slate.

WARNING Moving cultures across borders needs phytosanitary paperwork. Maitake cultures were once hand-carried back from Mycelia (Belgium) without it, which was an illegal import; about half of those cultures turned out excellent. Get the paperwork.

Our farm: plans and templates

FARM NOTE The business chapters describe other people's farms. This section gives the farm in Playa Negra the blank forms the book says it needs: a sales plan, a buyer list, a surplus plan, a waste line, a 12-month cash flow, a credit rule, an emergency plan and an accountant checklist. Prices are in colones (₡) first, with US$ at about ₡510 to US$1 in brackets. Anything not from Joseph's records is marked unconfirmed or OPEN. Fill the blanks from real sales, not hopes.

Sales plan template

Plan blocks from the weeks ahead, not from today's sales (Planning for surplus and buffers). The 130-bag split and Catawba's measured yields per block give the weekly crop below. Joseph's price is ₡13,000 a kilo for every mushroom (decided 6 Nov 2026; this replaces the earlier ₡10,000-13,000 oyster range and the assumed 20% premium for lion's mane and coral tooth).

Species Blocks Yield per block Weekly crop Price (₡/kg) Sales at those prices (₡)
Blue oyster 52 2.03 lb 106 lb (48 kg) 13,000 622,000
Lion's mane 46 1.63 lb 75 lb (34 kg) 13,000 442,000
Coral (comb) tooth 16 2.03 lb 32 lb (15 kg) 13,000 192,000
Golden oyster (A weeks) 16 1.28 lb 20 lb (9.3 kg) 13,000 121,000
Total 130 234 lb (106 kg) about 1,377,000 (US$2,700)

Phoenix oyster weeks (B weeks) use Catawba's Italian oyster as a stand-in, about 1.09 lb a block (17 lb, 7.9 kg, about ₡103,000 a week): sources have no measured figure for phoenix yet. Joseph now picks the 16-bag slot species himself each week; golden and phoenix are the examples.

Then say who buys each row.

Species Weekly kg target Buyer or channel Price agreed (₡/kg) Start date Who sells

RULE Raise prices before adding accounts, and do not sell cheap to dump surplus (Pricing). Do not grow what you cannot sell: sell before you scale.

Buyer list template

One row per buyer. Review it every month: a buyer who has stopped ordering is lost income you can still win back.

Buyer Type (restaurant, hotel, shop, market, other) Contact Species and kg a week Price (₡/kg) Delivery day Payment terms Share of weekly sales Last order Notes

RULE One-buyer cap. One California farm sold about 80% to one customer, who then stopped ordering for over a year with no warning (Build in redundancy). Fix a ceiling for any single buyer's share of weekly sales and keep to it. Joseph's ceiling: 30% (confirmed 6 Nov 2026). Mark the buyer list so over-dependence cannot be missed: shade or colour-code any buyer's row (in the farm app, in a distinct colour that is not the warning red used for faults) once their share reaches the ceiling, and use a lighter shade when they come within about 5 points of it. Joseph asked for this marking on 6 Nov 2026.

Credit rule

RULE Every buyer pays cash on delivery. Joseph's decision (6 Nov 2026): there are no credit terms, for new or old buyers. The book's examples: a farm that gave 15-30 day terms was owed US$30,000-40,000 at once when some buyers paid 45 days late or more, and now takes cash on delivery (Keep records, Pricing).

  • No terms, no credit limit and no payment days to set. If a buyer cannot pay on delivery, the delivery does not happen.
  • Write the rule on the price list so no buyer is surprised.
  • A skipped week costs more than it looks: a buyer who orders and then skips leaves product too old to sell the next week (One lost week).

Surplus and drying plan

"You are always going to have extra product" (Planning for surplus and buffers). Decide in advance what happens to it, in this order:

  1. Sell fresh at list price to the next buyer on the list, the same or next day. Fresh mushrooms carry a best-by of 7 days from harvest (Grading and packing).
  2. Dry it. Drying surplus lion's mane in a dehumidifier closet gave dry weight of about 10-11% of fresh, in about 24-48 hours at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) (Drying surplus, results). Dried product needs sealed, very dry packaging.
  3. Donate, with a receipt for the donation (Planning for surplus and buffers).
  4. Compost last, by the spent-block route (Our farm: waste route).

Do not discount to dump. A container can double as a dehydrator with a heating element and a fan.

OPEN Where the drying closet goes, who runs it, whether a dehumidifier closet works at 88% humidity without extra drying capacity, and who buys dried product are not decided.

The 25% waste line

FARM NOTE A Massachusetts farm wasted up to 66% of its mushrooms for a winter. Its owner built a calculator with a built-in 25% food-waste line, which showed the farm should cut production until sales caught up (Planning for surplus and buffers). Use the same line here: until you have measured your own waste, plan on selling 75% of the weekly crop.

At the figures above that is about 175 lb (79 kg) sold, or about ₡1,033,000 a week (US$2,020), instead of about ₡1.38 million. Plan costs against the lower figure. Log what goes to each of the four surplus steps every week, and replace 25% with the real number after a few months.

12-month cash flow template

A farm that makes its own blocks pays for everything long before it is paid. Plate to first blue oyster harvest takes about 8 weeks, so the first two months pay out with nothing coming in. The book's rules: budget about four times your estimate and at least double the time, and keep at least three months of operating cash (Financing and start-up capital, Cash flow).

Fill one column per month, in ₡. Lines marked ★ are known; the rest are yours.

Line M1 M2 M3 M4 M5 M6 M7 M8 M9 M10 M11 M12
Cash in
Fresh sales by buyer (from the sales plan, at 75%)
Dried product and other sales
Loans, savings added
Total cash in
Cash out
Electricity ★ about ₡362,000-422,000 a month on the binomic tariff (US$709-828)
Propane or fuel (steam, generator)
Substrate: sawdust, soy hulls, grain
Bags, filters, labels, packaging
Water treatment and consumables
Cultures and test blocks
Labour and CCSS contributions
Transport and delivery
Repairs and maintenance
Accountant, permits, insurance, municipal fees
Loan payments
Spare-block buffer (extra blocks)
Total cash out
Net for the month
Cash at end of month
Three months of operating cash (the floor)

CHECK Cash at the end of every month stays above the floor line. If it dips below, the answer is in the buyer list (who pays late) or the waste line (sales lower than planned), not in more blocks. Move each buyer's payment into the month they actually pay, not the month you delivered.

Emergency plan: floods, long power cuts, AC failure

FARM NOTE "Have a plan for floods and site emergencies before you need one" (Build in redundancy). Power cuts are the most likely here, so they get the most detail. Print this page, fill in the blanks and post it in the lab and by the generator.

What a power cut does (Power cuts, alarms and backup): blocks keep making heat, a room without cooling warms fast, and CO2 climbs fast because the exhaust fans stop. Cold weather cannot help in Playa Negra, where it is 25 °C (77 °F) and humid all year. Decide in advance what to save: the rooms producing the most heat first.

Event First 15 minutes First hour Same day Always
Power cut Note the start time. Check the culture fridge and cold rooms are shut. Walk the fruiting and incubation rooms: is CO2 rising? Start the generator if the cut is longer than a few minutes. Generator running on the emergency breakers only: 3, 4, 7, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16 and 18 in the real breaker box (lab HEPA units, fruiting fans and fogger, culture fridge, the two Fogel reach-ins, packing intake, incubation air; about 4,045 W, from the 8-9 Nov 2026 breaker list). Never run the heater and the air conditioners on the generator together. Check the incubation room first: it makes the most heat. Check fuel. Tell any buyer you will miss. Check CO2 and temperatures again. Write start time, end time, generator on or off, fuel used, what was affected, in the power-cut log. Total the hours without power each month.
AC failure Find which room and which unit. Check the second unit in that room. Open doors only if outside is cooler than inside. Move crop to the room with working AC if you can. Call the technician. Log the room temperature at the worst point. Order the failed part. Keep the contact for the HVAC person on this page.
Flood Cut power to the wet area at the breaker. Do not enter water with power on. Get people to safe ground first. Move boxed product, cultures and spawn up and out of the water path. Do not work through the chaos with the whole crew: assign one person to decide. Photograph everything for insurance. Check for contamination reservoirs: wet piles, cardboard, old equipment. Keep cultures and the culture fridge off the floor.

OPEN Fill in before the rainy season: propane or fuel on hand and the hours it runs the emergency list; the technician's phone number; who holds a key and a breaker map; which circuits the culture fridge, the logger alarm and the lab HEPA fan units sit on (the circuit numbers are known, the appliances on them are not); where the off-site cultures are; the insurance cover for crop and equipment; the phone number for ICE outages.

Accountant checklist for Costa Rica

WARNING This list is a set of questions to take to a local accountant and lawyer. It is not from Joseph's sources and states no legal fact. Confirm each item and its cost, and write the answer next to it.

Ask about Question Answer and date
Business structure Persona física or sociedad? What are the tax and liability differences?
Tax registration and e-invoicing Is the business registered with Hacienda? Which electronic invoicing (factura electrónica) system and software is required for sales to restaurants, shops and individuals?
VAT (IVA) Is fresh and dried mushroom product taxed or exempt, and does it differ by product? Can input VAT be claimed?
Health permit Does the farm and the packing area need a Ministry of Health operating permit (permiso sanitario de funcionamiento), and what does it require?
Municipal licence What commercial licence (patente) does the municipality require, and what is the yearly fee?
CCSS Registration as an employer with the CCSS; contributions for each worker; what a family member or casual worker needs.
Workers' insurance Is the INS workers' risk policy (póliza de riesgos del trabajo) required, and for whom?
Cultures and imports Does importing cultures from Cap n Stem (Maine) need a phytosanitary import permit from the SFE? How long, what cost, and can a small shipment travel with paperwork? Compare moving cultures across borders.
Environmental Is any environmental registration needed for a farm of this size and its waste?
Electricity Ask ICE for a quote on the commercial time-of-use tariffs; the farm is billed on the binomic tariff above 3,000 kWh a month. Is there a cheaper plan for a farm that runs 16-18 hours on steam days?
Records Which records, invoices and logs must be kept, and for how many years?
Prices How should the colón price list be stated if buyers ask for US$?

Key rules

  1. Decide "hobby or profit" first, then pick one of the three businesses (spawn, blocks or fresh) that you can run alone.
  2. Cost your own labour. A $2.50 materials block is not a $2.50 block until you make thousands a week.
  3. Plan on about 2 lb (0.9 kg) per 10 lb (4.5 kg) block and about 500 lb (227 kg) a week from one 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) room, with three weekly cohorts of about 250 blocks.
  4. Give incubation about twice the fruiting space: three weeks of capacity for fast species, far more for shiitake and maitake.
  5. Buy in what others do better (plates, grain masters, blocks for a second species) and resell to widen your range.
  6. Scale in one decisive leap to equipment that covers two rooms in a day or two; do not multiply small barrels.
  7. Each scale-up step must add speed without adding staff.
  8. Diversify suppliers for every ingredient, watch commodity prices, and never buy the cheapest grain.
  9. Treat 5% contamination as your whole margin, and diagnose it with logged data, one variable at a time.
  10. Hire with paid test days, explain the why behind every SOP, and rotate people so they see the whole process.
  11. Sell with free samples and dish ideas, raise prices before adding accounts, and be honest about medicinal claims.
  12. Our farm: use the sales plan, buyer list, cash flow, credit rule, emergency plan and accountant checklist in Our farm: plans and templates.

Open questions

  • No full profit and loss statement for a mushroom farm is available. The block-cost curve ($2.50 rising to about $9) is one block producer's own estimate.
  • What fraction of the room's volume the 12 x 24 ft full-capacity layout (500-600 lb, 227-272 kg, a week) fills was not stated, so it can't be checked directly against the 1/10-1/4 standard.
  • The small-business failure statistics are unconfirmed.
  • One farm's figure of 40 lb (18 kg) a week of restaurant orders is ambiguous: it is unclear whether it is per account or in total.
  • Yield figures for king oyster, lion's mane and oyster often do not state the block size.

chapters.html:
Suppliers, References and People

AT A GLANCE A directory of the companies, products, websites, books, people and strain codes that come up in professional mushroom growing, grouped by what you would use them for. Use it to find a supplier, check a name before you search, or trace where a strain came from. The rules people use most:

  • Many names were only ever heard spoken. Check every name marked "(spelling unverified)" before you search or contact anyone.
  • Strain codes get renamed by resellers. Ask for a strain's lineage instead of trusting its name.
  • Buy HEPA filters and FFUs from tested sources and read the "nines" (the filtration rating) on the label.
  • Log every heat-treatment run with a rugged logger such as MadgeTech.
  • Treat boiler feed water, whatever boiler brand you use.

How to use this chapter

This chapter lists every book, paper, person, website, company, product and strain code that the textbook's sources name, grouped by type. Each table gives the name, what it is, and what it is used for or known for. Many names were only heard, not seen written, so they are marked "(spelling unverified)" where the spelling or identity is uncertain. Likely duplicates are noted in Name variants and spelling notes rather than merged. Where a name was printed on a label, screen or whiteboard, that printed form is the more reliable one and is used here.

Prices are summarized in the price list in Chapter 22. How the equipment is used is covered in Chapter 6 and the chapters on each process.

Cap n Stem and its products

Cap n Stem, a Maine block and spawn producer, is the source of much of the practice in this book. Its people and products appear throughout.

It has not intentionally fruited mushrooms commercially for over a decade; its advice draws on client farms worldwide. The company name appears on its bag labels.

Books, papers and documents

Title What it is Used for
Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms (Paul Stamets) Cultivation book Soy plus sawdust; shiitake timing. Its still-air closet advice is outdated (use a flow hood; Chapter 4).

Extreme Ownership (Jocko Willink) Leadership book Staff mistakes are training failures (Chapter 22).
Outlive (Peter Attia) Healthspan book "Medicine 3.0".
The Fungal Pharmacy (Robert Rogers, presumed) Medicinal fungi book The colours of the "zhi" as symbolic.
Shennong Bencao Jing Han-dynasty materia medica Lingzhi as a superior herb.
Compendium of Materia Medica (Li Shizhen, 1590) Chinese pharmacopoeia
Soma (R. Gordon Wasson); The Road to Eleusis (Wasson, Hofmann, Ruck); LSD: My Problem Child (Hofmann); Food of the Gods (McKenna); The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross (Allegro); Brave New World (Huxley) Ethnomycology and spirituality
Der Führer in die Pilzkunde (Paul Kummer, 1871) Taxonomy Named the genus Pleurotus.
The Principles of Mushroom Growing and Mushroom Spawn Making (B.M. Duggar, USDA); Mushroom Growing (Duggar, 1915) USDA bulletin; book Early spawn making (title page reproduced in histories).
Sinden grain spawn patent (1932, Penn State) US patent The origin of grain spawn.
Papers by Costantin and Matruchot (1894), Brefeld (1908), Falck (1917), Etter (1929), Kaufert (1935), Block, Tsao and Han (1958), Bano and Srivastava (1963), Eugenio and Anderson (1968) Historical papers See Chapter 2.
Curtis (1781), Karsten (1881), Patouillard (1889), Murrill (1902), Stebbins (1949), Bose (1950s), Adaskaveg and Gilbertson (1986; unverified) Ganoderma papers See reishi.

Amycel bag-materials patent (unverified) Patent on bag polymers, Gurley values and patches

Roger Rabbit's notes on mushroom cultivation (compiled by dumbfounded1600; unverified) Forum compilation Bacteria shed by people; steam myths.
David Medlock's write-up (4 pages, AI-assisted) Not peer-reviewed Mineral dust and gill shape (Chapter 17).

People

Name Who they are Known for

John Donahue (also spelled Donoghue) Founder of Northwest Mycological Consultants (NMC) and author Bags, strains, sealers and the tumbler; his "land speed record".

Matt Noble Forum strain trader
