David Medlock (unverified) Grower Papers and a write-up on water and gill shape.
Cyrus Lester (unverified) Grower Sauna steamers; now uses a container.
James Shoop (unverified) Grower
Valentin Esteves (unverified) Grower Zip-tie bag closure (Chapter 6).
Alex (unverified) Grower A simple weekly schedule; a shiitake job.
David Law (unverified) Grower Dense trolleys in incubation.
Rob Evans Chef, Duckfat (Portland, Maine) Japanese maitake villages.
William Padilla-Brown Mycologist Influence of DNA work on the hobby.
Frank Herbert Author of Dune The chanterelle slurry story.
Dave Ramsey Finance author Running debt-free (Chapter 22).
Jocko Willink Author Extreme Ownership.
Frank Lockhart (unverified) Engineer at Primus Recommended MadgeTech loggers.
Historical figures Jacquin, Kummer, Costantin, Matruchot, Duggar, Brefeld, Falck, Etter, Sinden, Kaufert, Block, Tsao, Han, Bano, Srivastava, Eugenio, Anderson, Curtis, Karsten, Patouillard, Murrill, Stebbins, Bose, Shennong, Li Shizhen, Wasson, Hofmann, Huxley, McKenna, Allegro See Chapter 2.

Strain codes and named cultures

Strain names change hands; always ask for the lineage (Chapter 8).

Code Species and origin Notes
HeCNS / HECNS Lion's mane (Leighton Banks's wild clone) One of the two main US lion's mane strains; renamed by others (for example "Tree Beard").
HePow ("Pow") Lion's mane The other main US strain.
HcFF (label "121323-HCFF-2") Comb tooth (wild clone from Fungal Farm, Denmark)
PA CNS Chestnut (Pholiota adiposa) NMC, then New Hampshire Mushroom Co., then Cap n Stem.
POCNS (label "POCNS-17 053124") Cap n Stem's house blue oyster Prone to stroma; high yield.
3044, 3015, King Blue (unverified) Oyster and king codes Strains switched during a blotch outbreak.
JB Robust, low-yield P. ostreatus Far West Fungi.
PO 775 (unverified) Korean oyster strain Linked to a virus outbreak.
3782 Shiitake The 2013-14 shiitake revolution; small caps.
3790 Shiitake Cold-tolerant, dense; Far West Fungi.
JC Shiitake (cloned in 2018 at Cap n Stem) Big mushrooms; a niche strain.
KOM Shiitake (via "Sam", Texas) Expected to become a flagship.
Straw Shiitake (Aloha Medicinals) Late 2000s; erratic.
321 Shiitake (NMC) Cascadia Mushrooms' strain.
Conch King oyster (JT, Mushrooms Naturally) The US standard.
2603 (heard 2602/2603) King oyster (Mycelia)
Siberia King oyster Traded, given to North Spore, since lost.
9827 ("M4"?; unverified) Maitake (Mycelia) Cap n Stem's second most popular strain.
Shogun Maitake Tolerates warmer conditions than 9827.
494 Maitake (NMC) Inconsistent.
Oakshire (unverified) Maitake Untested.
Black Pearl / Black King / Cosmic Queen / Shimofuri Hiratake; "Aloha" and "Brat" versions (unverified) Black oyster (Hokuto hybrid)
Ganoderma lingzhi (Donahue line) Reishi Said to be high in some triterpenes (anecdotal).
NITE BP-1378 / BP-1379 Strains deposited in the Hokuto patent

Names that are probably the same

  • Brad Koons and Brad Coons are almost certainly the same person (Top Shelf Fungi).
  • John Donahue and John Donoghue are the same NMC founder.
  • Kyle Garone and Kyle Gironi (Far West Fungi) are probably the same person.
  • TR, T.R. Davis and Earth Angel may all be one producer (unverified).
  • "Plato's Sunlight" is an unverified hearing of a block supplier's name.
  • North Spore is also heard as "Norse sport", "nora spore" and "Norsepore".
  • Roger Abbott and "Roger Rabbit" appear to be the same forum figure (unverified).
  • The Fenrir system is also heard as the "fender system", and the Octa-Fenrir as "Octafender".

Key rules

  1. Check every "(unverified)" spelling before you search for or contact anyone.
  2. Buy HEPA filters and FFUs from tested sources and read the "nines" on the label.
  3. For steam, Sioux low-pressure boilers and Primus autoclaves are proven choices; treat the feed water whatever brand you use.
  4. Use MadgeTech or similar rugged loggers, and log every run.
  5. Strain codes get renamed by resellers, so ask for the lineage rather than trusting a name.
  6. Use the books listed (Stamets, Donahue, Arora) for background, but don't follow the classic still-air closet advice; work under a flow hood.
  7. Most suppliers here are in the US. Check local availability and the cost of shipping and duty before planning around a product.

Open questions

  • The exact identity of several suppliers (HHP, Plato's Sunlight, the Japanese bag and bagger makers, Pack mixers) is unconfirmed.
  • The deep-freeze study, the peroxide-tolerance study and the Amycel patent are not named precisely enough to find.
  • Some strain codes (3044, 3015, PO 775, Oakshire, M4) are as heard and unverified.

chapters.html:
Quick-Reference Cards

AT A GLANCE Ten one-screen cards for the working day: the process chain, grain, substrate, steam, room set points, species, water and cleaning, planning numbers, advice from three working farms, and the golden rules. Each card gives the number to use first and the range after it, with a link to the chapter that explains it. The numbers people reach for most:

  • Block: 10 lb (4.5 kg) of 50:50 Master's Mix at about 62% moisture, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag per 20 blocks.
  • Ultra-pasteurization: slowest block core 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h. Sterilization: core 121 °C (250 °F) for about 35 min.
  • Knock (inoculate) at a core of 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), never above about 38 °C (100 °F).
  • Incubate blocks at about 19 °C (66 °F) on the bag surface, CO2 1,500-3,000 ppm (exhaust on at 3,000, off at 1,500-2,500).
  • Fruit staple species at 16 °C (60 °F) to start, best 14-17 °C (58-62 °F), never above 18 °C (65 °F); CO2 cycled about 450-900 ppm, humidity swinging about 70-90%.

How to use these cards

These are the numbers most growers reach for, pulled from the subject chapters of this book. Each row gives the most commonly used value first and the range of other figures after it. Where growers use different values, the row says so and links to Settings and Their Ranges, which sets every such setting out with its conditions.

The numbers assume one baseline, the house practice of Cap n Stem, a Maine block and spawn farm: a 10 lb (4.5 kg) block in a filter-patch bag, 50:50 Master's Mix at about 62% moisture, one 6 lb (2.7 kg) spawn bag per twenty blocks, and incubation at about 19 °C (66 °F). If your block, recipe or climate differs, check the linked chapter before copying a number.

TIP Print a card and keep it in a sleeve on the wall of the room it covers. Each card fits one screen or one sheet.

Card 1: The process at a glance

From a frozen culture to a block ready to fruit. The full process is explained in How a Mushroom Farm Works, and each step in its own chapter.

Stage Key number Range and notes Details
Culture to block chain Cryo vial → slant → plate → G1 master of 4 lb (1.8 kg) → G2 of 6 lb (2.7 kg) → about 20 blocks per G2 No G3 and no block-to-block transfers Chapter 7, Chapter 9
Plate to masters 2 cuts of about 1 cm per master; up to about 12 masters per plate 4 cuts for slow strains; cut when growth is about 1 cm from the plate wall Chapter 7
Master to G2 1 master to about 12 G2 bags 6-24 is workable; one source uses about 20 (ranges) Chapter 9
Spawn rate 1 x 6 lb G2 per 20 x 10 lb blocks (about 3%) 12-30 blocks per bag; use a heavier rate for ultra-pasteurized substrate or slow species Chapter 11
Liquid culture 0.5% sugar; ready in 10-12 days (14 at most); about 20 mL per 6 lb master Cap n Stem's standard; many recipes elsewhere use 2-4% Chapter 7
Cryo storage -80 °C (-112 °F); about 3 mL of 10% glycerol per vial with the grains submerged; thaw at about 30 °C (86 °F) 5% glycerol in two sources; refresh every 6-12 months, or up to every 2-3 years (ranges) Chapter 8
Storage without a freezer Agar plugs in sterile water at about 1 °C (34 °F), cap slightly loose, sealed with parafilm Use for pink and golden oyster, which don't survive cryo Chapter 8

Card 2: Grain spawn

Full method: Grain Spawn. Sterilizing grain: Steam.

Item Value Notes
Grain USDA Grade 1, whole and clean. House mix: 3 parts rye to 1 part sorghum, plus gypsum and calcium carbonate (CaCO3) Chapter 9
Hydration targets (water as % of hydrated grain) Rye-millet mix: upper 40s %. Millet alone: at most about 45-47%. Rye alone: low 50s %. Oats: about 55% (oats can hold about 60%). Maitake spawn: 42-46% Chapter 9
Calcium additives in grain CaCO3 plus gypsum about 0.15% of wet weight; keep under 1% Prevents stroma; Chapter 9, Chapter 16
Sterilize grain Core at least 121 °C (250 °F) for at least 35 min. A vacuum autoclave cycle: 124 °C (255 °F) for 35 min Never just pasteurize spawn; Chapter 12
Incubate spawn About 16-18 °C (low to mid 60s °F); 17-18 °C (63-64 °F) ambient Cooler than blocks; Chapter 13
Store spawn 1-2 °C (34-36 °F); use within about 2 weeks (3 at most) At 6 °C (42 °F) spawn loses quality; lion's mane spawn 2 weeks at most; Chapter 15

Card 3: Substrate

Full method: Substrate. Bags and filling: Bags, Filters and Inoculation.

Item Value Notes
Master's Mix 50% hardwood sawdust : 50% soy hulls Never over 50% soy; avoid soybean meal; Chapter 10
Lean mix (shiitake, maitake) 70-80% hardwood : 20-30% wheat bran or midds Chapter 10, Chapter 20
Lion's mane 30-40% soy may beat 50:50 Chapter 20
Moisture, most species 61-63% Above about 68% invites bacteria; Chapter 10
Moisture, exceptions Shiitake 64-65%; king oyster 62-63%; maitake 60-61%; lion's mane 62% at most Chapter 20
Water already in the inputs Combo pellets about 7%; fuel pellets 7-15%; raw oak sawdust up to 70-80% Measure it before you add water; Chapter 10
pH and calcium pH about 6.5; gypsum as a buffer; CaCO3 1-4%, with care Pure grades only; Chapter 10
Block size 10 lb (4.5 kg) at most in small-patch polypropylene (PP) bags; 5 lb (2.3 kg) if incubation temperature is unstable A 12 lb (5.4 kg) block goes anaerobic (starved of oxygen) in the centre; Chapter 11
Fill About one-third substrate, two-thirds headspace Chapter 11

Card 4: Steam

Full method: Steam: Pasteurizing and Sterilizing. Boilers and generators: Equipment.

Item Value Notes
Ultra-pasteurization (UP) Core of the slowest block at 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) for at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h; no pressure Measure the core, not the air; hold times vary, see ranges
Sterilization Core at 121 °C (250 °F) for about 35 min Purge all air first; 15 psi (about 1 bar) on the gauge alone doesn't prove 121 °C
Overnight "quasi-pressure" method Bring the vessel to 15 psi and the cores to 93-100 °C (200-212 °F), switch the boiler off, and let it cool under pressure Used for shiitake and maitake; no hold time is given
Loading Fill to at most two-thirds to 80% of vessel volume, racked with gaps Steam must reach every bag
Boiler sizing About 250,000 BTU (about 73 kW) boiler per 10 ft (3 m) container of about 500 blocks a run; about 500,000 BTU (about 147 kW) for a 20-40 ft (6-12 m) container Published ratings for the same models differ; check with the manufacturer (ranges)
Cool and knock Pull blocks out hot into a HEPA positive-pressure room; knock at 27-32 °C (80-90 °F), never above about 38 °C (100 °F) Chapter 4, Chapter 11

RULE Put a logger in the core of the slowest-heating block on every cook. The air temperature in the vessel tells you nothing about the core.

Card 5: Room set points

Full method: Climate Control, Incubation, Fruit Rooms and Fruiting. The plenum is the conditioned air space that feeds the fruit rooms.

Room Temperature CO2 Humidity Light Notes
Lab and cool-down Comfortable; dump the heat outside n/a n/a n/a About 20% more supply air than return; about 20 Pa pressure step between rooms; Chapter 4
Spawn incubation About 16-18 °C (low to mid 60s °F) As for blocks n/a Dim Chapter 13
Block incubation 19 °C (66 °F) at the bag surface; core no more than 21-22 °C (70-72 °F) 1,500-3,000 ppm: exhaust on at 3,000, off at 1,500-2,500 by preference; never above 5,000 ppm where people work n/a Dim for most species; even light for shiitake and maitake Chapter 13, Chapter 18
Fruiting (staple species) Start at 16 °C (60 °F); best 14-17 °C (58-62 °F); 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) working range Exhaust on at 900 ppm, off at 600 (cycle about 450-900 ppm); 1,000 ppm at most Swing about 70-90% (some prefer 75-85%) 6,500 K daylight Chapter 14
Plenum feeding fruit rooms 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) About 450 ppm at most 40-50% n/a Chapter 5
Cold storage 1-4 °C (34-40 °F); spawn 1-2 °C (34-36 °F) n/a n/a n/a Chapter 15

Example CO2 control for a 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room: an exhaust fan of about 1,000 CFM (about 1,700 m³/h) switches on at 900 ppm and off at 600 ppm, with a damper admitting air from the plenum. Fans and each HEPA stage add about 1 °C (2 °F) to the air, so pre-cool the air ahead of them.

Card 6: Species at a glance

Fuller tables with every figure are in Growth Metrics by Species; growing notes are in Species Profiles. Where two values are given, they come from different growers or batches.

Species Substrate Incubation Fruiting temperature Fruiting notes Yield per 10 lb block
Blue oyster Master's Mix 10-14 days at about 19 °C (66 °F) 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) Keep CO2 low or stems stretch About 2 to about 4 lb (0.9-1.8 kg)
Black oyster Master's Mix About 10 days to fruitable; 2-3 weeks is better 10-18 °C (50-65 °F); 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) ideal Fruit from the side; harvest before the caps flip up About 2.6-2.9 lb (1.2-1.3 kg)
King oyster Master's Mix at 62-63% moisture 14-18 days 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) Bright light, high steady humidity, cycled CO2 About 2-2.25 lb (0.9-1.0 kg)
Lion's mane 30-40% soy, or Master's Mix; 62% moisture at most Plan 12 days (10-18 workable) 13-18 °C (55-65 °F) CO2 800 on / 450 off, or 900 on / 650 off; rack it above and away from shiitake, whose brown drips stain it About 2 lb + 1.5 lb (0.9 + 0.7 kg) over 2 flushes
Shiitake 20-30% bran or midds; 64-65% moisture About 12 weeks (6-14) until 75-80% of the surface is brown 10-16 °C (50-60 °F) for strain 3790 Shock to fruit (cold, soaking, smacking); pick while the cap rim is still curled under 3-5 lb (1.4-2.3 kg)
Maitake 20-40% supplement; 60-61% moisture 8-12 weeks to harvest, with light throughout About 16-21 °C (60s °F) Steady 90-93% humidity, slow constant air, its own room About 2 lb (0.9 kg)
Chestnut Master's Mix or combo pellets 2.5-3 weeks to white, then 1-2 weeks to ripen 13-16 °C (55-60 °F) CO2 under 900 ppm; low light; cut the clump 1/8-1/4 in (3-6 mm) above the block 2-3+ lb (0.9-1.4+ kg) on combo pellets
Pioppino Master's Mix About 3 weeks, kept cool 18-24 °C (65-75 °F) Open at the amber droplets, before the pin carpet; harvest 1.5-2 days after the carpet "Very high"; no figure given
Comb tooth Combo pellets, 50:50 About 10 days About 19-21 °C (upper 60s °F) None given Not stated
Reishi Logs or bags Months Not stated In-bag CO2 of 3,000-5,000 ppm gives antler forms Not stated

Card 7: Water and cleaning

Full method: Diseases, Pests and Water Quality, The Lab and Clean Practice, Safety.

Use Dose or method Notes
Humidifier water, routine Bleach or chlorine dioxide (ClO2) at 150-250 ppm Chapter 17
Humidifier water, blotch outbreak About 0.1% hydrogen peroxide: 1.5 qt of 3% peroxide per 10 gal of water (1.4 L per 38 L), changed every 3 days Short term only; growers differ on using peroxide at all, see ranges and Chapter 17
Surface cleaning 70% isopropyl alcohol, or bleach at up to about 400 ppm Never mix bleach with ammonia; Chapter 4, Chapter 18
Water treatment chain Particulate filter, then softener, then carbon, then reverse osmosis (RO) or steam; UV optional Chapter 17
Boiler feed water Filter, soften, carbon; blow down regularly Never feed a boiler RO or distilled water; Chapter 12

WARNING Bleach and ammonia together release toxic gas. Never mix them, and never use them one after the other on the same surface without rinsing.

Card 8: Planning numbers

Full method: Planning the Farm, Running the Business.

Item Value Notes
One 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room About 500-600 lb (230-270 kg) a week at full rolling capacity Three weekly cohorts of about 250 blocks; Chapter 3, Chapter 14
Incubation space About twice the fruiting space At least 3 weeks of production for fast species, far more for shiitake; Chapter 3, Chapter 13
Room loading About 1/10 to 1/4 of the room volume; never more than half for incubation Two hand widths between bags; see ranges
Block heat output 2 to 10 BTU/h per 10 lb block, depending on the source Size cooling for the high end; Chapter 5
Block cost About $2.50-3 in materials; with labour, climbs toward the $8.50-9 bought-in price Until you reach about 2,000-5,000 blocks a week; Chapter 22
Acceptable loss Treat a steady 5% contamination rate as your whole margin Chapter 16, Chapter 22
Drying 24-48 h at 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) with dehumidifiers; dried weight about 10% of fresh weight Keeps about 7 years sealed; Chapter 15

Card 9: Advice from three working farms

These come from three farms in different climates, set out in full in Advice from Other Growers.

  • Size air conditioning generously. Fruit at 14-17 °C (58-62 °F), and at 18 °C (65 °F) at most.
  • Give incubation at least twice the fruiting floor area, and 3-4 times for slow species.
  • Master's Mix is 50:50 as standard. In a hot climate, start it at 60:40 sawdust to soy, at 60-62% water counting what the materials already hold.
  • Fruit-room CO2: exhaust on at 1,000 ppm, off at 600 ppm. Let humidity swing between 78% and 90%.
  • Unload pasteurized bags within 3 h and cool them in HEPA-filtered air.

Key rules: the twelve golden rules

These rules recur across every part of the book. Each links to the chapter that explains it.

  1. Keep four separate climates: steam and mixing, lab and cool-down, incubation, and fruiting. Never share air between fruiting and the rest. See Chapter 3, Chapter 5.
  2. Move product one way (steam, lab, incubation, fruiting) and move air the opposite way. See Chapter 3.
  3. Measure the core of the slowest block with a logger on every cook. See Chapter 12.
  4. Pull cooked blocks hot into HEPA-filtered positive pressure and knock them the same day. See Chapter 4, Chapter 12.
  5. Never put a recirculating air conditioner, evaporator or circulation fan inside a lab, cool-down room or fruit room. See Chapter 4, Chapter 14.
  6. Keep HEPA hoods running at all times, and never spray them. See Chapter 4.
  7. Dose solids and water by weight, so every bag has the same moisture. See Chapter 10.
  8. Incubate at about 19 °C (66 °F) with space between bags, and avoid temperature swings and bumps. See Chapter 13.
  9. Control fruit-room CO2 with an exhaust fan on a CO2 controller, and keep the room under negative pressure. See Chapter 14.
  10. Treat humidifier water, and keep foggers out of the room or on outside air. See Chapter 17.
  11. Change one variable at a time, and keep data before blaming the spawn. See Chapter 16, Chapter 19.
  12. Wear a respirator when harvesting, especially shiitake and reishi. See Chapter 18.

chapters.title: Settings and Their Ranges
chapters.html:
Settings and Their Ranges

AT A GLANCE Many settings in mushroom growing have more than one figure in use. This chapter lists every such setting, by stage, with the value to start from, the full range that working growers use, and when each end of the range applies. Use it when a number in another chapter doesn't fit your farm. The settings people ask about most:

  • Ultra-pasteurization hold: slowest core above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 h and no more than 4-6 h, logged; longer holds at lower temperatures also work (steam).
  • Block incubation: 19 °C (66 °F) on the bag surface for 10 lb blocks, cooler for bigger blocks (incubation).
  • Fruiting: start at 16 °C (60 °F), best 14-17 °C (58-62 °F); CO2 exhaust on at 900 ppm and off at 600 ppm (fruiting).
  • Master's Mix: 50:50 sawdust to soy hulls as standard; on a hot, humid site, start at 60:40 (40% soy) (substrate).
  • Spawn rate: one 6 lb G2 bag per twenty 10 lb blocks, about 3% (bags and spawn).

How to read this chapter

Each row gives a setting, the value to start from, the full range reported with the conditions behind each figure, and the chapter that explains the setting. The starting value is Cap n Stem's figure wherever they give one. Other figures are listed with the conditions where they apply (climate, block size, species, equipment, scale): a different figure for a different context is not a contradiction. When the stakes are real, as with dosing chemicals or rating a boiler, check a primary source, or test on a few blocks with a data logger before changing the whole farm.

Many differences come from the same farm describing its practice years apart. A different figure can reflect a change in practice, not a mistake.

Figures from the three farms in Advice from Other Growers come from farms in different climates from the Maine farm behind most of this book's baseline. Treat a difference as another data point to test, not as a correction.

TIP The Quick-Reference Cards give only the starting value. Come here when you need to know how far you can move it.

How to choose between figures

Start from Cap n Stem's figure, then move only where your context differs from theirs: climate, block size, species, equipment or scale.

  1. When two figures differ and you can't tell which context fits yours, test both on a few blocks with a logger rather than averaging them.
  2. Prefer the figure repeated across several sources, and the later figure when the same grower changed practice.
  3. Recompute any unit conversion or arithmetic you are given before you use it. Several common slips are listed under Figures corrected.
  4. Treat chemical dosing figures (peroxide, bleach) as needing a primary source before you rely on them.
  5. A grower's numbers come from their own farm and climate. A hot, humid site argues for the cooler and leaner end of each range.

Culture and storage

Explained in Culture Work and Storing Cultures, Strains and Genetics.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Glycerol strength for cryo storage 10% 10% in most sources, and the later, more repeated figure of the Maine farm; 5% in two of its older sources; some industry labs use 30-35%, but cell death has been reported at 25-30% in shiitake Chapter 8
How long cryo cultures last Check every vial yearly; test-fruit anything older than 2-3 years before relying on it Refresh every 6-12 months (one routine); 2-3 years is comfortable; about 3 years; up to a decade (one report) Chapter 8
Sugar in liquid culture 0.5% (Cap n Stem's standard) Many recipes elsewhere use 2-4%. Cap n Stem tested 0.5% to 8% and had far fewer contaminations at 0.5% Chapter 7
Expansion ratios 2 cuts per master, 12 masters per plate, 12 G2 per master, 20 blocks per G2 (in theory 12 x 12 x 20 = 2,880 blocks from one plate) 1 master to 12 G2 in most sources; about 20 in one; 12-20 in another; masters per plate from about 4 to "30-some" Chapter 7, Chapter 9
G2 bags per master 12; 20 is workable on millet 12 in most sources, about 20 in one. High Country Fungi gets about 20 G2 from a 4 lb (1.8 kg) master. Millet's many small grains give many inoculation points, which is why 20 works Chapter 9
Plate incubation temperature 18-21 °C (65-70 °F) once growth is under way 27-29 °C (80-85 °F) for the first days in one source, but this is probably the air temperature near the hood, not a target; a hood at 21-27 °C (70-80 °F) in another Chapter 7
Culture generations (passages) Keep to few passages from banked stock Warnings about senescence (ageing and loss of vigour) and genetic drift: refresh from storage. Catawba Mushrooms normally works P1 to P4 but has run lines to P30-40 without trouble. Long lines can work, but the risk is the farm's to carry Chapter 7, Chapter 8
Agar for chestnut Either works PDA or PDYA (potato dextrose agar, with or without yeast) in one source; MYA (malt yeast agar) in another Chapter 7
Agar slurry and chestnut fruit form Unresolved Which method, slurry straight into bags or ordinary grain spawn, gave bigger chestnut caps is unclear Chapter 7
Liquid-culture sugar 0.5% (Cap n Stem) About double the usual sugar, used by one breeder only for single-generation liquid culture started fresh from a slant, never LC from LC Chapter 7

Grain spawn

Explained in Grain Spawn.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Grain moisture for lion's mane Depends on the grain: about 56% on oats About 56% on oats; about 46% on another grain. Oats hold more water Chapter 9, Chapter 20
Calcium additives Grain: about 0.15% in total, under 1%. Substrate: 1-4% calcium carbonate (CaCO3) The two figures are for different media; keep grain additives light Chapter 9, Chapter 10
Soaking grain to germinate endospores Don't soak long A common claim is that a long soak makes bacterial endospores (heat-resistant resting cells) germinate so the steam can kill them. In practice a long soak only starts fermentation Chapter 9, Chapter 12

Substrate

Explained in Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing.

RANGE Soy hull share in Master's Mix. Standard: 50:50 sawdust to soy hulls (Cap n Stem). Context: on a hot, humid site, start at 60:40 (40% soy) and raise it only if incubation temperature and blotch stay under control. High Country Fungi moved to 35-40% soy because 50% raised blotch and contamination; Catawba Mushrooms suggests starting at 45% or 40% soy. These are climate differences, not a disagreement about the recipe.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Dry matter in a 10 lb block About 3.8 lb (1.7 kg) at 62% moisture About 4 lb (1.8 kg) and about 3.3 lb (1.5 kg) in other sources; the figure depends on the moisture Chapter 11
Maitake substrate moisture 60-61% 54-57% reported by another grower; possibly a difference in how moisture was measured Chapter 10, Chapter 20
Maitake supplement share Within 20-40% 20-30%; about 30% soy; 35% soy Chapter 10, Chapter 20

Bags, filters and spawn rate

Explained in Bags, Filters and Inoculation.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Spawn rate 1 x 6 lb (2.7 kg) G2 per 20 x 10 lb (4.5 kg) blocks, about 3% High Country Fungi uses 6 lb per 15 x 11 lb (5 kg) blocks, about 3.6%. The slightly heavier rate suits ultra-pasteurized substrate Chapter 11
Unicorn filter patch letter order Check Unicorn's own specification Accounts differ on whether the T or the B patch is the most restrictive Chapter 11
Is the Tyvek (T) patch open or tight? Treat T as a tight patch One source says it passes more air than the A patch and dries bags; most others say it traps CO2 and puffs bags up. The explanation that went with the first view misread the Gurley number (see corrections) Chapter 11
Spawn bag patches versus substrate bag patches Not measured; test your own One source says substrate patches are more restrictive; another says spawn patches are Chapter 11, Chapter 13
Patch area Judge by whether the mycelium grows evenly from top to bottom of the bag Bag makers say more patch area is needed; one experienced farm is sceptical Chapter 11
Tyvek sleeve inside the bag Skip it Older teaching; in a steamer it filters nothing Chapter 12, Chapter 16

Steam

Explained in Steam: Pasteurizing and Sterilizing.

RANGE Ultra-pasteurization hold. Start from: the core of the slowest block above 93 °C (200 °F) for at least 2-3 h, and no more than 4-6 h, logged. Holds reported: 1-3 h, 2 h, 2-3 h, 3 h and 2-4 h; one source gives 1-3 h above 93 °C (200 °F) and calls 3 h overkill. Container steamers at the Maine farm run 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for about 3 h. A substrate temperature log sheet sets longer minimums: 4-6 h above 93 °C (200 °F), or 6-8 h above 88 °C (190 °F), and counts anything above 96 °C (205 °F) as overprocessing. High Country Fungi holds bags at 93 °C (200 °F) for 4-5 h. When to choose which: the shorter holds assume a fast-steaming boiler and a measured cold spot. With a slow heat-up or an unmeasured vessel, use the longer holds. Log your runs and compare yield and contamination before you settle on one.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
"10 hours" versus "3 hours" Both are right: 10 h is the whole cycle, 3 h is the hold Blocks in loose steam for about 10 h in total; held at 96-99 °C (205-210 °F) for 3 h of that Chapter 12
Temperature that kills moulds Ignore the differences: pasteurization already runs well above all of them About 43 °C (110 °F, a loose aside), about 60 °C (140 °F), about 66 °C (150 °F), about 71 °C (160 °F) Chapter 12, Chapter 16
Hobby-forum sterilizing rules Measure the core: time and temperature trade off Forum rules say "24 h", or "15 psi (about 1 bar) for 90 min to 2 h". Measured in the core, 35 min at 121 °C (250 °F) was enough Chapter 12
Safe temperature to inoculate Aim for a block core of 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); never at 38 °C (100 °F) or above Room temperature, about 30 °C (86 °F); 27-32 °C (80-90 °F); below 38 °C (100 °F). High Country Fungi finds even 27 °C (80 °F) can be too hot, and checks with an infrared thermometer Chapter 11, Chapter 12
Cooling blocks inside the vessel Pull blocks out hot into a HEPA-filtered room, unless the vessel itself is pressurized with HEPA air Never cool in the vessel; or cool in it only if it is pressurized with HEPA-filtered air Chapter 12, Chapter 16
Boiler ratings Check with the manufacturer The Sioux SF-25 has been given as about 1.1 million or about 500,000 BTU; the SF-11 as about 500,000 or about 250,000 BTU; the model prefix as "SF" or "SR" Chapter 12, Chapter 6
Sauna steam generator capacity Three 7 kW units per steam box of about 500 five-lb (2.3 kg) or 250 ten-lb (4.5 kg) blocks, about a 16 h run (Cap n Stem) Cap n Stem also ran about 500 five-lb blocks with two 7.5 kW units at one site. In their side-by-side test, units above 7 kW gave no extra steam Chapter 12
Sauna steamers per box Two to three 7 kW steamers per about 500 five-lb (2.3 kg) blocks in a tight, insulated box (Cap n Stem) Four steamers running 17 hours on a leaky, uninsulated wooden box. Seal and insulate the box before adding steamers Chapter 12

Incubation

Explained in Incubation and Climate Control and Monitoring.

RANGE Block incubation temperature. Start from 19 °C (66 °F) on the bag surface for 10 lb blocks. High Country Fungi sets 17 °C (62 °F) for 11 lb blocks and 18-19 °C (65-66 °F) for smaller ones; Catawba Mushrooms uses 18 °C (65 °F). When to choose which: bigger, richer blocks run hotter at the core, so set the room cooler for 11 lb blocks. In later notes High Country Fungi gives 17-18 °C (62-65 °F) for its blocks, with 19 °C (66-67 °F) as the ceiling.

RANGE Incubation CO2. Everyone agrees: keep it well under 5,000 ppm. Start from: exhaust on at about 3,000 ppm, off at 1,500-2,500 ppm depending on how much CO2 you are willing to tolerate, which gives the usual 1,500-3,000 ppm band. Other bands in use: 2,000-3,000 ppm; up to 2,500-3,000 ppm with the controller set to act at 3,500 ppm; about 2,500 ppm as ideal for shiitake. Context: in a hot climate, run toward the top of the band to save cooling, with the exhaust off at 2,000-2,500 ppm rather than 1,500, so it purges less hot outside air (a reviewed container-farm plan used 1,500-3,000 ppm). Tune it once blocks are in.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Core-to-air temperature gap Log inside a bag, and keep cores under about 22 °C (72 °F) Core above air by about 2 °C (3-4 °F); 2-3 °C (4-5 °F); about 3 °C (5-6 °F), rising to 4-5 °C (8-9 °F) Chapter 13
How full to load a room 1/10 to 1/4 of the room volume (Cap n Stem's standard) Incubation: never more than about half. The older one-third rule is still quoted. Context: a purpose-built 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) fruit room at full capacity gives 500-600 lb (230-270 kg) a week Chapter 3, Chapter 13, Chapter 14
Heat given off per block Size cooling for the high figure until you measure your own About 2, about 6, or about 10 BTU/h per 10 lb block Chapter 5, Chapter 13
Fresh air into incubation In a hot, humid climate: recirculate, and add a CO2-triggered exhaust as the safety valve Catawba Mushrooms suggests a damper intake from the plenum, or a portable air conditioner, to purge CO2. Cap n Stem (Erik Lomen) uses no fresh air at all: recirculate through the mini-splits, keep the room slightly negative, and let CO2 leak out or exhaust it near 3,000 ppm. Recirculating saves the most cooling Chapter 5, Chapter 13
Motion-sensor lights Dim light that stays dim; avoid sudden bright flashes One source says motion-triggered light is too strong a trigger for the blocks; others find it works well Chapter 9, Chapter 13
Light colour in incubation Depends on the species Warm light; 6,500 K for shiitake; red light in Asian practice Chapter 13
Humidifying incubation No humidifier in incubation (Cap n Stem: rooms at 16-21 °C, 60-70 °F, all year) In a very dry climate the air conditioner can dry the room enough that some growers add humidity Chapter 13

Fruiting

Explained in Fruit Rooms and Fruiting and Climate Control and Monitoring.

RANGE Fruit-room temperature. Start from 16 °C (60 °F), inside the best band of 14-17 °C (58-62 °F), with 18 °C (65 °F) as the ceiling. The general range for staple species is 13-18 °C (55-65 °F). High Country Fungi finds 14-16 °C (58-60 °F) best and treats 18 °C (65 °F) as the ceiling; Catawba Mushrooms uses 14-17 °C (58-62 °F). When to choose which: the cool end gives better shelf life and colour.

RANGE Fruit-room CO2. Start from exhaust on at 900 ppm, off at 600 ppm. Cycles in use run roughly 450-900 ppm; the same grower has given 450-900, 400-900 and 400-1,000 ppm. As controller set points: exhaust on at 900 ppm and off at 600 ppm, or on at 1,000 and off at 600 (Catawba Mushrooms). A band of 600-1,000 ppm is the consensus. A reviewed container-farm plan used 400-600 ppm, but that sits barely above outdoor air (about 410-420 ppm), so the fans would rarely stop.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Recirculating air Recirculate clean air only, never spore-laden fruiting air Never recirculate in fruit rooms (most sources); a published author recommends filtering and recirculating; a large king oyster farm mostly recirculates; recirculating is fine inside a clean plenum Chapter 5, Chapter 14
Constant or cycled fresh air Cycle for most species; maitake is the exception CO2-triggered "lung" cycling (the room breathes in and out on CO2); constant exhaust, used by several other growers; one farm's maitake method runs a slow fan constantly Chapter 5, Chapter 14
Active exhaust fan Use one, keep a spare, and clean it It is the only good way to control CO2 and keep the room negative; the cost is that it collects spores and wears out Chapter 5, Chapter 14
Humidity swings Swing for most species; keep it steady for maitake Swing about 70-90%; some growers prefer 75-85%, and High Country Fungi swings 78-90%; maitake wants a steady 90-93%; lion's mane is grown both ways Chapter 14
Fogger on a timer Use a humidity controller A timer is a budget option; it is also called improper because it worsens blotch Chapter 5, Chapter 14
Plenum size At least half the grow room's floor area Bigger is better, with no fixed ratio; at least half the grow room; High Country Fungi runs about 3/8 (98 sq ft against 256 sq ft, 9.1 m² against 23.8 m²). A smaller plenum needs more air conditioning for the makeup air Chapter 5
Hart misting system Consider TAC misting first; if you use Hart, size the compressor generously Hart cleared one farm's blotch, with about a 26 gal (98 L) tank and a 4.5 SCFM compressor called enough. Catawba Mushrooms recommends Hart but sizes the compressor at about 5 HP with an 80+ gal (300+ L) tank. High Country Fungi burned out a compressor and now rates TAC above Hart, using Hart only if TAC isn't available. Erik Lomen reports a farm that left Hart after three compressor failures, and describes TAC as a compressor-free alternative. The burnout supports the bigger compressor Chapter 5
Racks rusting in fruit rooms Coating and humidity decide it Racks rust quickly (one farm); little rust after a year (another) Chapter 6
Cleaning the fruit room Clean between every load at minimum Daily; daily only for maitake; between loads Chapter 14
Room sizes at one small farm Approximate 14 x 20 ft (4.3 x 6.1 m) rooms with a 20 x 28 ft (6.1 x 8.5 m) plenum; or 12 x 24 ft (3.7 x 7.3 m) rooms in a 15 x 24 ft (4.6 x 7.3 m) outbuilding. Both were given from memory Chapter 3, Chapter 14
Humidity instruments Never go without a CO2 meter; it is the one instrument to buy first A humidistat is not essential for a manually run room, but when misting is automatic a wet/dry-bulb humidistat is the most accurate control Chapter 14, Chapter 5
Steam as humidity Only steam put through a fine atomizer A raw steam hose into a fruit room soaks everything; never use a bare hose Chapter 14
Compressor for atomizing nozzles Size the compressor to the number of nozzles About 4.5 SCFM ran one demonstration room; a 10 CFM hardware-store compressor was far too small for a room of air-hungry nozzles needing about 40 CFM Chapter 14
Exhaust height in a long container Intake at the front, exhaust at the far end, one-way flow (Cap n Stem) In a long, narrow container, mounting the exhaust high stopped it pulling fog down before it spread Chapter 14
Holding the fruit room wet Swing RH between about 70% and 90%; don't hold it at 90% In a very humid climate (Houston), running wetter with shallow swings gave no blotch, because outside air keeps the swing shallow anyway Chapter 14

Lab and clean practice

Explained in The Lab and Clean Practice.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Spawn and substrate work in one lab Separate rooms remain the safer design; one lab is possible on a small farm with strict scheduling The rule is one room, one function. Cap n Stem did both in one lab for years: it works if the two jobs are separated in time and the hood is kept spotless, though "weird anomalies" crop up. See the single-lab routine Chapter 4
HEPA grade Buy tested units; prefer the higher grade Context decides it: "many nines" (99.99...%) for a production lab; 99.95-99.97% is the standard grade, and for small hobby hoods the old forum insistence on the highest grade is called doctrine Chapter 4
Cooling bags at the hoods A separate HEPA cool-down room is the ideal Done in front of the hoods at one farm; cooling at the hoods dries out bags, so a separate room is better Chapter 4
Hood warm-up Run fixed hoods all the time Never switch a hood off; a portable unit needs 20-30 min of running before use Chapter 4
Gloves Wear them in production Not needed for small culture work; required in production Chapter 4
Footbaths Labs: part of the entry routine in some. Fruit rooms: airflow matters more Context decides it: an alcohol bath or footbath at the lab entry is part of some labs' routine; at fruit-room doors they make little difference beside a clean plenum and one-way airflow Chapter 4
Still-air box and closet labs Fine for hobby cloning, not for production Context decides it: the worst approach for a production lab; enough for a beginner cloning wild or store-bought mushrooms Chapter 4
Hiring staff with lab experience Judge the person, and use paid test days A positive when it comes with a calm, steady temperament; a warning sign when the hire arrives sure they have it all figured out Chapter 4, Chapter 22

Water, disease and chemicals

Explained in Diseases, Pests and Water Quality and Safety.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Hydrogen peroxide in humidifier water Use it only as a short-term outbreak tool, and verify the thresholds Context decides it: the standing dose is bleach or ClO2; in an outbreak, about 0.1% for a short time is the rescue step. It is also listed among standard additives, and one older source ruled it out with no reason given Chapter 17
Peroxide thresholds The working recipe gives about 0.1%; check the original study Figures quoted: "over about 1% harms", "one-fifth of a percent", "0.025 = 2.5%", "0.001 = 0.1%" Chapter 17
Bleach strength for humidifier water Use the ppm figures: 150-250 ppm 150-250 ppm; 150-200 ppm. Two other figures are wrong: "2-4% = 200-400 ppm" is out by 100 times (200-400 ppm is 0.02-0.04%), and "biocide at 20%" is garbled Chapter 17, Chapter 18
Cause of rose comb (a deformed, bumpy growth on caps) Check water quality and air exchange first Air exchange and room management (one view); water quality almost every time (another) Chapter 14, Chapter 17
Crop lost to blotch All the figures are loose recollections "90%" (admitted to be made up), about 15%, about 20% Chapter 17
Chestnut intolerance in people Unsourced: treat it as anecdote All-or-nothing and "100% proven" (one view); individual cases only (another) Chapter 18

Species

Explained in Species Profiles and Growth Metrics by Species.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Black oyster parentage The patent is the strongest evidence: a multi-species hybrid Pleurotus ostreatus x ostreatus; king x blue oyster; the Hokuto patent, a multi-species hybrid Chapter 8, Chapter 20, Chapter 2
Black oyster timing Extra incubation doesn't hurt Fruitable at about 10 days, or 2-3 weeks; pins to harvest 10-14 days, or 4-5 days. "Pinning" may be defined differently in the two sources Chapter 20, Chapter 21
Black oyster: top or side fruiting Side fruiting Top fruiting is common, but one grower advises against it; side fruiting is at least as good Chapter 14
Lion's mane incubation Plan 12 days; 10-18 is workable About 10 days; about 12 days (10-18); about 2 weeks Chapter 20, Chapter 21
Lion's mane CO2 A narrow band under 900 ppm Exhaust on at 800, off at 450 ppm; or on at 900, off at 600-700 ppm Chapter 20
Shiitake timeline Judge by browning (75-80% of the surface), not the calendar About 12 weeks; 6-14 weeks depending on strain; the weeks given for each stage differ Chapter 13, Chapter 20
Shiitake substrate treatment Either method works: trial both on a few blocks Cap n Stem ultra-pasteurizes shiitake; other growers say sterilizing or the quasi-pressure method is better Chapter 12, Chapter 20
Shiitake strains 3782 and 3790 3782 is forgiving; 3790 yields better once your process is dialled in 3782 has been called both "higher" and "moderate" yielding; 3790 is higher-yielding when well managed Chapter 7, Chapter 20
Shiitake shocks One-block anecdotes: test your own strain Strain JC likes beating and 3790 likes cold (one view); cold delays 3790 (another) Chapter 14, Chapter 20
King oyster strains Conch does better with an excellent process Which of Conch and 2603 is more forgiving was never stated clearly Chapter 7, Chapter 20
Maitake light Follow the dedicated maitake protocol: light throughout incubation Light throughout incubation; or dim, then bright to pin; red or blue spectrum Chapter 13, Chapter 20
Chestnut timing Wait for the caramel-coloured ring Colonized in 2.5-3 weeks, or 2-3 weeks; pins to harvest in 7-12 days, or 2-3 weeks Chapter 20, Chapter 21
Chestnut: 5 lb versus 10 lb blocks on raw sawdust Both views agree that combo pellets doubled yield Going from 5 lb to 10 lb on raw sawdust gave no gain (one view), or about 20% more (another) Chapter 20, Chapter 22
Chestnut and light Some light, never intense Fruiting is partly triggered by light; strong light burns it Chapter 14
When to open pioppino bags At the fluff-and-amber-droplet stage, before the pin carpet A full pin carpet is the traditional cue but is a little late Chapter 14, Chapter 20
Oyster yield per 10 lb block Plan on 2 lb (0.9 kg) About 2 lb to about 4 lb (0.9-1.8 kg) Chapter 20, Chapter 22
Enoki fruiting temperature Treat enoki as a cold-fruiting species A warm-weather enoki strain pinned in summer heat for one California grower; treat it as warm only once a strain is proven Chapter 14, Chapter 20

Prices and business

Explained in Running the Business and Equipment.

Setting Start from Full range, and when it applies See
Cost of one block Cost your own labour About $2.50-3 in materials; with labour, the real cost climbs toward the $8.50-9 bought-in price until you reach a large scale Chapter 22
Price of a 2-yard mixer About $30,000 now About $8,000 and about $20,000 in earlier years; about $30,000 today in both accounts Chapter 6, Chapter 22
CO2 controller price A few hundred dollars About $300; about $230-250 Chapter 5
Savings from a Coroplast heat exchanger Second-hand and hypothetical: don't plan on it 85% heat recovery, and a monthly bill cut from $1,000 to $200 Chapter 5, Chapter 22

Figures corrected

Slips heard in talks that simple arithmetic or the sources themselves correct. Fungal Biology, Genetics and History has the full list.

Statement heard Correct version
72 G2 bags x 20 blocks = 288 blocks 1,440 blocks
200-400 ppm bleach is "2-4%" 0.02-0.04%
-80 °C is "-250-something" -80 °C = -112 °F
Duggar 1905 was a patent from Minnesota It was a USDA bulletin by a University of Missouri professor (shown on a slide)
A higher Gurley number means more airflow A higher Gurley number (seconds for a set volume of air to pass) means less air permeability

Key rules

  1. Start from the recommended value, and move along the range only for a reason you can name: block size, species, climate or equipment.
  2. When two figures differ and you can't tell which context fits yours, test both on a few blocks with a logger rather than averaging them.
  3. Prefer a figure that is repeated across sources, and the later one when a grower changed practice.
  4. Recompute any conversion or arithmetic before you use it.
  5. Get a primary source for chemical doses (peroxide, bleach), and use bleach figures in ppm, never in percent.
  6. On a hot, humid site, choose the cooler and leaner end of each range: less soy, cooler fruiting, a higher incubation CO2 band.
  7. Log the core of the slowest block on every cook, and judge any hold time by your own logged results.
  8. Keep fruit-room CO2 bands well above outdoor air (about 410-420 ppm): 600-1,000 ppm.

Open questions

  • Which Unicorn patch letter (T or B) is the most restrictive, and whether spawn or substrate patches are tighter: check Unicorn's own specification.
  • The safe threshold for hydrogen peroxide in humidifier water: the figures quoted don't agree, and the original study should be checked.
  • Whether the slurry method or grain spawn gave the bigger chestnut caps.
  • The true steam ratings of the Sioux SF-25 and SF-11 boilers.
  • Whether the lower maitake moisture figure (54-57%) reflects a different measuring method.

chapters.html:
Advice from Other Growers

AT A GLANCE Advice from three working farms in different climates on sizing, layout, climate, lab routine and equipment, with their numbers side by side. Their main messages:

  • Size air conditioning generously. Every one of them who undersized it regretted it.
  • Fruit cool: 14-17 °C (58-62 °F), and no warmer than 18 °C (65 °F) if you can help it.
  • Give incubation at least twice the fruiting floor area, and 3-4 times for shiitake, maitake or chestnut.
  • Master's Mix is 50:50 as standard. In a hot climate, start it leaner: 60:40 sawdust to soy hulls, at 60-62% total water.
  • Start a pasteurizing barrel as soon as it is loaded, hold the bags at 93 °C (200 °F) for 4-5 h, and unload them into HEPA-filtered air within 3 h.

The three farms

The advice comes from 2026 consultations with three growers. The same advice appears through the subject chapters of this book, and Settings and Their Ranges shows where their figures differ from the baseline used elsewhere.

  • High Country Fungi (Avery). Runs 11 lb (5 kg) Master's Mix blocks, pasteurized in barrels of the "Bubba's" style (a steam barrel). Fruits in a 16 x 16 ft (4.9 x 4.9 m) room behind a 7 x 14 ft (2.1 x 4.3 m) plenum, and buys genetics from Cap n Stem in Maine. The advice is a set of written answers to a grower's question list, 4 pages long (source).
  • Catawba Mushrooms (Ryan). Two grow rooms; about 70% of income from blue oyster; grosses about US$375,000 a year. The advice comes from a two-page consultation note on facility sizing, genetics, air-conditioning sizing, CO2 set points, tinctures, substrate ratios and the water feed for a Thor bagger (source).
  • Catawba's lab routine. A two-page note on the weekly lab day, culture rotation, slants, backup spawn, pests and market packaging; High Country Fungi follows parts of the same routine (source).
  • Ryan's facility review. A five-page review of a planned container farm (three 40 ft refrigerated containers plus one 20 ft container) in a hot, humid climate, covering layout, airflow, cooling, humidification and grain-cooking equipment. Its general lessons are in this chapter (source).
  • Cap n Stem (Erik Lomen). A Maine block and spawn farm. A recorded 49-minute video call on 8 May 2026 walked through a container-farm layout: lab layout and pressure, cooling hot blocks, incubation and fruit-room airflow, how racks move, cold storage, steam generation and boilers, water treatment and the TAC misting system (source).
  • High Country Fungi, 2026 follow-up. Voice notes and short videos from February to April 2026 on grain hydration in electric pressure cookers, incubation temperatures, summer cooling, yields and equipment (source). Their content is folded into the sections below.

Designing a small or container farm

AT A GLANCE Fix a weekly target first and size every room from it. Give incubation at least twice the fruiting floor. Keep dusty work out of the plenum. Oversize the cooling and the exhaust fans. Background: Planning the Farm, Climate Control.

Topic Advice See
Set a target Fix a clear weekly production target first, and size every room from it. Chapter 3, Chapter 22
Overall size Three 40 ft containers plus one 20 ft container give 640 sq ft (59 m²) for incubation and fruiting and 480 sq ft (45 m²) for everything else. That is small for a whole farm: realistic output is about 400-600 lb (180-270 kg) a week of fast species (lion's mane, oysters, black oyster). Container layouts can be expanded and repeated. Chapter 3
Incubation share At least twice the fruiting floor, and 3-4 times for shiitake, maitake or chestnut. Catawba's own incubation is too small. Chapter 3, Chapter 13
Handling Touch blocks as few times as possible, and use rolling racks wherever they fit. Chapter 6
Shelf width In an 8 ft (2.4 m) wide container, 24 x 48 in (61 x 122 cm) shelves leave too narrow an aisle; 18 x 48 in (46 x 122 cm) shelves leave room to move racks. Chapter 6
Ceiling height Low ceilings limit rolling racks to 4 tiers. Tall doors allow a 5th tier, but then racks can't roll between incubation and fruiting. Chapter 3, Chapter 6
Bagger The Fenrir bagger needs combo pellets. The Thor bagger needs a reliable water supply: Catawba uses a 7.5 gpm (28 L/min) pump fed from auxiliary tanks. Chapter 6, Chapter 10
Dusty work Keep mixing, bagging and dry-material storage out of the air plenum. Move them outside, or store material in a separate dry, dehumidified, ventilated space. Chapter 3, Chapter 10
Steam room It will be hot and steamy. Fit a heavy louvred exhaust fan, with an inline fan above the barrel ducted to it. Chapter 12
Fruit-room airflow Intake airflow (CFM) should be equal to or greater than exhaust. Use passive intakes or variable-speed EC fans, and filter boxes on the intakes. Exhaust fans are always undersized. Chapter 5, Chapter 14
Plenum At least half the grow room's floor area. Bring outside air in through an 8-10 in (20-25 cm) exterior intake with a damper and a filter box, and tune it as the CO2 demand becomes clear. Chapter 5, Chapter 25
Cooling Go big. Every grower who undersized air conditioning regretted it, and in a hot, humid climate extra capacity is an advantage. Chapter 5
Incubation cooling Mount the mini-split at the front or rear and blow it down the room, not over the racks, and add fans against temperature and CO2 layering. To purge CO2, use a damper intake from the plenum, or a portable air conditioner on the far side exhausting outdoors. Chapter 5, Chapter 13
Humidification Hydrofoggers carry a blotch risk. High Country Fungi now rates TAC misting above Hart; Catawba recommends Hart, with a compressor of about 5 HP and an 80+ gal (300+ L) tank. With other systems, use a Pola HP57 humidistat with a wet/dry bulb sensor. See the Hart range. Chapter 5, Chapter 17
Lab pressure Keep the clean room under positive pressure with a fan filter unit (FFU) in the wall, pushing HEPA-filtered air in from the next room. Chapter 4
Power Have a generator that can run the air conditioning, and split the supply into sub-panels by task. Chapter 3, Chapter 5

Layout lessons from Cap n Stem

These nine lessons come from walking through a container-farm plan. They apply to any small farm. See also Planning the Farm.

  1. Put fruiting at the far end with its own outside door, so harvest and packing leave without crossing clean areas.
  2. Keep incubation racks and fruiting racks separate. Incubation racks circulate through the clean side; fruiting racks stay put, and rust.
  3. Recirculate incubation air through the mini-splits with no fresh-air intake, keep the room slightly negative, and add fans. See incubation fresh air.
  4. Vent fruiting air outdoors only.
  5. Exhaust the lab while hot blocks cool, through a passive screened port, then close it.
  6. Use filters rated for high humidity in hot, humid climates.
  7. One long hood bench and one job at a time in a shared lab.
  8. Refrigerated (reefer) storage buys time off: park colonized blocks cold. See Chapter 15.
  9. Plan for boiler failure, and soften the water feeding any electric steam generator. See Chapter 12, Chapter 17.

Running one shared lab

AT A GLANCE A small farm often has one lab that does everything. Give each weekday one job, clean between jobs, keep one lab day for cultures, and keep backups at every level: P2 wedges, slants, water tubes and spare spawn. Background: The Lab and Clean Practice, Culture Work, Storing Cultures.

Procedure: a weekly routine for one lab

  1. Give each weekday one job: for example, steam on Monday, cool-down and inoculation on Tuesday, spawn preparation on Wednesday and agar on Thursday. Clean the lab between functions.
  2. Keep one lab day a week for cultures (Catawba uses Tuesday). Pour 5 sleeves of plates, seal them with grafting tape, and store them in a gasketed tote in the fridge.
  3. Split culture transfers into halves on alternate weeks. Move chestnut, maitake and enoki every other week.
  4. Transfer from the leading edge only, before the mycelium reaches the edge of the plate (lion's mane fails after it does).
  5. Make P2 plates and store them: cut 5 P2 wedges from each P1 plate (and drop wedges into jars), use one and refrigerate the rest.
  6. Bank each strain on 3-5 slants (poured at an angle in front of the hood, colonized for 2 weeks, then refrigerated for years) and in water tubes.
  7. Keep backup spawn: 2-5 bags of lion's mane or blue oyster, held for 4-6 weeks.
  8. Cool cooked bags in HEPA-filtered air: unload within 3 hours, cool them on wire racks in front of HEPA units, and check the temperature with an infrared thermometer, since even 27 °C (80 °F) can be too hot to inoculate.

CHECK Each Friday, every strain in use should have a fresh plate or P2 wedge in the fridge, its slants and water tube banked, and a backup spawn bag less than 6 weeks old.

Cooking grain in electric pressure cookers

High Country Fungi hydrates its millet in a row of electric pressure cookers instead of a kettle. The full method, with the reasons for each step, is in Grain Spawn.

Procedure: millet in electric pressure cookers

  1. Put about 8 lb (3.6 kg) of white millet and 4 lb (1.8 kg) of water in each cooker. With millet at 11-12% moisture this gives about 40% moisture. A light sprinkle of sawdust pellets on top is optional.
  2. Close the lid. It takes 10-12 min to reach pressure; then cook 12-15 min (13 min is typical, 14 min in a warm, dry room). Err towards undercooking.
  3. Turn each cooker off the moment its timer ends, or the keep-warm setting will scorch the bottom.
  4. Cool with the lids on for 1-1.5 h.
  5. Open and check: only a few burst kernels and no free water.
  6. Tip all the cookers into one drywall mixing basin, mix for even moisture, bag, and sterilize at once (High Country Fungi: 1 h 45 min at 17 psi (1.2 bar)). The whole batch takes 4-5 h.
  7. Give each cooker its own 15 A circuit.

CHECK Kernels intact with only a few burst, and no water pooled in the pot.

Species they grow

Species details are in Species Profiles.

  • Catawba's focus list: Italian, blue, golden and pink oyster, black pearl (18 days at 18 °C (65 °F) in black bags), lion's mane, coral tooth and pioppino.
  • High Country Fungi grows blue oyster (strain POCNS), golden and pink oyster, chestnut, pioppino, lion's mane, comb or coral tooth, black pearl, golden enoki and maitake, all from Cap n Stem genetics.
  • For a small container farm with limited incubation space, a realistic mix is lion's mane, oysters and black oyster, which are all fast species.

Most of these are US suppliers. Check local availability and import costs before planning around them.

Notes for hot climates

These two points are this book's own reasoning from the growers' advice, not advice the growers gave.

  • Don't set a fruit-room CO2 band near outdoor levels (about 410-420 ppm). With a band of 400-600 ppm, the exhaust would almost never stop, and it would keep pulling in hot, wet outside air for the air conditioning to treat. Catawba and the baseline in Fruit Rooms and Fruiting use roughly 600-1,000 ppm.
  • In a hot climate, run incubation at the top of the standard CO2 band (exhaust on at 3,000 ppm, off at 2,000-2,500 rather than 1,500; see Incubation), so the room purges hot outside air less often.

WHY Every purge of incubation or fruiting air brings in outside air that the air conditioning must cool and dry. In heat and humidity that air is the biggest load, so bands that purge less often save the most power.

Key rules

  1. Size air conditioning generously. Every grower who undersized it regretted it.
  2. Fruit at 14-17 °C (58-62 °F) for colour and shelf life, and never above 18 °C (65 °F) if you can help it.
  3. Give incubation at least twice the fruiting floor before adding fruit-room racks.
  4. Master's Mix is 50:50 as standard. In heat and humidity, start at 60:40 sawdust to soy and adjust from there.
  5. Measure the moisture already in your sawdust and pellets, and aim for 60-62% total.
  6. Start the barrel as soon as it is loaded, bring the bags to 93 °C (200 °F) and hold them there for 4-5 hours, then unload and cool them in HEPA-filtered air within 3 hours.
  7. Keep fruit-room intake equal to or greater than exhaust, with filtered intakes and speed-controlled fans.
  8. Swing fruit-room humidity between about 78% and 90%, and keep the floor dry.
  9. Run the lab on a fixed weekly day, transfer from the leading edge, and keep slants, water tubes and backup spawn.
  10. Gnat-proof everything: tape, magnetic screens, sticky traps on every shelf, and no compost near doors.
  11. Keep incubation and fruiting racks separate, and give the fruit room its own exit for harvest and packing.
  12. Recirculate incubation air, and exhaust fruit-room air and hot-lab air outdoors.

Open questions

These questions were put to the growers but not answered:

  • Which changes drove the biggest jumps in yield and fruit quality.
  • Which bag-production methods raised efficiency (the only pointer given was to look at one other farm's production space).
  • Whether to fruit all species in one room or in separate chambers.
  • How well filtered the outside air should be for each room. Airflow direction was covered, but not filter grades; specific high-humidity filter models were still to come from Cap n Stem.
  • Whether a mini-split can sit inside a fruit room, or should feed conditioned air in. The baseline in Climate Control feeds it in from a plenum.
  • Whether a farm that buys spawn should drop its lab, and whether to cook indoors or outdoors.

chapters.html:
Source Library

AT A GLANCE Every source behind this book, in one catalogue: 70 Cap n Stem (MycoWizards) member videos, 84 MycoWizards podcast conversations with other growers, and seven grower consultations and records. Each entry gives the length, what it covers, and which chapters of this book draw on it. Turn on Sources at the top of the page and every fact shows chips that link here.

How to use this library

  • Videos are sorted alphabetically by title; podcasts are listed by number, oldest first (Podcasts).
  • The short code under each title (for example agar-slurry) is the label used on the source chips, followed by a time stamp such as 0:13:15 (hours:minutes:seconds) or a page such as p3.
  • Used in lists the chapters of this book that carry facts from that source, worked out from the source chips themselves.
  • Some sources are dense technical walk-throughs; others are mostly conversation, speculation or deliberate fiction. Weight them accordingly (Weighting the sources).
  • Cap n Stem's own videos are the standard this book follows. Where a podcast guest's figure differs, the chapters give Cap n Stem's figure first and the guest's as context.

Weighting the sources

RULE Treat the conversation- and fiction-heavy sources (Cactus Hat Mushrooms, Massospora, Reishi Madness, Mycelium Man, Mon DI 2) lightly for technical facts.

TIP The densest technical sources are Fruit Room Design, Lab Design, To Pasteurize or Sterilize, Shiitake Cultivation, The Fenrir, Steam Generation and How to grow Maitake.

Podcast 30: Cultivating Shiitake Mushrooms

pod-30 · 25 Aug 2023 · 66 min · none (Erik of Cap n Stem) · Used in: 5 Climate Control and Monitoring, 10 Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing, 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation, 22 Running the Business

A solo walk-through of shiitake: why the US moved to shiitake and Chinese imports, the three maturation stages (colonize, popcorn/buckle, brown), trigger pinning, fruiting temperatures by strain, grading, cold storage and substrate coarseness. The general lesson for any species: incubation temperature must match how the substrate was heat-treated. Sterilized bags (15 psi, 121 C) tolerate warmer incubation (Far West Fungi runs 5 lb sterilized shiitake at 21-24 °C (70-75 °F)); ultra-pasteurized (93-100 °C (200-212 °F)) blocks let surviving thermophilic bacterial endospores wake up above about 19-21 °C (66-70 °F), giving duds and block-to-block yield swings, so hold 19-20 °C (66-68 °F) for 10 lb blocks (5 lb blocks have more leeway). Denser, more supplemented substrates push the case for sterilizing. Also: Cap n Stem's first 3,000 sq ft farm couldn't hold temperature because they didn't know how much heat blocks produce; cold rooms dry mushrooms, so use more evaporator and condenser capacity at lower fan speed, insulated floors and strip curtains.
