pod-52 · 04 Oct 2024 · 121 min · Eliah Thanhauser (co-founder, North Spore, Portland/Westbrook, Maine; spawn, kits, fresh mushrooms, education), recorded at their Mycology Outside event; other North Spore early staff join · Used in: 3 Planning the Farm and Its Layout, 5 Climate Control and Monitoring

North Spore's history from old mill buildings to a large purpose-built facility. Farm-useful points: early fruit rooms with low-pressure misters made so much water that stuck float-valve pumps flooded the floor below repeatedly; their first summer they had no cooling and grabbed window ACs off the roadside ("cooling... the continual problem with growing mushrooms"); know your neighbours before renting (a brewery next door means CO2 and shared ducts); their warehouse build-out ran about 500% over budget (new trench drains, pumps, electrical and water service; about half a million owed to the contractor before bank finance arrived); ultrasonic humidifiers fill with spores inside rooms, so put them outside the room and duct the mist in; many Asian farms grow a single species in low-tech shade houses.

Podcast 53: Dedikaryotization: Gregor Jones

pod-53 · 18 Oct 2024 · 47 min · Gregor Jones (Cap n Stem / MycoWizards lab; breeding work) · Used in: 8 Storing Cultures, Strains and Genetics

A lab method conversation on de-dikaryotization (blending cultures and hunting for clampless hyphae to recover monokaryons for breeding), tried so far on blue oyster and shiitake. No production, climate or business content.

Podcast 54: Tiger Sawgill: Thomas Roehl

pod-54 · 01 Nov 2024 · 75 min · Thomas Roehl (PhD student, Clark University, with David Hibbett; Lentinus tigrinus genetics) · Used in: 10 Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing, 14 Fruit Rooms and Fruiting

Research on the tiger sawgill (Lentinus tigrinus) and its two fruiting forms, mushroom development (inflating a pre-formed primordium vs building layers like polypores), iNaturalist data and a converted deli fridge as a fruiting chamber. One practical point from Cap n Stem: in-bag (high CO2) lion's mane gains water, not dry matter, as it grows on, while reishi keeps adding real mass.

Podcast 55: Sno Valley Mushrooms: Will Lockmiller

pod-55 · 15 Nov 2024 · 109 min · Will Lockmiller (Sno Valley Mushrooms, King County, Washington; grows about eight species from scratch on sawdust; sells blocks, substrate and spawn; consultant; runs a controls business for mushroom HVAC, humidification and CO2 automation), recorded live in front of an audience · Used in: 3 Planning the Farm and Its Layout, 5 Climate Control and Monitoring, 11 Bags, Filters and Inoculation, 14 Fruit Rooms and Fruiting, 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation, 18 Safety, 20 Species Profiles, 22 Running the Business

Will's path from Fungi Perfecti intern to an eight-species farm, with strong points on room design and species choice: US farms default to two room types (a shiitake room with slightly higher CO2, some condensing humidity and low light, and an "exotics" room for oyster, lion's mane and chestnut), while Asia also uses very cold rooms, very hot rooms, and shade houses used seasonally; most new farms make most of their money from two varieties, and mixing many species in one room "waters down the profitability"; choose species by data on what makes money in your climate, not garnish value (pink and yellow oyster draw people to the booth but aren't the earners); he picked 5 lb blocks for every product (shipping, handling, less core depth, tolerates a wider incubation temperature range when sterilized); shiitake is now his least profitable species; filter patches clog with water, spores or hard-water scale from humidifiers; CO2 exposure for staff; a mushroom is "a funny shape of water" (3 lb fresh dries to a quarter pound).

Podcast 56: Flying Saucer Farms: Clint Jurek

pod-56 · 29 Nov 2024 · 100 min · Clint Jurek (Flying Saucer Farms, outside Houston, coastal Texas, 2019-2024) · Used in: 3 Planning the Farm and Its Layout, 5 Climate Control and Monitoring, 6 Equipment, 10 Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing, 13 Incubation, 14 Fruit Rooms and Fruiting, 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation, 22 Running the Business

Clint is closing a profitable two-employee farm. About 40 of the 100 minutes are farm details (0:29-0:45); the rest is philosophy, management and why he chose not to scale. The hot, humid climate material (0:39-0:44) is short but directly relevant to a humid tropical site.

Podcast 57: Dr. Sara Webb: Mycelium In Microgravity

pod-57 · 13 Dec 2024 · 62 min · Dr. Sara Webb (astrophysicist, Australia; school space-science program) · Used in: 2 Fungal Biology, Genetics and History

A student research program that sent turkey tail, lion's mane and Cordyceps militaris cultures (from Cap n Stem) to the International Space Station, plus astronomy careers and outreach. Ground "analog" experiments grew mycelium on buckwheat and other grains; one batch drowned in too much liquid. No farm-relevant content.

Podcast 58: Wumbo Genetics

pod-58 · 27 Dec 2024 · 113 min · Maximilian (Wumbo Mycology; breeder, protoplast fusion; formerly grow-room manager at a large maitake and shiitake farm in Stockton, California, and its nutraceutical division) · Used in: 4 The Lab and Clean Practice, 18 Safety, 22 Running the Business

Mostly breeding methods (protoplast fusion with cold shock then heat shock), mycelium materials (paper, boards from extracted mushroom waste) and food plans. Farm-useful points: a large farm that scaled to 1,000-2,000 lb a week was shut down by fire marshals because the grow rooms had no sprinklers (power cords and outlets everywhere); Cap n Stem: selling only wholesale to distributors at about $4 a pound for oysters needs about 10,000 lb a week just to break even, so know how you'll sell before you build; Max's small lab shares one conditioned plenum tent that feeds filtered air to a 10x10 lab tent and an 8x8 incubation tent for positive pressure.

Podcast 59: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep1

pod-59 · 06 Jan 2025 · 15 min · Cap n Stem team only (Cap n Stem) · Used in: 18 Safety

The Cap n Stem team read and comment on the US National Organic Program's final rules for mushroom substrate. Producers argued organic substrate ingredients aren't consistently available and substitutions cause yield drops; under the rules, composted inputs and "inputs" carried over from older exemptions let large farms become certified organic overnight, which Cap n Stem calls an unfair game. Relevant only to farms planning organic certification.

Podcast 60: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep2

pod-60 · 08 Jan 2025 · 13 min · Cap n Stem team only (Daniel Ashley and Eric Lohman) · Used in: 22 Running the Business

The Cap n Stem team discuss a news headline about a fatal "psilocybin mushroom" case and mushroom misinformation (market customers who think lion's mane is psychedelic). No cultivation content.

Podcast 61: MadCap Mushrooms: Blake and Lindsey

pod-61 · 10 Jan 2025 · 145 min · Blake and Lindsey (MadCap Mushrooms, Vermont; started growing on the Mississippi coast while in the military) · Used in: 3 Planning the Farm and Its Layout, 5 Climate Control and Monitoring, 22 Running the Business

Mostly the couple's life stories (military, travel, psychedelics). Farm-useful points are few: on the humid Mississippi coast they grew indoors with no humidifier at all ("humid enough... that we didn't need any sort of humidity") until spores made them both wheeze, since they had no exhaust; white and pink oysters left layers of spores within two days; their Vermont farm (lab, incubation and fruiting in one room plus a hallway) maxes out at about 75 lb a week; one chef agreed to take 35-40 lb a week, flexible, which let them expand.

Podcast 62: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep3

pod-62 · 14 Jan 2025 · 10 min · Cap n Stem team only (Mike Vance and Eric Lohman) · Used in: background only

Cordyceps militaris culture-keeping and mating types (an ascomycete with two mating types; storing monokaryons matters for it, while shiitake and other basidiomycetes don't benefit from it), and "gatekeepers" of Cordyceps know-how. No production content for the main species in this book.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 63: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep4

pod-63 · 15 Jan 2025 · 8 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: 22 Running the Business

Meta (Instagram) took down the Cap n Stem account and other mushroom cultivator pages. No cultivation content.

Podcast 64: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep5

pod-64 · 20 Jan 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: background only

The Cap n Stem team recap mushroom festivals and announce giveaways. No cultivation content.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 65: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep6

pod-65 · 22 Jan 2025 · 18 min · Cap n Stem team only (Eric Lohman and Daniel Ashley) · Used in: 22 Running the Business

Cap n Stem stopped fruiting to specialize in spawn and substrate. Cap n Stem argues for specialization, a step-by-step path into vertical integration (start as a fruiter, then add substrate, then spawn and genetics), and that scale depends on local costs, including electricity.

Podcast 66: Open Fung: Phil Ross

pod-66 · 24 Jan 2025 · 107 min · Phil Ross (artist and mycomaterials pioneer; co-founder of MycoWorks; Open Fung project on open genetics and culture provenance) · Used in: 17 Diseases, Pests and Water Quality, 22 Running the Business

Mycelium materials, open science, naming fungi, and culture provenance (knowing a culture's history and checking it genetically, so you don't ship viruses, mites or the wrong organism to another farm). Cap n Stem: new farms often fail not from finance alone but from "some dumb mistake that created too much of a financial burden", because they didn't spend enough time learning the organism in their own environment. No production numbers.

Podcast 67: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep7

pod-67 · 27 Jan 2025 · 17 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: 20 Species Profiles

A study making gold nanoparticles with chestnut mushroom (Pholiota adiposa) polysaccharides for cancer research in mice. An aside from Cap n Stem: "nobody loves chestnuts... I don't know why we grow them anymore". No cultivation content.

Podcast 68: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep8

pod-68 · 29 Jan 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: background only

Off-topic news chat and giveaways (flow hoods, cultures). No cultivation content.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 69: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep9

pod-69 · 03 Feb 2025 · 16 min · Cap n Stem team only (Eric Lohman, Daniel Ashley, Michael Vance) · Used in: 9 Grain Spawn

Why spawn and colonizing blocks must ship refrigerated. Hard number: blocks in an open-air incubation environment make about 2 BTU per dry pound of substrate per hour (audio-checked); 160 ten-pound blocks packed tight on a pallet keep heating, and a dry (unrefrigerated) shipment arriving 4-10 days later is "trash, or at least half trash", even in shoulder seasons; freezing also kills cells. Cap n Stem logs block temperatures with data loggers inside blocks from incubation through shipping. Small spawn orders go same-day by airline cargo with ice packs and insulated boxes.

Podcast 70: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep10

pod-70 · 05 Feb 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: background only

Ross Ulbricht's pardon, dark-web history and privacy. No cultivation content.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 71: Highland Fungi: David Medlock

pod-71 · 07 Feb 2025 · 118 min · David Medlock (Highland Fungi, Elkins, West Virginia; mixed-species fresh grower; blocks, kits; ultrasonic fogging, 10 lb pasteurized blocks) · Used in: 5 Climate Control and Monitoring, 9 Grain Spawn, 20 Species Profiles

The fullest account in the sources of a rose comb (crowning) epidemic and how it was traced to humidifier water. Over a drought year his city water became mineral-heavy (plus chloramine); his ultrasonic fogger tank, topped up by float valve and fed back by condensate from the fog line, concentrated minerals, and fine white mineral dust settled on young pins. Rose comb spread from king and black oyster to big-cap blue, snow oyster and every gilled species except chestnut, while the same blocks fruited normally as kits in shops. It faded once he redirected the fog line, ran distilled water, then installed RO that removes chloramine (TDS about 600 in, 0 out). Also: how he piped fog in high through a perforated 6 inch pipe with a perforated CO2 exhaust pipe in the middle and a plenum dropping dry air ("if I see fog in my grow, it's water that hasn't absorbed into the air yet, and it's fallen back out"); keeping the fogger out of the grow room, clean and UV-treated; incubation held at 18-19 °C (64-66 °F) for 10 lb pasteurized blocks (mid-70s "asking for fruiting issues"); shiitake needs huge incubation space and tight HVAC and lighting; "super spawn" (G1 with about 30% hydrated sawdust or pellets) cut incubation about 1-1.5 weeks without running hotter; lion's mane cut on day 10, harvested by end of week 3; lion's mane pulls off the block when RH drops and day-night swings grow; VPD-based controllers compensate for temperature swings.

Podcast 72: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep11

pod-72 · 10 Feb 2025 · 13 min · Cap n Stem team only (Gregor Jones and Eric Lohman) · Used in: 2 Fungal Biology, Genetics and History

Results from the cultures sent to the ISS (see Podcast 57): turkey tail recovered fastest (about five days), lion's mane was slowest to leave the grain; side-by-side trials of "space" vs normal G1 planned. No production content.

Podcast 73: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep 12

pod-73 · 12 Feb 2025 · 16 min · Cap n Stem team only (Michael Vance and Eric Lohman) · Used in: 10 Substrate: Recipes, Moisture and Mixing

A listener in France asks whether soy-oil-extraction waste (hulls plus crushed beans) can replace soy hulls as a supplement. The Cap n Stem team: what soy hulls give is nitrogen, protein and fibre with a husk structure; other hulls (beet, cottonseed, oat), wheat bran and wheat middlings can do the same job; buckwheat flour has been used; David Medlock (Podcast 71) uses a high share of oats in ultra-pasteurized substrate; straw (fermented) can stand in; US growers have limited themselves to combo pellets or masters mix, but "it's not the only thing you can use".

Podcast 74: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep13

pod-74 · 17 Feb 2025 · 17 min · Cap n Stem team only (Mike Vance and Eric Lohman) · Used in: background only

The history of indoor morel cultivation patents (Ronald Ower's patent, his death, Gary Mills's later morel company), and that morels fruit differently from wood-rot species. Gary Mills now grows maitake on blocks with Japanese equipment. Not relevant to the main crops in this book.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 75: MycoWizards Broadcast: Ep14

pod-75 · 19 Feb 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only (Michael Vance, Daniel Ashley, Kate Higgins) · Used in: 22 Running the Business

How US tariffs on Canadian goods (combo pellets come from Canada) raise input prices, and whether to pass costs to customers. Cap n Stem keeps a "buffer" of surplus blocks to bail out farms whose own production failed or whose big customer changed orders.

Podcast 76: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 15

pod-76 · 24 Feb 2025 · 15 min · Cap n Stem team only · Used in: background only

Mycelium caskets made by a mushroom farm that diversified (about $1,200 for a human casket). Not relevant to the main crops in this book.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 77: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 16

pod-77 · 26 Feb 2025 · 13 min · Cap n Stem team only (Gregor Jones and Eric Lohman) · Used in: 8 Storing Cultures, Strains and Genetics

The first round of mechanical de-dikaryotization on nine strains (eight oysters including a pink and a gold, plus one shiitake) failed; literature suggests chemical methods work better for oysters. Wild oyster clones often smell great but never fruit well; wild lion's mane clones tend to fruit true. No production content.

Podcast 78: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 17

pod-78 · 10 Mar 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only (Eric Lohman and Michael Vance) · Used in: 22 Running the Business

A trip to France: Asian markets there sell large amounts of dried lion's mane, graded shiitake, tremella and cheap cordyceps; shiitake has barely entered European kitchens; the US has driven gourmet prices to "a penny per mushroom" efficiency. Not directly useful.

Podcast 79: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 18

pod-79 · 12 Mar 2025 · 13 min · Cap n Stem team only (Eric Lohman and Mike Vance) · Used in: 5 Climate Control and Monitoring

A grower (Enrique, Desert Moon Mushrooms) had lion's mane forming hundreds of small mounds ("cauliflower" effect), sometimes giving way to bacteria, and blue oysters turning blotchy. After ruling out light, bags, airflow and cleaning products, the cause was the burnt-out UV lamp treating the water going into his humidifier; replacing it fixed both. Cap n Stem: many farms suffer crop loss after crop loss from untreated water; well water and city water each have problems.

Podcast 80: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 19

pod-80 · 17 Mar 2025 · 14 min · Cap n Stem team only (Eric Lohman and Daniel Ashley) · Used in: 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation

Pennsylvania mushroom industry labour shortage and crop-loss insurance; button mushrooms in the US are picked small for yield and bruise easily, while Europe sells bigger, firmer ones; same yield-vs-size trade-off as shiitake. Not directly useful.

Podcast 81: MycoWizards Broadcast Ep: 20

pod-81 · 19 Mar 2025 · 12 min · Cap n Stem team only (Gregor Jones and Eric Lohman) · Used in: background only

Orchids and their fungal partners (mycorrhizal germination). Not relevant to the main crops in this book.

No facts used beyond what the manual already had.

Podcast 82: Will MacHugh and The Shiitake Battlefield

pod-82 · 16 May 2025 · 48 min · Will MacHugh (US shiitake block maker and farmer; data analyst who studied US customs import records) · Used in: 22 Running the Business

How imported Chinese shiitake logs (cheap cylindrical blocks, often under $1 each at first) wiped out large Pennsylvania block makers. Will found in public US Customs data that 3,583 shipping containers of shiitake logs entered the US in 2024, declared as "mushroom spawn"; by his ratios that is about 93 million lb of shiitake, about $400 million wholesale and $700 million retail. Country-of-origin labelling loopholes let imported blocks be sold as US-grown. Some Chinese companies now run US facilities (one in Bellingham has about 200,000 sq ft of shiitake fruiting space). He wants to grow grocery-friendly Japanese-style products.

Podcast 83: Feral Fungi: Jason Scott

pod-83 · 06 Sep 2025 · 133 min · Jason Scott (Feral Fungi; spagyric mushroom tinctures since 2016; teaches alchemy) · Used in: 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation, 22 Running the Business

Almost entirely about spagyric (alchemical) tincture making, its philosophy and history (Paracelsus, Rasa Shastra), festivals, and running a growing manufacturing business with integrity. There is nothing on cultivation, climate, cooling, containers or species choice. A few business points: in 2016 it was hard to buy even 10 lb of dried lion's mane; his process is a three-part extraction (organic alcohol in custom Soxhlets, water, and calcined minerals); growth only for its own sake doesn't pay staff a good wage; Erik notes Cap n Stem's revenue is in the millions but net barely funds its growth.

Podcast 84: Catawba Mushroom Partners: Ryan Hollums

pod-84 · 26 Oct 2026 · 75 min · Ryan Hollums (Catawba Mushrooms, western North Carolina; grower since 2013) · Used in: 3 Planning the Farm and Its Layout, 8 Storing Cultures, Strains and Genetics, 12 Steam: Pasteurizing and Sterilizing, 15 Harvest, Storage and Preservation, 17 Diseases, Pests and Water Quality, 20 Species Profiles, 22 Running the Business

Ryan's story from Alex's basement farm (about 150 lb/week) to 1,000-1,200 lb/week in a about 6,000 sq ft former furniture warehouse they are buying. It covers barrel steaming and its stratification problem (their biggest struggle), blotch brought in by flies, the choice of an autoclave over a boiler plus container steamer (partly because of the humid southeast's seasonal heat), autoclave buying advice, maitake trouble, sales through six farmers markets, and rack casters. No container or AC sizing talk.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.html:
Glossary

AT A GLANCE Short definitions of the words this book uses, A to Z. Links in the chapters jump here; links here jump back to the full explanation.

A

Agar. A jelly made from seaweed, mixed with nutrients and poured into dishes (plates) or tubes. Mycelium grows across it so you can see it, clean it up and pick the best growth. See Culture Work.

Air changes per hour (ACH). How many times an hour a fan replaces the whole volume of a room's air: fan airflow per hour divided by room volume. A 1,000 CFM fan moves 60,000 cu ft an hour, so in a room of about 2,900 cu ft (82 m³) it gives about 21 air changes per hour. See Air-exchange rate.

Airlock (sluice). A small room or vestibule between a dirtier and a cleaner area, with doors that are not opened at the same time, so dirty air and dust cannot flow straight through. See Sluices, airlocks and one-way movement.

Anemometer. A meter that measures air speed. Used to check a flow hood's face velocity. See The Lab.

Autoclave. A pressure vessel that sterilizes with steam at about 15 psi (1 bar) and 121 °C (250 °F). Ranges from a stovetop pressure cooker to a vacuum autoclave. See Steam.

Auto-fruiting. Mushrooms forming by themselves in spawn or a block before you trigger them, usually because it was held too long, warm or bright. See Grain Spawn.

B

Backdraft damper. A flap in a duct that lets air flow one way only, so outside air cannot blow back in when a fan is off.

Bacterial blotch. A bacterial disease of mushroom caps: yellow, tan or rusty patches and goopy lesions where water sits. Usually comes from the fruit room's humidifier water and warm, wet conditions. See Diseases.

Bagger. A machine that fills substrate bags. Volumetric baggers fill by volume from a hopper; load-cell fillers weigh in dry pellets and then add water. See Volumetric pneumatic baggers.

Band sealer. A continuous sealer that feeds bag tops through heated bands, sealing bags one after another at speed. See Bags.

Biological efficiency (BE). Fresh mushroom weight divided by the dry weight of the substrate, given as a percentage. At 100% BE, every 1 kg of dry substrate gives 1 kg of fresh mushrooms. See Growth Metrics by Species.

Block. A bag of colonized (or colonizing) substrate that will be fruited, typically 5-10 lb (2.3-4.5 kg) of moist sawdust mix; 10 lb is the norm. See Block sizes. Also called a fruiting block.

Boiler. A vessel that heats water into steam for pasteurizing substrate or running an autoclave. Farm boilers are usually low-pressure types (15 psi, 1 bar, or less). They need treated feed water, regular blowdown to flush sediment, and working safety switches. See Water treatment for boilers and steamers.

Bran and wheat midds. By-products of milling wheat, used as nitrogen supplements in sawdust substrate. Bran is the outer skin of the grain; midds (middlings) are bran mixed with the finer leftovers of milling. See Wheat midds, bran and other supplements.

BTU/h. British thermal units per hour, the US unit for heating and cooling power. 12,000 BTU/h (one "ton" of cooling) is about 3.5 kW.

Buller phenomenon (di-mon mating). When a dikaryon meets a monokaryon and passes one of its nuclei into it, turning the monokaryon into a new dikaryon. Breeders use it to make new strains. See Fungal genetics basics.

C

Calcium carbonate (CaCO3). Ground limestone or chalk. Added in tiny amounts to grain and substrate to buffer pH and stop loose starch clumping. Too much makes dense clumps that can lead to stroma. See Calcium additives and pH.

Casing. A layer of moist material (such as peat) spread over a substrate to hold water and help pinning. Used for king oyster on trays in some farms. See Fruiting.

Cell line. One culture plus every plate, spawn bag and block grown from it. Faults such as stroma or loss of vigour often run through a whole cell line. See Drift and domestication.

CFM. Cubic feet per minute, the US unit for fan airflow. 100 CFM is about 170 m³/h.

Chiller. A refrigeration machine that cools water (or water mixed with glycol, an antifreeze) instead of air. The cold liquid is pumped to a coil that cools air somewhere else, for example to precool fresh air before the main air conditioner. See Precooling the fresh air.

Chlorine dioxide (ClO2). A strong disinfectant used dissolved in water at a few parts per million, mainly to keep humidifier water free of bacteria. See Disinfecting humidifier water.

Clamp connection. A small bridge on the hyphae of most dikaryotic mushrooms, visible under a microscope. Its presence shows that two compatible nuclei are paired. See Biology.

Clean room. A room supplied with HEPA-filtered air at positive pressure, where cultures, grain and blocks are opened. See The Lab.

C:N ratio. Carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of a substrate. Wood is high in carbon; supplements such as soy hulls or bran add nitrogen. See Substrate.

CO2 (carbon dioxide). The gas mycelium and mushrooms breathe out. High CO2 helps colonization but makes long stems and small caps in fruiting. Measured in parts per million (ppm); outdoor air is about 400 ppm. See Climate Control.

Cobweb mould. A fast, wispy, grey-white mould that spreads like a spider's web. Early Neurospora can look like it, so check what the growth turns into. See Diagnosing problems in the bag.

Cold chain. Keeping a product cold without a break, from the farm's cooler through packing and transport to the customer. See The cold chain for blocks and spawn.

Colonization. Mycelium growing through grain or substrate until it is fully white and bound together.

Combo pellets. Pellets made from sawdust and a supplement (for example soy hulls) milled and pelleted together, so one product makes a complete substrate when water is added. See Substrate.

Contamination. Any unwanted organism (mould, bacteria, yeast) growing in a culture, spawn or block. See Contamination.

CoolBot. A controller that makes a window air conditioner run colder than it normally would, used to build cheap walk-in coolers. Not recommended for grow rooms: window units move too little air, their filters fail and they use a lot of energy. See Window units and CoolBot rooms.

Cool-down. The period after steaming when hot bags cool to inoculation temperature. Bags draw in air as they cool, so this air must be HEPA-filtered. The single biggest source of contamination. See Contamination.

Coroplast. Corrugated plastic sheet (like cardboard, but plastic). Used to build washable heat exchangers and light partitions. See Fruiting.

Cryovial. A small sealed tube for freezing cultures at -80 °C (-112 °F) in a glycerol solution for long-term storage. See Storing Cultures.

CSA (community-supported agriculture). A sales model in which customers pay a farm in advance for a season of produce. It brings cash in early in the year. See Cash flow.

Culture bank. A stored collection of strains (in the freezer, on slants or in other long-term storage) from which clean starting cultures can always be revived. See Storage methods compared.

D

Data logger. A small recording thermometer (or pressure recorder) placed in a block or vessel to prove each cook reached its time and temperature. See Steam.

Dedikaryotization. Splitting a dikaryon back into its two monokaryons, for example by blending mycelium and growing single fragments. Used in breeding. See Procedure: mechanical dedikaryotization.

Dew point. The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water starts to condense out of it. A cooling coil only takes water out of the air if the coil is colder than the air's dew point. See Precooling the fresh air.

Dikaryon. Mycelium whose cells carry two compatible nuclei, one from each parent. Only dikaryons normally fruit. See Biology.

Distributor. A company that buys from farms and resells to stores and restaurants. It pays less per pound than direct sales but takes larger volumes. See Grocery, distributors and wholesale.

E

Endospore. A tough resting form of some bacteria that survives ultra-pasteurization and wakes up later if the block is too wet or too hot. See Steam.

ERV (energy recovery ventilator). Like an HRV, it swaps stale room air for fresh outside air through a core that passes heat between the two streams, but it also passes some moisture. See HRVs and makeup air in incubation.

Evaporative cooling. Cooling air by evaporating water into it. It works well in dry climates, but in humid air it cools very little and adds water. The lowest temperature it can reach is the wet-bulb temperature. See Evaporative cooling.

Exudate. Liquid droplets that mycelium pushes out, often yellow or amber. Normal in small amounts for some species; heavy exudate can signal stress or a rich, undercooked mix.

F

FAE (fresh air exchange). Replacing room air with outside air to remove CO2. Controlled by fans that switch on CO2 readings. See Fruiting.

Fermented blocks (sour blocks). Blocks in which bacteria have taken hold, usually because they were too wet or sat warm for days between heat treatment and inoculation. They smell sour and go in the bin. See Colonizing blocks.

FFU (fan filter unit). A box with a fan and a HEPA filter, usually mounted in a ceiling or wall, that blows clean air into a room or work area. See The Lab.

Field capacity. The most water a material can hold while still draining freely. A substrate at about 60-61% moisture is near field capacity.

Filter patch. A breathable panel on a grow bag that lets gas in and out but keeps contaminants out. Patches come in grades from tight to open. See Bags.

Flow hood. A cabinet that blows a steady, smooth (laminar) stream of HEPA-filtered air across a work surface, so you can open plates and bags without contaminating them. See The Lab.

Flush. One wave of mushrooms from a block. Most blocks give one to three flushes. See Fruiting.

Fruit body. The mushroom itself: the part that grows from the mycelium to make and release spores.

Fruiting. The stage when a colonized block forms mushrooms, usually triggered by cutting the bag and changing CO2, humidity, temperature or light. See Fruiting.

Fruiting trigger. Whatever change tells a colonized block to start making mushrooms: usually cutting or opening the bag, together with fresh air, high humidity, light or a temperature drop. See Triggering fruiting: cutting.

G

G1, grain master. The first generation of grain spawn, inoculated from a plate or liquid culture. One master inoculates many G2 bags. See Grain Spawn.

G2. Second-generation grain spawn, made by breaking up a G1 master into fresh sterilized grain. Usually the spawn that goes into blocks. See Grain Spawn.

Gel pack. A sealed pack of gel that is chilled or frozen and packed with spawn or mushrooms to keep a shipment cool. See Spawn storage and shipping.

Glycerol. A thick, clear liquid used as a cryoprotectant: added to cultures before freezing so ice crystals do not destroy the cells. About 10% is the usual strength. See Cryoprotectant.

Gurley seconds. A measure of how hard it is for air to pass through a membrane: the seconds a set volume of air takes. A higher number means less airflow. See Bags.

Gusset. The folded side or bottom of a grow bag that lets it expand into a box shape. The weakest point of a bag. See Bags.

Guttation. Water droplets that mycelium or young mushrooms push out onto their surface; very visible in lion's mane.

Gypsum (calcium sulfate, CaSO4). A calcium additive used in tiny amounts with calcium carbonate in grain spawn, to soak up excess moisture and stop loose starch clumping. See Calcium additives and pH.

H

HDPE (high-density polyethylene). A tough, slippery, food-safe plastic sold in sheets and boards. Used for bagger parts, cutting boards and wear surfaces because it sheds water and wears well. See Equipment.

Headspace. The air space left in a bag above the substrate. It gives room for gas exchange and for shaking. See Bags.

Heat exchanger. A device that moves heat from one stream of air or water to another without mixing them, such as the core of an HRV or a water-to-air coil. See Sizing examples.

HEPA. High-efficiency particulate air filter: removes at least 99.97% of particles of 0.3 µm. The standard filter for labs, flow hoods and cool-down rooms.

HRV. Heat recovery ventilator: brings in fresh air while recovering heat (or coolness) from the air going out. See Climate Control.

Humidifier. A machine that adds water to the air, such as an ultrasonic fogger or a misting system. Its water quality largely decides a fruit room's risk of bacterial disease. See Water for humidifiers.

HWFP (hardwood fuel pellets). Compressed hardwood sawdust pellets sold for pellet stoves, used as a clean, consistent sawdust source. See Substrate.

Hydrogen peroxide. An oxidizing disinfectant that breaks down into water and oxygen, used to treat humidifier water and clean surfaces. See Hydrogen peroxide.

Hypha (plural hyphae). A single thread of mycelium, one cell wide.

I

Impulse sealer. A sealer that heats a wire for a moment to weld a bag closed. Too hot, and it burns tiny holes along the seal. See Bags.

Incubation. The stage when inoculated spawn or blocks are held in a warm, dark, controlled room while mycelium colonizes them. See Incubation.

Inoculation. Adding spawn or culture to sterilized grain or substrate. On many farms this step is called "the knock". See Bags and Inoculation.

L

Leading edge. The newest, outermost growth of mycelium on a plate, which is the healthiest tissue to transfer. See Culture Work.

Liquid culture (LC). Mycelium grown in sterile nutrient liquid in a jar, used to inoculate grain. Aerated liquid culture (ALC) has air bubbled through it. See Culture Work.

Load cell. An electronic weighing sensor. Load-cell fillers weigh each charge of pellets and water instead of measuring by volume. See Equipment.

LTL freight (less-than-truckload). Shipping one or a few pallets on a truck shared with other customers' freight; the usual way to ship blocks and bulk supplies. The delivery site must take a large truck. See Blocks in transit.

M

Master's Mix. The standard block substrate: hardwood sawdust and soy hulls, classically 50:50 by dry weight, hydrated to about 62% moisture (61-63% for most species). See Substrate.

MDF (medium-density fibreboard). A cheap board made of compressed wood fibre. It swells like a sponge when wet unless sealed, so keep it out of wet areas. See Equipment.

MEA (malt extract agar). A common agar recipe made with malt extract. MYA (malt yeast agar) adds yeast. See Agar media: which for which species.

Metabolites. Substances mycelium produces as it grows, often seen as yellow or orange droplets. Normal on some species' older grain.

Monokaryon. Mycelium with one type of nucleus per cell, grown from a single spore. It cannot normally fruit until it mates with a compatible monokaryon. See Biology.

Mycelium. The white thread-like network that is the main body of a fungus, growing through its food.

N

Negative pressure. A room kept at slightly lower air pressure than its surroundings, so air leaks in rather than out. Used for fruit rooms so spores do not spread to clean areas. See Fruiting.

Neurospora. A fast orange mould that spreads by powdery orange spores. It enters through bad seals or torn bags. Remove infected bags at once. See Contamination.

P

Parafilm. A stretchy wax film wrapped around plate edges to keep contaminants out.

Passage (P1, P2 ...). One transfer of a culture to fresh agar. P1 is the first plate grown from stored stock, P2 a transfer from that plate, and so on. Few passages from banked stock keep a strain vigorous; see senescence and Culture Work.

Pasteurization. Heating to kill most, but not all, microbes. In this book the main process is ultra-pasteurization. See Steam.

PCR (polymerase chain reaction). A lab method that copies a chosen piece of DNA millions of times, so it can be checked on a gel or sent out for sequencing. See PCR setup.

PDA and PDYA. Potato dextrose agar, and potato dextrose agar with yeast added: common agar recipes. See Agar media: which for which species.

PEX pipe. Flexible plastic (cross-linked polyethylene) water pipe, used for water lines to baggers, misting systems and sinks. See Equipment.

Pins (pinning). The tiny first mushrooms that appear on a block; "pinning" is the moment a block starts forming them. Also called primordia. See Fruit Rooms and Fruiting.

Plate. A shallow dish of agar used to grow and select mycelium. Also called a Petri dish.

Plenum. A small room or air space where air is conditioned (cooled, heated, humidified) before it is fed into the fruit room. See Fruiting.

Positive pressure. A room kept at slightly higher air pressure than its surroundings with filtered air, so air leaks out rather than in. Used for labs and cool-down rooms.

ppm. Parts per million. The unit for CO2 levels, and for chemical doses in water.

Precooling. Cooling, and ideally drying, outside air before it reaches the main air conditioner, so the air conditioner is not fighting hot, wet air. See Precooling the fresh air.

Pressure cooker. A sealed pot that reaches about 15 psi (1 bar) and 121 °C (250 °F): the smallest kind of autoclave. See Pressure cookers and tabletop units.

Primordia (singular primordium). Pins: the tiny first stage of a mushroom.

psi. Pounds per square inch, the unit for steam pressure. 15 psi is about 1 bar (100 kPa).

P-trap. A U-shaped bend in a drain pipe that holds water to block air and pests from coming back up the drain.

Q

Quaternary ammonium ("quat"). A family of surface disinfectants sold as cleaning concentrates. See Disinfectants.

R

Reefer. A refrigerated shipping container, often reused as a grow room or incubation room. See Planning.

Reverse osmosis (RO). Water filtering that forces water through a very fine membrane, removing most dissolved minerals. RO water suits humidifiers, but it is corrosive in a boiler. See The water treatment chain.

RH (relative humidity). How much water vapour the air holds, as a percentage of the most it could hold at that temperature. Fruit rooms usually swing between about 70% and 90% RH; some species need 90-95%. See Relative humidity.

Ribbon mixer. A trough mixer with a turning spiral blade (the ribbon) that mixes sawdust, supplement and water evenly. See Mixer practice.

Rose comb. A deformity where gill tissue grows on top of the cap. Linked to poor air exchange, over-humid rooms and mineral- or microbe-laden humidifier water. See Diseases.

S

Sauna steamer. An electric steam generator built for steam rooms, used by many small farms to steam substrate in barrels or boxes. See Sauna steam generators.

Sector (sectoring). A wedge of different-looking growth on a plate: faster, slower, thinner or a different texture. Sectors can be cut out and grown separately, either to remove them or to select from them. See Reading plates.

Senescence. A culture ageing and losing vigour after many transfers or a long time in growth. Shows as slow, weak or abnormal growth. See Storing Cultures.

Sequencing (DNA sequencing). Reading the code of a piece of DNA, usually done by an outside lab, to confirm a species or tell strains apart. See Why a farm does DNA work.

Shelf life. How long a harvested mushroom stays good enough to sell. It depends on the species, how mature it was when picked, and the cold chain. See Keeping quality by species.

Slant. A tube of agar set at an angle, used to store a culture for months. See Storing Cultures.

SOP. Standard operating procedure: a written step-by-step method every worker follows the same way.

Soy hulls. The outer husks of soybeans, sold as pellets: the standard nitrogen supplement in sawdust blocks and half of the masters mix. See Soy hulls.

Spawn. Grain (or sawdust) fully colonized by mycelium, used to inoculate substrate. See Grain Spawn.

Spawn rate. How much spawn is added per block, as a weight or a percentage of the substrate. See Bags and Inoculation.

Spore lung. An allergic lung illness from breathing large amounts of mushroom spores. Wear a respirator when harvesting. See Safety.

Steam generator. A machine, usually electric, that makes steam on demand for pasteurizing substrate. Smaller and simpler than a boiler. See Steam equipment.

Sterilization. Killing all living things, including bacterial endospores, with pressurized steam at 121 °C (250 °F). Used for grain and sterilized blocks. See Steam.

Strain. A particular genetic line of a species, kept as a culture, with its own speed, yield and form. See Culture Work.

Stripping. Removing the bag completely from a block to fruit it, as done for shiitake. See Fruiting.

Stroma. Hard, dense, hot, rubbery masses of mycelium, mostly in oyster grain spawn, that carry through to blocks and lower yield. It is not a contaminant. See Diseases.

Substrate. The food material a mushroom fruits from, such as sawdust and soy hulls. See Substrate.

Supplement. A nitrogen-rich addition to sawdust, such as soy hulls or wheat bran, that raises yield but also contamination risk.

T

Thermocouple. A temperature probe made of two joined wires. Thermocouple probes on a data logger read block core temperatures during a run. See Proving every run: data logging.

TIG welding. Tungsten inert gas welding: a precise welding method used for stainless steel and thin mild steel in farm-built equipment. See Equipment.

Tissue culture (clone). A culture started from a piece of mushroom flesh. It keeps the genetics of that mushroom. See Drift and domestication.

Trichoderma. The common green mould: white at first, then bright green as it spores. See Contamination.

Tyvek. A spun plastic sheet used as a tight filter patch on some bags. See Bags.

U

Ultra-pasteurization. Unpressurized steam that brings the block core to 93-100 °C (200-212 °F) and holds it for hours. Kills fungi and active bacteria but not bacterial endospores. Used for most sawdust blocks. See Steam.

Ultrasonic fogger. A humidifier that uses a vibrating disc under water to make a very fine fog. A fogger tank sitting in the room can spread disease; box it in and feed it outside air. See Designs ranked.

UV sterilizer. A lamp housing that water flows past, killing microbes with ultraviolet light; one step in a humidifier's water treatment. See The water treatment chain.

V

Vacuum autoclave. An autoclave that pulls several vacuum pulses to remove air before heating, so steam reaches every part of the load quickly and evenly. See Cycle types.

VPD (vapour pressure deficit). How much more water the air could hold at its current temperature. Unlike relative humidity, it allows for temperature, so one VPD setting means the same drying power at any temperature. See Humidity controllers and sensors.

W

Walk-in cooler. A refrigerated room you can walk into, used to cool and hold harvested mushrooms, spawn and sometimes blocks. See Where the cooler fits.

Wet-bulb temperature. The temperature shown by a thermometer wrapped in a wet wick. Compared with an ordinary (dry-bulb) reading, it gives true relative humidity, even in fog. It is also the lowest temperature that evaporative cooling can bring air down to, so the gap between the dry-bulb and wet-bulb readings shows how much an evaporative cooler can help. See Fruiting and Evaporative cooling.
